Anchoring the heart is the job of the fibrous pericardium, which attaches to the diaphragm and surrounding structures. Pick it for holding the heart in place.
questions.answerText: It lets the heart beat with little friction

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the fibrous and serous pericardium?
options: Both are muscular layers that help the heart contract
The fibrous layer reduces friction, and the serous layer anchors the heart
The fibrous layer lines the chambers, and the serous layer forms the valves
The fibrous layer anchors the heart, and the serous layer reduces friction
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium is a tough sac of dense connective tissue that anchors the heart in the mediastinum and prevents overfilling. The serous pericardium is a thin double membrane inside it, whose parietal and visceral layers enclose the fluid-filled pericardial cavity. That fluid lets the heart beat with little friction.
notes: Neither layer of the pericardium is muscle. The cardiac muscle is the myocardium, the middle layer of the heart wall.
This swaps the two roles. The tough dense connective tissue is the anchor, and the thin slippery membranes reduce friction.
Lining the chambers and covering the valves is the job of the endocardium. The pericardium is entirely outside the heart wall.
Correct. Fibrous anchors and protects, and serous reduces friction.
questions.answerText: The fibrous layer anchors the heart, and the serous layer reduces friction

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the epicardium and the endocardium?
options: The epicardium covers the outside, and the endocardium lines the chambers
The epicardium lines the chambers, and the endocardium covers the outside
Both are made of cardiac muscle that contracts
Both are layers of the fibrous pericardium
questions.why: Epi means upon and endo means within. The epicardium is the thin serous membrane on the outer surface of the heart, the same as the visceral layer of the serous pericardium. The endocardium is the smooth endothelium lining the chambers and covering the valves.
notes: Correct. Epicardium outside, endocardium inside.
This swaps the two. Use the prefixes: epi is on the outside, endo is on the inside.
Only the myocardium is cardiac muscle. The epicardium is a serous membrane and the endocardium is an endothelium.
The fibrous pericardium is a single tough layer of the sac. The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium, and the endocardium is not part of the pericardium at all.
questions.answerText: The epicardium covers the outside, and the endocardium lines the chambers

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the myocardium and the endocardium?
options: The myocardium forms a smooth lining, and the endocardium contracts
The myocardium covers the valves, and the endocardium anchors them
Both reduce friction between the heart and its sac
The myocardium contracts, and the endocardium forms a smooth lining
questions.why: The myocardium is the thick middle layer of cardiac muscle, and it does the contracting that pumps blood. The endocardium is a thin, smooth endothelium covering the inner surface of the myocardium, lining the chambers and covering the valves. One layer generates force and the other gives blood a smooth surface to flow across.
notes: This swaps the two roles. The thick muscle layer contracts, and the thin endothelium lines it.
The endocardium covers the valves, and the fibrous skeleton anchors them. The myocardium does neither, since valves have no muscle.
Reducing friction between the heart and its sac is the job of the serous pericardium and its fluid, outside the heart wall.
Correct. Myocardium contracts, and endocardium lines.
questions.answerText: The myocardium contracts, and the endocardium forms a smooth lining

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why does it matter that the endocardium is smooth?
options: It anchors the heart in the mediastinum
It gives blood a smooth surface to flow across
It lets the heart slide inside its sac
It lets the heart wall contract with force
questions.why: The endocardium is a smooth endothelium that lines every chamber, covers the valves, and continues into the lining of the great vessels. Because it is smooth, blood flows across it without catching or clotting. When the endocardium is damaged, for example by infection, the roughened surface disturbs flow and can harm the valves.
notes: Anchoring the heart is the job of the fibrous pericardium. Pick it for the tough sac holding the heart in place.
Correct. A smooth lining lets blood flow freely through the chambers and over the valves.
Sliding within the sac depends on the serous pericardium and its fluid, on the outside of the heart. Pick the serous pericardium for that job.
Contraction is the job of the myocardium. Pick it for the layer that generates force.
questions.answerText: It gives blood a smooth surface to flow across

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: A patient's heart pumps weakly because its wall cannot contract with normal force. Which layer of the heart wall is most likely damaged?
options: The myocardium
The endocardium
The fibrous pericardium
The epicardium
questions.why: The myocardium is the cardiac muscle layer, making up about ninety five percent of the wall thickness. It is the only layer that contracts, so damage to it directly weakens pumping. A heart attack, for example, kills a patch of myocardium when its coronary blood supply is blocked.
notes: Correct. The myocardium is the contracting layer.
The endocardium is a thin lining of the chambers and valves. Damage there can affect the valves, but it does not supply contractile force.
The fibrous pericardium is the outer sac, not part of the wall. Pick it for the layer that anchors the heart and limits overfilling.
The epicardium is a thin serous membrane on the heart surface with no contractile tissue. Pick it for the layer where the coronary vessels run.
questions.answerText: The myocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer of the heart wall is continuous with the inner lining of the great vessels?
options: The myocardium
The parietal pericardium
The endocardium
The epicardium
questions.why: The endocardium is an endothelium, a sheet of flat cells, and it continues without a break into the endothelium lining the great vessels. This gives blood one unbroken smooth surface from the vessels, through the chambers, and back out. The innermost layer of a blood vessel wall, the tunica intima, uses this same kind of lining.
notes: The myocardium is cardiac muscle that stops at the bases of the great vessels. Vessel walls contain smooth muscle in their tunica media instead.
The parietal pericardium lines the fibrous sac, outside the heart. Pick it for the serous layer facing the pericardial cavity from the sac side.
Correct. The endocardium continues into the lining of the great vessels.
The epicardium covers the outer surface of the heart. It does reflect onto the roots of the great vessels as part of the serous pericardium, but it does not line their inside.
questions.answerText: The endocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why are the walls of the atria thinner than the walls of the ventricles?
options: The atria pump blood out to the entire body
The atria are made of smooth muscle instead of cardiac muscle
The atria carry only oxygen-poor blood
The atria only push blood a short distance into the ventricles
questions.why: The atria are receiving chambers. Most blood flows from the atria into the ventricles on its own, and atrial contraction only tops off the ventricles a short distance below. Because so little force is needed, the atria have thin walls, while the ventricles need thick walls to push blood out through the circuits.
notes: Pumping blood to the body is the job of the left ventricle, the thickest chamber. Pick it for the systemic pump.
The atria are made of cardiac muscle, the same tissue as the ventricles, just in a thinner layer. Smooth muscle is found in vessel walls and hollow organs like the stomach.
Only the right atrium carries oxygen-poor blood. The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs, and oxygen content does not set wall thickness anyway.
Correct. A short push into the ventricles needs only a thin wall.
questions.answerText: The atria only push blood a short distance into the ventricles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why are the walls of the ventricles thicker than the walls of the atria?
options: They hold the valves that pump the blood
They must push blood out through a whole circuit
They receive blood from the great veins
They must stretch to store blood between beats
questions.why: The ventricles are the pumping chambers. The right ventricle pushes blood through the pulmonary circuit and the left ventricle pushes it through the systemic circuit, so each must generate far more force than an atrium. A thicker myocardium provides that force, and the left ventricle, with the longest circuit, is thickest of all.
notes: Valves do no pumping. They are passive flaps that open and close as pressure changes, so the muscle wall does all the work.
Correct. Pumping blood through a whole circuit requires thick muscle.
Receiving blood from the great veins is the job of the atria. Pick the atria for the chambers that collect venous return.
Storing blood between beats needs a stretchy, thin wall, which fits the atria better. Thick walls exist for force, not storage.
questions.answerText: They must push blood out through a whole circuit

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares pectinate muscles and trabeculae carneae?
options: Both are fibrous cords that hold the AV valves shut
Pectinate muscles line the atria, and trabeculae carneae line the ventricles
Pectinate muscles are in the ventricles, and trabeculae carneae are in the atria
Both are smooth areas found only in the outflow tracts
questions.why: Pectinate muscles are parallel, comb-like ridges on the inner walls of the atria and auricles. Trabeculae carneae are irregular, crisscrossing ridges on the inner walls of the ventricles. Both are ridges of myocardium, and their location tells you which chamber you are looking at in a dissected heart.
notes: The fibrous cords holding the AV valves are the chordae tendineae. Pick them for the heart strings attached to papillary muscles.
Correct. Pectinate muscles are atrial ridges, and trabeculae carneae are ventricular ridges.
This swaps their locations. Pectinate (comb-like) ridges belong to the atria, and trabeculae carneae belong to the ventricles.
The smooth outflow tracts are the conus arteriosus and aortic vestibule, which lack ridges. Pick those for the smooth passages leading to the semilunar valves.
questions.answerText: Pectinate muscles line the atria, and trabeculae carneae line the ventricles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the interatrial and interventricular septa?
options: The interatrial septum separates the atria, and the interventricular septum separates the ventricles
The interatrial septum separates the ventricles, and the interventricular septum separates the atria
Both septa are thin walls containing the fossa ovalis
Both septa separate the atria from the ventricles
questions.why: A septum is a dividing wall. The interatrial septum is the thin wall between the right and left atria, and it holds the fossa ovalis. The interventricular septum is the thick muscular wall between the right and left ventricles. Neither septum separates an atrium from a ventricle; that boundary is formed by the fibrous skeleton and the AV valves.
notes: Correct. Each septum is named for the chambers it separates.
This swaps the names. Read the root of each word: atrial for the atria and ventricular for the ventricles.
Only the interatrial septum is thin and holds the fossa ovalis. The interventricular septum is thick and muscular.
The atria are separated from the ventricles by the fibrous skeleton and the AV valves, not by either septum. Pick the AV valves for the openings between atria and ventricles.
questions.answerText: The interatrial septum separates the atria, and the interventricular septum separates the ventricles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why is the fossa ovalis found in the interatrial septum?
options: It marks where the fetal foramen ovale joined the atria
It is where the superior vena cava enters
It marks where the ductus arteriosus once attached
It is the opening where the coronary sinus drains
questions.why: Before birth, the foramen ovale was an opening in the interatrial septum that let blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. After birth, a flap seals it shut, leaving a shallow oval depression called the fossa ovalis. Its location simply marks where that fetal opening used to be.
notes: Correct. The fossa ovalis is the sealed site of the foramen ovale.
The superior vena cava enters the top of the right atrium, in the smooth posterior part called the sinus venarum. Pick it for where venous return from the upper body enters.
The ductus arteriosus connected the pulmonary trunk to the aorta and became the ligamentum arteriosum outside the heart. Pick it for the cord between those two vessels.
The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near the tricuspid valve, not as a depression in the septum. Pick it for the vessel draining the heart wall.
questions.answerText: It marks where the fetal foramen ovale joined the atria

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Fluid builds up in the pericardial cavity and presses on the heart from outside. Which heart function is most directly limited?
options: Oxygen pickup in the lungs
Closing of the valves
Spread of the electrical signal
Filling of the chambers
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium does not stretch much, so extra fluid in the pericardial cavity has nowhere to go but inward. That pressure squeezes the heart from outside and keeps the chambers from expanding to fill with blood. With less filling, less blood is pumped out with each beat.
notes: Oxygen pickup happens in the alveoli of the lungs, outside the pericardium. Pick the lungs for a problem with gas exchange.
Valves close because of pressure differences inside the heart, which outside fluid does not directly change. Pick valve closure for a problem with the cusps, chordae, or papillary muscles.
The electrical signal travels through the conduction system inside the heart wall. Pick the conduction system for a problem with the heartbeat's rhythm.
Correct. External pressure keeps the chambers from expanding and filling.
questions.answerText: Filling of the chambers

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Fluid fills the pericardial cavity until it squeezes the heart and limits how much it can fill. What is this condition called?
options: Myocardial infarction
Mitral valve prolapse
Cardiac tamponade
Endocarditis
questions.why: Cardiac tamponade is the buildup of fluid in the pericardial cavity that compresses the heart. Because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, the fluid presses inward and prevents the chambers from filling. The same fluid film that normally lets the heart glide can, in excess, stop it from working.
notes: A myocardial infarction is death of heart muscle when a coronary artery is blocked. Pick it for a heart attack, not for fluid around the heart.
Mitral valve prolapse is when the mitral cusps bulge back into the left atrium. Pick it for a valve problem involving the chordae tendineae.
Correct. Cardiac tamponade is fluid compressing the heart from the pericardial cavity.
Endocarditis is inflammation, often infection, of the endocardium lining the chambers and valves. Pick it for a problem on the inside of the heart.
questions.answerText: Cardiac tamponade

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: A knife enters the pericardial sac from the front of the chest. Which layer does it pierce first?
options: The myocardium
The visceral layer of the serous pericardium
The parietal layer of the serous pericardium
The fibrous pericardium
questions.why: From outside in, the layers around and of the heart are the fibrous pericardium, the parietal layer of the serous pericardium, the pericardial cavity, the visceral layer (epicardium), the myocardium, and the endocardium. A blade entering the sac would pierce the tough fibrous pericardium first. Bleeding into the pericardial cavity from such a wound can cause cardiac tamponade.
notes: The myocardium is the heart muscle itself, deep to the whole pericardium and the epicardium. Pick it for a wound that has reached the heart wall.
The visceral layer lies on the heart surface across the pericardial cavity. Pick it for the layer reached right before the heart muscle.
The parietal layer lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium, so it is the second layer reached. Pick it for the serous layer just deep to the fibrous sac.
Correct. The fibrous pericardium is the outermost layer of the sac.
questions.answerText: The fibrous pericardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: A heart attack destroys a patch of myocardium. Which ability of the heart is most directly reduced?
options: The gliding of the heart within its sac
The smoothness of the chamber lining
The anchoring of the heart in the mediastinum
The force of contraction
questions.why: The myocardium is the cardiac muscle layer that contracts to pump blood. When a coronary artery is blocked, the myocardium beyond it is starved of oxygen and dies, which is a myocardial infarction. Dead muscle cannot contract, so the heart pumps with less force.
notes: Gliding within the sac depends on the serous pericardium and its fluid. Pick it for a problem in the pericardial cavity.
The smoothness of the chamber lining depends on the endocardium. Pick it for damage to the inner lining or valves.
Anchoring depends on the fibrous pericardium. Pick it for the tough outer sac.
Correct. The myocardium generates the force of contraction.
questions.answerText: The force of contraction

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: An infection damages the thin lining that covers the surfaces of the heart valves. Which layer of the heart wall is infected?
options: The epicardium
The endocardium
The fibrous pericardium
The myocardium
questions.why: The valve cusps are covered by endocardium, the smooth endothelium that also lines the chambers. Infection of this layer is called endocarditis, and because the valves are covered by it, valve damage is a common result. A roughened valve surface may then fail to close cleanly.
notes: The epicardium covers the outside of the heart, far from the valves. Pick it for the surface layer where the coronary vessels run.
Correct. The endocardium covers the valves, so infection there is endocarditis.
The fibrous pericardium is part of the sac around the heart, not the wall. Pick it for the tough outer layer.
The myocardium is muscle and does not cover the valves. Pick it for a problem with contraction.
questions.answerText: The endocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: In a cross section through both ventricles, one has a thick wall and round cavity while the other is thin-walled and crescent-shaped. Which is the thick one, and why?
options: The left ventricle, because it pumps blood to the whole body
The right ventricle, because it receives blood from the whole body
The right ventricle, because it pumps blood to the lungs
The left ventricle, because it receives blood from the lungs
questions.why: The left ventricle drives the systemic circuit, sending blood to every tissue, which takes far more force than pushing blood to the nearby lungs. Its thick myocardium provides that force and gives it a round cavity in cross section. The thinner right ventricle wraps around it in a crescent shape.
notes: Correct. The left ventricle is thick because it powers the systemic circuit.
The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium, not directly from the body, and receiving blood does not require a thick wall.
The right ventricle does pump to the lungs, but that short circuit needs less force, so it is the thin, crescent-shaped one.
The chamber is right, but the reason is wrong. Receiving blood takes little force; wall thickness reflects pumping, not receiving.
questions.answerText: The left ventricle, because it pumps blood to the whole body

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: A baby is born with a hole in the interventricular septum. Which chambers can abnormally exchange blood?
options: The right atrium and right ventricle
The right and left ventricles
The right and left atria
The left atrium and left ventricle
questions.why: The interventricular septum is the thick wall between the right and left ventricles. A hole in it, called a ventricular septal defect, lets blood pass between the two ventricles. This mixes blood that should stay on separate sides of the heart.
notes: These chambers are normally connected through the tricuspid valve, so they are not separated by a septum. Pick them for a problem with the tricuspid valve.
Correct. The interventricular septum separates the two ventricles.
The atria are separated by the interatrial septum. Pick this pair for a hole in that wall, such as a patent foramen ovale.
These chambers are normally connected through the mitral valve. Pick them for a problem with the mitral valve.
questions.answerText: The right and left ventricles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: The foramen ovale fails to close after birth, leaving a hole in the interatrial septum. Which chambers can abnormally exchange blood?
options: The right and left atria
The right and left ventricles
The left atrium and left ventricle
The right ventricle and pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The interatrial septum separates the right and left atria. When the foramen ovale stays open after birth, a condition called a patent foramen ovale, blood can still pass between the two atria. Patent means open, and the condition is named for the fetal structure that failed to seal.
notes: Correct. A hole in the interatrial septum connects the two atria.
The ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum. Pick this pair for a ventricular septal defect.
The left atrium and left ventricle are normally joined through the mitral valve. A septal hole does not connect them.
The right ventricle and pulmonary trunk are normally joined through the pulmonary valve. Pick them for a pulmonary valve problem.
questions.answerText: The right and left atria

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: In a dissected heart, a student sees a muscular band stretching from the interventricular septum across the chamber to the base of a papillary muscle. Which chamber is she looking into?
options: The right atrium
The left ventricle
The left atrium
The right ventricle
questions.why: The band described is the moderator band, or septomarginal trabecula, and it is a landmark of the right ventricle. It runs from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle and carries part of the conduction system. Finding it is a reliable way to identify the right ventricle on a lab practical.
notes: The right atrium has pectinate muscles and the crista terminalis, not papillary muscles. Pick it when you see the fossa ovalis and the openings of the venae cavae.
The left ventricle has papillary muscles and trabeculae carneae but no moderator band. Pick it when you see the thickest wall and the mitral valve chordae.
The left atrium has no papillary muscles. Pick it when you see the openings of the four pulmonary veins.
Correct. The moderator band is found in the right ventricle.
questions.answerText: The right ventricle

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Where is the heart located?
options: In the left pleural cavity, surrounded by the left lung
In the abdominopelvic cavity, just below the diaphragm
In the mediastinum, between the lungs and resting on the diaphragm
In the dorsal body cavity, beside the vertebral column
questions.why: The heart sits in the mediastinum, the central region of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs. It rests on the diaphragm and is tilted so that about two thirds of its mass lies left of the midline. It is enclosed in its own pericardial sac, separate from the pleural cavities around the lungs.
notes: The left pleural cavity surrounds the left lung only. The heart leans left, but it sits in the mediastinum inside its own pericardium.
The abdominopelvic cavity lies below the diaphragm and holds organs such as the stomach and liver. The heart rests on top of the diaphragm, not under it.
Correct. The heart lies in the mediastinum between the lungs, on top of the diaphragm.
The dorsal body cavity holds the brain and spinal cord. Pick it for the cranial and vertebral cavities, not the heart.
questions.answerText: In the mediastinum, between the lungs and resting on the diaphragm

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: What type of tissue forms the myocardium, the thick middle layer of the heart wall?
options: Cardiac muscle tissue
Simple squamous epithelium
Dense irregular connective tissue
Smooth muscle tissue
questions.why: The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, making up about ninety five percent of its thickness, and it is built of cardiac muscle tissue arranged in spiraling bundles. This is the layer that actually contracts and pumps blood. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, so the myocardium is the one place you will see it.
notes: Correct. The myocardium is cardiac muscle, the only muscle tissue that forms the heart wall.

Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells. It forms the endothelium of the endocardium lining the chambers and the surface of the epicardium, so it fits a question about the inner or outer heart wall layers, not the myocardium.

Dense irregular connective tissue forms tough coverings such as the fibrous pericardium and the dermis. Choose it for the outer layer of the pericardial sac, which anchors the heart, not for the contracting middle layer of the wall.

Smooth muscle is the involuntary, nonstriated muscle in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels, such as the tunica media of an artery. It would be the answer if the question asked what muscle tissue narrows a blood vessel, not what forms the heart wall.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle tissue

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: What is the name of the smooth outflow tract of the left ventricle that leads blood to the aortic valve?
options: Aortic vestibule
Conus arteriosus
Fossa ovalis
Sinus venarum
questions.why: Most of the inner ventricular wall is covered in trabeculae carneae, which are irregular muscular ridges. Just below each semilunar valve the wall becomes smooth to form an outflow tract. In the left ventricle this smooth outflow tract is the aortic vestibule, and it leads blood up to the aortic valve.
notes: Correct. The aortic vestibule is the smooth outflow tract of the left ventricle.
The conus arteriosus is the matching smooth outflow tract of the right ventricle, leading to the pulmonary valve. It would be the answer if the question asked about the right ventricle.
The fossa ovalis is the oval depression in the interatrial septum left by the fetal foramen ovale. It would be the answer if the question asked about the remnant of a fetal shunt.
The sinus venarum is the smooth posterior part of the right atrium where the venae cavae empty. It would be the answer if the question asked where the venae cavae open into the heart.
questions.answerText: Aortic vestibule

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: What is the name of the smooth outflow tract of the right ventricle that leads blood to the pulmonary valve?
options: Crista terminalis
Moderator band
Conus arteriosus
Aortic vestibule
questions.why: The conus arteriosus is the smooth, funnel-shaped upper part of the right ventricle. It leads blood from the ridged main chamber up to the pulmonary valve and into the pulmonary trunk. Its smooth wall contrasts with the trabeculae carneae lining the rest of the ventricle.
notes: The crista terminalis is a ridge in the right atrium that separates its smooth posterior wall from its rough, pectinate anterior wall. It would be the answer if the question were about the inside of the right atrium.

The moderator band is a muscular band in the right ventricle that carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked which right ventricle structure carries conduction fibers.
Correct. The conus arteriosus leads from the right ventricle to the pulmonary valve.
The aortic vestibule is the smooth outflow tract of the left ventricle, leading to the aortic valve. It would be the answer if the question asked about the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: Conus arteriosus

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which heart chamber has the thickest wall and pumps blood into the aorta?
options: Left atrium
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
Right atrium
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta and out through the entire systemic circuit, from the head to the toes. Pushing blood that far takes far more force than sending it to the nearby lungs, so the left ventricle has the thickest myocardium (the heart muscle layer) of the four chambers. Its tip also forms the apex of the heart.
notes: The left atrium is a thin-walled receiving chamber that collects oxygen-rich blood from the pulmonary veins. It would be the answer if the question asked which chamber forms most of the base of the heart.
Correct. The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps into the aorta.

The right ventricle pumps blood only to the lungs through the pulmonary trunk, a short, low-pressure route, so its wall is thinner. Pick it if the question asked which chamber pumps into the pulmonary trunk.
The right atrium is a thin-walled receiving chamber that collects blood from the venae cavae and coronary sinus. Choose it if the question asked which chamber receives blood returning from the body.
questions.answerText: Left ventricle

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer of the heart wall is the same membrane as the visceral layer of the serous pericardium?
options: Epicardium
Fibrous pericardium
Endocardium
Myocardium
questions.why: The epicardium is the outermost layer of the heart wall, a thin serous membrane that covers the heart surface and carries fat and the coronary vessels. It is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium under a second name. You call it the epicardium when describing the heart wall and the visceral pericardium when describing the sac around the heart.
notes: Correct. The epicardium and the visceral serous pericardium are the same membrane.

The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer layer of the sac around the heart, not part of the heart wall. Choose it if the question asked which layer anchors the heart in the mediastinum and prevents overfilling.
The endocardium is the innermost layer, a smooth endothelium lining the chambers and covering the valves. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer lines the inside of the heart.
The myocardium is the thick middle layer made of cardiac muscle, the part of the wall that contracts. Pick it if the question asked which layer makes up most of the wall thickness.
questions.answerText: Epicardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer of the heart wall is made of cardiac muscle and does the work of contraction?
options: Myocardium
Parietal pericardium
Endocardium
Epicardium
questions.why: The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, built of cardiac muscle tissue arranged in spiraling bundles. It makes up about 95 percent of the wall thickness and is the only layer that contracts. The layers on either side of it are thin membranes that cover or line it.
notes: Correct. The myocardium is the cardiac muscle layer that contracts.

The parietal pericardium is the serous layer lining the inside of the fibrous pericardium, so it belongs to the sac rather than the heart wall. Choose it if the question asked which layer forms the outer boundary of the pericardial cavity.
The endocardium is the thin endothelial lining of the chambers and valves. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer lines the chambers and covers the valves.
The epicardium is the thin serous membrane on the outer surface of the heart, where fat and the coronary vessels run. Pick it if the question asked for the outermost layer of the heart wall.
questions.answerText: Myocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer of the heart wall is a smooth endothelium that lines the chambers and covers the valves?
options: Epicardium
Myocardium
Fibrous pericardium
Endocardium
questions.why: The endocardium is the innermost layer of the heart wall. It is a smooth sheet of endothelium (a single layer of flat cells) that lines every chamber and covers the valve cusps, so blood flows over a slick surface. It is continuous with the tunica intima, the lining of the great vessels.
notes: The epicardium covers the outside of the heart rather than lining the inside. Pick it if the question asked which layer is the same as the visceral serous pericardium.
The myocardium is the thick cardiac muscle layer in the middle of the wall. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer contracts to pump blood.
The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac of dense connective tissue around the whole heart. Choose it if the question asked what anchors the heart and keeps it from overfilling.
Correct. The endocardium lines the chambers and covers the valves.
questions.answerText: Endocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer around the heart is tough, inelastic dense connective tissue that anchors the heart in the mediastinum?
options: Endocardium
Parietal serous pericardium
Visceral serous pericardium
Fibrous pericardium
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium is the outermost layer of the sac around the heart. It is made of dense connective tissue, so it is tough and does not stretch much. That lets it anchor the heart to the surrounding structures of the mediastinum and keep the heart from overfilling with blood.
notes: The endocardium is the inner lining of the heart chambers and valves, not part of the pericardial sac. Choose it if the question asked which layer the blood touches inside the heart.

The parietal serous pericardium is a thin serous membrane lining the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium. Pick it if the question asked which layer forms the outer wall of the pericardial cavity.

The visceral serous pericardium lies directly on the heart surface and is also called the epicardium. It would be the answer if the question asked which pericardial layer is also part of the heart wall.
Correct. The fibrous pericardium is the tough anchoring layer of the sac.
questions.answerText: Fibrous pericardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: What is the name of the space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium, which holds a thin film of serous fluid?
options: Peritoneal cavity
Pericardial cavity
Pleural cavity
Mediastinum
questions.why: The pericardial cavity is the thin space between the two layers of the serous pericardium. It holds a small amount of serous fluid that reduces friction so the heart can glide as it beats. If too much fluid collects there, it presses on the heart and limits how much it can fill, a condition called cardiac tamponade.
notes: The peritoneal cavity is the space between the parietal and visceral peritoneum in the abdomen. Choose it if the question asked about the serous space around the abdominal organs.
Correct. The pericardial cavity holds the serous fluid between the two serous layers.

The pleural cavity is the fluid-filled space between the parietal and visceral pleurae around each lung. Pick it if the question asked about the space that lets the lungs glide against the chest wall.

The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity that holds the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. It would be the answer if the question asked where the whole heart sits, not the fluid space right around it.
questions.answerText: Pericardial cavity

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which wall separates the right atrium from the left atrium?
options: Interatrial septum
Fibrous skeleton
Crista terminalis
Interventricular septum
questions.why: The interatrial septum is the thin wall that divides the right atrium from the left atrium. It keeps oxygen-poor blood on the right side apart from oxygen-rich blood on the left. On its right atrial side you can find the fossa ovalis, an oval depression left over from the fetal foramen ovale.
notes: Correct. The interatrial septum divides the two atria.

The fibrous skeleton is the set of dense connective tissue rings around the four valve openings, which separates the atria from the ventricles rather than the left side from the right. It would be the answer if the question asked what anchors the valves and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles.

The crista terminalis is a ridge inside the right atrium that separates its smooth posterior wall from its rough, pectinate anterior wall. Choose it if the question asked about the ridge between the two parts of the right atrial wall.
The interventricular septum is the thick wall between the two ventricles. Pick it if the question asked which wall separates the right and left ventricles.
questions.answerText: Interatrial septum

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which wall separates the right ventricle from the left ventricle?
options: Interatrial septum
Moderator band
Interventricular septum
Coronary sulcus
questions.why: The interventricular septum is the thick muscular wall between the right and left ventricles. It keeps blood headed to the lungs separate from blood headed to the body. The AV bundle and the bundle branches of the conduction system run along this septum on their way toward the apex.
notes: The interatrial septum is the thinner wall between the two atria, where the fossa ovalis sits. Pick it if the question asked which wall separates the right and left atria.

The moderator band is a muscular band inside the right ventricle that carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked about the band that crosses the right ventricle.
Correct. The interventricular septum divides the two ventricles.

The coronary sulcus is the groove on the outside of the heart that circles between the atria and the ventricles and holds coronary vessels. Choose it if the question asked which external groove marks the boundary between the upper and lower chambers.
questions.answerText: Interventricular septum

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: In the adult heart, which feature is the shallow oval depression on the right atrial side of the interatrial septum?
options: Fossa ovalis
Foramen ovale
Auricle
Sinus venarum
questions.why: The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum, seen from inside the right atrium. It marks the spot where the foramen ovale, an opening between the atria, let fetal blood skip the lungs. After birth that opening seals, and the depression is what remains.
notes: Correct. The fossa ovalis is the oval depression in the interatrial septum.

The foramen ovale is the fetal opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. Pick it if the question asked about the fetal shunt itself rather than the depression it leaves behind.

An auricle is a small wrinkled pouch on the outside of each atrium that slightly increases its capacity. It would be the answer if the question asked about the ear-shaped flap on the surface of an atrium.

The sinus venarum is the smooth-walled posterior part of the right atrium, where the venae cavae empty. Choose it if the question asked which part of the right atrial wall is smooth and receives the venae cavae.
questions.answerText: Fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which parallel muscular ridges line the inner walls of the atria and the auricles?
options: Chordae tendineae
Papillary muscles
Pectinate muscles
Trabeculae carneae
questions.why: Pectinate muscles are parallel ridges of muscle on the inner walls of the atria and auricles. The name comes from the Latin word for comb, because the ridges line up like the teeth of a comb. In the right atrium they cover the rough anterior wall, which the crista terminalis separates from the smooth posterior wall.
notes: Chordae tendineae are fibrous cords, not muscle, that tie the cusps of the AV valves to the papillary muscles. Choose them if the question asked what keeps the AV valve cusps from flipping back into the atria.
Papillary muscles are cone-shaped projections of the ventricle wall that anchor the chordae tendineae. They would be the answer if the question asked what holds the cords of the AV valves.
Correct. Pectinate muscles are the comb-like ridges of the atria and auricles.
Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges on the inner walls of the ventricles, not the atria. Pick them if the question asked about the ridges inside the ventricles.
questions.answerText: Pectinate muscles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which irregular muscular ridges line the inner walls of the ventricles?
options: Crista terminalis
Pectinate muscles
Chordae tendineae
Trabeculae carneae
questions.why: Trabeculae carneae are the irregular ridges and bundles of muscle on the inner walls of both ventricles. The name means little beams of flesh. They give the ventricular lining a rough, crisscrossed look, unlike the orderly parallel pectinate muscles of the atria, which helps you tell the two kinds of chamber apart on a model.
notes: The crista terminalis is a single ridge in the right atrium marking where the smooth and rough parts of the wall meet. It would be the answer if the question asked about the ridge separating the sinus venarum from the pectinate wall.
Pectinate muscles are the parallel, comb-like ridges in the atria and auricles. Pick them if the question asked about the ridges on the atrial walls.
Chordae tendineae are thin fibrous cords attached to the AV valve cusps, not ridges of muscle on the wall. Choose them if the question asked what connects the valve cusps to the papillary muscles.
Correct. Trabeculae carneae are the irregular muscular ridges of the ventricles.
questions.answerText: Trabeculae carneae

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Fluid builds up in the pericardial cavity and squeezes the heart from outside. Which heart function is most directly limited?
options: How much oxygen the alveoli take up
How fully the ventricles can fill
How well the semilunar valves close
How fast the SA node fires
questions.why: The pericardial cavity sits between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium, and it normally holds only a thin film of fluid that lets the heart glide as it beats. The fibrous pericardium around it is tough and does not stretch, so extra fluid has nowhere to go and presses inward on the heart. The chambers cannot expand fully, and less blood enters the ventricles before each beat. This condition is called cardiac tamponade.
notes: Oxygen uptake happens across the alveolar walls in the lungs, which are wrapped by the pleurae, not the pericardium. This would fit a question about pneumonia or emphysema, where the exchange surface in the lungs is damaged.
Correct. Fluid pressing in from outside keeps the ventricles from expanding, so they fill with less blood.

The semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves at the exits of the ventricles, and their pocket-shaped cusps close on their own. Choose them for a question about backflow from the aorta or pulmonary trunk into a ventricle.

The SA node is the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium, and it keeps generating the beat on its own. Pick it if the question described a failing pacemaker or a rhythm that is too slow, not pressure on the outside of the heart.
questions.answerText: How fully the ventricles can fill

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why does long-term high blood pressure in the systemic arteries put extra strain on the left ventricle?
options: It must push against higher pressure in the aorta
It loses its blood supply from the coronary sinus
It receives less blood from the left atrium
It must push against higher pressure in the pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and out through the systemic circuit. In systemic hypertension, the pressure in those arteries stays high, so the ventricle has to squeeze harder with every beat to push blood out against it. Over time this extra workload strains the left ventricle and can thicken its wall.
notes: Correct. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, so higher systemic pressure means harder work with every beat.

The coronary sinus is a vein that drains the heart wall into the right atrium; it does not supply the ventricle. The heart wall is fed by the coronary arteries, so this choice mixes up drainage with supply.

Systemic hypertension raises the pressure the ventricle pumps against; it does not reduce the blood arriving from the left atrium. This choice confuses a problem with filling with a problem with pumping out.

The pulmonary trunk receives blood from the right ventricle, not the left. High pressure in the lung circuit would strain the right ventricle, so pick this for a question about the right side of the heart.
questions.answerText: It must push against higher pressure in the aorta

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why can inflammation of the endocardium damage the heart valves?
options: It makes up most of the wall's thickness
It anchors the heart in the mediastinum
It lines the chambers and covers the valves
It is the outer layer of the heart wall
questions.why: The endocardium is the innermost layer of the heart wall, a smooth endothelium that lines all four chambers. It also covers the surfaces of the valves and is continuous with the lining of the great vessels. Because the valves are covered by this same layer, inflammation or infection of the endocardium (endocarditis) can spread to the valve cusps and damage them.
notes: Most of the wall's thickness, about ninety five percent, is the myocardium, the layer of cardiac muscle. It would be the answer for a question about which layer contracts.

Anchoring the heart in the mediastinum is the job of the fibrous pericardium, the tough outer layer of the pericardial sac. Pick it for a question about what holds the heart in place and prevents overfilling.
Correct. The endocardium covers the valves, so its inflammation reaches them directly.
The outer layer of the heart wall is the epicardium, also called the visceral layer of the serous pericardium. Choose it for a question about the layer where the coronary vessels run.
questions.answerText: It lines the chambers and covers the valves

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why is the fossa ovalis considered a landmark of fetal circulation?
options: It marks where the umbilical vein was
It marks where the foramen ovale was
It marks where the ductus arteriosus was
It marks where the ductus venosus was
questions.why: The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum, the wall between the right and left atria. Before birth, an opening in that septum, the foramen ovale, let blood pass from the right atrium straight to the left atrium and bypass the lungs. After birth the opening seals, and the fossa ovalis is the mark it leaves behind.
notes: The umbilical vein carried blood from the placenta toward the liver, outside the heart. Its remnant is the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver, so pick it for a question about that ligament.
Correct. The fossa ovalis is the sealed remnant of the foramen ovale.

The ductus arteriosus was a vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, outside the heart. Its remnant is the ligamentum arteriosum, so pick that cord for a question about the ductus arteriosus.
The ductus venosus was the shunt through the fetal liver, and its remnant is the ligamentum venosum on the inferior surface of the liver. Choose it for a question about the liver bypass.
questions.answerText: It marks where the foramen ovale was

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall of the four chambers?
options: It holds the SA node in its wall
It pumps blood only to the nearby lungs
It receives blood from the venae cavae
It pumps blood to the entire body
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta and out through the systemic circuit, which reaches every tissue from head to toe. Pushing blood through that long, extensive circuit takes much more force than any other chamber needs. Its thick myocardium supplies that force, so it has the thickest wall of the four chambers.
notes: The SA node is in the wall of the right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava. It would be the answer for a question about where the pacemaker sits, not about wall thickness.
Pumping only to the nearby lungs describes the right ventricle, which has a thinner wall for exactly that reason. Pick it for a question about the right ventricle.
The venae cavae empty into the right atrium, a thin-walled receiving chamber. Choose the right atrium for a question about where blood from the body returns.
Correct. Driving blood through the entire body takes the most force, so the left ventricle has the most muscle.
questions.answerText: It pumps blood to the entire body

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Why is the wall of the right ventricle thinner than the wall of the left ventricle?
options: It pumps blood to the whole body
It receives blood from the pulmonary veins
It only receives blood and does not pump
It pumps blood only to the nearby lungs
questions.why: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk and through the pulmonary circuit, a short loop to the lungs right beside the heart. Moving blood through that short circuit takes much less force than pushing it through the entire body. The right ventricle therefore needs less muscle, and its wall is thinner than the left ventricle's.
notes: Pumping to the whole body is the job of the left ventricle, which is why its wall is the thickest. Pick it for a question about the left ventricle.
The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, not the right ventricle. Choose the left atrium for a question about where the pulmonary veins empty.
The right ventricle does pump, sending blood into the pulmonary trunk. Receiving blood with little pumping describes the atria, the thin-walled chambers that collect returning blood.
Correct. The short pulmonary circuit needs less force, so the right ventricle has a thinner wall.
questions.answerText: It pumps blood only to the nearby lungs

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which layer of the heart wall is the thick layer of cardiac muscle that does the contracting?
options: Epicardium
Fibrous pericardium
Endocardium
Myocardium
questions.why: The myocardium is the middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle tissue arranged in spiraling bundles. It makes up about 95 percent of the wall's thickness, and its contraction is what pumps blood out of the chambers. It is thickest in the left ventricle, which pumps blood to the whole body.
notes: The epicardium is the thin serous membrane on the outer surface of the heart, where fat and the coronary vessels run. Pick it if the question asked which layer is the same membrane as the visceral serous pericardium.

The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac of dense connective tissue that anchors the heart in the mediastinum. It contains no muscle; choose it for the layer that keeps the heart from overfilling.
The endocardium is the smooth endothelium lining the chambers and covering the valves. It would be the answer for the layer that is continuous with the lining of the great vessels.
Correct. The myocardium is the cardiac muscle layer and forms the bulk of the wall.
questions.answerText: Myocardium

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: What is the pericardium?
options: The serous membrane that surrounds each lung
The rings of dense connective tissue around the valves
The smooth lining of the heart chambers and valves
The double-walled sac that encloses the heart
questions.why: The pericardium is the double-walled sac that encloses the heart in the mediastinum. Its tough outer fibrous layer anchors the heart and keeps it from overfilling, and its inner serous layer folds back on itself to form a parietal layer and a visceral layer. The thin film of serous fluid between those two serous layers lets the heart beat without friction.
notes: That describes the pleura, the serous membrane of the lungs. It would be the answer for the membrane with a parietal layer on the thoracic wall and a visceral layer on the lung surface.

That describes the fibrous skeleton of the heart, which anchors the valves and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. Choose it if the question asked what holds the valve openings in shape.
That describes the endocardium, the innermost layer of the heart wall. Pick it if the question asked which layer lines the chambers and covers the valves.
Correct. The pericardium is the sac around the heart, with a fibrous outer layer and a serous inner layer.
questions.answerText: The double-walled sac that encloses the heart

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the fibrous pericardium and the serous pericardium?
options: The serous layer is tough and anchors the heart; the fibrous layer is a thin double membrane inside it
The fibrous layer lines the heart chambers; the serous layer lines the thoracic wall
The fibrous layer is tough and anchors the heart; the serous layer is a thin double membrane inside it
The fibrous layer is cardiac muscle that contracts; the serous layer is a thin membrane outside it
questions.why: The pericardium has two parts. The fibrous pericardium is the outer layer of dense, inelastic connective tissue that anchors the heart in the mediastinum and keeps it from overfilling. The serous pericardium sits inside it as a double membrane: its parietal layer lines the fibrous pericardium, and its visceral layer (the epicardium) covers the heart surface, with serous fluid between them.
notes: This swaps the two layers. The word fibrous is the clue: fibrous tissue is the tough, anchoring layer, while serous membranes are thin and secrete fluid. Students pick this when they mix up which name goes with which texture.

The lining of the chambers is the endocardium, and the membrane lining the thoracic wall is the parietal pleura. Neither is part of the pericardium; choose statements like these for questions about the inner heart wall or the lungs.
Correct. The fibrous layer is the tough anchor, and the serous layer is the thin double membrane that holds the lubricating fluid.

The muscle layer that contracts is the myocardium, the middle layer of the heart wall. The fibrous pericardium contains no muscle, so this option would fit only a question about what the myocardium does.
questions.answerText: The fibrous layer is tough and anchors the heart; the serous layer is a thin double membrane inside it

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Fluid builds up in the pericardial cavity and squeezes the heart, a condition called cardiac tamponade. Why does this keep the heart from filling properly?
options: The fluid presses on the heart from outside, so the chambers cannot expand
The fluid leaks through the wall into the chambers and dilutes the blood
The fluid stops the SA node from sending its signal to the atria
The fluid blocks the openings of the coronary arteries at the aorta
questions.why: The pericardial cavity is the space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium, and it normally holds only a thin film of fluid. Because the fibrous pericardium around it is tough and does not stretch, extra fluid has nowhere to go and presses inward on the heart. The chambers cannot expand fully between beats, so less blood fills them, even though the heart muscle itself is healthy.
notes: Correct. The trapped fluid compresses the heart from outside and limits how much each chamber can fill.

The pericardial cavity lies outside the heart wall, and fluid there does not pass through the myocardium into the chambers. Students choose this when they picture the pericardial cavity as connected to the inside of the heart.
The SA node is the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium, and fluid outside the heart does not switch it off. Pick an answer about the SA node for a question on what sets the heart rate.

The coronary arteries open from the base of the aorta, not into the pericardial cavity. A blocked coronary artery describes a myocardial infarction (heart attack), which starves the muscle of oxygen rather than squeezing the heart.
questions.answerText: The fluid presses on the heart from outside, so the chambers cannot expand

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which list names the four chambers of the heart?
options: Right and left atria, right and left ventricles
Right and left ventricles, conus arteriosus and aortic vestibule
Right and left atria, right and left auricles
Right and left atria, interatrial and interventricular septa
questions.why: The heart has four chambers. The two atria are the upper receiving chambers, taking in blood returning from the body and the lungs, and the two ventricles are the lower pumping chambers that send blood out into the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. The right side handles oxygen-poor blood and the left side handles oxygen-rich blood.
notes: Correct. Two atria receive blood and two ventricles pump it out.

The conus arteriosus and the aortic vestibule are the smooth outflow tracts of the right and left ventricles, leading to the pulmonary and aortic valves. They are parts of the ventricles, so they would be the answer only for a question about where blood leaves each ventricle.

The auricles are small wrinkled pouches on the outside of each atrium that slightly increase its capacity. They are parts of the atria, not separate chambers; pick them if the question asked for the ear-shaped flaps on the atria.
The interatrial and interventricular septa are walls that divide the chambers, not chambers themselves. Choose them if the question asked what separates the right side of the heart from the left.
questions.answerText: Right and left atria, right and left ventricles

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the walls of the atria and the ventricles?
options: The atria have thick walls because they push blood out through the great arteries
The atria are thick-walled pumping chambers; the ventricles are thin-walled receiving chambers
The atria and ventricles have walls of equal thickness because they move the same blood
The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers; the ventricles are thick-walled pumping chambers
questions.why: The atria receive blood returning to the heart and only need to push it a short distance down into the ventricles, so their walls are thin. The ventricles must pump blood out of the heart into the pulmonary trunk and aorta, so they have thick muscular walls. Wall thickness tracks the work each chamber does, which is also why the left ventricle is thicker than the right.
notes: The great arteries, the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, leave from the ventricles, not the atria. The atria send blood only into the ventricles below them, so this mistakes which chambers connect to the arteries.

This reverses the two roles. The atria receive blood from veins and the ventricles pump it into arteries, so the ventricles are the thick ones. Students choose this when they forget that the atria sit on top as receiving chambers.
The chambers do move the same blood, but not with the same effort. Wall thickness depends on how hard a chamber must push, so the pumping ventricles are much thicker than the receiving atria.
Correct. Receiving chambers are thin, and pumping chambers are thick.
questions.answerText: The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers; the ventricles are thick-walled pumping chambers

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: A newborn has a hole in the interventricular septum. Which two kinds of blood can now mix that the septum normally keeps apart?
options: Oxygen-poor blood of the pulmonary trunk and oxygen-rich blood of the aorta
Oxygen-poor blood of the right atrium and oxygen-rich blood of the left atrium
Oxygen-rich blood of the left ventricle and blood already in the aorta
Oxygen-poor blood of the right ventricle and oxygen-rich blood of the left ventricle
questions.why: The interventricular septum is the thick wall between the two ventricles. The right ventricle holds oxygen-poor blood headed for the lungs and the left ventricle holds oxygen-rich blood headed for the body, so the septum keeps the pulmonary and systemic circuits separate at the pumping chambers. A hole in it lets the two kinds of blood mix.
notes: The pulmonary trunk and the aorta are linked before birth by the ductus arteriosus, a vessel outside the heart. Pick this for a question about a patent ductus arteriosus, the fetal shunt that failed to close.
The atria are separated by the interatrial septum, not the interventricular septum. A hole there, such as a foramen ovale that never closed, would be the answer if the defect were between the atria.
The left ventricle and the aorta are separated by the aortic valve, not by a septum. Choose this pairing for a question about what happens when the aortic valve fails to close.
Correct. The septum divides the two ventricles, so a hole there mixes right ventricle blood with left ventricle blood.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-poor blood of the right ventricle and oxygen-rich blood of the left ventricle

questions.topic: Heart: pericardium, wall, chambers and surface features
questions.q: On an opened heart model, one chamber has pectinate muscles on its rough anterior wall, a smooth posterior part where two large veins empty, and an oval depression on its septal wall. Which chamber is this, and where does it send its blood?
options: The right atrium, which sends blood to the right ventricle.
The left atrium, which sends blood to the left ventricle.
The right ventricle, which sends blood to the pulmonary trunk.
The right atrium, which sends blood to the pulmonary trunk.
questions.why: Pectinate muscles line the atria, and the smooth posterior part where the two venae cavae empty is the sinus venarum, found in the right atrium. The oval depression is the fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum. The right atrium passes its blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
notes: Correct. The sinus venarum and the fossa ovalis mark the right atrium, which empties into the right ventricle.

The left atrium does send blood to the left ventricle, but it receives the four pulmonary veins, and the sinus venarum where the venae cavae empty is in the right atrium. Pick it for the chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.
The right ventricle does pump into the pulmonary trunk, but its walls carry trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles, not pectinate muscles, and no veins empty into it.
The chamber is the right atrium, but the right atrium does not send blood into the pulmonary trunk. That is the job of the right ventricle, through the pulmonary valve.
questions.answerText: The right atrium, which sends blood to the right ventricle.

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which chamber receives blood from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae?
options: The right atrium
The left ventricle
The right ventricle
The left atrium
questions.why: The superior and inferior venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood from the body, and both empty into the right atrium. This makes the right atrium the first stop in the heart for blood coming back from the systemic circuit. From there, blood passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
notes: Correct. Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta. Pick it if the question asked which chamber pumps blood to the body.
The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, not directly from the venae cavae. Pick it if the question asked which chamber pumps blood to the lungs.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins. Pick it if the question asked where the pulmonary veins empty.
questions.answerText: The right atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Blood leaving the right ventricle enters which vessel?
options: The pulmonary veins
The aorta
The pulmonary trunk
The superior vena cava
questions.why: When the right ventricle contracts, blood passes through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. The pulmonary trunk then splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry the oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. This is the start of the pulmonary circuit.
notes: The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs back to the left atrium, so they bring blood into the heart. Pick them for the return trip from the lungs.
The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle and carries it to the body. Pick it if the question asked where blood goes when it leaves the left ventricle.
Correct. The right ventricle empties into the pulmonary trunk, which leads to the lungs.
The superior vena cava returns blood from the upper body to the right atrium. Pick it if the question asked which vessel drains the head and arms.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
options: The aortic valve
The mitral valve
The tricuspid valve
The pulmonary valve
questions.why: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, sitting between the right atrium and the right ventricle. It has three cusps, which gives it its name. When the right ventricle contracts, the tricuspid valve closes so blood does not flow back into the right atrium.
notes: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve at the exit of the left ventricle, leading into the aorta. Pick it for the left ventricle's outflow.
The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and left ventricle. Pick it if the question asked about the left side.
Correct. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve is the semilunar valve at the exit of the right ventricle, leading into the pulmonary trunk. Pick it if the question asked about the right ventricle's outflow.
questions.answerText: The tricuspid valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle?
options: The pulmonary valve
The tricuspid valve
The mitral valve
The aortic valve
questions.why: The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and the left ventricle. It is also called the bicuspid valve because it has two cusps, and it is the only heart valve with two. It closes when the left ventricle contracts so blood does not flow back into the left atrium.
notes: The pulmonary valve is the semilunar valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. Pick it for the right ventricle's outflow.
The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, between the right atrium and right ventricle. Pick it if the question asked about the right side.
Correct. The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle.
The aortic valve is the semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta. Pick it if the question asked which valve blood crosses as it leaves the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: The mitral valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk?
options: The pulmonary valve
The tricuspid valve
The mitral valve
The aortic valve
questions.why: The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve with three pocket-shaped cusps, sitting at the outflow of the right ventricle where the pulmonary trunk begins. It opens when the right ventricle contracts and closes afterward so blood in the pulmonary trunk cannot fall back into the ventricle. Each ventricle has an inflow valve and an outflow valve, and the pulmonary valve is the right ventricle's outflow valve.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary valve guards the right ventricle's exit into the pulmonary trunk.
The tricuspid valve is the inflow valve of the right ventricle, between the right atrium and right ventricle. Pick it if the question asked which valve blood crosses to enter the right ventricle.
The mitral valve is the inflow valve of the left ventricle, between the left atrium and left ventricle. Pick it for the left side's atrioventricular valve.
The aortic valve guards the exit of the left ventricle into the aorta. Pick it if the question asked about the left ventricle's outflow.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which valve guards the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta?
options: The pulmonary valve
The tricuspid valve
The aortic valve
The mitral valve
questions.why: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve at the outflow of the left ventricle, where the aorta begins. When the left ventricle contracts, the aortic valve opens and blood surges into the aorta. When the ventricle relaxes, the valve closes so blood in the aorta cannot flow back into the ventricle.
notes: The pulmonary valve guards the right ventricle's exit into the pulmonary trunk. Pick it if the question asked about the right ventricle's outflow.
The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, between the right atrium and right ventricle. Pick it for the right side's inflow valve.
Correct. The aortic valve guards the left ventricle's exit into the aorta.
The mitral valve is the inflow valve of the left ventricle, between the left atrium and left ventricle. Pick it if the question asked which valve blood crosses to enter the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: The aortic valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: How many cusps does the tricuspid valve have?
options: Six
Three
Two
Four
questions.why: The tricuspid valve has three cusps, and its name says so: tri means three and cusp means a flap. A cusp is one of the leaflets that meet to close a valve opening. The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, and its three cusps are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles in the right ventricle.
notes: Six is a misconception, perhaps from adding the cusps of two valves together. A single valve has two or three cusps.
Correct. The tricuspid valve has three cusps, as its name says.
Two cusps belong to the mitral valve, which is why it is also called the bicuspid valve. Pick two if the question asked about the left atrioventricular valve.
No heart valve normally has four cusps. Students who choose four may be counting the four valves of the heart rather than the flaps of one valve.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which two valves are the atrioventricular valves?
options: The pulmonary and aortic valves
The tricuspid and mitral valves
The tricuspid and pulmonary valves
The mitral and aortic valves
questions.why: Atrioventricular valves sit between an atrium and a ventricle, which is what the name means. The tricuspid valve is on the right side and the mitral valve is on the left side. Both have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles that hold them shut when the ventricles contract.
notes: The pulmonary and aortic valves are the semilunar valves, at the exits of the ventricles into the great arteries. Pick this pair if the question asked which valves are semilunar.
Correct. The tricuspid and mitral valves sit between the atria and ventricles.
This pair joins the right ventricle's inflow and outflow valves. It would fit a question about the two valves of the right ventricle, but only the tricuspid is atrioventricular.
This pair joins the left ventricle's inflow and outflow valves. It would fit a question about the two valves of the left ventricle, but only the mitral is atrioventricular.
questions.answerText: The tricuspid and mitral valves

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which structures are the strong fibrous cords that tie the cusps of an atrioventricular valve to the ventricle wall?
options: The papillary muscles
The trabeculae carneae
The chordae tendineae
The pectinate muscles
questions.why: The chordae tendineae are thin, strong cords of fibrous tissue that run from the edges of the atrioventricular valve cusps down to the papillary muscles. They work like the strings of a parachute, keeping the cusps from flipping back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts. Their name means tendinous cords, which describes their tough, string-like look.
notes: The papillary muscles are the cone-shaped muscle projections that the chordae tendineae attach to. They anchor the cords rather than being the cords, so pick them if the question asked what the chordae attach to.
The trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges on the inner walls of the ventricles. Pick them if the question asked about the ridged texture of the ventricle walls.
Correct. The chordae tendineae are the fibrous cords that tie the cusps to the ventricle wall.
The pectinate muscles are parallel muscular ridges on the walls of the atria and auricles. Pick them for a question about the ridges inside the atria.
questions.answerText: The chordae tendineae

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: What are the cone-shaped muscle projections of the ventricle wall that anchor the chordae tendineae?
options: The trabeculae carneae
The papillary muscles
The pectinate muscles
The auricles
questions.why: The papillary muscles are cone-shaped projections that rise from the inner wall of each ventricle. The chordae tendineae run from their tips to the cusps of the atrioventricular valves. When the ventricle contracts, the papillary muscles tighten the cords so the valve stays shut against the pressure.
notes: The trabeculae carneae are the general irregular ridges covering the inner ventricle walls. They are in the same chamber, but they do not anchor the valve cords, so pick them for the ridged texture of the ventricle wall.
Correct. The papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae.
The pectinate muscles are parallel ridges on the walls of the atria and auricles, not in the ventricles. Pick them for a question about the comb-like ridges inside the atria.
The auricles are wrinkled pouches on the outside of each atrium. Pick them if the question asked about the ear-shaped flaps on the atria.
questions.answerText: The papillary muscles

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: When the left ventricle contracts, which valve closes to keep blood from flowing back into the left atrium?
options: The tricuspid valve
The pulmonary valve
The aortic valve
The mitral valve
questions.why: Each valve prevents backflow into the chamber behind it. The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, so when the left ventricle squeezes, the mitral valve snaps shut and blood cannot return to the left atrium. Blood is then forced out through the open aortic valve instead.
notes: The tricuspid valve prevents backflow into the right atrium when the right ventricle contracts. Pick it for the right side.
The pulmonary valve guards the exit of the right ventricle. Pick it for backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle.

The aortic valve opens, not closes, when the left ventricle contracts, letting blood into the aorta. It closes afterward to prevent backflow into the left ventricle, so pick it for backflow from the aorta.
Correct. The mitral valve closes to prevent backflow into the left atrium.
questions.answerText: The mitral valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which two valves have pocket-shaped cusps and no chordae tendineae?
options: The mitral and aortic valves
The tricuspid and mitral valves
The tricuspid and pulmonary valves
The pulmonary and aortic valves
questions.why: The pulmonary and aortic valves are the semilunar valves, named for their half-moon shaped cusps. Each cusp is a small pocket that fills with blood when flow tries to reverse, and the filled pockets press together to seal the opening. Because they close themselves this way, they need no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.
