notes: The tricuspid valve is the entrance to the right ventricle from the right atrium. It would be the answer if blood leaked from the right ventricle back into the right atrium.
Correct. The pulmonary valve separates the pulmonary trunk from the right ventricle.
The mitral valve separates the left atrium and left ventricle. It would be the answer if blood leaked from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
The aortic valve is the matching semilunar valve on the left side. It would be the answer if blood fell back from the aorta into the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A patient's left ventricle must work much harder than normal to push blood into the aorta because the valve between them is stiff and narrowed (stenotic). Which valve is affected?
options: Tricuspid valve
Pulmonary valve
Aortic valve
Mitral valve
questions.why: A stenotic valve is stiff and narrowed, so it does not open fully and blood has trouble getting through. The valve that blood must pass to go from the left ventricle into the aorta is the aortic valve. When it is narrowed, the left ventricle has to push harder to move the same amount of blood.
notes: The tricuspid valve is the entrance to the right ventricle from the right atrium. It would be the answer if blood had trouble moving from the right atrium into the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve is the exit from the right ventricle. It would be the answer if the right ventricle were struggling to push blood into the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. The aortic valve is the passage from the left ventricle into the aorta.
The mitral valve is the entrance to the left ventricle from the left atrium. A stenotic mitral valve would slow blood moving from the left atrium into the left ventricle instead.
questions.answerText: Aortic valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A patient's right ventricle must work much harder than normal to push blood into the pulmonary trunk because the valve between them is stiff and narrowed (stenotic). Which valve is affected?
options: Mitral valve
Pulmonary valve
Tricuspid valve
Aortic valve
questions.why: A stenotic valve does not open fully, which narrows the passage for blood. Blood leaving the right ventricle must pass the pulmonary valve to enter the pulmonary trunk. If that valve is narrowed, the right ventricle has to push harder to send blood to the lungs.
notes: The mitral valve is the entrance to the left ventricle from the left atrium. It would be the answer if blood had trouble moving from the left atrium into the left ventricle.
Correct. The pulmonary valve is the passage from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
The tricuspid valve is the entrance to the right ventricle, not its exit. A narrowed tricuspid valve would slow blood moving from the right atrium into the right ventricle.
The aortic valve is the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta. It would be the answer if the left ventricle were struggling to push blood into the aorta.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Blood travels from the left atrium out to the systemic arteries. Which two heart valves does it cross, in order?
options: Aortic valve, then mitral valve
Tricuspid valve, then pulmonary valve
Mitral valve, then pulmonary valve
Mitral valve, then aortic valve
questions.why: From the left atrium, blood crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle then pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta, which branches into the systemic arteries. On each side of the heart, the atrioventricular valve comes first and the semilunar valve second.
notes: These are the right two valves in the wrong order. Blood has to enter the left ventricle through the mitral valve before the ventricle can pump it out through the aortic valve.
The tricuspid and pulmonary valves are the right-side valves. They would be the answer for blood traveling from the right atrium to the lungs.
The mitral valve is right, but the pulmonary valve is the exit from the right ventricle, not the left. It would fit only if the question were about blood leaving the right ventricle for the lungs.
Correct. The mitral valve comes first, then the aortic valve.
questions.answerText: Mitral valve, then aortic valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A student traces blood from the right atrium to the pulmonary arteries and writes: right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, aortic valve, pulmonary trunk, pulmonary arteries. Which correction fixes the trace?
options: Replace the pulmonary trunk with the aorta
Replace the aortic valve with the pulmonary valve
Replace the tricuspid valve with the mitral valve
Swap the right atrium and the right ventricle
questions.why: The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs through the pulmonary valve, which opens into the pulmonary trunk. The aortic valve belongs to the left ventricle and opens into the aorta. Swapping in the pulmonary valve makes every structure in the trace belong to the right side of the heart, which is what the pulmonary circuit needs.
notes: The pulmonary trunk is correct, since it is the vessel that branches into the pulmonary arteries. The aorta would fit only if the trace were heading to the body instead of the lungs.
Correct. The right ventricle empties through the pulmonary valve, not the aortic valve.
The tricuspid valve is already correct, since it separates the right atrium from the right ventricle. The mitral valve would be correct only in a trace through the left side of the heart.
The order of the chambers is already correct. Blood enters the right atrium first and the right ventricle second, so swapping them would add an error.
questions.answerText: Replace the aortic valve with the pulmonary valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A red blood cell leaves a vein in the foot and travels to the left ventricle. In what order does it pass through the other three chambers?
options: Right ventricle, right atrium, left atrium
Right atrium, left atrium
Left atrium, right atrium, right ventricle
Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium
questions.why: Blood from the foot returns through the leg veins and the inferior vena cava to the right atrium. It crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary circuit to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium, and the mitral valve lets it into the left ventricle.
notes: This reverses the right atrium and right ventricle. The atrium is the receiving chamber for blood from the venae cavae, so it comes before the ventricle.

This route skips the right ventricle and the lungs by going straight from the right atrium to the left atrium. That shortcut exists only in the fetus, through the foramen ovale, so it would be the answer for fetal circulation, not an adult.
Venous blood from the body never enters the left atrium first. The left atrium receives blood only from the lungs, so it must come after the right heart and the pulmonary circuit.
Correct. The cell passes the right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, and left atrium before reaching the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A student traces oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the body and writes: pulmonary veins, left atrium, tricuspid valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta. Which correction fixes the trace?
options: Replace the aortic valve with the pulmonary valve
Swap the left atrium and the left ventricle
Replace the pulmonary veins with the pulmonary arteries
Replace the tricuspid valve with the mitral valve
questions.why: On the left side of the heart, blood crosses the mitral valve to move from the left atrium into the left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is the right-side atrioventricular valve, between the right atrium and right ventricle. Every other step in the student's trace is already correct.
notes: The aortic valve is already correct as the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta. The pulmonary valve would fit only in a trace from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The chamber order is already correct. The pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium first, and the left ventricle comes after the atrioventricular valve, so swapping them would add an error.

The pulmonary veins are already correct, since they carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry blood into the lungs, so they would belong in a trace from the right ventricle.
Correct. The mitral valve, not the tricuspid, separates the left atrium from the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: Replace the tricuspid valve with the mitral valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A student traces oxygen-poor blood from the body to the lungs and writes: venae cavae, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary veins. Which correction fixes the trace?
options: Replace the tricuspid valve with the mitral valve
Replace the pulmonary valve with the aortic valve
Replace the right atrium with the left atrium
Replace the pulmonary veins with the pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The pulmonary valve opens into the pulmonary trunk, which branches into the pulmonary arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. The pulmonary veins run the other way, carrying oxygen-rich blood out of the lungs to the left atrium. Every other step in the student's trace is already correct.
notes: The tricuspid valve is already correct, since it separates the right atrium from the right ventricle. The mitral valve belongs in a trace through the left side of the heart.
The pulmonary valve is already correct as the exit from the right ventricle. The aortic valve is the exit from the left ventricle and would belong in a trace that ends at the aorta.
The right atrium is already correct, because the venae cavae empty into it. The left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins, so it would belong in a trace from the lungs to the body.
Correct. Blood passing the pulmonary valve enters the pulmonary trunk, not the pulmonary veins.
questions.answerText: Replace the pulmonary veins with the pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which heart chamber receives blood from the superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, and the coronary sinus?
options: Left ventricle
Left atrium
Right ventricle
Right atrium
questions.why: The right atrium is the receiving chamber for oxygen-poor blood coming back to the heart. The superior vena cava brings blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs, the inferior vena cava brings blood from the trunk and lower limbs, and the coronary sinus brings blood that has already served the heart wall. All three empty into the right atrium, which then passes the blood through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.
notes: The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta. Choose it if the question asked which chamber sends blood out to the whole body.

The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins, not blood returning from the body. Pick it if the question asked which chamber the pulmonary veins drain into.

The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and pumps it into the pulmonary trunk. It would be the answer if the question asked which chamber sends blood to the lungs.
Correct. The venae cavae and the coronary sinus all empty into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: Right atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which heart chamber receives oxygen-rich blood from the four pulmonary veins?
options: Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
questions.why: The pulmonary veins carry blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs back to the heart, and all four of them open into the left atrium. From there the blood passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it out to the body. The left atrium is where the pulmonary circuit ends and the blood begins its trip through the left side of the heart.
notes: The right ventricle receives oxygen-poor blood from the right atrium and sends it toward the lungs. Choose it if the question asked which chamber pumps into the pulmonary trunk.
The left ventricle is the next stop after the left atrium, receiving blood through the mitral valve. It would be the answer if the question asked which chamber pumps blood into the aorta.
Correct. All four pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium.

The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae and from the heart wall through the coronary sinus. Pick it if the question listed those vessels instead of the pulmonary veins.
questions.answerText: Left atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which heart chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?
options: Left ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
Right ventricle
questions.why: The right ventricle receives oxygen-poor blood from the right atrium and, when it contracts, pushes that blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. The pulmonary trunk then splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry the blood to the lungs. This makes the right ventricle the pump for the pulmonary circuit, the loop between the heart and the lungs.
notes: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, starting the systemic circuit. Pick it if the question asked which chamber pumps into the aorta.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the pulmonary veins and passes it to the left ventricle. Choose it if the question asked where blood returning from the lungs first enters the heart.

The right atrium is a receiving chamber that passes blood down through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. It would be the answer if the question asked which chamber receives the venae cavae.
Correct. The right ventricle sends blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
questions.answerText: Right ventricle

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which fibrous cords tie the cusps of the atrioventricular valves to the papillary muscles?
options: Moderator band
Trabeculae carneae
Chordae tendineae
Pectinate muscles
questions.why: The chordae tendineae are strong fibrous cords, often called the heart strings, that connect the cusps of the tricuspid and mitral valves to the papillary muscles. When the ventricle contracts, the cords hold the cusps in place so the valve cannot flip back into the atrium. Only the atrioventricular valves have chordae tendineae, because the semilunar valves close on their own as their cusps fill with blood.
notes: The moderator band is a muscular band in the right ventricle that carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle. Choose it if the question asked which band crosses the right ventricle carrying conduction fibers.
Trabeculae carneae are irregular ridges of muscle on the ventricle walls, not cords attached to the valves. Pick them if the question asked about the rough muscular ridges lining the ventricles.
Correct. The chordae tendineae tie the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles.
Pectinate muscles are parallel muscular ridges on the walls of the atria and auricles. They would be the answer if the question asked about the comb-like ridges inside the atria.
questions.answerText: Chordae tendineae

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which cone-shaped muscular projections of the ventricle wall anchor the chordae tendineae?
options: Pectinate muscles
Papillary muscles
Trabeculae carneae
Crista terminalis
questions.why: Papillary muscles are cone-shaped projections of the ventricle wall, and the chordae tendineae attach to their tips. When the ventricle contracts, the papillary muscles contract with it and pull on the chordae, holding the AV valve cusps shut against the pressure inside the ventricle. If a papillary muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack, the valve can fail and leak.
notes: Pectinate muscles are parallel ridges on the walls of the atria and auricles, and they have no connection to the valves. Pick them if the question asked about the comb-like ridges in the atria.
Correct. The papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae in the ventricles.

Trabeculae carneae are the irregular ridges that roughen the rest of the ventricle wall, but they do not anchor the valve cords. They would be the answer if the question asked about the crisscrossed muscular ridges lining the ventricles.

The crista terminalis is a ridge in the right atrium that separates the smooth posterior wall from the pectinate anterior wall. Choose it if the question asked about the landmark ridge inside the right atrium.
questions.answerText: Papillary muscles

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which pair of heart valves has no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles, because their pocket-shaped cusps fill with blood and close on their own?
options: Tricuspid and mitral valves
Mitral and aortic valves
Pulmonary and aortic valves
Tricuspid and pulmonary valves
questions.why: The pulmonary and aortic valves are the semilunar valves, guarding the exits of the ventricles. Their cusps are shaped like small pockets, so when the ventricles relax, blood falling back fills the pockets and presses them together to seal the opening. Because they close themselves this way, they need no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles, which belong only to the atrioventricular valves.
notes: The tricuspid and mitral valves are the atrioventricular valves, and they are the ones that do have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Pick this pair if the question asked which valves are held shut by cords during ventricular contraction.

This pair mixes one valve of each type, since the mitral valve is an AV valve with chordae and the aortic valve is semilunar. Students choose it when they group the two left-sided valves together instead of grouping by valve type.
Correct. The semilunar valves, pulmonary and aortic, have no chordae tendineae.

This pair mixes one valve of each type, since the tricuspid valve is an AV valve with chordae and the pulmonary valve is semilunar. Students choose it when they group the two right-sided valves together instead of grouping by valve type.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary and aortic valves

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: After a heart attack, a papillary muscle in the left ventricle is damaged, and its chordae tendineae can no longer hold the valve cusps shut. When the left ventricle contracts, into which chamber will some blood leak backward?
options: Left atrium
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
Right atrium
questions.why: The papillary muscles of the left ventricle anchor the chordae tendineae of the mitral valve, the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle. When the ventricle contracts, these structures normally hold the mitral cusps closed so blood can only go out into the aorta. If a papillary muscle fails, the cusps can be pushed back and some blood leaks backward into the left atrium.
notes: Correct. A failing mitral valve lets blood leak back into the left atrium.

The left ventricle is the chamber doing the contracting, so it is where the leaking blood comes from, not where it goes. Students choose it when they lose track of which side of the mitral valve is upstream.

The right ventricle is separated from the left ventricle by the interventricular septum, which a papillary muscle problem does not open. Choose it only if the question described a hole in the interventricular septum.

The right atrium is on the other side of the heart and is separated from the left ventricle by septa, not by the mitral valve. Pick it if the damaged papillary muscle had been in the right ventricle, which would let blood leak back through the tricuspid valve.
questions.answerText: Left atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A heart murmur is caused by blood leaking backward through a valve that does not close cleanly. What kind of valve problem is this?
options: Heart block
Valve regurgitation
Cardiac tamponade
Valve stenosis
questions.why: Each heart valve should seal completely when it closes so blood moves in only one direction. A valve that fails to seal lets blood slip backward, and this is called regurgitation (the valve is also described as incompetent or insufficient). The backward jet of blood is turbulent, and that turbulence is the swishing sound heard through a stethoscope as a murmur.
notes: Heart block is a conduction problem in which the signal is delayed or stopped at the AV node, so the atria and ventricles beat out of step. It is an electrical disorder and does not involve a leaking valve.
Correct. Regurgitation means a valve leaks and lets blood flow backward, and the turbulence is heard as a murmur.
Cardiac tamponade is fluid in the pericardial cavity compressing the heart from outside. It would be the answer if the question described the heart being squeezed so that it cannot fill.

Stenosis is a valve whose opening has become narrowed and stiff, so it does not open fully and blood is squeezed forward through a smaller hole. Pick stenosis when a question describes blocked forward flow out of a chamber, not backflow.
questions.answerText: Valve regurgitation

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A heart attack damages a papillary muscle in the left ventricle, and the mitral valve begins to fail. What best explains the failure?
options: The coronary sinus is blocked, so blood backs up into the valve
The chordae lose their anchor, so the cusps swing into the atrium
The SA node loses its blood supply, so the valve gets no signal to close
The pericardium loses its anchor, so the heart shifts out of position
questions.why: The mitral valve is an atrioventricular valve, and its cusps are tied to the ventricle wall by the chordae tendineae, which are anchored on the papillary muscles. When the ventricle contracts, the papillary muscles hold those cords tight so the cusps cannot be forced back into the left atrium. If a papillary muscle dies, the cords lose their anchor, the cusps can prolapse (bulge backward) into the atrium, and blood leaks backward.
notes: The coronary sinus is the large vein on the posterior heart that drains the cardiac veins into the right atrium. It would be the answer for a question about where blood from the heart wall returns, not about how a valve is held shut.
Correct. Without a working papillary muscle, the chordae cannot hold the mitral cusps shut against a contracting ventricle.

The SA node is the pacemaker in the right atrium, and valves do not close because of electrical signals; they move passively with the pressure of the blood on each side. Pick the SA node for a question about what sets the heart rate.

The pericardium is the sac around the whole heart and anchors it in the mediastinum, but it does not hold the valve cusps. Choose it for a question about what keeps the heart in place or prevents overfilling.
questions.answerText: The chordae lose their anchor, so the cusps swing into the atrium

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In aortic stenosis, the aortic valve opening is narrowed and stiff. Why does this strain the left ventricle?
options: Its inflow from the left atrium is blocked
Its pacemaker signal is slowed
Blood leaks back into it from the aorta
It must push blood through a smaller exit
questions.why: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta, the exit through which the left ventricle sends blood to the body. Stenosis means the valve opening has become narrowed and stiff, so it does not open fully. The left ventricle has to squeeze much harder to push the same amount of blood through the smaller opening, which strains its wall.
notes: Blood enters the left ventricle from the left atrium through the mitral valve, not the aortic valve. A narrowed mitral valve would be the answer for blocked inflow.
The SA node is in the right atrial wall and sets the heart rate on its own. Valves do not control it, so this choice mixes up the valves with the conduction system.
Backflow from the aorta into the ventricle describes aortic regurgitation, a leaky valve that fails to close. Pick it when the valve does not seal, not when it does not open fully.
Correct. The left ventricle has to push harder to get blood through the narrowed aortic valve.
questions.answerText: It must push blood through a smaller exit

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In pulmonary stenosis, the pulmonary valve is narrowed. Which chamber is strained, and why?
options: The right ventricle, because its exit to the lungs is narrowed
The left ventricle, because its exit into the aorta is narrowed
The right atrium, because its exit into the right ventricle is narrowed
The left atrium, because its exit into the left ventricle is narrowed
questions.why: The pulmonary valve is the semilunar valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. When it is narrowed (stenosis), the right ventricle has to squeeze harder to push blood through the smaller opening toward the lungs. The extra workload falls on the chamber just upstream of the narrowed valve, which is the right ventricle.
notes: Correct. The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary valve, so it bears the extra workload.
The left ventricle's exit is the aortic valve. This describes aortic stenosis, so pick it if the narrowed valve led into the aorta.
The right atrium empties through the tricuspid valve, not the pulmonary valve. A narrowed tricuspid valve would be the answer for strain on the right atrium.
The left atrium empties through the mitral valve, on the opposite side of the heart from the pulmonary valve. It would be strained by a narrowed mitral valve.
questions.answerText: The right ventricle, because its exit to the lungs is narrowed

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Why do the AV valves have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles while the semilunar valves do not?
options: The semilunar valves are held shut by the pericardium
Contracting ventricles could push the AV cusps backward
The AV valves open toward the arteries and need strength
The semilunar valves are too small to need any support
questions.why: The AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) sit between each atrium and ventricle. When a ventricle contracts, the blood pushes up against their cusps, and without support the cusps could be forced back into the atrium. The chordae tendineae tie the cusps to the papillary muscles, which hold the cords tight so the cusps stay shut. The semilunar valves have pocket-shaped cusps that fill with blood from above and close themselves, so they need no cords.
notes: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac around the whole heart. It anchors the heart and prevents overfilling, but it does not touch the valves, so pick it for a question about the pericardial sac.
Correct. The cords and papillary muscles keep the AV cusps from being forced back into the atria.
The AV valves open from the atria into the ventricles, not toward the arteries. The valves that open into arteries are the semilunar valves, the pulmonary and aortic valves.
Size is not the reason. The semilunar valves close on their own because their pocket-shaped cusps fill with blood flowing back toward them, a shape that needs no anchors.
questions.answerText: Contracting ventricles could push the AV cusps backward

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Why is it important that each heart valve lets blood flow in only one direction?
options: One-way valves insulate the atria from the ventricles
One-way valves keep the two sides' blood from mixing
One-way valves set the heart rate
Backflow would reduce the blood moving forward
questions.why: Each chamber squeezes blood toward the next part of the pathway, and the valves make sure it goes forward. If a valve leaks, part of every squeeze sends blood back where it came from instead of onward. Less blood moves forward to the lungs or body with each beat, and the heart has to work harder to make up the difference. A leaky valve is described as regurgitation.
notes: Electrical insulation between the atria and ventricles comes from the fibrous skeleton, the dense connective tissue rings around the valves. Pick the fibrous skeleton for a question about why the AV bundle is the only electrical route.

Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood are kept apart by the interatrial and interventricular septa, the walls between the left and right sides. Choose the septa for a question about keeping the two circuits separate.
The heart rate is set by the SA node, the pacemaker in the right atrial wall. Valves open and close passively with blood pressure and play no part in timing.
Correct. One-way flow makes sure each squeeze sends blood onward instead of backward.
questions.answerText: Backflow would reduce the blood moving forward

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which pair names the two atrioventricular (AV) valves and where each one sits?
options: Tricuspid (right atrium to right ventricle) and mitral (left atrium to left ventricle)
Tricuspid (right atrium to right ventricle) and pulmonary (right ventricle to pulmonary trunk)
Pulmonary (right ventricle to pulmonary trunk) and aortic (left ventricle to aorta)
Mitral (right atrium to right ventricle) and tricuspid (left atrium to left ventricle)
questions.why: The atrioventricular valves sit between each atrium and the ventricle below it, which is where their name comes from. The tricuspid valve, with three cusps, guards the right side, and the mitral (bicuspid) valve, with two cusps, guards the left side. Both are held in place by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, which the semilunar valves lack.
notes: Correct. The tricuspid is on the right side and the mitral is on the left.
The tricuspid is an AV valve, but the pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve. This pair would fit a question asking for the two valves on the right side of the heart.
These are the two semilunar valves, which guard the exits from the ventricles into the great arteries. Pick this pair if the question asked for the semilunar valves.
The two AV valves are named here but placed on the wrong sides. The mitral valve is on the left, between the left atrium and left ventricle, and the tricuspid is on the right.
questions.answerText: Tricuspid (right atrium to right ventricle) and mitral (left atrium to left ventricle)

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which pair names the two semilunar valves and where each one sits?
options: Mitral (left atrium to left ventricle) and aortic (left ventricle to aorta)
Tricuspid (right atrium to right ventricle) and mitral (left atrium to left ventricle)
Aortic (right ventricle to pulmonary trunk) and pulmonary (left ventricle to aorta)
Pulmonary (right ventricle to pulmonary trunk) and aortic (left ventricle to aorta)
questions.why: The semilunar valves guard the exits from the two ventricles into the great arteries. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, and the aortic valve sits between the left ventricle and the aorta. Each has three pocket-shaped cusps that fill with blood and close on their own, so they need no chordae tendineae.
notes: The mitral is an AV valve and the aortic is a semilunar valve. This pair would be correct for a question asking which two valves are on the left side of the heart.
These are the two atrioventricular valves, between each atrium and ventricle. Pick this pair if the question asked for the AV valves.

The names are right but the locations are swapped. Each semilunar valve is named for the artery it opens into: the pulmonary valve opens into the pulmonary trunk and the aortic valve opens into the aorta.
Correct. Each semilunar valve sits at the exit of a ventricle and is named for the artery it opens into.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary (right ventricle to pulmonary trunk) and aortic (left ventricle to aorta)

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: How many cusps do the tricuspid valve and the mitral valve each have?
options: Tricuspid two, mitral three
Both have three cusps
Both have two cusps
Tricuspid three, mitral two
questions.why: The tricuspid valve, between the right atrium and right ventricle, has three cusps, as its name says (tri- means three). The mitral valve, between the left atrium and left ventricle, has two cusps, which is why it is also called the bicuspid valve. The two semilunar valves, pulmonary and aortic, each have three cusps.
notes: This swaps the counts. The tricuspid name gives away its three cusps, and the mitral valve's other name, bicuspid, gives away its two.
Three cusps is right for the tricuspid valve and for both semilunar valves, but the mitral valve has only two. Students choose this when they lump the mitral in with the three-cusped valves.
Two cusps is right only for the mitral (bicuspid) valve. Students pick this when they forget that tri- in tricuspid means three.
Correct. Three cusps on the right AV valve and two on the left.
questions.answerText: Tricuspid three, mitral two

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the backflow each type of heart valve prevents?
options: AV valves prevent backflow into the venae cavae; semilunar valves prevent backflow into the atria
AV valves prevent backflow into the atria; semilunar valves prevent backflow into the ventricles
AV valves prevent backflow into the ventricles; semilunar valves prevent backflow into the atria
Both AV and semilunar valves prevent backflow from the ventricles into the atria
questions.why: Each valve stops blood from flowing back into the chamber it just left. The AV valves sit between the atria and ventricles, so when the ventricles contract they close and keep blood from being pushed back up into the atria. The semilunar valves sit at the ventricle exits, so when the ventricles relax they close and keep blood in the pulmonary trunk and aorta from falling back into the ventricles.
notes: The AV valves sit between the atria and the ventricles, not at the openings of the venae cavae, and the semilunar valves are nowhere near the atria. This option mixes up where each valve sits along the pathway.
Correct. Each valve protects the chamber just upstream of it.
This reverses the two jobs. A valve keeps blood from returning to the chamber upstream of it, and the atria are upstream of the AV valves while the ventricles are upstream of the semilunar valves.
Only the AV valves stand between the atria and the ventricles. The semilunar valves guard the ventricle exits, so they keep blood from falling back out of the great arteries into the ventricles.
questions.answerText: AV valves prevent backflow into the atria; semilunar valves prevent backflow into the ventricles

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: When the left ventricle contracts, blood slips backward through the mitral valve into the left atrium, heard as a murmur. Which structural failure could cause this?
options: Damaged pectinate muscles
A torn chordae tendineae cord
A narrowed coronary sinus
A thinned interatrial septum
questions.why: The chordae tendineae are fibrous cords that tie the cusps of an AV valve to the papillary muscles of the ventricle wall. When the ventricle contracts, they hold the cusps shut so the cusps cannot flip back into the atrium. If a cord tears or a papillary muscle is damaged, part of the cusp is no longer held, so the valve leaks and blood slips back into the left atrium.
notes: Pectinate muscles are parallel muscular ridges on the inner walls of the atria and auricles, and they have no connection to the valve cusps. Pick them if the question asked which ridges line the inside of the atria.
Correct. Without the cord holding it, the cusp is pushed back into the atrium and the valve leaks.

The coronary sinus is the large vein on the back of the heart that drains the cardiac veins into the right atrium. A problem there affects drainage of the heart wall, not the closing of the mitral valve; choose it for a question about where cardiac veins empty.
The interatrial septum is the wall between the two atria. Weakness there would affect blood moving between the atria, not blood leaking back through the mitral valve from the ventricle.
questions.answerText: A torn chordae tendineae cord

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: From which vessels does the right atrium receive blood?
options: The four pulmonary veins returning from the lungs
The pulmonary trunk and the pulmonary arteries
The aorta and the coronary arteries at its base
The superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus
questions.why: The right atrium is the receiving chamber for oxygen-poor blood. The superior vena cava brings blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs, the inferior vena cava brings blood from the trunk and lower limbs, and the coronary sinus brings blood that has already supplied the heart wall. All of it then passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
notes: The four pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them if the question asked what empties into the left atrium.

The pulmonary trunk and its pulmonary arteries carry blood out of the right ventricle toward the lungs. They would be the answer if the question asked where blood goes after it leaves the right ventricle.

The aorta and coronary arteries carry blood away from the heart. The aorta leaves the left ventricle and the coronary arteries branch from its base; choose them for a question on where the heart wall gets its oxygen-rich supply.
Correct. Blood from the body returns through the two venae cavae, and blood from the heart wall returns through the coronary sinus.
questions.answerText: The superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which circuit does each side of the heart drive?
options: The right side drives the pulmonary circuit; the left side drives the systemic circuit
The right side drives the systemic circuit; the left side drives the pulmonary circuit
The atria drive the pulmonary circuit; the ventricles drive the systemic circuit
The right side drives both circuits; the left side only receives blood
questions.why: The heart works as two pumps side by side. The right side receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and pumps it through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs, which is the pulmonary circuit. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it through the aorta to the rest of the body, which is the systemic circuit.
notes: Correct. Right side to the lungs, left side to the body.
This swaps the two sides. The right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk, which goes to the lungs, and the left ventricle opens into the aorta, which goes to the body.

Both circuits are driven by ventricles, one on each side. The atria are receiving chambers that only pass blood down to the ventricles, so this mixes up the top-and-bottom split of the heart with the right-and-left split.
Each side of the heart both receives and pumps. The left ventricle is the strongest pump in the heart, sending blood out through the aorta, so it does far more than receive.
questions.answerText: The right side drives the pulmonary circuit; the left side drives the systemic circuit

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Blood moves from the right atrium to the pulmonary trunk. Which two valves does it cross, in order?
options: Tricuspid valve, then aortic valve
Pulmonary valve, then tricuspid valve
Tricuspid valve, then pulmonary valve
Mitral valve, then aortic valve
questions.why: Blood leaving the right atrium first passes through the tricuspid valve, the AV valve on the right side, into the right ventricle. When the right ventricle contracts, the blood passes through the pulmonary valve, a semilunar valve, into the pulmonary trunk. Both valves are on the right side because this blood has not yet been to the lungs.
notes: The tricuspid valve is right, but the aortic valve leads from the left ventricle into the aorta. Students choose this when they forget that the right ventricle empties into the pulmonary trunk.
These are the right valves but in reverse order. Blood must cross the AV valve into the ventricle before it can leave the ventricle through the semilunar valve.
Correct. The AV valve comes first, then the semilunar valve.
These are the matching valves on the left side of the heart, crossed by blood going from the left atrium to the aorta. Pick this pair if the question started at the left atrium.
questions.answerText: Tricuspid valve, then pulmonary valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Trace a drop of blood from the right atrium until it enters the aorta. Which sequence is correct?
options: Tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, lungs, left ventricle, mitral valve, left atrium, aortic valve
Tricuspid valve, right ventricle, aortic valve, lungs, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, pulmonary valve
Tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, lungs, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve
Mitral valve, right ventricle, aortic valve, lungs, left atrium, tricuspid valve, left ventricle, pulmonary valve
questions.why: Blood leaving the right atrium crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. It returns oxygen-rich through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve into the aorta. Each side follows the same pattern: atrium, AV valve, ventricle, semilunar valve.
notes: This sends blood from the lungs into the left ventricle first. Returning blood always enters an atrium first, so the pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium, which then fills the left ventricle through the mitral valve.
This swaps the two semilunar valves. The right ventricle opens through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, and the left ventricle opens through the aortic valve into the aorta.
Correct. Each side runs atrium, AV valve, ventricle, semilunar valve, with the lungs in between.

This swaps the valves between the two sides. The tricuspid and pulmonary valves belong to the right side, and the mitral and aortic valves belong to the left, so the right ventricle cannot open through an aortic valve.
questions.answerText: Tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, lungs, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Which structure is a cone-shaped muscular projection of the ventricle wall that anchors the chordae tendineae?
options: Trabeculae carneae
Moderator band
Papillary muscle
Pectinate muscles
questions.why: The papillary muscles are cone-shaped projections of the ventricle wall that rise into each ventricle. The chordae tendineae run from their tips to the cusps of the AV valve above, so together they hold the valve shut against the pressure of a contracting ventricle. If a papillary muscle is damaged, the valve it anchors can fail and leak.
notes: The trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges covering the inner walls of the ventricles, but they do not anchor the chordae. Pick them for a question about the rough, ridged surface inside the ventricles.

The moderator band is a muscular band in the right ventricle that carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle. Choose it if the question asked which band crosses the right ventricle carrying conduction fibers.
Correct. The papillary muscles are the anchors at the lower end of the chordae tendineae.
The pectinate muscles are parallel ridges on the walls of the atria and auricles, not the ventricles. They would be the answer for the ridges inside the atria.
questions.answerText: Papillary muscle

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: How do the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles keep an AV valve from failing?
options: They carry the electrical signal from the atria to the valve cusps
They pull the semilunar valve cusps closed after each heartbeat
They pull the AV valve cusps open so the ventricles can fill
They hold the cusps shut against the pressure of a contracting ventricle
questions.why: When a ventricle contracts, the rising pressure pushes the AV valve cusps up toward the atrium. The papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae, which act like tethers that keep the cusps from being pushed inside out into the atrium. The valve stays sealed, so blood leaves through the semilunar valve instead of flowing back into the atrium.
notes: The chordae tendineae are fibrous cords, not conducting tissue. The signal reaches the ventricles through the AV bundle, so choose a conduction structure if the question asked how the signal crosses into the ventricles.

Only the AV valves have chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. The semilunar valves have pocket-shaped cusps that fill with blood and close themselves; students pick this when they assume every valve has the same anchoring structures.

AV valves open because blood pushes them open as the ventricles fill, not because cords pull on them. Students choose this when they picture the chordae as ropes that open the valve rather than tethers that keep it from flipping back.
Correct. The cords and their muscle anchors keep the cusps from flipping back into the atrium.
questions.answerText: They hold the cusps shut against the pressure of a contracting ventricle

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In a dissected heart, a valve has cusps tied by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, and the chamber below it has a moderator band. Which valve is this, and backflow into which chamber does it prevent?
options: The mitral valve, preventing backflow into the left atrium.
The tricuspid valve, preventing backflow into the right atrium.
The pulmonary valve, preventing backflow into the right ventricle.
The tricuspid valve, preventing backflow into the right ventricle.
questions.why: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles belong only to the atrioventricular valves, so the valve is the tricuspid or the mitral. The moderator band is a muscular band in the right ventricle, which makes this the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle. It keeps blood from flowing back into the right atrium.
notes: The mitral valve also has chordae tendineae, but it opens into the left ventricle, which has no moderator band. Pick it for the atrioventricular valve on the left side.
Correct. Chordae point to an atrioventricular valve, and the moderator band places it on the right side.
The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve with no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles. It guards the exit from the right ventricle and prevents backflow into the right ventricle.
The valve is the tricuspid, but it prevents backflow into the right atrium above it, not the right ventricle. Backflow into the right ventricle is stopped by the pulmonary valve.
questions.answerText: The tricuspid valve, preventing backflow into the right atrium.

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In one complete trip through the heart, from the venae cavae to the aorta, how many valves does a drop of blood cross?
options: Two valves
Four valves
Three valves
Six valves
questions.why: Blood crosses the tricuspid and pulmonary valves on the right side, goes to the lungs, then crosses the mitral and aortic valves on the left side. That is all four heart valves, each crossed once per loop.
notes: Two is the count for one side only, such as the tricuspid and pulmonary valves on the right. The full loop also crosses the two valves on the left side.
Correct. The drop crosses the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves.
No valve is skipped in the normal pathway. Three would leave one out, for example the pulmonary valve on the way to the lungs.
The heart has only four valves, and blood crosses each once per loop. Six would count valves that the heart does not have.
questions.answerText: Four valves

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In the pathway of blood, where does blood go after it passes the pulmonary valve and before it enters the left atrium?
options: The lungs
The body tissues
The heart wall
The liver
questions.why: After the pulmonary valve, blood enters the pulmonary trunk, which branches to the lungs. In the lungs it picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, then returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary trunk carries blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins bring it back to the left atrium.
Blood reaches the body tissues after the aortic valve, on the left side. Blood that has just passed the pulmonary valve is in the pulmonary circuit.
The heart wall gets its blood from the coronary arteries, which leave the base of the aorta. That blood drains to the right atrium through the coronary sinus, not to the left atrium.
The liver is reached from the systemic side, after the aorta. Blood in the pulmonary circuit does not pass through it.
questions.answerText: The lungs

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: In one full loop of the pathway, from the venae cavae back out through the aorta, how many times does a drop of blood pass through the heart?
options: Once, entering on the right side and leaving on the left
Twice, once through the right side and once through the left
Twice, both times through the right side
Four times, once through each of the four chambers
questions.why: The pathway is a full loop with the lungs in the middle. Blood enters the right side from the body, leaves for the lungs, comes back into the left side, and then leaves for the body. That makes two passes through the heart in one loop, one on each side.
notes: Blood cannot cross straight from the right side to the left in the adult heart, because the septum separates them. It has to leave for the lungs and come back, which makes two passes.
Correct. The drop passes through the right side, goes to the lungs, and comes back through the left side.
Blood coming back from the lungs enters the left atrium, not the right side. The right side only handles blood returning from the body.
The drop does reach all four chambers, but it moves through them in two passes: the right atrium and right ventricle on the first, the left atrium and left ventricle on the second.
questions.answerText: Twice, once through the right side and once through the left

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: Blood in the right ventricle is about to be pumped out. Is it oxygen-rich or oxygen-poor, and where is it headed?
options: Oxygen-rich, headed to the body
Oxygen-poor, headed to the lungs
Oxygen-poor, headed to the body
Oxygen-rich, headed to the lungs
questions.why: The right ventricle holds blood that has just come back from the body through the right atrium, so it is oxygen-poor. It pumps that blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and out to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
notes: Oxygen-rich blood headed to the body is in the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta.
Correct. The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
The blood is oxygen-poor, but the right ventricle sends it to the lungs, not the body. Only the left ventricle pumps to the body.
Blood headed to the lungs has not picked up oxygen yet. It becomes oxygen-rich in the lungs and returns in the pulmonary veins.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-poor, headed to the lungs

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A clot breaks loose from a vein in the arm and travels with the normal flow of blood. Which heart valve does it cross first, and in which organ is it most likely to lodge after it leaves the heart?
options: The mitral valve, then it lodges in the brain
The tricuspid valve, then it lodges in the brain
The pulmonary valve, then it lodges in the liver
The tricuspid valve, then it lodges in the lungs
questions.why: Blood from an arm vein returns through the superior vena cava to the right atrium, so the first valve the clot crosses is the tricuspid. The right ventricle then pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and the arteries of the lungs, where it lodges. A deep vein clot from the leg takes the same route to cause a pulmonary embolism.
notes: The mitral valve is on the left side, which a clot from a vein reaches only after passing through the lungs. Mitral valve then brain describes a route on the arterial side.
The first valve is right, but the right ventricle pumps the clot to the lungs, not the body. It would have to pass through the lungs and the left heart to reach the brain.
The pulmonary valve is the second valve crossed, after the tricuspid. Blood leaving through the pulmonary valve goes to the lungs, not the liver.
Correct. Venous blood reaches the right heart first, and the right ventricle sends the clot to the lungs.
questions.answerText: The tricuspid valve, then it lodges in the lungs

questions.topic: Heart valves and blood flow through the heart
questions.q: A drop of blood is in the pulmonary trunk. After it goes to the lungs and comes back to the heart, which valve will it cross second?
options: The mitral valve
The pulmonary valve
The aortic valve
The tricuspid valve
questions.why: From the lungs, blood returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium. The first valve it crosses is the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and the second is the aortic valve as the left ventricle pumps it into the aorta.
notes: The mitral valve is the first valve crossed after returning from the lungs, between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The question asks for the second.
The drop has already passed the pulmonary valve to reach the pulmonary trunk. It will not meet that valve again until it has gone around the body.
Correct. Mitral first, then aortic, on the way out to the body.
The tricuspid valve is on the right side and is crossed by blood returning from the body. Blood from the lungs enters the left side.
questions.answerText: The aortic valve

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which great vessel carries blood from the left ventricle out to the body?
options: The pulmonary trunk
The superior vena cava
The aorta
The coronary sinus
questions.why: The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It leaves the left ventricle, passing through the aortic valve, and carries oxygen-rich blood to every part of the body through its branches. This makes it the start of the systemic circuit.
notes: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Pick it if the question asked which vessel leaves the right ventricle.

The superior vena cava returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs to the right atrium. It brings blood into the heart, so pick it for a question about venous return from the upper body.
Correct. The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle to the body.
The coronary sinus is a vein on the back of the heart that drains the heart wall into the right atrium. Pick it for a question about where the cardiac veins empty.
questions.answerText: The aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: How many pulmonary veins return blood to the left atrium?
options: Four
Two
Six
One
questions.why: Four pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, typically two from each lung. On the posterior surface of a heart model they appear as four openings entering the left atrium. No other chamber receives the pulmonary veins, so counting four openings on the back of the heart is a quick way to spot the left atrium.
notes: Correct. Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, enter the left atrium.
Two is the number of pulmonary veins from each lung, not the total. Students who choose two have counted one side only.
Six is an overcount. Each lung typically sends only two pulmonary veins to the left atrium, so students who choose six are guessing rather than counting the openings on the left atrium.
One vessel describes the pulmonary trunk, which leaves the right ventricle as a single vessel before splitting. Pick one for the number of pulmonary trunks.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: After the aorta rises out of the left ventricle, which part of it curves over the top of the heart before turning downward?
options: The descending thoracic aorta
The ascending aorta
The aortic arch
The abdominal aorta
questions.why: The aorta has named parts along its path. It begins as the ascending aorta rising from the left ventricle, then curves over the top of the heart as the aortic arch, and then runs down behind the heart as the descending thoracic aorta. After passing through the diaphragm it becomes the abdominal aorta.
notes: The descending thoracic aorta is the segment after the arch, running down along the vertebral column behind the heart. Pick it for the part of the aorta in the posterior thorax.

The ascending aorta is the short first segment that rises straight up from the left ventricle, before the curve. The coronary arteries branch from its base, so pick it for a question about where the coronary arteries begin.
Correct. The aortic arch is the curved segment over the top of the heart.
The abdominal aorta is the segment below the diaphragm, in the abdomen. Pick it for a question about the aorta's branches to the abdominal organs.
questions.answerText: The aortic arch

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The coronary sinus empties the blood it collects into which chamber?
options: The right ventricle
The left atrium
The left ventricle
The right atrium
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a large vein in the groove on the posterior heart that collects blood from the cardiac veins. It empties into the right atrium, the same chamber that receives the venae cavae. That makes sense, because blood that has fed the heart wall is oxygen-poor and needs to go to the lungs like the rest of the body's venous blood.
notes: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve. Pick it if the question asked which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins. Pick it if the question asked where the pulmonary veins empty.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta. Pick it if the question asked which chamber feeds the coronary arteries through the aorta.
Correct. The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: The right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: From where do the right and left coronary arteries branch?
options: From the coronary sinus
From the base of the aorta
From the aortic arch
From the pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The two coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta. They leave the base of the ascending aorta, just above the aortic valve, and run in the grooves on the heart's surface to supply the heart wall. Because they branch off right at the start, the heart wall is the first tissue to receive freshly oxygenated blood from the left ventricle.
notes: The coronary sinus is a vein that collects blood from the heart wall and empties into the right atrium. It drains the heart rather than supplying it, so pick it for venous drainage.
Correct. The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta, just above the aortic valve.

The aortic arch is the curved segment above the heart, whose branches supply the head, neck, and upper limbs. Pick it for the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries, not the coronary arteries.
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It gives off the pulmonary arteries, so pick it if the question asked where the pulmonary arteries begin.
questions.answerText: From the base of the aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A central venous catheter is placed in a vein near the collarbone and threaded toward the heart. Which great vessel does it pass through to enter the right atrium from above?
options: The pulmonary trunk
The superior vena cava
The aorta
The inferior vena cava
questions.why: Veins of the head, neck, and upper limbs all drain into the superior vena cava, which empties into the top of the right atrium. A catheter threaded from a vein near the collarbone follows that same venous path. It travels with the flow of blood toward the heart and enters the right atrium from above.
notes: The pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. A catheter would reach it only after passing through the right atrium and right ventricle, not on the way in.
Correct. A line from the upper body follows the superior vena cava into the right atrium.
The aorta is an artery carrying blood away from the left ventricle. A venous catheter travels with venous blood toward the heart, so it would not reach the aorta.
The inferior vena cava returns blood from the trunk and lower limbs, entering the right atrium from below. Pick it for a catheter threaded up from a vein in the groin.
questions.answerText: The superior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A blood clot breaks loose from a deep vein in the leg. Which great vessel carries it into the right atrium?
options: The pulmonary veins
The superior vena cava
The coronary sinus
The inferior vena cava
questions.why: Veins of the lower limbs drain upward into the inferior vena cava, which returns blood from the trunk and legs to the right atrium. A clot that breaks loose in a leg vein rides that venous flow into the right atrium. From there it passes through the right ventricle and can lodge in the lungs, which is why leg clots are dangerous.
notes: The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium. A clot from the leg reaches the right side of the heart first, so it would not travel in the pulmonary veins.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs. Pick it if the clot had started in a vein of the arm.
The coronary sinus collects blood from the heart wall's own veins and empties into the right atrium. Pick it for venous blood coming from the myocardium, not from the legs.
Correct. The inferior vena cava carries blood from the legs into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: The inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the anterior interventricular artery, also called the LAD, on the front of the heart?
options: The great cardiac vein
The middle cardiac vein
The anterior cardiac veins
The small cardiac vein
questions.why: The cardiac veins travel in the same grooves as the coronary arteries. The great cardiac vein runs up the anterior interventricular sulcus beside the anterior interventricular artery, the LAD. It then curves around to the back of the heart and drains into the coronary sinus.
notes: Correct. The great cardiac vein runs beside the anterior interventricular artery.
The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery on the back of the heart. Pick it if the question asked which vein travels with the posterior interventricular artery.
The anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle directly into the right atrium, skipping the coronary sinus. Pick them if the question asked which veins bypass the coronary sinus.
The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the right border of the heart. Pick it if the question asked which vein travels with the right marginal artery.
questions.answerText: The great cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The pulmonary trunk divides into which vessels?
options: The right and left pulmonary arteries
The right and left pulmonary veins
The right and left coronary arteries
The right and left brachiocephalic arteries
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle as one short, wide vessel and then splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one to each lung. They are called arteries because they carry blood away from the heart, even though that blood is oxygen-poor. In the lungs the blood picks up oxygen and returns in the pulmonary veins.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary trunk divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs back to the left atrium. They bring blood toward the heart, so pick them for the return trip from the lungs.
The right and left coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta to supply the heart wall. Pick them for the heart's own blood supply.

There is only one brachiocephalic artery, on the right, and it branches from the aortic arch, not the pulmonary trunk. Students may be thinking of the right and left brachiocephalic veins, which join to form the superior vena cava.
questions.answerText: The right and left pulmonary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The aorta, the largest artery in the body, receives blood directly from which chamber?
options: The left atrium
The right atrium
The left ventricle
The right ventricle
questions.why: The aorta begins at the aortic valve, at the outflow of the left ventricle. When the left ventricle contracts, it pushes oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body. That is why the left ventricle has the thickest wall of the four chambers.
notes: The left atrium passes blood into the left ventricle through the mitral valve. It is one step before the aorta, so pick it for the chamber that receives the pulmonary veins.
The right atrium receives blood from the body through the venae cavae. Pick it if the question asked where oxygen-poor blood first enters the heart.
Correct. The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta. Pick it if the question asked which chamber sends blood to the lungs.
questions.answerText: The left ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, yet they are still classified as veins. Why?
options: They have thicker walls than arteries
They carry blood toward the heart
They carry oxygen-poor blood
They carry blood away from the heart
questions.why: Arteries and veins are named for the direction of flow, not for how much oxygen the blood carries. Any vessel that carries blood away from the heart is an artery, and any vessel that carries blood toward the heart is a vein. The pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs back to the left atrium, so they are veins even though that blood is rich in oxygen.
notes: Veins generally have thinner walls than arteries of similar size, because venous blood is under lower pressure. Pick thicker walls for a question about what distinguishes arteries.
Correct. Veins are defined by carrying blood toward the heart.

The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, which is the point of the question. Students who pick this are using the rule of thumb that veins carry oxygen-poor blood, which fails in the pulmonary circuit.
Carrying blood away from the heart is what defines an artery. Pick this for the pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs.
questions.answerText: They carry blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Blood supplying the heart wall flows from the aorta to the coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, and cardiac veins. Which vessel does it enter next, before reaching the right atrium?
options: The superior vena cava
The coronary sinus
The inferior vena cava
The pulmonary veins
questions.why: The coronary circulation runs from the aorta to the coronary arteries, through the capillaries of the myocardium, into the cardiac veins, and then into the coronary sinus. The coronary sinus is a large vein in the groove on the back of the heart that empties into the right atrium. A few small anterior cardiac veins skip the sinus and drain straight into the right atrium.
notes: The superior vena cava returns blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs to the right atrium. It does not collect blood from the heart wall, so pick it for upper body drainage.
Correct. The cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
The inferior vena cava returns blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium. Pick it for drainage from below the diaphragm, not from the heart wall.
The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them for the end of the pulmonary circuit.
questions.answerText: The coronary sinus

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which coronary artery gives rise to the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery?
options: The posterior interventricular artery
The right marginal artery
The right coronary artery
The left coronary artery
questions.why: The left coronary artery leaves the base of the aorta and quickly splits into two main branches. The anterior interventricular artery, often called the LAD, runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles, and the circumflex artery curves around the left side in the coronary sulcus. Together they supply the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, the anterior septum, and the apex.
notes: The posterior interventricular artery runs down the back of the heart between the ventricles and usually comes from the right coronary artery. It is a branch itself, not the source of the circumflex.
The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery running along the right border of the heart. It does not give rise to other main coronary branches.
The right coronary artery gives off the right marginal artery and, in most people, the posterior interventricular artery. Pick it if the question asked which artery gives rise to those branches.
Correct. The left coronary artery branches into the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries.
questions.answerText: The left coronary artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A clot blocks a coronary artery, and the patch of heart muscle beyond the blockage begins to die. What is this event called?
options: A myocardial infarction
Cardiac tamponade
A heart murmur
An aneurysm
questions.why: The coronary arteries are the heart's own supply line, and they are fairly narrow. When one is blocked, the myocardium it feeds is starved of oxygen and its muscle begins to die. Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery is a myocardial infarction, commonly called a heart attack.
notes: Correct. Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery is a myocardial infarction.
Cardiac tamponade is fluid building up in the pericardial cavity and squeezing the heart from outside. Pick it for a heart compressed by fluid, not one starved by a blocked artery.
A heart murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow, often from a valve that does not close cleanly. Pick it for a question about a leaky or narrowed valve.
An aneurysm is a weakened, bulging section of an artery wall. Pick it for a question about a ballooning vessel, not a blocked one.
questions.answerText: A myocardial infarction

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The heart's chambers are always full of blood, yet the heart needs its own coronary arteries. Why can't the heart wall simply take what it needs from the blood in its chambers?
options: The wall is too thick for oxygen to diffuse in from the chambers
Heart muscle uses so little oxygen that a small separate supply is enough
The endocardium is a solid barrier that blocks all contact with the blood
The blood in the chambers has already lost all of its oxygen
questions.why: Oxygen can diffuse only a very short distance through tissue. The myocardium is far too thick for oxygen in the chamber blood to reach its deeper layers, so only the innermost lining can be fed that way. The coronary arteries solve this by branching into capillaries throughout the muscle, which is why a blocked coronary artery starves heart tissue even when the chambers are full.
notes: Correct. The thick myocardium needs vessels that bring blood into its depth.
This is backward. Heart muscle has a very high oxygen demand, which is why its cells are packed with mitochondria and why it is damaged so quickly when its supply is blocked.
The endocardium is a thin, smooth endothelium, and the innermost layer of the wall can in fact receive some oxygen from chamber blood. The barrier is the thickness of the myocardium, not the lining.
Blood in the left atrium and left ventricle is freshly oxygenated from the lungs. The problem is reaching the deep muscle, not a lack of oxygen in the chamber blood.
questions.answerText: The wall is too thick for oxygen to diffuse in from the chambers

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessels return blood from the body to the right atrium?
options: The right and left pulmonary arteries
The superior and inferior venae cavae
The right and left brachiocephalic veins
The four pulmonary veins
questions.why: The superior vena cava returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs, and the inferior vena cava returns it from the trunk and lower limbs. Both empty directly into the right atrium. Together with the coronary sinus, they bring all of the systemic venous return back to the heart.
notes: The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs. Pick them for the branches of the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. The superior and inferior venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
The brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava, so they drain into it rather than into the heart. Pick them for the veins that merge to make the SVC.
The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them for blood coming back from the pulmonary circuit.
questions.answerText: The superior and inferior venae cavae

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium?
options: The inferior vena cava
The middle cardiac vein
The coronary sinus
The great cardiac vein
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a large vein on the posterior surface of the heart, lying in the groove between the atria and ventricles. It collects blood from the cardiac veins that drain the heart wall and empties into the right atrium. The flow of the heart's own supply is aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium.
notes: The inferior vena cava returns blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium. Pick it for systemic venous return from below the diaphragm.
The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery and empties into the coronary sinus. Pick it for the vein in the posterior interventricular groove.
Correct. The coronary sinus collects the cardiac veins and drains into the right atrium.
The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus, not straight into the atrium. Pick it for the vein alongside the LAD.
questions.answerText: The coronary sinus

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessels return blood from the lungs to the left atrium?
options: The four pulmonary veins
The pulmonary trunk
The two pulmonary arteries
The superior and inferior venae cavae
questions.why: Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, carry oxygen-rich blood back to the left atrium. They are one of the few veins in the body that carry oxygen-rich blood. Remember that veins are defined by carrying blood toward the heart, not by how much oxygen the blood holds.
notes: Correct. Four pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and carries blood toward the lungs. Pick it for the large vessel at the start of the pulmonary circuit.
The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs. Pick them for the vessels leaving the pulmonary trunk.
The venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium. Pick them for systemic venous return.
questions.answerText: The four pulmonary veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs?
options: The superior vena cava
The pulmonary veins
The aorta
The pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, passing through the pulmonary valve, and soon divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries that enter the lungs. It carries oxygen-poor blood, even though it is an artery. Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart.
notes: The superior vena cava returns blood from the head, neck, and arms to the right atrium. Pick it for venous return from the upper body.
The pulmonary veins carry blood back from the lungs into the left atrium. Pick them for blood returning to the heart from the lungs.
The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries oxygen-rich blood to the body. Pick it for the start of the systemic circuit.
Correct. The pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood from the left ventricle to the body?
options: The inferior vena cava
The pulmonary veins
The pulmonary trunk
The aorta
questions.why: The aorta, the largest artery in the body, leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve. It arches over the heart and then descends through the thorax and abdomen, giving off branches that carry oxygen-rich blood to every part of the body. Its first branches, the coronary arteries, supply the heart wall itself.
