notes: The inferior vena cava carries blood toward the heart from the trunk and lower limbs. Pick it for venous return entering the right atrium.
The pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them for the vessels that fill the left side of the heart.
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and carries blood to the lungs. Pick it for the start of the pulmonary circuit.
Correct. The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle to the body.
questions.answerText: The aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus all empty into which chamber?
options: The right ventricle
The left ventricle
The left atrium
The right atrium
questions.why: All three vessels carry oxygen-poor blood back to the heart. The venae cavae drain the body, and the coronary sinus drains the heart wall itself. They all empty into the right atrium, the receiving chamber for systemic venous return.
notes: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium, not directly from any vein. Pick it for the chamber feeding the pulmonary trunk.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps into the aorta. Pick it for the systemic pump.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the four pulmonary veins. Pick it for blood returning from the lungs.
Correct. All three empty into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: The right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which chamber receives oxygen-rich blood through four vessels?
options: The left ventricle
The right ventricle
The left atrium
The right atrium
questions.why: Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, deliver oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium. The left atrium then passes this blood through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The number four is a good clue on a lab practical when you are identifying the left atrium from behind.
notes: The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium through the mitral valve, not directly from veins. Pick it for the chamber feeding the aorta.
The right ventricle receives oxygen-poor blood from the right atrium. Pick it for the chamber feeding the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. The four pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium.
The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from three large veins, the two venae cavae and the coronary sinus, plus a few small anterior cardiac veins. Pick it for systemic venous return.
questions.answerText: The left atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which chamber sends blood into the pulmonary trunk?
options: The left ventricle
The right ventricle
The right atrium
The left atrium
questions.why: The right ventricle contracts and pushes oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. The trunk then splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries headed for the lungs. The smooth outflow path leading up to the pulmonary valve is the conus arteriosus.
notes: The left ventricle pumps into the aorta. Pick it for the start of the systemic circuit.
Correct. The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk.
The right atrium sends blood down into the right ventricle, not into an artery. Pick it for the chamber receiving the venae cavae.
The left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins. Pick it for the end of the pulmonary circuit.
questions.answerText: The right ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which chamber sends blood into the aorta?
options: The left atrium
The left ventricle
The right atrium
The right ventricle
questions.why: The left ventricle contracts with force and pushes oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. The smooth outflow path leading to the aortic valve is the aortic vestibule. From the aorta, blood reaches every tissue of the body.
notes: The left atrium sends blood down through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. Pick it for the chamber receiving the pulmonary veins.
Correct. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta.
The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body. Pick it for the chamber where the venae cavae empty.
The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk. Pick it for the start of the pulmonary circuit.
questions.answerText: The left ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student writes: pulmonary veins carry blood away from the heart. Which statement corrects this?
options: Pulmonary veins carry blood toward the heart, into the right atrium
Pulmonary veins carry blood toward the heart, into the left atrium
Pulmonary veins carry blood away from the heart, out of the left ventricle
Pulmonary veins carry blood away from the heart, out of the right ventricle
questions.why: By definition, veins carry blood toward the heart and arteries carry it away. The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium. The vessel carrying blood away from the heart to the lungs is the pulmonary trunk and its pulmonary arteries.
notes: The direction is right, but the right atrium receives the venae cavae and coronary sinus, not the pulmonary veins. Pick the right atrium for systemic venous return.
Correct. Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs into the left atrium.
Blood leaving the left ventricle travels in the aorta. Pick the aorta for the vessel carrying blood away to the body.
Blood leaving the right ventricle travels in the pulmonary trunk, an artery. This choice repeats the student's error of calling an outgoing vessel a vein.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary veins carry blood toward the heart, into the left atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student writes: the pulmonary trunk leaves the left ventricle. Which statement corrects this?
options: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle
The pulmonary trunk enters the left atrium
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right atrium
The pulmonary trunk leaves the left atrium
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, so it must leave the chamber that holds oxygen-poor blood ready to be pumped. That chamber is the right ventricle. The left ventricle is connected to the aorta instead.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle.
The vessels entering the left atrium are the pulmonary veins. The pulmonary trunk carries blood away from the heart, not into it.
The right atrium is a receiving chamber that sends blood to the right ventricle. No artery leaves an atrium.
The left atrium receives the pulmonary veins and has no outgoing artery. Pick it for where blood from the lungs arrives.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student writes: the aorta leaves the right ventricle. Which statement corrects this?
options: The aorta leaves the right atrium
The aorta enters the right atrium
The aorta leaves the left atrium
The aorta leaves the left ventricle
questions.why: The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood to the body, so it leaves the chamber that holds oxygen-rich blood ready to be pumped, the left ventricle. Blood passes through the aortic valve to enter it. The right ventricle is connected to the pulmonary trunk instead.
notes: The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and sends it to the right ventricle. No artery leaves it.
The vessels entering the right atrium are the venae cavae and the coronary sinus. The aorta carries blood away from the heart, not into it.
The left atrium sends blood down into the left ventricle and has no outgoing artery. Pick it for the chamber receiving the pulmonary veins.
Correct. The aorta leaves the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: The aorta leaves the left ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A clot blocks blood returning from the lower body to the heart. Which vessel is blocked, and which chamber receives less blood?
options: The pulmonary veins and the left atrium
The superior vena cava and the right atrium
The inferior vena cava and the right atrium
The inferior vena cava and the left atrium
questions.why: The inferior vena cava carries oxygen-poor blood from the trunk and lower limbs up to the heart. It empties into the right atrium, so a clot in it reduces the blood reaching that chamber. Both venae cavae drain into the right atrium; only the location of the clot tells you which one.
notes: The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them for a blockage in the return from the lungs.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs. Pick it for a clot blocking return from the upper body.
Correct. Blood from the lower body returns through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium.
The vessel is right, but the inferior vena cava empties into the right atrium, not the left. Pick the left atrium only for vessels coming from the lungs.
questions.answerText: The inferior vena cava and the right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A clot blocks blood returning from the head, neck, and arms. Which vessel is most likely involved?
options: The superior vena cava
The inferior vena cava
The pulmonary veins
The coronary sinus
questions.why: The superior vena cava collects oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs and empties it into the top of the right atrium. It forms where the right and left brachiocephalic veins join. A clot there backs up blood in the upper body.
notes: Correct. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and arms.
The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs. Pick it for blocked return from below the diaphragm.
The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick them for blocked return from the lungs.
The coronary sinus drains the heart wall into the right atrium. Pick it for venous return from the myocardium.
questions.answerText: The superior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student says the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-poor blood to the heart. Which correction is accurate?
options: They carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium
They carry oxygen-poor blood from the lungs to the right atrium
They carry oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the lungs
They carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
questions.why: The pulmonary veins drain the lungs, where blood has just picked up oxygen, so they carry oxygen-rich blood. They empty into the left atrium. They are still veins because a vein is defined by direction, carrying blood toward the heart, not by how much oxygen the blood holds.
notes: Correct. Pulmonary veins bring freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
This keeps the student's error and adds another one. Blood leaving the lungs has just been oxygenated, and the right atrium receives the venae cavae and coronary sinus, not the pulmonary veins.
Blood moving from the heart to the lungs travels in arteries, not veins. This describes no real vessel; the left ventricle actually sends its blood to the body through the aorta.

This describes the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is the right statement for those vessels, which count as arteries because they carry blood away from the heart.
questions.answerText: They carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student says arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood. Which vessels prove this statement wrong?
options: Coronary arteries
Pulmonary arteries
Aorta
Pulmonary veins
questions.why: An artery is any vessel that carries blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary arteries, branches of the pulmonary trunk, carry oxygen-poor blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs. They are true arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood, so the student's rule does not hold.
notes: The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta and carry oxygen-rich blood to the myocardium. They follow the usual pattern and would be the answer for the blood supply of the heart wall.
Correct. The pulmonary arteries are arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.

The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood away from the left ventricle, so it fits the student's rule rather than breaking it. It would be the answer for the largest artery or the start of the systemic circuit.
The pulmonary veins are the exception to a different rule. They carry oxygen-rich blood toward the heart, so they disprove the claim that veins always carry oxygen-poor blood.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student says veins always carry oxygen-poor blood. Which vessels prove this statement wrong?
options: Venae cavae
Pulmonary arteries
Pulmonary veins
Cardiac veins
questions.why: A vein is any vessel that carries blood toward the heart. The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs, where it has just picked up oxygen, back to the left atrium, so they are veins that carry oxygen-rich blood. Direction, not oxygen content, decides whether a vessel is an artery or a vein.
notes: The superior and inferior venae cavae carry oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium. They follow the student's rule and would be the answer for where systemic blood returns to the heart.
The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart. They break the opposite rule, that arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, but they are not veins.
Correct. The pulmonary veins are veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.
The cardiac veins drain oxygen-poor blood from the myocardium into the coronary sinus. They fit the usual pattern and would be the answer for the venous drainage of the heart wall.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What are the great vessels of the heart?
options: The coronary arteries running in the grooves on the heart surface
The small vessels branching through the lung tissue
The largest arteries and veins of the lower limbs
The large arteries and veins attached to the base of the heart
questions.why: The great vessels are the large arteries and veins that enter and leave the heart at its base, the broad superior surface. They are the superior and inferior venae cavae, the pulmonary trunk, the pulmonary veins, and the aorta. Together they carry all the blood moving into and out of the heart's chambers.
notes: The coronary arteries run in the grooves (sulci) on the heart's surface and supply the heart wall itself. They are small and would be the answer for coronary circulation, not the great vessels.

Vessels branching through the lung tissue are branches of the pulmonary arteries and veins plus the small bronchial vessels. They would be the answer for the blood supply within the lungs, not the vessels attached to the heart.
The large vessels of the lower limbs, such as the femoral artery and great saphenous vein, are far from the heart. They are part of the systemic circuit but are not attached to the heart.
Correct. The great vessels are the large vessels attached at the base of the heart.
questions.answerText: The large arteries and veins attached to the base of the heart

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The superior vena cava returns blood from which regions?
options: The lungs
Head, neck, and upper limbs
Lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis
The heart wall
questions.why: The superior vena cava is the large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the regions above the heart, the head, neck, and upper limbs, into the right atrium. Its partner, the inferior vena cava, returns blood from the regions below. Both empty into the right atrium.
notes: Blood from the lungs returns through the four pulmonary veins to the left atrium. This would be the answer for the pulmonary veins.
Correct. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs.
The lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis drain into the inferior vena cava. Choose this for the other vena cava, which enters the right atrium from below.
Blood from the heart wall drains through the cardiac veins into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium. Choose the heart wall for the coronary sinus.
questions.answerText: Head, neck, and upper limbs

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The inferior vena cava returns blood from which regions?
options: Head, neck, and upper limbs
The lungs
The heart wall
Lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis
questions.why: The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the regions below the diaphragm, including the lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis. It runs up along the posterior abdominal wall, passes through the diaphragm, and empties into the right atrium.
notes: The head, neck, and upper limbs drain into the superior vena cava. Choose this for the vena cava that enters the right atrium from above.
Blood from the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It never enters a vena cava.
The heart wall drains through the cardiac veins into the coronary sinus. Pick the heart wall for a question about the coronary sinus.
Correct. The inferior vena cava drains the regions below the diaphragm.
questions.answerText: Lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The superior vena cava empties into which chamber?
options: Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
questions.why: The superior vena cava carries oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs and opens into the upper part of the right atrium. The right atrium is the receiving chamber for all blood returning from the systemic circuit, so both venae cavae end there.
notes: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve. No vein empties directly into a ventricle; ventricles pump blood out into arteries.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta. It would be the answer for the chamber that starts the systemic circuit.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the pulmonary veins, not the venae cavae. Choose it for where blood returning from the lungs enters.
Correct. The superior vena cava opens into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: Right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The superior vena cava, the inferior vena cava, and the coronary sinus all empty into which chamber?
options: Right ventricle
Right atrium
Left atrium
Left ventricle
questions.why: All three of these veins carry oxygen-poor blood back to the heart, and all three empty into the right atrium. The superior vena cava drains the upper body, the inferior vena cava drains the lower body, and the coronary sinus drains the heart wall. The right atrium is the collecting chamber for the systemic circuit.
notes: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium, not directly from any vein. It is the answer for the chamber that pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. All three return oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium.
The left atrium receives only the four pulmonary veins, which bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. Choose it for where pulmonary blood returns.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and sends it into the aorta. No vein drains directly into it.
questions.answerText: Right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which great vessel carries blood away from the right ventricle?
options: Superior vena cava
Pulmonary trunk
Aorta
Pulmonary veins
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk is the large artery that leaves the right ventricle, beyond the pulmonary valve. It carries oxygen-poor blood upward and then splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which lead to the lungs. It is the first vessel of the pulmonary circuit.
notes: The superior vena cava brings blood into the right atrium from the upper body. It carries blood toward the heart, so it cannot carry blood away from a ventricle.
Correct. The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle.
The aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle, not the right. It is the left-side counterpart and would be the answer for the vessel leaving the left ventricle.
The pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium. They are the answer for the vessels returning blood at the end of the pulmonary circuit.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: How many pulmonary veins usually empty into the left atrium, and what kind of blood do they carry?
options: Four, carrying oxygen-poor blood
Four, carrying oxygen-rich blood
Two, carrying oxygen-poor blood
Two, carrying oxygen-rich blood
questions.why: Usually four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, empty into the left atrium. They carry oxygen-rich blood, because the blood has just picked up oxygen in the lungs. These veins complete the pulmonary circuit and deliver blood to the left side of the heart for pumping to the body.
notes: The count is right, but the blood is not. Blood in the pulmonary veins has just left the lungs and is oxygen-rich; oxygen-poor blood enters the lungs through the pulmonary arteries.
Correct. Four pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium.
Both parts are off. Each lung usually sends two pulmonary veins, four in all, and blood leaving the lungs is oxygen-rich. Oxygen-poor blood travels to the lungs in the pulmonary arteries.
The oxygen content is right, but the count is not. Each lung usually sends two pulmonary veins, so the left atrium receives four; students often guess two by picturing one vein per lung.
questions.answerText: Four, carrying oxygen-rich blood

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What is the largest artery in the body?
options: Aorta
Femoral artery
Common carotid artery
Pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It leaves the left ventricle, arches over the heart, and descends through the thorax and abdomen, giving off branches that supply every region of the body. It is an elastic artery, so it stretches with each heartbeat and recoils between beats to keep blood moving.
notes: Correct. The aorta is the largest artery in the body.
The femoral artery is the main artery of the thigh, a muscular artery well downstream of the aorta. It would be the answer for the large artery of the anterior thigh.
The common carotid arteries carry blood up the neck to the head. Choose them for the main arteries of the neck, not the largest artery.
The pulmonary trunk is a large elastic artery leaving the right ventricle, but it is short and smaller than the aorta. It would be the answer for the artery that carries blood toward the lungs.
questions.answerText: Aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the blood the aorta carries?
options: Oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
Oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium
Oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body
Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium
questions.why: The aorta receives oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle through the aortic valve. Its branches then carry that blood to every region of the body, which makes the aorta the main trunk of the systemic circuit.
notes: This describes the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Choose this statement for the vessel leaving the right ventricle.
This describes the superior and inferior venae cavae, which return oxygen-poor blood from the body. It fits the veins that enter the right atrium.
Correct. The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body.
This describes the pulmonary veins, which bring oxygen-rich blood back from the lungs. It would be correct for the vessels entering the left atrium.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What is coronary circulation?
options: The flow of blood between the heart and the lungs
The flow of blood from the heart to the head and neck
The blood supply and drainage of the heart wall itself
The flow of blood through the four chambers of the heart
questions.why: Coronary circulation is the heart's own blood supply. The blood passing through the chambers does not nourish the thick myocardium, so the heart wall gets its oxygen from the coronary arteries, which leave the base of the aorta. Cardiac veins then drain the wall into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
notes: Blood flowing between the heart and the lungs is the pulmonary circuit. Choose it for the loop that oxygenates blood.
Blood flowing to the head and neck travels in branches of the aortic arch, such as the common carotid arteries. That is part of the systemic circuit, not the heart's own supply.
Correct. Coronary circulation supplies and drains the heart wall.
The path through the four chambers is the pathway of blood through the heart. This blood passes through the heart but does not supply its wall, which is why the coronary vessels are needed.
questions.answerText: The blood supply and drainage of the heart wall itself

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Where do the coronary arteries originate?
options: From the aortic arch
At the base of the aorta
From the pulmonary trunk
From the coronary sinus
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta. They arise from its base, just above the aortic valve, and then run in the grooves on the heart's surface to supply the myocardium. Branching this early means the heart wall receives oxygen-rich blood straight from the left ventricle.
notes: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery. Choose the arch for the arteries to the head and upper limbs; the coronary arteries arise earlier, at the base of the ascending aorta.
Correct. The coronary arteries leave the base of the aorta, just above the aortic valve.
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, so it would be a poor source for the heart wall. No coronary artery branches from it.
The coronary sinus is a vein that collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties into the right atrium. It is the drain of the coronary circulation, not its source.
questions.answerText: At the base of the aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What tissue do the coronary arteries supply?
options: The organs of the abdomen
The tissues of the head and neck
The alveolar walls of the lungs
The myocardium of the heart wall
questions.why: The coronary arteries supply the heart wall, above all the myocardium, the thick layer of cardiac muscle that does the pumping. The myocardium works nonstop and needs a steady supply of oxygen, but it cannot draw enough from the blood passing through the chambers, so it relies on its own arteries.
notes: The abdominal organs are supplied by branches of the abdominal aorta, such as the celiac trunk and mesenteric arteries. That would be the answer for the digestive tract's blood supply.
The head and neck are supplied by the common carotid and vertebral arteries, branches of the aortic arch and subclavian arteries. Choose them for the arteries of the neck.
The lungs receive blood from the pulmonary arteries, which bring oxygen-poor blood for gas exchange, and from small bronchial arteries. The coronary arteries do not reach the lungs.
Correct. The coronary arteries feed the myocardium.
questions.answerText: The myocardium of the heart wall

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel collects blood from most of the cardiac veins?
options: Great cardiac vein
Coronary sinus
Superior vena cava
Inferior vena cava
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a large vein on the posterior surface of the heart, lying in the groove between the atria and ventricles. The great, middle, and small cardiac veins all drain into it, and it empties into the right atrium. A few small anterior cardiac veins bypass it and drain straight into the right atrium, which is why it collects most, not all, of the heart's venous blood.
notes: The great cardiac vein is one of the veins that drains into the coronary sinus. It runs with the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) and would be the answer for the vein in the anterior interventricular groove.
Correct. The coronary sinus collects the cardiac veins.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs into the right atrium. It does not receive the cardiac veins.
The inferior vena cava drains the lower limbs, abdomen, and pelvis into the right atrium. The cardiac veins do not join it.
questions.answerText: Coronary sinus

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The coronary sinus empties into which chamber?
options: Right atrium
Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Left atrium
questions.why: The coronary sinus carries oxygen-poor blood drained from the heart wall, so it returns that blood to the same chamber that receives the venae cavae, the right atrium. From there the blood joins the rest of the systemic return and heads to the lungs.
notes: Correct. The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium.
The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, not directly from the coronary sinus. It is the answer for the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the aorta. No vein empties into it.
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the pulmonary veins. Oxygen-poor blood from the heart wall does not go there; choose it for where pulmonary blood returns.
questions.answerText: Right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What are the two main coronary arteries?
options: Anterior and posterior interventricular arteries
Right and left marginal arteries
Right and left coronary arteries
Right and left pulmonary arteries
questions.why: The two main coronary arteries are the right coronary artery (RCA) and the left coronary artery (LCA). Both leave the base of the aorta and run in the grooves on the heart's surface. Each then gives off smaller named branches that spread over the myocardium.
notes: The anterior and posterior interventricular arteries are branches, not the main coronary arteries. The anterior one (LAD) comes from the left coronary artery and the posterior one (PDA) usually comes from the right.

The right and left marginal arteries are smaller branches running along the heart's borders. The right marginal comes from the right coronary artery and the left marginal from the left coronary artery.
Correct. The RCA and LCA are the two main coronary arteries.
The right and left pulmonary arteries are branches of the pulmonary trunk that carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Choose them for the pulmonary circuit, not the heart's own supply.
questions.answerText: Right and left coronary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which two arteries are the main branches of the right coronary artery?
options: Anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries
Right marginal and circumflex arteries
Right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries
Anterior and posterior interventricular arteries
questions.why: The right coronary artery runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle. It gives off the right marginal artery along the right border of the heart and, in most people, continues around to the back of the heart as the posterior interventricular artery, also called the posterior descending artery (PDA).
notes: The anterior interventricular artery (LAD) and the circumflex artery are the main branches of the left coronary artery. Choose this pair for the left side.
The right marginal artery is a right coronary branch, but the circumflex artery belongs to the left coronary artery. This pair mixes one branch from each side.
Correct. The right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries branch from the RCA.

These two arteries run in the anterior and posterior interventricular grooves, but they come from different main arteries. The anterior one comes from the left coronary artery, so only the posterior one is a right coronary branch.
questions.answerText: Right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What is another name for the posterior interventricular artery?
options: Posterior descending artery
Right marginal artery
Circumflex artery
Left anterior descending artery
questions.why: The posterior interventricular artery is also called the posterior descending artery, or PDA, because it descends along the posterior interventricular groove toward the apex. In most people it is a branch of the right coronary artery, and it supplies the posterior part of the interventricular septum.
notes: Correct. The posterior interventricular artery is the posterior descending artery (PDA).
The right marginal artery is the other main branch of the right coronary artery, running along the heart's right border. It is a separate vessel, not another name for the PDA.

The circumflex artery is a branch of the left coronary artery that wraps around the left side of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and ventricle. It is a separate vessel with its own course.

The left anterior descending artery (LAD) is the other name for the anterior interventricular artery, the left coronary branch on the front of the heart. It is the PDA's counterpart on the anterior surface.
questions.answerText: Posterior descending artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which arteries are main branches of the left coronary artery?
options: Anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries
Posterior interventricular and circumflex arteries
Anterior interventricular and right marginal arteries
Right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries
questions.why: The left coronary artery is short. Soon after leaving the aorta it divides into the anterior interventricular artery, better known as the LAD, which runs down the front of the heart between the ventricles, and the circumflex artery, which curves around the left side in the groove between the left atrium and ventricle. These branches supply most of the left side of the heart.
notes: Correct. The LAD and the circumflex artery branch from the left coronary artery.
The circumflex is a left coronary branch, but the posterior interventricular artery usually comes from the right coronary artery. This pair mixes one branch from each side.
The anterior interventricular artery belongs to the left coronary artery, but the right marginal artery belongs to the right. This pair mixes the two sides.
The right marginal and posterior interventricular arteries are the main branches of the right coronary artery. Choose this pair for the right side.
questions.answerText: Anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The LAD, or left anterior descending artery, is also called which artery?
options: Circumflex artery
Right marginal artery
Posterior interventricular artery
Anterior interventricular artery
questions.why: LAD stands for left anterior descending artery, the clinical name for the anterior interventricular artery. It is a branch of the left coronary artery that descends toward the apex along the anterior interventricular groove, the groove on the front of the heart that marks the septum between the ventricles. The great cardiac vein runs beside it.
notes: The circumflex artery is the other main branch of the left coronary artery, curving around the left side of the heart. It does not descend along the front of the septum.
The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery running along the right border of the heart. It would be the answer for the artery that the small cardiac vein accompanies.

The posterior interventricular artery is the PDA, the posterior descending artery, which usually branches from the right coronary artery. It runs on the back of the heart and is the LAD's posterior counterpart.
Correct. The LAD is the anterior interventricular artery.
questions.answerText: Anterior interventricular artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which coronary artery usually supplies the SA and AV nodes?
options: Right coronary artery
Left coronary artery
Left marginal artery
Anterior interventricular artery
questions.why: In most people the right coronary artery supplies both the SA node, the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium, and the AV node, in the floor of the right atrium. This fits its location, since the RCA runs along the right side of the heart. It is also why a blockage of the RCA can cause rhythm problems as well as muscle damage.
notes: Correct. The RCA usually supplies both nodes.

The left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, left ventricle, anterior septum, and apex. In a minority of people one of its branches supplies the SA node, but the usual source of both nodes is the right coronary artery.
The left marginal artery runs along the left border of the heart and supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle. It is far from the right atrium, where both nodes sit.

The anterior interventricular artery (LAD) runs down the front of the septum and supplies the anterior septum, much of the left ventricle, and the apex. Choose it for a question about the artery to the front of the left ventricle.
questions.answerText: Right coronary artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: In the usual pattern, which artery supplies the apex of the heart?
options: Left subclavian artery
Pulmonary trunk
Left coronary artery
Right coronary artery
questions.why: In the usual pattern, the left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, the left ventricle, the anterior part of the interventricular septum, and the apex. Its anterior interventricular branch, the LAD, runs down the front of the heart toward the apex. The apex is the tip of the left ventricle, so it makes sense that the left coronary artery serves it.
notes: The left subclavian artery is the third branch of the aortic arch and supplies the left upper limb. Choose it for the artery heading toward the left arm.
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It does not supply the heart wall, and it would be the answer for the vessel leaving the right ventricle.
Correct. The left coronary artery, through the LAD, supplies the apex.

The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, the posterior septum, and usually the SA and AV nodes. Choose it for a question about the conduction nodes or the right ventricle.
questions.answerText: Left coronary artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the LAD (anterior interventricular artery)?
options: Middle cardiac vein
Small cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
Great cardiac vein
questions.why: The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular groove beside the LAD, draining the front of the heart. It then curves around to the posterior surface and empties into the coronary sinus. Cardiac veins travel in the same grooves as the coronary arteries, so learning the arteries gives you the veins.
notes: The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery (PDA) on the back of the heart. Choose it for the vein in the posterior interventricular groove.
The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the right border of the heart. It would be the answer for the vein beside that right coronary branch.

The anterior cardiac veins drain the front of the right ventricle straight into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. Pick them for the veins that skip the coronary sinus, not for the vein paired with the LAD.
Correct. The great cardiac vein accompanies the LAD.
questions.answerText: Great cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the posterior interventricular artery (PDA)?
options: Middle cardiac vein
Great cardiac vein
Coronary sinus
Small cardiac vein
questions.why: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove beside the PDA, draining the back of both ventricles. It empties into the coronary sinus near where the sinus opens into the right atrium. Its name fits its position, in the middle of the posterior surface between the two ventricles.
notes: Correct. The middle cardiac vein accompanies the PDA.
The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) on the front of the heart. It is the anterior counterpart of the middle cardiac vein.
The coronary sinus is the large collecting vein in the posterior groove between the atria and ventricles. It receives the middle cardiac vein but does not run beside the PDA itself.
The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the right border of the heart. Choose it for the vein beside that branch.
questions.answerText: Middle cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the right marginal artery?
options: Great cardiac vein
Small cardiac vein
Middle cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
questions.why: The small cardiac vein runs along the right border of the heart with the right marginal artery, draining that part of the right side of the heart. It ends by joining the coronary sinus. Like the other named cardiac veins, it shares a groove with a coronary artery branch.
notes: The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) on the front of the heart. It would be the answer for the vein paired with the LAD.
Correct. The small cardiac vein accompanies the right marginal artery.
The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery (PDA) in the posterior interventricular groove. Choose it for the vein on the back of the heart between the ventricles.
The anterior cardiac veins drain the front of the right ventricle directly into the right atrium, skipping the coronary sinus. They are not the vein paired with the right marginal artery.
questions.answerText: Small cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What is a myocardial infarction?
options: Inflammation of the serous pericardium
Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery
A leaky valve that lets blood flow backward
Fluid squeezing the heart within the pericardial cavity
questions.why: Myocardial infarction is the medical name for a heart attack. Myo means muscle, cardial means heart, and an infarction is an area of tissue that dies because its blood supply is cut off. When a coronary artery is blocked, the myocardium beyond the blockage is starved of oxygen and its muscle begins to die.
notes: Inflammation of the pericardium is pericarditis. Choose that for a problem with the sac around the heart, not death of the heart muscle.
Correct. A myocardial infarction is death of heart muscle after its coronary supply is blocked.
A valve that does not close cleanly lets blood leak backward, which can be heard as a murmur. That is a valve problem and would be the answer for what produces a heart murmur.
Fluid building up in the pericardial cavity and squeezing the heart is cardiac tamponade. It limits how much the heart can fill, but it is not caused by a blocked coronary artery.
questions.answerText: Death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces blood through the coronary circulation?
options: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, left atrium
Pulmonary trunk, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium
Aorta, cardiac veins, myocardial capillaries, coronary arteries, coronary sinus, right atrium
Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium
questions.why: Coronary blood starts in the aorta, where the coronary arteries branch off its base. The arteries feed the capillaries of the myocardium, where oxygen and nutrients pass to the muscle. The blood then drains into the cardiac veins, which empty into the coronary sinus, and the coronary sinus returns it to the right atrium.
notes: Every step is right except the last. The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium; the left atrium receives only the pulmonary veins from the lungs.
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and gives off no coronary branches. The coronary arteries arise from the base of the aorta, so the trace must start there.
This puts the veins before the arteries. Blood always flows from arteries into capillaries and then into veins, so the cardiac veins come after the capillaries.
Correct. Aorta, coronary arteries, capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium.
questions.answerText: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why does the heart need its own coronary circulation?
options: The coronary vessels carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs
All four heart chambers hold only oxygen-poor blood
The deep myocardium cannot get enough oxygen from chamber blood
The coronary vessels pump blood to assist the ventricles
questions.why: The myocardium is thick and works without rest, so it needs a large, steady supply of oxygen and nutrients. The blood rushing through the chambers can reach only the innermost cells of the wall, so the rest of the muscle depends on the coronary arteries. These arteries bring oxygen-rich blood into the wall itself and spread it through capillaries in the muscle.
notes: Carrying oxygen-poor blood to the lungs is the job of the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries. Choose that for the pulmonary circuit, not for the heart's own supply.

Only the right chambers hold oxygen-poor blood; the left atrium and left ventricle are full of oxygen-rich blood. The real issue is reaching the deep muscle of the wall, not the oxygen content of the chamber blood.
Correct. The deep myocardium depends on the coronary arteries for its oxygen.
Vessels do not pump blood; only the heart's chambers do. This choice confuses the coronary arteries, which supply the wall, with the ventricles, which do the pumping.
questions.answerText: The deep myocardium cannot get enough oxygen from chamber blood

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why can a blocked coronary artery cause a heart attack?
options: The blocked artery stops blood from leaving the left ventricle
The myocardium beyond the blockage loses oxygen and begins to die
The blockage also closes the coronary sinus so the wall cannot drain
The blockage reverses blood flow through the aortic valve
questions.why: Each coronary artery is the supply line for its own patch of myocardium. If it is blocked, the muscle downstream receives no oxygen-rich blood, and before long those cells begin to die. That area of dead muscle is a myocardial infarction, or heart attack, and it weakens the heart's ability to pump.
notes: The coronary arteries supply the heart wall; they are not the path blood takes out of the left ventricle. Blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve into the aorta, which stays open in a heart attack.
Correct. Muscle beyond the blockage is starved of oxygen and dies.
The coronary sinus is the vein that drains the heart wall, and an arterial blockage does not close it. A problem with the coronary sinus would affect drainage, not the oxygen supply.
The aortic valve keeps blood from falling back from the aorta into the left ventricle, and a coronary blockage does not reverse it. A leaking valve would produce a murmur, not death of heart muscle.
questions.answerText: The myocardium beyond the blockage loses oxygen and begins to die

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the pulmonary veins with the venae cavae?
options: Pulmonary veins bring oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium; venae cavae bring oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium
Pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium; venae cavae bring oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium
Both bring oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium of the heart
Pulmonary veins carry blood away from the heart; venae cavae carry blood toward it
questions.why: Both sets of vessels are veins, because both carry blood toward the heart, but they serve different circuits. The pulmonary veins end the pulmonary circuit, bringing oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium. The superior and inferior venae cavae end the systemic circuit, bringing oxygen-poor blood from the body into the right atrium.
notes: This swaps every detail between the two. Blood from the lungs is oxygen-rich and enters the left side, while blood from the body is oxygen-poor and enters the right side.
Correct. The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium and the venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium.
Only the venae cavae carry oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, which is the main thing that sets them apart.
All veins carry blood toward the heart, including the pulmonary veins. Carrying blood away from the heart would make a vessel an artery, as with the pulmonary trunk.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium; venae cavae bring oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the pulmonary trunk with the aorta?
options: Both leave the left ventricle, one heading to the lungs and one to the body
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle; the aorta leaves the left ventricle
The pulmonary trunk leaves the left ventricle; the aorta leaves the right ventricle
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-rich blood; the aorta carries oxygen-poor blood
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk and the aorta are the two great arteries leaving the heart, and each comes from a different ventricle. The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs, and the aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body. Having one outflow vessel per ventricle is what keeps the two circuits separate.
notes: Each ventricle has its own outflow vessel, and the left ventricle opens only into the aorta. The pulmonary trunk comes from the right ventricle, which is why the two sides of the heart can serve two separate circuits.
Correct. The right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle opens into the aorta.
This reverses the sides. The right ventricle drives the pulmonary circuit to the lungs, and the left ventricle drives the systemic circuit to the body.
This reverses the oxygen content. The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to be oxygenated in the lungs, and the aorta carries oxygen-rich blood out to the body.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle; the aorta leaves the left ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why are the pulmonary arteries unusual among arteries?
options: They carry blood toward the heart instead of away from it
They branch directly from the left ventricle
They have no tunica media in their walls
They carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart
questions.why: Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. They are still arteries because an artery is defined by direction: it carries blood away from the heart. In the lungs this blood picks up oxygen before returning in the pulmonary veins.
notes: Carrying blood toward the heart would make them veins. The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart, like every artery; what is unusual is the oxygen content of that blood.
The pulmonary arteries branch from the pulmonary trunk, which leaves the right ventricle. The left ventricle's only outflow vessel is the aorta.
The pulmonary arteries have all three tunics, including a tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. A wall made of only the tunica intima belongs to a capillary.
Correct. They are arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.
questions.answerText: They carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why are the pulmonary veins unusual among veins?
options: They carry oxygen-rich blood toward the heart
They empty into the right atrium
They have thicker walls than the aorta
They carry blood away from the heart
questions.why: Most veins carry oxygen-poor blood back from the tissues, but the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They are still veins because they carry blood toward the heart. Their blood has just been oxygenated in the lung capillaries.
notes: Correct. They are veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.
The pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium. The right atrium receives the venae cavae and the coronary sinus, which carry oxygen-poor blood.
Veins, including the pulmonary veins, have thinner walls than arteries, and the aorta has one of the thickest walls of any vessel. This choice reverses the usual artery and vein wall pattern.
No vein carries blood away from the heart; that would make it an artery. The pulmonary veins carry blood toward the heart, like all veins.
questions.answerText: They carry oxygen-rich blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the regions supplied by the right and left coronary arteries?
options: The right supplies the anterior septum; the left supplies the posterior septum
The right supplies the left ventricle and the apex; the left supplies the right ventricle and the two nodes
Both supply only the atria, since the ventricles are fed by the blood in their chambers
The right feeds most of the right ventricle and usually the nodes; the left, most of the left ventricle and apex
questions.why: In the usual pattern, the right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior septum, and usually the SA and AV nodes. The left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, the anterior septum, and the apex. Each artery mainly feeds the side of the heart it travels along.
notes: This reverses the septum. The LAD, a left coronary branch, supplies the anterior septum, and the PDA, usually a right coronary branch, supplies the posterior septum.
This swaps the two sides. The left coronary artery is the one that reaches the apex and most of the left ventricle, while the right coronary artery usually feeds the nodes in the right atrium.

Both coronary arteries supply the ventricles as well as the atria, and the thick ventricular walls need them most. The blood passing through the chambers does not nourish the deep myocardium, which is why coronary arteries exist.
Correct. Each coronary artery mainly supplies its own side of the heart.
questions.answerText: The right feeds most of the right ventricle and usually the nodes; the left, most of the left ventricle and apex

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why is the LAD (anterior interventricular artery) considered so clinically important?
options: It is the only artery that supplies the right atrium
It carries blood out of the right ventricle to the lungs
It feeds the anterior septum, much of the left ventricle, and the apex
It drains blood from the heart wall into the coronary sinus
questions.why: The LAD runs down the front of the heart in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior part of the interventricular septum, much of the front wall of the left ventricle, and the apex. The left ventricle pumps blood to the entire body, so losing the LAD's territory takes out a large share of the heart's pumping muscle.
notes: The right atrium is supplied mainly by the right coronary artery, which runs along the right side of the heart. Choose the RCA for the right atrium and the nodes within it.
Carrying blood from the right ventricle to the lungs is the job of the pulmonary trunk. The LAD is a small artery on the heart surface, not a great vessel.
Correct. The LAD feeds a large part of the left ventricle, the anterior septum, and the apex.
Draining the heart wall into the coronary sinus is the job of the cardiac veins. The great cardiac vein runs beside the LAD, so it would be the answer for the vein that drains the LAD's territory.
questions.answerText: It feeds the anterior septum, much of the left ventricle, and the apex

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Most cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus. Which veins bypass it and drain straight into the right atrium?
options: Small cardiac vein
Great cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
Middle cardiac vein
questions.why: The anterior cardiac veins are small veins on the front of the right ventricle. Instead of joining the coronary sinus, they open directly into the right atrium. All the other named cardiac veins empty into the coronary sinus first, and the coronary sinus then empties into the right atrium.
notes: The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery and empties into the coronary sinus. It would be the answer for the vein along the heart's right border.

The great cardiac vein runs with the LAD on the front of the heart and then curves around to empty into the coronary sinus. It is the answer for the vein paired with the anterior interventricular artery.
Correct. The anterior cardiac veins skip the coronary sinus and open into the right atrium.
The middle cardiac vein runs with the PDA on the back of the heart and empties into the coronary sinus. Choose it for the vein in the posterior interventricular groove.
questions.answerText: Anterior cardiac veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The coronary arteries are small. Why is a problem in them so serious?
options: They supply the myocardium that pumps blood for the entire body
They are the main vessels returning blood to the right atrium
They form the valves that keep blood flowing forward
They carry all of the blood leaving the left ventricle
questions.why: The coronary arteries carry only a small share of the blood the heart pumps, but that blood feeds the myocardium, the muscle that drives both circulations. If they fail, the heart muscle weakens or dies, and every organ loses its blood supply as the pump fails. Their importance comes from what they feed, not from their size.
notes: Correct. They feed the muscle that powers the whole circulation.
Returning blood to the right atrium is the job of the venae cavae and the coronary sinus. The coronary arteries deliver blood to the heart wall rather than draining it.
The valves are flaps of endocardium over a connective tissue core, not arteries. Choose the valves for a question about one-way flow through the heart.
Nearly all the blood leaving the left ventricle enters the aorta and travels to the body. Only a small fraction enters the coronary arteries at the aortic base.
questions.answerText: They supply the myocardium that pumps blood for the entire body

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement correctly pairs the cardiac veins with the arteries they run beside?
options: Great with the LAD, middle with the PDA, small with the right marginal artery
Great with the PDA, middle with the LAD, small with the right marginal artery
Great with the LAD, middle with the right marginal artery, small with the PDA
Great with the right marginal artery, middle with the PDA, small with the LAD
questions.why: Each named cardiac vein travels in the same groove as a coronary artery. The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) on the front, the middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery (PDA) on the back, and the small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the right border. All three end in the coronary sinus.
notes: Correct. Great with the LAD, middle with the PDA, small with the right marginal artery.
This swaps the great and middle cardiac veins. The great cardiac vein is on the front of the heart with the LAD, and the middle cardiac vein is on the back with the PDA.
The great cardiac vein is paired correctly here, but the middle and small cardiac veins are swapped. The middle vein runs with the PDA and the small vein runs with the right marginal artery.
This swaps the great and small cardiac veins. The small cardiac vein runs along the right border with the right marginal artery, and the great cardiac vein runs with the LAD.
questions.answerText: Great with the LAD, middle with the PDA, small with the right marginal artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A patient with a blocked right coronary artery develops an abnormal heart rhythm. Which structures, usually supplied by the RCA, best explain this?
options: SA and AV nodes
Pulmonary and aortic valves
Anterior septum and apex
Left atrium and left auricle
questions.why: In most people the right coronary artery supplies the SA node, the pacemaker that starts each beat, and the AV node, which passes the signal on to the ventricles. If the RCA is blocked, these nodal cells are starved of oxygen and may not fire or conduct normally. That is why an RCA blockage can cause a rhythm problem in addition to damaged muscle.
notes: Correct. The RCA usually feeds both nodes, so its blockage can disturb the rhythm.
The semilunar valve cusps are thin flaps of endocardium and connective tissue that do not set the rhythm. They would be the answer for a question about preventing backflow from the great arteries.
The anterior septum and apex are supplied by the LAD, a branch of the left coronary artery. Damage there would follow an LAD blockage and mainly weaken the left ventricle.
The left atrium and its auricle are supplied by the left coronary artery, mainly through the circumflex branch. They hold no node and would point to a left coronary problem.
questions.answerText: SA and AV nodes

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A patient has a blockage in the LAD. Which region of the heart is most at risk?
options: Anterior septum, front of the left ventricle, and apex
Right border of the right ventricle
Posterior septum and the back of both ventricles
Right atrium, SA node, and AV node
questions.why: The LAD runs down the front of the heart in the anterior interventricular groove. It supplies the anterior part of the interventricular septum, much of the front wall of the left ventricle, and the apex. A blockage here starves those areas of oxygen, so they are the regions where heart muscle would die.
notes: Correct. These are the regions the LAD supplies.
The right border of the heart is supplied by the right marginal artery, a branch of the right coronary artery. It would be at risk if that branch were blocked.
The posterior septum and the back of the ventricles are supplied by the posterior interventricular artery (PDA), usually a branch of the right coronary artery. That region fits a blockage of the PDA.
The right atrium and both nodes are usually supplied by the right coronary artery. Choose them for an RCA blockage, especially one that causes a rhythm problem.
questions.answerText: Anterior septum, front of the left ventricle, and apex

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Coronary artery disease narrows the coronary arteries. Why can this lead to pumping failure?
options: The narrowed arteries let blood leak backward through the valves
The narrowed arteries block blood from entering the right atrium
The pericardium thickens and stops the heart from beating
The myocardium receives too little oxygen and contracts more weakly
questions.why: Coronary artery disease is a narrowing of the coronary arteries, usually by fatty plaques in the vessel wall (atherosclerosis). Less blood reaches the myocardium, so the muscle cells run short of oxygen and cannot contract with full force. If the supply drops far enough, muscle dies, and the weakened wall cannot pump enough blood for the body.
notes: Backward leak through a valve happens when a valve fails to close, producing a murmur. Coronary disease affects the supply to the muscle, not the valve cusps directly.

Blood enters the right atrium through the venae cavae and coronary sinus, and narrowed coronary arteries do not block those veins. Choose the venae cavae for a question about blood returning from the body.
Excess fluid in the pericardial cavity can restrict filling, as in cardiac tamponade. That is a problem of the sac around the heart, not of the arteries feeding the muscle.
Correct. Starved muscle contracts weakly, so the heart pumps less.
questions.answerText: The myocardium receives too little oxygen and contracts more weakly

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: If the coronary sinus were blocked, which flow would be impaired?
options: Blood flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk
Blood flow from the lungs into the left atrium
Arterial supply from the aorta into the myocardium
Venous drainage from the heart wall into the right atrium
questions.why: The coronary sinus is the large vein that collects blood from the great, middle, and small cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium. A blockage there would back up the venous drainage of most of the heart wall. Only the small anterior cardiac veins, which open directly into the right atrium, would still drain normally.
notes: Flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk passes through the pulmonary valve. It is part of the pulmonary circuit and does not involve the coronary sinus.
Flow from the lungs into the left atrium travels in the pulmonary veins. That would be the answer for a blockage of the pulmonary veins.
The arterial supply to the myocardium comes from the coronary arteries at the base of the aorta. A blocked coronary artery, not the coronary sinus, would cut that supply.
Correct. The coronary sinus drains most of the heart wall into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: Venous drainage from the heart wall into the right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A blockage of the left coronary artery would cause the greatest loss of pumping muscle in which chamber?
options: Left atrium
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
Right atrium
questions.why: The left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, the anterior septum, and the apex. The left ventricle has the thickest wall of the four chambers and pumps blood to the whole body, so a left coronary blockage destroys the most pumping muscle there. This is why left coronary blockages tend to be the most dangerous.
notes: The left atrium is also supplied by the left coronary artery, but its wall is thin and it does little of the pumping. The thick-walled left ventricle has far more muscle at stake.
Correct. The left ventricle has the most muscle in the left coronary territory.
Most of the right ventricle is supplied by the right coronary artery. Choose it for a question about an RCA blockage.
The right atrium is supplied mainly by the right coronary artery. It would be threatened by an RCA blockage, not a left coronary one.
questions.answerText: Left ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The right coronary artery supplies most of the wall of which ventricle, making it the ventricle most threatened by an RCA blockage?
options: Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Both ventricles equally
Neither ventricle, only the atria
questions.why: The right coronary artery runs in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle and supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, and the posterior septum. Because it feeds most of the right ventricular wall, the right ventricle is the ventricle most threatened when the RCA is blocked, and pumping to the lungs suffers.
notes: Correct. Most of the right ventricle depends on the RCA.
Most of the left ventricle is supplied by the left coronary artery, and the RCA feeds only part of it. The left ventricle would be the answer for a left coronary blockage.
The two ventricles are not supplied equally by either artery. The right coronary artery feeds most of the right ventricle, while the left coronary artery feeds most of the left ventricle.
The RCA does supply the right atrium, but it also supplies most of the right ventricle. The ventricular muscle is where an RCA blockage does the most pumping damage.
questions.answerText: Right ventricle

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Depending on where it occurs, a myocardial infarction can cause problems beyond weaker pumping. Which statement best explains why?
options: An infarction blocks the venae cavae so blood cannot return
An infarction destroys the fibrous pericardium that anchors the heart
An infarction spreads to the lungs through the pulmonary veins
The dying area may include conduction tissue or papillary muscles
questions.why: An infarction kills whatever myocardium the blocked artery supplied. Depending on the location, that patch may include conduction tissue such as the SA node, AV node, or bundle branches, which disturbs the rhythm, or a papillary muscle, which can let an atrioventricular valve fail. So the result can be a rhythm problem or a leaking valve as well as weaker pumping.
notes: The venae cavae are large veins outside the heart wall, and an infarction does not block them. A blocked vena cava would stop blood returning from the body, a different problem from dying heart muscle.
The fibrous pericardium is a dense connective tissue sac outside the heart wall, with its own blood supply. An infarction damages heart muscle, not the pericardial sac.

An infarction is a local area of dead heart muscle and does not spread through the pulmonary veins, which carry blood from the lungs toward the heart. This choice invents a route the damage cannot take.
Correct. Conduction tissue and papillary muscles are myocardium too, so they can die in an infarction.
questions.answerText: The dying area may include conduction tissue or papillary muscles

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why can a coronary artery blockage lead to papillary muscle damage and a leaking valve?
options: Papillary muscles are ventricular myocardium fed by the coronary arteries
Papillary muscles are conduction tissue that stops firing first
Papillary muscles sit inside the aorta beside the coronary openings
Papillary muscles are dense connective tissue fed by blood in the atria
questions.why: Papillary muscles are cone-shaped projections of the ventricular wall, so they are myocardium supplied by the coronary arteries like the rest of the wall. They anchor the chordae tendineae that hold the atrioventricular valves shut. If a blockage kills a papillary muscle, the chordae lose their anchor and the tricuspid or mitral valve can fail, letting blood leak back into the atrium.
notes: Correct. Papillary muscles are myocardium and lose their supply when a coronary artery is blocked.

Papillary muscles are contractile myocardium, not conduction tissue, although the moderator band carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle. Choose the conduction system for a question about rhythm, not valve support.
Papillary muscles project from the inner walls of the ventricles, not from the aorta. The aortic valve is a semilunar valve and has no papillary muscles or chordae tendineae.

Papillary muscles are cardiac muscle, not dense connective tissue; the chordae tendineae are the fibrous cords. Blood in the chambers also does not nourish the deep wall, which is why the coronary arteries are needed.
questions.answerText: Papillary muscles are ventricular myocardium fed by the coronary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why is damage to the apex especially serious in a left coronary blockage?
options: The apex is where the pulmonary veins enter the heart
The apex holds the aortic valve, which would stop closing
The apex contains the SA node that starts every heartbeat
It is formed by the left ventricle, the chamber that pumps blood to the body
questions.why: The apex is the blunt inferior tip of the heart, and it is formed by the left ventricle. Its muscle is supplied by the left coronary artery through the LAD. If that muscle dies, the left ventricle, which pumps blood into the aorta and out to the whole body, loses part of its pumping wall.
notes: The pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base of the heart, the opposite end from the apex. Choose the base for where the great vessels attach.
The aortic valve sits at the base of the heart, at the exit of the left ventricle into the aorta. It is at the opposite end from the apex.
The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava, far from the apex. It would be the answer for where each heartbeat starts.
Correct. The apex is left ventricle muscle, and the left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body.
questions.answerText: It is formed by the left ventricle, the chamber that pumps blood to the body

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which statement best explains why coronary circulation and the conduction system are linked clinically?
options: Coronary arteries feed the conduction tissue, so a blockage can disturb the rhythm
The conduction system pumps blood through the coronary arteries
Coronary veins carry the electrical signal from the SA node to the ventricles
The conduction system is made of blood vessels that branch from the aorta
questions.why: The conduction system is made of specialized cardiac muscle cells, and like all myocardium it depends on the coronary arteries for oxygen. The right coronary artery usually feeds the SA and AV nodes, and coronary branches that enter the septum supply the AV bundle and bundle branches. A coronary blockage can therefore starve conduction tissue and cause a rhythm problem in addition to killing contractile muscle.
notes: Correct. Conduction tissue depends on the coronary supply, so a blockage can affect rhythm.
The conduction system carries an electrical signal; it does not pump blood. The contraction of the myocardium is what moves blood, including into the coronary arteries from the aorta.
Veins carry blood, not electrical signals. The signal travels from the SA node to the ventricles through the AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers.
The conduction system is made of specialized cardiac muscle cells, not blood vessels. The vessels branching from the base of the aorta are the coronary arteries.
questions.answerText: Coronary arteries feed the conduction tissue, so a blockage can disturb the rhythm

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces coronary circulation from the aorta back to the right atrium?
options: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, coronary sinus, cardiac veins, right atrium
Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium
Aorta, cardiac veins, myocardial capillaries, coronary arteries, coronary sinus, right atrium
Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, left atrium
questions.why: The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta and carry oxygen-rich blood to the capillaries of the myocardium, the heart muscle. Cardiac veins collect the blood from those capillaries and empty into the coronary sinus, a large vein on the posterior heart. The coronary sinus then opens into the right atrium.
notes: This sequence reverses the coronary sinus and the cardiac veins. The cardiac veins are the smaller tributaries that feed into the coronary sinus, and the coronary sinus is the last vessel before the heart chamber.
Correct. This is the coronary route from the aorta to the right atrium.

This sequence puts the cardiac veins before the capillaries. Veins carry blood away from capillaries, so the coronary arteries must come first, feeding the capillaries, and the cardiac veins come after.

This sequence ends in the left atrium, which receives blood only from the pulmonary veins. The coronary sinus returns oxygen-poor blood, so it empties into the right atrium with the rest of the body's venous return.
questions.answerText: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: In coronary circulation, blood that has passed through the capillaries of the myocardium enters which vessels next?
options: Coronary sinus
Cardiac veins
Pulmonary veins
Coronary arteries
questions.why: The heart wall has its own circulation. Coronary arteries feed the capillaries of the myocardium, and after exchange in those capillaries the blood collects into the cardiac veins. The cardiac veins then drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
notes: The coronary sinus is one step later. It collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties into the right atrium, so it would be the answer if the question started at the cardiac veins.
Correct. Myocardial capillaries drain into the cardiac veins.
The pulmonary veins drain the lungs into the left atrium and play no part in draining the heart wall. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels leave the lung capillaries.

The coronary arteries come before the capillaries, carrying oxygen-rich blood from the aorta to the heart muscle. They would be the answer if the question asked what supplies the myocardial capillaries.
questions.answerText: Cardiac veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the anterior interventricular artery, the LAD, and drains into the coronary sinus?
options: Middle cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
Small cardiac vein
Great cardiac vein
questions.why: Each named cardiac vein travels in the same groove as a coronary artery.
