The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus with the anterior interventricular artery, also called the left anterior descending artery or LAD. It carries blood from that region around to the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
notes: The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery on the back of the heart. It would be the answer if the question named the posterior interventricular artery, the PDA.
The anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle straight into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. They would be the answer if the question asked which veins skip the coronary sinus.
The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the lower right border of the heart. It would be the answer if the question named the right marginal artery.
Correct. The great cardiac vein travels with the LAD.
questions.answerText: Great cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the posterior interventricular artery, the PDA, and drains into the coronary sinus?
options: Middle cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
Small cardiac vein
Great cardiac vein
questions.why: The middle cardiac vein lies in the posterior interventricular sulcus, the groove on the back of the heart between the two ventricles. The posterior interventricular artery, also called the posterior descending artery or PDA, runs in the same groove. The middle cardiac vein carries blood from that region into the coronary sinus and on to the right atrium.
notes: Correct. The middle cardiac vein travels with the PDA.

The anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle directly into the right atrium without joining the coronary sinus. They would be the answer if the question asked which veins bypass the coronary sinus.
The small cardiac vein runs with the right marginal artery along the lower right border. It would be the answer if the question named the right marginal artery.
The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery on the front of the heart. It would be the answer if the question named the LAD.
questions.answerText: Middle cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which cardiac vein runs alongside the right marginal artery and drains into the coronary sinus?
options: Middle cardiac vein
Great cardiac vein
Small cardiac vein
Anterior cardiac veins
questions.why: The small cardiac vein runs along the lower right border of the heart with the right marginal artery, a branch of the right coronary artery. It carries blood from that area into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium. Learning the arteries makes the veins easier, because each named vein shares a groove with an artery.
notes: The middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery on the back of the heart. It would be the answer if the question named the PDA.
The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery on the front of the heart. It would be the answer if the question named the LAD.
Correct. The small cardiac vein travels with the right marginal artery.

The anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle straight into the right atrium, so they never join the coronary sinus. They would be the answer if the question asked which veins skip the coronary sinus.
questions.answerText: Small cardiac vein

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs returns to the right atrium through which vessel?
options: Superior vena cava
Coronary sinus
Pulmonary veins
Inferior vena cava
questions.why: The superior vena cava collects venous blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs and empties into the top of the right atrium. Together with the inferior vena cava from below, it returns the systemic circuit's oxygen-poor blood to the heart.
notes: Correct. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs.
The coronary sinus collects blood from the heart wall itself through the cardiac veins. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood from the myocardium returns to the right atrium.
The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, not oxygen-poor blood from the body. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood returns from the lungs.
The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs and enters the right atrium from below. It would be the answer if the blood were coming from the legs or abdomen.
questions.answerText: Superior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Oxygen-poor blood from the trunk and lower limbs returns to the right atrium through which vessel?
options: Coronary sinus
Hepatic portal vein
Inferior vena cava
Superior vena cava
questions.why: The inferior vena cava is the large vein that collects blood from the trunk and lower limbs. It runs up through the abdomen beside the aorta and empties into the lower part of the right atrium. Along with the superior vena cava, it ends the systemic circuit.
notes: The coronary sinus drains the heart wall through the cardiac veins. It would be the answer if the question asked where the cardiac veins empty.
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver, not to the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood from the intestines reaches the liver.
Correct. The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs, entering the right atrium from above. It would be the answer if the blood were coming from the arms or head.
questions.answerText: Inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The right and left coronary arteries, which supply the heart wall, branch from which part of the circulation?
options: Pulmonary trunk
Coronary sinus
Aortic arch
Base of the aorta
questions.why: The two coronary arteries leave the base of the aorta, just beyond the aortic valve, so they receive oxygen-rich blood as soon as it leaves the left ventricle. They then run in the grooves on the heart's surface and branch over the myocardium.
notes: The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, so it could not supply the heart wall with oxygen. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel branches into the pulmonary arteries.
The coronary sinus is a vein that collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question asked where the heart wall's venous blood drains.

The aortic arch is farther along the aorta and gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries. It would be the answer if the question asked where the arteries to the head and upper limbs arise.
Correct. The coronary arteries arise from the base of the aorta.
questions.answerText: Base of the aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The great, middle, and small cardiac veins all empty into which structure before their blood reaches the right atrium?
options: Inferior vena cava
Coronary sinus
Superior vena cava
Pulmonary veins
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a large vein on the posterior surface of the heart. The great, middle, and small cardiac veins drain into it, and it empties into the right atrium. Only the small anterior cardiac veins skip it and drain the right ventricle straight into the right atrium.
notes: The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs into the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood from the legs returns to the heart.
Correct. The named cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs into the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood from the arms returns to the heart.
The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood returns from the lungs.
questions.answerText: Coronary sinus

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which great vessel returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs to the right atrium?
options: Coronary sinus
Pulmonary trunk
Superior vena cava
Inferior vena cava
questions.why: The superior vena cava is the large vein that collects oxygen-poor blood from the upper body, including the head, neck, and upper limbs. It enters the top of the right atrium. Its partner, the inferior vena cava, brings blood from below and enters the bottom of the same chamber.
notes: The coronary sinus is the large vein on the back of the heart that collects blood from the heart wall itself. Choose it if the question asked which vessel returns blood from the cardiac veins to the right atrium.
The pulmonary trunk is an artery that carries blood away from the right ventricle toward the lungs. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel leaves the right ventricle.
Correct. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs into the right atrium.
The inferior vena cava returns oxygen-poor blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium. Pick it if the question asked which vessel drains the lower body.
questions.answerText: Superior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which great vessel returns oxygen-poor blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium?
options: Superior vena cava
Aorta
Coronary sinus
Inferior vena cava
questions.why: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body. It runs up the back of the abdomen beside the aorta, passes through the diaphragm, and empties into the lower part of the right atrium. It carries oxygen-poor blood from the abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs.
notes: The superior vena cava returns blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs to the top of the right atrium. Pick it if the question asked which vessel drains the upper body.

The aorta is the main artery leaving the left ventricle, carrying oxygen-rich blood away from the heart. Choose it if the question asked which vessel sends blood out to the body, not back to the heart.

The coronary sinus collects blood from the heart wall through the cardiac veins and empties into the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood from the myocardium returns to the heart chambers.
Correct. The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs.
questions.answerText: Inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel is the largest artery in the body, carrying oxygen-rich blood away from the left ventricle?
options: Aorta
Pulmonary trunk
Brachiocephalic trunk
Common carotid artery
questions.why: The aorta leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve, arches over the heart, and runs down through the thorax and abdomen. Every systemic artery in the body branches off it directly or indirectly. It is an elastic artery, so it stretches with each heartbeat and recoils between beats to keep blood moving.
notes: Correct. The aorta is the largest artery in the body.

The pulmonary trunk is also a large elastic artery, but it leaves the right ventricle and carries oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs. Pick it if the question asked which artery begins the pulmonary circuit.

The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch of the aortic arch, supplying the right side of the head and neck and the right upper limb. It would be the answer if the question asked for the first vessel to branch off the aortic arch.
The common carotid arteries are branches that carry blood up the neck to the head. Choose one if the question asked which artery supplies the head and neck.
questions.answerText: Aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which great vessel carries blood out of the right ventricle?
options: Pulmonary trunk
Superior vena cava
Aorta
Pulmonary veins
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one to each lung. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is oxygen-poor. This is a reminder that arteries and veins are named by direction of flow, not by how much oxygen they carry.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary trunk carries blood out of the right ventricle toward the lungs.
The superior vena cava brings oxygen-poor blood from the upper body into the right atrium. Choose it if the question asked which vessel returns blood from the head and upper limbs.
The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood out of the left ventricle to the body. Pick it if the question asked which vessel leaves the left ventricle.

The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium, so they bring blood toward the heart. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels return blood from the lungs.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessels return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium?
options: Cardiac veins
Venae cavae
Pulmonary veins
Pulmonary arteries
questions.why: The four pulmonary veins, usually two from each lung, carry blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs back to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, even though their blood is oxygen-rich. Together with the pulmonary arteries they form the pulmonary circuit.
notes: The cardiac veins drain blood from the heart wall and mostly empty into the coronary sinus. Choose them if the question asked which veins drain the myocardium.
The venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels empty into the right atrium.
Correct. The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium.
The pulmonary arteries branch from the pulmonary trunk and carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs. Pick them if the question asked which vessels take blood into the lungs.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which large vein on the posterior surface of the heart collects the cardiac veins and empties into the right atrium?
options: Coronary sinus
Anterior cardiac veins
Great cardiac vein
Inferior vena cava
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a wide vein lying in the groove between the atria and ventricles on the back of the heart. The great, middle, and small cardiac veins drain into it, and it empties into the right atrium. The coronary flow runs aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium.
notes: Correct. The coronary sinus collects the cardiac veins and empties into the right atrium.
The anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. Choose them if the question asked which cardiac veins skip the coronary sinus.

The great cardiac vein runs with the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) and drains into the coronary sinus rather than straight into a chamber. Pick it if the question asked which cardiac vein travels beside the LAD.

The inferior vena cava returns blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium, not blood from the heart wall. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel drains the lower body.
questions.answerText: Coronary sinus

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A coronary artery is blocked, and the patch of heart muscle it supplies dies. What is this event called?
options: Stroke
Cardiac tamponade
Myocardial infarction
Aneurysm
questions.why: The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta and are the heart wall's own blood supply. When one is blocked, the myocardium beyond the blockage is starved of oxygen and its muscle cells begin to die. Death of tissue from lost blood supply is called an infarction, so death of heart muscle is a myocardial infarction, the medical term for a heart attack.
notes: A stroke is loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery. It would be the answer if the blocked vessel supplied brain tissue rather than the heart wall.

Cardiac tamponade is fluid building up in the pericardial cavity and squeezing the heart from outside. Pick it when fluid around the heart limits how much the heart can fill, not when an artery is blocked.
Correct. A myocardial infarction is the death of heart muscle after its coronary blood supply is cut off.

An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall, most often in the aorta or the arteries of the brain. Choose it when a wall is stretching outward and might rupture, not when a lumen is blocked.
questions.answerText: Myocardial infarction

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Plaque gradually narrows the arteries that supply the heart wall. Which disorder fits?
options: Cardiac tamponade
Coronary artery disease
Heart block
Peripheral artery disease
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries and their branches leave the base of the aorta and supply the myocardium. Coronary artery disease is narrowing of these vessels, usually by atherosclerotic plaque. A narrowed coronary artery can starve the heart muscle of oxygen, and if it becomes fully blocked, the result is a myocardial infarction.
notes: Cardiac tamponade is fluid filling the pericardial cavity and squeezing the heart from outside. It would be the answer for a problem with heart filling, not narrowed vessels.
Correct. Coronary artery disease is narrowing of the coronary arteries that feed the heart wall.

Heart block is a conduction disorder at the AV node that makes the atria and ventricles beat out of step. It is an electrical problem, so choose it for a rhythm question rather than narrowed arteries.
Peripheral artery disease is the same plaque narrowing in the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs. Pick it when a question describes leg pain on walking.
questions.answerText: Coronary artery disease

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student says that veins always carry oxygen-poor blood. Which fact shows this statement is wrong?
options: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-rich blood to the lungs
The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium
The coronary sinus carries oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium
The venae cavae carry oxygen-rich blood to the right atrium
questions.why: Vessels are named by the direction they carry blood, not by how much oxygen it holds: arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it toward the heart. The four pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs, where it has just picked up oxygen, to the left atrium. They are veins carrying oxygen-rich blood, which disproves the rule.
notes: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, not oxygen-rich blood. They are the exception to the matching rule that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood.
Correct. The pulmonary veins are veins that carry oxygen-rich blood.
The coronary sinus carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart wall and empties into the right atrium, not the left. Choose it for a question about how the myocardium drains.

The superior and inferior venae cavae carry oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium. They fit the student's rule, so pick them for a question about where systemic blood returns to the heart.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A student says that arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood. Which vessels show this statement is wrong?
options: The pulmonary veins
The renal arteries
The pulmonary arteries
The coronary arteries
questions.why: An artery is any vessel that carries blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content. The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood returned from the body into the pulmonary trunk, which splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries headed to the lungs. They are arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood, so they disprove the student's rule.
notes: The pulmonary veins are the exception on the other side, veins carrying oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They would be the answer if the student had claimed that veins always carry oxygen-poor blood.
The renal arteries branch from the abdominal aorta and carry oxygen-rich blood to the kidneys. They follow the usual pattern, so choose them for a question about the kidney's blood supply.
Correct. The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta and carry oxygen-rich blood to the myocardium. They follow the usual pattern, so pick them for a question about the heart wall's own blood supply.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A blockage in the right coronary artery causes a rhythm problem as well as damaged muscle. What anatomy explains the rhythm problem?
options: It usually supplies the left atrium
It usually supplies the apex of the heart
It usually supplies the SA and AV nodes
It usually supplies the anterior septum
questions.why: The SA node and AV node are part of the conduction system, the specialized cells that start and relay each heartbeat. In most people both nodes get their blood from the right coronary artery. When the RCA is blocked, the nodes can be starved of oxygen along with the muscle, so the beat may slow, become irregular, or be blocked at the AV node.
notes: The left atrium is supplied by the left coronary artery, mainly through its circumflex branch. Choose it for a question about the regions the left coronary artery feeds.
The apex is supplied by the left coronary artery, mainly through the anterior interventricular artery (the LAD). Pick the apex for a question about what a LAD blockage damages.
Correct. The RCA supplies the SA and AV nodes in most people.
The anterior part of the interventricular septum is supplied by the LAD, a branch of the left coronary artery. The RCA's posterior interventricular branch supplies the posterior septum instead.
questions.answerText: It usually supplies the SA and AV nodes

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Why can a blockage of the anterior interventricular artery (the LAD) be especially dangerous?
options: It supplies the right atrium and right ventricle
It supplies much of the left ventricle and apex
It drains the heart wall into the coronary sinus
It is the only vessel supplying the SA node
questions.why: The anterior interventricular artery, also called the left anterior descending artery (LAD), is a branch of the left coronary artery that runs in the groove between the ventricles on the front of the heart. It supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the anterior part of the interventricular septum, and the apex. The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, so losing a large area of its muscle seriously weakens the heart's pumping.
notes: The right atrium and most of the right ventricle are supplied by the right coronary artery. Pick it for a question about what an RCA blockage damages.
Correct. The LAD feeds a large part of the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber.

Draining the heart wall is the job of the cardiac veins and the coronary sinus. The great cardiac vein runs beside the LAD, but the LAD itself is an artery that delivers blood rather than draining it.
The SA node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery, not the LAD. Choose the RCA for a question about why a blockage causes a rhythm problem.
questions.answerText: It supplies much of the left ventricle and apex

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
options: The pulmonary trunk
The coronary sinus
The base of the aorta
The aortic arch
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries branch off the base of the aorta, just above the aortic valve, so they are the first branches the aorta gives off. From there they run in the grooves on the heart's surface and branch over the myocardium. This gives the heart wall first access to the oxygen-rich blood leaving the left ventricle.
notes: The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and has no coronary branches. Choose it for a question about which vessel splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries.

The coronary sinus is a vein on the back of the heart that collects blood from the cardiac veins and drains into the right atrium. It would be the answer for where coronary blood ends up, not where the arteries begin.
Correct. The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, just above the aortic valve.

The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery, which supply the head, neck, and upper limbs. Pick it if the question asked where those three branches arise.
questions.answerText: The base of the aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which two arteries come directly off the aorta to supply the heart wall?
options: The circumflex and marginal arteries
The anterior and posterior interventricular arteries
The right and left pulmonary arteries
The right and left coronary arteries
questions.why: The two coronary arteries, right and left, leave the base of the aorta and supply the myocardium. The right coronary artery serves the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, and usually the SA and AV nodes, while the left coronary artery serves the left atrium, the left ventricle, and the anterior septum. Every other named coronary artery is a branch of one of these two.
notes: The circumflex and left marginal arteries are branches of the left coronary artery, and the right marginal artery comes off the right. Choose them for a question about branches that run along the sides of the heart.

These are branches, not the two main coronary arteries. The anterior interventricular artery is a branch of the left coronary artery and the posterior interventricular artery usually comes off the right; pick them if the question asked which arteries run in the interventricular grooves.
The right and left pulmonary arteries branch from the pulmonary trunk and carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood reaches each lung.
Correct. The right and left coronary arteries are the two main vessels, and the rest are their branches.
questions.answerText: The right and left coronary arteries

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What does the coronary sinus do?
options: Drains the right ventricle wall directly into the right atrium
Carries oxygen-rich blood from the aorta into the myocardium
Collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium
Collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the left atrium
questions.why: The coronary sinus is a large vein in the groove on the posterior surface of the heart. The great, middle, and small cardiac veins drain into it, and it empties that oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium. Along with the two venae cavae, it is one of the three large veins that empty into the right atrium; only the small anterior cardiac veins enter the right atrium on their own.
notes: That describes the anterior cardiac veins, which bypass the coronary sinus and empty straight into the right atrium. Pick it if the question asked which cardiac veins skip the coronary sinus.
That is the job of the coronary arteries, which leave the base of the aorta and branch over the myocardium. Choose this for a question about how the heart wall gets its oxygen supply.
Correct. The coronary sinus is the collecting vein of the heart wall, and it opens into the right atrium.

The coronary sinus does collect the cardiac veins, but it carries oxygen-poor blood, which returns to the right side of the heart. Students pick this when they confuse it with the pulmonary veins, which are the vessels that empty into the left atrium.
questions.answerText: Collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which sequence traces blood through the coronary circulation, from the aorta back into the heart?
options: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium
Pulmonary trunk, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium
Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, left atrium
Aorta, cardiac veins, myocardial capillaries, coronary arteries, coronary sinus, right atrium
questions.why: The heart wall is supplied like any other organ: arteries, then capillaries, then veins. Oxygen-rich blood leaves the base of the aorta in the coronary arteries, delivers oxygen in the capillaries of the myocardium, and drains into the cardiac veins. The cardiac veins empty into the coronary sinus, which returns the oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium.
notes: Correct. Arteries, capillaries, veins, then the coronary sinus into the right atrium.
The pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and gives off no coronary arteries. The coronary arteries branch from the aorta, which carries the oxygen-rich blood the heart muscle needs.

Everything is in order until the last step. Oxygen-poor blood from the heart wall returns to the right atrium, just like blood from the rest of the body; the left atrium receives only the pulmonary veins.
This puts the veins before the arteries. Blood always passes from arteries to capillaries to veins, so the cardiac veins come after the capillaries, not before them.
questions.answerText: Aorta, coronary arteries, myocardial capillaries, cardiac veins, coronary sinus, right atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A clot blocks a branch of the left coronary artery. The patch of myocardium beyond the block is starved of oxygen and begins to die. What is this event called?
options: Cardiac tamponade
Heart block
Myocardial infarction
Aneurysm
questions.why: A myocardial infarction, commonly called a heart attack, is death of heart muscle caused by a blocked coronary artery. The coronary arteries are the heart wall's own supply line, and they are narrow, so a block cuts off oxygen to every cell downstream of it. Infarction means tissue death from loss of blood supply, and myocardial names the heart muscle layer that is affected.
notes: Cardiac tamponade is fluid building up in the pericardial cavity and squeezing the heart from outside. Pick it if the scenario described fluid around the heart limiting how much it can fill.

Heart block is a conduction disorder in which the electrical signal is delayed or stopped at the AV node. It would be the answer if the scenario described the atria and ventricles beating out of step.
Correct. A blocked coronary artery leads to death of the heart muscle it supplies.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall that can rupture. Choose it for a scenario about a bulging aorta or brain artery, not a blocked coronary artery.
questions.answerText: Myocardial infarction

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: Which vessel is the largest artery in the body, carrying oxygen-rich blood out of the left ventricle?
options: Inferior vena cava
Aorta
Common carotid artery
Pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve, arches over the heart, and descends through the thorax and abdomen, giving off branches that carry oxygen-rich blood to every part of the body. Its first branches are the coronary arteries, which supply the heart wall itself.
notes: The inferior vena cava is a vein, not an artery, and it returns oxygen-poor blood from the trunk and lower limbs to the right atrium. Choose it for a question about the large vein draining the lower body.
Correct. The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the whole body.
The common carotid arteries carry blood up the neck to the head and are much smaller than the aorta. They would be the answer for a question about the main arteries supplying the head and neck.

The pulmonary trunk is also a large artery leaving the heart, but it leaves the right ventricle and carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Pick it if the question asked which vessel the right ventricle pumps into.
questions.answerText: Aorta

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: What does the pulmonary trunk carry, and where does it take it?
options: Oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium
Oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs
Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium
Oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and carries oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs. It soon splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one to each lung, where the blood picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. Because it carries blood away from the heart, it counts as an arterial vessel even though its blood is low in oxygen.
notes: That describes the superior and inferior venae cavae, which return oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium. They would be the answer for the vessels that empty into the right atrium.
Correct. The pulmonary trunk takes oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
That describes the pulmonary veins, which return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Pick it if the question asked what the left atrium receives.
That describes the aorta, which leaves the left ventricle and supplies the whole body. Choose it for the vessel the left ventricle pumps into.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: How many pulmonary veins return blood to the heart, and which chamber do they enter?
options: Four, entering the right atrium
Two, entering the left ventricle
Four, entering the left atrium
Two, entering the left atrium
questions.why: There are four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, and all four empty into the left atrium. They carry oxygen-rich blood that has just passed through the lungs. From the left atrium, that blood crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle to be pumped out to the body.
notes: Four is right, but the right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the venae cavae and coronary sinus. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, so they return to the left side of the heart.
Returning blood always enters an atrium before a ventricle, so no vein empties straight into the left ventricle. Students pick this when they skip the left atrium in the pathway.
Correct. Four pulmonary veins, two from each lung, all entering the left atrium.
The left atrium is right, but there are two veins from each lung, four in all. Students choose two when they count one vein per lung.
questions.answerText: Four, entering the left atrium

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood. Why are they still called arteries and veins?
options: Vessels are named by which ventricle pumps blood into them
Vessels are named by wall thickness, and these have unusually thin walls
Vessels are named by the direction they carry blood relative to the heart
Vessels are named by the oxygen content of the blood they carry
questions.why: Arteries are defined as vessels that carry blood away from the heart, and veins as vessels that carry blood toward it. The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs, so they are arteries even though that blood is low in oxygen. The pulmonary veins carry blood back to the left atrium, so they are veins even though that blood has just picked up oxygen in the lungs.
notes: Both ventricles pump into arteries, the right into the pulmonary trunk and the left into the aorta, and no ventricle pumps into a vein. Students choose this when they try to link each vessel name to one side of the heart.

Arteries do usually have thicker walls than veins, but wall thickness is a feature of each vessel type, not the basis for its name. Pick wall thickness for a question about telling an artery from a vein on a slide.
Correct. Direction of flow, away from or toward the heart, is what defines an artery or a vein.

This is the rule students often learn first, that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry oxygen-poor blood. It works for the systemic circuit, but it is not how vessels are named, which is why the pulmonary vessels seem to break it.
questions.answerText: Vessels are named by the direction they carry blood relative to the heart

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A drop of blood leaves the right ventricle and travels to the left atrium. Which sequence of vessels does it pass through?
options: Pulmonary veins, lung capillaries, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary trunk
Pulmonary trunk, pulmonary veins, lung capillaries, pulmonary arteries
Aorta, pulmonary arteries, lung capillaries, pulmonary veins
Pulmonary trunk, pulmonary arteries, lung capillaries, pulmonary veins
questions.why: The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. Those arteries branch down to the capillaries around the alveoli, where the blood picks up oxygen. The blood then collects into the pulmonary veins, which carry it back to the left atrium, completing the pulmonary circuit.
notes: These are the right vessels traced in reverse, from the left atrium back to the right ventricle. Blood leaves the heart in arteries and returns in veins, so the pulmonary trunk comes first.
This puts the veins before the capillaries. Blood moves from arteries to capillaries to veins, so the pulmonary arteries come before the lung capillaries and the pulmonary veins come after them.
The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries blood to the body, not the lungs. Pick the aorta as the starting vessel only if the question traced blood from the left ventricle.
Correct. Trunk, arteries, capillaries, then veins back to the left atrium.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary trunk, pulmonary arteries, lung capillaries, pulmonary veins

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: A catheter is pushed up the descending thoracic aorta and around the aortic arch toward the ascending aorta. Which branch of the arch does it pass first?
options: The left subclavian artery
The brachiocephalic trunk
The left common carotid artery
The right subclavian artery
questions.why: Moving from the right side of the body to the left, the arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery. A catheter coming up from the descending aorta travels the arch from left to right, so it meets the branches in reverse order. The left subclavian is the first one it passes.
notes: Correct. Coming from the descending aorta, the catheter meets the left subclavian first.
The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch, on the right side of the arch, so a catheter coming from the descending aorta passes it last.
The left common carotid is the middle branch of the arch. The catheter passes the left subclavian before reaching it.
The right subclavian does not leave the arch at all. It is one of the two branches of the brachiocephalic trunk.
questions.answerText: The left subclavian artery

questions.topic: Great vessels and coronary circulation
questions.q: On a heart model, you follow the great vessel that leaves the right ventricle upward. A short fibrous cord ties it to the larger vessel that curves over the top of the heart. Which two vessels does the cord join, and which circuit does each serve?
options: Pulmonary trunk, systemic circuit; aorta, pulmonary circuit
Pulmonary veins, pulmonary circuit; aorta, systemic circuit
Pulmonary trunk, pulmonary circuit; aorta, systemic circuit
Aorta, systemic circuit; superior vena cava, systemic circuit
questions.why: The great vessel that leaves the right ventricle is the pulmonary trunk, which carries blood to the lungs in the pulmonary circuit. The short cord is the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, and it ties the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, curves over the heart as the aortic arch, and carries blood to the body in the systemic circuit.
notes: The two vessels are right, but the circuits are reversed. The pulmonary trunk carries blood to the lungs, and the aorta carries blood to the body.
The pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium; they do not leave the right ventricle. The vessel leaving the right ventricle is the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. The cord, the ligamentum arteriosum, joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
The aorta leaves the left ventricle, and the superior vena cava empties into the right atrium. Neither one is the vessel that leaves the right ventricle.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary trunk, pulmonary circuit; aorta, systemic circuit

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which two cell junctions are found in the intercalated discs that join cardiac muscle cells?
options: Desmosomes and hemidesmosomes
Tight junctions and gap junctions
Hemidesmosomes and tight junctions
Desmosomes and gap junctions
questions.why: Intercalated discs are the dark bands where neighboring cardiac muscle cells meet end to end. Desmosomes hold the cells together so they do not pull apart when the heart contracts, and gap junctions are small channels that let the electrical signal pass directly from one cell to the next. Working together, these two junctions let the whole heart wall contract as one coordinated unit.
notes: Desmosomes are correct, but hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to its basement membrane rather than to a neighboring cell. Pick hemidesmosomes for a question about what keeps the epidermis attached to the basement membrane.

Gap junctions are present in intercalated discs, but tight junctions are not. Tight junctions seal neighboring epithelial cells together so material cannot leak between them, so pick them for a question about the leak-proof lining of the intestine or bladder.

Neither of these junctions joins cardiac cells end to end. Hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to the basement membrane beneath it, and tight junctions seal epithelial cells together, so this pair fits questions about epithelium.
Correct. Desmosomes provide adhesion and gap junctions provide electrical coupling in the intercalated discs.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes and gap junctions

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which structural feature is unique to cardiac muscle and joins its cells end to end?
options: Intercalated discs
Terminal cisterns
Striations
Fascicles
questions.why: Intercalated discs are the junctions where one cardiac muscle cell meets the next, and they show up on a slide as dark lines crossing the fibers. They contain desmosomes that hold the cells together and gap junctions that pass the electrical signal from cell to cell. Because no other muscle tissue has them, intercalated discs are the quickest way to identify cardiac muscle.
notes: Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiac cells end to end and are found only in cardiac muscle.
Terminal cisterns are the enlarged end sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum inside a skeletal muscle fiber, sitting on either side of a T tubule. Pick them for a question about the parts of a triad.

Striations are the light and dark bands made by lined-up contractile proteins, and both skeletal and cardiac muscle have them, so they are not unique to cardiac muscle. Pick striations for a question about what skeletal and cardiac muscle share.

Fascicles are bundles of skeletal muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium, and they are a feature of a whole skeletal muscle, not a junction between cells. Pick them for a question about what the perimysium surrounds.
questions.answerText: Intercalated discs

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Cardiac muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs that contain gap junctions. Why are the gap junctions essential for the heart to work as a pump?
options: They isolate each cell so it beats on its own rhythm
They pass the signal so the cells contract together
They store blood between cells for later ejection
They hold the cells together so they do not pull apart
questions.why: Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells end to end. They contain two kinds of junctions: desmosomes, which hold the cells together against the force of contraction, and gap junctions, which let the electrical signal pass directly from one cell to the next. This coupling lets the whole heart muscle contract together as a single pump.
notes: Isolated cells would beat out of step and the heart could not pump. This is the opposite of what gap junctions do.
Correct. Gap junctions electrically couple the cardiac cells.
Blood is held in the heart's chambers, not between muscle cells. Intercalated discs are cell junctions, not storage spaces.
This is the job of the desmosomes in the intercalated discs. Pick desmosomes for the mechanical adhesion between cardiac cells.
questions.answerText: They pass the signal so the cells contract together

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What type of muscle tissue forms the myocardium?
options: Smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle
Dense regular connective tissue
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: The myocardium is built of cardiac muscle, an involuntary, striated muscle tissue found nowhere else in the body. Its cells are short and branched and joined end to end by intercalated discs. That connected structure lets the whole heart contract as one coordinated unit.
notes: Smooth muscle is involuntary but lacks striations, and it lines hollow organs such as the stomach and blood vessels. Pick it for the muscle in the wall of an artery or the gut.
Correct. Cardiac muscle forms the myocardium.
Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, with parallel collagen fibers. It is not muscle, so pick it for a question about tendons.
Skeletal muscle is striated but voluntary and attaches to bones. Pick it for a muscle you can move on command, such as the biceps.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What are the specialized junctions where neighboring cardiomyocytes meet end to end called?
options: T tubules
Sarcomeres
Chordae tendineae
Intercalated discs
questions.why: Intercalated discs are the specialized junctions where cardiac muscle cells join end to end. Under the microscope they look like dark lines crossing the fibers, and they are one of the easiest ways to identify cardiac muscle. They hold the cells together and let the contraction signal pass from one cell to the next.
notes: T tubules are inward folds of the muscle cell membrane that carry the signal deep into the cell. They are inside a single cell, not junctions between cells.
A sarcomere is the repeating contractile unit inside a muscle cell, and rows of sarcomeres create the striations. Pick it for a question about the basic unit of contraction.
Chordae tendineae are fibrous cords that tie valve cusps to papillary muscles. Pick them for a question about what holds the atrioventricular valves in place.
Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiomyocytes end to end.
questions.answerText: Intercalated discs

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Within the intercalated discs, which junctions let the contraction signal pass directly from one cardiomyocyte to the next?
options: Gap junctions
Tight junctions
Desmosomes
Sarcomeres
questions.why: Gap junctions are tiny protein channels that connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells. In the intercalated discs they let the electrical signal for contraction pass straight from one cardiomyocyte to the next. This is why the heart muscle contracts as one coordinated unit rather than cell by cell.
notes: Correct. Gap junctions are channels that pass the contraction signal from cell to cell.

Tight junctions seal neighboring cells together to block leakage between them, as in the lining of the intestine. They are not part of the intercalated disc, so pick them for a question about epithelial seals.
Desmosomes are the other junction in the intercalated discs, but they anchor cells together rather than pass signals. Pick desmosomes if the question asked what keeps the cells from pulling apart.
A sarcomere is the contractile unit inside a muscle cell, made of thick and thin filaments. It is not a junction between cells, so pick it for a question about the unit of contraction.
questions.answerText: Gap junctions

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Within the intercalated discs, which junctions anchor cardiomyocytes so they do not pull apart during contraction?
options: Desmosomes
Gap junctions
Tight junctions
Mitochondria
questions.why: Desmosomes are anchoring junctions that rivet neighboring cells together with protein fibers. Cardiac muscle pulls hard with every heartbeat, so the desmosomes in the intercalated discs keep the cells from tearing apart under that strain. Desmosomes are also common in other tissues that are stretched, such as the epidermis.
notes: Correct. Desmosomes anchor cardiomyocytes so they do not pull apart.
Gap junctions are the channels in the intercalated discs that pass the contraction signal between cells. Pick them if the question asked how the signal spreads from cell to cell.
Tight junctions seal cells together to block leakage, as in the lining of the gut. They are not part of the intercalated disc, so pick them for a question about leak-proof epithelial seals.
Mitochondria are organelles that make ATP, and cardiac muscle is packed with them. They power contraction but do not hold cells together, so pick them for a question about the cell's energy supply.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Under the microscope, a tissue shows short, branching, striated cells, each with one central nucleus, joined end to end by dark crossing lines. Which tissue is it?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle
Skeletal muscle
questions.why: Cardiac muscle cells are short and branched, with striations and usually one central nucleus. The dark lines crossing the fibers are intercalated discs, the junctions where cells meet end to end, and they are found only in cardiac muscle. Branching plus intercalated discs is the quickest way to identify this tissue on a slide.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue has wavy parallel collagen fibers with flattened fibroblast nuclei between them. Pick it for a slide of a tendon or ligament.
Correct. Branching striated cells with one nucleus and intercalated discs are cardiac muscle.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with one central nucleus but have no striations and no intercalated discs. Pick smooth muscle for a slide of unstriped, tapered cells.
Skeletal muscle fibers are striated but long, unbranched, and multinucleated, with nuclei pushed to the edges. Pick skeletal muscle for a slide of long cylinders with many peripheral nuclei.
questions.answerText: Cardiac muscle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Cardiac muscle shares one feature with skeletal muscle and a different feature with smooth muscle. Which statement is correct?
options: It is multinucleated like skeletal muscle and involuntary like smooth muscle
It is striated like skeletal muscle and involuntary like smooth muscle
It is voluntary like skeletal muscle and unstriated like smooth muscle
It is striated like smooth muscle and voluntary like skeletal muscle
questions.why: Cardiac muscle is striated, like skeletal muscle, because both are built from orderly rows of sarcomeres. It is also involuntary, like smooth muscle, so you cannot consciously control your heartbeat. That combination of striated and involuntary is unique to cardiac muscle.
notes: The second half is right, but cardiac muscle cells usually have one central nucleus. Long multinucleated fibers are a feature of skeletal muscle only.
Correct. Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle and involuntary like smooth muscle.
Both halves are wrong. Cardiac muscle is not under conscious control and it is striated. This statement describes neither cardiac muscle nor any other single tissue.
Smooth muscle is the one muscle tissue without striations, and cardiac muscle is involuntary. Both halves of this statement are mixed up.
questions.answerText: It is striated like skeletal muscle and involuntary like smooth muscle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: An intercalated disc contains which pair of cell junctions?
options: Tight junctions and desmosomes
Desmosomes and gap junctions
Tight junctions and gap junctions
Synapses and gap junctions
questions.why: Each intercalated disc does two jobs, and each job has its own junction. Desmosomes anchor the cells together so they do not tear apart when the heart contracts, and gap junctions are channels that pass the contraction signal straight from cell to cell. Together they let the heart work as one strong, coordinated unit.
notes: Desmosomes are correct, but tight junctions belong to epithelial sheets, not cardiac muscle. This pair would fit a question about junctions in an epithelium.
Correct. Intercalated discs contain desmosomes for anchoring and gap junctions for signaling.
Gap junctions are correct, but tight junctions are not found in intercalated discs. Tight junctions seal epithelial cells to stop leakage, so pick them for the lining of the gut.

A synapse is the junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell, such as at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle. Cardiomyocytes pass the signal to each other through gap junctions instead.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes and gap junctions

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Suppose the gap junctions between cardiomyocytes stopped working. What would be most directly lost?
options: The supply of ATP to the contracting cells
The direct spread of the contraction signal from cell to cell
The anchoring of the chordae tendineae to the ventricle wall
The anchoring that keeps cells from pulling apart
questions.why: Gap junctions are channels in the intercalated discs that let the electrical signal pass straight from one cardiomyocyte to the next. Without them, the signal could not sweep across the heart muscle, and the cells would no longer contract together as a coordinated unit. That coordinated squeeze is what makes the heart an effective pump.
notes: ATP comes from the mitochondria, which fill about a quarter of each cardiomyocyte. Pick this if the question asked what the mitochondria supply.
Correct. Gap junctions pass the contraction signal from cell to cell, so losing them breaks the coordinated contraction.
The chordae tendineae attach to the papillary muscles, which are part of the ventricle wall. Gap junctions do not hold them, so pick this for a question about papillary muscle damage.
Anchoring cells together is the job of the desmosomes. Pick this if the question asked what would fail if the desmosomes broke down.
questions.answerText: The direct spread of the contraction signal from cell to cell

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Mitochondria fill about a quarter of the volume of each cardiomyocyte. Why does cardiac muscle need so many?
options: To pass the contraction signal between cells
To hold neighboring cells together
To store oxygen for times when blood flow stops
To make the energy for constant, lifelong contraction
questions.why: Mitochondria are the organelles that make ATP, the energy molecule that powers muscle contraction. The heart contracts about once a second for an entire lifetime and cannot pause to rest, so its cells need a large, steady supply of ATP. Packing each cardiomyocyte with mitochondria meets that demand, which also makes the heart heavily dependent on a constant oxygen supply.
notes: Passing the contraction signal between cells is the job of the gap junctions in the intercalated discs. Pick this for a question about gap junctions.
Holding neighboring cells together is the job of the desmosomes in the intercalated discs. Pick this for a question about desmosomes.
Mitochondria do not store oxygen. Oxygen is held in muscle by myoglobin, a protein, and the heart has only a small reserve, which is why it is damaged quickly when blood flow stops.
Correct. Abundant mitochondria supply ATP for the heart's nonstop work.
questions.answerText: To make the energy for constant, lifelong contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The signal for each heartbeat starts at the SA node, spreads across the atria, and then pauses briefly at the AV node before reaching the ventricles. Why is this short delay useful?
options: It lets the right and left ventricles contract at different times
It lets the atria finish filling the ventricles first
It lets the ventricles contract first so the atria can fill
It gives the SA node time to make the next signal
questions.why: For the heart to pump well, the ventricles should be full before they squeeze. The brief hold at the AV node gives the atria time to contract and push their last blood into the ventricles. Then the signal travels on through the AV bundle, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, and the ventricles contract with a full load.
notes: The right and left ventricles contract together, since the signal reaches both through the bundle branches at nearly the same time. The delay separates the atria from the ventricles, not the two ventricles from each other.
Correct. The AV node delay lets the atria finish filling the ventricles.
This reverses the order. The atria contract first and the ventricles follow, so the delay lets ventricular filling finish before ventricular contraction.
The SA node sets its own rhythm and does not wait on the AV node. The pause affects how the signal passes to the ventricles, not when the next beat starts.
questions.answerText: It lets the atria finish filling the ventricles first

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which structure of the cardiac conduction system is the natural pacemaker of the heart?
options: The atrioventricular node
The sinoatrial node
The Purkinje fibers
The atrioventricular bundle
questions.why: The sinoatrial (SA) node is a small cluster of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium. It fires on its own faster than any other part of the conduction system, about 60 to 100 times a minute, so its signal sets the pace for the whole heart. That is why it is called the natural pacemaker, and it is the first stop in the conduction pathway.
notes: The AV node sits in the floor of the right atrium and briefly delays the signal before passing it on to the ventricles. It is the answer for where the signal pauses, and it can act as a slower backup pacemaker if the SA node fails, but it is not the normal pacemaker.
Correct. The SA node fires first and fastest, so it sets the heart's rhythm.

The Purkinje fibers are the last part of the pathway, spreading the signal through the walls of both ventricles. Pick them if the question asked which structure hands the signal to the ventricular muscle cells.
The AV bundle, also called the bundle of His, carries the signal into the interventricular septum. Choose it if the question asked for the only electrical link between the atria and the ventricles.
questions.answerText: The sinoatrial node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In which chamber wall is the sinoatrial node located?
options: The wall of the right ventricle
The wall of the left ventricle
The wall of the right atrium
The wall of the left atrium
questions.why: The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium, close to where the superior vena cava empties into that chamber. This placement fits the order of the heartbeat. The signal starts at the top of the heart in an atrium, spreads across both atria so they contract first, and only then travels down to the ventricles.
notes: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk and receives the signal late, through the right bundle branch and the Purkinje fibers. Pick it if the question asked which chamber sends blood to the lungs.

The left ventricle has the thickest wall in the heart and receives the signal near the end of the pathway, through the Purkinje fibers. It would fit a question about which chamber pumps blood into the aorta.
Correct. The SA node lies in the right atrial wall near the opening of the superior vena cava.

The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and holds no named node of the conduction system. Students pick it because they remember the SA node is in an atrium, but it is the right atrium, not the left.
questions.answerText: The wall of the right atrium

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The sinoatrial node lies near the opening of which large vein?
options: The inferior vena cava
The superior vena cava
The coronary sinus
A pulmonary vein
questions.why: The SA node lies in the upper part of the right atrial wall, near the opening of the superior vena cava, the large vein that returns blood from the head, neck and upper limbs. This puts the pacemaker high on the heart, so the signal starts at the top and travels downward toward the apex.
notes: The inferior vena cava also opens into the right atrium, but lower down, bringing blood from the trunk and lower limbs. It would be the answer if the question asked which vein returns blood from below the diaphragm.
Correct. The SA node sits in the right atrial wall near where the superior vena cava enters.

The coronary sinus collects blood from the heart's own cardiac veins and opens low on the posterior wall of the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel returns blood from the heart wall itself.
The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, not the right atrium where the SA node sits. Pick them if the question asked which vessels empty into the left atrium.
questions.answerText: The superior vena cava

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Where is the atrioventricular node located?
options: In the floor of the right atrium
In the superior interventricular septum
In the wall of the left ventricle
Throughout both ventricle walls
questions.why: The AV node lies in the floor of the right atrium, close to the interatrial septum, the wall between the two atria. This spot sits right at the junction of the atria and the ventricles, which suits its job. It collects the signal after it crosses the atria, holds it briefly, and then passes it down into the AV bundle.
notes: Correct. The AV node sits in the right atrial floor next to the interatrial septum.

The superior part of the interventricular septum holds the AV bundle, also called the bundle of His, the next structure after the AV node. Pick this location if the question asked where the AV bundle lies.
The left ventricle wall contains Purkinje fibers but no node. Students sometimes place the AV node in a ventricle because of the word ventricular in its name, but the node sits on the atrial side.
This describes the Purkinje fibers, the final part of the pathway. It would be correct if the question asked where the Purkinje fibers are found.
questions.answerText: In the floor of the right atrium

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What is the other name for the atrioventricular bundle?
options: The cardiac plexus
The bundle of His
The Purkinje fibers
The bundle branches
questions.why: The atrioventricular (AV) bundle is also called the bundle of His, after the anatomist who described it. Both names refer to the same short strand of conducting cells that runs from the AV node into the superior interventricular septum. Textbooks, lab lists and ECG reports use the two names interchangeably, so you need to recognize both.
notes: The cardiac plexus is a network of autonomic nerve fibers near the base of the heart, not part of the conduction system itself. Pick it if the question asked how sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves reach the nodes.
Correct. The AV bundle and the bundle of His are the same structure.

The Purkinje fibers are a separate, later part of the pathway, spread through the walls of both ventricles. They would be the answer if the question asked which fibers deliver the signal to the ventricular muscle.

The right and left bundle branches are what the AV bundle splits into, and they run down either side of the interventricular septum. Choose them if the question asked which structures come right after the bundle of His.
questions.answerText: The bundle of His

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In which part of the heart does the atrioventricular bundle lie?
options: The upper interventricular septum
The floor of the right atrium
The wall of the right atrium
The apex of the heart
questions.why: The AV bundle runs from the AV node into the superior part of the interventricular septum, the muscular wall between the two ventricles. To get there it crosses the fibrous skeleton, a framework of dense connective tissue that electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. That makes the AV bundle the only electrical bridge between the upper and lower chambers, and just below this point it splits into the right and left bundle branches.
notes: Correct. The AV bundle lies in the upper part of the interventricular septum.
The floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum is where the AV node sits, one step before the AV bundle. Pick it if the question asked for the location of the AV node.
The wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava holds the SA node. Pick it if the question asked where the pacemaker is.
The apex is the pointed bottom of the heart, where the bundle branches deliver the signal to the Purkinje fibers. It would fit a question about where ventricular contraction begins.
questions.answerText: The upper interventricular septum

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: How many bundle branches carry the signal down the interventricular septum?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.why: The AV bundle divides into two bundle branches, a right bundle branch and a left bundle branch. They run down the right and left sides of the interventricular septum toward the apex, so each ventricle gets its own branch of the signal. At the apex they pass the signal on to the Purkinje fibers.
notes: One is the number of AV bundles. Students who confuse the single bundle of His with the branches it splits into tend to pick this number.
Correct. There is a right bundle branch and a left bundle branch, one for each ventricle.
Three may come from counting the AV bundle together with its two branches. The bundle itself divides into just two branches, one for each ventricle.
Four matches the number of heart chambers, which is a common mix-up. Only the two ventricles receive bundle branches, so there are two, not four.
questions.answerText: Two

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Where are the Purkinje fibers located?
options: In the floor of the right atrium
Throughout the walls of both ventricles
In the superior interventricular septum
In the wall of the right atrium
questions.why: The Purkinje fibers branch through the walls of both ventricles, spreading out from the apex into the ventricular muscle. They are the last part of the conduction pathway and hand the signal directly to the contractile cells, the ordinary working heart muscle cells. Because they fan out from the bottom of the heart, the ventricles contract from the apex upward.
notes: The floor of the right atrium, near the interatrial septum, holds the AV node. Pick this location if the question asked where the signal pauses before entering the ventricles.
Correct. The Purkinje fibers spread through the walls of both ventricles.
The superior interventricular septum holds the AV bundle, which comes before the bundle branches and the Purkinje fibers. Choose it if the question asked where the bundle of His lies.
The right atrial wall holds the SA node near the superior vena cava. It would be correct if the question asked where the pacemaker sits.
questions.answerText: Throughout the walls of both ventricles

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which region of the brain contains the cardiac centers that adjust heart rate?
options: The medulla oblongata
The midbrain
The cerebellum
The thalamus
questions.why: The cardiac centers are regions of the medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, autonomic nerves travel to the heart and reach the SA and AV nodes through the cardiac plexus, where they speed up or slow down the rate the SA node sets. The medulla also holds centers for breathing, which is one reason damage to it is so dangerous.
notes: Correct. The cardiac centers sit in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem.

The midbrain is the upper part of the brainstem, above the pons, and holds visual and auditory reflex centers. Students pick it because it is part of the brainstem, but the cardiac centers are lower down, in the medulla.
The cerebellum sits behind the brainstem and coordinates balance and smooth movement. Pick it if the question asked which brain region fine-tunes skeletal muscle movement.
The thalamus is part of the diencephalon and relays sensory information to the cerebral cortex. It would be the answer for the brain's main sensory relay station.
questions.answerText: The medulla oblongata

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What is the cardiac plexus?
options: A cluster of pacemaker cells in the right atrial wall
A strand of conducting cells in the interventricular septum
A fine network of conducting fibers in the ventricle walls
A network of autonomic nerve fibers near the base of the heart
questions.why: The cardiac plexus is a network of autonomic nerve fibers near the base of the heart, close to the great vessels. Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers pass through it to reach the SA and AV nodes, where they adjust the heart rate. It is part of the heart's nerve supply, not part of the conduction system itself.
notes: This describes the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker. Pick it if the question asked what the SA node is.

This describes the AV bundle, or bundle of His. Choose it if the question asked for the only electrical link between the atria and the ventricles. The plexus is made of nerve fibers, not conducting muscle cells.
This describes the Purkinje fibers, the last part of the conduction pathway. It would be correct if the question asked what delivers the signal to the ventricular muscle.
Correct. The cardiac plexus is the nerve network that carries autonomic fibers to the nodes.
questions.answerText: A network of autonomic nerve fibers near the base of the heart

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart rate?
options: The vagus nerve
The phrenic nerve
The trigeminal nerve
The facial nerve
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibers reach the heart in the vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, which leaves the medulla and travels down through the neck into the thorax. Its fibers join the cardiac plexus and end at the SA and AV nodes, where they slow the heart rate. The name vagus means wandering, which fits a cranial nerve that reaches all the way into the thorax and abdomen.
notes: Correct. The vagus nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart.

The phrenic nerve comes from the cervical plexus and runs down through the thorax alongside the pericardium to reach the diaphragm. Students pick it because it passes right beside the heart, but it does not adjust heart rate. Pick it if the question asked which nerve travels to the diaphragm.
The trigeminal nerve, cranial nerve V, is the main sensory nerve of the face and has three divisions. Choose it if the question asked which cranial nerve carries touch and pain from the face.
The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, exits the skull near the ear and spreads across the face. It would be the answer for a cranial nerve that branches over the face, not one that reaches the heart.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which conduction structure fires fastest, about 60 to 100 times a minute, and therefore sets the heart rate?
options: The bundle branches
The Purkinje fibers
The atrioventricular node
The sinoatrial node
questions.why: Several parts of the conduction system can fire on their own, but the SA node fires fastest, about 60 to 100 times a minute. Because its signal arrives before the slower sites have a chance to fire, it sets the pace for the entire heart. A normal rhythm started by the SA node is called a sinus rhythm.
notes: The bundle branches carry the signal down both sides of the interventricular septum and do not set the rate. Pick them if the question asked which structures run toward the apex from the AV bundle.

The Purkinje fibers can fire on their own only very slowly, so they never set the normal pace. They would be correct if the question asked which structures spread the signal through the ventricle walls.

The AV node can fire on its own, but more slowly than the SA node, so normally it just relays the signal after a short delay. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure takes over as a backup pacemaker if the SA node fails.
Correct. The SA node is the fastest site, so it sets the heart rate.
questions.answerText: The sinoatrial node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which conduction structure is the only electrical link between the atria and the ventricles?
options: The Purkinje fibers
The bundle branches
The sinoatrial node
The atrioventricular bundle
questions.why: The atria and ventricles are separated by the fibrous skeleton, a framework of dense connective tissue that does not conduct electrical signals. The AV bundle, or bundle of His, is the one strand of conducting tissue that passes through it, so every normal heartbeat must travel this route to reach the ventricles. This is why damage at the AV node or AV bundle can disconnect the atrial beat from the ventricular beat.
notes: The Purkinje fibers spread the signal within the ventricle walls and do not cross between the atria and the ventricles. Choose them if the question asked which structures reach the contractile cells of the ventricles.
The bundle branches are already below the fibrous skeleton, carrying the signal down the septum between the ventricles. They would be correct if the question asked what the AV bundle divides into.
The SA node is the pacemaker in the right atrial wall and starts the signal, but it sits entirely on the atrial side. Pick it if the question asked which structure fires first.
Correct. The AV bundle is the only conducting path through the fibrous skeleton.
questions.answerText: The atrioventricular bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, which structure comes just before the bundle branches?
options: The atrioventricular node
The atrioventricular bundle
The Purkinje fibers
The sinoatrial node
questions.why: The pathway runs SA node, across the atria, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, then Purkinje fibers. The AV bundle sits directly before the bundle branches because it is the single trunk that divides into the right and left branches at the top of the interventricular septum.
notes: The AV node comes two steps before the bundle branches, with the AV bundle between them. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure lies just before the AV bundle.
Correct. The AV bundle divides into the bundle branches.
The Purkinje fibers come just after the bundle branches, not before them. Choose them if the question asked which structure the bundle branches hand the signal to.
The SA node is the first structure in the pathway, several steps before the bundle branches. Pick it if the question asked which structure starts each heartbeat.
questions.answerText: The atrioventricular bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which conduction structure delivers the signal directly to the contractile cells of the ventricle walls?
options: The atrioventricular node
The Purkinje fibers
The bundle branches
The atrioventricular bundle
questions.why: The Purkinje fibers branch through the walls of both ventricles and connect with the contractile cells, the ordinary cardiac muscle cells that do the pumping. They are the final link in the conduction pathway. Once the Purkinje fibers deliver the signal, the ventricular muscle contracts.
notes: The AV node is in the floor of the right atrium and delays the signal before it enters the ventricles. It would be correct if the question asked where the signal pauses.
Correct. The Purkinje fibers are the last step, handing the signal to the working ventricular muscle.

The bundle branches carry the signal down the interventricular septum toward the apex, one step before the Purkinje fibers. Pick them if the question asked which structures run down either side of the septum.
The AV bundle carries the signal from the AV node into the top of the interventricular septum. Choose it if the question asked for the only electrical bridge between the atria and the ventricles.
questions.answerText: The Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: At which structure of the conduction system does the signal pause briefly before entering the ventricles?
options: The bundle branches
The Purkinje fibers
The sinoatrial node
The atrioventricular node
questions.why: After the signal spreads across both atria, it reaches the AV node in the floor of the right atrium and slows down there for a fraction of a second. This brief delay gives the atria time to finish squeezing their blood into the ventricles before the ventricles are signaled to contract. After the pause, the signal continues into the AV bundle.
