To hold cells together during forceful contractions
To pass the electrical signal to the next cell
To keep the valve cusps from flipping backward
questions.why: Every heartbeat pulls hard on the cardiomyocytes, and the heart keeps beating for a lifetime. Desmosomes are anchoring junctions in the intercalated discs that rivet neighboring cells together, so the force of contraction is shared across the wall instead of pulling cells apart.
notes: Setting the pace is the job of the SA node, the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium. Choose it for what starts each heartbeat, not for what holds cells together.
Correct. Desmosomes keep cardiomyocytes attached under the strain of contraction.
Passing the signal is the job of gap junctions, the channel junctions in the same intercalated discs. This would be the answer for how the signal spreads between cells.
Keeping the atrioventricular valve cusps from flipping back is the job of the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Pick them for a question about stopping backflow into the atria.
questions.answerText: To hold cells together during forceful contractions

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: How does the branching of cardiomyocytes help the heart work?
options: It lets each cell contract independently of the others
It anchors the myocardium firmly to the fibrous pericardium
It links each cell to several neighbors in a connected network
It gives each cell several nuclei for faster repair
questions.why: Each cardiomyocyte splits into branches that join several neighboring cells at intercalated discs. This builds an interconnected network, so the contraction signal spreads in many directions at once and the wall squeezes in a coordinated way. A row of unbranched cells could pass the signal along only a single line.
notes: This is the opposite of what branching does. Cardiac cells are linked so they contract together; separate units contracting on their own is closer to how skeletal muscle uses its motor units.

The myocardium is not attached to the fibrous pericardium; the serous pericardium and the pericardial cavity lie between them. The fibrous pericardium anchors the whole heart in the mediastinum, which would be the answer for what holds the heart in place.
Correct. Branching connects each cell to several others so the signal spreads through a network.
Cardiomyocytes usually have a single central nucleus, and branching does not add nuclei. Several nuclei per cell is a feature of skeletal muscle fibers, so this choice mixes up the two tissues.
questions.answerText: It links each cell to several neighbors in a connected network

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A disease weakens the desmosomes in a patient's intercalated discs. What is the most likely result in the heart wall?
options: The chordae tendineae detach from the valves
The cells lose their striations
Cardiomyocytes pull apart during contraction
The SA node stops generating impulses
questions.why: Desmosomes are the anchoring junctions in the intercalated discs that hold cardiomyocytes together. Each contraction pulls on these connections, so if the desmosomes are weak the cells can be pulled apart under the strain. The wall then loses its strength as one continuous sheet of muscle.
notes: Chordae tendineae are fibrous cords tying the atrioventricular valve cusps to the papillary muscles, and desmosomes do not attach them. They would be the answer for a question about a valve flipping back into the atrium.
Striations come from the ordered sarcomeres inside each cell, not from the junctions between cells. They would be affected by a problem with the contractile filaments themselves, not with desmosomes.
Correct. Without strong desmosomes, the pull of each beat can separate the cells.

The SA node is a cluster of specialized pacemaker cells in the right atrial wall that starts each beat. Choose it for a question about where the heartbeat begins, which does not depend on the anchoring junctions.
questions.answerText: Cardiomyocytes pull apart during contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which pair of structures gives cardiomyocytes both electrical and mechanical coordination with their neighbors?
options: T tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum inside each cell
Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles in the ventricles
Gap junctions and desmosomes in the intercalated discs
SA node and AV node in the right atrium
questions.why: The intercalated disc contains two kinds of junction with complementary jobs. Gap junctions are channels that pass the electrical signal from cell to cell, which gives electrical coordination, and desmosomes rivet the cells together so they pull as one, which gives mechanical coordination. Together they let the myocardium behave like a single unit.
notes: T tubules and the sarcoplasmic reticulum work inside a single muscle cell, carrying the signal inward and storing calcium. They would be the answer for structures within one cell, not for links between neighboring cells.
Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles hold the atrioventricular valves shut when the ventricles contract. Pick them for a question about preventing backflow into the atria.
Correct. Gap junctions coordinate the cells electrically and desmosomes coordinate them mechanically.
The SA and AV nodes are parts of the conduction system that start and delay the heartbeat. They set the timing of the whole heart, but they do not join individual cells to one another.
questions.answerText: Gap junctions and desmosomes in the intercalated discs

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Cardiac muscle acts as a functional syncytium, meaning its separate cells contract together as if they were one large cell. Which feature makes this possible?
options: Desmosomes within the intercalated discs
Abundant mitochondria in each cell
A single central nucleus in each cell
Gap junctions within the intercalated discs
questions.why: A syncytium is a mass of cytoplasm that works as one cell. Cardiomyocytes are separate cells, but the gap junctions in their intercalated discs connect their cytoplasm so the electrical signal passes straight through. Because every cell receives the signal almost at once, the whole chamber contracts together, which is why the myocardium is called a functional syncytium.
notes: Desmosomes hold the cells together mechanically, but they do not pass the signal, so on their own they could not make the cells contract in unison. Choose them for what stops cells from pulling apart.

Abundant mitochondria, about a quarter of the cell volume, supply the energy for constant contraction. Pick them for a question about how heart muscle keeps working without tiring, not about how cells act as one unit.

Having one central nucleus helps you recognize a cardiomyocyte on a slide, but it does nothing to link cells. It would be the answer for how cardiac cells differ from multinucleated skeletal muscle fibers.
Correct. Gap junctions pass the signal through the cells so they contract as one unit.
questions.answerText: Gap junctions within the intercalated discs

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What is the cardiac conduction system?
options: Nerves from the brainstem that start each heartbeat
Valves and cords that keep blood moving in one direction
Coronary vessels that supply oxygen to the heart wall
Specialized heart muscle cells that start and spread each beat
questions.why: The cardiac conduction system is a network of specialized cardiac muscle cells, about one percent of the cardiac fibers, that generates the signal for each heartbeat and spreads it in a fixed order. It runs from the SA node across the atria to the AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers. This order makes the atria contract first and the ventricles second.
notes: Nerves from the cardiac centers in the medulla oblongata only speed up or slow down the heart. They do not start the beat, which is why a transplanted heart with its nerves cut still beats.
The valves, chordae tendineae, and papillary muscles keep blood flowing in one direction. Choose them for a question about preventing backflow, not about the electrical signal.
The coronary vessels deliver oxygen to the heart wall and drain it. They would be the answer for coronary circulation, not for what generates the heartbeat.
Correct. The conduction system is specialized cardiac muscle that starts and spreads the beat.
questions.answerText: Specialized heart muscle cells that start and spread each beat

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What is autorhythmicity?
options: Skeletal muscle's ability to contract when we choose
The heart's ability to set its own rhythm without nerve input
The steady, rhythmic closing of the heart valves
The brainstem's control of heart rate through the vagus nerve
questions.why: Autorhythmicity means self-rhythm: the heart's built-in ability to generate its own beat without a signal from the nervous system. It belongs to the conducting cells of the conduction system, especially the SA node, which fires on its own about sixty to one hundred times a minute. Nerves can adjust this rate, but they do not create it.
notes: Contracting on command describes voluntary skeletal muscle, which needs a nerve signal for every contraction. Cardiac muscle is different because it starts its own beat.
Correct. Autorhythmicity is the heart generating its own beat.
Valves open and close passively as pressures change in the chambers; they do not create a rhythm. Choose the valves for a question about one-way blood flow.
The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart rate. That is nervous adjustment of the rate, the opposite of the heart setting its own rhythm.
questions.answerText: The heart's ability to set its own rhythm without nerve input

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What are the conducting cells of the heart?
options: Endothelial cells that line the heart chambers
Ordinary working cardiomyocytes that contract when signaled
Neurons in the cardiac plexus that start each heartbeat
Non-contractile cells that generate and carry the signal
questions.why: Conducting cells are specialized cardiac muscle cells that do little or no contracting. Their job is to generate the electrical signal and carry it through the heart along the conduction pathway. They make up the SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers.
notes: Endothelial cells form the smooth endocardium lining the chambers and covering the valves. They would be the answer for the inner layer of the heart wall.

Ordinary working cardiomyocytes are the contractile cells. They make up most of the myocardium and contract when the signal reaches them, so they would be the answer for the cells that generate force.
The cardiac plexus is a network of autonomic nerve fibers near the base of the heart that adjusts the rate. Its fibers change the pace but do not start the heartbeat.
Correct. Conducting cells generate and carry the signal rather than contract.
questions.answerText: Non-contractile cells that generate and carry the signal

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What are the contractile cells of the heart?
options: Purkinje fibers lining the ventricle walls
Pacemaker cells clustered in the SA node
Fibroblasts that build the fibrous skeleton
Working cardiomyocytes that contract when signaled
questions.why: Contractile cells are the ordinary working cardiomyocytes that make up most of the myocardium. They do not start the signal themselves; they contract when the signal from the conduction system reaches them. Their combined contraction is what squeezes blood out of the chambers.
notes: Purkinje fibers are conducting cells that deliver the signal to the contractile cells of the ventricle walls. Choose them for the last part of the conduction pathway.
Pacemaker cells of the SA node are conducting cells that generate the signal. They are the answer for where each heartbeat starts, not for the cells that do the squeezing.
Fibroblasts make the dense connective tissue of the fibrous skeleton, which anchors the valves and insulates the atria from the ventricles. They are not muscle cells and do not contract.
Correct. Contractile cells are the working cardiomyocytes that generate force.
questions.answerText: Working cardiomyocytes that contract when signaled

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker?
options: Purkinje fibers
SA node
AV bundle
AV node
questions.why: The SA node, or sinoatrial node, is the heart's natural pacemaker. It sits in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava and fires faster than any other part of the conduction system, about sixty to one hundred times a minute. Because it fires first, it sets the pace for the whole heart.
notes: Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricle walls at the end of the pathway. Choose them for the structures that deliver the signal to the ventricular contractile cells.
Correct. The SA node fires first and sets the heart rate.
The AV bundle (bundle of His) carries the signal from the AV node into the interventricular septum. It is the only electrical bridge between atria and ventricles, not the starting point.

The AV node, in the floor of the right atrium, receives the signal from the atria and delays it briefly before passing it on. It can take over as a slower backup pacemaker if the SA node fails, but it is not the normal pacemaker.
questions.answerText: SA node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What does SA node stand for?
options: Sinoatrial node
Septal arterial node
Atrioventricular node
Semilunar atrial node
questions.why: SA stands for sinoatrial. The name points to its location: the sino part refers to the sinus venarum, the smooth-walled part of the right atrium where the venae cavae empty, and atrial tells you the node sits in an atrium. It lies in the right atrial wall near the opening of the superior vena cava.
notes: Correct. SA stands for sinoatrial.
There is no septal arterial node. The S in SA comes from sinus, and the node is made of specialized muscle cells, not an artery.
Atrioventricular is what AV stands for in the AV node, the second node in the pathway, at the junction between the right atrium and the ventricles. Choose it for the AV node.
Semilunar describes the half-moon cusps of the pulmonary and aortic valves, not a node. This mix-up comes from seeing the letter S in both terms.
questions.answerText: Sinoatrial node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What does AV node stand for?
options: Apical ventricular node
Aortic valve node
Arteriovenous node
Atrioventricular node
questions.why: AV stands for atrioventricular, meaning it relates to both an atrium and a ventricle. The AV node sits in the floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum, at the junction where the signal must cross from the atria to the ventricles. It delays the signal briefly and then passes it into the AV bundle.
notes: There is no apical ventricular node. The apex is where the bundle branches carry the signal, but the AV node itself sits in the floor of the right atrium.

AV is also used as an abbreviation for the aortic valve, which is why this mix-up is common. The aortic valve is the semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta, not part of the conduction system.
Arteriovenous describes a direct connection from an artery to a vein, as in an arteriovenous anastomosis. Choose it for a vessel that bypasses capillaries, not for a node.
Correct. AV stands for atrioventricular.
questions.answerText: Atrioventricular node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What is the AV bundle also called?
options: Bundle branches
Crista terminalis
Bundle of His
Moderator band
questions.why: The AV bundle, or atrioventricular bundle, is also called the bundle of His. It picks up the signal from the AV node and carries it into the superior part of the interventricular septum. It is the only electrical link between the atria and the ventricles, and it soon splits into the right and left bundle branches.
notes: The bundle branches are the next step after the bundle of His, carrying the signal down each side of the septum. They are what the AV bundle divides into, not another name for it.

The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the right atrium separating its smooth posterior wall from the rough, pectinate anterior wall. It is a surface landmark, not part of the conduction pathway.
Correct. The AV bundle is the bundle of His.

The moderator band, or septomarginal trabecula, is a muscular band in the right ventricle that carries part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle. Choose it for that band, not for the AV bundle.
questions.answerText: Bundle of His

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Where is the AV bundle located?
options: Floor of the right atrium
Right atrial wall near the superior vena cava
Superior interventricular septum
Walls of both ventricles
questions.why: The AV bundle lies in the superior part of the interventricular septum, just below the AV node. It is the one place where the signal can pass through the fibrous skeleton that otherwise insulates the atria from the ventricles. From there it divides into the right and left bundle branches, which run down the septum.
notes: The floor of the right atrium, near the interatrial septum, is where the AV node sits. Choose this location for the AV node, one step earlier in the pathway.
The wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava is the location of the SA node. It would be the answer for where the pacemaker sits.
Correct. The AV bundle runs in the upper interventricular septum.
The walls of both ventricles hold the Purkinje fibers, which spread the signal to the contractile cells. Choose this location for the last step of the pathway.
questions.answerText: Superior interventricular septum

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The right and left bundle branches carry the signal toward which part of the heart?
options: AV node
Base of the heart
Apex of the heart
Both atria
questions.why: The right and left bundle branches carry the signal down both sides of the interventricular septum toward the apex, the inferior tip of the heart. From there the Purkinje fibers spread it up through the ventricle walls. This route makes the ventricles contract from the apex upward.
notes: The AV node lies upstream of the bundle branches, and the signal has already passed through it. Choose the AV node for the step that delays the signal before the AV bundle.

The base is the broad superior surface where the great vessels attach. The Purkinje fibers eventually spread the signal back up toward the base, but the bundle branches carry it the other way, down toward the apex.
Correct. The bundle branches carry the signal down the septum toward the apex.
The atria received the signal from the SA node at the start of the beat. The bundle branches are in the ventricular septum and carry the signal away from the atria.
questions.answerText: Apex of the heart

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What do the Purkinje fibers do?
options: Delay the signal so the atria can empty
Spread the signal through the ventricle walls
Set the pace of the heartbeat
Carry the signal across the fibrous skeleton
questions.why: Purkinje fibers are the last part of the conduction system. They branch from the bundle branches and run throughout the walls of both ventricles, delivering the signal to the contractile cells. Because they reach the apex first and then spread upward, the ventricles contract from the apex toward the base.
notes: Delaying the signal so the atria can finish emptying is the job of the AV node. It would be the answer for the brief pause between atrial and ventricular contraction.
Correct. Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to the ventricular contractile cells.
Setting the pace is the job of the SA node in the wall of the right atrium. Choose it for the structure that starts each beat.

Carrying the signal across the fibrous skeleton from the atria to the ventricles is the job of the AV bundle, or bundle of His. Pick it for the only electrical bridge between the upper and lower chambers.
questions.answerText: Spread the signal through the ventricle walls

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which sequence traces the cardiac conduction pathway in the correct order?
options: SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches, AV bundle
SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
SA node, AV bundle, AV node, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches
questions.why: The SA node fires first and the signal spreads across both atria, which contract. The signal then reaches the AV node, where it pauses briefly, and passes into the AV bundle in the upper interventricular septum. The right and left bundle branches carry it down the septum toward the apex, and the Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricle walls so the ventricles contract.
notes: This sends the signal backward through the ventricles. The AV bundle comes right after the AV node, and the Purkinje fibers are the last step, not the middle.
Correct. SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.
This swaps the two nodes. The SA node is the pacemaker and always fires first; the AV node receives the signal only after it has crossed the atria.

This puts the AV bundle before the AV node and the Purkinje fibers before the bundle branches. The AV node must pass the signal to the bundle, and the bundle branches must carry it down the septum before the Purkinje fibers spread it.
questions.answerText: SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why does the SA node, rather than another part of the conduction system, normally set the heart rate?
options: It lies closest to the ventricles
It receives a direct signal from the brain for each beat
It is the largest node in the heart
It fires fastest, so it starts each beat before other sites can
questions.why: Several parts of the conduction system can generate signals on their own, but the SA node fires fastest, about sixty to one hundred times a minute. Because it fires first, its signal sweeps through the heart before the slower sites reach their own firing point. That is why the SA node normally sets the pace for the whole heart.
notes: The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, farther from the ventricles than the AV node. Its position near the top of the heart helps the atria contract first, but distance to the ventricles is not why it sets the rate.
Nerves from the brainstem only speed up or slow down the SA node; they do not start each beat. A transplanted heart with its nerves cut still beats at its own rate.
Size does not decide which site sets the pace; firing speed does. This choice treats the pacemaker as a matter of size, which is a common guess but not the reason.
Correct. The fastest site fires first and sets the pace.
questions.answerText: It fires fastest, so it starts each beat before other sites can

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is the AV bundle so important to the heartbeat?
options: It holds the atrioventricular valves shut during contraction
It is the only electrical bridge from the atria to the ventricles
It sets the heart rate for all four chambers
It spreads the signal through the ventricle walls
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton, the dense connective tissue around the valves, separates the atria from the ventricles and does not conduct electrical signals. The AV bundle passes through this barrier in the upper interventricular septum, so it is the only route by which the signal can reach the ventricles. Without it, the ventricles would not receive the signal from the atria.
notes: Holding the atrioventricular valves shut is the job of the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Choose them for a question about preventing backflow into the atria.
Correct. The AV bundle is the only electrical link through the fibrous skeleton.
Setting the heart rate is the job of the SA node, which fires fastest. The AV bundle only carries the signal it is given.
Spreading the signal through the ventricle walls is the job of the Purkinje fibers, at the end of the pathway. The AV bundle comes earlier, carrying the signal into the septum.
questions.answerText: It is the only electrical bridge from the atria to the ventricles

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The right and left bundle branches run down which structure?
options: Wall of the right atrium
Outer surface of the ventricles
Interatrial septum
Interventricular septum
questions.why: After the AV bundle enters the top of the interventricular septum, it splits into the right and left bundle branches. These run down the right and left sides of the septum toward the apex. Because they travel inside the septum, damage to the septum, such as an infarction there, can interrupt the signal to the ventricles.
notes: The wall of the right atrium holds the SA node, near the opening of the superior vena cava. Choose it for the location of the pacemaker.
The outer surface of the ventricles is where the coronary arteries and cardiac veins run in their grooves. The bundle branches run inside the septum, not on the surface.
The interatrial septum is the wall between the two atria, where the fossa ovalis sits. The AV node lies near it, but the bundle branches are lower, in the ventricular septum.
Correct. The bundle branches run down both sides of the interventricular septum.
questions.answerText: Interventricular septum

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The ventricles contract from the apex upward. What does this accomplish?
options: It pushes blood upward toward the outflow valves at the base
It lets the ventricles fill from below
It keeps the atrioventricular valves open during contraction
It pushes blood back into the atria
questions.why: The pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles at the base of the heart, at the top. Because the Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to the apex first, contraction starts at the bottom and moves upward, squeezing blood toward the semilunar valves much like squeezing a toothpaste tube from the closed end. This wringing action empties the ventricles efficiently into the great arteries.
notes: Correct. Apex-to-base contraction drives blood toward the exits at the base.
The ventricles fill while they are relaxed, from the atria above through the atrioventricular valves. Contraction is for emptying, not filling.
The atrioventricular valves close, not open, when the ventricles contract. Keeping them open would let blood leak back into the atria.

Blood is kept from going back into the atria by the closed atrioventricular valves, held by the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Pushing blood back into the atria would be backflow, which the heart is built to prevent.
questions.answerText: It pushes blood upward toward the outflow valves at the base

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares conducting cells and contractile cells in the heart?
options: Conducting cells generate and carry the signal; contractile cells generate force
Conducting cells generate force; contractile cells carry the signal
Conducting cells are nerve cells; contractile cells are cardiac muscle cells
Both contract strongly, but only contractile cells have gap junctions
questions.why: Both kinds of cell are cardiac muscle, but they have different jobs. Conducting cells, such as those in the SA node, AV node, and Purkinje fibers, generate the electrical signal and carry it through the heart with little or no contraction. Contractile cells are the ordinary working cardiomyocytes that make up most of the myocardium and generate the force that pumps blood when the signal reaches them.
notes: Correct. Conducting cells handle the signal and contractile cells do the pumping.
This swaps the two jobs. Contractile cells are named for what they do, contracting, while conducting cells conduct the signal.
Conducting cells are specialized cardiac muscle cells, not neurons. Nerves reach the heart through the cardiac plexus, but they only adjust the rate set by the conducting cells.
Conducting cells do little or no contracting, and gap junctions link cardiac cells of both kinds so the signal can pass between them. This choice gets both halves wrong.
questions.answerText: Conducting cells generate and carry the signal; contractile cells generate force

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the SA node and the AV node?
options: The AV node starts each beat; the SA node delays the signal and passes it on
The SA node signals the ventricles directly; the AV node controls only the atria
The SA node starts each beat; the AV node delays the signal and passes it on
Both nodes sit in the interventricular septum and send the signal to the apex
questions.why: The SA node, in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, is the pacemaker that fires first and starts each heartbeat. The signal spreads across the atria to the AV node, in the floor of the right atrium, which holds it briefly so the atria can finish emptying. The AV node then passes the signal into the AV bundle and on to the ventricles.
notes: This swaps the two nodes. The SA node fires fastest and so starts the beat; the AV node is the second stop, where the signal pauses.
The SA node's signal cannot reach the ventricles directly because the fibrous skeleton insulates them from the atria. It must pass through the AV node and AV bundle first.
Correct. The SA node starts the beat and the AV node delays and relays it.
Both nodes are in the right atrium, not the interventricular septum. The structures in the septum are the AV bundle and the bundle branches.
questions.answerText: The SA node starts each beat; the AV node delays the signal and passes it on

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which conduction structure passes through the fibrous skeleton to connect the atria electrically to the ventricles?
options: Purkinje fibers
SA node
Moderator band
AV bundle
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton is a set of dense connective tissue rings around the valves that electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles. The AV bundle, or bundle of His, is the one conduction pathway that crosses it, carrying the signal from the AV node into the top of the interventricular septum. Every signal the ventricles receive comes through this bridge.
notes: Purkinje fibers are in the ventricle walls, beyond the fibrous skeleton. They spread the signal after it has already crossed over.
The SA node starts the signal in the wall of the right atrium, but it lies entirely within the atrium. It is the answer for the pacemaker, not the bridge.

The moderator band is a muscular band inside the right ventricle that carries part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle. It lies within the ventricle and does not cross the fibrous skeleton.
Correct. The AV bundle is the bridge through the fibrous skeleton.
questions.answerText: AV bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which pair of conduction structures spreads the signal through the ventricles?
options: SA node and bundle branches
AV node and AV bundle
Bundle branches and Purkinje fibers
SA node and AV node
questions.why: Once the signal crosses into the ventricles through the AV bundle, the right and left bundle branches carry it down both sides of the interventricular septum toward the apex. The Purkinje fibers then spread it through the walls of both ventricles to the contractile cells. These two structures are the ventricular part of the conduction system.
notes: The bundle branches are ventricular, but the SA node is in the right atrium. This pair mixes the first and fourth steps of the pathway.

The AV node and AV bundle carry the signal from the atria to the top of the septum, the bridge into the ventricles. They hand the signal off to the bundle branches but do not spread it through the ventricle walls.
Correct. The bundle branches and Purkinje fibers distribute the signal through the ventricles.
The SA and AV nodes are both in the right atrium. They start and delay the signal, so they are the answer for the atrial part of the pathway.
questions.answerText: Bundle branches and Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why must the atria contract before the ventricles?
options: So the atria can receive blood from the ventricles
So the semilunar valves stay closed
So the coronary arteries can supply the atria first
So the ventricles are filled before they eject blood
questions.why: The ventricles are the main pumps, and they can only push out the blood they hold. When the atria contract first, they top off the ventricles with a final push of blood. The ventricles then contract while full, which is why the conduction system is arranged so the atria go first and the ventricles second.
notes: Blood never flows from the ventricles back into the atria in a normal heart; the atrioventricular valves prevent it. The atria receive blood from veins, not from the ventricles.

The semilunar valves stay closed while the ventricles fill and open when the ventricles contract. The order of atrial and ventricular contraction is about filling the ventricles, not holding these valves shut.
The coronary arteries supply all of the heart wall and are not the reason for the contraction order. This choice links two unrelated systems.
Correct. Atrial contraction tops off the ventricles before they pump.
questions.answerText: So the ventricles are filled before they eject blood

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What would happen if the ventricles contracted before the atria had emptied into them?
options: The aortic valve would stay closed permanently
The ventricles would eject less blood, being underfilled
Blood would flow from the aorta back into the lungs
The ventricles would eject more blood than usual
questions.why: The atria finish filling the ventricles with their final contraction. If the ventricles contracted first, they would squeeze down before that last push of blood arrived, so each beat would send out less blood. The atria would also be pushing against closed atrioventricular valves, so their contraction would be wasted.
notes: The aortic valve still opens whenever the left ventricle contracts with enough force. The problem would be a smaller volume of blood, not a valve that never opens.
Correct. Underfilled ventricles pump out less blood.
There is no direct route from the aorta back to the lungs in an adult heart, and the aortic valve stops backflow into the ventricle. This choice invents a path blood cannot take.
Less filling means less blood to eject, not more. A ventricle can only push out what it holds.
questions.answerText: The ventricles would eject less blood, being underfilled

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how autorhythmicity differs from nervous control of the heart?
options: Nerves start each beat; autorhythmicity only adjusts the rate
Autorhythmicity starts the beat; nerves only speed it up or slow it down
Autorhythmicity controls the atria; nerves control the ventricles
Both start the beat, so the heart stops if either is lost
questions.why: Autorhythmicity is the heart's built-in ability to generate its own beat, centered on the SA node. The autonomic nerves, sympathetic fibers that speed the rate and parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve that slow it, only adjust the pace the SA node already sets. A transplanted heart, whose nerves have been cut, still beats on its own.
notes: This reverses the roles. The conduction system starts every beat, and the nerves change how fast it happens.
Correct. The heart starts its own beat, and nerves adjust the rate.

Both systems affect the whole heart rather than splitting it into atria and ventricles. The SA node starts the beat for all four chambers, and the nerves reach the SA and AV nodes to adjust the overall rate.
The heart does not stop when its nerves are lost, as heart transplants show. Only the conduction system is needed to start the beat.
questions.answerText: Autorhythmicity starts the beat; nerves only speed it up or slow it down

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A patient's AV node is damaged, so the signal is delayed or stopped there. What timing problem can result?
options: The SA node is forced to fire faster
The atria stop receiving the signal
The atria and ventricles beat out of step
The atrioventricular valves stay open
questions.why: A block at the AV node is called heart block. The SA node still fires and the atria still contract, but the signal is delayed or stopped before it reaches the ventricles. The ventricles may then beat late, skip beats, or beat at a slower rate of their own, so the atria and ventricles fall out of step.
notes: AV node damage does not change how fast the SA node fires. A fast resting rate would be tachycardia, a different disorder.
The atria receive the signal from the SA node before it ever reaches the AV node, so they still contract. The problem lies downstream, between the atria and the ventricles.
Correct. A block at the AV node disconnects atrial and ventricular timing.

The atrioventricular valves close because of pressure changes when the ventricles contract, and the chordae tendineae hold them shut. AV node damage affects the timing signal, not the valves themselves.
questions.answerText: The atria and ventricles beat out of step

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: If the brief delay at the AV node disappeared, how would ventricular filling be affected?
options: The ventricles would contract before the atria finished emptying
Filling would not change, because the delay has no purpose
The ventricles would fill more completely than usual
The atria would contract after the ventricles
questions.why: The pause at the AV node holds the signal just long enough for the atria to finish pushing blood into the ventricles. Without it, the signal would race into the ventricles while the atria were still contracting, and the ventricles would squeeze down before they were completely full. Each beat would then pump out less blood.
notes: Correct. Without the delay, the ventricles would contract before they were full.
The delay is essential timing, not a flaw. It is what lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
Removing the delay would cut filling short, not improve it. The delay exists to give the ventricles extra filling time.
The atria would still fire first, since the SA node sits in the atrium. The problem is that the ventricles would follow too soon, overlapping with atrial contraction.
questions.answerText: The ventricles would contract before the atria finished emptying

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: If the AV bundle is blocked, what major conduction problem occurs?
options: The Purkinje fibers fire faster to compensate
The SA node stops firing altogether
The atria no longer receive the signal
The signal cannot reach the ventricles normally
questions.why: The AV bundle is the only electrical bridge through the fibrous skeleton between the atria and the ventricles. If it is blocked, the signal from the SA node still spreads across the atria but cannot reach the ventricles normally. The atria and ventricles then lose their coordination, a form of heart block.
notes: If the ventricles lose the signal from above, cells lower in the conduction system may take over, but they fire more slowly than the SA node, not faster. This choice reverses that pattern.
The SA node lies upstream in the right atrium and keeps firing normally. A block in the AV bundle does not reach back to the pacemaker.
The atria get the signal from the SA node before it reaches the AV bundle, so they still contract. The loss is on the ventricular side of the block.
Correct. With the bridge blocked, the signal cannot cross to the ventricles normally.
questions.answerText: The signal cannot reach the ventricles normally

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Damage to the bundle branches would most directly affect which chambers?
options: Right atrium only
Both ventricles
Both atria
Left atrium only
questions.why: The bundle branches run down the right and left sides of the interventricular septum and feed the Purkinje fibers in the ventricle walls. Damage to them, called a bundle branch block, delays or blocks the signal to the ventricle on the affected side. The atria are upstream and still receive the signal normally.
notes: The right atrium holds the SA and AV nodes, which lie above the bundle branches. Damage to the bundle branches would not change how the right atrium receives its signal.
Correct. The bundle branches serve the ventricles.
The atria get the signal from the SA node before it reaches the AV node and bundle. Since the bundle branches are downstream of the atria, damage to them leaves atrial contraction intact.
The left atrium receives the signal as it spreads across both atria from the SA node. It is upstream of the bundle branches and would contract normally.
questions.answerText: Both ventricles

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Damage to the Purkinje fibers would most directly impair what?
options: Coordinated contraction of the ventricle walls
Contraction of the atria
The delay of the signal at the AV node
The pacing of the heartbeat by the SA node
questions.why: Purkinje fibers run throughout the walls of both ventricles and deliver the signal to the contractile cells, starting at the apex and spreading upward. If they are damaged, parts of the ventricle wall receive the signal late or out of order, so the ventricles cannot squeeze in a smooth, coordinated way and pump less effectively.
notes: Correct. Purkinje damage disrupts the orderly squeeze of the ventricles.
The atria contract when the signal spreads from the SA node across their walls. Purkinje fibers are only in the ventricles, so atrial contraction would continue.
The AV node delay happens before the signal reaches the ventricles. Purkinje fibers are downstream of it, so their damage would not change that pause.
The SA node sits at the very start of the pathway in the right atrium. Damage at the far end, in the ventricle walls, does not change how the SA node paces the heart.
questions.answerText: Coordinated contraction of the ventricle walls

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A transplanted heart has had all of its nerves cut, yet it still beats. What explains this?
options: The papillary muscles set the heart's rhythm
The vagus nerve regrows into the heart within minutes
The conduction system generates its own signals
The brain sends signals through the blood to the heart
questions.why: The heartbeat starts inside the heart itself. The SA node and the rest of the conduction system are autorhythmic, meaning they generate their own signals without input from the nervous system. Cutting the nerves removes only the ability to speed up or slow down the rate, so a transplanted heart beats at the SA node's own pace.
notes: Papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae to hold the atrioventricular valves shut. They are contractile muscle, not pacemaker tissue.
Cut nerves do not regrow within minutes, and the vagus nerve only slows the heart anyway. The transplanted heart beats right away because it never needed nerves to start each beat.
Correct. The conduction system starts each beat on its own.
Some hormones carried in the blood can raise the heart rate, but they adjust the pace rather than starting each beat. The signal for each beat comes from the SA node.
questions.answerText: The conduction system generates its own signals

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: If the SA node fails, what can take over pacing the heart?
options: The vagus nerve, which then starts each beat
The cardiac centers of the medulla oblongata
The fibrous skeleton around the valves
Another conduction site or an artificial pacemaker
questions.why: Other parts of the conduction system, such as the AV node, can generate signals on their own, though more slowly than the SA node. If the SA node fails, one of these sites can take over as an ectopic pacemaker, meaning a pacemaker outside its normal location. When this backup is not enough, an implanted artificial pacemaker can deliver timed signals instead.
notes: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart rate. It can only adjust the pace, never start the beat.
The cardiac centers in the medulla oblongata adjust the rate through autonomic nerves. They do not generate the beat, which is why a heart beats even when its nerves are cut.
The fibrous skeleton is dense connective tissue that insulates the atria from the ventricles. It cannot conduct a signal, let alone start one.
Correct. A backup site in the conduction system or an implanted device can take over.
questions.answerText: Another conduction site or an artificial pacemaker

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is an ectopic pacemaker considered abnormal?
options: The delay at the AV node grows longer
The nerves to the heart have been cut
A site outside the SA node takes over the rhythm
The SA node fires faster than its usual rate
questions.why: Ectopic means out of place. An ectopic pacemaker is any site outside the SA node that takes over setting the heart's rhythm. Because the beat no longer starts in the normal place, the signal may spread in an unusual order, and the normal pacing sequence of the heart is lost.
notes: A longer delay at the AV node is a form of heart block. The beat still starts in the SA node, so this is a conduction problem, not an ectopic pacemaker.
Cutting the heart's nerves, as in a transplant, leaves the SA node in charge. The heart still beats from its normal pacemaker.
Correct. Ectopic means the rhythm starts somewhere other than the SA node.
An SA node firing too fast is tachycardia, an abnormal rate. The pacemaker is still in its normal place, so it is not ectopic.
questions.answerText: A site outside the SA node takes over the rhythm

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Suppose the ventricles contracted from the base downward instead of from the apex upward. Why would this be inefficient?
options: The atrioventricular valves would never open
The coronary arteries would carry blood backward
Blood would be pushed away from the outflow valves
The atria would contract after the ventricles
questions.why: The pulmonary and aortic valves sit at the base of the ventricles, at the top of the heart. Contracting from the apex upward squeezes blood toward those exits. If contraction began at the base, it would push blood down toward the closed apex, away from the valves, so less blood would leave with each beat.
notes: The atrioventricular valves open when the ventricles relax and fill, which would still happen. The problem would be emptying the ventricles, not filling them.
Coronary blood flow runs from the aorta into the heart wall regardless of how the ventricles contract. The direction of ventricular contraction does not reverse it.
Correct. Base-first contraction would push blood away from the exits at the base.
The order of atrial and ventricular contraction is set by the SA node and the AV node delay, not by the direction the ventricles squeeze. This choice mixes up two different timing ideas.
questions.answerText: Blood would be pushed away from the outflow valves

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A patient's atria contract normally, but the signal never reaches the ventricles. Where is the block most likely to be?
options: At the AV node or AV bundle
At the SA node
In the Purkinje fibers
In the walls of the atria
questions.why: If the atria contract normally, the SA node fired and the signal crossed the atrial walls. The ventricles receive that signal only through the AV node and then the AV bundle, the single bridge through the fibrous skeleton. A signal that stops between the atria and the ventricles must therefore be blocked at the AV node or AV bundle, which is what heart block means.
notes: Correct. The AV node and AV bundle are the only route from atria to ventricles.
If the SA node had failed, the atria would not receive a normal signal either. The atria are contracting here, so the pacemaker is working.
Purkinje fibers are the last step, inside the ventricle walls. Damage there would make ventricular contraction disorganized, but the signal would already have crossed into the ventricles.
The signal has already spread across the atrial walls, since the atria are contracting. A block there would affect the atria themselves.
questions.answerText: At the AV node or AV bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A student says nerves from the brain start each heartbeat. Which correction is accurate?
options: The conduction system starts each beat; nerves only adjust the rate
Hormones in the blood start each heartbeat instead
Nerves start the beat in the atria, and the SA node starts it in the ventricles
The papillary muscles start each beat by pulling on the valves
questions.why: The heartbeat starts in the SA node, part of the heart's own conduction system. Autonomic nerves reach the SA and AV nodes through the cardiac plexus and only speed up or slow down the rate the SA node already sets. That is why a transplanted heart, with its nerves cut, still beats.
notes: Correct. The SA node starts the beat; nerves only change its pace.
Some hormones in the blood can raise the heart rate, but like the nerves they adjust the pace rather than start the beat. The signal for each beat comes from the SA node.
Nerves do not start the beat in any chamber. The SA node starts each beat, and the signal travels through the atria and on to the ventricles through the conduction pathway.
Papillary muscles anchor the chordae tendineae to hold the atrioventricular valves shut during ventricular contraction. They respond to the signal; they do not create it.
questions.answerText: The conduction system starts each beat; nerves only adjust the rate

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is the AV bundle described as the only electrical bridge between the atria and the ventricles?
options: The fibrous skeleton blocks the signal everywhere else
It is the largest bundle of nerves in the heart
It carries blood between the atria and the ventricles
It is the only cardiac tissue with gap junctions
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton is a set of dense connective tissue rings around the four valves. Connective tissue does not conduct the electrical signal, so this layer insulates the atria from the ventricles all the way around. The AV bundle is the one strand of conducting tissue that passes through it, so every signal to the ventricles has to cross there.
notes: Correct. The insulating fibrous skeleton leaves the AV bundle as the only path.
The AV bundle is specialized cardiac muscle, not a bundle of nerves. The nerves that reach the heart only adjust the rate and do not carry the beat from atria to ventricles.
Blood passes from the atria to the ventricles through the atrioventricular valves, not through the AV bundle. The AV bundle carries an electrical signal, not blood.
Gap junctions link cardiomyocytes throughout the heart, in both the atria and the ventricles. They are not unique to the AV bundle, so they cannot explain why it is the only bridge.
questions.answerText: The fibrous skeleton blocks the signal everywhere else

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium. Which chambers does its signal reach first?
options: Left ventricle only
Both atria
Right ventricle only
Both ventricles
questions.why: Because the SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium, its signal spreads across both atria first, and the atria contract. Only after that does the signal reach the AV node, pause, and travel through the AV bundle to the ventricles. Placing the pacemaker in an atrium is what makes the atria contract before the ventricles.
notes: The left ventricle receives the signal through the left bundle branch and Purkinje fibers, after the atria. It is reached late, not first.
Correct. The signal spreads across both atria before anything else.
The right ventricle receives the signal through the right bundle branch, late in the pathway. It is never the first chamber to receive the signal from the SA node.
The ventricles receive the signal last, after it has crossed the atria and passed through the AV node and AV bundle. They would be the answer for where the Purkinje fibers deliver the signal.
questions.answerText: Both atria

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver instead of contracting, but the ventricles keep pumping. What is the main effect?
options: The ventricles fill less completely, but blood still circulates
The ventricles stop receiving any blood
All blood flow stops immediately
The pulmonary circuit stops while the systemic circuit continues
questions.why: Much of ventricular filling happens as blood flows from the atria into the relaxed ventricles, and atrial contraction adds a final top-off. If the atria only quiver, that last push is lost, so the ventricles fill less completely and pump somewhat less. Because the ventricles still contract, blood keeps circulating, which is why atrial fibrillation is common and treatable rather than an immediate emergency.
notes: Correct. Filling is less efficient, but the ventricles keep the blood moving.
Blood still flows from the atria into the ventricles through the open atrioventricular valves while the ventricles relax. Losing the atrial contraction reduces filling but does not stop it.
Blood flow stops only when the ventricles fail to pump, as in ventricular fibrillation. Here the ventricles are still contracting, so blood keeps moving.
Both circuits are driven by the ventricles, which are still working. Losing atrial contraction affects both sides and does not shut down one circuit.
questions.answerText: The ventricles fill less completely, but blood still circulates

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In ventricular fibrillation, the signals in the ventricles are rapid and disorganized. Why is this life-threatening?
options: The atria stop receiving blood from the veins
The coronary sinus overfills with blood
The valves seal shut and cannot open again
The ventricles quiver and move almost no blood
questions.why: Pumping depends on the ventricle walls squeezing together in order, from the apex upward. In ventricular fibrillation the signals are chaotic, so the muscle only quivers and moves little or no blood into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. The body and the heart wall itself lose their blood supply within minutes, which is why it is treated as an emergency with a defibrillator.
notes: The atria still receive blood from the veins in ventricular fibrillation. The failure is in the ventricles, which cannot push blood out.
The coronary sinus drains the heart wall and is not the reason this rhythm is deadly. The danger is that the ventricles stop sending blood to the body.
The valves open and close with pressure changes and are not sealed shut by disorganized signals. The problem is a lack of effective contraction, not stuck valves.
Correct. Quivering ventricles move almost no blood.
questions.answerText: The ventricles quiver and move almost no blood

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: How does the order of the conduction pathway match the pathway of blood through the heart?
options: The atria are signaled first, filling the ventricles before they pump
All four chambers are signaled at once so blood moves in both directions
The signal follows the blood from the aorta back to the venae cavae
The ventricles are signaled first so they push blood up into the atria
questions.why: Blood moves from the atria into the ventricles and then out into the great arteries. The conduction system mirrors this: the SA node fires the atria first, the AV node delays the signal while the atria empty, and then the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers fire the ventricles from the apex upward. Electrical order produces mechanical order, so blood keeps moving forward.
notes: Correct. The atria fire first and fill the ventricles, then the ventricles fire and pump.
The atria and ventricles are deliberately signaled at different times, with the AV node delay between them. Contracting all four chambers together would leave the ventricles underfilled.
The signal travels through conduction tissue inside the heart, not along the blood vessels. It starts in the SA node in the right atrium, not in the aorta.
Blood never moves from the ventricles up into the atria in a normal heart; the atrioventricular valves prevent it. Signaling the ventricles first would mean they contract before they are full.
questions.answerText: The atria are signaled first, filling the ventricles before they pump

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why does damage near the interventricular septum threaten the conduction system?
options: The AV bundle and bundle branches run through the septum
The SA node lies deep within the ventricular septum
The coronary sinus runs down the inside of the septum
The fossa ovalis lies in the ventricular septum
questions.why: The AV bundle enters the top of the interventricular septum and splits into the right and left bundle branches, which run down both sides of it toward the apex. Damage to the septum, such as an infarction after an LAD blockage, can cut these pathways and block the signal to one or both ventricles.
notes: Correct. The septum carries the AV bundle and both bundle branches.
The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava, not in the ventricular septum. Choose that location for the pacemaker.
The coronary sinus runs on the posterior surface of the heart in the groove between the atria and ventricles. It is a vein draining the heart wall, not a conduction pathway.
The fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale. It lies in the wall between the atria and has nothing to do with conduction.
questions.answerText: The AV bundle and bundle branches run through the septum

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which is more immediately life-threatening, failure of atrial conduction or failure of ventricular conduction?
options: Neither, because nerves can take over the heartbeat
Both equally, because all four chambers pump equally
Ventricular failure, since ventricles pump blood out
Atrial failure, because the atria hold the pacemaker
questions.why: The ventricles are the main pumps that send blood into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. If atrial conduction fails, the ventricles still contract and blood still circulates, as in atrial fibrillation, which is common and treatable. If ventricular conduction fails, as in ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles cannot pump and blood flow stops, which is a life-threatening emergency.
notes: Nerves cannot take over the heartbeat; they only adjust the rate set by the conduction system. Fibrillating ventricles need a defibrillator, not nervous input.
The chambers do not pump equally; the thick-walled ventricles do most of the work, while the thin-walled atria mainly fill the ventricles. That difference is why ventricular failure is worse.
Correct. Without effective ventricles, blood stops leaving the heart.
The SA node is in the right atrium, but the atria themselves only top off the ventricles. Losing atrial contraction reduces filling while the ventricles keep the blood moving.
questions.answerText: Ventricular failure, since ventricles pump blood out

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, after the SA node fires, where does the signal travel next?
options: Across both atria
Into the AV node
Through the Purkinje fibers
Down the bundle branches
questions.why: The SA node, the sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium, is the pacemaker that fires first. Its signal spreads through both atria, and the atria contract. Only after crossing the atria does the signal reach the AV node, where it pauses before passing on to the ventricles.
notes: Correct. The signal from the SA node spreads across both atria first.

The AV node is the next named structure, but the signal first has to spread across the atrial walls to reach it. The AV node would be the answer if the question started after the signal had crossed the atria.
The Purkinje fibers are the last part of the pathway, spreading the signal through the ventricle walls. They would be the answer if the question started at the bundle branches.
The bundle branches run down the interventricular septum and come after the AV node and AV bundle. They would be the answer if the question started at the AV bundle.
questions.answerText: Across both atria

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, after the signal spreads across the atria, which structure does it reach next?
options: AV bundle
SA node
Bundle branches
AV node
questions.why: The AV node, the atrioventricular node in the floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum, collects the signal after it crosses the atria. The signal pauses there briefly, which gives the atria time to finish emptying into the ventricles. Then the signal passes into the AV bundle.
notes: The AV bundle comes one step after the AV node, carrying the signal into the interventricular septum. It would be the answer if the question started at the AV node.
The SA node is where the signal starts, before it spreads across the atria. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure fires first.
The bundle branches run down both sides of the interventricular septum, two steps after the AV node. They would be the answer if the question started at the AV bundle.
Correct. The signal crosses the atria and then reaches the AV node.
questions.answerText: AV node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, after the brief delay at the AV node, the signal passes into which structure?
options: Bundle branches
SA node
Purkinje fibers
AV bundle
questions.why: The AV bundle, also called the bundle of His, carries the signal from the AV node into the upper part of the interventricular septum. The fibrous skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles, so the AV bundle is the only electrical bridge between them. It then splits into the right and left bundle branches.
notes: The bundle branches come after the AV bundle, carrying the signal down both sides of the septum. They would be the answer if the question started at the AV bundle.
The SA node is the pacemaker where the signal begins, at the very start of the pathway. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure fires first.
The Purkinje fibers are the final part of the pathway in the ventricle walls. They would be the answer if the question started at the bundle branches.
Correct. The AV node passes the signal into the AV bundle.
questions.answerText: AV bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, the AV bundle passes the signal to which structures next?
options: Right and left bundle branches
AV node
Atrial walls
Purkinje fibers
questions.why: The AV bundle divides at the top of the interventricular septum into the right and left bundle branches. The bundle branches carry the signal down both sides of the septum toward the apex of the heart. From there the signal enters the Purkinje fibers.
notes: Correct. The AV bundle splits into the right and left bundle branches.
The AV node comes before the AV bundle, not after it. It would be the answer if the question asked where the signal goes after crossing the atria.
The atrial walls receive the signal at the start of the pathway, right after the SA node fires. They would be the answer if the question started at the SA node.
The Purkinje fibers come after the bundle branches and spread the signal through the ventricle walls. They would be the answer if the question started at the bundle branches.
questions.answerText: Right and left bundle branches

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, the bundle branches pass the signal to which structures?
options: Purkinje fibers
SA node
AV bundle
AV node
questions.why: The bundle branches carry the signal down the interventricular septum toward the apex. There they connect with the Purkinje fibers, which run throughout the walls of both ventricles. The Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to the contractile cells, so the ventricles contract from the apex upward.
notes: Correct. The bundle branches hand the signal to the Purkinje fibers.
The SA node is the pacemaker at the very start of the pathway. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure sets the heart rate.
The AV bundle comes before the bundle branches, carrying the signal into the septum. It would be the answer if the question started at the AV node.
The AV node is two steps earlier, where the signal pauses on the floor of the right atrium. It would be the answer if the question started at the atria.
questions.answerText: Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In the cardiac conduction pathway, the Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to which cells?
options: Conducting cells of the AV node
Conducting cells of the SA node
Contractile cells of the ventricular walls
Contractile cells of the atrial walls
questions.why: The Purkinje fibers are the last part of the conduction system. They spread through the walls of both ventricles and hand the signal to the contractile cells, the ordinary working cardiac muscle cells. Those cells then contract, starting at the apex and moving upward, which pushes blood toward the semilunar valves.
notes: The AV node is a conducting structure in the floor of the right atrium, near the middle of the pathway. It would be the answer if the question started at the atria.
The SA node is where each heartbeat's signal begins, not where it ends. It would be the answer if the question asked which structure acts as the pacemaker.
Correct. The Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to the contractile cells of the ventricles.
The contractile cells of the atrial walls receive the signal at the start of the pathway, straight from the SA node. They would be the answer if the question started at the SA node.
questions.answerText: Contractile cells of the ventricular walls

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces the cardiac conduction pathway from the pacemaker to ventricular contraction?
options: SA node, across the atria, AV bundle, AV node, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
SA node, across the atria, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
SA node, across the atria, AV node, AV bundle, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches
AV node, across the atria, SA node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
questions.why: The SA node in the right atrium fires first and the signal spreads across both atria. It reaches the AV node, pauses briefly, and then enters the AV bundle in the interventricular septum. The bundle branches carry it down toward the apex, and the Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricle walls so the ventricles contract.
notes: This sequence swaps the AV node and AV bundle. The AV node collects the signal from the atria first and then passes it into the AV bundle in the septum.
Correct. This is the conduction pathway in order.
This sequence swaps the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. The bundle branches run down the septum first, and the Purkinje fibers at the end spread the signal into the ventricle walls.
This sequence starts at the AV node. The SA node is the pacemaker that fires first, so it must lead the pathway, and the AV node comes after the atria.
questions.answerText: SA node, across the atria, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Damage to the AV node prevents it from passing signals normally to the ventricles. What is the most likely result?
options: The atria quiver from rapid, disorganized signals
The ventricles quiver and pump no blood
The atria and ventricles beat out of step
The SA node stops firing and the atria stop
questions.why: The AV node collects the signal from the atria and, through the AV bundle, is the only electrical route to the ventricles, because the fibrous skeleton insulates everything else. When the signal is delayed or stopped at the AV node, the atria and ventricles can no longer beat in their normal order. This is called heart block.
notes: Rapid, disorganized signals that make the atria quiver describe atrial fibrillation. It would be the answer if the question asked what happens when chaotic signals arise in the atria.
Quivering ventricles that pump no blood describe ventricular fibrillation, a life-threatening emergency. It would be the answer if the question asked what a defibrillator is used to treat.
Correct. A damaged AV node disconnects the atria from the ventricles, so they beat out of step.

The SA node lies upstream of the AV node, in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, so damage at the AV node does not stop it. The atria keep receiving signals from the SA node. This would fit a question about a failing SA node.
questions.answerText: The atria and ventricles beat out of step

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which part of the cardiac conduction system is the natural pacemaker of the heart?
options: Purkinje fibers
AV bundle
AV node
SA node
questions.why: The sinoatrial (SA) node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. It fires faster than any other part of the conduction system, about 60 to 100 times a minute, so it sets the pace for the whole heart. Its signal spreads across both atria and then on to the AV node.
notes: Purkinje fibers are the last step in the pathway, spreading the signal through the walls of both ventricles. They would be the answer if the question asked which fibers deliver the signal to the ventricular muscle.
The AV bundle carries the signal from the AV node into the interventricular septum. Choose it if the question asked which structure is the only electrical bridge from the atria to the ventricles.
The AV node sits in the floor of the right atrium and briefly delays the signal before passing it to the ventricles. Pick it if the question asked where the signal pauses.
Correct. The SA node is the pacemaker that sets the heart rate.
questions.answerText: SA node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: At which point in the conduction pathway does the signal pause briefly so the atria can finish emptying before the ventricles contract?
options: SA node
Purkinje fibers
Bundle branches
AV node
questions.why: The atrioventricular (AV) node lies in the floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum. When the signal from the atria reaches it, the AV node holds it for a moment before passing it on. That short delay gives the atria time to push their last blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
notes: The SA node starts each heartbeat in the wall of the right atrium, one step earlier in the pathway. Pick it if the question asked which structure is the natural pacemaker.
Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricle walls at the end of the pathway, with no delay. Choose them if the question asked which fibers trigger the ventricular muscle to contract.

The bundle branches carry the signal down the right and left sides of the interventricular septum toward the apex. They would be the answer if the question asked which structures run down both sides of the septum.
Correct. The AV node delays the signal so the atria can finish emptying.
questions.answerText: AV node

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which part of the conduction system is the only electrical bridge from the atria to the ventricles?
options: SA node
Purkinje fibers
Bundle branches
AV bundle
questions.why: The atria and ventricles are separated by the fibrous skeleton, rings of dense connective tissue that do not conduct electrical signals. The AV bundle, also called the bundle of His, is the one route through that insulation, carrying the signal from the AV node into the top of the interventricular septum. A block at this point can disconnect the beat of the atria from the beat of the ventricles.
notes: The SA node starts the heartbeat in the right atrium but does not cross into the ventricles. Pick it if the question asked which structure sets the heart rate.
Purkinje fibers lie in the walls of the ventricles and are the final step of the pathway. Choose them if the question asked which fibers deliver the signal to the ventricular muscle cells.

The bundle branches are already on the ventricular side, carrying the signal down both sides of the septum after the AV bundle. They would be the answer if the question asked which structures run toward the apex.
Correct. The AV bundle is the only electrical link through the fibrous skeleton.
questions.answerText: AV bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which conduction fibers spread the signal through the walls of both ventricles?
options: Bundle branches
AV bundle
Purkinje fibers
SA node
questions.why: Purkinje fibers are the last part of the conduction pathway. They branch out from the bundle branches near the apex and run through the walls of both ventricles, delivering the signal to the contractile muscle cells. Because the signal reaches the apex first, the ventricles contract from the apex upward and squeeze blood toward the arteries at the top.
notes: The bundle branches carry the signal down the right and left sides of the interventricular septum toward the apex, one step before the Purkinje fibers. They would be the answer if the question asked which structures run down the septum.

The AV bundle carries the signal from the AV node into the top of the interventricular septum, well before it reaches the ventricle walls. Pick it if the question asked for the only electrical bridge between atria and ventricles.
Correct. Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricular walls.
The SA node starts the signal in the wall of the right atrium. Choose it if the question asked which structure is the pacemaker.
questions.answerText: Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: After disease damages the AV node, the atria and ventricles beat out of step with each other. Which disorder fits?
options: Heart block
Cardiac tamponade
Atrial fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles, so the AV node and AV bundle are the only electrical route between them. Heart block is the disorder in which the signal is delayed or stopped at the AV node. When the signal cannot get through reliably, the atria keep following the SA node while the ventricles fall out of step with them.
notes: Correct. Heart block is a delay or stop of the signal at the AV node, which lets the atria and ventricles beat out of step.
Cardiac tamponade is fluid in the pericardial cavity that squeezes the heart from outside. It limits filling but does not disconnect the atrial and ventricular rhythms.

Atrial fibrillation is rapid, disorganized signaling within the atria themselves, so the atria quiver instead of contracting. Pick it if the problem started in the atrial walls rather than at the AV node.

Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic signaling in the ventricles, so they quiver and pump no blood. It would be the answer for a sudden collapse with no effective heartbeat, not a steady mismatch between atria and ventricles.
questions.answerText: Heart block

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A patient's ventricles quiver rapidly and move no blood at all. Which rhythm disorder is this?
options: Ventricular fibrillation
Heart block
Atrial fibrillation
Tachycardia
questions.why: Fibrillation means rapid, disorganized electrical signals that make heart muscle quiver instead of contracting together. When this happens in the ventricles, the pumping chambers cannot squeeze in a coordinated way, so no blood is pushed into the aorta or pulmonary trunk. That is why ventricular fibrillation is a life-threatening emergency.
notes: Correct. Chaotic signals make the ventricles quiver, so they pump no blood.
Heart block is a delay or stop of the signal at the AV node, so the atria and ventricles beat out of step. The ventricles still contract, just not in time with the atria.
Atrial fibrillation is the same kind of chaotic quivering, but in the atria. The ventricles can still pump, so choose it when the upper chambers quiver and blood is still moving.
Tachycardia is an abnormally fast resting heart rate in which the beats are still organized, so blood keeps moving. It would fit a question about a heart beating too fast to fill well between beats.
questions.answerText: Ventricular fibrillation

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A patient's SA node can no longer pace the heart normally. Which treatment takes over its job?
options: A replacement heart valve
A coronary artery bypass
An artificial pacemaker
A defibrillator shock
questions.why: The SA node is the natural pacemaker, a cluster of conducting cells in the right atrial wall that sets the pace of every heartbeat. An artificial pacemaker is a small implanted device that delivers a timed electrical signal to the heart, so it can take over for a failing SA node or carry the signal past a block at the AV node. It restores an ordered beat by supplying the signal the heart is no longer making on its own.
