notes: A replacement valve fixes a valve that leaks or is narrowed, which is a problem of one-way blood flow. Pick it for regurgitation or stenosis, not for a pacing failure.

A coronary bypass reroutes blood around a blocked coronary artery to feed the myocardium. It would be the answer for coronary artery disease, where heart muscle is starved of blood, not for a pacing problem.
Correct. An implanted pacemaker supplies the timed signal that the failing SA node can no longer provide.

A defibrillator delivers one strong shock that stops chaotic signals all at once so the SA node can restart the rhythm. It is the answer for ventricular fibrillation, but it does not provide an ongoing beat when the SA node itself fails.
questions.answerText: An artificial pacemaker

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A student says that nerves from the brain start each heartbeat. Which statement corrects this?
options: The AV node starts each beat, and the SA node delays it
The SA node starts it, and nerves only adjust the rate
The Purkinje fibers start each beat, and the atria follow
The vagus nerve starts each beat, and the SA node relays it
questions.why: The heart has autorhythmicity, the built-in ability to generate its own rhythm. The SA node, in the wall of the right atrium, fires first and sets the pace of the whole heart without any signal from the nervous system. Autonomic nerves reaching the heart through the cardiac plexus only adjust that pace, with sympathetic nerves speeding it and the vagus nerve slowing it. A transplanted heart, whose nerves have been cut, still beats.
notes: The AV node, in the floor of the right atrium, delays the signal briefly before passing it to the ventricles, and the SA node fires before it. Choose the AV node for a question about the built-in delay.
Correct. The SA node sets the beat on its own, and autonomic nerves only speed it up or slow it down.
Purkinje fibers are the last part of the pathway, spreading the signal through the ventricle walls. Pick them for a question about how the signal reaches the ventricular muscle, not where it begins.
The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart rate, but it does not start the beat. Pick the vagus nerve for a question about which nerve slows the heart.
questions.answerText: The SA node starts it, and nerves only adjust the rate

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is the brief delay of the signal at the AV node useful for pumping?
options: It lets the ventricles finish emptying before the atria contract
It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
It gives the SA node time to recover between beats
It keeps the semilunar valves shut until the atria fill
questions.why: In the conduction pathway, the signal from the SA node spreads across the atria, which contract, and then reaches the AV node in the floor of the right atrium. The AV node holds the signal for a brief moment before passing it to the AV bundle and the ventricles. That pause gives the atria time to finish emptying their blood into the ventricles, so the ventricles are full before they contract.
notes: This reverses the order. The atria contract first and the ventricles second, and the delay protects that atria-then-ventricles order.
Correct. The pause lets the ventricles fill completely before they contract.
The SA node fires on its own schedule at the start of the pathway. The AV node delay happens after the SA node has already fired, so it is not there to give the SA node a rest.

The semilunar valves open and close with the pressure of blood in the ventricles and great arteries, not with the AV node signal. Choose them for a question about preventing backflow from the aorta or pulmonary trunk.
questions.answerText: It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why are the gap junctions in the intercalated discs important for the myocardium?
options: They anchor cells so they do not pull apart
They insulate the atria from the ventricles
They pass the signal directly between cells
They set the pace of the heartbeat
questions.why: Intercalated discs are the specialized junctions where neighboring cardiac muscle cells meet end to end. The gap junctions within them are channels that let the electrical signal pass directly from one cell to the next. Because the signal spreads so quickly from cell to cell, the myocardium contracts as one coordinated unit rather than cell by cell.
notes: Anchoring cells so they do not pull apart is the job of desmosomes, the other junction in the intercalated disc. Pick desmosomes for a question about holding cells together during forceful contraction.

Insulating the atria from the ventricles is the job of the fibrous skeleton, the dense connective tissue rings around the valves. Choose it for a question about why the AV bundle is the only electrical route between the chambers.
Correct. Gap junctions pass the signal cell to cell so the myocardium contracts as a unit.
Setting the pace of the heartbeat is the job of the SA node, the pacemaker in the right atrial wall. Gap junctions spread the signal but do not start it.
questions.answerText: They pass the signal directly between cells

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why are the desmosomes in the intercalated discs important for the myocardium?
options: They pass the signal from cell to cell
They keep cells attached during contraction
They anchor the chordae tendineae
They form rings around the heart valves
questions.why: Desmosomes are anchoring junctions within the intercalated discs, the places where neighboring cardiac muscle cells meet end to end. The heart contracts forcefully with every beat for an entire lifetime, which tends to pull the cells apart. Desmosomes bind the cells tightly together, so the myocardium holds together and pulls as a single unit.
notes: Passing the electrical signal between cells is the job of gap junctions, the other junction in the intercalated disc. Pick gap junctions for a question about how the myocardium contracts as one unit.
Correct. Desmosomes hold cardiac muscle cells together against the pull of each beat.
The chordae tendineae are anchored to the ventricle wall by the papillary muscles. Choose papillary muscles for a question about what holds the cords of the AV valves in place.
The rings of dense connective tissue around the valves are the fibrous skeleton. It would be the answer for a question about what anchors the valves and insulates the atria from the ventricles.
questions.answerText: They keep cells attached during contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why does ventricular fibrillation need a shock from a defibrillator?
options: It removes fluid from the pericardial cavity
It stops the chaos so the SA node can take over
It permanently replaces the SA node as the pacemaker
It reopens a blocked coronary artery
questions.why: In ventricular fibrillation, rapid, disorganized signals make the ventricles quiver instead of contracting, so they move no blood. A defibrillator delivers one strong shock that stops all the chaotic electrical activity at the same moment. With that chaos cleared, the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker, has a chance to restart the heart in its normal rhythm.
notes: Removing fluid from the pericardial cavity treats cardiac tamponade, where the heart is squeezed from outside. Choose it for a filling problem, not chaotic electrical signals.
Correct. The shock clears the chaos so the SA node can restart a normal rhythm.

Taking over permanently as the pacemaker is the job of an implanted artificial pacemaker, which delivers a timed signal with every beat. A defibrillator gives a single shock rather than an ongoing beat.
Reopening a blocked coronary artery treats a heart attack by restoring blood to the myocardium. Pick it for coronary artery disease, not a rhythm problem.
questions.answerText: It stops the chaos so the SA node can take over

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is atrial fibrillation usually less immediately life-threatening than ventricular fibrillation?
options: The AV node blocks every atrial signal
The SA node keeps full control of the atria
The ventricles can still pump blood
The atria pump most of the blood to the body
questions.why: In atrial fibrillation, chaotic signals make the atria quiver instead of contracting, but signals still pass through the AV node and the ventricles keep contracting. The ventricles are the main pumps, and the atria mainly top them off, so blood still moves to the lungs and body. In ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles themselves quiver and no blood is pumped at all, which is an immediate emergency.
notes: If the AV node blocked every atrial signal, the ventricles would lose their normal signal entirely, which describes complete heart block. In atrial fibrillation, many signals still pass through the AV node, so the ventricles keep beating, though irregularly.

In atrial fibrillation, disorganized signals throughout the atria override the SA node's normal pace. Students choose this when they assume the pacemaker still controls the atria, which is exactly what is lost.
Correct. In atrial fibrillation the ventricles keep pumping, so blood still moves.
The atria are thin-walled chambers that mainly receive blood and top off the ventricles. The ventricles do the real pumping to the lungs and body, which is why losing them is far more dangerous.
questions.answerText: The ventricles can still pump blood

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Where is the SA node, the heart's pacemaker, located?
options: In the superior part of the interventricular septum
Throughout the walls of both ventricles
In the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava
In the floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum
questions.why: The SA (sinoatrial) node sits in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. It fires faster than any other part of the conduction system, about 60 to 100 times a minute, so it sets the pace for the whole heart. From there the signal spreads across both atria toward the AV node.
notes: That is where the AV bundle (bundle of His) runs, carrying the signal from the AV node into the septum. Choose it for the only electrical bridge between the atria and the ventricles.

That describes the Purkinje fibers, the last part of the pathway, which deliver the signal to the contractile cells of the ventricles. They would be the answer for the structures that spread the signal through the ventricle walls.
Correct. The SA node is in the right atrial wall near where the superior vena cava enters.
That is the location of the AV node, the second stop in the pathway, which delays the signal before passing it to the ventricles. Pick it if the question asked where the signal pauses.
questions.answerText: In the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What does the AV node do in the cardiac conduction pathway?
options: Carries the signal down both sides of the interventricular septum
Delays the signal briefly, then passes it on to the ventricles
Spreads the signal through the walls of both ventricles
Fires first and sets the pace of the whole heart
questions.why: The AV (atrioventricular) node sits in the floor of the right atrium near the interatrial septum. The signal from the SA node reaches it after crossing the atria, and the AV node holds that signal for a brief moment before sending it into the AV bundle. That delay gives the atria time to finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
notes: That is the job of the right and left bundle branches, which run down the septum toward the apex. They would be the answer for the step between the AV bundle and the Purkinje fibers.
Correct. The AV node is the brief holding point between the atria and the ventricles.
That is the job of the Purkinje fibers, which deliver the signal to the contractile cells of the ventricle walls. Choose them for the final step of the pathway.
That is the job of the SA node, the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium. Pick it if the question asked which structure starts each heartbeat.
questions.answerText: Delays the signal briefly, then passes it on to the ventricles

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: The atria and ventricles are electrically insulated from each other. Which structure is the only electrical bridge that carries the signal across?
options: The fibrous skeleton
The AV bundle
The Purkinje fibers
The moderator band
questions.why: The fibrous skeleton, a set of dense connective tissue rings around the valves, insulates the atria from the ventricles, so the signal cannot spread directly from atrial muscle to ventricular muscle. The AV bundle, also called the bundle of His, is the one route through. It carries the signal from the AV node into the superior part of the interventricular septum, which is why a block here disconnects the atria from the ventricles.
notes: The fibrous skeleton is the insulator, not the bridge. Its rings of dense connective tissue anchor the valves and stop the signal from crossing anywhere except the AV bundle; pick it if the question asked what electrically separates the atria from the ventricles.
Correct. The AV bundle is the single electrical path from the atria into the ventricles.

The Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricle walls at the end of the pathway, well after it has crossed from the atria. Choose them for the structures that deliver the signal to the ventricular muscle cells.

The moderator band is a muscular band in the right ventricle that carries part of the conduction system to the anterior papillary muscle. It lies entirely within the ventricle, so it would be the answer only for a question about that band in the right ventricle.
questions.answerText: The AV bundle

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which sequence gives the cardiac conduction pathway from the pacemaker to the ventricle walls?
options: SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
SA node, AV node, AV bundle, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches
SA node, AV bundle, AV node, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
questions.why: The signal starts at the SA node in the right atrium and spreads across both atria to the AV node, where it pauses briefly. It then travels through the AV bundle into the interventricular septum, down the right and left bundle branches toward the apex, and out through the Purkinje fibers into the ventricle walls. This order makes the atria contract first and the ventricles second, with the ventricles squeezing from the apex upward.
notes: Correct. Pacemaker, pause, bridge, branches, then the ventricle walls.
This starts at the AV node, but the SA node is the pacemaker that fires first. Students pick this when they mix up the two nodes because their names look alike.
This puts the Purkinje fibers before the bundle branches. The branches carry the signal down the septum first, and the Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricle walls at the very end.
This puts the AV bundle before the AV node. The node is the holding point in the floor of the right atrium, and the bundle carries the signal out of it into the septum.
questions.answerText: SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Why is the brief pause at the AV node essential to a normal heartbeat?
options: It keeps the signal from spreading across the walls of the atria
It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
It lets the ventricles contract before the atria begin to contract
It lets the SA node rest so it can fire again on the next beat
questions.why: The atria contract first to top off the ventricles, and the ventricles contract second to pump blood out. If the signal passed straight to the ventricles, both would contract almost at once and the ventricles would squeeze before they were full. The AV node's short delay holds the signal just long enough for the atria to finish emptying, which keeps the two halves of the heartbeat in the right order.
notes: The signal has already spread across both atria by the time it reaches the AV node, and that spread is what makes the atria contract. Pick a statement about atrial spread if the question asked what happens between the SA node and the AV node.
Correct. The delay keeps atrial contraction ahead of ventricular contraction.
This reverses the normal order. The atria contract first and the ventricles second, and the delay exists to protect that order, not to flip it.

The SA node fires again on its own rhythm and does not need the AV node to pause for it. Students choose this when they think of the delay as a rest period for the pacemaker rather than timing between chambers.
questions.answerText: It lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What are intercalated discs?
options: Junctions where neighboring cardiac muscle cells meet end to end
Fibrous cords that tie the valve cusps to the papillary muscles
Rings of dense connective tissue around the four valve openings
Clusters of conducting cells that set the pace of the heartbeat
questions.why: Intercalated discs are the specialized junctions where neighboring cardiomyocytes (cardiac muscle cells) join end to end. Under the microscope they appear as dark lines crossing the fibers, and they are one of the features that identify cardiac muscle tissue. They hold the cells together and let the signal to contract pass from one cell to the next, so the heart contracts as one coordinated unit.
notes: Correct. Intercalated discs are the end-to-end junctions between cardiac muscle cells.
That describes the chordae tendineae of the AV valves. They would be the answer for the structures that keep the AV valve cusps from flipping back into the atria.

That describes the fibrous skeleton of the heart, which anchors the valves and insulates the atria from the ventricles. Pick it if the question asked what electrically separates the upper and lower chambers.
That describes the SA node, the pacemaker in the wall of the right atrium. Choose it for a question about which structure starts each heartbeat.
questions.answerText: Junctions where neighboring cardiac muscle cells meet end to end

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: An intercalated disc contains two kinds of cell junction. Which statement correctly matches each junction to its job?
options: Desmosomes anchor the cells together; gap junctions let the signal pass between cells
Desmosomes anchor the cells together; tight junctions let the signal pass between cells
Tight junctions seal the cells together; desmosomes let the signal pass between cells
Gap junctions anchor the cells together; desmosomes let the signal pass between cells
questions.why: An intercalated disc holds two kinds of junction with two different jobs. Desmosomes are anchoring junctions that rivet neighboring cells together so they do not pull apart when the heart contracts. Gap junctions are channels that connect the insides of neighboring cells, so the contraction signal passes directly from cell to cell and the myocardium contracts as a unit.
notes: Correct. Desmosomes hold the cells together, and gap junctions pass the signal.
Desmosomes are right, but tight junctions seal cells and do not carry a signal. The signal-passing junction in the intercalated disc is the gap junction.

Tight junctions seal neighboring epithelial cells to block leaks between them, and they are not the junctions of the intercalated disc. Pick tight junctions for a question about how epithelium keeps material from slipping between its cells.
This swaps the two jobs. Gap junctions are open channels between cells, which suits passing a signal, while desmosomes are mechanical anchors.
questions.answerText: Desmosomes anchor the cells together; gap junctions let the signal pass between cells

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: Which description fits a cardiomyocyte, a cardiac muscle cell?
options: A spindle-shaped cell with one central nucleus and no visible striations
A short, branching cell with many peripheral nuclei and few mitochondria
A long, cylindrical cell with many nuclei pushed to the edge of the cell
A short, branching cell with usually one central nucleus and many mitochondria
questions.why: A cardiomyocyte is a short cell that branches to connect with its neighbors, usually with a single central nucleus, and it is striated like skeletal muscle. It is packed with mitochondria, about a quarter of the cell volume, because the heart works constantly for a lifetime and needs a steady energy supply. These features, plus intercalated discs, are how you recognize cardiac muscle on a slide.
notes: That describes a smooth muscle cell, found in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels. It would be the answer for a muscle cell that has no striations.
Short and branching is right, but cardiomyocytes usually have one central nucleus and are rich in mitochondria. Students choose this when they blend the features of cardiac and skeletal muscle.
That describes a skeletal muscle fiber, which is long, cylindrical, and multinucleated with its nuclei at the edge. Pick it if the question asked about the muscle cells attached to bones.
Correct. Short, branching, one central nucleus, and rich in mitochondria.
questions.answerText: A short, branching cell with usually one central nucleus and many mitochondria

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: How do the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves affect the heart rate?
options: Parasympathetic fibers in the phrenic nerve slow the rate; sympathetic nerves speed it
Sympathetic nerves speed the rate; parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve slow it
These nerves start each heartbeat, so the heart stops beating if they are cut
Sympathetic nerves slow the rate; parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve speed it
questions.why: The heart sets its own beat through the SA node, but autonomic nerves reaching the SA and AV nodes through the cardiac plexus can adjust the pace. Sympathetic nerves speed the heart rate, as during exercise or stress, and parasympathetic fibers carried in the vagus nerve slow it. These nerves only adjust the rate; they do not start the heartbeat.
notes: The phrenic nerve runs to the diaphragm, not the heart. The parasympathetic fibers to the heart travel in the vagus nerve; pick the phrenic nerve for a question about which nerve reaches the diaphragm.
Correct. Sympathetic speeds the heart, and the vagus nerve slows it.
The heart is autorhythmic, meaning the SA node starts each beat on its own. A transplanted heart has had its nerves cut and still beats, which shows the nerves only adjust the rate.
This reverses the two divisions. The sympathetic division prepares the body for activity and speeds the heart, while the vagus nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that slow it.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic nerves speed the rate; parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve slow it

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: What joins neighboring cardiac muscle cells, and which two kinds of cell junctions does it contain?
options: Intercalated discs, containing desmosomes and gap junctions
Intercalated discs, containing tight junctions and hemidesmosomes
T tubules, containing desmosomes and gap junctions
The endomysium, containing tight junctions and gap junctions
questions.why: Cardiac muscle cells are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which show up on a slide as dark lines crossing the fibers. Desmosomes in the discs hold the cells together so they do not pull apart as the heart contracts. Gap junctions are small channels that let the electrical signal pass directly from cell to cell, so the heart muscle contracts as a coordinated unit.
notes: Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiac cells with desmosomes for adhesion and gap junctions for electrical coupling.

Intercalated discs are right, but tight junctions seal epithelial cells to stop leakage between them, and hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane. Pick those junctions if the question asked about epithelium.

T tubules are inward tunnels of the sarcolemma that carry the signal into a single muscle cell, not connections between cells. They would be the answer if the question asked how a signal reaches deep inside a fiber.
The endomysium is the connective tissue sheath around each muscle fiber, not a junction between cells. Choose it if the question asked what wraps each skeletal muscle fiber.
questions.answerText: Intercalated discs, containing desmosomes and gap junctions

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A student labels a high-power drawing of cardiac muscle. Where the end of one cardiomyocyte meets the next, a dark line crosses the fiber, and the student labels it a Z disc. Why is that label wrong, and what is the line?
options: It lies inside one cell, so it is an intercalated disc.
It joins two separate cells, so it is an intercalated disc.
It joins two separate cells, so it is an M line.
It borders one sarcomere, so it is a desmosome.
questions.why: A Z disc is the border of a sarcomere, and it repeats many times inside a single cell along each myofibril. The dark line where two cardiomyocytes meet end to end is an intercalated disc, a junction between cells. Its desmosomes keep the cells from pulling apart, and its gap junctions let the signal pass from cell to cell.
notes: Intercalated disc is the right name, but the reason is wrong. Intercalated discs sit between neighboring cells; the lines that repeat inside one cell are Z discs.
Correct. A line where two cells meet is a cell junction, the intercalated disc.
The line does join two cells, but an M line is the protein line in the center of the H zone, inside one sarcomere. It anchors thick filaments, not neighboring cells.
Desmosomes are found within the intercalated disc, but they are not the whole dark line, and they do not border a sarcomere. The sarcomere border is the Z disc.
questions.answerText: It joins two separate cells, so it is an intercalated disc.

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A student draws a cardiomyocyte as a long, unbranched cylinder with five nuclei pressed against its edge. Which correction would make the drawing look like cardiac muscle instead of skeletal muscle?
options: Remove the striations and make the cell spindle-shaped.
Keep the long shape but move all five nuclei to the center.
Make the cell longer and add more nuclei along its edge.
Make the cell short and branching, with one central nucleus.
questions.why: A long cylinder with many nuclei at the edge is a skeletal muscle fiber. A cardiomyocyte is short and branching and usually has a single central nucleus, and it joins its neighbors end to end at intercalated discs. Both tissues are striated, so the stripes stay in the drawing.
notes: Spindle-shaped cells without striations describe smooth muscle. Cardiac muscle is striated, so removing the stripes would make the drawing wrong in a new way.
Moving the nuclei inward helps, but a cardiomyocyte usually has one nucleus, not five, and it is short and branching rather than a long unbranched cylinder.
A longer fiber with more nuclei at the edge looks even more like skeletal muscle. Skeletal fibers are the long, multinucleated cells.
Correct. Cardiomyocytes are short, branching cells, usually with one central nucleus.
questions.answerText: Make the cell short and branching, with one central nucleus.

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: In a heart transplant, every nerve fiber that reached the old heart through the cardiac plexus is cut and not reconnected. Which autonomic supply does the new heart lose, and does it still beat?
options: It loses both the sympathetic and the vagal fibers, and it still beats.
It loses only the sympathetic fibers, and it still beats.
It loses only the vagal fibers, and it still beats.
It loses both the sympathetic and the vagal fibers, and it stops beating.
questions.why: The cardiac plexus is the network of autonomic fibers near the base of the heart through which both supplies reach the nodes: the sympathetic nerves that speed the heart and the parasympathetic fibers, carried in the vagus nerve, that slow it. Cutting the plexus removes both. The new heart still beats because these nerves only adjust the pace the SA node already sets.
notes: Correct. Both sets reach the heart through the cardiac plexus, and the SA node keeps setting the beat without them.
The vagal parasympathetic fibers also reach the heart through the cardiac plexus, so they are cut too, not only the sympathetic fibers.
The sympathetic nerves also reach the heart through the cardiac plexus, so they are cut along with the vagal fibers.
Both sets are lost, but these nerves only adjust the pace. The heartbeat starts in the heart's own conduction system, so the new heart keeps beating.
questions.answerText: It loses both the sympathetic and the vagal fibers, and it still beats.

questions.topic: Cardiac muscle and the conduction system
questions.q: A tumor in the thorax presses on the vagus nerve and blocks the fibers it carries to the cardiac plexus. Which nerve input to the heart is lost, and which still reaches it?
options: The sympathetic speeding is lost; parasympathetic slowing remains.
Both are lost, because the vagus carries every nerve to the heart.
The parasympathetic slowing is lost; sympathetic speeding remains.
Neither is lost, because the cardiac centers bypass the vagus nerve.
questions.why: The parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart travel in the vagus nerve, so blocking the vagus removes the slowing input. The sympathetic nerves that speed the heart are a separate set that also reaches the heart through the cardiac plexus, so they still get through. The SA node keeps setting the beat either way.
notes: This reverses the two sources. The vagus carries the parasympathetic fibers, which slow the heart; the speeding fibers are sympathetic and do not travel in the vagus.
The vagus carries only the parasympathetic supply to the heart. The sympathetic nerves reach the cardiac plexus by a separate route.
Correct. Only the vagal, parasympathetic input is blocked.

The parasympathetic fibers to the heart travel in the vagus nerve, so blocking it does remove the slowing input. The cardiac centers in the medulla adjust the rate through these nerves, not around them.
questions.answerText: The parasympathetic slowing is lost; sympathetic speeding remains.

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the lumen of a blood vessel?
options: The outermost connective tissue layer of the wall
The smooth muscle layer of the wall
The hollow channel the blood flows through
The endothelial lining of the wall
questions.why: The lumen is the hollow interior of a vessel, the open channel the blood flows through. The vessel wall surrounds it in layers, starting with the endothelium that faces the lumen. On a slide, an artery's lumen is small and round, while a vein's lumen is wider and often looks collapsed.
notes: The outermost connective tissue layer is the tunica externa, made mostly of collagen. Pick it if the question asked which layer anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue.
The smooth muscle layer is the tunica media, which changes the vessel's diameter. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is thickest in an artery.
Correct. The lumen is the open space inside the vessel.
The endothelial lining is the simple squamous epithelium of the tunica intima, which faces the lumen but is part of the wall. Choose it if the question asked what tissue lines the inside of a vessel.
questions.answerText: The hollow channel the blood flows through

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
options: An artery
A capillary
A venule
A vein
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and the definition is about direction, not oxygen content. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and are still arteries. A handy link is that artery and away both start with the letter a.
notes: Correct. Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
A capillary is the tiny exchange vessel between an arteriole and a venule. It would be the answer if the question asked where gases and nutrients cross between blood and tissue.
A venule is the smallest vein, collecting blood from a capillary bed on its way back toward the heart. Choose it if the question asked which vessel drains a capillary bed.
A vein carries blood toward the heart. Pick it if the question asked which vessel returns blood to the heart.
questions.answerText: An artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of blood vessel carries blood toward the heart?
options: A vein
An arteriole
An artery
A capillary
questions.why: Veins carry blood toward the heart, under low pressure. As with arteries, the definition is about direction, not oxygen: most veins carry oxygen-poor blood, but the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart and are still veins. Because the pressure is low, many veins have valves to keep blood moving the right way.
notes: Correct. Veins return blood to the heart.
An arteriole is the smallest artery, still carrying blood away from the heart toward a capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel controls flow into a capillary bed.
An artery carries blood away from the heart, under high pressure. Pick it if the question asked which vessel leaves the heart.

A capillary connects arterioles to venules and is where exchange happens, so it carries blood neither directly away from nor toward the heart. Choose it if the question asked about the exchange vessel.
questions.answerText: A vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which is the smallest type of blood vessel, where exchange between the blood and the tissues takes place?
options: A venule
An arteriole
A capillary
A muscular artery
questions.why: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels and the only ones thin enough for exchange. Their wall is just the tunica intima, a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane. Gases, nutrients and wastes cross this thin wall between the blood and the surrounding tissue.
notes: A venule is the smallest vein, collecting blood after it leaves the capillaries. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel drains a capillary bed.

An arteriole is the smallest artery, feeding a capillary bed, but its wall has smooth muscle and is too thick for exchange. Pick it if the question asked which vessel controls how much blood enters a capillary bed.
Correct. Capillaries are the exchange vessels.

A muscular artery is a medium-sized artery, such as the brachial or femoral artery, that distributes blood to organs. Choose it if the question asked which artery type has a tunica media that is mostly smooth muscle.
questions.answerText: A capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the innermost tunic of a vessel wall called?
options: The tunica intima
The tunica media
The tunica externa
The tunica adventitia
questions.why: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of the vessel wall, facing the lumen. It is a lining of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane, and it is continuous with the endocardium inside the heart. Intima comes from the same root as intimate, meaning innermost.
notes: Correct. The tunica intima is the innermost tunic.
The tunica media is the middle layer, built of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer sets the vessel's diameter.
The tunica externa is the outermost layer, made mostly of collagen, which anchors the vessel. Pick it if the question asked for the outer layer of the wall.
Tunica adventitia is another name for the tunica externa, the outermost layer. Students pick it because it sounds unfamiliar, but it is just an alternate name for the outer tunic.
questions.answerText: The tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the middle layer of a vessel wall?
options: The tunica externa
The basement membrane
The tunica media
The tunica intima
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer, between the tunica intima and the tunica externa. It is made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, and its smooth muscle sets the vessel's diameter. It is the thickest layer in arteries, which is why arteries hold their round shape on a slide.
notes: The tunica externa is the outermost layer, mostly collagen, anchoring the vessel to nearby tissue. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is thickest in a vein.
The basement membrane is the thin layer the endothelium rests on, part of the tunica intima rather than a separate tunic. Choose it if the question asked what the endothelial cells sit on.
Correct. The tunica media is the middle layer.
The tunica intima is the innermost layer, an endothelial lining on a basement membrane. Pick it if the question asked which layer faces the lumen.
questions.answerText: The tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What tissue makes up the tunica media?
options: Skeletal muscle fibers
Simple squamous endothelium
Smooth muscle and elastic fibers
Mostly collagen fibers
questions.why: The tunica media is built of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. The smooth muscle contracts or relaxes to narrow or widen the vessel, and the elastic fibers let the wall stretch and recoil with each heartbeat. This is the layer that does the active work of controlling vessel diameter.
notes: Skeletal muscle is voluntary muscle attached to bones and is not found in vessel walls. Students pick it because they know the media is muscular, but vessel walls use involuntary smooth muscle.
Simple squamous endothelium lines the tunica intima, the innermost layer. Pick it if the question asked what tissue lines the lumen.
Correct. Smooth muscle and elastic fibers make up the middle tunic.
Mostly collagen fibers describe the tunica externa, the outer anchoring layer. It would be the answer if the question asked what the outermost tunic is made of.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle and elastic fibers

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What type of epithelium lines the tunica intima?
options: Simple columnar epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium (endothelium)
Stratified squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
questions.why: The tunica intima is lined by simple squamous epithelium, a single layer of flat cells, which in blood vessels is called endothelium. A single flat layer gives blood a smooth surface to flow over and, in capillaries, makes exchange easy because the wall is so thin. It rests on a basement membrane.
notes: Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells specialized for absorption and secretion, as in the stomach and intestines. It would be the answer if the question asked what lines the digestive tract.
Correct. Endothelium is simple squamous epithelium lining the vessels.
Stratified squamous epithelium is many layers thick and protects surfaces that face friction, like the skin and the esophagus. Pick it if the question asked what lines a surface exposed to wear.
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium, usually ciliated, lines most of the respiratory airways such as the trachea. Choose it if the question asked what lines the trachea.
questions.answerText: Simple squamous epithelium (endothelium)

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is made mostly of collagen fibers and anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue?
options: The tunica media
The tunica externa
The tunica intima
The endothelium
questions.why: The tunica externa is the outermost layer, made mostly of collagen fibers with some nerves and small vessels. Collagen is tough and resists stretch, so this layer protects the vessel and anchors it to nearby tissue. It is the thickest layer in veins.
notes: The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. Pick it if the question asked which layer controls vessel diameter.
Correct. The collagen-rich tunica externa anchors the vessel.
The tunica intima is the innermost layer, an endothelial lining on a basement membrane. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer faces the lumen.
The endothelium is the simple squamous lining of the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked what single layer of cells lines the lumen.
questions.answerText: The tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessels are the smallest arteries?
options: Arterioles
Venules
Sinusoids
Capillaries
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, with walls of just one or two layers of smooth muscle. They lead into capillary beds and adjust how much blood enters each bed by narrowing or widening. The ending -ole means small, so arteriole means small artery.
notes: Correct. Arterioles are the smallest arteries.
Venules are the smallest veins, on the return side after the capillaries. Pick them if the question asked which vessels collect blood from a capillary bed.
Sinusoids are a leaky type of capillary found in organs like the liver and spleen. Choose them if the question asked which capillary type lets whole cells cross.
Capillaries are smaller than arterioles, but they are exchange vessels, not arteries. They would be the answer if the question asked for the smallest blood vessel overall.
questions.answerText: Arterioles

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which arteries are the largest, including the aorta?
options: Muscular arteries
Arterioles
Elastic arteries
Metarterioles
questions.why: Elastic arteries are the largest arteries, including the aorta, pulmonary trunk, brachiocephalic, subclavian, common carotid and common iliac arteries. Their thick tunica media is dominated by elastic tissue, so they stretch with each heartbeat and recoil between beats. That recoil keeps blood moving while the ventricles relax.
notes: Muscular arteries are medium-sized, such as the brachial, radial and femoral arteries, with a tunica media that is mostly smooth muscle. Pick them if the question asked which arteries distribute blood to specific organs.
Arterioles are the smallest arteries, controlling flow into capillary beds. They would be the answer if the question asked for the smallest arteries.
Correct. Elastic arteries are the largest, and the aorta is the classic example.

A metarteriole is the tapered terminal end of an arteriole where it meets a capillary bed, so it is even smaller. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment joins an arteriole to its capillaries.
questions.answerText: Elastic arteries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a capillary bed?
options: A direct channel from an artery to a vein
The tapered terminal end of an arteriole
A network of capillaries fed by one arteriole
A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance
questions.why: A capillary bed is a network of roughly ten to one hundred capillaries supplied by a single arteriole, entering through its tapered end, the metarteriole. Blood flows through the bed and drains into a venule. Spreading the blood through many fine capillaries gives a large surface for exchange with the tissue.
notes: A direct channel from an artery to a vein that skips the capillaries is an arteriovenous anastomosis. Pick it if the question asked what lets blood bypass capillaries entirely.

The tapered terminal end of an arteriole is the metarteriole, which feeds the capillary bed rather than being the bed itself. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment joins an arteriole to its capillaries.
Correct. A capillary bed is the network of capillaries supplied by one arteriole.
A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance is a precapillary sphincter. It would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes the entrance to a capillary.
questions.answerText: A network of capillaries fed by one arteriole

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a precapillary sphincter?
options: The endothelial lining of a sinusoid
A flap of the tunica intima inside a vein
A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance
A network of capillaries fed by one arteriole
questions.why: A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle where a capillary branches off the metarteriole. When it contracts, it closes the capillary's entrance, and when it relaxes, blood flows in. This lets the body open or close parts of a capillary bed depending on the tissue's needs.
notes: The endothelial lining of a sinusoid is a leaky, gapped wall, not a muscular ring. It would be the answer if the question asked what lines the wide capillaries of the liver.
A flap of the tunica intima inside a vein is a venous valve, which keeps blood from flowing backward. Pick it if the question asked what prevents backflow in limb veins.
Correct. A precapillary sphincter is a smooth muscle ring guarding a capillary entrance.
A network of capillaries fed by one arteriole is a capillary bed. Choose it if the question asked what a capillary bed is.
questions.answerText: A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What are venous valves made from?
options: Rings of smooth muscle from the tunica media
Flaps of the tunica intima
Folds of skeletal muscle around the vein
Bundles of collagen from the tunica externa
questions.why: Venous valves are thin flaps of the tunica intima, the endothelial lining, that project into the lumen of a vein. They open as blood moves toward the heart and fall closed if blood starts to slide backward. They are most common in the limb veins, where blood must travel uphill against gravity.
notes: Rings of smooth muscle from the tunica media change the diameter of a vessel, and at a capillary entrance they form a precapillary sphincter. Pick this if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary's entrance.
Correct. Venous valves are folds of the innermost tunic.

Skeletal muscle around the deep veins squeezes them during movement, which is the skeletal muscle pump, but it is outside the vein and does not form the valves. Choose it if the question asked what pushes venous blood toward the heart when you walk.
Collagen bundles make up the tunica externa, which anchors the vessel to nearby tissue. It would be the answer if the question asked what the outermost layer of a vein is made of.
questions.answerText: Flaps of the tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the thickest layer in an artery?
options: The tunica intima
The tunica media
The basement membrane
The tunica externa
questions.why: In an artery the tunica media, the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, is the thickest layer. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, and a thick muscular, elastic media lets the wall withstand that pressure and control the vessel's diameter. This thick media is why an artery holds its round shape on a slide.
notes: The tunica intima is a thin endothelial lining on a basement membrane and is never the thickest layer. Pick it if the question asked which tunic is the only one in a capillary wall.
Correct. The tunica media is the thickest tunic in an artery.
The basement membrane is a very thin layer under the endothelium, part of the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked what the endothelial cells rest on.
The tunica externa is the thickest layer in a vein, not an artery. It would be correct if the question asked about the thickest tunic of a vein.
questions.answerText: The tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic makes up the entire wall of a capillary?
options: The tunica intima
The tunica media
The tunica externa
All three tunics, each very thin
questions.why: A capillary wall is only the tunica intima: a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane. Capillaries lack a tunica media and a tunica externa entirely. This one-cell-thick wall is what makes exchange possible between the blood and the tissues.
notes: Correct. The capillary wall is just the tunica intima.
The tunica media is the smooth muscle and elastic layer of arteries and veins. Capillaries have none, so pick the media if the question asked which layer is thickest in an artery.
The tunica externa is the collagen-rich outer layer of arteries and veins, and capillaries lack it. It would be the answer if the question asked which tunic is thickest in a vein.
Students often assume every vessel has all three tunics, just scaled down. Capillaries are the exception: they keep only the inner lining so the wall stays thin enough for exchange.
questions.answerText: The tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Compared with its matching artery, how do a vein's wall and lumen differ?
options: A thicker wall and a wider lumen
A thinner wall and a wider lumen
A thicker wall and a narrower lumen
A thinner wall and a narrower lumen
questions.why: Veins carry blood back to the heart under low pressure, so they do not need the thick muscular tunica media of an artery. They have the same three tunics but a thinner media, a thicker externa, and a wider lumen. On a slide the artery holds its round shape while the vein often looks collapsed.
notes: A vein does have a wider lumen, but its wall is thinner, not thicker. Students mix this up because the tunica externa is thicker in veins, yet the overall wall is still thinner.
Correct. A vein has a thinner wall and a wider lumen than its artery.
This describes the artery, not the vein. Arteries have thick walls and narrower lumens because they carry blood under high pressure.
A vein's wall is thinner, but its lumen is wider, not narrower. The wide lumen is why veins hold so much of the body's blood at rest.
questions.answerText: A thinner wall and a wider lumen

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessels have valves in their walls?
options: Arterioles
Arteries
Veins
Capillaries
questions.why: Veins, especially those in the limbs, have valves formed from flaps of the tunica intima. Blood in veins moves at low pressure and often has to travel uphill against gravity, so the valves keep it from sliding backward. Arteries do not need valves because the high pressure from the heart keeps their blood moving forward.
notes: Arterioles are the smallest arteries and control flow into capillary beds with smooth muscle, not valves. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels act as gatekeepers to capillary beds.
Arteries carry blood under high pressure from the heart, which keeps it moving forward without valves. Pick them if the question asked which vessels have the thickest tunica media.
Correct. Veins have valves to prevent backflow.
Capillaries have walls only one cell thick and no valves. Choose them if the question asked where exchange between blood and tissue happens.
questions.answerText: Veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel type has a wall made of a single tunic, the tunica intima only?
options: Venules
Muscular arteries
Capillaries
Arterioles
questions.why: Capillaries are the only vessels whose wall is just the tunica intima, an endothelium on a basement membrane. They lack both the tunica media and the tunica externa. A wall this thin is what allows gases, nutrients and wastes to cross between the blood and the tissues.
notes: Venules have thin, porous walls, and beyond the first postcapillary venules they gain smooth muscle. They would be correct if the question asked which vessels collect blood from capillaries.
Muscular arteries have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle, up to forty layers. Choose them if the question asked which arteries distribute blood to specific organs.
Correct. Capillaries have only the tunica intima.
Arterioles have one or two layers of smooth muscle in their tunica media, so their wall is more than the intima. Pick them if the question asked which vessels control blood flow into a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: Capillaries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessels are the smallest veins?
options: Venules
Capillaries
Sinusoids
Arterioles
questions.why: Venules are the smallest veins. They collect blood as it drains from a capillary bed and merge to form larger veins. The ending -ule means small, just as arteriole means small artery.
notes: Correct. Venules are the smallest veins.
Capillaries are the exchange vessels between arterioles and venules, and they are neither arteries nor veins. Choose them if the question asked for the smallest blood vessel overall.
Sinusoids are a wide, leaky type of capillary, not veins. They would be the answer if the question asked which capillary type lets whole cells cross.
Arterioles are the smallest arteries, on the delivery side before the capillaries. Pick them if the question asked for the smallest arteries.
questions.answerText: Venules

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel type carries blood under high pressure and has a thick wall with a heavy tunica media?
options: Venules
Arteries
Veins
Capillaries
questions.why: Arteries receive blood pushed out by the ventricles, so they carry it under the highest pressure in the system. Their thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers lets them withstand that pressure and control their diameter. The thick wall is why arteries keep a round shape when cut.
notes: Venules are the smallest veins, with thin, porous walls and low pressure. Choose them if the question asked which vessels collect blood from capillary beds.
Correct. Arteries are the high-pressure vessels with a thick tunica media.
Veins carry blood under low pressure and have thinner walls with a lighter tunica media. Pick them if the question asked which vessels have valves and a wide lumen.
Capillaries have no tunica media at all, just a single layer of endothelium. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels are built for exchange.
questions.answerText: Arteries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type has an unbroken endothelial lining and is the most common type?
options: The fenestrated capillary
The continuous capillary
The sinusoid
The postcapillary venule
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining, interrupted only by narrow clefts between the cells. They are the most common type, found in muscle, skin, the lungs and the central nervous system. Their tight wall keeps most substances from leaking out, which is especially important in the brain.
notes: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores called fenestrations in the endothelium for rapid filtration or absorption. Pick them if the question asked about the capillaries of the kidney or small intestine.
Correct. Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the most common.
Sinusoids are wide, leaky capillaries with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. They would be the answer if the question asked which capillaries let whole cells pass, as in the liver.
The postcapillary venule is the first venule after a capillary bed, loosely joined and very porous. Students pick it because its name contains capillary, but it is a small vein, not a capillary type.
questions.answerText: The continuous capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type has an endothelium with small pores called fenestrations?
options: The metarteriole
The sinusoid
The continuous capillary
The fenestrated capillary
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, called fenestrations (from the Latin word for windows), through their endothelial cells. These pores let fluid and small molecules move quickly, so these capillaries are found where rapid filtration or absorption happens. Examples include the kidney, the small intestine, the choroid plexus and most endocrine glands.
notes: A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole that feeds a capillary bed, not a type of capillary. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment joins an arteriole to its capillaries.

Sinusoids also have openings, but theirs are large, with wide gaps between cells and an incomplete basement membrane. They would be the answer if the question asked which capillaries let whole blood cells cross.
Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining with no pores, only narrow clefts between cells. Pick them if the question asked which capillaries are most common or which serve the brain.
Correct. Fenestrated capillaries have small pores in the endothelium.
questions.answerText: The fenestrated capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type is a wide, leaky vessel with large gaps between its cells?
options: The metarteriole
The sinusoid
The fenestrated capillary
The continuous capillary
questions.why: Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large fenestrations, wide clefts between cells, and an incomplete basement membrane. They are the leakiest capillary type, built for tissues where whole cells or large proteins must cross. They are found in the liver, spleen, red bone marrow, anterior pituitary and adrenal glands.
notes: A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole leading into a capillary bed, not a capillary type. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment feeds a capillary bed.
Correct. Sinusoids are the wide, leaky capillaries.

Fenestrated capillaries have small pores but an intact basement membrane, so they are leaky to fluid and small molecules but not to cells. Pick them if the question asked about the kidney or small intestine.
Continuous capillaries are the tightest type, with an unbroken lining. They would be the answer if the question asked which capillaries keep most substances out of the brain.
questions.answerText: The sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which arteries have a tunica media that is mostly smooth muscle and distribute blood to specific organs?
options: Elastic arteries
Muscular arteries
Arterioles
Metarterioles
questions.why: Muscular arteries are medium-sized arteries, such as the femoral, axillary, brachial and radial arteries. Their tunica media is mostly smooth muscle, up to forty layers thick, which lets them distribute blood to specific organs and hold vascular tone. They sit between the large elastic arteries and the tiny arterioles in size.
notes: Elastic arteries, such as the aorta, have a tunica media dominated by elastic tissue rather than smooth muscle. Pick them if the question asked which arteries stretch and recoil with each heartbeat.
Correct. Muscular arteries have a smooth-muscle media and deliver blood to organs.

Arterioles also have smooth muscle, but only one or two layers, and they control flow into capillary beds rather than delivering blood to whole organs. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels are the gatekeepers of capillary beds.
Metarterioles are the tapered terminal ends of arterioles, where they join a capillary bed. Choose them if the question asked which segment leads directly into capillaries.
questions.answerText: Muscular arteries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the correct order of the five vessel types as blood flows from the heart and back?
options: Artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein
Artery, capillary, arteriole, vein, venule
Arteriole, artery, capillary, vein, venule
Vein, venule, capillary, arteriole, artery
questions.why: Arteries leave the heart and branch into smaller arterioles, which feed the capillaries where exchange happens. The capillaries then merge into venules, which join to form veins that return blood to the heart. The sequence gets smaller toward the capillaries and larger again on the way back.
notes: Correct. Blood flows artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein.
This order puts the capillary before the arteriole and the vein before the venule. Arterioles feed capillaries, and venules drain into veins, so both pairs are reversed.
This order starts with an arteriole and ends with a venule. Blood leaves the heart in a large artery first and returns through a large vein last.
This is the correct sequence run backward, from the vein side to the artery side. It would describe the order if blood flowed toward the tissues through veins, which it does not.
questions.answerText: Artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A guard stands motionless for hours, and blood pools in the veins of his legs. What normally helps push this blood back toward the heart that is missing here?
options: Closing of the precapillary sphincters in the legs
Contraction of the smooth muscle in the leg arteries
Contractions of the leg muscles squeezing the deep veins
Recoil of the aorta between heartbeats
questions.why: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so they rely on help to move it uphill from the legs. When you walk, contracting leg muscles squeeze the deep veins, and the venous valves let the blood move only toward the heart; this is the skeletal muscle pump. Standing still turns that pump off, so blood pools in the leg veins.
notes: Precapillary sphincters open or close capillary entrances to control flow into a capillary bed. They would be the answer if the question asked what regulates blood entering individual capillaries.

Smooth muscle in the leg arteries narrows or widens them to adjust delivery, but it works on the arterial side and does not push venous blood upward. Pick it if the question asked what causes vasoconstriction of an artery.
Correct. The skeletal muscle pump, idle while standing still, normally pushes leg vein blood upward.

The aorta's elastic recoil keeps blood moving forward through the arteries between beats, but its push is mostly used up by the time blood reaches the veins. Choose it if the question asked what keeps arterial blood moving while the ventricles relax.
questions.answerText: Contractions of the leg muscles squeezing the deep veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which group of vessels, taken together, holds the largest share of the body's blood at rest?
options: The arteries
The arterioles
The capillaries
The veins
questions.why: At rest, the veins hold roughly sixty percent of the body's blood, so they are called blood reservoirs. Their thin walls and wide lumens let them stretch and hold a large volume at low pressure. When the body needs more circulating blood, some of this stored volume can be moved back toward the heart.
notes: Arteries have thick walls and narrower lumens and hold a much smaller share of the blood at any moment. Pick them if the question asked which vessels carry blood under the highest pressure.
Arterioles are small vessels that regulate flow into capillary beds and hold little blood. Choose them if the question asked which vessels are the gatekeepers of capillary beds.
Capillaries are enormous in number, but each is tiny, so together they hold only a small share of the blood. They would be the answer if the question asked where exchange takes place.
Correct. The veins act as the body's blood reservoir.
questions.answerText: The veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On a slide, a vessel wall is a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, with no tunica media and no tunica externa. Which vessel type is it?
options: A vein
A muscular artery
A capillary
An arteriole
questions.why: A wall made of only endothelium on a basement membrane is the tunica intima alone, and the capillary is the only vessel built this way. Lacking the other two tunics keeps the wall as thin as possible. That thinness is what lets gases, nutrients and wastes pass between the blood and the tissue.
notes: A vein has all three tunics, with a thin media, a thick externa and a wide lumen. Choose it if the slide showed a collapsed-looking vessel with a thick outer layer.
A muscular artery has a thick tunica media of many smooth muscle layers. It would be the answer if the slide showed a round vessel with a heavy muscular wall.
Correct. Only a capillary has an endothelium with no media or externa.
An arteriole has one or two layers of smooth muscle in a tunica media around its endothelium. Pick it if the slide showed a tiny vessel with a thin ring of muscle.
questions.answerText: A capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel has a thinner wall and a wider lumen than its matching artery, with valves along its course. Which vessel type is it?
options: An arteriole
An elastic artery
A vein
A capillary
questions.why: Three clues point to a vein: a thinner wall, a wider lumen, and valves. Veins carry blood back to the heart under low pressure, so they need less muscle, and their valves keep the slow-moving blood from flowing backward. Arteries lack valves and have thicker, more muscular walls.
notes: An arteriole is a small artery with smooth muscle and no valves. Choose it if the description mentioned the vessel that controls flow into a capillary bed.
An elastic artery, such as the aorta, has a thick wall rich in elastic tissue and no valves. Pick it if the description mentioned a large artery that stretches and recoils with each heartbeat.
Correct. A thin wall, wide lumen and valves identify a vein.
A capillary has a wall only one cell thick and no valves. It would be the answer if the description mentioned an endothelium with no tunica media or externa.
questions.answerText: A vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A capillary in the liver is wide and leaky, with large gaps between its endothelial cells so whole blood cells can cross. Which capillary type is it?
options: A fenestrated capillary
A continuous capillary
A metarteriole
A sinusoid
questions.why: Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, with large fenestrations, wide gaps between cells, and an incomplete basement membrane. In the liver, this lets large proteins and even whole cells move between the blood and the liver tissue. Capillary type always follows the job of the tissue.
notes: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores but an intact basement membrane, so they pass fluid and small molecules but not cells. They would be the answer if the question described the kidney or small intestine.
Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the tightest type. Pick them if the question described the capillaries of the brain, skin or muscle.
A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole that feeds a capillary bed, not a capillary itself. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment leads into the capillaries.
Correct. The wide, leaky capillaries of the liver are sinusoids.
questions.answerText: A sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A capillary in the kidney has an endothelium pierced by small pores for rapid filtration. Which capillary type is it?
options: A metarteriole
A continuous capillary
A fenestrated capillary
A sinusoid
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, called fenestrations, through their endothelium. These pores let fluid and small molecules pass quickly, which suits places where filtration or absorption must happen fast. The kidney, small intestine, choroid plexus and most endocrine glands all use this type.
notes: A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole leading into a capillary bed. Choose it if the question asked which vessel segment feeds a capillary bed.
Continuous capillaries have no pores, only narrow clefts between cells. Pick them if the question described the tight capillaries of the brain.
Correct. Small endothelial pores for filtration identify a fenestrated capillary.

Sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, much leakier than small pores. They would be the answer if the question described capillaries that let whole cells cross, as in the liver or spleen.
questions.answerText: A fenestrated capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which of these is an example of an elastic artery?
options: The femoral artery
The brachial artery
The common carotid artery
The radial artery
questions.why: Elastic arteries are the largest arteries, close to the heart, with a tunica media dominated by elastic tissue. The aorta, pulmonary trunk, brachiocephalic, subclavian, common carotid and common iliac arteries are all elastic arteries. They stretch with each heartbeat and recoil between beats to keep blood moving.
notes: The femoral artery is a muscular artery, a medium-sized vessel with a smooth-muscle media that delivers blood to the thigh. Pick it if the question asked for an example of a muscular artery.
The brachial artery is a muscular artery in the arm, used when measuring blood pressure. Choose it if the question asked for an example of a muscular artery.
Correct. The common carotid is a large elastic artery near the heart.
The radial artery is a muscular artery in the forearm, the one used to take a pulse at the wrist. It would be correct if the question asked for a muscular artery example.
questions.answerText: The common carotid artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel is the smallest type of artery and acts as a gatekeeper that controls how much blood enters a capillary bed?
options: An arteriole
A capillary
A venule
A muscular artery
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, with one or two layers of smooth muscle in their walls. By narrowing or widening, they control how much blood flows into the capillary bed they supply. They are also the main site of resistance to blood flow in the circulation.
notes: Correct. Arterioles are the smallest arteries and the gatekeepers of capillary beds.
A capillary is the exchange vessel inside the bed, downstream of the gate, and has no smooth muscle to control flow. Choose it if the question asked where exchange takes place.
A venule is the smallest vein, collecting blood after it leaves the capillaries. Pick it if the question asked which vessel drains a capillary bed.
A muscular artery is a medium-sized artery that distributes blood to whole organs. It would be the answer if the question asked about arteries like the brachial or femoral.
questions.answerText: An arteriole

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which structure is a direct channel that lets blood bypass the capillaries of a bed when exchange is not needed?
options: A portal system
A precapillary sphincter
A vascular shunt
A capillary bed
questions.why: A vascular shunt is a direct channel through a capillary bed that lets blood travel from the arteriole side to the venule side without entering the capillaries. When the precapillary sphincters close, blood takes the shunt instead. This lets the body send blood past tissues that do not need exchange at the moment.
notes: A portal system sends blood through two capillary beds in series, adding exchange rather than skipping it. Choose it if the question described the route from the digestive organs through the liver.

A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle that opens or closes the entrance to a capillary. It decides whether blood enters a capillary, so pick it if the question asked what controls a capillary's entrance.
Correct. A vascular shunt carries blood past the capillaries.
A capillary bed is the network of capillaries where exchange happens, which the shunt goes around. Pick it if the question asked what a single arteriole supplies.
questions.answerText: A vascular shunt

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: At which vessel type do white blood cells usually leave the bloodstream to enter the tissues?
options: Vein
Venule
Arteriole
Elastic artery
questions.why: Venules, especially the postcapillary venules that receive blood straight from the capillaries, have thin walls whose cells are loosely joined and very porous. White blood cells slip between these cells to leave the blood and enter the surrounding tissue. This is why venules are described as the main exit point for white blood cells.
notes: Veins have thicker walls with all three tunics and carry blood back to the heart. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels have valves and act as blood reservoirs.
Correct. White blood cells usually leave the blood through the porous walls of venules.
Arterioles have a ring of smooth muscle and control flow into capillary beds, not the exit of white blood cells. Pick them if the question asked which vessels regulate blood flow into a bed.
Elastic arteries, like the aorta, have thick elastic walls and carry blood under high pressure. Choose them if the question asked which arteries stretch and recoil with each heartbeat.
questions.answerText: Venule

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the middle layer whose smooth muscle sets the diameter of the vessel?
options: The tunica media
The tunica externa
The tunica intima
The basement membrane
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer, made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. When its smooth muscle contracts, the vessel narrows (vasoconstriction), and when it relaxes, the vessel widens (vasodilation). This is how vessels adjust how much blood flows through them.
notes: Correct. The smooth muscle of the tunica media sets vessel diameter.
The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors the vessel, with no smooth muscle to squeeze it. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is thickest in veins.
The tunica intima is the innermost endothelial lining and has no muscle to change the diameter. Pick it if the question asked which layer faces the lumen.
The basement membrane is the thin layer the endothelium rests on, part of the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked what supports the endothelial cells.
questions.answerText: The tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the order of the three tunics of a vessel wall, from the lumen outward?
options: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa
Tunica intima, tunica externa, tunica media
Tunica media, tunica intima, tunica externa
Tunica externa, tunica media, tunica intima
questions.why: Starting at the lumen, the tunica intima comes first as the endothelial lining. The tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers surrounds it, and the collagen-rich tunica externa forms the outer covering. The names match the order: intima for innermost, media for middle, externa for external.
notes: Correct. Intima, media, then externa, from the lumen outward.
This order swaps the media and the externa. The muscular media lies in the middle, with the collagen externa wrapped around it.
This order puts the media first, but the endothelial lining of the intima always faces the lumen. Students sometimes pick it because the media is the thickest and most noticeable layer in an artery.
This is the correct order read from the outside in. It would be right if the question asked for the tunics from the outer surface toward the lumen.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the order of the three capillary types from the tightest, least leaky wall to the leakiest wall?
options: Continuous capillary, sinusoid, fenestrated capillary
Fenestrated capillary, continuous capillary, sinusoid
Continuous capillary, fenestrated capillary, sinusoid
Sinusoid, fenestrated capillary, continuous capillary
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the tightest. Fenestrated capillaries add small pores that pass fluid and small molecules quickly. Sinusoids are the leakiest, with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane so even whole cells can cross. The capillary type is matched to how much the tissue needs to let through.
notes: This order places sinusoids in the middle, but their large gaps make them leakier than fenestrated capillaries with small pores.
This order puts fenestrated capillaries ahead of continuous ones. Continuous capillaries have no pores at all, so they are tighter than fenestrated ones.
Correct. Continuous, then fenestrated, then sinusoid.
This is the correct order reversed, from leakiest to tightest. It would be right if the question asked for the leakiest type first.
questions.answerText: Continuous capillary, fenestrated capillary, sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the order of the three sizes of artery, from largest to smallest?
options: Muscular artery, elastic artery, arteriole
Arteriole, muscular artery, elastic artery
Elastic artery, muscular artery, arteriole
Elastic artery, arteriole, muscular artery
questions.why: Elastic arteries such as the aorta are the largest and sit closest to the heart. They branch into medium-sized muscular arteries, such as the brachial and femoral, which distribute blood to organs. Muscular arteries then branch into the microscopic arterioles that feed capillary beds.
notes: This order puts muscular arteries ahead of elastic ones. The elastic arteries, like the aorta, are the largest because they receive blood straight from the heart.
This is the correct order reversed, from smallest to largest. It would be right if the question asked for the sizes from smallest to largest.
Correct. Elastic arteries, then muscular arteries, then arterioles.
This order places arterioles in the middle, but arterioles are the smallest arteries, the last branches before the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Elastic artery, muscular artery, arteriole

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which choice correctly matches each tunic to its main tissue?
options: Intima is elastic fibers, media is collagen, externa is endothelium
Intima is mostly collagen, media is endothelium, externa is smooth muscle
Intima is endothelium, media is smooth muscle, externa is collagen
