Intima is smooth muscle, media is collagen, externa is endothelium
questions.why: The tunica intima is a lining of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane, facing the lumen. The tunica media is smooth muscle and elastic fibers, which set the vessel's diameter. The tunica externa is mostly collagen, which anchors the vessel to the tissue around it.
notes: This match places the endothelium on the outside of the vessel, but endothelium always lines the lumen. Elastic fibers are part of the media, not the intima's main tissue.
This match puts collagen on the inside and endothelium in the middle. The endothelium must face the lumen to give blood a smooth surface, so it belongs to the intima.
Correct. Endothelium, then smooth muscle and elastic fibers, then collagen.
This match moves every tissue one layer inward. Smooth muscle belongs in the middle layer, and the endothelium lines the inside, not the outside.
questions.answerText: Intima is endothelium, media is smooth muscle, externa is collagen

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On a slide, an artery and its matching vein sit side by side. Which description fits the pair?
options: The vein is round with a thick media; the artery looks collapsed with a thick externa
The artery is round with a thick media; the vein looks collapsed with a thick externa
The artery looks collapsed because its lumen is wider than the vein's
Both are round, but the vein has the thicker tunica media
questions.why: Arteries and veins have the same three tunics in different proportions. The artery's thick, muscular tunica media holds it open and round, while the vein has a thin media, a thick collagen externa and a wide lumen, so it often looks flattened or collapsed. This is usually the fastest way to tell the pair apart on a slide.
notes: This reverses the two vessels. The artery's thick media keeps it round, and the vein's thin wall lets it collapse.
Correct. A round, thick-media artery beside a collapsed, thick-externa vein is the classic pair.
The vein is the one with the wider lumen, and it is the vein that collapses. Students pick this when they link a wide lumen to the artery instead of the vein.
The artery, not the vein, has the thicker tunica media, because it carries blood under higher pressure. The vein's thickest layer is the tunica externa.
questions.answerText: The artery is round with a thick media; the vein looks collapsed with a thick externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the order of these vessels by wall thickness, from thickest to thinnest: capillary, vein, artery?
options: Vein, artery, capillary
Capillary, vein, artery
Artery, vein, capillary
Artery, capillary, vein
questions.why: Arteries have the thickest walls, with a heavy tunica media to handle high pressure. Veins have all three tunics but a thinner media, so their walls are thinner than those of matching arteries. Capillaries have the thinnest walls of all, just one layer of endothelium, so exchange can happen across them.
notes: This order puts the vein ahead of the artery. Veins carry blood at low pressure and have thinner walls than their matching arteries.
This is the correct order reversed, from thinnest to thickest. It would be right if the question asked for the thinnest wall first.
Correct. Artery, then vein, then capillary.
This order places the capillary in the middle, but with a wall only one cell thick it is thinner than any vein.
questions.answerText: Artery, vein, capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: How many tunics make up the wall of an artery or a vein?
options: Two
Five
Three
Four
questions.why: Arteries and veins both have three tunics: the tunica intima, the tunica media and the tunica externa. The two vessel types differ in the thickness of these layers, not in their number. Capillaries are the exception, with only the tunica intima.
notes: Two might come from counting only the muscle and connective tissue layers and forgetting the endothelial lining. Arteries and veins have all three tunics.
Five matches the number of vessel types (artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein), a common mix-up. The question asks about layers in one wall, and there are three.
Correct. Intima, media and externa make three tunics.
Four may come from counting the basement membrane or an elastic lamina as a separate tunic. Those are parts of or borders between the three tunics, not extra tunics.
questions.answerText: Three

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the thickest layer in a vein?
options: The basement membrane
The tunica externa
The tunica intima
The tunica media
questions.why: In a vein, the tunica externa, the outer collagen layer, is the thickest tunic. Veins carry blood under low pressure, so they need only a thin tunica media, and their collagen externa provides most of the support. This is the reverse of an artery, where the muscular tunica media is thickest.
notes: The basement membrane is a thin sheet under the endothelium, part of the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked what the endothelial cells rest on.
Correct. The tunica externa is the thickest layer in a vein.
The tunica intima is a thin endothelial lining in every vessel and is never the thickest layer of a vein. Pick it if the question asked which layer forms the venous valves.
The tunica media is the thickest layer in an artery, not a vein. Students pick it because they carry over the artery rule, but veins have a thin media.
questions.answerText: The tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which small vessels within the tunica externa supply the wall of a large vessel such as the aorta?
options: The vascular sinuses
The vasa vasorum
The coronary arteries
The metarterioles
questions.why: The vasa vasorum, meaning vessels of the vessels, are small blood vessels in the tunica externa that supply the wall of a large vessel. The wall of a large artery like the aorta is too thick to be nourished only by the blood flowing through its lumen. These small vessels are easy to see in the outer layer of the aorta on a slide.
notes: Vascular sinuses are thin-walled veins with no smooth muscle, such as the dural venous sinuses and the coronary sinus. Choose them if the question asked about veins supported by surrounding dense connective tissue.
Correct. The vasa vasorum supply the walls of large vessels.
The coronary arteries supply the heart wall, not the walls of other vessels. Pick them if the question asked which vessels feed the myocardium.
Metarterioles are the tapered ends of arterioles that feed capillary beds in tissues. They would be the answer if the question asked which segment joins an arteriole to its capillaries.
questions.answerText: The vasa vasorum

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Blood flows through the hollow central channel of a vessel. What is this channel called?
options: The anastomosis
The tunic
The lumen
The fenestration
questions.why: The lumen is the hollow interior of a vessel, the channel blood flows through. It is surrounded by the vessel wall, starting with the endothelium of the tunica intima. Comparing lumens on a slide helps tell vessels apart, since veins have a wider lumen than their matching arteries.
notes: An anastomosis is a place where two vessels join to give blood an alternate route. Choose it if the question asked what protects a tissue when one vessel is blocked.
A tunic is one of the layers of the vessel wall around the lumen, not the space itself. Pick it if the question asked for the general name of a wall layer.
Correct. The lumen is the channel inside the vessel.
A fenestration is a small pore in the endothelium of certain capillaries. It would be the answer if the question asked about the windows in kidney or intestinal capillaries.
questions.answerText: The lumen

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What are the flaps of the tunica intima in limb veins that keep blood from flowing backward called?
options: Fenestrations
Anastomoses
Venous valves
Precapillary sphincters
questions.why: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that project into the lumen of a vein. They open as blood moves toward the heart and close if it starts to flow backward. They are most common in limb veins, where blood must travel uphill at low pressure, and they can sometimes be seen as small bumps along a forearm vein.
notes: Fenestrations are small pores in the endothelium of some capillaries, which let fluid pass quickly. Pick them if the question asked about the pores in kidney capillaries.
Anastomoses are junctions between vessels that give blood an alternate route. Choose them if the question asked what keeps a tissue supplied when one vessel is blocked.
Correct. Venous valves are the intimal flaps that stop backflow.
Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle that open or close the entrance to a capillary. They would be the answer if the question asked what controls blood entering a single capillary.
questions.answerText: Venous valves

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the narrowing of a vessel caused by contraction of the smooth muscle in its wall called?
options: Vasodilation
Atherosclerosis
Vasoconstriction
Aneurysm
questions.why: Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of a vessel as the smooth muscle of its tunica media contracts. Vaso means vessel and constriction means narrowing. It reduces blood flow through that vessel and is one way arterioles control how much blood reaches a capillary bed.
notes: Vasodilation is the opposite, the widening of a vessel as its smooth muscle relaxes. Pick it if the question asked what happens when the tunica media relaxes.
Atherosclerosis also narrows an artery, but the cause is fatty plaque building up in the wall, not muscle contraction. It would be the answer if the question asked about narrowing caused by plaque.
Correct. Vasoconstriction is narrowing from smooth muscle contraction.
An aneurysm is a weakened area of a vessel wall that balloons outward, the opposite of narrowing. Choose it if the question asked about a bulge in an artery wall.
questions.answerText: Vasoconstriction

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the tapered terminal end of an arteriole, where it joins a capillary bed, called?
options: The postcapillary venule
The metarteriole
The precapillary sphincter
The muscular artery
questions.why: The metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole, where it meets a capillary bed. Capillaries branch off it, and precapillary sphincters at those branch points open or close each capillary's entrance. Its far end has no smooth muscle and forms a thoroughfare channel that leads straight to a venule.
notes: The postcapillary venule is on the opposite side of the capillary bed, receiving blood as it leaves the capillaries. Pick it if the question asked which vessel first drains a capillary bed.
Correct. The metarteriole is the arteriole's tapered end at the capillary bed.

The precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle on the metarteriole at the entrance to a capillary, not the arteriole's end itself. It would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary.
A muscular artery is a much larger, medium-sized artery that distributes blood to organs. Choose it if the question asked about arteries like the brachial or femoral.
questions.answerText: The metarteriole

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which structure is a ring of smooth muscle that opens or closes the entrance to a capillary?
options: A precapillary sphincter
A fenestration
A venous valve
An anastomosis
questions.why: A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle on the metarteriole at the point where a capillary branches off. When it contracts, blood is kept out of that capillary, and when it relaxes, blood flows in. A sphincter is any ring of muscle that closes an opening, which is exactly its job here.
notes: Correct. A precapillary sphincter guards a capillary's entrance.
A fenestration is a small pore in the endothelium of some capillaries. Choose it if the question asked about the windows in fenestrated capillaries.
A venous valve is a flap of the tunica intima in a vein that prevents backflow, with no muscle in it. Pick it if the question asked what keeps limb vein blood moving toward the heart.
An anastomosis is a junction where two vessels meet, giving an alternate route. It would be the answer if the question asked what keeps a tissue supplied when one vessel is blocked.
questions.answerText: A precapillary sphincter

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Sinusoids are found where even whole blood cells must cross the capillary wall. Which of these tissues contains sinusoids?
options: Skeletal muscle
The brain
The small intestine
Red bone marrow
questions.why: Sinusoids are wide, leaky capillaries with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. Red bone marrow uses them so newly made blood cells can move from the marrow into the bloodstream. Sinusoids are also found in the liver, spleen, anterior pituitary and adrenal glands.
notes: Skeletal muscle has continuous capillaries, the most common type. It would be the answer if the question asked where continuous capillaries are found.
The brain has continuous capillaries, the tightest type, which keep most substances out of brain tissue. Pick it if the question asked where continuous capillaries matter most.
The small intestine has fenestrated capillaries, whose small pores speed the absorption of nutrients. Choose it if the question asked where fenestrated capillaries are found.
Correct. Red bone marrow has sinusoids so new blood cells can enter the blood.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Contracting limb muscles squeeze the deep veins and push blood toward the heart. What is this mechanism called?
options: Elastic recoil
The skeletal muscle pump
Vasoconstriction
The precapillary sphincter
questions.why: The skeletal muscle pump is the squeezing of deep veins by the surrounding skeletal muscles as they contract during movement. Each squeeze pushes blood forward, and the venous valves stop it from sliding back. This is one of the main ways low-pressure venous blood returns from the limbs to the heart.
notes: Elastic recoil is the springing back of elastic arteries like the aorta between heartbeats. Choose it if the question asked what keeps arterial blood moving while the ventricles relax.
Correct. The skeletal muscle pump moves blood through the deep veins.

Vasoconstriction is narrowing of a vessel by the smooth muscle in its own wall, not squeezing by nearby skeletal muscle. Pick it if the question asked what happens when a vessel's tunica media contracts.
A precapillary sphincter is a smooth muscle ring that controls entry into a capillary, far from the deep veins. It would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary entrance.
questions.answerText: The skeletal muscle pump

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In the vascular sequence, what do capillaries merge into as blood starts back toward the heart?
options: Arterioles
Elastic arteries
Metarterioles
Venules
questions.why: After exchange in the capillary bed, the capillaries merge into venules, the smallest veins. Venules then join to form larger veins that return blood to the heart. The full sequence is artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein.
notes: Arterioles come before the capillaries, feeding blood into the bed. Pick them if the question asked which vessels supply a capillary bed.

Elastic arteries, like the aorta, are the largest arteries near the heart, at the very start of the sequence. They would be the answer if the question asked which arteries stretch and recoil with each heartbeat.
Metarterioles are the tapered ends of arterioles on the arterial side of the bed. Choose them if the question asked which vessel segment leads into the capillaries.
Correct. Capillaries drain into venules.
questions.answerText: Venules

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Blood is drawn and an IV line is placed in a forearm vessel because it is close to the surface, thin-walled, and at low pressure. Which vessel type is used?
options: An arteriole
A vein
An artery
A capillary
questions.why: Veins are used for blood draws and IV lines because they sit close to the surface, have thin walls with wide lumens, and carry blood at low pressure. That makes them easy to enter with a needle and slow to bleed afterward. Their valves can even be seen as small bumps along a forearm vein.
notes: Arterioles are microscopic arteries buried in the tissues, too small and too deep to use. Choose them if the question asked which vessels control flow into a capillary bed.
Correct. A superficial, thin-walled, low-pressure vein is used.

Arteries carry blood under high pressure, have thick walls, and usually lie deeper, so puncturing one bleeds more and is harder to control. Pick an artery if the question asked where you feel a pulse.

Capillaries are far too small for a needle or IV line, though a finger stick does draw a drop of capillary blood. They would be the answer if the question asked where exchange with the tissues happens.
questions.answerText: A vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The brain needs capillaries that keep most substances in the blood out of the brain tissue. Which capillary type fits this job?
options: The postcapillary venule
The sinusoid
The continuous capillary
The fenestrated capillary
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining with only narrow clefts between cells, so they are the tightest type. In the brain the cells are joined especially tightly, which keeps most substances in the blood from reaching brain tissue. Capillary type is always matched to what the tissue needs to let through.
notes: The postcapillary venule is a small, very porous vein that drains a capillary bed, not a capillary type, and it is where white blood cells leave the blood. Choose it if the question asked where white blood cells exit the bloodstream.
Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, letting even whole cells cross. They would be the answer if the question described the liver, spleen or red bone marrow.
Correct. Tight continuous capillaries protect the brain.
Fenestrated capillaries have pores built for fast filtration and absorption, the opposite of what the brain needs. Pick them if the question described the kidney or small intestine.
questions.answerText: The continuous capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Following blood from the heart to a tissue, it has just left an arteriole. Which vessel does it enter next?
options: An elastic artery
A venule
A capillary
A vein
questions.why: Arterioles are the last vessels on the arterial side, and they feed directly into the capillaries of a capillary bed. In the capillaries, gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with the tissue. From there blood drains into venules and then veins.
notes: An elastic artery, like the aorta, is at the start of the sequence near the heart, before the arterioles. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel blood enters when it leaves the left ventricle.
A venule comes after the capillaries, collecting the blood that has passed through the bed. Choose it if the question asked which vessel blood enters after leaving a capillary.
Correct. Arterioles empty into capillaries.
A vein comes at the end of the sequence, after the capillaries and venules. Pick it if the question asked which vessel carries blood back to the heart.
questions.answerText: A capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The far end of a metarteriole has no smooth muscle and runs straight from the arteriole to a venule. What is this channel called?
options: A precapillary sphincter
An arteriovenous anastomosis
A thoroughfare channel
A postcapillary venule
questions.why: A thoroughfare channel is the distal end of a metarteriole, which has no smooth muscle and leads straight to a venule. It gives blood a direct route through the capillary bed. When the precapillary sphincters close, blood can pass through this channel instead of entering the capillaries.
notes: A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance, while this channel has no muscle at all. Pick it if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary.
An arteriovenous anastomosis connects an artery directly to a vein, outside the capillary bed. Choose it if the question described an artery linked straight to a vein with no capillaries involved.
Correct. The muscle-free end of the metarteriole is the thoroughfare channel.

A postcapillary venule is the first small vein receiving blood from the capillaries, where the thoroughfare channel empties. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel first drains a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: A thoroughfare channel

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A capillary wall is a single layer of flat endothelial cells, with no muscle or connective tissue layers. Why does this thin wall suit the capillary's job?
options: It keeps all blood cells and proteins inside the vessel
It makes the distance for diffusion as short as possible
It makes the vessel strong enough for high arterial pressure
It lets the capillary narrow and widen to control flow
questions.why: Capillaries are the exchange vessels, and gases, nutrients and wastes cross their walls mainly by diffusion, the movement of substances from higher to lower concentration. Diffusion is fastest over short distances. A wall only one flat cell thick keeps the distance between the blood and the tissue as short as possible.
notes: Thinness does not decide what stays inside; that depends on the capillary type, and sinusoids are thin yet let whole cells cross. This choice confuses the thickness of the wall with how tightly its cells are joined.
Correct. A one-cell wall gives the shortest diffusion distance.
A thin wall is weaker, not stronger, which is why capillaries sit downstream of arterioles where pressure has already dropped. Thick walls for high pressure describe arteries.
Narrowing and widening require smooth muscle, which capillaries lack. That job belongs to arterioles and precapillary sphincters upstream of the capillaries.
questions.answerText: It makes the distance for diffusion as short as possible

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls, while veins of similar size have thinner walls. Why does this difference fit each vessel's job?
options: Arteries face high pressure from the heart; veins carry low-pressure blood back
Veins carry blood at higher pressure, so their thin walls stretch to absorb it
Arteries need thick walls to hold the larger share of the body's blood
Arteries need thick walls so exchange can happen across them
questions.why: Arteries receive blood forced out by the ventricles, so they must withstand high pressure, and their thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers lets them stretch, recoil and control their diameter. By the time blood reaches the veins, most of that pressure is gone. Veins can therefore have thinner walls, relying on valves and nearby muscles to keep blood moving.
notes: Correct. Wall thickness matches the pressure each vessel carries.
This reverses the pressures. Arteries carry the high-pressure blood, and veins carry low-pressure blood back to the heart.
Veins, not arteries, hold the largest share of the body's blood, about sixty percent at rest. Their thin walls and wide lumens are what let them act as reservoirs.
Exchange happens only across thin capillary walls, and a thick wall would block it. Pick capillaries if the question asked which vessels are built for exchange.
questions.answerText: Arteries face high pressure from the heart; veins carry low-pressure blood back

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Veins, especially in the legs, contain one-way valves that arteries lack. Why do veins need valves while arteries do not?
options: Valves in veins filter debris out of the returning blood
Valves in veins speed blood up to match arterial pressure
Valves keep blood from flowing too quickly into the capillaries
Low-pressure venous blood, often moving uphill, can slide backward
questions.why: Arterial blood is pushed forward by high pressure from the heart, so it does not tend to flow backward. Venous blood moves at low pressure and, in the legs, has to travel uphill against gravity. Valves made from flaps of the tunica intima close if blood starts to slide back, so each push from nearby muscles moves blood only toward the heart.
notes: Venous valves are simple flaps with no filtering role. Filtering of blood happens in organs like the spleen and the kidneys, not in vein walls.
Valves do not add pressure or speed; they only prevent backward flow. Students pick this when they confuse a valve with a pump.
Veins are downstream of the capillaries, so their valves cannot control flow into capillaries. That job belongs to arterioles and precapillary sphincters on the arterial side.
Correct. Low pressure and gravity make valves necessary in veins.
questions.answerText: Low-pressure venous blood, often moving uphill, can slide backward

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Arterioles have smooth muscle in their walls that can tighten or relax. Why does this muscular control matter for the body?
options: The muscle pumps blood forward like a small heart
The muscle lets nutrients pass through the arteriole wall
It lets arterioles send more blood to tissues that need it
The muscle keeps blood from flowing backward toward the heart
questions.why: Arterioles are the gatekeepers of capillary beds. When their smooth muscle relaxes (vasodilation), more blood flows into that bed, and when it contracts (vasoconstriction), less does. This lets the body shift blood to active tissues, such as working muscles during exercise, and away from tissues that need less at the moment.
notes: Vessel smooth muscle holds or changes diameter; it does not beat rhythmically to pump blood. The heart is the only pump in the system.
Arteriole walls are too thick for exchange, and their muscle does not help substances cross. Nutrients cross in the capillaries, whose walls are one cell thick.
Correct. Adjusting their diameter lets arterioles direct blood where it is needed.
Preventing backflow is the job of venous valves in veins. Arterial blood is already pushed forward by the pressure from the heart.
questions.answerText: It lets arterioles send more blood to tissues that need it

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The aorta has an especially high proportion of elastic tissue in its wall. Why is this elasticity valuable right where blood leaves the heart?
options: It lets oxygen and nutrients pass through the aortic wall
It lets the aorta contract on its own to pump blood like a second heart
It keeps the aorta rigid so it cannot expand
It stretches with each surge, then recoils to push blood between beats
questions.why: With each contraction, the left ventricle pushes a surge of blood into the aorta. The elastic wall stretches to absorb that surge, then recoils while the ventricles relax, pushing blood onward between beats. This smooths the flow, and when elastic arteries stiffen with age, that cushioning is lost and the strain shows up in smaller vessels downstream.
notes: The aortic wall is far too thick for exchange, and its own outer layers are supplied by the vasa vasorum. Oxygen and nutrients reach tissues only across capillary walls.
Elastic tissue recoils passively but cannot contract on its own, and the aorta does not pump. Students pick this when they confuse elastic recoil with muscle contraction.
Elastic tissue does the opposite of making a wall rigid; it lets it stretch and spring back. Stiffness is what happens when elastic arteries lose that tissue with age.
Correct. Stretch and recoil keep blood moving between heartbeats.
questions.answerText: It stretches with each surge, then recoils to push blood between beats

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Blood flow slows dramatically as it passes through capillary beds compared with arteries. Why is slow flow through capillaries useful?
options: It allows more time for exchange with the tissue
Capillaries actually have the fastest flow in the body
It lets the capillaries hold most of the body's blood
It gives platelets time to seal the capillary wall
questions.why: Capillaries are where exchange happens, and exchange takes time because substances cross the wall by diffusion. Blood slows in the capillaries because it is spread across an enormous number of tiny vessels. That slower pace gives oxygen, nutrients and wastes more time to cross between the blood and the tissue.
notes: Correct. Slow flow allows more time for exchange.
Flow is slowest, not fastest, in the capillaries. Students pick this because each capillary is so narrow, but the total cross-section of all capillaries together is huge, which slows the flow.
The veins, not the capillaries, hold the largest share of the blood, about sixty percent at rest. Choose the veins if the question asked which vessels act as blood reservoirs.
Platelets seal a vessel only after it is injured, and slow flow is not about clotting. This choice mixes up normal exchange with the response to bleeding.
questions.answerText: It allows more time for exchange with the tissue

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells pass through almost single file. Why is this tight fit useful?
options: It squeezes oxygen out of the red cells by pressure
It keeps white blood cells from entering the capillary
It keeps each red cell close to the wall for gas exchange
It filters worn-out red blood cells out of circulation
questions.why: Oxygen and carbon dioxide move between red blood cells and tissue by diffusion, which works best over short distances. When red cells pass through a capillary almost single file, each one presses close to the thin endothelial wall. That keeps the path for gases between the cell and the tissue very short.
notes: Oxygen leaves red cells by diffusion toward the tissue, not because the cells are squeezed. Students pick this when they picture the capillary wringing the cells out like a sponge.
White blood cells do pass through capillaries and usually leave the blood at venules. The tight fit is about exchange, not about keeping white cells out.
Correct. Single-file flow keeps each red cell close to the wall for exchange.
Worn-out red blood cells are removed mainly in the spleen, which uses leaky sinusoids for that job. Pick the spleen if the question asked where old red cells are filtered out.
questions.answerText: It keeps each red cell close to the wall for gas exchange

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which structure is a fenestrated sheet of elastic fibers at the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media?
options: The vasa vasorum
The external elastic lamina
The basement membrane
The internal elastic lamina
questions.why: The internal elastic lamina is a sheet of elastic fibers with small openings that marks the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media. Internal tells you it is the inner of the two elastic sheets. It is easy to see in arteries as a wavy line just outside the endothelium.
notes: The vasa vasorum are small blood vessels in the tunica externa that supply the walls of large vessels. Choose them if the question asked how the wall of the aorta gets its own blood supply.
The external elastic lamina is the outer elastic sheet, separating the tunica media from the tunica externa. Pick it if the question asked which boundary lies between the media and the externa.

The basement membrane is the thin layer the endothelium rests on, inside the tunica intima, and it is not made of elastic fibers. It would be the answer if the question asked what supports the endothelial cells.
Correct. The internal elastic lamina separates the intima from the media.
questions.answerText: The internal elastic lamina

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On an artery slide, you find the internal and external elastic laminae. Which layer lies between them?
options: The tunica externa
The tunica media
The tunica intima
The lumen
questions.why: The internal elastic lamina marks the inner edge of the tunica media, and the external elastic lamina marks its outer edge. So everything between the two elastic sheets is the tunica media. Measuring how thick that band is helps you decide whether you are looking at an artery, with a thick media, or a vein, with a thin one.
notes: The tunica externa lies outside the external elastic lamina. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is found beyond the outer elastic sheet.
Correct. The two elastic laminae border the tunica media.
The tunica intima lies inside the internal elastic lamina, between it and the lumen. Pick it if the question asked which layer is found on the lumen side of the internal elastic lamina.
The lumen is the open channel in the center of the vessel, inside the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked where the blood flows.
questions.answerText: The tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vascular sinus is a vein with a thin endothelial wall and no smooth muscle, supported by the dense connective tissue around it. Which of these is a vascular sinus?
options: The coronary sinus
The maxillary sinus
The femoral vein
The great saphenous vein
questions.why: The coronary sinus on the back of the heart is a vascular sinus. It collects blood from the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium, and its wall is thin endothelium without smooth muscle. The dural venous sinuses of the brain are the other main example.
notes: Correct. The coronary sinus is a vascular sinus.

The maxillary sinus is an air-filled paranasal sinus in the maxilla, not a blood vessel at all. Students pick it because of the shared word sinus, so choose it only for a question about the paranasal sinuses.
The femoral vein is a large deep vein of the thigh with a normal three-layered wall. It would be the answer if the question asked which deep vein runs with the femoral artery.

The great saphenous vein is a long superficial vein of the leg with all three tunics, including smooth muscle, and valves along its length. Pick it if the question asked for the longest superficial vein of the lower limb.
questions.answerText: The coronary sinus

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Avascular tissues have no capillaries at all. Which of these tissues is avascular?
options: The liver
Skeletal muscle
Cartilage
Red bone marrow
questions.why: Avascular means without vessels. Cartilage, the cornea and lens of the eye, and the covering and lining epithelia have no capillaries of their own. They get nutrients by diffusion from nearby tissue, which is one reason cartilage heals so slowly.
notes: The liver is very well supplied with blood and contains sinusoids, the leakiest capillary type. It would be the answer if the question asked which organ has sinusoids that receive blood from the hepatic portal vein.
Skeletal muscle is richly supplied with continuous capillaries to meet its high demand for oxygen. Pick it if the question asked where continuous capillaries are commonly found.
Correct. Cartilage has no capillaries.
Red bone marrow contains sinusoids so new blood cells can enter the bloodstream. Choose it if the question asked where blood cells are made.
questions.answerText: Cartilage

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the widening of a vessel as the smooth muscle in its wall relaxes called?
options: Vasodilation
Vasoconstriction
Aneurysm
Vascular tone
questions.why: Vasodilation is the widening of a vessel when the smooth muscle of its tunica media relaxes. A wider lumen lets more blood flow through. Arterioles use vasodilation to send extra blood into capillary beds of tissues that need it, such as working muscles.
notes: Correct. Vasodilation is widening from smooth muscle relaxation.
Vasoconstriction is the opposite, narrowing of a vessel as its smooth muscle contracts. Pick it if the question asked what happens when the tunica media contracts.
An aneurysm is a bulge in a weakened artery wall, a disorder rather than a normal response of smooth muscle. Choose it if the question asked about a balloon-like swelling that can rupture.

Vascular tone is the partial contraction a vessel holds at rest, which stiffens the wall and keeps up pressure. It would be the answer if the question asked about the vessel's resting state rather than a change in diameter.
questions.answerText: Vasodilation

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Chronically high blood sugar damages capillaries, harming capillary-rich organs such as the retina and kidneys. What makes up the wall of a capillary, the part that is injured?
options: A thick layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers
Three layers, like the wall of a small artery
A single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane
An outer coat of loose connective tissue
questions.why: A capillary wall is only the tunica intima: one layer of simple squamous endothelium resting on a basement membrane. That thinness is what makes capillaries the exchange vessels, since gases and nutrients cross easily. It also means there is little protecting them, so damage to the endothelium directly harms organs that depend on dense capillary beds.
notes: Smooth muscle and elastic fibers make up the tunica media, the thick middle layer of arteries. Capillaries have no tunica media, so pick this for a question about the layer that lets arteries constrict.
Arteries and veins have three tunics, but capillaries have only one. Students choose this when they assume every vessel shares the same layered plan.
Correct. The capillary wall is a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, the tunica intima alone.
An outer coat of connective tissue is the tunica externa, found on arteries and veins. Capillaries lack it, so choose this for a question about the outermost tunic of larger vessels.
questions.answerText: A single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a blood vessel?
options: A cord of dense tissue linking muscle to bone
A tube that carries lymph back to the veins
A tube that carries air into the lungs
A tube that carries blood through the body
questions.why: A blood vessel is a tube that carries blood through the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries allow exchange with the tissues, and veins carry blood back toward the heart. Together with the heart, the vessels form the cardiovascular system.
notes: A cord of dense connective tissue linking muscle to bone is a tendon. Choose it for a question about how muscles attach to bones.
A tube that carries lymph is a lymphatic vessel. Lymphatic vessels return excess tissue fluid to the veins and would be the answer for the lymphatic system.
Tubes that carry air into the lungs are airways such as the trachea and bronchi. They belong to the respiratory system.
Correct. A blood vessel is a tube for blood.
questions.answerText: A tube that carries blood through the body

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is an artery?
options: A vessel that always carries oxygen-rich blood
The smallest vessel, where exchange occurs
A vessel that carries blood toward the heart
A vessel that carries blood away from the heart
questions.why: An artery is any vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but the definition is about direction, not oxygen; the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and are still arteries. Arteries have thick walls with a heavy tunica media to handle high pressure.
notes: This is a common misconception. The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood, so oxygen content cannot define an artery; direction away from the heart does.
The smallest vessel, where exchange occurs, is a capillary. It would be the answer for the vessel whose wall is only the tunica intima.
A vessel that carries blood toward the heart is a vein. Choose this definition for the venae cavae or the pulmonary veins.
Correct. Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
questions.answerText: A vessel that carries blood away from the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a vein?
options: A vessel that carries blood away from the heart
A vessel that carries blood toward the heart
A vessel that always carries oxygen-poor blood
A vessel whose wall is only endothelium
questions.why: A vein is any vessel that carries blood toward the heart. Most veins carry oxygen-poor blood, but the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood and are still veins, because the definition depends on direction. Veins have thinner walls and wider lumens than arteries, and many have valves.
notes: A vessel that carries blood away from the heart is an artery. Choose this definition for the aorta or the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. Veins carry blood toward the heart.
This is a common misconception. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, so oxygen content cannot define a vein; direction toward the heart does.
A vessel whose wall is only endothelium on a basement membrane is a capillary. It would be the answer for the exchange vessels.
questions.answerText: A vessel that carries blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a capillary?
options: A small artery that controls flow into capillaries
The largest artery, leaving the left ventricle
The smallest vessel, where exchange with tissues occurs
A small vein that collects blood from capillaries
questions.why: A capillary is the smallest blood vessel, connecting an arteriole to a venule. Its wall is a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, so it is thin enough for gases, nutrients, and wastes to pass between the blood and the tissues. This exchange is the whole point of the circulation.
notes: A small artery that controls flow into capillaries is an arteriole. Its smooth muscle narrows or widens it to adjust how much blood enters a capillary bed.
The largest artery, leaving the left ventricle, is the aorta. It is a thick-walled elastic artery built to handle high pressure, the opposite of a capillary.
Correct. Capillaries are the tiny exchange vessels.
A small vein that collects blood from capillaries is a venule. Choose it for the vessel that drains a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: The smallest vessel, where exchange with tissues occurs

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists the vessels blood passes through, starting from the heart?
options: Arteries, venules, capillaries, arterioles, veins
Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins
Arteries, capillaries, arterioles, venules, veins
Veins, venules, capillaries, arterioles, arteries
questions.why: Blood leaves the heart in arteries, which branch into smaller arterioles. Arterioles feed the capillaries, where exchange with the tissues happens. Capillaries merge into venules, and venules join to form veins, which carry blood back to the heart.
notes: This swaps arterioles and venules. Arterioles are the small arteries leading into capillaries, and venules are the small veins leading out of them.
Correct. Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins.
This places capillaries before arterioles. Arteries must branch into arterioles before reaching the capillaries.
This is the sequence run backward, from veins to arteries. Blood flows away from the heart in arteries first and returns in veins, not the reverse.
questions.answerText: Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which set names the three tunics of an artery or vein wall?
options: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa
Epicardium, myocardium, endocardium
Epidermis, dermis, hypodermis
Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa
questions.why: The wall of an artery or vein is built in three concentric layers called tunics. From the inside out they are the tunica intima, a lining of endothelium; the tunica media, smooth muscle and elastic fibers; and the tunica externa, mostly collagen. A capillary keeps only the tunica intima.
notes: The mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis externa are layers of the digestive tract wall. Choose them for a question about the wall of the stomach or intestine.
The epicardium, myocardium, and endocardium are the three layers of the heart wall. The endocardium is continuous with the tunica intima, but this set names the heart's layers.
The epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis are the layers of the skin and the tissue beneath it. They belong to the integumentary system.
Correct. These are the three tunics of a vessel wall.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the innermost layer of a vessel wall?
options: Tunica externa
Tunica media
Tunica intima
Tunica albuginea
questions.why: The tunica intima is the innermost tunic, the one in direct contact with the blood. It is a lining of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane, and it is continuous with the endocardium of the heart. Intima shares a root with intimate, meaning innermost.
notes: The tunica externa is the outermost tunic, mostly collagen, that anchors the vessel. It would be the answer for the outer layer.
The tunica media is the middle tunic, made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. Choose it for the layer that sets the vessel's diameter.
Correct. The tunica intima is the innermost layer.
The tunica albuginea is the dense connective tissue capsule around the testis and the ovary, not a layer of a vessel wall. The shared word tunica makes it easy to confuse.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the outermost layer of a vessel wall?
options: Basement membrane
Tunica externa
Tunica media
Tunica intima
questions.why: The tunica externa is the outermost tunic of a vessel wall. It is made mostly of collagen fibers, with nerves and small vessels, and it anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue. In large vessels it holds the vasa vasorum, small vessels that supply the wall itself.
notes: The basement membrane is the thin layer under the endothelium, part of the tunica intima. It sits on the inner side of the wall, not the outside.
Correct. The tunica externa is the outermost layer.
The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. It would be the answer for the layer that controls the vessel's diameter.
The tunica intima is the innermost layer, lining the lumen. Choose it for the endothelium that touches the blood.
questions.answerText: Tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What tissue lines the tunica intima?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple squamous endothelium
Dense collagen fibers
Smooth muscle with elastic fibers
questions.why: The tunica intima is lined by endothelium, a simple squamous epithelium: one layer of flat cells resting on a basement membrane. Its smooth surface lets blood flow with little friction, and its thinness is what makes exchange possible in capillaries, where the intima is the only layer.
notes: Stratified squamous epithelium is many layers thick and resists abrasion, as in the epidermis and the lining of the esophagus. It would be far too thick for a vessel lining.
Correct. The intima is a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a basement membrane.
Dense collagen fibers make up most of the tunica externa, the outermost layer. It would be the answer for the layer that anchors the vessel.
Smooth muscle with elastic fibers makes up the tunica media, the middle layer. Choose it for the layer that changes vessel diameter.
questions.answerText: Simple squamous endothelium

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the only layer of a capillary wall?
options: Tunica media
Tunica intima
Vasa vasorum
Tunica externa
questions.why: A capillary wall is only the tunica intima: a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane. It has no tunica media and no tunica externa. That extreme thinness is what lets gases, nutrients, and wastes cross between the blood and the tissues.
notes: The tunica media is the smooth muscle layer of arteries and veins. Capillaries have none; flow into them is controlled upstream by arterioles and precapillary sphincters.
Correct. A capillary is just the tunica intima.
The vasa vasorum are small vessels in the tunica externa that supply the walls of large vessels such as the aorta. A capillary is far too thin to need them.
The tunica externa is the collagen-rich outer layer of arteries and veins. Capillaries lack it entirely, so choose it for the layer that anchors larger vessels.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What does the tunica media contain?
options: Smooth muscle and elastic fibers
Mostly collagen fibers
Skeletal muscle fibers
Simple squamous endothelium
questions.why: The tunica media is made of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibers arranged in rings around the vessel. The smooth muscle contracts or relaxes to narrow or widen the vessel, and the elastic fibers let the wall stretch and recoil with each heartbeat. Elastic arteries such as the aorta have a media dominated by elastic tissue, while muscular arteries have a media made mostly of smooth muscle.
notes: Correct. The tunica media is smooth muscle and elastic fibers.
Mostly collagen fibers describes the tunica externa, the outermost layer that anchors the vessel. It would be the answer for that layer.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary muscle attached to bones, and it is not found in vessel walls. Vessel walls use smooth muscle, which works without conscious control.
Simple squamous endothelium lines the tunica intima, the innermost layer. Choose it for the layer touching the blood.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle and elastic fibers

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is the thickest layer in an artery wall?
options: Tunica intima
Tunica externa
Tunica media
Basement membrane
questions.why: In arteries the tunica media is the thickest layer. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, and the thick band of smooth muscle and elastic fibers lets them withstand that pressure, stretch with each beat, and control their diameter. In veins, by contrast, the tunica externa is usually the thickest layer.
notes: The tunica intima is a thin lining of endothelium and is the thinnest tunic in arteries. It would be the answer for the only layer a capillary has.
The tunica externa is usually the thickest layer in veins, not arteries. Choose it for a question about vein walls.
Correct. Arteries have a thick tunica media.
The basement membrane is a very thin sheet beneath the endothelium, part of the tunica intima. It is far from the thickest layer.
questions.answerText: Tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What does the smooth muscle of the tunica media control?
options: Vessel diameter
Direction of flow through valves
Production of blood cells
Exchange of gases with tissues
questions.why: The smooth muscle of the tunica media wraps around the vessel. When it contracts, the vessel narrows (vasoconstriction); when it relaxes, the vessel widens (vasodilation). Changing the diameter adjusts how much blood flows through the vessel and helps maintain blood pressure.
notes: Correct. Smooth muscle in the media narrows or widens the vessel.
One-way flow in veins is maintained by venous valves, which are folds of the tunica intima. The smooth muscle of the media does not form valves.
Blood cells are produced in red bone marrow, not in vessel walls. That would be the answer for a question about hematopoiesis.
Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of capillaries, which have no tunica media at all. Choose capillaries for a question about where exchange occurs.
questions.answerText: Vessel diameter

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What does the tunica externa mostly contain?
options: Endothelial cells
Collagen fibers
Smooth muscle cells
Cardiac muscle cells
questions.why: The tunica externa is made mostly of collagen fibers, along with nerves and small blood vessels. Collagen is strong and resists stretching, so this layer protects the vessel and anchors it to surrounding tissues. In large vessels it also carries the vasa vasorum, which supply the outer part of the wall.
notes: Endothelial cells form the lining of the tunica intima, the innermost layer. They would be the answer for the layer in contact with blood.
Correct. The tunica externa is mostly collagen.
Smooth muscle is the main component of the tunica media, the middle layer. Choose it for the layer that changes vessel diameter.
Cardiac muscle is found in the heart wall, not in vessel walls. Choose it for the myocardium.
questions.answerText: Collagen fibers

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the main job of the tunica externa?
options: Changing the vessel's diameter
Allowing exchange with the tissues
Anchoring the vessel to surrounding tissue
Lining the lumen with a smooth surface
questions.why: The tunica externa is the outer, collagen-rich layer, and its main job is to anchor the vessel to the surrounding tissue and protect it from overstretching. Its collagen fibers blend into the connective tissue around the vessel, holding it in place. It also carries nerves and, in large vessels, the vasa vasorum.
notes: Changing the vessel's diameter is the job of the smooth muscle in the tunica media. That would be the answer for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
Exchange with tissues happens across capillary walls, which are only the tunica intima. The thick collagen of the externa would block exchange, which is why capillaries lack it.
Correct. The tunica externa anchors and protects the vessel.
Lining the lumen with a smooth surface is the job of the endothelium of the tunica intima. Choose the intima for the layer that touches blood.
questions.answerText: Anchoring the vessel to surrounding tissue

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares arteries and veins by direction of flow?
options: Arteries carry blood toward the heart; veins carry blood away from it
Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry oxygen-poor blood, in every case
Both carry blood away from the heart, at different pressures
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward it
questions.why: Direction relative to the heart is what defines arteries and veins. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry blood toward it. This rule holds without exception, while oxygen content does not, since the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.
notes: This reverses the two definitions. A handy check is that artery and away both start with the same letter.

This is true for most vessels but fails for the pulmonary circuit. The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, so oxygen content cannot be the defining rule.
Only arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. Arteries do run at higher pressure, but that is a difference in pressure, not in direction.
Correct. Arteries go away from the heart and veins return to it.
questions.answerText: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward it

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the walls of arteries and veins?
options: Veins have thicker walls; arteries have thinner walls and wider lumens
Arteries have only a tunica intima; veins have all three tunics
Arteries have thicker walls; veins have thinner walls and wider lumens
Both have identical walls and differ only in the direction of flow
questions.why: Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so they have thick walls with a heavy tunica media, and on a slide they keep a round shape. Veins carry blood under low pressure, so they have thinner walls, a thinner media, and a wider lumen, and they often look collapsed on a slide. Both have the same three tunics, just in different proportions.
notes: This reverses the pattern. Arteries need thick walls to withstand high pressure, while veins run at low pressure and have thinner walls.
A wall made of only the tunica intima belongs to a capillary. Arteries and veins both have all three tunics.
Correct. Arteries are thick-walled; veins are thinner-walled with wider lumens.
Arteries and veins have the same three tunics, but the proportions differ, especially the thickness of the tunica media. Those differences are how you tell them apart on a slide.
questions.answerText: Arteries have thicker walls; veins have thinner walls and wider lumens

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares capillaries with arteries and veins?
options: Capillaries carry blood only toward the heart; arteries and veins carry it away
Capillaries have the thickest walls; arteries and veins are the exchange vessels
Capillaries have all three tunics; arteries and veins have only the tunica intima
Capillaries are thin exchange vessels; arteries and veins are transport vessels
questions.why: Arteries and veins are transport vessels: their three-layered walls carry blood to and from the tissues but are too thick for exchange. Capillaries have only the tunica intima, a single layer of endothelium, so gases, nutrients, and wastes can cross between blood and tissue. Exchange happens only at the capillary level.
notes: Capillaries connect arterioles to venules, so blood in them moves from the arterial side to the venous side. Carrying blood toward the heart describes veins, not capillaries.
Capillaries have the thinnest walls of any vessel, a single layer of endothelium. Arteries and veins are too thick for exchange, so this reverses both halves.
This reverses the layers. Arteries and veins have all three tunics, while capillaries have only the tunica intima.
Correct. Capillaries exchange; arteries and veins transport.
questions.answerText: Capillaries are thin exchange vessels; arteries and veins are transport vessels

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why do capillaries have only a tunica intima?
options: A thin wall lets materials pass between blood and tissues
A thin wall lets capillaries withstand the highest pressure
Lacking a media lets capillaries contract more strongly
Capillaries need no lining because they hold no blood
questions.why: A capillary wall is just endothelium on a basement membrane, a single cell thick. That short distance lets O2, CO2, nutrients, and wastes pass quickly between the blood and the tissue fluid. A tunica media or externa would add layers that block this exchange, so capillaries lack them.
notes: Correct. The thin wall is what makes exchange possible.
Thin walls withstand less pressure, not more. Arteries handle the highest pressure, which is why they have the thickest tunica media.
Without a tunica media, capillaries have no smooth muscle layer to contract. Flow into them is controlled upstream by the arterioles and precapillary sphincters.
Capillaries are full of blood, and their endothelial lining is exactly what holds it. This choice misreads the single layer as no lining at all.
questions.answerText: A thin wall lets materials pass between blood and tissues

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why is the tunica externa built mainly of collagen fibers?
options: Collagen lets gases pass through the wall
Collagen recoils to push blood along between heartbeats
Collagen contracts to change the vessel's diameter
Collagen is strong, so it anchors and protects the vessel
questions.why: Collagen fibers are strong and resist being stretched, much like the fibers of a rope. In the tunica externa they protect the vessel from overstretching and blend into the surrounding connective tissue, which anchors the vessel in place. Stretch and recoil come from elastic fibers in the media, and changes in diameter come from smooth muscle.
notes: Gases pass through the thin endothelium of capillaries, which have no tunica externa at all. A thick collagen layer would block exchange rather than allow it.

Stretching and recoiling to keep blood moving between beats is the job of elastic fibers, which are concentrated in the tunica media of elastic arteries such as the aorta. Choose elastic fibers for that recoil.
Collagen is a protein fiber and cannot contract. Changing diameter is the job of the smooth muscle in the tunica media.
Correct. Strong collagen fibers anchor and protect the vessel.
questions.answerText: Collagen is strong, so it anchors and protects the vessel

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares arterioles with larger arteries?
options: Arterioles are larger than arteries and carry blood to the lungs
Arterioles are the smallest arteries and control flow into capillary beds
Arterioles have no smooth muscle and serve as the exchange vessels
Arterioles are the smallest veins and collect blood from capillaries
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, with thin walls holding only one or two layers of smooth muscle. As arteries branch down into arterioles, the arterioles become the control valves of the circulation: by constricting or dilating, they adjust how much blood flows into each capillary bed. Larger arteries mainly carry and distribute blood under high pressure.
notes: Arterioles are smaller than arteries, as the ending -ole (small) suggests. Blood reaches the lungs through the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries.
Correct. Arterioles are the smallest arteries and regulate entry into capillary beds.
Arterioles do have smooth muscle, one or two layers, and that is how they control flow. The exchange vessels with no smooth muscle are the capillaries.
The smallest veins, which collect blood from capillaries, are venules. Choose venules for the vessels draining a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: Arterioles are the smallest arteries and control flow into capillary beds

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares venules and veins?
options: Venules carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart
Venules feed blood into capillaries; veins drain the capillaries
Venules are larger than veins and have the thickest walls
Venules collect blood from capillaries; veins carry it on toward the heart
questions.why: Venules are the smallest veins. They collect blood as it leaves a capillary bed and merge into larger veins, which carry the blood back toward the heart under low pressure. Venule walls are thin and porous, while veins have all three tunics, a wide lumen, and often valves.
notes: Venules are veins, so they carry blood toward the heart, not away from it. Vessels carrying blood away from the heart are arteries and arterioles.
Feeding blood into capillaries is the job of arterioles. Venules are the vessels that drain capillaries, which this choice wrongly gives to veins.
Venules are the smallest veins, as the ending -ule (small) suggests, and their walls are thin and porous. Larger veins come after them.
Correct. Venules gather blood from capillaries and veins carry it home to the heart.
questions.answerText: Venules collect blood from capillaries; veins carry it on toward the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are capillaries called exchange vessels?
options: They pass blood between the right and left sides of the heart
Gases, nutrients, and wastes cross their thin walls
They trade blood cells directly with lymphatic vessels
They are where the heart exchanges blood with the great vessels
questions.why: Capillaries are called exchange vessels because their walls, a single layer of endothelium, are thin enough for materials to cross. O2 and nutrients leave the blood and enter the tissues, while CO2 and wastes move from the tissues into the blood. Arteries and veins only carry blood; the actual delivery happens in the capillaries.
notes: The right and left sides of the heart are linked through the lungs by the pulmonary circuit, not by capillaries passing blood between them. In an adult heart no blood passes directly between the two sides.
Correct. Exchange happens across the thin capillary wall.

Lymphatic capillaries pick up excess tissue fluid that leaks out of blood capillaries, but blood capillaries do not trade blood cells directly with them. That idea fits a question about how lymph forms, not why capillaries are exchange vessels.
The heart connects to the great vessels through its valves, not through capillaries. Choose the semilunar valves for where blood passes from the ventricles into the great arteries.
questions.answerText: Gases, nutrients, and wastes cross their thin walls

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel type carries blood directly into a capillary bed?
options: Veins
Elastic arteries
Venules
Arterioles
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, and they deliver blood into capillary beds. Their smooth muscle, along with precapillary sphincters at the entrance to the capillaries, adjusts how much blood enters each bed. On the other side of the bed, venules collect the blood and carry it on toward the veins.
notes: Veins receive blood from venules and carry it back toward the heart. They are two steps downstream of the capillaries.

Elastic arteries, such as the aorta and common carotid arteries, are the large arteries near the heart. They branch into muscular arteries and then arterioles long before blood reaches the capillaries.
Venules are on the other side of the capillary bed, draining it. Choose them for the vessels that receive blood leaving the capillaries.
Correct. Arterioles feed the capillary beds.
questions.answerText: Arterioles

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel type directly drains a capillary bed?
options: Venules
Arterioles
Muscular arteries
Large veins
questions.why: Venules are the smallest veins, and they collect blood as it leaves a capillary bed. The first ones, the postcapillary venules, have thin, porous walls; they then merge into larger venules and veins. This makes venules the direct drain of every capillary bed.
notes: Correct. Venules collect blood from the capillaries.
Arterioles feed blood into a capillary bed rather than draining it. Choose them for the vessels that control how much blood enters the capillaries.
Muscular arteries, such as the brachial and femoral arteries, distribute blood to organs well upstream of the capillaries. They carry blood away from the heart, not out of a capillary bed.
Large veins receive blood only after venules have collected it from the capillaries. They are farther downstream on the return trip to the heart.
questions.answerText: Venules

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic is most involved in vasoconstriction?
options: Tunica media
Tunica intima
Tunica externa
Basement membrane
questions.why: Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of a vessel when the smooth muscle in its wall contracts. That smooth muscle is in the tunica media, arranged in rings around the vessel, so contracting it squeezes the lumen smaller. Relaxing the same muscle widens the vessel, which is vasodilation.
notes: Correct. The smooth muscle of the tunica media narrows the vessel.
The tunica intima is a thin lining of endothelium with no smooth muscle layer. It provides the smooth surface for blood flow but does not squeeze the vessel.
The tunica externa is mostly collagen, which cannot contract. It anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue.
The basement membrane is a thin sheet beneath the endothelium, part of the tunica intima. It has no contractile cells.
questions.answerText: Tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which tunic forms the valves found in many veins?
options: Tunica intima
Tunica media
Tunica externa
Vasa vasorum
questions.why: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that project into the lumen of many veins, especially in the limbs. Blood moving toward the heart pushes the flaps open, while blood that starts to slip backward fills them and pushes them shut. This keeps low-pressure venous blood moving in one direction.
notes: Correct. Venous valves are folds of the tunica intima.
The tunica media is the smooth muscle layer that changes vessel diameter. It does not fold inward to form valves.
The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors the vessel. It lies on the outside of the wall and cannot form flaps inside the lumen.
The vasa vasorum are small vessels in the tunica externa that supply the wall of large vessels. They are blood vessels, not valve flaps.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A large vessel must be held firmly in place among the surrounding tissues. Which part of its wall does this?
options: Internal elastic lamina
Tunica externa
Tunica intima
Tunica media
questions.why: The tunica externa is the outermost tunic, made mostly of collagen fibers that blend into the connective tissue around the vessel. These fibers tie the vessel to its surroundings and keep it from shifting or overstretching. In large vessels this layer is thick and also carries the vasa vasorum.
notes: The internal elastic lamina is a sheet of elastic fibers at the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media. It marks the inner edge of the media and plays no anchoring role.
Correct. The collagen of the tunica externa anchors the vessel.
The tunica intima is the innermost lining touching the blood. It is on the wrong side of the wall to anchor the vessel to its surroundings.
The tunica media is the smooth muscle and elastic layer that changes vessel diameter and lets the wall stretch and recoil. It sits in the middle of the wall and does not attach to surrounding tissue.
questions.answerText: Tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel has a thick tunica media and carries blood away from the heart. What type of vessel is it?
options: Venule
Capillary
Vein
Artery
questions.why: Two clues point to an artery. Carrying blood away from the heart is the definition of an artery, and a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers is the wall arteries need to handle high pressure. On a slide, this thick media also helps an artery keep its round shape.
notes: A venule is a small vein that drains a capillary bed, with thin, porous walls. It carries blood toward the heart, not away.
A capillary has no tunica media at all, only the tunica intima. Choose it for a vessel whose wall is a single layer of endothelium.
A vein carries blood toward the heart and has a thin tunica media with a thicker tunica externa. It would be the answer for a thin-walled vessel with a wide lumen and valves.
Correct. A thick media and flow away from the heart mark an artery.
questions.answerText: Artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel on a slide has a thin wall, a wide lumen, and valves. What type of vessel is it?
options: Vein
Arteriole
Capillary
Artery
questions.why: A thin wall, a wide lumen, and valves are the signature of a vein. Veins carry blood at low pressure, so they need less muscle in the tunica media, and their valves, flaps of the tunica intima, stop blood from flowing backward. On a slide, a vein often looks collapsed next to its round partner artery.
notes: Correct. Thin wall, wide lumen, and valves identify a vein.
An arteriole is a tiny artery with one or two layers of smooth muscle that controls flow into capillaries. It has no valves and a narrow lumen.
A capillary is a single layer of endothelium, far smaller than a vein, with no valves. It would be the answer for the exchange vessel.
An artery has a thick wall with a heavy tunica media and a relatively narrow lumen, and it has no valves along its length. Choose it for a thick-walled vessel carrying blood away from the heart.
questions.answerText: Vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel wall consists only of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane. What type of vessel is it?
options: Vein
Arteriole
Capillary
Elastic artery
questions.why: A wall made of only simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane is the tunica intima alone, and the vessel built that way is a capillary. Arteries and veins add a tunica media and a tunica externa. The single thin layer is what lets capillaries exchange materials with the tissues.
notes: A vein has all three tunics, with a thin media and a thicker externa, plus valves in many limb veins. It would be the answer for a thin-walled vessel with a wide lumen and valves.
An arteriole has endothelium plus one or two layers of smooth muscle in its tunica media. That muscle layer is what lets it control flow into the capillaries.
Correct. A wall of endothelium alone is a capillary.
An elastic artery, such as the aorta, has a thick tunica media full of elastic sheets and a well-developed tunica externa. It is the opposite extreme from a single-layered wall.
questions.answerText: Capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says veins always carry oxygen-poor blood. What actually defines a vessel as an artery or a vein?
options: The direction it carries blood relative to the heart
The oxygen content of the blood it carries
The overall thickness of its wall
Whether or not it has valves along its length
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood toward it, and that direction is the defining rule. Oxygen content does not work as a rule, because the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood. Wall thickness and valves are typical features but not the definition.
notes: Correct. Direction relative to the heart defines arteries and veins.

Oxygen content works for most vessels but fails in the pulmonary circuit, where the arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the veins carry oxygen-rich blood. That exception is why the student's rule is wrong.
Arteries usually have thicker walls than veins, and that helps you tell them apart on a slide. But wall thickness follows from the pressure each carries; it is a feature, not the definition.
Many veins, especially in the limbs, have valves, but not all do, so valves are a feature rather than the definition. Choose valves for a question about how veins prevent backflow.
questions.answerText: The direction it carries blood relative to the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why does the vascular sequence place capillaries between arterioles and venules?
options: Capillaries oxygenate the blood in every tissue
Exchange with tissues must happen before blood returns to the heart
Capillaries add pressure to push blood into the veins
Capillaries filter blood cells out before they reach the veins
questions.why: Arterioles deliver blood to the capillaries, and venules carry it away. Placing the capillaries in the middle means blood always passes through the exchange vessels, unloading O2 and nutrients and picking up CO2 and wastes, before it starts back to the heart. Without that middle step, blood would return to the heart without having served the tissues.
notes: Blood picks up oxygen only in the capillaries of the lungs. In other tissues the capillaries do the reverse, releasing oxygen to the cells.
Correct. Capillaries sit in the middle so exchange happens before blood heads back.
Pressure drops as blood passes through the capillaries; they do not add any. The pressure that moves blood comes from the heart's pumping.
Capillaries do not filter blood cells out; red blood cells pass through them single file and continue into the venules. Removing old blood cells is the job of the spleen and liver.
questions.answerText: Exchange with tissues must happen before blood returns to the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why is the tunica intima important in both large vessels and capillaries?
options: It is the endothelial lining blood touches in every vessel
It contains the smooth muscle that controls diameter
It anchors every vessel to the surrounding tissue
It forms the valves found in all arteries
questions.why: The tunica intima is the one tunic every vessel has, from the aorta down to the smallest capillary. Its endothelium forms a smooth, continuous lining that blood flows over with little friction, and it is continuous with the endocardium of the heart. In capillaries this same layer is the whole wall, so it is also the surface where exchange happens.
notes: Correct. Every vessel, large or small, is lined by the endothelium of the intima.
Smooth muscle that controls diameter is in the tunica media, which capillaries lack. It cannot be the reason the intima matters in every vessel.
Anchoring a vessel to surrounding tissue is the job of the tunica externa, which capillaries also lack. Choose the externa for that role in larger vessels.
Valves made from the tunica intima are found in many veins, especially in the limbs, not in arteries. Choose venous valves for a question about stopping backflow in veins.
questions.answerText: It is the endothelial lining blood touches in every vessel

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each tunic to its function?
options: Intima changes diameter, media anchors the vessel, externa lines the lumen
Intima anchors the vessel, media lines the lumen, externa changes diameter
Intima lines the lumen, media changes diameter, externa anchors the vessel
Intima lines the lumen, media anchors the vessel, externa changes diameter
