questions.why: Each tunic's tissue explains its job. The tunica intima is smooth endothelium, so it lines the lumen and gives blood a low-friction surface. The tunica media is smooth muscle and elastic fibers, so it narrows or widens the vessel and lets it stretch and recoil. The tunica externa is mostly collagen, so it anchors and protects the vessel.
notes: This shifts every function one layer over. Changing diameter needs smooth muscle, which is in the media, not in the thin endothelium of the intima.
This also scrambles all three. The lining that touches blood has to be the innermost layer, the intima, and anchoring has to be done by the outermost layer, the externa.
Correct. Intima lines, media adjusts diameter, externa anchors.
The intima is matched correctly, but the media and externa are swapped. Collagen in the externa cannot contract to change diameter, and smooth muscle in the media does not anchor the vessel.
questions.answerText: Intima lines the lumen, media changes diameter, externa anchors the vessel

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which description matches an elastic artery?
options: A thin-walled vessel with a wide lumen and valves
A large artery near the heart with a media rich in elastic fibers
A microscopic artery with one or two layers of smooth muscle
A medium-sized artery with a media made mostly of smooth muscle
questions.why: Elastic arteries are the largest arteries, sitting closest to the heart, such as the aorta, pulmonary trunk, and common carotid arteries. Their tunica media is packed with elastic lamellae (sheets of elastic fibers), so the wall stretches when the ventricles push blood in and recoils between beats. That recoil keeps blood moving forward while the heart relaxes.
notes: This describes a vein, which carries blood back to the heart under low pressure. Choose it if the question asked how a vein differs from the artery it travels with.
Correct. Elastic arteries like the aorta are large, close to the heart, and full of elastic fibers that let them stretch and recoil.
This describes an arteriole, the smallest artery, which adjusts how much blood enters a capillary bed. It would be the answer for the vessel that regulates flow into capillaries.

This describes a muscular artery, such as the femoral or brachial artery, whose media can hold dozens of smooth muscle layers. Pick it if the question asked which arteries distribute blood to specific organs.
questions.answerText: A large artery near the heart with a media rich in elastic fibers

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement describes muscular arteries?
options: Low-pressure vessels that carry blood back toward the heart
Medium-sized arteries that distribute blood to specific organs
Very large arteries that stretch and recoil with each heartbeat
Microscopic arteries that open and close individual capillary beds
questions.why: Muscular arteries are the medium-sized arteries that carry blood from the elastic arteries to individual organs and body regions. The femoral, axillary, brachial, and radial arteries are examples. Their thick smooth muscle layer lets them hold vascular tone (a steady partial contraction) and adjust their diameter, which is why they are also called distributing arteries.
notes: This describes veins, which return blood to the heart. Choose it if the question asked which vessels rely on valves and the skeletal muscle pump.
Correct. Muscular arteries such as the brachial and femoral arteries distribute blood to particular organs and regions.
This describes elastic arteries such as the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Pick it if the question asked which arteries keep blood moving between heartbeats by recoiling.
This describes arterioles, the smallest arteries, along with the precapillary sphincters at their ends. They would be the answer for the vessels that control blood flow into a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: Medium-sized arteries that distribute blood to specific organs

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which layer makes up most of the wall of a muscular artery?
options: Tunica externa
Tunica media
External elastic lamina
Tunica intima
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer of a vessel wall, made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. In a muscular artery this layer can hold up to forty layers of smooth muscle, making it by far the thickest part of the wall. That heavy muscle is what lets these arteries narrow or widen to control how much blood reaches an organ.
notes: The tunica externa is the outer layer of mostly collagen fibers that anchors the vessel. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is thickest in a vein.
Correct. The tunica media, packed with smooth muscle, is the dominant layer of a muscular artery.

The external elastic lamina is a thin elastic sheet marking the boundary between the media and the externa, and it is thin in muscular arteries. Choose it if the question asked what separates the middle layer from the outer layer.
The tunica intima is the thin inner lining of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane. Pick it if the question asked which layer is the only one a capillary has.
questions.answerText: Tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is the main job of arterioles?
options: Stretching and recoiling to push blood between heartbeats
Regulating how much blood enters a capillary bed
Serving as the main site of exchange with tissue cells
Collecting blood as it drains out of a capillary bed
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, with only one or two layers of smooth muscle in their walls. When that muscle contracts (vasoconstriction) the arteriole narrows and less blood enters the capillary bed downstream; when it relaxes (vasodilation) more blood flows in. Because of this, arterioles are the chief site of resistance in the circulation.
notes: This is the job of elastic arteries such as the aorta. Pick it if the question asked which vessels cushion each heartbeat and keep blood flowing while the ventricles relax.
Correct. Arterioles set how much blood reaches each capillary bed by narrowing or widening.
This is the job of capillaries, whose walls are only endothelium thin enough for gases and nutrients to cross. Choose it if the question asked where exchange with tissues happens.
This is the job of venules, the smallest veins. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels receive blood leaving the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Regulating how much blood enters a capillary bed

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why is the wall of a capillary only a single layer of cells thick?
options: So the vessel can hold most of the body's blood at rest
So the vessel can stretch and recoil under high pressure
So the vessel can constrict and set resistance to flow
So materials can cross quickly between blood and tissue
questions.why: Capillaries are the exchange vessels of the body. Their wall is just the tunica intima, a single layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane, with no media or externa. The shorter the distance, the faster oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and wastes can move between the blood and the surrounding cells.
notes: The veins as a group act as blood reservoirs, holding about sixty percent of the blood at rest because of their wide lumens. This would fit a question about why veins are called capacitance or reservoir vessels.
Stretch and recoil depend on a thick, elastic tunica media, which is the design of elastic arteries like the aorta. Pick that idea if the question asked why the aorta has so many elastic fibers.
Constricting to set resistance requires smooth muscle, which capillaries lack. This describes arterioles, the answer if the question asked which vessels are the chief site of resistance.
Correct. A one-cell-thick wall gives the shortest possible path for exchange.
questions.answerText: So materials can cross quickly between blood and tissue

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which list names the three types of capillary?
options: Elastic, muscular, and arteriole
Continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid
Postcapillary venule, muscular venule, and vein
Tunica intima, tunica media, and tunica externa
questions.why: Capillaries come in three builds that differ in how leaky they are. Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining, fenestrated capillaries have small pores (fenestrations, from the Latin word for windows), and sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large gaps. The type found in a tissue matches what that tissue needs to move in or out of the blood.
notes: These are the three sizes of artery, from largest to smallest. Pick this list if the question asked how arteries are classified.
Correct. Continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid are the three capillary types, from tightest to leakiest.
These are the vessels on the venous side, in the order blood reaches them after leaving the capillaries. They would be the answer for the sequence of vessels draining a capillary bed.
These are the three tunics of an artery or vein wall, from inside to outside. Choose this list if the question asked about the layers of a vessel wall.
questions.answerText: Continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which description fits a continuous capillary?
options: A wide, winding vessel with large gaps and a patchy basement membrane
A metarteriole end with no smooth muscle that runs straight to a venule
An endothelium perforated by small pores called fenestrations
An unbroken endothelial lining interrupted only by small clefts
questions.why: A continuous capillary has endothelial cells joined edge to edge in an unbroken sheet. The only openings are intercellular clefts, narrow gaps between neighboring cells that let water and small solutes through. This is the most common and the least leaky capillary type, found in muscle, skin, lungs, and the central nervous system.
notes: This describes a sinusoid, the leakiest capillary type. It would be the answer if the question asked which capillaries let whole cells cross, as in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow.

This describes a thoroughfare channel, the distal end of a metarteriole that acts as a direct route from arteriole to venule. Choose it if the question asked how blood can pass through a capillary bed without entering the true capillaries.
Pores in the endothelium define a fenestrated capillary. Pick this if the question asked which capillary type is found in the kidney and small intestine.
Correct. Continuous capillaries have a complete lining broken only by intercellular clefts.
questions.answerText: An unbroken endothelial lining interrupted only by small clefts

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In which group of tissues are continuous capillaries most common?
options: Skeletal muscle, skin, and lungs
Kidney, small intestine, and endocrine glands
Cartilage, cornea, and covering epithelia
Liver, spleen, and red bone marrow
questions.why: Continuous capillaries are the most common type in the body. They are found in skeletal muscle, skin, the lungs, and the central nervous system, where steady, controlled exchange is needed without large leaks. Their unbroken lining lets small molecules and gases cross while keeping larger proteins and cells inside the vessel.
notes: Correct. Muscle, skin, and lungs are classic locations of continuous capillaries.
These tissues have fenestrated capillaries, whose pores allow rapid filtration or absorption. Pick this group if the question asked where fenestrated capillaries are found.
These tissues are avascular, meaning they have no capillaries at all and get nutrients by diffusion from nearby tissue. Choose this group if the question asked which tissues lack a blood supply.
These organs have sinusoids, the leakiest capillaries, wide enough for whole cells to cross. They would be the answer if the question asked where sinusoids are located.
questions.answerText: Skeletal muscle, skin, and lungs

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a fenestrated capillary?
options: A direct channel that lets blood skip a capillary bed
A capillary whose endothelium has small pores
A wide, leaky capillary with large gaps between cells
A capillary with an unbroken endothelial lining
questions.why: Fenestra is Latin for window, and a fenestrated capillary has small pores through its endothelial cells. These pores let fluid and small solutes pass much faster than through a continuous capillary, while blood cells and most proteins stay inside. Fenestrated capillaries sit where rapid filtration or absorption happens, such as the kidney and small intestine.
notes: A direct channel that bypasses capillaries is a vascular shunt, not a type of capillary. Choose it if the question asked how blood can skip a capillary bed when exchange is not needed.
Correct. Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, the fenestrations, in their endothelium.
Large gaps describe a sinusoid. It would be the answer if the question asked which capillary lets whole cells cross the wall.
An unbroken lining describes a continuous capillary. Pick it if the question asked about the most common capillary type, found in muscle, skin, and the brain.
questions.answerText: A capillary whose endothelium has small pores

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Where are fenestrated capillaries found?
options: Brain and skeletal muscle
Liver and spleen
Kidney and small intestine
Cartilage and cornea
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries are placed where fluid must move quickly across the vessel wall. In the kidney they allow rapid filtration of plasma, and in the small intestine they allow absorbed nutrients to enter the blood quickly. They are also found in the choroid plexus of the brain ventricles and in most endocrine glands.
notes: The brain and skeletal muscle have continuous capillaries with an unbroken lining. This pair would be the answer if the question asked where the tightest capillaries are found.
The liver and spleen have sinusoids, wider and leakier than fenestrated capillaries. Pick this pair if the question asked where whole cells cross capillary walls.
Correct. The kidney and small intestine both rely on fenestrated capillaries for rapid filtration and absorption.
Cartilage and the cornea are avascular and have no capillaries at all. Choose this pair if the question asked which tissues lack blood vessels.
questions.answerText: Kidney and small intestine

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which description matches a sinusoid?
options: A capillary with small pores in an otherwise intact endothelium
A capillary with an unbroken lining joined by narrow clefts
A thin-walled vein with no smooth muscle, held open by connective tissue
A wide, winding capillary with large gaps and a patchy basement membrane
questions.why: A sinusoid is the leakiest kind of capillary. It is wide and winding, with large fenestrations, wide clefts between cells, and an incomplete basement membrane. These openings are big enough for large proteins and even whole blood cells to pass, which suits organs like the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow.
notes: Small pores in an intact lining describe a fenestrated capillary. Pick it if the question asked which capillary type allows rapid filtration in the kidney.
An unbroken lining with narrow clefts describes a continuous capillary. It would be the answer if the question asked about capillaries in skin, muscle, or the brain.

This describes a vascular sinus, such as the dural venous sinuses or the coronary sinus. The names sound alike, but a vascular sinus is a vein, not a capillary. Choose it if the question asked about a vein supported by dense connective tissue.
Correct. Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane.
questions.answerText: A wide, winding capillary with large gaps and a patchy basement membrane

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In which group of organs are sinusoids found?
options: Skin, skeletal muscle, and lungs
Liver, spleen, and red bone marrow
Cartilage, cornea, and lens
Kidney, small intestine, and choroid plexus
questions.why: Sinusoids are found where large materials or whole cells must cross the vessel wall. In red bone marrow newly made blood cells enter the bloodstream, in the spleen blood cells move between the blood and the splenic tissue, and in the liver plasma proteins and other large molecules pass freely. Sinusoids also occur in the anterior pituitary and adrenal glands.
notes: These tissues have continuous capillaries, the tightest and most common type. This group would be the answer for where continuous capillaries are found.
Correct. The liver, spleen, and red bone marrow all have sinusoids.
These tissues are avascular and have no capillaries. Choose this group if the question asked which tissues get nutrients only by diffusion.
These sites have fenestrated capillaries, built for rapid filtration and absorption. Pick this group if the question asked where fenestrated capillaries are found.
questions.answerText: Liver, spleen, and red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a vascular shunt?
options: An arrangement that routes blood through two capillary beds in a row
A direct channel that lets blood bypass the capillaries of a bed
A network of capillaries supplied by a single metarteriole
A ring of smooth muscle that opens or closes a capillary entrance
questions.why: A vascular shunt is a direct channel connecting the arteriole side of a capillary bed to the venule side. When exchange is not needed, blood can travel through the shunt and skip the true capillaries. This lets the body send blood past a tissue that does not need it at the moment.
notes: This describes a portal system, such as the hepatic portal system. Choose it if the question asked about blood passing through two capillary beds before returning to the heart.
Correct. A vascular shunt lets blood travel past a capillary bed without passing through its capillaries.
This describes a capillary bed, the network of ten to one hundred capillaries fed by one metarteriole. It would be the answer if the question asked what a metarteriole supplies.

This describes a precapillary sphincter, the ring of smooth muscle that controls whether blood enters a capillary. Pick it if the question asked what opens or closes the entrance to an individual capillary.
questions.answerText: A direct channel that lets blood bypass the capillaries of a bed

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What is a venule?
options: The smallest artery, controlling flow into a capillary bed
The smallest vein, collecting blood as it leaves a capillary bed
The tapered end of an arteriole at the edge of a capillary bed
The exchange vessel whose wall is only endothelium
questions.why: Venules are the smallest veins. The postcapillary venule receives blood straight from the capillaries, and it is loosely joined and very porous, which makes it the site where white blood cells leave the bloodstream. Venules then merge into larger veins that carry blood back toward the heart.
notes: The smallest artery is the arteriole. Pick it if the question asked which vessel regulates how much blood enters a capillary bed.
Correct. A venule is the smallest vein, draining blood from a capillary bed.
This describes a metarteriole, the tapered end of an arteriole where it meets the capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel directly supplies a capillary bed.
This describes a capillary, whose wall is only the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked which vessel is the main site of exchange.
questions.answerText: The smallest vein, collecting blood as it leaves a capillary bed

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Compared with the artery it travels beside, how is a vein built?
options: Thinner wall, wider lumen, and valves
Only a tunica intima, with no media or externa
Thinner wall, narrower lumen, and no valves
Thicker wall, narrower lumen, and no valves
questions.why: A vein has the same three tunics as an artery, but in different proportions. Because it carries blood under low pressure, its tunica media is thin, its tunica externa is the thickest layer, and its lumen is wide. Many veins, especially in the limbs, also have valves that keep blood from flowing backward. On a slide the vein often looks collapsed next to its round artery.
notes: Correct. Veins have thinner walls, wider lumens, and valves compared with their matching arteries.
A wall of only tunica intima describes a capillary. Choose it if the question asked which vessel lacks a tunica media and tunica externa.
This mixes the two vessels. A vein does have a thinner wall, but its lumen is wider than the artery's, not narrower, and many veins have valves.
This is the artery side of the comparison, built thick to handle high pressure. Pick it if the question asked how an artery differs from its matching vein.
questions.answerText: Thinner wall, wider lumen, and valves

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What are venous valves?
options: Cusps anchored by chordae tendineae inside the heart
Folds of the tunica intima that keep blood from flowing backward
Rings of smooth muscle that open and close capillary entrances
Bands of elastic fibers that help the vein wall recoil
questions.why: Venous valves are small flaps formed from the tunica intima, the inner lining of the vein. They point toward the heart, so blood can push them open while moving forward, but backflow catches them and closes them. This matters because blood in veins is under low pressure and, in the limbs, must often travel upward against gravity.
notes: These are the atrioventricular valves of the heart, the tricuspid and mitral valves. They would be the answer if the question asked which heart valves are held by chordae tendineae.
Correct. Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that block backward flow.
These are precapillary sphincters, found at the entrance to capillaries on the arterial side. Pick them if the question asked what controls blood entering an individual capillary.

Veins do not depend on elastic recoil, and valves are not elastic bands. Elastic recoil is the job of the elastic arteries, the answer if the question asked how the aorta keeps blood moving between beats.
questions.answerText: Folds of the tunica intima that keep blood from flowing backward

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In which vessels are valves most common?
options: Arterioles
Elastic arteries
Capillary beds
Veins of the limbs
questions.why: Valves are a feature of veins, and they are most common in the veins of the arms and especially the legs. Blood in these veins is under low pressure and must return to the heart against gravity. The valves, together with the squeezing of nearby skeletal muscles, keep that blood moving toward the heart instead of sliding back down.
notes: Arterioles carry blood toward capillaries under enough pressure that backflow is not a problem, so they lack valves. They would be the answer for the vessels that set resistance to flow.

Elastic arteries such as the aorta have no valves along their length; the aortic and pulmonary valves belong to the heart. Elastic arteries would be the answer if the question asked which vessels stretch and recoil with each heartbeat.
Capillaries have only an endothelial wall and no valves. Pick them if the question asked where exchange between blood and tissue happens.
Correct. Limb veins carry low-pressure blood against gravity, so they have many valves.
questions.answerText: Veins of the limbs

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares elastic and muscular arteries?
options: Elastic arteries have more layers of smooth muscle in their media than muscular arteries do
Elastic arteries regulate flow into capillary beds, while muscular arteries collect blood from them
Muscular arteries stretch and recoil near the heart, while elastic arteries distribute blood to organs
Elastic arteries stretch and recoil near the heart, while muscular arteries distribute blood to organs
questions.why: Elastic arteries, like the aorta and common carotid, are the large vessels closest to the heart. Their elastic-rich media stretches with each heartbeat and recoils between beats, keeping blood moving. Muscular arteries, like the brachial and femoral, come next and deliver blood to specific organs, using their thick smooth muscle to adjust diameter.
notes: It is the reverse. Muscular arteries have the most smooth muscle, up to about forty layers, while elastic arteries are dominated by elastic lamellae.

Regulating flow into capillary beds is the job of arterioles, and collecting blood from capillaries is the job of venules. Pick those vessels if the question asked about the two ends of a capillary bed.
This swaps the two types. It is a common mix-up because both are arteries, but the elastic fibers are what let the aorta stretch and recoil, not smooth muscle.
Correct. Elastic arteries cushion and propel blood near the heart, and muscular arteries distribute it to organs.
questions.answerText: Elastic arteries stretch and recoil near the heart, while muscular arteries distribute blood to organs

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares continuous and fenestrated capillaries?
options: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining, while fenestrated capillaries have small pores
Both types are leaky enough to let whole blood cells cross the wall
Fenestrated capillaries have an unbroken lining, while continuous capillaries have small pores
Continuous capillaries have large gaps for cells, while fenestrated capillaries have none
questions.why: A continuous capillary has an unbroken endothelial lining with only narrow clefts between cells, so exchange is controlled and slow. A fenestrated capillary has small pores through its endothelial cells, which lets fluid and small solutes move across much faster. That is why continuous capillaries suit muscle and skin, while fenestrated capillaries suit the kidney and small intestine.
notes: Correct. The unbroken lining versus the small pores is the defining difference.
Neither type lets whole blood cells cross. Only sinusoids, found in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow, have gaps that large.
This swaps the two. The word fenestrated means windowed, which is the clue that those capillaries are the ones with pores.
Large gaps that let cells pass belong to sinusoids, not continuous capillaries. Pick a statement like this if it compared sinusoids with tighter capillaries.
questions.answerText: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining, while fenestrated capillaries have small pores

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares fenestrated capillaries and sinusoids?
options: Sinusoids have small pores, while fenestrated capillaries have large gaps and are leakier
Both have a complete basement membrane that keeps whole cells inside
Sinusoids have an unbroken lining, while fenestrated capillaries have small pores
Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, while sinusoids have large gaps and are leakier
questions.why: Both fenestrated capillaries and sinusoids have openings in their walls, but the size differs. Fenestrated capillaries have small pores that let fluid and small solutes through. Sinusoids are wide and winding, with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, so they let large proteins and even whole cells cross. Sinusoids are therefore the leakiest capillary type.
notes: This swaps the two. Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, which is why the liver, spleen, and bone marrow use them.
Sinusoids have an incomplete basement membrane, which is part of what lets whole cells pass. A complete basement membrane fits continuous and fenestrated capillaries only.
An unbroken lining describes a continuous capillary, not a sinusoid. Pick a statement like this if it compared continuous and fenestrated capillaries.
Correct. Small pores in fenestrated capillaries, large gaps in sinusoids.
questions.answerText: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, while sinusoids have large gaps and are leakier

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which order ranks the capillary types from least leaky to most leaky?
options: Sinusoid, fenestrated, continuous
Fenestrated, continuous, sinusoid
Continuous, sinusoid, fenestrated
Continuous, fenestrated, sinusoid
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the tightest. Fenestrated capillaries add small pores, so they are leakier and allow rapid filtration. Sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, so they are the leakiest and can pass whole cells. Leakiness rises as you move from tissues that need a tight barrier to tissues where cells must cross.
notes: This is the right sequence read backward, from most leaky to least leaky. It would be the answer if the question asked for the order from leakiest to tightest.
This places fenestrated capillaries as the tightest, but their pores make them leakier than continuous capillaries, which have an unbroken lining.
This puts sinusoids in the middle, but sinusoids are the leakiest type because their gaps are larger than the small pores of fenestrated capillaries.
Correct. Leakiness increases from continuous to fenestrated to sinusoid.
questions.answerText: Continuous, fenestrated, sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are fenestrated capillaries a good fit for the kidney?
options: Their large gaps let whole blood cells leave the vessel
Their pores let fluid filter out of the blood quickly
Their unbroken lining keeps most substances in the blood
Their thick smooth muscle wall withstands arterial pressure
questions.why: The kidney filters a large volume of plasma every day to begin forming urine. Fenestrated capillaries have small pores that let water and small solutes leave the blood quickly, while blood cells and most proteins stay inside. That combination of speed and selectivity is exactly what filtration requires.
notes: Large gaps that let whole cells leave describe sinusoids. Pick this if the question asked why the liver, spleen, or red bone marrow uses sinusoids.
Correct. Small pores make rapid filtration possible while keeping cells in the blood.
An unbroken lining describes continuous capillaries, which limit leakage. This would be the answer if the question asked why the brain or skeletal muscle uses continuous capillaries.
Capillaries have no smooth muscle at all; their wall is only endothelium. A thick muscular wall describes muscular arteries, the answer if the question asked which vessels distribute blood to organs.
questions.answerText: Their pores let fluid filter out of the blood quickly

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are fenestrated capillaries a good fit for the small intestine?
options: Their pores let absorbed nutrients enter the blood quickly
Their valves keep absorbed nutrients from flowing backward
Their wide gaps let blood cells pass into the gut wall
Their tight, unbroken lining blocks absorbed nutrients
questions.why: After a meal, the small intestine absorbs large amounts of digested nutrients and water. The capillaries in its villi are fenestrated, so their small pores let these absorbed materials move into the blood rapidly. This is the same design the kidney uses for filtration, simply working in the opposite direction.
notes: Correct. The pores of fenestrated capillaries let absorbed nutrients reach the blood quickly.
Capillaries do not have valves. Valves are found in veins, especially limb veins, and would be the answer if the question asked what prevents backflow in the legs.
Gaps wide enough for blood cells describe sinusoids. Pick this if the question asked about capillaries in the spleen or red bone marrow.
A tight, unbroken lining describes continuous capillaries, which would slow absorption. This fits a question about why brain capillaries keep most substances out.
questions.answerText: Their pores let absorbed nutrients enter the blood quickly

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are sinusoids useful in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow?
options: Their thick tunica media lets them handle arterial pressure
Their unbroken lining keeps most substances from leaving
Their large gaps let big molecules and whole cells cross the wall
Their small pores allow rapid filtration of fluid only
questions.why: Each of these organs moves large materials between blood and tissue. Red bone marrow releases newly made blood cells, the spleen handles blood cells moving in and out of its tissue, and the liver exchanges large proteins with the blood. Sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, so these large materials can pass easily.
notes: Capillaries, including sinusoids, have no tunica media. A thick media describes arteries, the answer if the question asked which vessels carry blood under high pressure.
An unbroken lining describes continuous capillaries. This would be the answer if the question asked why muscle and skin capillaries limit leakage.
Correct. Large gaps make sinusoids the right capillary where cells and big molecules must cross.
Small pores that filter fluid describe fenestrated capillaries. Pick this if the question asked why the kidney or small intestine uses fenestrated capillaries.
questions.answerText: Their large gaps let big molecules and whole cells cross the wall

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are continuous capillaries the type found in skeletal muscle and skin?
options: They allow steady exchange while limiting leakage
They let blood bypass the tissue when exchange is not needed
They filter large volumes of fluid out of the blood quickly
They let whole blood cells move freely into the tissue
questions.why: Muscle and skin need a steady supply of oxygen and nutrients, but they do not need to filter large volumes of fluid or move cells across the vessel wall. Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining with only narrow clefts, so gases and small molecules cross while proteins and cells stay inside. This keeps exchange controlled and prevents unnecessary fluid loss into the tissue.
notes: Correct. Continuous capillaries give controlled exchange with little leakage.
Bypassing a tissue is the job of a vascular shunt, not a type of capillary. Choose it if the question asked how blood skips a capillary bed.
Rapid filtration of large fluid volumes is the job of fenestrated capillaries. This would be the answer if the question asked about capillaries in the kidney.
Letting whole cells cross is the job of sinusoids. Pick this if the question asked why red bone marrow or the spleen uses sinusoids.
questions.answerText: They allow steady exchange while limiting leakage

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares capillaries and venules?
options: Capillaries regulate flow into a bed, while venules carry blood under high pressure
Both have a tunica media of several smooth muscle layers
Capillaries are where exchange happens, while venules collect blood draining from capillary beds
Venules are where exchange happens, while capillaries collect blood draining from venules
questions.why: Capillaries connect arterioles to venules and are the main exchange vessels, with walls only one cell thick. Venules are the smallest veins and come right after the capillaries, collecting the blood that leaves a capillary bed. Postcapillary venules are porous and are where white blood cells leave the bloodstream, but the main job of exchange belongs to capillaries.
notes: Regulating flow into a capillary bed is the job of arterioles and precapillary sphincters, and veins and venules carry blood under low pressure, not high. Pick arterioles if the question asked what controls entry into a bed.
Capillaries have no tunica media, and venules have at most one or two layers of smooth muscle. Several layers of smooth muscle would describe arteries.
Correct. Exchange happens in capillaries, and venules drain them.
This reverses the sequence. Blood flows from capillaries into venules, not the other way around.
questions.answerText: Capillaries are where exchange happens, while venules collect blood draining from capillary beds

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A superficial vein on a patient's forearm shows a row of small bumps along its length. What do the bumps most likely mark?
options: Lymph nodes
Arteriovenous anastomoses
Precapillary sphincters
Venous valves
questions.why: Veins in the limbs have valves, flaps of the tunica intima that keep blood flowing toward the heart. Blood collects slightly just behind each valve, so in a superficial vein the valves can show up as small bumps along the vessel. Phlebotomists notice these when choosing where to draw blood.
notes: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs that filter lymph and cluster in places like the axilla and groin. They are not strung along a vein, and they would be the answer if the question asked where lymph is filtered.

Arteriovenous anastomoses are direct artery-to-vein connections that bypass capillaries, mostly in places like the skin of the fingers. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood can skip a capillary bed.

Precapillary sphincters are microscopic rings of smooth muscle at the entrance to capillaries. They cannot be seen through the skin, and they would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary.
Correct. The small bumps along a superficial vein mark the positions of its valves.
questions.answerText: Venous valves

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A tissue must move fluid out of the blood quickly but should keep blood cells inside the vessel. Which capillary type fits best?
options: Continuous capillary
Sinusoid
Fenestrated capillary
Arteriole
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores in their endothelium. These pores let water and small solutes leave the blood rapidly, but they are too small for blood cells to pass. That is the combination this tissue needs, and it is why fenestrated capillaries are found in the kidney, small intestine, and choroid plexus.
notes: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining that limits leakage, so fluid would move too slowly. Pick them if the tissue needed a tight barrier, as in the brain.
Sinusoids are leaky enough to let whole cells pass, which this tissue wants to prevent. They would be the answer if the tissue needed cells to cross, as in red bone marrow.
Correct. Fenestrated capillaries allow rapid fluid movement while keeping cells inside.
An arteriole is a small artery with smooth muscle, not an exchange vessel. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel controls how much blood reaches the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Fenestrated capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In red bone marrow, newly made blood cells must pass through the vessel wall into the bloodstream. Which capillary type fits this job?
options: Postcapillary venule
Fenestrated capillary
Sinusoid
Continuous capillary
questions.why: Whole blood cells are far too large to fit through the small pores of a fenestrated capillary or the narrow clefts of a continuous capillary. Sinusoids are wide and winding, with large gaps between cells and an incomplete basement membrane. Those openings are big enough for new blood cells to squeeze into the bloodstream, which is why red bone marrow, the spleen, and the liver use sinusoids.
notes: Postcapillary venules are where white blood cells leave the blood to enter tissues, which is the opposite direction from this question. They would be the answer if the question asked where leukocytes exit the bloodstream.
Fenestrated capillaries have small pores that pass fluid and small solutes but not cells. Pick them if the tissue needed rapid filtration, as in the kidney.
Correct. Only sinusoids have gaps large enough for whole cells to pass.
Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the tightest type. They would be the answer if the tissue needed to keep most substances out, as in the brain.
questions.answerText: Sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A tissue needs to keep most substances inside the blood and allow only controlled exchange. Which capillary type fits best?
options: Fenestrated capillary
Continuous capillary
Sinusoid
Thoroughfare channel
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining, broken only by narrow intercellular clefts. Gases and small molecules can cross, but proteins and cells stay in the blood. This tight, controlled barrier suits skin, skeletal muscle, the lungs, and especially the central nervous system.
notes: Fenestrated capillaries have pores that let fluid move quickly, so they are leakier than this tissue wants. Pick them if the tissue needed rapid filtration or absorption.
Correct. Continuous capillaries form the tightest exchange barrier.
Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, wide enough for whole cells. They would be the answer if large materials needed to cross, as in the liver.

A thoroughfare channel is the distal end of a metarteriole that carries blood straight from arteriole to venule, not a barrier type. Choose it if the question asked about a direct route through a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: Continuous capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are the capillaries of the brain built as especially tight continuous capillaries?
options: To let blood bypass the brain when it is resting
To keep most blood substances away from neurons
To let new blood cells enter the bloodstream quickly
To filter large volumes of fluid, as the kidney does
questions.why: Neurons are very sensitive to changes in their chemical surroundings. Brain capillaries are continuous capillaries with very tight connections between their endothelial cells, which keeps most substances in the blood from reaching the neural tissue. This protective arrangement is called the blood-brain barrier.
notes: The brain needs a constant blood supply and does not shut it off when resting. Bypassing capillaries is the job of vascular shunts, the answer if the question asked how blood skips a capillary bed.
Correct. Tight brain capillaries protect neural tissue from most substances in the blood.
Releasing new blood cells is the job of sinusoids in red bone marrow. Pick this if the question asked why marrow capillaries are so leaky.
Filtering large volumes of fluid is the job of fenestrated capillaries in the kidney. This would be the answer if the question asked why kidney capillaries have pores.
questions.answerText: To keep most blood substances away from neurons

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are the capillaries of the liver built as leaky sinusoids?
options: So blood can skip the liver on its way to the heart
So the liver can keep plasma proteins out of its tissue
So large molecules move freely to and from liver cells
So the liver can filter urine out of the blood
questions.why: The liver processes much of what is in the blood, taking up nutrients and other absorbed materials and releasing large plasma proteins it makes. Sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, so blood comes into close contact with liver cells and large molecules move freely in both directions.
notes: Skipping the liver happens in the fetus through the ductus venosus, a shunt, not through sinusoids. Choose that idea if the question asked how fetal blood bypasses the liver.
The liver actually releases plasma proteins into the blood, so it needs leaky capillaries, not a barrier. Keeping substances out is the role of tight continuous capillaries, as in the brain.
Correct. Leaky sinusoids let large materials move freely between blood and liver cells.
Filtering urine from the blood is the job of the kidney, which uses fenestrated capillaries. Pick the kidney if the question asked where blood is filtered to start forming urine.
questions.answerText: So large molecules move freely to and from liver cells

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The precapillary sphincters of a capillary bed close. Where does the blood arriving at that bed go?
options: Out through the vessel wall into the tissue
Backward into the arteriole toward the heart
Through the closed capillaries at higher speed
Through a vascular shunt straight to the venule
questions.why: Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle at the entrance to each capillary. When they close, blood cannot enter the true capillaries. Instead it travels through the vascular shunt, the direct channel through the bed (the metarteriole and its thoroughfare channel), and drains into the venule without exchange taking place.
notes: Blood stays inside the vessels. Movement of fluid out into tissue happens across open capillary walls, the answer if the question asked where exchange occurs.

Blood keeps moving forward, driven by pressure from the arterial side, and does not flow back toward the heart. Backward flow would be a problem in veins with failed valves, the answer if the question asked about varicose veins.
A closed sphincter blocks the capillary, so no blood enters it at all. This would only fit if the sphincters were open.
Correct. With the sphincters closed, blood takes the shunt directly to the venule.
questions.answerText: Through a vascular shunt straight to the venule

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: One valve in a leg vein no longer closes properly and lets blood flow backward. What happens locally?
options: Blood leaks out into the tissue above the valve
The vein wall thickens and narrows its lumen
Blood pools in the vein segment below the failed valve
Blood pools in the artery that supplies the leg
questions.why: In the leg, venous blood is moving upward toward the heart. A working valve catches any blood that slides back. When a valve fails, blood falls back through it and collects in the segment of vein below (farther from the heart), raising pressure there and stretching that part of the vein.
notes: Blood falls back below the failed valve, not above it, because it is pulled down by gravity. The segment above still has working valves holding blood in place.
Wall thickening and a narrowed lumen describe arteriosclerosis, which affects arteries. Pick that if the question asked about stiff, thickened artery walls.
Correct. Backflow through a failed valve makes blood pool in the segment below it.

Arteries do not depend on venous valves, so the artery supplying the leg is not affected. Pooling in an artery would not fit any common disorder; narrowing of a leg artery is peripheral artery disease.
questions.answerText: Blood pools in the vein segment below the failed valve

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why is a vein more likely than an artery to collapse when it is cut?
options: Its valves close and pull the wall inward
It has no tunica externa to hold its shape
Its wall has more elastic fibers than an artery wall
Its wall is thinner and the pressure inside it is lower
questions.why: Arteries have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, so they hold their round shape even when empty. Veins have a thin media and carry blood under low pressure, so there is little to keep the wall open. That is why a vein looks collapsed next to its artery on a slide and why a cut vein flattens.
notes: Valves are flaps that block backflow; they do not pull the wall inward. Choose valves if the question asked what keeps blood moving toward the heart in the limbs.
Veins do have a tunica externa; in fact it is the thickest layer of a vein. Pick the tunica externa if the question asked which layer is thickest in a vein.
Arteries, not veins, have the most elastic tissue, which helps them keep their shape. More elastic fibers would make a vessel less likely to collapse, which describes the aorta.
Correct. A thin wall and low internal pressure let a vein collapse.
questions.answerText: Its wall is thinner and the pressure inside it is lower

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says that every blood vessel has three tunics. Which correction is accurate?
options: Arteries have three tunics, but veins have only the intima and externa
Capillaries have only a tunica externa, which gives them their strength
Arteries and veins have three, but capillaries have only the tunica intima
All vessels, including the smallest capillaries, have the same three tunics
questions.why: The walls of arteries and veins are built from three layers: the tunica intima (endothelial lining), the tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic fibers), and the tunica externa (collagen). A capillary wall is only the tunica intima, endothelium on a basement membrane. That single thin layer is what makes capillaries suited for exchange.
notes: Veins have all three tunics, just in different proportions, with a thin media and a thick externa. Pick a statement about proportions if the question asked how veins differ from arteries.
A capillary's single layer is the tunica intima, not the externa, and capillaries are not built for strength. The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors larger vessels.
Correct. Capillaries are the exception, with only the tunica intima.
This repeats the student's error. If capillaries had a media and externa, their walls would be too thick for efficient exchange.
questions.answerText: Arteries and veins have three, but capillaries have only the tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says capillaries are strong, high-pressure vessels. Which correction is accurate?
options: Capillaries are the strongest vessels because blood moves slowly in them
Capillaries have the thickest tunica media of any vessel
Veins, not arteries, carry blood at the highest pressure
Capillaries are thin exchange vessels, and arteries carry the high pressure
questions.why: Capillaries have walls only one endothelial cell thick, built for exchange rather than strength. By the time blood reaches them, the arterioles upstream have already lowered its pressure. The high-pressure vessels are the arteries, whose thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers can withstand the force of each heartbeat.
notes: Slow flow does not make a vessel strong. Capillaries are the thinnest vessels, and the slow flow simply gives more time for exchange.
Capillaries have no tunica media at all. The thickest media belongs to arteries, the answer if the question asked which vessels resist high pressure.
Veins carry blood under the lowest pressure, which is why they need valves. Pick veins if the question asked which vessels rely on valves and the skeletal muscle pump.
Correct. Capillaries are thin exchange vessels, and the arteries handle high pressure.
questions.answerText: Capillaries are thin exchange vessels, and arteries carry the high pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says veins push blood back to the heart with thick muscular walls. Which correction is accurate?
options: Veins rely on elastic recoil, as the aorta does
Veins have the thickest tunica media of any vessel
Veins are thin-walled and rely on valves and muscle pumps
Veins rely on precapillary sphincters to push blood forward
questions.why: Veins carry blood under low pressure and have a thin tunica media, so they cannot push blood on their own. Instead, contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the deep veins (the skeletal muscle pump), and valves make sure the squeezed blood can only move toward the heart. Together these keep venous return going, especially from the legs.
notes: Elastic recoil is how elastic arteries like the aorta keep blood moving between heartbeats. It would be the answer if the question asked about the aorta.
Arteries have the thickest tunica media, not veins. Pick arteries if the question asked which vessels have the most smooth muscle.
Correct. Thin-walled veins depend on valves and the skeletal muscle pump.
Precapillary sphincters control entry into capillaries on the arterial side and do not push blood. Choose them if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary.
questions.answerText: Veins are thin-walled and rely on valves and muscle pumps

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says arterioles mainly collect blood leaving capillaries. Which correction is accurate?
options: Arterioles return blood to the heart under low pressure
Arterioles are the exchange vessels where gases cross the wall
Arterioles feed capillary beds and regulate how much enters
Arterioles stretch and recoil to cushion each heartbeat
questions.why: Arterioles are on the arterial side of the capillary bed. They are the smallest arteries, and their one or two layers of smooth muscle narrow or widen to control how much blood reaches the capillaries. The vessels that collect blood leaving capillaries are the venules, on the other side of the bed.
notes: Returning blood to the heart under low pressure is the job of veins. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels have valves and wide lumens.
Exchange happens in capillaries, whose walls are only endothelium. Pick capillaries if the question asked where gases and nutrients cross into tissue.
Correct. Arterioles feed capillary beds and regulate the flow into them.
Stretching and recoiling is the job of elastic arteries like the aorta. Choose them if the question asked which vessels keep blood moving between heartbeats.
questions.answerText: Arterioles feed capillary beds and regulate how much enters

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says venules regulate how much blood enters a capillary bed. Which correction is accurate?
options: Venules stretch and recoil to propel blood forward
Venules carry blood away from the heart into capillaries
Venules are the main vessels where exchange happens
Venules collect blood as it leaves capillary beds
questions.why: Venules are the smallest veins, located on the outflow side of the capillary bed. They receive blood after it has passed through the capillaries and carry it on toward larger veins. Entry into the bed is controlled upstream by arterioles and precapillary sphincters.
notes: Stretch and recoil is the job of elastic arteries like the aorta. Pick them if the question asked how blood keeps moving between heartbeats.
Carrying blood away from the heart into capillaries is the job of arterioles. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels feed a capillary bed.

Capillaries are the main exchange vessels, although postcapillary venules are porous and are where white blood cells leave the blood. Choose capillaries if the question asked where most exchange happens.
Correct. Venules drain capillary beds; they do not control entry into them.
questions.answerText: Venules collect blood as it leaves capillary beds

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Capillaries in the brain, kidney, and liver are all called capillaries, yet they differ greatly in how leaky they are. What explains this?
options: Capillaries in different organs have different numbers of tunics
Leakier capillaries are older capillaries that have worn thin
Capillaries come in three structural types matched to each tissue's job
Leakiness depends only on how hard the heart is pumping
questions.why: All capillaries have a wall of endothelium on a basement membrane, but that wall is built three different ways. Continuous capillaries in the brain are tight, fenestrated capillaries in the kidney have small pores for filtration, and sinusoids in the liver have large gaps for large molecules and cells. The structure follows what each tissue needs to move across the wall.
notes: Every capillary has only one tunic, the tunica intima. The number of tunics distinguishes capillaries from arteries and veins, not one capillary from another.
Leakiness is a built-in design feature, not a sign of wear. Sinusoids are leaky in healthy young organs because the tissue needs large materials to cross.
Correct. Continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoid capillaries are built differently for different jobs.
Pumping force affects blood pressure, but it does not explain why brain capillaries stay tight while liver capillaries stay leaky. The difference is in the wall structure itself.
questions.answerText: Capillaries come in three structural types matched to each tissue's job

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are venous valves especially important in veins below the level of the heart?
options: Veins below the heart carry oxygen-rich blood that must not mix with arterial blood
Blood must rise against gravity at low pressure, and valves stop it from sliding back
Arteries below the heart carry blood at such high pressure that veins must resist it
Capillaries below the heart lack endothelium, so valves replace the lining
questions.why: Blood in the veins of the legs and lower body is under low pressure and has to travel upward to reach the heart. Without help, gravity would pull it back down. Venous valves let blood move only toward the heart, and each squeeze from nearby skeletal muscles pushes blood up past the next valve.
notes: Systemic veins below the heart carry oxygen-poor blood, not oxygen-rich blood. Oxygen-rich venous blood is found in the pulmonary veins and, before birth, the umbilical vein.
Correct. Valves keep low-pressure blood from falling back against gravity.
Venous valves have nothing to do with arterial pressure. High arterial pressure is the reason arteries have thick walls, the answer if the question asked why arteries have a heavy tunica media.
All capillaries have an endothelial lining, and capillaries have no valves. The endothelium would be the answer if the question asked what forms the entire capillary wall.
questions.answerText: Blood must rise against gravity at low pressure, and valves stop it from sliding back

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: How does vessel wall structure match the pressure each vessel carries?
options: Arteries and veins have identical walls, and only valves differ
Capillaries have the thickest walls because they hold the highest pressure
Veins have a thick media for high pressure, while arteries have thin walls for low pressure
Arteries have a thick media for high pressure, while veins have thin walls for low pressure
questions.why: Blood leaves the heart under high pressure, so arteries have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers that can withstand and smooth out each heartbeat. By the time blood reaches the veins, its pressure is low, so veins have thinner walls, a thin media, and a wide lumen. Veins make up for low pressure with valves and the skeletal muscle pump.
notes: Arteries and veins have the same three tunics but in very different proportions. The difference in tunica media thickness is the main way to tell them apart on a slide.
Capillaries have the thinnest walls of all, only endothelium, and they do not hold the highest pressure. Pick capillaries if the question asked where exchange happens.
This swaps arteries and veins. The thick media belongs to arteries because they receive blood directly from the heart.
Correct. Thick arterial walls handle high pressure, and thin venous walls carry low-pressure blood.
questions.answerText: Arteries have a thick media for high pressure, while veins have thin walls for low pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What are the vasa vasorum?
options: Elastic sheets at the border of the tunica intima and media
Flaps of the tunica intima that block backward flow
Rings of smooth muscle at the entrance to capillaries
Small vessels in the externa that supply a large vessel's wall
questions.why: Vasa vasorum means vessels of the vessels. The wall of a large artery or vein, such as the aorta, is too thick to be nourished only by the blood flowing through its lumen. Tiny vessels running in the tunica externa supply the outer parts of the wall, and they are easy to see on a section of the aorta.
notes: This describes the internal elastic lamina. Pick it if the question asked what marks the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media.
This describes venous valves. Choose them if the question asked what keeps blood moving toward the heart in limb veins.
This describes precapillary sphincters. They would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes the entrance to a capillary.
Correct. The vasa vasorum are small vessels in the tunica externa that nourish a large vessel's wall.
questions.answerText: Small vessels in the externa that supply a large vessel's wall

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which pair are examples of vascular sinuses?
options: Paranasal sinuses and the maxillary sinus
Liver sinusoids and spleen sinusoids
Dural venous sinuses and the coronary sinus
Aortic arch and pulmonary trunk
questions.why: A vascular sinus is a vein whose wall is only thin endothelium with no smooth muscle, so it relies on surrounding dense connective tissue for support. The dural venous sinuses, held within the dura mater around the brain, and the coronary sinus on the back of the heart are the classic examples. Both are veins despite the word sinus in their names.
notes: Paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull bones, not blood vessels. They would be the answer if the question asked about spaces that open into the nasal cavity.
Sinusoids are the leakiest type of capillary, not veins. Pick them if the question asked which capillaries let whole cells cross in the liver and spleen.
Correct. The dural venous sinuses and the coronary sinus are vascular sinuses.
The aortic arch and pulmonary trunk are elastic arteries, not veins. Choose them if the question asked for examples of elastic arteries.
questions.answerText: Dural venous sinuses and the coronary sinus

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are blood draws and IV lines placed in veins rather than arteries?
options: Veins are near the surface, thin-walled, and under low pressure
Veins have no valves that could block the needle
Veins have thicker walls that seal tightly around a needle
Veins carry oxygen-rich blood that gives more accurate results
questions.why: Many veins run just under the skin, while most arteries lie deeper. A vein has a thin wall and a wide lumen and carries blood under low pressure, so a needle enters it easily and the puncture bleeds slowly afterward. An artery's high pressure would make a puncture bleed much more forcefully.
notes: Correct. Surface position, thin walls, and low pressure make veins the safer choice.
Many limb veins do have valves; they can even be seen as small bumps along a forearm vein. The valves are a reason to pick a straight stretch of vein, not a reason veins are chosen.
Veins have thinner walls than arteries, not thicker ones. Thick walls describe arteries, which is part of why they are harder to puncture.
Systemic veins carry oxygen-poor blood, not oxygen-rich blood. Oxygen-rich blood is found in systemic arteries and the pulmonary veins.
questions.answerText: Veins are near the surface, thin-walled, and under low pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The precapillary sphincters guarding a capillary bed contract and close. What happens to exchange between blood and tissue in that bed?
options: Exchange stays the same because capillaries fill from the venules
Exchange increases because blood is forced into those capillaries
Exchange decreases because blood is diverted away from those capillaries
Exchange stays the same because arterioles exchange gases too
questions.why: A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the entrance to a capillary. When it closes, blood cannot enter that capillary and flows past the bed through other channels instead. Since capillaries are the only vessels thin enough for exchange, less blood in the bed means less exchange with the surrounding tissue.
notes: Venules drain blood out of capillaries and do not refill them from the far end. This choice reflects the mistaken idea that blood can flow backward into a capillary bed from the venous side.
This reverses the effect. A closed sphincter blocks the entrance to the capillary, so blood is kept out rather than forced in. More exchange would happen if the sphincters opened.
Correct. Closed sphincters send blood around the bed, so exchange in it drops.
Arterioles have walls of smooth muscle and are not thin enough for exchange; only capillaries are. This choice confuses the vessel that controls flow with the vessel where exchange happens.
questions.answerText: Exchange decreases because blood is diverted away from those capillaries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In the systemic circuit, which type of vessel receives blood directly from a capillary bed?
options: Arteriole
Vein
Venule
Artery
questions.why: Capillaries merge into venules, the smallest veins, as blood leaves a capillary bed. The first of these, the postcapillary venule, has a thin and very porous wall. Venules then join to form veins, which carry the blood back toward the heart.
notes: Arterioles feed blood into a capillary bed from the arterial side. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessel delivers blood to a capillary bed.
Veins are one step later, formed as venules merge. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels venules drain into.
Correct. Venules collect blood as it leaves the capillaries.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart and branch into arterioles before any capillary is reached. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessel the aorta branches into.
questions.answerText: Venule

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In an ordinary systemic route (artery, arteriole, ?, venule, vein), which vessel fills the gap between the arteriole and the venule?
options: Capillary
Vein
Muscular artery
Elastic artery
questions.why: Arterioles deliver blood to capillaries, and capillaries drain into venules. The capillary is the smallest vessel, with a wall made only of the tunica intima (endothelium on a basement membrane). That thin wall is what makes it the only vessel where exchange with the tissues happens.
notes: Correct. The capillary sits between the arteriole and the venule.
A vein comes after the venule, as venules merge on the way back to the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked what venules drain into.

A muscular artery, such as the brachial or femoral artery, is larger than an arteriole and comes before it. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel type distributes blood to specific organs.

An elastic artery, such as the aorta, is the largest kind of artery and sits right next to the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel stretches and recoils with each heartbeat.
questions.answerText: Capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of blood vessel is defined as carrying blood away from the heart?
options: Artery
Capillary
Venule
Vein
questions.why: Arteries are named by direction of flow: they carry blood away from the heart. Most carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, which shows that the name depends on direction and not on oxygen content. Because arteries carry blood under high pressure, they have thick walls with a heavy tunica media.
notes: Correct. Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
A capillary connects an arteriole to a venule and is where exchange with the tissues happens. Choose it if the question asked which vessel trades gases and nutrients with the tissues.
A venule is the smallest kind of vein, collecting blood as it leaves a capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel first receives blood from the capillaries.
A vein carries blood toward the heart under low pressure. Pick it if the question asked about vessels that return blood to the heart.
questions.answerText: Artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of blood vessel is defined as carrying blood toward the heart?
options: Artery
Capillary
Vein
Arteriole
questions.why: Veins are named by direction of flow: they carry blood toward the heart. Most carry oxygen-poor blood, but the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium, so oxygen content is not what makes a vessel a vein. Veins work under low pressure, so their walls are thinner than those of the matching arteries.
notes: An artery carries blood away from the heart under high pressure. Pick it if the question asked about vessels leaving the heart.
A capillary is the exchange vessel between an arteriole and a venule. Choose it if the question asked where gases and nutrients cross into the tissues.
Correct. Veins carry blood toward the heart.

An arteriole is the smallest kind of artery, still carrying blood away from the heart, and it controls how much blood enters a capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel regulates flow into the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel has a wall made of only a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, which makes it the site of exchange with the tissues?
options: Muscular artery
Venule
Arteriole
Capillary
questions.why: A capillary wall is just the tunica intima, a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a basement membrane, with no tunica media or tunica externa. That thin wall lets gases, nutrients, and wastes cross between the blood and the tissue fluid. Capillaries connect arterioles to venules and are the only vessels thin enough for this exchange.
notes: A muscular artery has a thick tunica media of many smooth muscle layers and distributes blood to specific organs. Choose it if the question asked about a medium-sized artery such as the brachial or femoral.

A venule is the smallest vein, collecting blood as it leaves the capillaries, and the larger venules add smooth muscle to the wall. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel drains a capillary bed.
An arteriole is the smallest artery, with one or two layers of smooth muscle around its lining. Pick it if the question asked which vessel controls how much blood enters a capillary bed.
Correct. The capillary wall is a single layer of endothelium, built for exchange.
questions.answerText: Capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which layer of a blood vessel wall is the innermost lining of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane?
options: Tunica intima
Tunica media
Tunica externa
External elastic lamina
questions.why: The tunica intima is the innermost of the three tunics and the layer the blood touches. It is a smooth lining of endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) on a basement membrane, and it is continuous with the endocardium of the heart. It is also the only layer a capillary has.
notes: Correct. The tunica intima is the endothelial lining of the vessel.
The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. Pick it if the question asked which layer changes the diameter of the vessel.
The tunica externa is the outermost layer, mostly collagen fibers, that anchors the vessel. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is the thickest in a vein.

The external elastic lamina is a sheet of elastic fibers between the tunica media and the tunica externa, not a lining. Choose it if the question asked what marks the outer boundary of the tunica media.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which layer of a blood vessel wall is made mainly of smooth muscle and elastic fibers and sets the diameter of the vessel?
options: Tunica intima
Tunica media
Tunica externa
Endothelium
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer of the vessel wall, built of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. When its smooth muscle contracts the vessel narrows (vasoconstriction), and when it relaxes the vessel widens (vasodilation). It is the thickest layer in arteries, which is why arteries hold their round shape on a slide.
notes: The tunica intima is the innermost endothelial lining, with no smooth muscle of its own. Pick it if the question asked which layer the blood touches.
Correct. The tunica media is the smooth muscle layer that controls vessel diameter.
The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors the vessel and carries small nerves and vessels. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is the thickest in a vein.
The endothelium is the single layer of flat cells that makes up the tunica intima. Choose it if the question asked what kind of cells line every vessel and form the whole wall of a capillary.
questions.answerText: Tunica media

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which layer of a blood vessel wall is made mostly of collagen fibers and anchors the vessel to the surrounding tissue?
options: Tunica externa
Tunica media
Tunica intima
Internal elastic lamina
questions.why: The tunica externa is the outermost layer of a vessel wall. It is mostly collagen fibers, with small nerves and vessels running through it, and it ties the vessel to the tissue around it. It is the thickest layer in veins, and in large vessels it carries the vasa vasorum, the tiny vessels that supply the wall itself.
notes: Correct. The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors the vessel.
The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. Pick it if the question asked which layer is the thickest in an artery.
The tunica intima is the endothelial lining on the inside of the vessel. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is continuous with the endocardium.
The internal elastic lamina is a sheet of elastic fibers at the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media. Choose it if the question asked what marks the inner edge of the middle layer.
questions.answerText: Tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of artery is the largest, with a tunica media dominated by elastic fibers that stretch and recoil with each heartbeat?
options: Metarteriole
Arteriole
Muscular artery
Elastic artery
questions.why: Elastic arteries are the large arteries closest to the heart, such as the aorta, pulmonary trunk, brachiocephalic trunk, and common carotid arteries. Their tunica media is packed with elastic fibers, so they stretch when the ventricles push blood into them and recoil between beats. That recoil keeps blood moving forward even while the ventricles are relaxing.
notes: A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole where it joins a capillary bed. Choose it if the question asked which vessel directly supplies a network of capillaries.
An arteriole is the smallest artery, with only one or two layers of smooth muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel controls flow into a capillary bed.

A muscular artery is a medium-sized artery whose tunica media is mostly smooth muscle, such as the brachial or femoral artery. Pick it if the question asked which artery type distributes blood to specific organs.
Correct. Elastic arteries are the large, stretchy arteries near the heart.
questions.answerText: Elastic artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which type of artery is medium-sized, has a tunica media made mostly of smooth muscle, and distributes blood to specific organs?
options: Elastic artery
Metarteriole
Arteriole
Muscular artery
questions.why: Muscular arteries, also called distributing arteries, carry blood from the elastic arteries out to individual organs and regions. Examples include the axillary, brachial, radial, and femoral arteries. Their thick tunica media of smooth muscle, up to about forty layers, lets them hold steady tone and adjust how much blood each region receives.
notes: An elastic artery is a large artery near the heart whose tunica media is dominated by elastic fibers. Pick it if the question asked about the aorta or the pulmonary trunk.
A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole at the start of a capillary bed. Choose it if the question asked where the precapillary sphincters sit.
An arteriole is much smaller, with only one or two layers of smooth muscle. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel controls flow into a capillary bed.
Correct. Muscular arteries distribute blood to specific organs.
questions.answerText: Muscular artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel is the smallest type of artery, with one or two layers of smooth muscle, and controls how much blood enters a capillary bed?
options: Arteriole
Capillary
Muscular artery
Venule
questions.why: Arterioles are microscopic arteries with a thin tunica media of one or two smooth muscle layers. When that muscle contracts or relaxes, the arteriole narrows or widens and changes how much blood flows into the capillary bed downstream. Because they can change their diameter so easily, arterioles are the main site of resistance in the circulation.
notes: Correct. Arterioles regulate flow into the capillary beds.
A capillary has no smooth muscle at all, only an endothelial lining, so it cannot control flow. Choose it if the question asked which vessel is the site of exchange.
A muscular artery is a medium-sized artery with many layers of smooth muscle that distributes blood to whole organs. It would be the answer if the question asked about the brachial or femoral artery.
A venule is the smallest vein, collecting blood after it leaves a capillary bed rather than controlling what enters it. Pick it if the question asked which vessel drains the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Arteriole

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type has an unbroken endothelial lining, interrupted only by small intercellular clefts?
options: Thoroughfare channel
Sinusoid
Continuous capillary
Fenestrated capillary
questions.why: Continuous capillaries are the most common type.
