Their endothelial cells form an unbroken lining, with only narrow clefts between neighboring cells, so they let less through than the other types. They are found in muscle, skin, the lungs, and the central nervous system, where the tight capillaries of the brain help keep most substances out.
notes: A thoroughfare channel is the end of a metarteriole that acts as a direct route from arteriole to venule, not a type of capillary wall. Choose it if the question asked which channel lets blood bypass a capillary bed.

A sinusoid is a wide, leaky capillary with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. It would be the answer if the question asked which capillary lets whole cells cross, as in the liver and spleen.
Correct. Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining.

A fenestrated capillary has small pores, called fenestrations, through its endothelium. Pick it if the question asked which capillary type is found where rapid filtration or absorption happens, such as the kidney.
questions.answerText: Continuous capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type has small pores in its endothelium and is found where rapid filtration or absorption happens, such as the kidney and small intestine?
options: Sinusoid
Fenestrated capillary
Postcapillary venule
Continuous capillary
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, called fenestrations (from the Latin for windows), through their endothelial cells. The pores let fluid and small solutes move across quickly. They are found where fast filtration or absorption is the job, including the kidney, the small intestine, the choroid plexus, and most endocrine glands.
notes: A sinusoid has much larger gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, wide enough for whole cells to pass. It would be the answer if the question asked about the capillaries of the liver, spleen, or red bone marrow.
Correct. Fenestrated capillaries have pores for rapid filtration and absorption.
A postcapillary venule is the first vein-side vessel to receive blood from a capillary bed, not a capillary. Choose it if the question asked where white blood cells leave the bloodstream.
A continuous capillary has an unbroken lining with no pores. Pick it if the question asked about the most common capillary type, found in muscle, skin, and the brain.
questions.answerText: Fenestrated capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type is wide and winding, with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, so that whole cells can cross its wall?
options: Continuous capillary
Postcapillary venule
Sinusoid
Fenestrated capillary
questions.why: Sinusoids, also called sinusoidal capillaries, are the leakiest capillaries. They are wide and winding, with large fenestrations, wide clefts, and an incomplete basement membrane. That build lets proteins and even whole blood cells pass, which is why sinusoids are found in the liver, spleen, red bone marrow, anterior pituitary, and adrenal glands.
notes: A continuous capillary has an unbroken lining and lets the least through. It would be the answer if the question asked about the most common capillary type or the tight capillaries of the brain.

A postcapillary venule receives blood from a capillary bed and has porous walls, but it is the start of the venous side, not a capillary. Choose it if the question asked which vessel collects blood just after the capillaries.
Correct. Sinusoids are the wide, leaky capillaries that let whole cells cross.
A fenestrated capillary has small pores that let fluid and small solutes through, but not whole cells. Pick it if the question asked about the capillaries of the kidney or small intestine.
questions.answerText: Sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel carries blood under low pressure, has a thin tunica media and a wide lumen, and contains valves in the limbs?
options: Muscular artery
Elastic artery
Vein
Arteriole
questions.why: Veins return blood to the heart under low pressure, so they do not need a thick muscular wall. They have a thin tunica media, a relatively thick tunica externa, and a wide lumen, and on a slide they often look collapsed next to their round companion artery. Venous valves, flaps of the tunica intima, keep blood from sliding backward, especially in the limbs where blood must travel up against gravity.
notes: A muscular artery has a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and carries blood under high pressure to organs. It would be the answer if the question asked about a distributing artery such as the brachial artery.
An elastic artery is a large, high-pressure artery near the heart with a thick, elastic tunica media. Pick it if the question asked about the aorta or pulmonary trunk.
Correct. Veins are thin-walled, low-pressure vessels with valves.
An arteriole is a tiny artery that controls flow into capillaries, and it has no valves. Choose it if the question asked which vessel is the main site of resistance.
questions.answerText: Vein

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which structures keep blood in the limb veins from flowing backward as it returns to the heart under low pressure?
options: Precapillary sphincters
Venous valves
Semilunar valves
Elastic laminae
questions.why: Blood in the veins moves under low pressure, and in the limbs it often has to travel upward against gravity. Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that open as blood moves toward the heart and close if it starts to slide back. Working with the skeletal muscle pump, which squeezes the deep veins as limb muscles contract, they keep venous blood moving one way.
notes: Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle at the entrance to a capillary bed that open or close to control inflow. Pick them if the question asked what controls whether blood enters a particular capillary bed.
Correct. Venous valves keep blood in the limb veins moving toward the heart.

Semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves of the heart, at the exits of the ventricles. They would be the answer if the question asked which valves keep blood from falling back into the ventricles.

The internal and external elastic laminae are sheets of elastic fibers at the boundaries of the tunica media, and they do not control the direction of flow. Choose them if the question asked what marks the edges of the middle layer of an artery on a slide.
questions.answerText: Venous valves

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the wall of a capillary with the wall of an artery?
options: A capillary has only the tunica intima, while an artery has all three tunics
A capillary has all three tunics, but each is thinner than in an artery
A capillary has a tunica media of smooth muscle but no tunica externa
A capillary has only a tunica externa, while an artery has all three tunics
questions.why: An artery wall has three tunics: the tunica intima lining, a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, and an outer tunica externa of collagen. A capillary keeps only the innermost layer, the endothelium on its basement membrane. That single thin layer is what lets gases, nutrients, and wastes cross between the blood and the tissues.
notes: Correct. A capillary wall is only the tunica intima.

Capillaries do not have thinner versions of all three tunics; they lack the tunica media and tunica externa entirely. Students choose this when they picture a capillary as a scaled-down artery rather than a single cell layer.

Capillaries have no smooth muscle at all, which is why they cannot change their own diameter. Students choose this when they confuse a capillary with an arteriole, which does have one or two layers of smooth muscle.

The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer, and capillaries do not have it. Students choose this when they mix up the innermost and outermost tunics; the layer capillaries keep is the inner endothelial lining.
questions.answerText: A capillary has only the tunica intima, while an artery has all three tunics

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On a slide, a vessel has a thick tunica media packed with smooth muscle. What job is this wall built for?
options: Withstanding high pressure and changing diameter
Exchanging gases and nutrients with the tissues
Letting whole blood cells pass through its wall
Holding a large reserve of blood at low pressure
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer of a vessel wall, made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. It is the thickest layer in arteries, because arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure and need a strong wall to withstand it. Its smooth muscle can also contract or relax to narrow or widen the vessel (vasoconstriction and vasodilation), which adjusts how much blood flows through.
notes: Correct. A thick, muscular media is the mark of an artery, built for high pressure and for changing diameter.

Exchange happens in capillaries, whose wall is only the tunica intima, a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane. Pick exchange for a vessel with no media at all, the thinnest wall in the body.
Letting whole cells cross is the job of sinusoids, the leaky capillaries of the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow. They have no tunica media, so this does not match a thick muscular wall.

Veins hold the largest share of the body's blood at rest and run at low pressure, with a thin media and a thick tunica externa. Choose this for a vessel with a wide, collapsed-looking lumen and a thin middle layer.
questions.answerText: Withstanding high pressure and changing diameter

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The kidney must filter fluid out of its blood rapidly while keeping blood cells inside the vessels. Which capillary type fits this job?
options: Sinusoid
Fenestrated capillary
Postcapillary venule
Continuous capillary
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, called fenestrations, through their endothelial cells. The pores let fluid and small dissolved substances move out quickly, while their small size and the intact basement membrane keep blood cells inside. That combination fits places that filter or absorb rapidly, such as the kidney, the small intestine, and most endocrine glands.
notes: Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane, leaky enough to let whole cells through. Choose them for the liver, spleen, or red bone marrow, but not where blood cells must stay inside.
Correct. Its small pores allow rapid filtration of fluid while keeping blood cells in the vessel.

A postcapillary venule is the small vessel that collects blood after it leaves a capillary bed, and it is where white blood cells leave the bloodstream. It is not a capillary type, so it would fit a question about where blood drains from a capillary bed.

Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining with only narrow clefts between cells, so they are the least leaky type. Pick them for muscle, skin, lungs, or the brain, where movement across the wall is slower and more controlled.
questions.answerText: Fenestrated capillary

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: In red bone marrow, newly made blood cells must move from the tissue into the bloodstream. Which capillary type makes this possible?
options: Arteriole
Sinusoid
Fenestrated capillary
Continuous capillary
questions.why: Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large openings in the endothelium, wide gaps between cells, and an incomplete basement membrane. These gaps are big enough for whole cells to pass through the wall. That is why sinusoids are found in red bone marrow, where new blood cells enter the circulation, as well as in the liver and spleen.
notes: An arteriole is the smallest artery, with one or two layers of smooth muscle that adjust flow into a capillary bed. It is not an exchange vessel, so it would fit a question about controlling blood flow, not about cells crossing a wall.
Correct. Sinusoids have gaps large enough for whole blood cells to cross the wall.

Fenestrated capillaries have small pores that let fluid and small molecules through quickly, but the pores are far too small for cells. Pick them for the kidney or small intestine, where fast filtration or absorption is the job.

Continuous capillaries have an unbroken lining and are the tightest type, found in muscle, skin, lungs, and the brain. They would be the answer if the goal were to keep most substances inside the blood.
questions.answerText: Sinusoid

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A student says capillaries have all three tunics, just thinner. Which statement correctly describes the capillary wall?
options: It has only the tunica externa
It has only the tunica intima
It has all three tunics, each one cell thick
It has only the tunica media
questions.why: A capillary wall is only the innermost layer of a vessel, the tunica intima: a single layer of simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane. Capillaries lack a tunica media and a tunica externa entirely. That makes their wall thin enough for gases, nutrients, and wastes to cross between the blood and the tissues.
notes: The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors a vessel and is thickest in veins. Choose it for a question about the outermost layer of a vein, not a capillary.
Correct. A capillary wall is just endothelium on a basement membrane, the tunica intima.
This is the misconception in the question. Arteries and veins have all three tunics, but a capillary has only the innermost one.
The tunica media is the smooth muscle and elastic layer that is thickest in arteries. Pick it for a question about what lets an artery change its diameter; capillaries have none.
questions.answerText: It has only the tunica intima

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are superficial veins, rather than arteries, used for IV lines?
options: They carry oxygen-rich blood straight to the tissues
They lack valves, so fluid can flow either way
They are deep, thick-walled, and under high pressure
They are superficial, thin, wide, and low pressure
questions.why: Veins return blood to the heart under low pressure, so their walls are thinner and their lumens wider than those of the matching arteries. Many limb veins also run just under the skin, where they are easy to see and reach. A needle enters a thin, wide vein easily, and because the pressure is low, the site bleeds slowly when the needle comes out. The same features make veins the usual choice for routine blood draws.
notes: Systemic veins carry oxygen-poor blood toward the heart, not oxygen-rich blood to the tissues. This choice describes systemic arteries.

Limb veins actually have many valves, flaps of the tunica intima that keep blood flowing toward the heart. They can even be seen as small bumps along a forearm vein, so this choice is a misconception about vein anatomy.
Deep, thick-walled, high-pressure vessels are arteries. Those features are why arteries are avoided for routine IV lines, so pick this description for a question about artery walls.
Correct. Superficial veins are easy to reach, easy to enter, and slow to bleed.
questions.answerText: They are superficial, thin, wide, and low pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are arteries not the usual choice for routine blood draws?
options: They carry too little blood to sample from
They are deep, thick-walled, and high pressure
They have valves inside that block the needle
They are thin-walled and collapse too easily
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. Most run deeper in the body than the superficial veins, which makes them harder to find and enter. Because of the high pressure, a puncture also bleeds more forcefully, so arteries are saved for special tests rather than routine draws.
notes: Arteries carry plenty of blood under high pressure. This misconception confuses arteries with tiny vessels like capillaries, which hold too little blood to draw from.
Correct. Depth, thick walls, and high pressure make arteries harder to enter and quicker to bleed.
Arteries do not have valves; valves are found in veins, especially in the limbs. This choice comes from mixing up the two vessel types.
A thin wall that looks collapsed on a slide describes a vein, not an artery. Pick it for a question about why veins look flattened next to their matching arteries.
questions.answerText: They are deep, thick-walled, and high pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are valves especially important in the veins below the heart?
options: They raise venous pressure to arterial levels
They stop blood sliding back down against gravity
They let blood exchange gases through the vein wall
They stop blood from entering the capillary beds
questions.why: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that let blood move only toward the heart. Blood in the veins below the heart, especially in the legs, travels upward against gravity under low pressure. Each valve closes if blood starts to slide back down, so blood moves up the vein in short steps toward the heart. When these valves fail, blood pools and causes varicose veins.
notes: Valves only control direction; they do not raise venous pressure. Pressure in veins stays low, which is why they need valves in the first place.
Correct. Valves stop backflow where blood must climb against gravity at low pressure.
Exchange of gases happens across the thin wall of capillaries, not veins. Pick capillaries for a question about where gases and nutrients cross.
Entry into capillary beds is controlled by arterioles and precapillary sphincters on the arterial side. Choose them for a question about directing flow into a tissue.
questions.answerText: They stop blood sliding back down against gravity

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why does walking help move blood back to the heart from the legs?
options: Walking makes the veins contract on their own like the heart
Contracting leg muscles squeeze the deep veins
Walking widens the leg arteries
Walking makes the venous valves open both ways
questions.why: Deep veins of the legs run between the leg muscles. When the muscles contract during walking, they squeeze those veins and push blood forward, and the venous valves keep it from flowing back down. This is called the skeletal muscle pump, and it is a major help to venous return from the legs, where blood must move upward against gravity at low pressure.
notes: Veins have a thin tunica media and do not pump rhythmically the way the heart does. Students choose this when they assume veins pump blood on their own.
Correct. The skeletal muscle pump squeezes deep veins, and the valves keep blood moving toward the heart.
Wider arteries bring more blood into the legs, which is a separate effect. It does not push blood back up the veins, so pick it only for a question about delivering blood to working muscles.
Venous valves only open toward the heart, and their whole job is to close when blood flows backward. This misconception would undo what the valves do.
questions.answerText: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the deep veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are sinusoids the capillary type found in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow?
options: Their wide gaps let large molecules and cells cross
Their unbroken lining keeps most substances in the blood
Their smooth muscle controls how much blood enters
Their small pores allow rapid filtration of fluid
questions.why: Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large openings in the endothelium, wide gaps between cells, and an incomplete basement membrane. Those gaps let large molecules, and even whole cells, pass through the wall. The liver exchanges large proteins with the blood, the spleen handles whole blood cells, and red bone marrow releases newly made blood cells, so all three need this leaky build.
notes: Correct. The wide gaps of sinusoids let large molecules and whole cells pass.
An unbroken lining describes continuous capillaries, the tightest type, found in muscle, skin, lungs, and the brain. Pick it for tissues that must keep most substances inside the blood.
Capillaries have no smooth muscle at all; their wall is only endothelium on a basement membrane. Smooth muscle that controls flow describes arterioles and precapillary sphincters.

Small pores describe fenestrated capillaries, found in the kidney, small intestine, and most endocrine glands. They would be the answer for rapid filtration or absorption, but their pores are too small for cells.
questions.answerText: Their wide gaps let large molecules and cells cross

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are continuous capillaries the least leaky capillary type?
options: Their lining is unbroken except for narrow clefts
Their basement membrane is incomplete
Their endothelial cells contain small pores
They have a thick tunica media around the endothelium
questions.why: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelial lining, with neighboring cells joined closely and interrupted only by narrow intercellular clefts. With no pores and no large gaps, only small substances can pass, so most material stays inside the blood. They are the most common type, found in muscle, skin, lungs, and the central nervous system, where the tight lining helps protect the brain.
notes: Correct. An unbroken lining with only narrow clefts makes continuous capillaries the tightest type.
An incomplete basement membrane is a feature of sinusoids, the leakiest type. It would be the answer for a question about how whole cells cross in the liver, spleen, or bone marrow.
Small pores, called fenestrations, describe fenestrated capillaries. Pick them for a question about rapid filtration in the kidney or absorption in the small intestine.
No capillary has a tunica media; the wall is only endothelium on a basement membrane. A thick tunica media describes an artery.
questions.answerText: Their lining is unbroken except for narrow clefts

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are fenestrated capillaries found in the kidney and the small intestine?
options: Their large gaps let whole blood cells pass through
Their thick walls withstand high pressure
Their pores allow fast filtration and absorption
Their unbroken lining keeps substances in
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries have small pores, called fenestrations, in their endothelial cells. These pores let fluid and small dissolved substances move across the wall much faster than in continuous capillaries. The kidney filters large volumes of fluid out of the blood, and the small intestine absorbs digested nutrients into the blood, so both depend on this rapid movement.
notes: Letting whole blood cells pass describes sinusoids, the leakiest capillaries, found in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow. The kidney and intestine need fluid to move, not cells.
Capillaries have thin walls made of a single layer of endothelium, never thick walls. Thick walls that withstand high pressure describe arteries.
Correct. Fenestrations let fluid and small solutes cross quickly, which filtration and absorption require.
An unbroken lining describes continuous capillaries, which keep most substances in the blood. Choose them for muscle, skin, lungs, or the brain.
questions.answerText: Their pores allow fast filtration and absorption

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Why are capillary walls so thin?
options: A thin wall lets materials cross quickly
A thin wall lets capillaries withstand high pressure
A thin wall lets capillaries hold most of the blood
A thin wall lets capillaries change diameter quickly
questions.why: Capillaries are the exchange vessels, where gases, nutrients, and wastes move between the blood and the tissues. Their wall is only the tunica intima, a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a basement membrane. That keeps the distance between blood and tissue fluid very short, so materials can cross quickly.
notes: Correct. A one-cell-thick wall keeps the exchange distance short.
Withstanding high pressure takes a thick wall, like the heavy tunica media of an artery. Pick arteries for a question about which vessels handle high pressure.
The veins, not the capillaries, hold the largest share of the body's blood at rest, roughly sixty percent. Choose veins for a question about blood reservoirs.
Changing diameter takes smooth muscle, which capillaries lack. Arterioles, with one or two layers of smooth muscle, are the answer for a question about adjusting flow into a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: A thin wall lets materials cross quickly

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which list gives the three tunics of a blood vessel wall in order from innermost to outermost?
options: Tunica media, tunica intima, tunica externa
Tunica intima, tunica externa, tunica media
Tunica externa, tunica media, tunica intima
Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa
questions.why: The tunica intima is the innermost layer, an endothelial lining in direct contact with the blood. The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, and the tunica externa is the outer layer of mostly collagen fibers that anchors the vessel. The names follow the order: intima means innermost, media means middle, and externa means outer.
notes: This places the muscle layer innermost, but the tunica media sits in the middle, between the endothelial lining and the outer collagen layer. Its name, media, means middle.
This places the tunica externa in the middle, but externa means outer. The muscular tunica media is the middle layer.
These are the right three tunics, but listed from the outside in. Pick this order if the question asked for the layers from outermost to innermost.
Correct. Intima, media, externa, from the lumen outward.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What tissue forms the tunica intima of a blood vessel?
options: Simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane
Smooth muscle and elastic fibers
Stratified squamous epithelium on a basement membrane
Mostly collagen fibers with nerves and small vessels
questions.why: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of a vessel wall, and it is lined by endothelium, a single layer of flat (simple squamous) cells resting on a basement membrane. This smooth, thin lining reduces friction as blood flows past and is continuous with the endocardium inside the heart. In a capillary, this layer is the entire wall.
notes: Correct. The intima is a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a basement membrane.
Smooth muscle and elastic fibers make up the tunica media, the middle layer. Pick this if the question asked which layer changes a vessel's diameter.

Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers and protects surfaces that take friction, such as the skin and the lining of the esophagus. It would be the answer for a protective lining, not a thin vessel lining that blood flows across.
Collagen fibers with nerves and small vessels make up the tunica externa, the outer layer that anchors the vessel. Choose it for the layer that contains the vasa vasorum.
questions.answerText: Simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: What does the tunica media contain, and what does it control?
options: Collagen fibers and small vessels; it anchors the vessel in place
Endothelium on a basement membrane; it reduces friction with the blood
Cardiac muscle and elastic fibers; it pumps blood along the vessel
Smooth muscle and elastic fibers; it controls the vessel's diameter
questions.why: The tunica media is the middle layer of the vessel wall, made of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. When its smooth muscle contracts, the vessel narrows (vasoconstriction), and when it relaxes, the vessel widens (vasodilation). It is the thickest layer in arteries, which helps them handle blood under high pressure.
notes: Collagen fibers with small vessels form the tunica externa, which anchors the vessel to surrounding tissue. It would be the answer for the outermost tunic, the thickest layer in veins.
Endothelium on a basement membrane is the tunica intima, the smooth inner lining. Pick it if the question asked which layer is in direct contact with the blood.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall, and blood vessels do not pump blood. Students choose this when they confuse the smooth muscle in vessel walls with heart muscle.
Correct. The smooth muscle of the media narrows or widens the vessel.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle and elastic fibers; it controls the vessel's diameter

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A capillary wall is built from only one of the three tunics. Which one, and why only that layer?
options: Tunica intima and media, because the wall must be thin but strong
Tunica externa only, because the capillary must be anchored in tissue
Tunica media only, because the capillary must control its own diameter
Tunica intima only, because exchange needs the thinnest possible wall
questions.why: A capillary wall is just the tunica intima: a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane. Capillaries are the exchange vessels, where gases, nutrients, and wastes cross between the blood and the tissues, and that exchange works best across the thinnest possible barrier. Adding smooth muscle or a collagen coat would only slow the crossing.
notes: A capillary has no tunica media, so its wall is not two layers. Students choose this when they assume every vessel needs muscle; the precapillary sphincters that control entry into a capillary sit on the metarteriole, not the capillary itself.
The tunica externa is the collagen layer that anchors larger vessels, and capillaries lack it too. Choose it for the thickest layer of a vein.
The tunica media is the smooth muscle layer that changes vessel diameter, and capillaries lack it. Pick it for a question about how arterioles adjust blood flow into a capillary bed.
Correct. The capillary wall is endothelium on a basement membrane, which keeps the exchange barrier as thin as possible.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima only, because exchange needs the thinnest possible wall

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel on a slide has a thick middle layer packed with smooth muscle and elastic fibers, and it holds a round shape. Which vessel type is it most likely to be?
options: A vein
A venule
A capillary
An artery
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so their tunica media is thick, with plenty of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. That thick middle layer is why an artery keeps its round shape on a slide. A vein has the same three tunics, but its media is thin and its outer externa is the thickest layer, so it usually looks collapsed.
notes: A vein has a thin tunica media, a thick tunica externa, and a wide lumen, so it often looks collapsed on a slide. Pick it if the vessel had a thin wall and an irregular, flattened shape.
A venule is a small vein with a thin, porous wall that collects blood from capillaries. It would be the answer for a tiny thin-walled vessel just downstream of a capillary bed.
A capillary wall is only endothelium and a basement membrane, with no tunica media at all. Choose it for a vessel whose wall is a single layer of flat cells.
Correct. A thick muscular media and a round shape point to an artery.
questions.answerText: An artery

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which list gives the five vessel types in the order blood passes through them, starting from the heart?
options: Arteries, venules, capillaries, arterioles, veins
Arterioles, arteries, capillaries, veins, venules
Veins, venules, capillaries, arterioles, arteries
Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins
questions.why: Blood leaves the heart in arteries, which branch into smaller arterioles. Arterioles feed the capillaries, where exchange with the tissues happens, and the capillaries merge into venules, the smallest veins. Venules join into veins, which carry blood back to the heart.
notes: This swaps arterioles and venules. Arterioles are the small arteries leading into a capillary bed, and venules are the small veins draining out of it.
This puts the small vessels before the large ones on each side. Blood goes from the large arteries into the smaller arterioles, and on the return trip the small venules merge into larger veins.
This is the correct sequence run backward, from veins to arteries. Blood leaves the heart in arteries and returns in veins, so this order fits only a question that asked for the sequence in reverse.
Correct. Arteries branch down to capillaries, and venules merge back up into veins.
questions.answerText: Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which statement correctly defines arteries and veins?
options: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood; veins carry oxygen-poor blood
Arteries carry blood at low pressure; veins carry blood at high pressure
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward the heart
Arteries carry blood toward the heart; veins carry blood away from the heart
questions.why: Arteries and veins are defined by the direction of blood flow relative to the heart. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry blood back toward it. This is why the pulmonary arteries count as arteries even though they carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.
notes: This is true in the systemic circuit, but it is not the definition. The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood, so oxygen content cannot be the rule.
This reverses the pressures. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, which is why they have thick muscular walls, while veins carry blood under low pressure and rely on valves.
Correct. Direction of flow is what defines the two vessel types.
This reverses the two definitions. A helpful memory aid is that artery and away both start with the letter a.
questions.answerText: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which vessel type is the main exchange vessel, where gases and nutrients cross between blood and tissue?
options: Capillaries
Arterioles
Veins
Elastic arteries
questions.why: Capillaries are the exchange vessels of the body. Their walls are only the tunica intima, a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, so oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide, and wastes can cross easily between the blood and the surrounding tissue. Every other vessel type has a thicker wall built for carrying or controlling blood rather than exchanging with the tissues.
notes: Correct. Capillaries have the thin walls that make exchange possible.
Arterioles are the smallest arteries, with one or two layers of smooth muscle. Pick them if the question asked which vessels adjust how much blood enters a capillary bed.
Veins carry blood back to the heart under low pressure and hold most of the blood volume at rest. Choose them for a question about blood reservoirs or vessels with valves.
Elastic arteries, like the aorta and pulmonary trunk, stretch with each heartbeat and recoil between beats. They would be the answer for vessels that keep blood moving while the ventricles relax.
questions.answerText: Capillaries

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Arterioles have walls made mostly of smooth muscle. What does that allow them to do?
options: Adjust how much blood enters a capillary bed
Let gases cross between blood and tissue
Hold the largest share of the blood at rest
Stretch and recoil to keep blood moving between beats
questions.why: Arterioles are the smallest arteries, and their walls are mostly one or two layers of smooth muscle. When that muscle contracts, the arteriole narrows and less blood flows into the capillary bed it feeds; when it relaxes, the arteriole widens and more blood flows in. This lets the body send more blood to active tissues and less to resting ones.
notes: Correct. Their smooth muscle lets arterioles open or narrow the entrance to a capillary bed.
Gas exchange happens across capillary walls, which are only endothelium. Arterioles have muscle in their walls, so they control flow rather than exchange material.
Veins, not arterioles, hold the largest share of the blood at rest, roughly 60 percent. Choose this for a question about the blood reservoirs of the body.

Stretching and recoiling to keep blood moving between beats is the job of elastic arteries like the aorta, whose walls are rich in elastic fibers. Pick this for a question about the largest arteries near the heart.
questions.answerText: Adjust how much blood enters a capillary bed

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A phlebotomist draws blood from a vein in the arm rather than an artery. Which set of features makes the vein the safer choice?
options: Its thick tunica media clamps shut around the needle to stop the bleeding
It lies closer to the surface, has a thinner wall, and carries blood at low pressure
Its wall is a single layer of endothelium, so the needle passes through easily
It lies deeper, has a thicker wall, and carries blood at high pressure
questions.why: Veins used for blood draws sit close to the surface, so they are easy to find and reach. Their walls are thinner, with a thin tunica media, and their lumen is wide, so a needle enters easily. Because veins carry blood under low pressure, the puncture bleeds slowly and is easy to stop with gentle pressure, unlike an artery.
notes: Veins have a thin tunica media, not a thick one, and vessel walls do not clamp around a needle. Students choose this when they confuse veins with muscular arteries.
Correct. Surface position, a thin wall, and low pressure make a vein easy to enter and slow to bleed.
A wall made only of endothelium describes a capillary, which is far too small to hold a needle. Choose this description for a question about the exchange vessels.

That describes an artery, which generally lies deeper, has a thick muscular wall, and carries blood under high pressure. Pick this set of features if the question asked why an arterial puncture is harder and bleeds more.
questions.answerText: It lies closer to the surface, has a thinner wall, and carries blood at low pressure

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which list names the three kinds of artery in order from largest to smallest?
options: Elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles
Elastic arteries, arterioles, muscular arteries
Arterioles, muscular arteries, elastic arteries
Muscular arteries, elastic arteries, arterioles
questions.why: Elastic arteries are the largest, near the heart (the aorta, pulmonary trunk, and their major branches), with a tunica media rich in elastic fibers that stretches and recoils with each beat. Muscular arteries are medium-sized, like the brachial and femoral arteries, with a media made mostly of smooth muscle that distributes blood to specific organs. Arterioles are the smallest, with one or two layers of smooth muscle that control flow into capillary beds.
notes: Correct. Elastic arteries branch into muscular arteries, which branch into arterioles.
This puts arterioles in the middle, but arterioles are the smallest arteries, the last before the capillaries. Muscular arteries come between the elastic arteries and the arterioles.
These are the right three kinds listed from smallest to largest. Pick this order if the question asked for the arteries from smallest to largest.
This swaps the first two. The largest arteries, right next to the heart, are the elastic ones, and the muscular arteries branch from them to reach specific organs.
questions.answerText: Elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Which capillary type is the leakiest, letting even whole blood cells cross, and where is it found?
options: Continuous, in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow
Continuous, in muscle, skin, and the brain
Fenestrated, in the kidney and small intestine
Sinusoid, in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow
questions.why: Sinusoids are wide, winding capillaries with large openings in the endothelium, an incomplete basement membrane, and wide gaps between cells. They are found where whole cells or large molecules must pass between the blood and the tissue, such as the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow. Newly made blood cells leaving the red bone marrow, for example, cross into the blood through sinusoid walls.
notes: The locations belong to sinusoids, but continuous capillaries are the tightest type, not the leakiest. Students pick this when they remember the organs but mix up the capillary name.

Continuous capillaries are the least leaky type, with an unbroken lining, and these are their correct locations. Choose this pairing for the most common capillary type, or the tight capillaries of the brain.

Fenestrated capillaries have small pores that let fluid and small molecules through quickly, but not whole cells. Pick this pairing if the question asked about the capillaries built for rapid filtration and absorption.
Correct. Sinusoids are the leakiest capillaries, found where whole cells must cross.
questions.answerText: Sinusoid, in the liver, spleen, and red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On an artery slide, you find two wavy elastic sheets in the wall. Between them is a thick band of smooth muscle, and outside the outer sheet is a collagen layer holding tiny blood vessels. Which tunic lies between the sheets, and what are the tiny vessels?
options: The tunica intima; the tiny vessels are the vasa vasorum.
The tunica media; the tiny vessels are capillaries of the intima.
The tunica media; the tiny vessels are the vasa vasorum.
The tunica externa; the tiny vessels are metarterioles.
questions.why: The internal elastic lamina marks the inner edge of the tunica media and the external elastic lamina marks its outer edge, so the smooth muscle between them is the tunica media. Outside the external lamina is the tunica externa, mostly collagen. The small vessels in it are the vasa vasorum, which supply the wall of a large vessel.
notes: The tunica intima lies inside the internal elastic lamina and is a thin lining of endothelium on a basement membrane. It has no thick band of smooth muscle.
The middle layer is right, but the tiny vessels sit in the collagen layer outside the outer sheet, the tunica externa. They are the vasa vasorum.
Correct. The two laminae frame the tunica media, and the vessels in the externa are the vasa vasorum.

The tunica externa is the collagen layer outside the outer sheet, not the smooth muscle between the sheets. Metarterioles are the tapered ends of arterioles at a capillary bed, not vessels in an artery wall.
questions.answerText: The tunica media; the tiny vessels are the vasa vasorum.

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: A vessel on a slide has a wall made only of endothelium on a basement membrane. If you follow it upstream until smooth muscle first appears in the wall, which vessel have you reached, and which tunic has appeared?
options: A venule; the tunica externa has appeared.
An arteriole; the tunica externa has appeared.
An elastic artery; the tunica intima has appeared.
An arteriole; the tunica media has appeared.
questions.why: A wall of only endothelium on a basement membrane is a capillary, which has the tunica intima alone. Upstream of a capillary is an arteriole, whose wall has one to two layers of smooth muscle. Smooth muscle belongs to the tunica media, so that is the tunic that has been added.
notes: Venules lie downstream of capillaries, not upstream, and the collagen tunica externa is not the smooth muscle layer.
The vessel is right, but smooth muscle belongs to the tunica media. The tunica externa is mostly collagen.
The tunica intima is the layer the capillary already has. An elastic artery such as the aorta is far upstream, with smaller arteries and arterioles in between.
Correct. Arterioles feed capillaries, and their smooth muscle is a tunica media.
questions.answerText: An arteriole; the tunica media has appeared.

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: The endocardium lining the heart chambers continues into the great vessels. Which tunic of a vessel wall is it continuous with, and what tissue do the two share?
options: The tunica media; both contain smooth muscle.
The tunica externa; both are mostly collagen fibers.
The tunica intima; both contain cardiac muscle.
The tunica intima; both are a lining of endothelium.
questions.why: The endocardium is a smooth endothelium lining the chambers and covering the valves, and it is continuous with the lining of the great vessels. In a vessel, that lining is the tunica intima, simple squamous endothelium on a basement membrane. The same layer is the only one a capillary has.
notes: The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers. The endocardium is a thin endothelial lining with no smooth muscle.
The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors a vessel. The endocardium is the innermost layer of the heart, so it lines up with the innermost tunic.
The tunica intima is right, but it is endothelium, not muscle. Cardiac muscle is found in the myocardium, the middle layer of the heart wall.
Correct. The endocardium and the tunica intima are one continuous endothelial lining.
questions.answerText: The tunica intima; both are a lining of endothelium.

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On a slide, a thin, very porous vessel sits just downstream of a capillary bed, and white blood cells are squeezing through its wall into the tissue. Which vessel type is it?
options: A postcapillary venule
A metarteriole
A muscular artery
A continuous capillary
questions.why: Blood leaving a capillary bed enters the venules, and the first one is the postcapillary venule, which is loosely joined and very porous. Venules are where white blood cells leave the bloodstream to enter the tissues. The vessel's place downstream of the bed and the cells crossing its wall both point to it.
notes: Correct. The postcapillary venule drains the bed and is where white cells leave the blood.
A metarteriole is the tapered end of an arteriole where it joins a capillary bed. It is upstream of the capillaries, not downstream.
A muscular artery has a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and distributes blood to organs. It is neither thin nor porous, and it lies far upstream of a capillary bed.
A continuous capillary has an unbroken lining interrupted only by small clefts. It is part of the capillary bed, not the vessel that drains it.
questions.answerText: A postcapillary venule

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: On a slide of a capillary bed, two tiny vessels each have one or two layers of smooth muscle in their walls. One carries blood into the bed, and the other lies just downstream, collecting blood that has passed through it. Which vessel is each, and what does each do?
options: Into the bed is a venule that collects blood; downstream is an arteriole that controls flow
Both are arterioles, one feeding the bed and one controlling the flow out of it
Into the bed is an arteriole that controls flow; downstream is a venule that collects blood
Into the bed is a muscular artery; downstream is a vein carrying blood to the heart
questions.why: An arteriole and a muscular venule can both have one or two layers of smooth muscle, so the wall alone does not tell them apart. The direction of flow does. The arteriole carries blood into the capillary bed and adjusts how much enters it, and the venule collects the blood drained from the capillaries on its way back toward the heart.
notes: This swaps the two. Venules lie downstream of a capillary bed and collect blood leaving it, while the arteriole upstream controls how much blood enters.
Arterioles carry blood away from the heart into a capillary bed, so neither one drains it. The small muscular vessel downstream of the bed is a muscular venule.
Correct. Direction of flow tells them apart: the arteriole feeds the bed and the muscular venule collects from it.
A muscular artery has up to forty layers of smooth muscle, and blood reaches a vein only after the venules. Both vessels here are far smaller.
questions.answerText: Into the bed is an arteriole that controls flow; downstream is a venule that collects blood

questions.topic: Blood vessel histology and vessel types
questions.q: Two artery slides are compared. One has a tunica media packed with elastic lamellae and well-defined elastic laminae. The other has up to forty layers of smooth muscle and a thin external elastic lamina. One came from the aorta and one from the brachial artery. Which match is correct?
options: The elastic slide is the brachial artery; the muscular slide is the aorta.
Both slides are elastic arteries, cut at different levels of one vessel.
Both slides are muscular arteries; the aorta has the more muscle layers.
The elastic slide is the aorta; the muscular slide is the brachial artery.
questions.why: An elastic artery has a thick tunica media dominated by elastic lamellae, and the aorta is the main example. A muscular artery has a media of mostly smooth muscle, up to forty layers, with a thin external elastic lamina, and the brachial artery is a muscular artery. Elastic arteries stretch and recoil near the heart, while muscular arteries distribute blood to specific organs.
notes: This reverses the two. The brachial artery is a muscular artery, and the aorta, which stretches and recoils with each heartbeat, is an elastic artery.
The slide with up to forty smooth muscle layers and a thin external lamina is a muscular artery, not an elastic one. The brachial artery is a muscular artery.
The aorta is an elastic artery, not a muscular one. Its media is dominated by elastic lamellae so it can stretch with each heartbeat.
Correct. Elastic lamellae mark the aorta, and many smooth muscle layers mark the brachial artery.
questions.answerText: The elastic slide is the aorta; the muscular slide is the brachial artery.

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the characteristic shape of a mature erythrocyte?
options: A biconcave disc
A small irregular fragment
A sickle-shaped crescent
A smooth sphere
questions.why: A mature erythrocyte is a biconcave disc, a round disc that is thinner in the center than at the rim. This shape gives the cell about 30 percent more surface area than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds gas exchange. It also lets the cell bend and fold through the narrowest capillaries.
notes: Correct. The red cell is a disc thinner at its center.
A small fragment of cytoplasm describes a platelet, which breaks off a megakaryocyte. Pick it for a question about thrombocytes.
A rigid, curved sickle shape is seen in sickle cell disease, where abnormal hemoglobin distorts the cell. It is a disease shape, not the normal one.
A sphere would have less surface area for the same volume and could not fold as easily. The biconcave shape gains about 30 percent more surface than a sphere.
questions.answerText: A biconcave disc

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the approximate diameter of an erythrocyte?
options: About 7.5 um
About 10 to 12 um
About 1 um
About 2 to 4 um
questions.why: An erythrocyte is about 7.5 micrometers (um) across. That is a useful ruler on a blood smear, because other cells can be sized against it. Platelets are much smaller, and the leukocytes are larger.
notes: Correct. A red cell is about 7.5 micrometers across.
About 10 to 12 um is roughly the size of a neutrophil, which is larger than a red cell. Leukocytes are bigger than erythrocytes.
About 1 um is roughly how thin a red cell is at its center, not how wide it is. Students who choose it mix up thickness with diameter.
About 2 to 4 um is the size of a platelet, a small cell fragment. Choose it for the smallest formed element.
questions.answerText: About 7.5 um

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Where is a mature erythrocyte thinnest?
options: At its center
It is evenly thick throughout
Over its nucleus
At its rim
questions.why: An erythrocyte is a biconcave disc, which means both faces are pressed inward. That makes the cell thinnest in the center and thickest at the rim. On a stained smear this shows up as a pale center, because less hemoglobin is stacked there.
notes: Correct. Both faces dip inward, so the center is the thinnest part.
A disc of even thickness would be a flat coin. The red cell is thinner in the middle, which is what gives it extra surface area.
A mature erythrocyte has no nucleus, having ejected it during development. A nucleus would be the answer for a leukocyte.
The rim is the thickest part of the disc. Students who pick it reverse the biconcave shape.
questions.answerText: At its center

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What advantage does the biconcave disc shape give an erythrocyte?
options: Extra room inside for organelles
A rigid shape that holds its form in narrow vessels
A smaller surface that slows the loss of gases
More surface area and flexibility
questions.why: The biconcave shape gives an erythrocyte about 30 percent more surface area than a sphere of the same volume, so gases move in and out more quickly. The thin, flexible disc can also bend and fold to squeeze single file through capillaries narrower than itself. Both features serve the job of carrying oxygen.
notes: A mature red cell has ejected its nucleus and most organelles. The space goes to hemoglobin instead.
A rigid red cell is a problem, not an advantage. In sickle cell disease rigid cells cannot fold and jam the capillaries.
This reverses the advantage. The biconcave shape increases surface area so gases move faster.
Correct. Extra surface speeds gas exchange and flexibility lets the cell pass narrow capillaries.
questions.answerText: More surface area and flexibility

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which statement about the nucleus of a mature erythrocyte is correct?
options: It has one large round nucleus
It has no nucleus, because it was ejected
It has a kidney-shaped nucleus
It has a nucleus with three to five lobes
questions.why: During development the erythrocyte ejects its nucleus, so a mature red cell is anucleate, meaning it has no nucleus. This frees more space for hemoglobin. On a smear, a red cell shows a pale center but no stained nucleus, which sets it apart from every leukocyte.
notes: A large round nucleus filling most of the cell is the look of a lymphocyte. Pick it for that agranulocyte.
Correct. Mature red cells are anucleate.
A kidney-shaped nucleus belongs to a monocyte, the largest leukocyte.
A nucleus with three to five lobes belongs to a neutrophil, the most numerous leukocyte.
questions.answerText: It has no nucleus, because it was ejected

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Besides a nucleus, what else does a mature erythrocyte lack?
options: Its hemoglobin molecules
A flexible plasma membrane
Mitochondria and other organelles
The iron in its heme groups
questions.why: As an erythrocyte matures, it ejects its nucleus and loses most of its organelles, including its mitochondria. What is left is a flexible membrane packed with hemoglobin. Losing these structures makes room for more hemoglobin, but it also means the cell cannot divide or repair itself.
notes: Hemoglobin is what fills the mature erythrocyte. It is the one thing the cell keeps in abundance.
Every cell needs a plasma membrane. The red cell membrane is flexible, which lets it fold through capillaries.
Correct. The red cell gives up its organelles to make room for hemoglobin.
Iron sits in the heme groups of hemoglobin, so a red cell is full of it. Iron is what lets hemoglobin bind oxygen.
questions.answerText: Mitochondria and other organelles

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Because it lacks a nucleus and organelles, a mature erythrocyte cannot do which of the following?
options: Divide or make new proteins
Carry oxygen
Hold hemoglobin
Bend through capillaries
questions.why: Cell division and protein synthesis both depend on a nucleus, which holds the DNA instructions, and on organelles such as ribosomes. A mature erythrocyte has ejected its nucleus and most organelles, so it cannot divide or replace its proteins. That is why red cells wear out after about 120 days and must be replaced by the bone marrow.
notes: Correct. Without a nucleus or ribosomes the cell cannot divide or build proteins.
Carrying oxygen is the main job of the red cell, done by hemoglobin. No nucleus is needed for it.
Holding hemoglobin is exactly what the red cell is built for. Losing the nucleus makes more room for it.
Bending through capillaries depends on the flexible plasma membrane and biconcave shape, not on a nucleus.
questions.answerText: Divide or make new proteins

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the average lifespan of an erythrocyte?
options: About 10 days
About 1 year
About 120 days
About 120 hours
questions.why: An erythrocyte lives about 120 days, roughly four months. Without a nucleus it cannot repair itself, so it gradually wears out and becomes less flexible. Worn cells are then broken down in the spleen and liver, and new ones are made in the red bone marrow.
notes: About 10 days is closer to the lifespan of a platelet. Red cells last much longer.
A year is too long. Without a nucleus to repair it, a red cell wears out in about four months.
Correct. Red cells last about four months.
About 120 hours is only five days. Students who pick it have the right number with the wrong unit.
questions.answerText: About 120 days

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A blood cell is an anucleate biconcave disc about 7.5 um across, with no organelles and a lifespan of about 120 days. What is it?
options: A platelet
An erythrocyte
A neutrophil
A lymphocyte
questions.why: Each clue points to the erythrocyte. It has no nucleus and no organelles, it is a biconcave disc about 7.5 um across, and it lives about 120 days before the spleen and liver remove it. No other formed element has this combination.
notes: A platelet is a small fragment of cytoplasm, about 2 to 4 um, not a biconcave disc. Pick it for a fragment from a megakaryocyte.
Correct. Every clue matches the red blood cell.
A neutrophil is a complete cell with a three to five lobed nucleus and fine pale granules. It has a nucleus, so it cannot be anucleate.
A lymphocyte is a nucleated agranulocyte with a large round nucleus. Its nucleus rules it out.
questions.answerText: An erythrocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What feature is used to divide the leukocytes into two structural classes?
options: Whether a nucleus is present
Whether the cell carries hemoglobin
Whether the cell is larger than a red cell
Whether visible cytoplasmic granules are present
questions.why: Leukocytes are sorted into granulocytes, which have granules in their cytoplasm that are visible with a light microscope after staining, and agranulocytes, which do not. The granulocytes are the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. The agranulocytes are the lymphocytes and monocytes.
notes: All leukocytes are complete cells with a nucleus. Lacking a nucleus is a feature of the mature erythrocyte.
Hemoglobin is carried by erythrocytes, not leukocytes. No leukocyte is classed by hemoglobin content.
All leukocytes are larger than red cells, so size cannot split them into two classes.
Correct. Granulocytes have visible granules and agranulocytes do not.
questions.answerText: Whether visible cytoplasmic granules are present

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: To which class of leukocytes do the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils belong?
options: The granulocytes
The erythrocytes
The thrombocytes
The agranulocytes
questions.why: Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils all have cytoplasmic granules that are visible after staining, so they are called granulocytes. They all develop from the myeloblast and have lobed nuclei. The other two leukocytes, lymphocytes and monocytes, are agranulocytes.
notes: Correct. All three have visible cytoplasmic granules.
Erythrocytes are the red blood cells, which have no nucleus and no granules. They are not leukocytes at all.
Thrombocyte is another name for the platelet, a cell fragment. It is not a class of leukocyte.
The agranulocytes are the lymphocytes and monocytes, which lack visible granules. Pick this class for those two cells.
questions.answerText: The granulocytes

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which two leukocytes are classified as agranulocytes?
options: Neutrophils and eosinophils
Lymphocytes and monocytes
Eosinophils and basophils
Neutrophils and basophils
questions.why: Agranulocytes are the leukocytes without visible cytoplasmic granules after staining. There are two of them: the lymphocyte, with a large round nucleus, and the monocyte, the largest leukocyte, with a kidney-shaped nucleus. The other three leukocytes are granulocytes.
notes: Neutrophils have fine pale granules and eosinophils have red-orange ones. Both are granulocytes.
Correct. These two lack visible granules.
Eosinophils have coarse red-orange granules and basophils have large dark granules. Both are granulocytes.
Neutrophils and basophils both have visible granules, so they are granulocytes. Pick this pair for a question about granulocytes.
questions.answerText: Lymphocytes and monocytes

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the most numerous in normal blood?
options: The neutrophil
The basophil
The lymphocyte
The monocyte
questions.why: Neutrophils make up more than half of all circulating leukocytes, which makes them the most numerous. They are the first responders to infection, engulfing and digesting bacteria. The mnemonic Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas lists the leukocytes from most to least numerous, starting with neutrophils.
notes: Correct. Neutrophils are more than half of all leukocytes.
Basophils are the rarest leukocyte, at the end of the mnemonic. Pick them for the least numerous white cell.
Lymphocytes are the second most numerous leukocyte. They come right after neutrophils in the mnemonic.
Monocytes are in the middle of the count, third in the mnemonic. They are the largest leukocyte, not the most numerous.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Roughly what percentage of circulating leukocytes are neutrophils?
options: Less than 1 percent
About 20 to 40 percent
About 2 to 8 percent
About 50 to 70 percent
questions.why: Neutrophils make up roughly 50 to 70 percent of the leukocytes in a normal differential count, which is more than all the other types combined. Exact ranges vary slightly between labs and textbooks, but neutrophils are always the clear majority. A rise in neutrophils often signals a bacterial infection.
notes: This is the share of basophils, the rarest leukocyte.
This is the share of lymphocytes, the second most numerous leukocyte.
This is the share of monocytes, the largest leukocyte.
Correct. Neutrophils are more than half of all leukocytes.
questions.answerText: About 50 to 70 percent

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the characteristic nuclear shape of a neutrophil?
options: Three to five connected lobes
A kidney-shaped nucleus
A two-lobed nucleus
A single large round nucleus
questions.why: A mature neutrophil has a nucleus divided into three to five lobes joined by thin strands. This multi-lobed nucleus, along with fine pale granules, makes it easy to pick out on a smear. Because the nucleus takes many shapes, the neutrophil is also called a polymorphonuclear cell.
notes: Correct. The multi-lobed nucleus is the signature of a neutrophil.
A kidney-shaped nucleus belongs to a monocyte, the largest leukocyte.
A two-lobed, or bilobed, nucleus belongs to an eosinophil, which also has coarse red-orange granules.
A large round nucleus filling most of the cell belongs to a lymphocyte.
questions.answerText: Three to five connected lobes

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Because of its many-lobed nucleus, the neutrophil is also called what?
options: A macrophage
A mast cell
A polymorphonuclear cell
A plasma cell
questions.why: Poly means many and morpho means shape, so polymorphonuclear means having a nucleus of many shapes. The neutrophil earns this name because its nucleus is divided into three to five lobes that vary from cell to cell. Clinicians often shorten the term to PMN.
notes: A macrophage is a monocyte that has left the blood and matured in a tissue. Pick it for the large phagocyte of the tissues.
A mast cell is a tissue cell similar to the basophil that releases histamine. It is not another name for the neutrophil.
Correct. The name describes its many-lobed nucleus.
A plasma cell is an activated B lymphocyte that makes antibodies. Pick it for antibody production.
questions.answerText: A polymorphonuclear cell

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Roughly what percentage of circulating leukocytes are eosinophils?
options: About 50 to 70 percent
About 20 to 40 percent
Less than 1 percent
About 1 to 4 percent
questions.why: Eosinophils make up only a small share of leukocytes, roughly 1 to 4 percent. They are fourth in the most-to-least order of Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. Their numbers rise in parasitic infections and allergic reactions.
notes: This is the share of neutrophils, the most numerous leukocyte.
This is the share of lymphocytes, the second most numerous leukocyte.
This is the share of basophils, the rarest leukocyte, which come after eosinophils in the count.
Correct. Eosinophils are a small share of leukocytes.
questions.answerText: About 1 to 4 percent

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the characteristic nuclear shape of an eosinophil?
options: A two-lobed nucleus
A large round nucleus filling most of the cell
A nucleus with three to five lobes
A kidney-shaped nucleus
questions.why: An eosinophil has a nucleus with two lobes, often described as looking like a pair of earmuffs or a telephone receiver. Together with its coarse red-orange granules, this makes the eosinophil easy to recognize on a stained smear.
notes: Correct. The bilobed nucleus plus red-orange granules marks an eosinophil.
A large round nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm belongs to a lymphocyte.
Three to five lobes is the neutrophil nucleus. Pick it for the most numerous leukocyte.
A kidney-shaped nucleus belongs to the monocyte, the largest leukocyte.
questions.answerText: A two-lobed nucleus

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the rarest in normal blood, at less than 1 percent?
options: The eosinophil
The basophil
The monocyte
The lymphocyte
questions.why: Basophils make up less than 1 percent of leukocytes, so they are the rarest and come last in Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. They have large dark granules that release histamine and other mediators of inflammation. Finding one on a smear usually takes some searching.
notes: Eosinophils are uncommon, about 1 to 4 percent, but they are more numerous than basophils.
Correct. Basophils are the rarest leukocyte.
Monocytes are about 2 to 8 percent of leukocytes. They are the largest leukocyte, not the rarest.
Lymphocytes are the second most numerous leukocyte. They are common on any smear.
questions.answerText: The basophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which two substances are found in the granules of a basophil?
options: Fibrinogen and serotonin
Major basic protein and peroxidase
Histamine and heparin
Perforin and granzymes
questions.why: Basophil granules contain histamine, which widens blood vessels and makes them leaky during inflammation, and heparin, which prevents clotting. Releasing these substances helps start an inflammatory response. Mast cells in the tissues carry the same chemicals.
notes: These are carried in platelet granules, fibrinogen in alpha granules and serotonin in dense granules. Pick them for platelets.
Major basic protein and related enzymes are in eosinophil granules. Pick them for the parasite-fighting granulocyte.
Correct. These are the classic contents of basophil granules.
Perforin and granzymes are stored by natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells, which use them to kill infected cells.
questions.answerText: Histamine and heparin

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Why is the nucleus of a basophil often difficult to see on a stained smear?
options: It has been ejected from the cell
It is very small and stains pale
Large dark granules cover it
It is hidden by hemoglobin
questions.why: A basophil has a lobed nucleus, but its cytoplasm is packed with large granules that stain dark purple to blue-black. These granules sit over the nucleus and hide much of it. The dark, crowded look of the cell is what identifies it.
notes: Ejecting the nucleus happens only in the red cell line. Basophils are complete cells and keep their nucleus.
The basophil nucleus is not tiny or pale. It is simply covered by the dark granules.
Correct. The dark granules cover much of the nucleus.
Hemoglobin is found in erythrocytes, not basophils. Students who pick this mix up the red pigment with the dark granules.
questions.answerText: Large dark granules cover it

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which tissue cell is structurally similar to the circulating basophil?
options: The macrophage
The plasma cell
The mast cell
The fibroblast
questions.why: Mast cells live in connective tissues, especially near blood vessels, and contain granules of histamine and heparin much like basophils. Both cells release these chemicals to start inflammation and allergic reactions. The basophil circulates in blood, while the mast cell stays in the tissues.
notes: A macrophage is the tissue form of the monocyte, a large phagocyte. Pick it for the cell a monocyte becomes.
A plasma cell is the antibody-making cell that develops from a B lymphocyte.
Correct. Mast cells resemble basophils and carry histamine and heparin.
A fibroblast is the cell of connective tissue proper that makes fibers and ground substance. It is not related to basophils.
questions.answerText: The mast cell

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Roughly what percentage of circulating leukocytes are lymphocytes?
options: About 2 to 8 percent
About 50 to 70 percent
About 20 to 40 percent
Less than 1 percent
questions.why: Lymphocytes make up roughly 20 to 40 percent of leukocytes, second only to neutrophils. Exact ranges vary a little between sources, but lymphocytes are always the second most common white cell. They are the core of specific immunity and include the B cells and T cells.
notes: This is the share of monocytes, the largest leukocyte.
This is the share of neutrophils, the most numerous leukocyte.
Correct. Lymphocytes are the second most numerous leukocyte.
This is the share of basophils, the rarest leukocyte.
questions.answerText: About 20 to 40 percent

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What does the nucleus of a lymphocyte look like?
options: A kidney-shaped nucleus
A nucleus with three to five lobes
A two-lobed nucleus
A large round nucleus
questions.why: A lymphocyte has a large, round, dark-staining nucleus that fills nearly the entire cell. Only a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm shows around the edge. This look sets it apart from the monocyte, which is larger and has a kidney-shaped nucleus.
notes: A kidney-shaped nucleus belongs to the monocyte, the largest leukocyte.
Three to five lobes belongs to the neutrophil, the most numerous leukocyte.
A two-lobed nucleus belongs to the eosinophil, which also has red-orange granules.
Correct. A big round nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm marks a lymphocyte.
questions.answerText: A large round nucleus

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which list names the three kinds of lymphocytes?
options: Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells
Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils
Monocytes, macrophages, and mast cells
questions.why: Lymphocytes come in three kinds. B lymphocytes become plasma cells that make antibodies, T lymphocytes direct and carry out cell-based immune responses, and natural killer cells destroy infected or abnormal cells. All three come from the lymphoid line and look similar on a smear.
notes: These are the three kinds of formed elements in blood. Pick this list for the cellular part of blood.
Correct. These are the three kinds of lymphocytes.
These are the three granulocytes. Pick this list for leukocytes with visible granules.
A monocyte matures into a macrophage, and the mast cell resembles a basophil. None of these is a lymphocyte.
questions.answerText: B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: When a B lymphocyte is activated, into what cell does it develop?
options: A mast cell
A plasma cell
A macrophage
A megakaryocyte
questions.why: An activated B lymphocyte develops into a plasma cell. Plasma cells make and release antibodies, the gamma globulins of the plasma. This is why gamma globulins are the one group of plasma proteins not made in the liver.
notes: A mast cell is a tissue cell similar to a basophil, with histamine and heparin granules.
Correct. Activated B cells become antibody-making plasma cells.
A macrophage develops from a monocyte that leaves the blood. Pick it for the large tissue phagocyte.
A megakaryocyte is the giant marrow cell that breaks into platelets.
questions.answerText: A plasma cell

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Roughly what percentage of circulating leukocytes are monocytes?
options: About 20 to 40 percent
Less than 1 percent
About 50 to 70 percent
About 2 to 8 percent
questions.why: Monocytes make up roughly 2 to 8 percent of leukocytes. They are third in the most-to-least order of Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. Although they are not very numerous, they are the largest leukocytes and become macrophages in the tissues.
notes: This is the share of lymphocytes, the second most numerous leukocyte.
This is the share of basophils, the rarest leukocyte.
This is the share of neutrophils, the most numerous leukocyte.
Correct. Monocytes are a small share of leukocytes.
questions.answerText: About 2 to 8 percent

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the characteristic nuclear shape of a monocyte?
options: A large round nucleus filling most of the cell
A nucleus with three to five lobes
A two-lobed nucleus
A kidney-shaped nucleus
questions.why: A monocyte has a large nucleus with an indentation on one side, giving it a kidney or horseshoe shape. Combined with its large size and pale gray-blue cytoplasm with no visible granules, this identifies the monocyte on a smear.
notes: A large round nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm belongs to a lymphocyte, the other agranulocyte.
Three to five lobes belongs to a neutrophil.
A two-lobed nucleus belongs to an eosinophil.
Correct. The indented, kidney-shaped nucleus marks a monocyte.
questions.answerText: A kidney-shaped nucleus

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the largest of the five?
options: The lymphocyte
The monocyte
The basophil
The neutrophil
questions.why: The monocyte is the largest leukocyte, noticeably bigger than the red cells around it on a smear. Its size fits its job, since after leaving the blood it matures into a macrophage that engulfs debris and pathogens.
notes: Most lymphocytes are small, about the size of a red cell. Pick the lymphocyte for the large round nucleus, not the largest size.
Correct. The monocyte is the largest leukocyte.
The basophil is the rarest leukocyte. It is not the largest.
The neutrophil is the most numerous leukocyte, but it is smaller than a monocyte.
questions.answerText: The monocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: When a monocyte leaves the blood and enters a tissue, into what cell does it mature?
options: A neutrophil
A macrophage
A plasma cell
A mast cell
questions.why: Monocytes circulate in the blood for a short time, then leave it, mostly through the loosely joined walls of the venules, and enter the tissues. There they enlarge and mature into macrophages, large phagocytes that engulf debris and pathogens. Macrophages in the spleen and liver also remove worn-out red cells.
notes: A neutrophil is a separate granulocyte that develops from the myeloblast. Monocytes do not turn into neutrophils.
Correct. Monocytes become macrophages in the tissues.
A plasma cell develops from an activated B lymphocyte. Pick it for antibody production.
A mast cell is a tissue cell similar to the basophil, carrying histamine and heparin.
questions.answerText: A macrophage

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which list puts the five leukocytes in order from most to least numerous?
options: Neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, monocytes, basophils
Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils
Lymphocytes, neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils
Basophils, eosinophils, monocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils
questions.why: The mnemonic Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas gives the order from most to least numerous: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils. Neutrophils are more than half of all leukocytes, while basophils are less than 1 percent. This order is the answer to the differential count question.
notes: This swaps monocytes and eosinophils. Monocytes are more numerous and come third.
Correct. This matches Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas.
This swaps the first two. Neutrophils, not lymphocytes, are the most numerous.
