This is the correct sequence written backward, from least to most numerous.
questions.answerText: Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A leukocyte has fine pale granules and a nucleus with three to five lobes, and it is the most numerous white cell. Which cell is it?
options: The neutrophil
The eosinophil
The basophil
The monocyte
questions.why: Each clue fits the neutrophil. It has fine, pale granules that are hard to see, a nucleus with three to five lobes, and it outnumbers every other leukocyte. It is the first responder to infection, engulfing and digesting bacteria.
notes: Correct. Pale granules, a multi-lobed nucleus, and the highest count identify the neutrophil.
The eosinophil has coarse red-orange granules and a two-lobed nucleus, and it is uncommon.
The basophil has large dark granules that hide its nucleus, and it is the rarest leukocyte.
The monocyte is an agranulocyte with a kidney-shaped nucleus. It has no visible granules.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A granulocyte has a two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules. Which cell is it?
options: The neutrophil
The eosinophil
The basophil
The lymphocyte
questions.why: A two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules are the two features that identify an eosinophil on a smear. Eosinophils attack parasites and help moderate allergic reactions.
notes: The neutrophil has fine pale granules and a nucleus with three to five lobes.
Correct. A bilobed nucleus and red-orange granules mark the eosinophil.
The basophil has large dark purple granules that hide its nucleus.
The lymphocyte is an agranulocyte with a large round nucleus and no visible granules.
questions.answerText: The eosinophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: On a blood smear, which statement correctly distinguishes a lymphocyte from a monocyte?
options: Lymphocyte has a three to five lobed nucleus; monocyte has a two-lobed nucleus
Lymphocyte has visible granules; monocyte has none
Lymphocyte is larger with a kidney-shaped nucleus; monocyte has a round nucleus
Lymphocyte has a round nucleus; monocyte is larger with a kidney-shaped one
questions.why: Both cells are agranulocytes, so granules cannot tell them apart. The lymphocyte has a round nucleus that fills almost the whole cell, leaving only a thin rim of cytoplasm. The monocyte is the largest leukocyte and has more cytoplasm around an indented, kidney-shaped nucleus.
notes: These nuclear shapes belong to the neutrophil and the eosinophil. Neither fits a lymphocyte or a monocyte.
Neither cell has visible granules, since both are agranulocytes. Granules separate granulocytes from agranulocytes, not these two cells.
This swaps the two cells. The monocyte is the larger cell with the kidney-shaped nucleus.
Correct. Nucleus shape and cell size separate the two agranulocytes.
questions.answerText: Lymphocyte has a round nucleus; monocyte is larger with a kidney-shaped one

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is a platelet, in structural terms?
options: A type of granulocyte
An immature red cell
A complete nucleated cell
A fragment of a megakaryocyte
questions.why: A platelet is a small piece of cytoplasm wrapped in membrane that has broken off a megakaryocyte, a giant cell in red bone marrow. It has no nucleus, so it is a cell fragment rather than a whole cell. Platelets gather at a vessel injury to form a plug and help build a clot.
notes: Granulocytes are leukocytes with lobed nuclei and visible granules, such as neutrophils. Platelets are fragments, not leukocytes.
An immature red cell in the blood is a reticulocyte, which still has ribosome remnants.
Complete nucleated cells in blood are the leukocytes. Platelets lack a nucleus.
Correct. Platelets are pieces of megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
questions.answerText: A fragment of a megakaryocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is another name for a platelet?
options: A leukocyte
A thrombocyte
An erythrocyte
A megakaryocyte
questions.why: Platelets are also called thrombocytes, from thrombo, meaning clot. The name reflects their job, since platelets gather at a vessel injury, form a plug, and help the clotting proteins build a clot. Despite the cyte ending, a thrombocyte is a cell fragment, not a whole cell.
notes: A leukocyte is a white blood cell, a complete nucleated cell that defends the body.
Correct. Thrombocyte is the other name for a platelet.
An erythrocyte is a red blood cell, the oxygen carrier. Pick it for the most numerous formed element.
A megakaryocyte is the giant marrow cell that breaks apart to form platelets. It is the parent cell, not the platelet itself.
questions.answerText: A thrombocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the approximate diameter of a platelet?
options: About 2 to 4 um
About 7.5 um
About 50 um
About 10 to 12 um
questions.why: Platelets are tiny, about 2 to 4 micrometers (um) across, much smaller than the 7.5 um erythrocyte. On a smear they look like small purple specks scattered between the red cells. Their small size fits the fact that they are fragments of a larger cell.
notes: Correct. Platelets are the smallest formed elements.
About 7.5 um is the diameter of an erythrocyte. Platelets are much smaller than red cells.
About 50 um is larger than any circulating blood cell. Students who pick it confuse the platelet with the giant megakaryocyte that produces it.
About 10 to 12 um is roughly the size of a neutrophil, which is larger than a red cell.
questions.answerText: About 2 to 4 um

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the normal platelet count in blood?
options: About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
About 4 to 6 million per microliter
About 20,000 to 40,000 per microliter
About 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter
questions.why: A normal platelet count is about 150,000 to 400,000 platelets per microliter of blood. Platelets are intermediate in number, fewer than red cells but more than white cells. A count well below the normal range is called thrombocytopenia and raises the risk of bleeding.
notes: Correct. Platelets are intermediate in number among the formed elements.
This is roughly the normal red cell count. Erythrocytes are by far the most numerous formed element.
A count this low is well below normal. It would be thrombocytopenia, with a high risk of bleeding.
This is roughly the normal white cell count. Leukocytes are the least numerous formed element.
questions.answerText: About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the normal total white blood cell count?
options: About 4 to 6 million per microliter
About 40,000 to 110,000 per microliter
About 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter
About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
questions.why: A normal total leukocyte count is roughly 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter of blood, with slight differences between labs. Leukocytes are the least numerous formed element. A count well above this range can point toward infection or leukemia, and a count well below it is leukopenia.
notes: This is roughly the normal red cell count. Erythrocytes are by far the most numerous formed element.
This is ten times the normal range. A count this high would point toward a serious problem such as leukemia.
Correct. Leukocytes are the least numerous formed element.
This is the normal platelet count. Platelets outnumber white cells.
questions.answerText: About 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A white cell has a lobed nucleus almost hidden by large dark granules of histamine and heparin, and it is the rarest leukocyte. Which cell is it?
options: The eosinophil
The monocyte
The basophil
The neutrophil
questions.why: Each clue fits the basophil. Its large, dark granules contain histamine and heparin and cover much of its lobed nucleus, and it makes up less than 1 percent of leukocytes. Its job is to release histamine and other mediators during inflammation.
notes: The eosinophil has coarse red-orange granules and a clearly visible two-lobed nucleus.
The monocyte is an agranulocyte with a kidney-shaped nucleus and no visible granules.
Correct. Dark histamine granules and rarity identify the basophil.
The neutrophil has fine pale granules and is the most numerous leukocyte.
questions.answerText: The basophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A leukocyte is the largest of the five, is an agranulocyte with a kidney-shaped nucleus, and matures into a macrophage. Which cell is it?
options: The lymphocyte
The neutrophil
The monocyte
The eosinophil
questions.why: Each clue points to the monocyte. It is the largest leukocyte, has no visible granules, and has an indented, kidney-shaped nucleus. After it leaves the blood and enters the tissues, it matures into a macrophage that engulfs debris and pathogens.
notes: The lymphocyte is also an agranulocyte, but it is smaller and has a round nucleus. Activated B lymphocytes become plasma cells, not macrophages.
The neutrophil is a granulocyte with a three to five lobed nucleus. It does not become a macrophage.
Correct. Size, nucleus shape, and the macrophage fate identify the monocyte.
The eosinophil is a granulocyte with a two-lobed nucleus and red-orange granules.
questions.answerText: The monocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A formed element is a small membrane-bound fragment about 2 to 4 um across, with no nucleus, that breaks off a megakaryocyte. What is it?
options: A platelet
An erythrocyte
A reticulocyte
A neutrophil
questions.why: Each clue points to the platelet. It is a small fragment of megakaryocyte cytoplasm, about 2 to 4 um across, with no nucleus. Platelets gather at a vessel injury, form a plug, and help the clotting proteins build a clot.
notes: Correct. A small, nucleus-free fragment of a megakaryocyte is a platelet.
An erythrocyte is a whole biconcave cell about 7.5 um across, packed with hemoglobin. Pick it for a question about the oxygen-carrying cell.
A reticulocyte is an immature red cell with ribosome remnants. It forms in the red cell line, not from a megakaryocyte.
A neutrophil is a complete cell with a lobed nucleus and fine pale granules. It is not a fragment.
questions.answerText: A platelet

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: When the five leukocytes are listed from most to least numerous, which one falls in the middle position?
options: The monocyte
The lymphocyte
The neutrophil
The eosinophil
questions.why: The order from most to least numerous is neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, remembered as Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. The third of five is the middle position, and that is the monocyte. Monkeys sits in the middle of the mnemonic.
notes: Correct. Monocytes are third of five.
Lymphocytes are second in the order, just ahead of monocytes.
Neutrophils are first, the most numerous leukocyte.
Eosinophils are fourth in the order, just after monocytes.
questions.answerText: The monocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Lymphocytes are the main cells of lymphatic tissue. How is a lymphocyte classified as a blood cell?
options: A granular white blood cell
A red blood cell
An agranular white blood cell
A platelet
questions.why: Lymphocytes are leukocytes, or white blood cells, and they belong to the agranular group because their cytoplasm lacks visible granules on a stained smear. On a slide a lymphocyte shows a large, round nucleus that fills most of the cell, with only a thin rim of cytoplasm. Monocytes are the other agranular white blood cell.
notes: Granular white blood cells are the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, which show stained granules in their cytoplasm. Pick this for a question about one of those three.
Red blood cells carry oxygen, have no nucleus, and look like biconcave discs. Choose this for a question about erythrocytes, not cells of lymphatic tissue.
Correct. A lymphocyte is an agranular white blood cell.
Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood clot, not whole cells with a nucleus. They fit a question about clotting.
questions.answerText: An agranular white blood cell

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which formed element is also called the red blood cell?
options: The megakaryocyte
The erythrocyte
The platelet
The leukocyte
questions.why: Erythrocyte is the formal name for a red blood cell, from the Greek erythro, meaning red, and cyte, meaning cell. Erythrocytes are by far the most numerous formed elements, and their job is to carry oxygen bound to hemoglobin. Learning these word parts helps with the other formed elements too: leuko means white.
notes: A megakaryocyte is a giant cell in red bone marrow whose cytoplasm breaks apart into platelets, and it is not found circulating as a formed element. It would be the answer for where platelets come from.
Correct. The erythrocyte is the red blood cell.
Platelets, also called thrombocytes, are small cell fragments that help with clotting. Choose platelets for a question about plugging a damaged vessel.
Leukocyte means white cell, so leukocytes are the white blood cells that defend the body. Pick the leukocyte for a question about the formed elements that fight infection.
questions.answerText: The erythrocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the shape of a mature erythrocyte?
options: A flat plate
A branching cell
A biconcave disc
A sphere
questions.why: A mature erythrocyte is a biconcave disc, a round disc that is thinner in the center and thicker at the rim, pinched in on both sides. This shape gives about 30 percent more surface area than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds gas exchange. Its flexible membrane also lets the disc fold to squeeze through narrow capillaries.
notes: A flat plate is a misreading of the word platelet, which is a small cell fragment, not a red cell shape. Pick platelets for a question about the formed element named for its small plate-like form.
A branching cell describes cells such as neurons or dendritic cells with long processes. Choose a branching shape for a question about the shape of a neuron.
Correct. A mature erythrocyte is a biconcave disc.

A sphere would give less surface area for gas exchange than a biconcave disc of the same volume. Students who pick it are picturing a generic round cell rather than the pinched-in disc seen on a smear.
questions.answerText: A biconcave disc

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which formed elements are the white blood cells?
options: Leukocytes
Platelets
Erythrocytes
Megakaryocytes
questions.why: Leukocytes are the white blood cells, from leuko, meaning white. They are the only formed elements that are complete cells with a nucleus, and they defend the body against infection. There are five types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.
notes: Correct. Leukocytes are the white blood cells.
Platelets are cell fragments that help with clotting, not white blood cells. Choose them for a question about plugging a damaged vessel.
Erythrocytes are the red blood cells that carry oxygen. Pick them for a question about the most numerous formed element.
Megakaryocytes are giant cells in red bone marrow that produce platelets, and they do not circulate as white blood cells. They would be the answer for the source of platelets.
questions.answerText: Leukocytes

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the most numerous and the first responder to infection?
options: The basophil
The lymphocyte
The neutrophil
The monocyte
questions.why: Neutrophils are the most numerous leukocytes and the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection, where they engulf and digest bacteria. On a smear they have a nucleus with three to five lobes and fine pale granules. The memory aid Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas lists the leukocytes from most to least numerous, starting with neutrophils.
notes: Basophils are the rarest leukocytes and release histamine in inflammation. Choose the basophil for a question about the least numerous leukocyte.

Lymphocytes are the second most numerous leukocytes and form the core of specific immunity, including T cells and B cells. Pick the lymphocyte for a question about the leukocyte with a large round nucleus filling most of the cell.
Correct. The neutrophil is the most numerous leukocyte and the first responder.
Monocytes are the largest leukocytes and mature into macrophages in the tissues. They would be the answer for the leukocyte with a kidney-shaped nucleus.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the rarest and releases histamine during inflammation?
options: The neutrophil
The basophil
The eosinophil
The lymphocyte
questions.why: Basophils are the least numerous leukocytes. Their large dark granules contain histamine and other chemicals that they release during inflammation, and the granules are so dense they often hide the lobed nucleus. On a smear, those dark purple granules are the quickest way to spot one.
notes: Neutrophils are the most numerous leukocytes, the opposite end of the count from basophils. Choose the neutrophil for a question about the first responder to bacterial infection.
Correct. The basophil is the rarest leukocyte and releases histamine.

Eosinophils have a two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules, and they attack parasites and moderate allergic reactions. Pick the eosinophil for a question about defense against parasitic worms.
Lymphocytes are agranulocytes with a large round nucleus, and they include the T and B cells. They would be the answer for the core cells of specific immunity.
questions.answerText: The basophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the largest and matures into a macrophage after leaving the blood?
options: The neutrophil
The lymphocyte
The eosinophil
The monocyte
questions.why: Monocytes are the largest leukocytes, with a kidney-shaped or horseshoe-shaped nucleus and no visible granules. They leave the blood and enter the tissues, where they mature into macrophages that engulf debris and pathogens. Macrophages in lymph nodes, the spleen, and other organs all trace back to monocytes.
notes: Neutrophils also engulf bacteria, but they stay neutrophils and do not become macrophages. Pick the neutrophil for a question about the most numerous leukocyte with a three-to-five-lobed nucleus.
Lymphocytes are agranulocytes like monocytes, but most are small, with a round nucleus filling nearly the whole cell. They would be the answer for the leukocytes that include T cells and B cells.
Eosinophils have a two-lobed nucleus and red-orange granules and fight parasites. Choose the eosinophil for a question about defense against parasites.
Correct. The monocyte is the largest leukocyte and becomes a macrophage.
questions.answerText: The monocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A lab report uses the term thrombocyte. Which formed element is being named?
options: The platelet
The leukocyte
The erythrocyte
The hemocytoblast
questions.why: Thrombocyte is another name for a platelet, from thrombo, meaning clot. Platelets are small fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm that gather and stick at a vessel injury, forming a plug and helping build a clot. A low platelet count is called thrombocytopenia, which uses the same root.
notes: Correct. A thrombocyte is a platelet.
The leukocyte is the white blood cell, named from leuko, meaning white. Choose it for a question about the formed elements that fight infection.
The erythrocyte is the red blood cell, named from erythro, meaning red. Pick it for a question about the oxygen-carrying cell.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell in red bone marrow that gives rise to every formed element, and it does not circulate. It would be the answer for the cell all blood cells come from.
questions.answerText: The platelet

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which formed element is a small cell fragment rather than a complete cell?
options: The leukocyte
The platelet
The erythrocyte
The reticulocyte
questions.why: A platelet is a small, membrane-bound fragment of cytoplasm that breaks off a megakaryocyte, a giant cell in the red bone marrow. Because it is a fragment, it has no nucleus and is not a whole cell. Platelets gather at a vessel injury, stick together to form a plug, and help the clotting proteins build a clot.
notes: A leukocyte is a complete cell with a nucleus. Choose it for a question about which formed elements are the only complete, nucleated cells.
Correct. The platelet is a cell fragment, not a complete cell.
An erythrocyte has no nucleus as a mature cell, but it is a whole cell that ejected its nucleus during development, not a fragment. Pick the erythrocyte for a question about the oxygen-carrying cell.
A reticulocyte is a whole immature red blood cell that still holds ribosome remnants. It would be the answer for the stage just before a mature erythrocyte.
questions.answerText: The platelet

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which leukocytes are agranulocytes, lacking visible cytoplasmic granules?
options: Eosinophils and basophils
Neutrophils and eosinophils
Neutrophils and basophils
Lymphocytes and monocytes
questions.why: Leukocytes are sorted into two groups by whether granules show in their cytoplasm on a stained smear. Granulocytes, which are neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, have visible granules and lobed nuclei. Agranulocytes, which are lymphocytes and monocytes, lack visible granules and have a single round or kidney-shaped nucleus.
notes: Eosinophils and basophils are both granulocytes with very visible granules, red-orange and dark purple. Choose this pair for a question about leukocytes involved in allergic reactions.
Neutrophils and eosinophils are both granulocytes, with fine pale granules and coarse red-orange granules. Pick this pair for a question about granulocytes with lobed nuclei.
Neutrophils and basophils are both granulocytes, the most numerous and the rarest leukocytes. This pair would answer a question about the two ends of the differential count.
Correct. Lymphocytes and monocytes are the agranulocytes.
questions.answerText: Lymphocytes and monocytes

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which statement explains why a mature erythrocyte has no nucleus?
options: Its nucleus breaks into three to five small lobes
It ejects its nucleus to make room for hemoglobin
It never had a nucleus at any stage of development
Its nucleus is hidden under dense dark granules
questions.why: Developing red blood cells in the marrow do have a nucleus, but they eject it, along with most organelles, before entering circulation. This leaves more space inside the cell for hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein. The trade-off is that a mature red cell cannot divide or repair itself, so it lasts only about 120 days.
notes: A nucleus with three to five lobes describes a neutrophil. Choose this for a question about identifying the most numerous leukocyte.
Correct. The erythrocyte ejects its nucleus to make room for hemoglobin.
Developing red cells start out with a nucleus and lose it during maturation. This choice confuses a red cell with a platelet, which is a fragment and never had its own nucleus.
A nucleus hidden by dense dark granules describes a basophil. Pick this for a question about identifying a basophil on a smear.
questions.answerText: It ejects its nucleus to make room for hemoglobin

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: About how long does an erythrocyte circulate before it is broken down?
options: About 1 year
About 120 days
About 7 days
About 10 years
questions.why: An erythrocyte lives about 120 days, roughly four months. Because it has no nucleus, it cannot make new proteins to repair itself, so its membrane gradually wears out. Worn cells are then removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver, and the iron is saved for reuse.
notes: A year is about three times too long for a red cell. Without a nucleus to repair itself, an erythrocyte wears out in about four months.
Correct. An erythrocyte lives about 120 days.
About a week is far too short for a red cell. Students who pick this may be thinking of platelets, which last only about 5 to 9 days.
Ten years is far beyond any red cell's life. This choice confuses circulating blood cells with long-lived cells such as some memory lymphocytes or bone cells.
questions.answerText: About 120 days

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Mature red blood cells are biconcave discs, pinched in on both sides. How does this shape help them do their job?
options: It adds surface area and lets the cell bend through capillaries
It makes the cell rigid so it keeps its shape in narrow vessels
It leaves room for a large nucleus in the center of the cell
It gives the cell a sticky surface that helps form clots
questions.why: A biconcave disc has about 30 percent more surface area than a sphere of the same volume, so oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out faster. The thin, flexible disc can also fold to squeeze single file through capillaries narrower than itself. Both features serve the red cell's job of picking up and delivering gases in every tissue.
notes: Correct. The shape adds surface area and flexibility.
Rigidity is a problem, not a benefit, for red cells. A rigid, curved red cell is what happens in sickle cell disease, so pick rigidity for a question about why sickled cells block capillaries.
A mature red cell has no nucleus at all, and the pinched-in center is just thin cytoplasm. This choice comes from assuming every cell keeps a nucleus; leukocytes are the formed elements that do.
Sticking together at an injury is the job of platelets, not red cells. Choose a sticky surface for a question about how platelets form a plug.
questions.answerText: It adds surface area and lets the cell bend through capillaries

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: White blood cells can squeeze out of blood vessels into the tissues, while red blood cells stay inside. Why is this ability essential to white cells?
options: To form clots on the outside of damaged vessels
To deliver oxygen to tissues outside the vessels
To return excess tissue fluid to the lymphatics
To reach infection in the tissues and fight it there
questions.why: Most infections and injuries happen in the tissues, not inside the bloodstream. Leukocytes use the blood mainly as a highway, then squeeze between the loosely joined cells of the postcapillary venules to reach the problem. Monocytes, for example, leave the blood and mature into macrophages that engulf debris and pathogens in the tissues.
notes: Plugging and clotting a damaged vessel is the job of platelets and the clotting proteins. Choose this for a question about what platelets do at a cut.
Oxygen delivery is the job of red cells, and they do it from inside the capillaries as oxygen diffuses out. Pick oxygen delivery for a question about erythrocytes.
Returning excess tissue fluid is the job of lymphatic capillaries, which take up interstitial fluid as lymph. This would be the answer for a question about the lymphatic system's fluid balance role.
Correct. White cells leave the blood to fight infection where it is.
questions.answerText: To reach infection in the tissues and fight it there

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Platelets gather within seconds at the site of a cut. What do they do there?
options: They engulf bacteria that entered the wound
They stick together to plug the damaged vessel
They secrete antibodies against invading microbes
They carry oxygen to the injured tissue
questions.why: Platelets gather and stick at a vessel injury, piling up to form a plug that slows bleeding almost at once. They also help the clotting proteins, such as fibrinogen, build a firmer clot around the plug. Because they are small, numerous fragments already circulating everywhere, they can respond faster than any process that needs new cells.
notes: Engulfing bacteria is the job of phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages. Choose this for a question about the first responder to bacterial infection.
Correct. Platelets stick together to plug the vessel and support clotting.
Secreting antibodies is the job of plasma cells, which come from B cells. This would be the answer for a question about humoral immunity.
Carrying oxygen is the job of erythrocytes, using hemoglobin. Pick this for a question about red blood cells.
questions.answerText: They stick together to plug the damaged vessel

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria. Why is this helpful for a cell whose job is carrying oxygen?
options: It lets the cell make more hemoglobin as it travels
It lets the cell store oxygen in its membrane
It means the cell does not use up the oxygen it carries
It lets the cell divide faster in the bloodstream
questions.why: Mitochondria are the organelles that use oxygen to make most of a cell's energy. A mature red cell has ejected its mitochondria, along with its nucleus, so it makes its small energy supply without oxygen. As a result, nearly all the oxygen it picks up in the lungs is delivered to the tissues instead of being consumed on the way.
notes: A mature red cell cannot make new hemoglobin, because it has no nucleus or ribosomes left to build proteins. Its hemoglobin is all made while it is still developing in the marrow.
Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin inside the cell, not stored in the membrane. This choice misplaces the oxygen; the membrane's important trait is its flexibility.
Correct. Without mitochondria, the red cell does not burn the oxygen it carries.
A mature red cell cannot divide at all, because it has no nucleus. New red cells come only from stem cells in red bone marrow.
questions.answerText: It means the cell does not use up the oxygen it carries

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which list names the three formed elements of blood?
options: Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and plasma
Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and fibrinogen
Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
Erythrocytes, platelets, and megakaryocytes
questions.why: The formed elements are the cells and cell fragments suspended in plasma. They are erythrocytes (red blood cells), leukocytes (white blood cells), and platelets (thrombocytes, which are cell fragments). Together they make up about 45 percent of blood volume.
notes: Plasma is the liquid matrix that the formed elements float in, not a formed element itself. Pick plasma if the question asked for the other main component of blood.
Fibrinogen is a plasma protein dissolved in the fluid, not a cell or cell fragment. It would be the answer if the question asked which plasma protein forms a clot.
Correct. Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets are the three formed elements.
Megakaryocytes are giant cells that stay in the red bone marrow and break apart to make platelets. Choose them if the question asked which cell produces platelets.
questions.answerText: Erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: What is the shape of a mature erythrocyte, and what does it lack?
options: A small cell fragment with no nucleus or disc shape
A biconcave disc with no nucleus
A biconcave disc with one central nucleus
A round cell with a multi-lobed nucleus
questions.why: A mature erythrocyte is a biconcave disc, thinner in the center than at the rim, which gives it more surface area for gas exchange and lets it fold through narrow capillaries. It ejects its nucleus and most organelles as it matures, leaving more room for hemoglobin. On a smear the thin center shows up as a pale central area.
notes: This describes a platelet, a fragment of megakaryocyte cytoplasm. It would be the answer if the question asked which formed element is not a whole cell.
Correct. The erythrocyte is a biconcave disc without a nucleus.

The shape is right, but a mature red cell has no nucleus at all. Students pick this when they assume every blood cell must have one; the pale center on a smear is the thin middle of the disc, not a nucleus.
A round cell with a multi-lobed nucleus is a neutrophil, the most numerous leukocyte. Pick this description if the question asked how to recognize a neutrophil on a smear.
questions.answerText: A biconcave disc with no nucleus

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which list names the five types of leukocytes?
options: Neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and basophil
Neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and reticulocyte
Neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and platelet
Neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and megakaryocyte
questions.why: The five leukocytes are neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are granulocytes with visible granules, while lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes. The phrase Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas lists them from most to least numerous.
notes: Correct. These are the five leukocytes.
A reticulocyte is an immature erythrocyte that still holds ribosome remnants. Pick it if the question asked which young red cell is released from the marrow.
A platelet is a fragment of cytoplasm, a separate formed element, not a leukocyte. It would be the answer if the question asked which formed element helps form clots.
A megakaryocyte is the giant marrow cell that fragments into platelets; it does not circulate as a white blood cell. Choose it if the question asked where platelets come from.
questions.answerText: Neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, and basophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: Which formed element is the most numerous in blood, and which is the least numerous?
options: Erythrocytes most, platelets least
Leukocytes most, erythrocytes least
Platelets most, leukocytes least
Erythrocytes most, leukocytes least
questions.why: Erythrocytes are by far the most numerous formed element, which is why the red cell layer fills nearly half of a spun tube. Leukocytes are the least numerous, and together with the platelets they form only the thin buffy coat. Platelets fall in between: far fewer than red cells, but more numerous than white cells.
notes: Erythrocytes are the most numerous, but platelets outnumber leukocytes. Students pick this because platelets are the smallest, mixing up size with number.
This reverses the true order. Leukocytes are the rarest formed element, which is why a spun tube shows only a thin pale buffy coat.
Platelets are intermediate in number, far fewer than erythrocytes. This choice confuses the smallest formed element with the most common one.
Correct. Erythrocytes are most numerous and leukocytes least numerous.
questions.answerText: Erythrocytes most, leukocytes least

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: A platelet is counted as a formed element even though it is not a whole cell. What is a platelet, and what does it do?
options: A whole cell with a kidney-shaped nucleus that becomes a macrophage
A fragment of megakaryocyte cytoplasm that helps form a clot
A plasma protein that turns into fibrin threads in a clot
An immature erythrocyte that still holds ribosome remnants
questions.why: A platelet, also called a thrombocyte, is a small membrane-bound fragment of cytoplasm, not a complete cell. Platelets form when a megakaryocyte, a giant cell in the red bone marrow, breaks its cytoplasm into thousands of pieces. At a vessel injury, platelets gather and stick to form a plug and help the clotting proteins build a clot.
notes: This describes a monocyte, the largest leukocyte, which leaves the blood to become a macrophage. It would be the answer if the question asked which white cell has a kidney-shaped nucleus.
Correct. A platelet is a piece of megakaryocyte cytoplasm that acts in clotting.
This describes fibrinogen, a plasma protein dissolved in the fluid rather than a formed element. Choose it if the question asked which protein forms the threads of a clot.
This describes a reticulocyte, a young red blood cell. Pick it if the question asked which immature cell makes up about 1 to 2 percent of circulating red cells.
questions.answerText: A fragment of megakaryocyte cytoplasm that helps form a clot

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: On a blood smear, which leukocyte has a nucleus with three to five lobes and fine, pale granules, and is the most numerous white blood cell?
options: The monocyte
The basophil
The eosinophil
The neutrophil
questions.why: The neutrophil is identified by its multi-lobed nucleus, usually three to five lobes, and its fine, pale granules. It is the most numerous leukocyte and the first responder to infection, engulfing and digesting bacteria. On a smear you should look at the shape of the nucleus first and the granules second.
notes: The monocyte is the largest leukocyte, with a kidney-shaped nucleus and no visible granules. Choose it if the smear showed a large cell with a curved, kidney-shaped nucleus.
The basophil has a nucleus hidden by large, dark granules and is the rarest leukocyte. It would be the answer if the granules were so dark you could barely see the nucleus.
The eosinophil has a two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules. Pick it if the smear showed a bilobed nucleus with bright red-orange granules.
Correct. A multi-lobed nucleus with fine pale granules marks a neutrophil.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: On a blood smear, one white cell has a two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules, and the cell beside it has a kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant pale cytoplasm. Which cells are they, and which group does each belong to?
options: Neutrophil, a granulocyte; lymphocyte, an agranulocyte
Eosinophil, a granulocyte; monocyte, an agranulocyte
Eosinophil, an agranulocyte; monocyte, a granulocyte
Basophil, a granulocyte; monocyte, an agranulocyte
questions.why: A two-lobed nucleus with coarse red-orange granules identifies the eosinophil, one of the three granulocytes. A kidney-shaped nucleus in a large cell with abundant pale cytoplasm identifies the monocyte, one of the two agranulocytes. Reading the nucleus first and the granules second sorts nearly every white cell on a smear.
notes: A neutrophil has three to five lobes and fine pale granules, and a lymphocyte has a large round nucleus that fills almost the whole cell. Neither matches these nuclei.
Correct. The two-lobed cell is an eosinophil, a granulocyte, and the kidney-shaped one is a monocyte, an agranulocyte.
The cells are named correctly, but the groups are swapped. Eosinophils have visible granules, so they are granulocytes, and monocytes lack them.
A basophil's lobed nucleus is hidden by large dark granules, not shown clearly beside red-orange ones. The monocyte half of this answer is right.
questions.answerText: Eosinophil, a granulocyte; monocyte, an agranulocyte

questions.topic: Formed elements: blood cells and platelets
questions.q: In a differential count, a white cell with a large round nucleus that fills almost the whole cell keeps turning up. Which cell is it, and where does it rank among the five by number?
options: A monocyte, the second most numerous
A lymphocyte, the second most numerous
A lymphocyte, the most numerous
A neutrophil, the most numerous
questions.why: A large round nucleus filling almost the whole cell, with only a thin rim of cytoplasm, is a lymphocyte. From most to least numerous the leukocytes run neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, so the lymphocyte ranks second.
notes: A monocyte has a kidney-shaped nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm, and it ranks third in number.
Correct. The round-nucleus cell is a lymphocyte, second only to the neutrophil.
The cell is a lymphocyte, but neutrophils are the most numerous leukocyte. Lymphocytes come second.
Neutrophils are the most numerous, but their nucleus has three to five lobes, not one large round nucleus.
questions.answerText: A lymphocyte, the second most numerous

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The fossa ovalis is an oval depression in the wall between the two atria. Why does it exist in the adult heart?
options: It is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, a fetal vessel that let blood bypass the lungs
It is the site of the SA node, where each heartbeat begins
It is the opening where the coronary sinus drains into the right atrium
It is the remnant of the foramen ovale, a fetal opening that let blood bypass the lungs
questions.why: Before birth the lungs are filled with fluid and not yet used for breathing, so the fetus has shortcuts that send blood around them. The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass straight from the right atrium to the left atrium. After birth it normally closes, leaving a shallow oval dip called the fossa ovalis.
notes: The ductus arteriosus is a different fetal shunt, a short vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Its adult remnant is the ligamentum arteriosum, so pick it for that ligament.
The SA node sits in the wall of the right atrium near where the superior vena cava enters, not in the fossa ovalis. Pick it for the pacemaker of the heart.
The coronary sinus does open into the right atrium, but its opening is a hole for draining blood, not a sealed depression. Pick it for where the cardiac veins empty.
Correct. The fossa ovalis marks the closed foramen ovale, a fetal shortcut between the atria.
questions.answerText: It is the remnant of the foramen ovale, a fetal opening that let blood bypass the lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is an anastomosis?
options: A flap of the tunica intima inside a vein
A junction of two vessels that offers an alternate route
Two capillary beds connected in series by a vein
A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance
questions.why: An anastomosis is a place where two vessels join, so blood has more than one path to reach a tissue. If one route is blocked, blood can still arrive through the other. Anastomoses are common around joints and in the brain, and an arteriovenous anastomosis is a special type that connects an artery directly to a vein.
notes: A flap of the tunica intima inside a vein is a venous valve. Choose it if the question asked what keeps blood from flowing backward in a limb vein.
Correct. An anastomosis is a junction of vessels that offers an alternate route.

Two capillary beds connected in series by a vein describes a portal system, such as the hepatic portal system. Pick it if the question asked about blood passing through two capillary beds before returning to the heart.
A ring of smooth muscle at a capillary entrance is a precapillary sphincter. It would be the answer if the question asked what opens or closes a capillary's entrance.
questions.answerText: A junction of two vessels that offers an alternate route

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which circuit runs from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side?
options: The hepatic portal circulation
The coronary circulation
The systemic circuit
The pulmonary circuit
questions.why: The pulmonary circuit carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the lungs. There the blood picks up oxygen and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Pulmonary refers to the lungs, which is the destination of this short loop.
notes: The hepatic portal circulation carries blood from the digestive organs through the liver before it returns to the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked how absorbed nutrients reach the liver.
The coronary circulation supplies the heart wall itself through the coronary arteries and cardiac veins. Choose it if the question asked which vessels feed the heart muscle.
The systemic circuit runs from the left side of the heart out to the body and back to the right side. Pick it if the question asked which circuit supplies the body's tissues.
Correct. The pulmonary circuit links the right heart, the lungs and the left heart.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary circuit

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A vessel structure is a direct connection from an artery to a vein that bypasses the capillaries. Which structure is it?
options: A venous valve
A capillary bed
An arteriovenous anastomosis
A portal system
questions.why: An arteriovenous anastomosis connects an artery directly to a vein, so blood skips the capillaries entirely. The name tells you its ends: arterio for the artery and venous for the vein, joined by an anastomosis, a junction between vessels. Because no capillaries are involved, no exchange happens along this route.
notes: A venous valve is a flap of the tunica intima that keeps blood from flowing backward in a vein. Choose it if the question asked what prevents backflow in limb veins.
A capillary bed is the network of capillaries where exchange happens, which this connection bypasses. It would be the answer if the question asked what one arteriole feeds.
Correct. An arteriovenous anastomosis links an artery straight to a vein.
A portal system passes blood through two capillary beds in series, the opposite of skipping capillaries. Pick it if the question described the route through the liver from the digestive organs.
questions.answerText: An arteriovenous anastomosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Blood passes through two capillary beds in series before returning to the heart, as in the route through the liver. What is this arrangement called?
options: An anastomosis
The pulmonary circuit
A portal system
A vascular shunt
questions.why: In a portal system, blood flows through one capillary bed, collects into a portal vein, and then passes through a second capillary bed before heading back to the heart. The hepatic portal system carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver this way, so the liver can process absorbed nutrients first. Most routes have only one capillary bed between an artery and a vein.
notes: An anastomosis is a junction where two vessels join to give blood an alternate route. Pick it if the question asked what keeps blood flowing to a tissue when one path is blocked.

The pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right heart to the lungs and back to the left heart, through one set of capillaries. It would be the answer if the question asked which circuit brings blood to the lungs.
Correct. Two capillary beds in series define a portal system.
A vascular shunt lets blood bypass the capillaries of a bed, which is the opposite of adding a second bed. Choose it if the question described blood skipping exchange when it is not needed.
questions.answerText: A portal system

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In the hepatic portal system, in what order does blood pass these structures after leaving the arteries of the digestive organs?
options: Liver sinusoids, hepatic portal vein, digestive organ capillaries, hepatic veins
Digestive organ capillaries, hepatic portal vein, liver sinusoids, hepatic veins
Digestive organ capillaries, hepatic veins, liver sinusoids, hepatic portal vein
Hepatic portal vein, digestive organ capillaries, liver sinusoids, hepatic veins
questions.why: A portal system has two capillary beds in series. Blood first passes through the capillaries of the digestive organs, where it picks up absorbed nutrients, then drains into the hepatic portal vein. That vein carries it to the second capillary bed, the sinusoids of the liver, and the hepatic veins finally return it toward the heart through the inferior vena cava.
notes: This order puts the liver first, but blood reaches the liver only after collecting nutrients in the digestive organs. Starting at the liver would skip the reason the portal system exists.
Correct. Digestive capillaries, portal vein, liver sinusoids, then hepatic veins.
This order swaps the hepatic portal vein and the hepatic veins. The portal vein brings blood into the liver, while the hepatic veins carry it out toward the heart.
This order starts with the portal vein, but a portal vein always connects two capillary beds, so a capillary bed has to come before it.
questions.answerText: Digestive organ capillaries, hepatic portal vein, liver sinusoids, hepatic veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which choice correctly matches each circuit or arrangement to its route: the pulmonary circuit, the systemic circuit, and the hepatic portal system?
options: Pulmonary to the body, systemic to the lungs, hepatic portal to the heart
Pulmonary to the lungs, systemic to the body, hepatic portal through the liver
Pulmonary to the liver, systemic to the lungs, hepatic portal to the body
Pulmonary to the body, systemic to the liver, hepatic portal to the lungs
questions.why: The pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right heart to the lungs and back to the left heart. The systemic circuit carries blood from the left heart out to the body and back to the right heart. The hepatic portal system is a detour within the systemic circuit that routes blood from the digestive organs through the liver.
notes: This swaps the pulmonary and systemic circuits. Pulmonary refers to the lungs, so the pulmonary circuit goes to the lungs, and the hepatic portal system does not go to the heart.
Correct. Lungs, body, and liver, in that order.
This sends the pulmonary circuit to the liver and the systemic circuit to the lungs. Only the hepatic portal system involves the liver, and only the pulmonary circuit involves the lungs.
This match gets all three routes wrong. The word pulmonary, meaning lungs, and the word hepatic, meaning liver, give away the correct matches.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary to the lungs, systemic to the body, hepatic portal through the liver

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which portal system links the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary?
options: The hepatic portal system
The hypophyseal portal system
The coronary circulation
The pulmonary circuit
questions.why: The hypophyseal portal system connects capillaries in the hypothalamus to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary. Like any portal system, it passes blood through two capillary beds in series before the blood returns to the heart. Hypophysis is another name for the pituitary gland, which gives the system its name.
notes: The hepatic portal system routes blood from the digestive organs through the liver. Pick it if the question asked which portal system carries absorbed nutrients to the liver.
Correct. The hypophyseal portal system links the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.
The coronary circulation supplies the heart wall through the coronary arteries and cardiac veins. Choose it if the question asked which vessels feed the heart muscle.

The pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right heart to the lungs and back, with one capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which circuit brings blood to the lungs for oxygen.
questions.answerText: The hypophyseal portal system

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a place where two vessels join, giving blood an alternate route if one path is blocked, called?
options: A fenestration
An anastomosis
A precapillary sphincter
A portal system
questions.why: An anastomosis is a junction where two vessels join, so a tissue can be reached by more than one path. If one vessel is blocked, blood can still arrive through the other. This backup arrangement protects tissues such as those around joints and in the brain.
notes: A fenestration is a small pore in the endothelium of some capillaries. Choose it if the question asked about the windows in kidney or intestinal capillaries.
Correct. An anastomosis is a junction that gives blood an alternate route.
A precapillary sphincter is a smooth muscle ring that opens or closes a capillary's entrance. It would be the answer if the question asked what controls blood entering a single capillary.

A portal system passes blood through two capillary beds in series, as in the route through the liver. Pick it if the question asked about blood crossing two capillary beds before returning to the heart.
questions.answerText: An anastomosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Atherosclerotic plaque slowly narrows the lumen of an artery. Why does this narrowing threaten the tissue downstream?
options: The plaque weakens the wall until it balloons outward and bursts
Less blood gets through, so the tissue receives less oxygen
The plaque blocks the veins that drain the tissue
The narrowing speeds flow and floods the tissue with oxygen
questions.why: In atherosclerosis, fatty plaque builds up in the artery wall and bulges inward, narrowing the lumen. Less blood can pass through a narrower channel, so the tissue supplied by that artery receives less oxygen. A clot can also form on the rough plaque and suddenly block the vessel, which is how plaques in the coronary arteries cause heart attacks.
notes: A wall that weakens and balloons outward describes an aneurysm, not a narrowing plaque. Pick it if the question asked about a bulge in an artery wall that can rupture.
Correct. Reduced flow through the narrowed lumen starves the tissue of oxygen.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of arteries, not veins, and the problem is reduced delivery into the tissue. A blocked drainage vein would fit a question about varicose veins or a venous clot.
A narrower channel lets less blood through, not more. This choice confuses a faster jet through a tight spot with more total delivery to the tissue.
questions.answerText: Less blood gets through, so the tissue receives less oxygen

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In atherosclerosis, what is an atheroma?
options: A clot of fibrin and platelets sitting in the vessel lumen
A balloon-like outward bulge of a weakened artery wall
A deposit of fatty material, cells, and debris within the artery wall
A twisted, swollen superficial vein with failed valves
questions.why: An atheroma, also called a plaque, is the lesion that defines atherosclerosis. It is a deposit of fatty material, cells, and debris that builds up inside the artery wall itself, starting where the smooth inner lining (the tunica intima) has been injured. As it grows it bulges into the lumen, the open channel of the vessel, and narrows it.
notes: A clot of fibrin and platelets in the lumen is a thrombus. A thrombus can form on top of a roughened plaque, but it sits in the channel rather than in the wall, so choose it if the question asks what a thrombus is.
A balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall is an aneurysm. The wall pushes outward rather than filling with plaque, so pick this if the question asks what defines an aneurysm.
Correct. An atheroma is the fatty plaque that builds up within the artery wall.
A twisted, swollen superficial vein with failed valves is a varicose vein. That is a disorder of a vein, not of an artery wall, so it fits a question about pooled blood in the legs.
questions.answerText: A deposit of fatty material, cells, and debris within the artery wall

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which structural change defines an aneurysm?
options: A clot lodged in an artery of the lung
A balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall
Inflammation along the wall of a vein
A fatty plaque growing within an artery wall
questions.why: An aneurysm is a weak spot in an artery wall that balloons outward. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so a weakened area stretches and bulges instead of holding its shape. Aneurysms are most common in the aorta and in the arteries of the brain, and the danger is that the thin bulge can rupture.
notes: A clot lodged in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism. It blocks the vessel rather than stretching its wall, so it fits a question about a clot that traveled from a deep leg vein.
Correct. An aneurysm is an outward, balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall.
Inflammation along a vein wall is phlebitis, which causes pain, redness, and tenderness along the vein. Choose it for a question about an inflamed vein, not a weakened artery.
A fatty plaque growing within the wall is an atheroma, the lesion of atherosclerosis. It bulges inward and narrows the lumen, so pick it if the question asks what defines atherosclerosis.
questions.answerText: A balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, where does the umbilical vein carry blood?
options: From the fetus to the placenta
From the placenta to the fetus
From the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
From the right atrium to the left atrium
questions.why: The placenta is where fetal blood picks up oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood, so the vessel leaving the placenta carries the richest blood in the fetus. That vessel is the single umbilical vein, which runs through the umbilical cord to the fetus. It is called a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, even though its blood is oxygen-rich.
notes: Blood traveling from the fetus back to the placenta is carried by the two umbilical arteries, and it is oxygen-poor. Pick this direction if the question asks about the umbilical arteries.
Correct. The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.
Blood moving from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta uses the ductus arteriosus, a short vessel that lets blood skip the lungs. It fits a question about that shunt, not the umbilical vein.
Blood passing from the right atrium to the left atrium uses the foramen ovale, an opening in the interatrial septum. Choose this if the question asks what the foramen ovale does.
questions.answerText: From the placenta to the fetus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In which part of the fetal heart is the foramen ovale located?
options: The interatrial septum
The interventricular septum
The wall of the inferior vena cava
The wall of the pulmonary trunk
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum, the wall between the right and left atria. It lets blood pass directly from the right atrium to the left atrium, so that blood skips the right ventricle and the lungs, which are not yet used for gas exchange. After birth it closes and leaves a shallow depression called the fossa ovalis.
notes: Correct. The foramen ovale is an opening in the wall between the two atria.

The interventricular septum separates the right and left ventricles and has no normal fetal opening. Pick it if the question asks which wall divides the ventricles; a hole there is a defect, not a fetal shunt.
The inferior vena cava is where the ductus venosus empties after carrying blood through the liver. It fits a question about the end of the ductus venosus, not the foramen ovale.
The pulmonary trunk is where the ductus arteriosus begins, carrying blood from the trunk into the aorta. Choose it for a question about where the ductus arteriosus attaches.
questions.answerText: The interatrial septum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which description matches varicose veins?
options: Arteries narrowed by fatty plaque
Superficial veins twisted and swollen from failed valves
Deep veins blocked by a stationary blood clot
Veins that are inflamed, red, and tender
questions.why: Veins carry blood under low pressure and rely on one-way valves to keep it moving toward the heart. When the valves in superficial veins fail, blood flows backward and pools, so the veins stretch, twist, and bulge visibly under the skin. This is most common in the legs, where blood has to climb against gravity.
notes: Arteries narrowed by fatty plaque describe atherosclerosis, a disease of the high-pressure side of the circulation. Choose it for a question about plaque in an artery wall.
Correct. Varicose veins are superficial veins that twist and swell when their valves fail.
A clot blocking a deep vein is a deep vein thrombosis, usually in the leg. Pick it if the question asks about a clot that could break free and travel to the lungs.
Inflamed, red, tender veins describe phlebitis. It is an inflammation of the vein wall rather than pooled blood from failed valves, so it fits a question about an inflamed vein.
questions.answerText: Superficial veins twisted and swollen from failed valves

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ductus arteriosus is a short fetal vessel that connects which two structures?
options: The pulmonary veins and the left atrium
The right atrium and the left atrium
The umbilical vein and the inferior vena cava
The pulmonary trunk and the aorta
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus runs from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Blood that enters the right ventricle and is pumped into the pulmonary trunk can cross straight into the aorta instead of going to the collapsed fetal lungs. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, a short cord between the same two vessels.
notes: The pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium in both the fetus and the adult. That is a normal connection rather than a shunt, so it fits a question about where blood returning from the lungs enters the heart.
The right and left atria are connected by the foramen ovale, an opening in the interatrial septum. Choose this pair for a question about the foramen ovale.
The umbilical vein is connected to the inferior vena cava by the ductus venosus, the shunt that lets blood bypass the liver. Pick this pair if the question asks what the ductus venosus links.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
questions.answerText: The pulmonary trunk and the aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a thrombus?
options: A clot fragment that breaks free and lodges elsewhere
A fatty deposit within the artery wall
A balloon-like bulge in an artery wall
A clot that forms in place and can block the vessel
questions.why: A thrombus is a blood clot that forms and stays attached inside a vessel. In atherosclerosis, the roughened surface of a plaque is a common place for one to form, and it can suddenly block the vessel. If a piece breaks off and travels, that moving clot is then called an embolus.
notes: A clot fragment that breaks free and travels is an embolus. Pick it if the question asks what forms when part of a thrombus breaks loose, as in a pulmonary embolism.
A fatty deposit within the wall is an atheroma, or plaque. A thrombus can form on top of a plaque, but the plaque itself is not a clot, so choose this for a question about atheromas.
A balloon-like bulge in an artery wall is an aneurysm, a weakening of the wall rather than a clot. Pick it if the question asks what an aneurysm is.
Correct. A thrombus is a clot that forms in place inside a vessel and can block it.
questions.answerText: A clot that forms in place and can block the vessel

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How many umbilical arteries does a fetus have, and what do they carry?
options: Two arteries carrying oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
One artery carrying oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta
Two arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta
One artery carrying oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
questions.why: The umbilical cord normally holds two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. The arteries carry blood away from the fetal heart, so they take oxygen-poor, waste-laden blood from the fetus to the placenta, where it is refreshed. The single umbilical vein brings the oxygen-rich blood back.
notes: This mixes the correct number with the umbilical vein's direction and oxygen content. Students choose it when they assume arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood, but the name follows direction from the heart, not oxygen level.
This has the right direction and oxygen content but the wrong number. The single vessel in the cord is the vein; there are two umbilical arteries.
Correct. Two umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta.
One vessel carrying oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus describes the umbilical vein, not the arteries. Pick it if the question asks about the umbilical vein.
questions.answerText: Two arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the general term for the stiffening and thickening of artery walls?
options: Arteriosclerosis
Atherosclerosis
Phlebitis
Hypertension
questions.why: Arteriosclerosis is the broad term for artery walls that become thicker and stiffer, so they lose their ability to stretch and recoil. The name means hardening of the arteries. Atherosclerosis is its most common form, the one caused specifically by fatty plaque in the wall.
notes: Correct. Arteriosclerosis is the general term for stiff, thickened artery walls.
Atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis, the specific one caused by fatty plaque in the wall. Pick it if the question asks about plaque buildup rather than the general term.
Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, causing pain, redness, and tenderness along the vein. Choose it for a question about an inflamed vein, not stiff arteries.
Hypertension is chronically high pressure within the arteries. It strains vessel walls over time, but it names the pressure, not the wall change, so pick it for a question about high blood pressure.
questions.answerText: Arteriosclerosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a deep vein thrombosis?
options: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg
A twisted, swollen vein near the skin
A clot lodged in an artery of the lung
Inflammation along the wall of a vein
questions.why: A deep vein thrombosis is a clot that forms in one of the deep veins, most often in the leg, where blood moves slowly under low pressure. It matters because of where the clot can go. If it breaks free, it rides the normal venous return to the right side of the heart and on to the lungs.
notes: Correct. A deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg.
A twisted, swollen vein near the skin is a varicose vein, caused by failed valves rather than a clot. Choose it for a question about superficial veins that bulge visibly.
A clot lodged in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism, often the result of a deep vein thrombosis that broke loose. Pick it if the question asks where a traveling leg clot ends up.
Inflammation along a vein wall is phlebitis. It can accompany a clot, but it names the inflammation, so pick it for a question about a red, tender vein.
questions.answerText: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: An atherosclerotic plaque starts with injury to which layer of the artery wall?
options: The tunica intima, the endothelial lining
The valves that line the inside of the vessel
The tunica externa, the outer connective tissue layer
The tunica media, the smooth muscle layer
questions.why: Atherosclerosis begins with damage to the endothelium, the smooth simple squamous lining of the tunica intima. That lining is the layer in direct contact with the blood. Once it is injured, fatty material, cells, and debris collect in the wall at that spot and the plaque begins to grow inward toward the lumen.
notes: Correct. The injury that starts a plaque is in the tunica intima, the endothelial lining.
Arteries away from the heart do not have valves; one-way valves are a feature of veins. This fits a question about what fails in varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency.
The tunica externa is the outer connective tissue layer that anchors the vessel to nearby structures. Choose it for a question about the outermost tunic, not the one touching the blood.
The tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, the thickest layer in arteries. Pick it if the question asks which layer lets an artery constrict and dilate.
questions.answerText: The tunica intima, the endothelial lining

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A fetus routes blood around its collapsed lungs. Which two shunts together accomplish this lung bypass?
options: The umbilical vein and the ductus venosus
The foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus
The ductus venosus and the foramen ovale
The ductus venosus and the ductus arteriosus
questions.why: Two shunts keep most blood away from the fetal lungs. The foramen ovale lets blood cross from the right atrium to the left atrium before it ever reaches the right ventricle. Blood that does enter the pulmonary trunk can cross through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta. The third shunt, the ductus venosus, bypasses the liver, not the lungs.
notes: The umbilical vein and the ductus venosus are the route oxygen-rich blood takes from the placenta through the liver toward the inferior vena cava. Pick this pair for a question about the path from the placenta, not the lung bypass.
Correct. The foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus together route blood around the lungs.
This pair includes the ductus venosus, which bypasses the liver. Only the foramen ovale in this pair skips the lungs, so it would fit a question about one liver shunt and one lung shunt.
This pair also includes the ductus venosus, the liver bypass. Students pick it when they remember that both names start with ductus and assume both skip the lungs.
questions.answerText: The foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ductus venosus passes through which fetal organ, letting most blood bypass it?
options: The kidneys
The spleen
The lungs
The liver
questions.why: The ductus venosus is a shunt that runs through the fetal liver. Oxygen-rich blood arriving in the umbilical vein can flow through it straight toward the inferior vena cava instead of passing through the liver tissue. The placenta handles much of the work the liver will do after birth, so this detour costs the fetus very little.
notes: The kidneys have no fetal bypass shunt. This choice comes from guessing an abdominal organ; the fetal shunts only skip the liver and the lungs.
The spleen has no fetal shunt. Students may choose it because it sits near the liver in the upper abdomen, but the ductus venosus is named for its connection to the venous system through the liver.
The lungs are bypassed by two other shunts, the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. Pick the lungs if the question asks what organ those two shunts route blood around.
Correct. The ductus venosus carries blood through the liver so most of it skips the liver tissue.
questions.answerText: The liver

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Atherosclerosis narrowing the coronary arteries produces which named disorder?
options: Peripheral artery disease
Stroke
Hypertension
Coronary artery disease
questions.why: The coronary arteries supply the myocardium, the muscle of the heart wall. When atherosclerotic plaque narrows them, the disorder is called coronary artery disease. It can starve the heart muscle of oxygen and lead to a heart attack. The same plaque in other arteries gets a different name based on location.
notes: Peripheral artery disease is the same plaque narrowing the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs. Pick it if the narrowed vessel is a leg artery.
A stroke is a loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery. Choose it when the narrowed or ruptured vessel supplies the brain.
Hypertension is chronically high pressure within the arteries. It names a pressure problem, not narrowing of one vessel, so pick it for a question about high blood pressure.
Correct. Plaque narrowing the coronary arteries is coronary artery disease.
questions.answerText: Coronary artery disease

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Hemorrhoids are best classified as which kind of vessel disorder?
options: Atherosclerosis of the rectal arteries
Varicose veins of the rectal and anal region
An aneurysm of a rectal artery
Inflammation of a rectal vein
questions.why: Hemorrhoids are varicose veins in the rectal and anal region. Just as in the legs, the veins there stretch, swell, and bulge when blood pools in them. They are a venous disorder, which fits the general pattern that vein problems involve pooled blood under low pressure.
notes: Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque narrowing an artery. Students choose it because hemorrhoids involve swollen vessels, but hemorrhoids are veins, and plaque is an artery problem.
Correct. Hemorrhoids are varicose veins of the rectal and anal region.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall, most common in the aorta and brain arteries. Pick it for a question about a weakened artery that could rupture.
Inflammation of a vein is phlebitis. Choose it if the question describes pain, redness, and tenderness along a vein rather than swollen, pooled veins.
questions.answerText: Varicose veins of the rectal and anal region

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot from a leg vein breaks free and lodges in an artery of the lung. What is this disorder called?
options: Phlebitis
Pulmonary embolism
Chronic venous insufficiency
Deep vein thrombosis
questions.why: An embolus is a clot or fragment that travels through the bloodstream and lodges somewhere else. When that clot ends up in an artery of the lung, the disorder is a pulmonary embolism. It is a life-threatening emergency because it blocks blood flow to part of the lung, and the clot most often comes from a deep vein of the leg.
notes: Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, with pain, redness, and tenderness along it. Choose it for a question about an inflamed vein, not a traveling clot.
Correct. A traveling clot that lodges in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism.
Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term failure of the leg vein valves, causing swelling and skin changes in the lower leg. It fits a question about persistent leg swelling from failed valves.
A deep vein thrombosis is the clot while it is still in the deep leg vein. Pick it if the question describes where the clot first forms rather than where it lodges.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary embolism

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: After birth the umbilical vein closes. Which adult structure does it leave behind?
options: The ligamentum arteriosum
The fossa ovalis
The ligamentum venosum
The ligamentum teres
questions.why: Once the cord is cut, the umbilical vein no longer carries blood and closes into a fibrous cord called the ligamentum teres, also known as the round ligament of the liver. It runs from the umbilicus to the liver in the free edge of the falciform ligament, following the path the vein once took.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, a short cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Choose it for a question about that shunt.
The fossa ovalis is the shallow depression left in the interatrial septum when the foramen ovale closes. It fits a question about the foramen ovale.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, the shunt that ran through the liver. Pick it if the question asks what the ductus venosus becomes.
Correct. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver.
questions.answerText: The ligamentum teres

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Peripheral artery disease is the narrowing of arteries in which region?
options: The coronary arteries of the heart wall
The aorta and its main trunk
The limbs, usually the legs
The arteries of the brain
questions.why: Peripheral artery disease is atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries that supply the limbs, most often the legs. The word peripheral points to vessels away from the body's core. Because the leg muscles are starved of blood, the typical sign is pain in the legs during walking that eases with rest.
notes: Narrowing of the coronary arteries is coronary artery disease, which can starve the heart wall. Choose it for a question about plaque in the vessels of the heart.
The aorta is a common site for an aneurysm, a balloon-like bulge of a weakened wall. Pick it if the question asks where aneurysms commonly form.
Correct. Peripheral artery disease narrows the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs.
Narrowing of the brain arteries can lead to a stroke, a loss of blood supply to part of the brain. Pick the brain arteries if the question asks where narrowing causes a stroke.
questions.answerText: The limbs, usually the legs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The foramen ovale closes after birth. Which adult landmark does it leave?
options: The ligamentum arteriosum
The medial umbilical ligaments
The ligamentum venosum
The fossa ovalis
questions.why: When the lungs inflate at birth, pressure in the left atrium rises and the flap over the foramen ovale is pressed shut. The sealed opening leaves a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum called the fossa ovalis, visible from the right atrium. It is the one fetal remnant that is a depression rather than a cord, because the foramen ovale was a hole, not a vessel.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, a short cord between the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Choose it for a question about that shunt.
