The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the two umbilical arteries, paired cords on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. They fit a question about the umbilical arteries.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Pick it for a question about the liver shunt.
Correct. The foramen ovale leaves the fossa ovalis, a shallow depression in the interatrial septum.
questions.answerText: The fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which adult structures are the remnants of the paired umbilical arteries?
options: The ligamentum arteriosum
The ligamentum teres
The medial umbilical ligaments
The ligamentum venosum
questions.why: After birth the two umbilical arteries no longer carry blood to the placenta, and most of each one closes into a fibrous cord. These cords are the medial umbilical ligaments, which run up the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus. There are two of them because there were two arteries.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus. Students choose it because the word arteriosum sounds like artery, but it lies between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, not in the abdominal wall.
The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the single umbilical vein, running to the liver in the falciform ligament. Pick it for a question about the umbilical vein.
Correct. The two umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, a cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Choose it for a question about the liver shunt.
questions.answerText: The medial umbilical ligaments

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: As an atheroma grows in an artery wall, how does it change the vessel's channel?
options: It blocks the valves that keep arterial blood moving one way
It stiffens only the outer layer and leaves the lumen unchanged
It bulges outward and widens the lumen
It bulges inward and narrows the lumen
questions.why: An atheroma builds up within the wall just beneath the endothelium, so as it grows it pushes into the lumen, the open channel where blood flows. A narrower lumen carries less blood to the tissue downstream. That reduced flow is what links atherosclerosis to coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral artery disease.
notes: Arteries away from the heart have no valves; one-way valves belong to veins. This fits a question about what fails in varicose veins.
Plaque forms in the inner part of the wall, not the outer layer, and it does change the lumen. Students choose this when they picture arteriosclerosis as only a hardened outer coat.
An outward bulge describes an aneurysm, where a weakened wall balloons outward. Pick it if the question asks how an aneurysm changes the vessel's shape.
Correct. A growing plaque bulges inward and narrows the lumen.
questions.answerText: It bulges inward and narrows the lumen

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Chronic venous insufficiency results from the long-term failure of which structures?
options: The walls of the aorta and large arteries
The valves of the leg veins
The interatrial septum of the heart
The endothelial lining of the coronary arteries
questions.why: Leg veins depend on one-way valves to keep blood moving up toward the heart against gravity. In chronic venous insufficiency those valves fail over a long period, so blood pools in the lower leg. The result is persistent swelling and skin changes around the ankles and lower leg.
notes: Weakness or stiffening of the aorta and large artery walls fits an aneurysm or arteriosclerosis. Choose it for a question about the high-pressure arterial side.
Correct. Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term failure of the leg vein valves.
The interatrial septum holds the fossa ovalis; if the foramen ovale fails to seal, the result is a patent foramen ovale. It fits a question about that fetal opening.
Injury to the endothelial lining of the coronary arteries is where atherosclerosis begins, leading to coronary artery disease. Pick it for a question about how coronary plaque starts.
questions.answerText: The valves of the leg veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ductus arteriosus closes after birth. Which adult cord does it become?
options: The ligamentum venosum
The ligamentum teres
The fossa ovalis
The ligamentum arteriosum
questions.why: Once the lungs take over gas exchange, blood no longer needs to skip them, and the ductus arteriosus closes. It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, a short fibrous cord that still connects the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch. The remnant keeps a piece of the original name, which makes the pair easy to match.
notes: The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, the liver shunt. Pick it when the question names the ductus venosus.
The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein, running to the liver in the falciform ligament. Choose it for a question about the umbilical vein.
The fossa ovalis is the depression left by the foramen ovale in the interatrial septum. It fits a question about the opening between the atria.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
questions.answerText: The ligamentum arteriosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: On a diagram of a fetal heart, a short vessel runs from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Which shunt is it?
options: The ductus venosus
The foramen ovale
The umbilical vein
The ductus arteriosus
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is the short vessel linking the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Because fetal lung tissue resists blood flow, most blood pumped into the pulmonary trunk takes this shortcut into the aorta and out to the body. Its location between two great arteries is the clue to its name.
notes: The ductus venosus is a shunt inside the liver, carrying blood from the umbilical vein toward the inferior vena cava. Pick it for a diagram of the fetal liver.
The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum, not a vessel. Choose it if the diagram shows a hole between the two atria.
The umbilical vein runs in the umbilical cord, bringing oxygen-rich blood from the placenta. It fits a question about the vessel arriving from the placenta.
Correct. The vessel between the pulmonary trunk and aorta is the ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: The ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A fetal shunt is described as an opening that lets blood pass directly from one atrium to the other. Which shunt is it?
options: The ductus venosus
An umbilical artery
The ductus arteriosus
The foramen ovale
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum. Blood entering the right atrium from the inferior vena cava can pass straight through it into the left atrium, skipping the right ventricle and the lungs. The word foramen means opening, which fits a hole in a wall rather than a vessel.
notes: The ductus venosus is a vessel that carries blood through the liver toward the inferior vena cava. Choose it for a description of the liver bypass.
An umbilical artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta in the umbilical cord. It fits a description of a vessel in the cord leading away from the fetus.
The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, not an opening between the atria. Pick it if the description names those two great arteries.
Correct. The opening between the two atria is the foramen ovale.
questions.answerText: The foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: An adult liver shows a fibrous cord on its inferior surface that ends at the inferior vena cava. Which fetal shunt did this cord once carry blood as?
options: An umbilical artery
The ductus arteriosus
The umbilical vein
The ductus venosus
questions.why: The ductus venosus carried blood through the fetal liver toward the inferior vena cava. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver that still reaches the inferior vena cava. Its position on the liver and its connection to the vena cava both point back to the ductus venosus.
notes: An umbilical artery leaves a medial umbilical ligament on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. Choose it for a cord on the abdominal wall, not the liver.
The ductus arteriosus leaves the ligamentum arteriosum, a cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta in the thorax. Pick it if the cord were found above the heart.

The umbilical vein leaves the ligamentum teres, which reaches the liver from the umbilicus in the free edge of the falciform ligament. Pick it for a cord running from the umbilicus to the liver, not one ending at the vena cava.
Correct. The cord on the inferior liver surface ending at the inferior vena cava is the ligamentum venosum, left by the ductus venosus.
questions.answerText: The ductus venosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A vessel disorder is described as a balloon-like outpouching commonly found in the aorta or brain arteries. Which disorder is it?
options: Hypertension
A stroke
Atherosclerosis
An aneurysm
questions.why: An aneurysm is a weakened area of an artery wall that bulges outward like a balloon. The aorta and the arteries of the brain are the most common sites. The high pressure in arteries keeps stretching the thin bulge, which is why an aneurysm can rupture and bleed.
notes: Hypertension is chronically high pressure within the arteries. It can stress a weak wall, but it is not a bulge itself, so choose it for a description of high blood pressure.
A stroke is a loss of blood supply to part of the brain. A ruptured brain aneurysm can cause one, but the stroke is the result, so pick it for a description of brain tissue losing its supply.
Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque that bulges inward and narrows an artery. Pick it if the description is of a narrowed vessel rather than an outward bulge.
Correct. A balloon-like outpouching of an artery wall is an aneurysm.
questions.answerText: An aneurysm

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A vessel disorder is described as a loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery. Which disorder is it?
options: A stroke
Coronary artery disease
Phlebitis
Peripheral artery disease
questions.why: A stroke happens when part of the brain loses its blood supply, either because an artery is blocked, often by atherosclerosis or a clot, or because it bursts. Brain tissue begins to die within minutes without blood. It is one of the main diseases that atherosclerosis causes, named for its location in the brain.
notes: Correct. Loss of blood supply to part of the brain is a stroke.
Coronary artery disease is narrowing of the coronary arteries that supply the heart wall. Pick it if the description involves the heart muscle rather than the brain.
Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, causing pain, redness, and tenderness. It fits a description of an inflamed vein, not an artery supplying the brain.
Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs. Choose it for a description of leg pain during walking.
questions.answerText: A stroke

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a cadaver, paired fibrous cords run up the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus. Which fetal vessels are these the remnants of?
options: The ductus venosus
The umbilical vein
The umbilical arteries
The ductus arteriosus
questions.why: The two umbilical arteries carried oxygen-poor blood from the fetus out through the umbilicus to the placenta. After birth they close into the medial umbilical ligaments, which run up the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus. The fact that the cords are paired matches the two arteries.
notes: The ductus venosus leaves the ligamentum venosum on the inferior surface of the liver. Choose it if the cord were found on the liver.
The umbilical vein is single, and its remnant, the ligamentum teres, runs from the umbilicus up to the liver. Pick it for a single cord heading to the liver, not a pair on the abdominal wall.
Correct. Paired cords on the inner anterior abdominal wall are the medial umbilical ligaments, left by the umbilical arteries.
The ductus arteriosus leaves the ligamentum arteriosum in the thorax, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. It fits a cord found above the heart.
questions.answerText: The umbilical arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A fetal shunt is described as passing through the liver and emptying toward the inferior vena cava. Which shunt is it?
options: The foramen ovale
The ductus venosus
The ductus arteriosus
An umbilical artery
questions.why: The ductus venosus carries oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein through the liver and on toward the inferior vena cava, so most of it skips the liver tissue. From the vena cava the blood enters the right atrium. Its name, venosus, reflects that it links two parts of the venous system.
notes: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum, letting blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. Pick it for a description of a hole between the atria.
Correct. The shunt through the liver toward the inferior vena cava is the ductus venosus.
The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, letting blood skip the lungs. Choose it for a description involving the great arteries.
An umbilical artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta. It fits a description of a vessel in the umbilical cord leading away from the fetus.
questions.answerText: The ductus venosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient's superficial leg veins have become twisted and bulge visibly under the skin. Which disorder is this?
options: An aortic aneurysm
Varicose veins
Deep vein thrombosis
Pulmonary embolism
questions.why: Varicose veins are superficial veins whose one-way valves have failed. Blood flows backward and pools, so the veins stretch, twist, and bulge where they can be seen under the skin. The legs are the usual site because blood there has to return to the heart against gravity.
notes: An aortic aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge of a weakened aortic wall. It is an artery disorder deep in the trunk, so it fits a description of a bulging aorta, not leg veins.
Correct. Twisted, bulging superficial veins in the legs are varicose veins.
A deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg. It is hidden in the deep tissues rather than visible under the skin, so pick it if the description is a clot in a deep vein.
A pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in an artery of the lung, often one that traveled from a deep leg vein. Choose it for a description of a clot blocking blood flow to the lung.
questions.answerText: Varicose veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In an adult heart, the interatrial septum shows a shallow oval depression where an opening once sat. Which fetal structure left this depression?
options: The umbilical vein
The ductus venosus
The ductus arteriosus
The foramen ovale
questions.why: The shallow depression is the fossa ovalis, and it marks where the foramen ovale used to be. In the fetus the foramen ovale was an opening in the interatrial septum that let blood pass from the right atrium to the left. Because it was a hole rather than a vessel, it closes into a depression instead of a fibrous cord.
notes: The umbilical vein leaves the ligamentum teres, which runs from the umbilicus to the liver. It fits a cord in the falciform ligament, not a mark inside the heart.
The ductus venosus leaves the ligamentum venosum on the inferior surface of the liver. Choose it if the remnant were found on the liver.
The ductus arteriosus leaves a cord, the ligamentum arteriosum, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the remnant were a cord outside the heart near the great arteries.
Correct. The fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum is the remnant of the foramen ovale.
questions.answerText: The foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A vessel runs in the umbilical cord and carries oxygen-rich blood toward the fetus. Which vessel is it?
options: The ductus venosus
The ductus arteriosus
An umbilical artery
The umbilical vein
questions.why: The umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta, where it has picked up oxygen and nutrients, through the cord to the fetus. It is a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, even though its blood is oxygen-rich. This is a good reminder that vessels are named by direction of flow, not by oxygen content.
notes: The ductus venosus continues on from the umbilical vein inside the fetal liver, not in the cord. Choose it for a vessel that carries blood through the liver toward the inferior vena cava.
The ductus arteriosus lies in the fetal chest between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. It fits a description of the lung bypass, not a vessel in the cord.
An umbilical artery also runs in the cord, but it carries oxygen-poor blood away from the fetus to the placenta. Pick it if the question describes flow toward the placenta.
Correct. The umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta toward the fetus.
questions.answerText: The umbilical vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a newborn, the ductus arteriosus fails to seal, leaving an abnormal connection between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. What is this condition called?
options: Patent ductus arteriosus
Ligamentum arteriosum
Patent foramen ovale
Aortic aneurysm
questions.why: Patent means open. When the ductus arteriosus stays open after birth instead of closing, the condition is named patent ductus arteriosus, after the fetal structure that failed to seal. It leaves an abnormal connection between the pulmonary and systemic sides of the circulation.
notes: Correct. A ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth is a patent ductus arteriosus.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the normal cord left when the ductus arteriosus closes as expected. Choose it for a question about the healthy adult remnant, not a failure to close.
A patent foramen ovale is the opening in the interatrial septum that fails to seal. Pick it if the open connection is between the two atria.
An aortic aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge of a weakened aortic wall. It fits a question about a weakened artery that could rupture, not a fetal shunt that stayed open.
questions.answerText: Patent ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A disorder is described as fatty plaques building up within artery walls, beginning at an injured inner lining. Which disorder is it?
options: Atherosclerosis
Varicose veins
An aneurysm
Phlebitis
questions.why: Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the endothelium of the tunica intima, the smooth inner lining of an artery. Fatty material, cells, and debris then collect in the wall at that spot as a plaque, or atheroma, which bulges into the lumen and narrows it. It is the root of most heart attacks and strokes.
notes: Correct. Fatty plaque building up in artery walls is atherosclerosis.
Varicose veins are superficial veins twisted and swollen from failed valves. They fit a description of pooled blood in veins, not plaque in arteries.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall. Pick it if the description is an outward bulge rather than a plaque.
Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, causing pain, redness, and tenderness. Choose it for a description of an inflamed vein, not plaque in an artery.
questions.answerText: Atherosclerosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Trace oxygen-rich fetal blood from the placenta to the heart. Which sequence is correct?
options: Umbilical vein, then foramen ovale, then ductus venosus, then left atrium
Ductus venosus, then umbilical vein, then aorta, then right atrium
Umbilical artery, then ductus arteriosus, then aorta, then right atrium
Umbilical vein, then ductus venosus, then inferior vena cava, then right atrium
questions.why: Oxygen-rich blood leaves the placenta in the umbilical vein and travels through the cord to the fetus. At the liver, most of it takes the ductus venosus, which skips the liver tissue and empties toward the inferior vena cava. The inferior vena cava then delivers it to the right atrium, where much of it will cross the foramen ovale.
notes: The foramen ovale is inside the heart, between the atria, so blood cannot reach it before passing through the liver shunt. This order would fit only if the foramen ovale came after the right atrium.
This reverses the first two steps. Blood must arrive in the umbilical vein before it can enter the ductus venosus, and it reaches the heart by the inferior vena cava, not the aorta.

Umbilical arteries carry blood away from the fetus to the placenta, and the ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. This sequence runs in the wrong direction and mixes in the lung bypass.
Correct. Umbilical vein, ductus venosus, inferior vena cava, then right atrium.
questions.answerText: Umbilical vein, then ductus venosus, then inferior vena cava, then right atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Match each fetal structure to its adult remnant: umbilical vein, ductus venosus, foramen ovale. Which set of pairings is fully correct?
options: Umbilical vein to ligamentum teres, ductus venosus to ligamentum venosum, foramen ovale to fossa ovalis
Umbilical vein to ligamentum venosum, ductus venosus to fossa ovalis, foramen ovale to ligamentum teres
Umbilical vein to ligamentum arteriosum, ductus venosus to fossa ovalis, foramen ovale to ligamentum teres
Umbilical vein to fossa ovalis, ductus venosus to ligamentum teres, foramen ovale to ligamentum venosum
questions.why: Each remnant keeps a clue to the original. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the foramen ovale, an oval hole, becomes the fossa ovalis, an oval depression. The umbilical vein is the odd name out: it becomes the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver, running in the free edge of the falciform ligament.
notes: Correct. Ligamentum teres, ligamentum venosum, and fossa ovalis, in that order.
This set swaps the umbilical vein and ductus venosus remnants. The ligamentum venosum belongs to the ductus venosus, since the names match, and the fossa ovalis belongs to the foramen ovale.
This set uses the ligamentum arteriosum, which is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, a structure not in this list. Choose that pairing only for a question that includes the ductus arteriosus.

This set sends the umbilical vein to the fossa ovalis, but the fossa ovalis is a depression in the heart left by the foramen ovale. The umbilical vein becomes a cord running to the liver, the ligamentum teres.
questions.answerText: Umbilical vein to ligamentum teres, ductus venosus to ligamentum venosum, foramen ovale to fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot breaks free from a deep leg vein and lodges in a lung artery. Which route does it follow?
options: Deep leg vein, then thoracic duct, then right atrium and right ventricle, then pulmonary artery
Deep leg vein, then inferior vena cava, then right atrium and right ventricle, then pulmonary artery
Deep leg vein, then aorta, then left atrium and left ventricle, then pulmonary artery
Deep leg vein, then pulmonary vein, then left atrium and left ventricle, then pulmonary artery
questions.why: A loose clot simply follows the normal venous return. Leg veins drain upward into the inferior vena cava, which empties into the right atrium. The right ventricle then pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk and arteries, and the first vessels narrow enough to trap the clot are in the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism.
notes: The thoracic duct is a lymphatic vessel that returns lymph to the left subclavian vein, not a path for venous blood from the leg. Pick it for a question about where lymph from the leg drains.
Correct. The clot travels up the inferior vena cava, through the right heart, and into a pulmonary artery.

The aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle to the body, so venous blood from the leg never enters it directly. This route would fit an arterial clot heading out to the body, not one returning from a vein.
Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium. A clot can only reach them after passing through the lungs, so this order runs the pulmonary circuit backward.
questions.answerText: Deep leg vein, then inferior vena cava, then right atrium and right ventricle, then pulmonary artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Oxygen-rich blood travels from the placenta into the fetal body. In what order does it reach the three fetal shunts: ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus?
options: Foramen ovale first, then ductus venosus, then ductus arteriosus
Ductus venosus first, then ductus arteriosus, then foramen ovale
Ductus arteriosus first, then foramen ovale, then ductus venosus
Ductus venosus first, then foramen ovale, then ductus arteriosus
questions.why: Blood from the placenta arrives in the umbilical vein and meets the ductus venosus first, at the liver. It then flows through the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, where the foramen ovale lets much of it cross to the left atrium. Blood that instead enters the right ventricle is pumped into the pulmonary trunk, where the ductus arteriosus carries it on to the aorta.
notes: The foramen ovale is in the heart, so blood cannot reach it before passing the liver. The ductus venosus has to come first because the umbilical vein reaches the liver before the heart.

This puts the ductus arteriosus before the foramen ovale. The atria come before the ventricle and pulmonary trunk, so blood meets the opening between the atria before the vessel between the great arteries.
This is the full reverse of the real path. It would describe blood traveling back from the great arteries toward the placenta, which is not how fetal blood flows.
Correct. Ductus venosus, then foramen ovale, then ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus first, then foramen ovale, then ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Atherosclerosis gets a different disease name depending on which artery it narrows. Match a coronary artery, a leg artery, and a brain artery to the named disorder.
options: Coronary artery to coronary artery disease, leg artery to stroke, brain artery to peripheral artery disease
Coronary artery to peripheral artery disease, leg artery to stroke, brain artery to coronary artery disease
Coronary artery to stroke, leg artery to coronary artery disease, brain artery to peripheral artery disease
Coronary artery to coronary artery disease, leg artery to peripheral artery disease, brain artery to stroke
questions.why: The wall change is the same in every case, a fatty plaque narrowing the lumen, but the disease is named for the tissue that loses blood. Narrowed coronary arteries starve the heart wall, causing coronary artery disease. Narrowed limb arteries cause peripheral artery disease, and a blocked or burst brain artery causes a stroke.
notes: This set gets the coronary artery right but swaps the other two. Peripheral artery disease belongs to the leg, and a stroke to the brain.
This set is fully scrambled. Peripheral means away from the body's core, so peripheral artery disease belongs to the limbs, not the heart.
This set scrambles all three. Stroke always involves the brain, and coronary artery disease always involves the arteries of the heart wall.
Correct. Coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, then stroke.
questions.answerText: Coronary artery to coronary artery disease, leg artery to peripheral artery disease, brain artery to stroke

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is atherosclerosis?
options: Fatty plaque building up within artery walls
A balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall
A blood clot lodged in a deep vein of the leg
Inflammation of the wall of a vein
questions.why: Atherosclerosis is a slow, structural disease of arteries in which fatty plaques, called atheromas, build up within the wall. It begins where the endothelium of the tunica intima is injured. As plaques grow they narrow the lumen, which is why atherosclerosis underlies coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, and most strokes.
notes: Correct. Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque building up within artery walls.
A balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall is an aneurysm. Pick it if the question asks what an aneurysm is.
A clot in a deep leg vein is a deep vein thrombosis, a venous disorder. Choose it if the question asks about a clot that could travel to the lungs.
Inflammation of a vein wall is phlebitis. It fits a question about a red, tender vein, not plaque in an artery.
questions.answerText: Fatty plaque building up within artery walls

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis are related?
options: Atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis
Arteriosclerosis affects arteries, while atherosclerosis affects veins
They are two names for the same disorder of veins
Arteriosclerosis is a form of atherosclerosis found only in the coronary arteries
questions.why: Arteriosclerosis is the general term for artery walls that become stiff and thick, the broad hardening of the arteries. Atherosclerosis is one specific kind, the form caused by fatty plaque building up in the wall, and it is by far the most common. So every case of atherosclerosis is a kind of arteriosclerosis, but not the other way around.
notes: Correct. Atherosclerosis is the most common form of the broader condition, arteriosclerosis.
Both disorders affect arteries; the arter- and athero- roots do not mark artery versus vein. Venous disorders include varicose veins, phlebitis, and deep vein thrombosis.
Both terms describe arteries, not veins, and they are not exact synonyms. Students pick this because the names look so alike, but one is the category and the other is a type within it.
This reverses the relationship. Arteriosclerosis is the broad category and atherosclerosis is the specific form, and neither term is limited to the coronary arteries.
questions.answerText: Atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is phlebitis?
options: Inflammation of a vein
Failure of the valves in the leg veins
Twisted, swollen superficial veins
A clot in a deep vein of the leg
questions.why: The root phleb- means vein and the suffix -itis means inflammation, so phlebitis is inflammation of a vein. It causes pain, redness, and tenderness along the course of the vein. Like other venous disorders, it involves the low-pressure side of the circulation.
notes: Correct. Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein.
Long-term failure of the leg vein valves is chronic venous insufficiency, which causes lasting swelling of the lower leg. Choose it for a question about failed valves.
Twisted, swollen superficial veins are varicose veins, caused by valve failure and pooled blood. They fit a question about veins that bulge visibly under the skin.
A clot in a deep leg vein is a deep vein thrombosis. Inflammation can accompany a clot, but pick this if the question asks about the clot itself.
questions.answerText: Inflammation of a vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which three fetal shunts route blood around the liver and the lungs?
options: The umbilical vein, umbilical arteries, and placenta
The ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus
The umbilical vein, ductus venosus, and ductus arteriosus
The fossa ovalis, ligamentum venosum, and ligamentum arteriosum
questions.why: A shunt is a vessel or opening that routes blood around an organ. The fetus has three: the ductus venosus skips most of the liver, while the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus both route blood around the collapsed lungs. All three close after birth when the lungs and liver take over their normal work.
notes: The umbilical vessels and the placenta carry blood between the fetus and mother, but they are not shunts around an organ. Pick this set if the question asks which structures connect the fetus to the placenta.
Correct. The ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus are the three fetal shunts.
The umbilical vein is not a shunt; it brings blood from the placenta to the fetus. This set swaps it in for the foramen ovale, which is the shunt between the atria.
These are the adult remnants of the shunts after they close. Choose this set for a question about what the fetal shunts become after birth.
questions.answerText: The ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient feels pain in the calf muscles when walking that eases with rest, because narrowed arteries cannot deliver enough blood to the working muscles. Which disorder is this?
options: Phlebitis
Varicose veins
Coronary artery disease
Peripheral artery disease
questions.why: Peripheral artery disease is atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs. At rest the narrowed vessels can still keep up, but walking raises the muscles' demand for blood beyond what the narrow lumen can carry, so the muscles hurt. When the person rests, demand drops and the pain eases.
notes: Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, causing redness and tenderness along the vein. It fits a red, tender vein, not muscle pain that comes and goes with walking.
Varicose veins are twisted superficial veins from failed valves. They can make legs ache, but they are a vein problem, so choose them for visibly bulging veins rather than starved muscles.
Coronary artery disease is the same plaque narrowing the arteries of the heart wall. Pick it if the pain were in the chest from a starved myocardium.
Correct. Leg pain on walking from narrowed limb arteries is peripheral artery disease.
questions.answerText: Peripheral artery disease

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which adult remnant is a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver that reaches the inferior vena cava?
options: The fossa ovalis
The ligamentum arteriosum
The ligamentum venosum
The medial umbilical ligaments
questions.why: The ligamentum venosum is what remains of the ductus venosus, the fetal shunt that carried blood through the liver toward the inferior vena cava. After birth the shunt closes into a fibrous cord that sits on the inferior surface of the liver. The name keeps the venosum from ductus venosus, which makes the pair easy to match.
notes: The fossa ovalis is a shallow depression in the interatrial septum of the heart, left by the foramen ovale. Choose it for a question about a mark inside the heart.
The ligamentum arteriosum lies in the thorax, a short cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the question asks what the ductus arteriosus becomes.
Correct. The ligamentum venosum is the cord on the inferior surface of the liver, left by the ductus venosus.
The medial umbilical ligaments are paired cords on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall, left by the umbilical arteries. They fit a question about cords on the abdominal wall.
questions.answerText: The ligamentum venosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot forms in a deep vein of the leg, breaks free, and travels through the venous return. Where does it most likely lodge?
options: In a coronary artery of the heart wall
In an artery of the other leg
In an artery of the brain
In an artery of the lung
questions.why: A clot from a leg vein follows the normal route of venous blood. It rides up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium and right ventricle and is pumped into the pulmonary arteries. As those arteries branch and narrow in the lungs, the clot gets stuck, which is a pulmonary embolism.
notes: Coronary arteries branch from the aorta, which is on the left side of the heart. A venous clot reaches the lungs before it could ever reach the aorta, so this fits a clot that started in the left heart.
Arteries of the legs are reached from the aorta, not from the veins. A clot from a leg vein has to pass through the right heart and lungs first, so it cannot travel straight to another leg.
Brain arteries are also supplied from the aorta. A clot that blocks a brain artery causes a stroke, so pick this for a clot that began on the arterial side, such as on a plaque in a neck artery.
Correct. A loose venous clot from the leg lodges in an artery of the lung.
questions.answerText: In an artery of the lung

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: An atherosclerotic plaque narrows an artery of the leg. What is the named disorder in this location?
options: Coronary artery disease
Peripheral artery disease
Hypertension
Stroke
questions.why: Atherosclerosis takes its disease name from where it happens. When plaque narrows the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs, the disorder is peripheral artery disease. The leg muscles are starved of blood, so the classic sign is pain on walking.
notes: Coronary artery disease is plaque narrowing the arteries of the heart wall. Pick it if the narrowed artery were a coronary artery.
Correct. Plaque narrowing a leg artery is peripheral artery disease.
Hypertension is chronically high pressure within the arteries throughout the body, not narrowing of one leg artery. It fits a question about high blood pressure.
A stroke is a loss of blood supply to part of the brain. Choose it if the blocked or burst artery supplied the brain.
questions.answerText: Peripheral artery disease

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a newborn, the opening in the interatrial septum fails to seal after birth. What is this condition called?
options: Fossa ovalis
Patent foramen ovale
Ligamentum venosum
Patent ductus arteriosus
questions.why: The opening in the interatrial septum is the foramen ovale, and patent means open. When it stays open after birth, the condition is called patent foramen ovale, named for the fetal structure that failed to seal. It leaves an abnormal connection between the right and left atria.
notes: The fossa ovalis is the normal depression left when the foramen ovale closes as it should. Choose it for a question about the healthy adult remnant.
Correct. An interatrial opening that stays open is a patent foramen ovale.
The ligamentum venosum is the normal remnant of the ductus venosus on the liver. It fits a question about what the liver shunt becomes.
A patent ductus arteriosus is an open connection between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the vessel between the great arteries failed to close.
questions.answerText: Patent foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A weakened spot in the wall of the aorta balloons outward. Which disorder is this, and why is it dangerous?
options: Atherosclerosis, because it narrows the lumen
A pulmonary embolism, because it blocks a lung artery
An aneurysm, because it can rupture
Phlebitis, because the vessel wall is inflamed
questions.why: A weakened artery wall that bulges outward is an aneurysm, and the aorta is one of the most common sites. The danger is rupture: the thin, stretched bulge can burst under arterial pressure and cause severe internal bleeding. The disorder widens the vessel rather than narrowing it.
notes: Atherosclerosis narrows an artery with plaque that bulges inward. Pick it if the vessel were narrowed rather than ballooned outward.
A pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in a lung artery, usually from a deep leg vein. It fits a question about a traveling clot, not a weakened aortic wall.
Correct. An outward bulge of a weakened aortic wall is an aneurysm, dangerous because it can rupture.
Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, not a bulging artery. Choose it for a vein that is red, tender, and painful.
questions.answerText: An aneurysm, because it can rupture

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: At birth the lungs inflate and the placenta is cut off. What normally happens to the fetal shunts?
options: They widen to carry more blood into the inflated lungs
They close and are left behind as ligaments or remnants
They disappear completely and leave no trace
They stay open for life as backup routes around the lungs
questions.why: Once the newborn breathes and the placenta is gone, there is no longer a reason to route blood around the lungs or liver. Each shunt closes in the hours and weeks after birth and leaves a remnant: the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, the ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, and the foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.
notes: The shunts carry blood away from the lungs, not into them, so widening them would work against the newborn. After birth, blood reaches the lungs through the pulmonary arteries once the shunts close.
Correct. The shunts close and remain as small ligaments or, for the foramen ovale, a depression.
Each shunt leaves something behind that can be found in an adult, such as the fossa ovalis in the heart or the ligamentum venosum on the liver. Students pick this when they forget the remnants.
Shunts that stay open after birth are abnormal and get their own names, such as patent ductus arteriosus and patent foramen ovale. This describes a defect, not the normal outcome.
questions.answerText: They close and are left behind as ligaments or remnants

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Before birth, the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus route blood away from the lungs, and both close after birth. Why is bypassing the lungs appropriate only before birth?
options: The fetal lungs already exchange gases with the amniotic fluid
Blood reaching the fetal lungs would carry oxygen away from them
The fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange
The fetal heart is too weak to pump blood into the lungs
questions.why: A fetus does not breathe air, so its lungs are collapsed and filled with fluid, and the placenta handles gas exchange. Sending all the blood through the lungs would be wasted effort, so most of it is shunted past them, with only a small share reaching the lungs to supply the growing tissue. At birth the lungs inflate and take over gas exchange, so the shunts are no longer needed.
notes: The fetal lungs do not exchange gases with amniotic fluid; all fetal gas exchange happens at the placenta. This misconception comes from the fact that the lungs are filled with fluid.
This misreads the reason for the bypass. The lungs are skipped because they are not yet exchanging gases, so sending blood there would not help oxygenate it.
Correct. Because the fetal lungs are not used for gas exchange, blood is shunted around them until birth.
The fetal heart pumps blood strongly through the whole body and out to the placenta. The shunts exist because the lungs are not in use, not because the heart lacks strength.
questions.answerText: The fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Before birth, where does fetal blood pick up oxygen and nutrients and give up its wastes?
options: The fetal liver
The fetal lungs
The placenta
The amniotic fluid
questions.why: The placenta is the organ where fetal blood and maternal blood come close enough to exchange materials, without mixing. Fetal blood picks up oxygen and nutrients there and gives up carbon dioxide and wastes. The umbilical arteries bring oxygen-poor blood to the placenta, and the umbilical vein carries the refreshed blood back to the fetus.
notes: The fetal liver is largely bypassed by the ductus venosus, since the placenta handles much of its filtering. Choose it for a question about which organ the ductus venosus skips.
The fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange before birth, which is why blood is shunted around them. Pick the lungs if the question asks where gas exchange happens after birth.
Correct. The placenta is where fetal blood exchanges oxygen, nutrients, and wastes with the mother's blood.
The amniotic fluid surrounds and cushions the fetus but is not where its blood exchanges gases. Students choose it because the fetus is bathed in it, but no blood vessels exchange materials with it.
questions.answerText: The placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In atherosclerosis, plaque narrows and roughens an artery. Why does this put the tissue downstream at risk?
options: Plaque affects only the artery wall itself and never the tissue it supplies
A narrowed artery speeds blood up, flooding the tissue with too much oxygen
Less blood gets through, and a clot on the rough plaque can block it completely
Narrowing forces arterial blood backward into the veins of that tissue
questions.why: A plaque bulges into the lumen, so less blood can reach the tissue the artery supplies. The plaque surface is also rough, and a thrombus, or clot, can form on it and suddenly block the vessel completely. Either way, the downstream tissue loses its oxygen supply, which is how plaque leads to heart attacks, strokes, and leg pain.
notes: The whole point of the named diseases, such as coronary artery disease and stroke, is that the tissue downstream suffers. Students choose this when they think of plaque only as a wall problem.
Narrowing does not deliver extra oxygen; the tissue gets less blood, not more. This misconception treats a narrowed pipe like a nozzle that boosts delivery.
Correct. Narrowing reduces flow, and a clot on the rough plaque can block the artery entirely.

Arteries do not empty backward into veins; blood still has to pass forward through capillaries to reach the veins. This mixes up arterial narrowing with the backflow that happens when vein valves fail.
questions.answerText: Less blood gets through, and a clot on the rough plaque can block it completely

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Aneurysms are a disorder of arteries rather than veins. Which statement best explains why a weak spot is so risky in an artery wall?
options: Arteries lack a muscular middle layer, so any weak spot leaks
Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so a weak spot balloons and can burst
Arteries have one-way valves that tear apart at a weak spot
Arteries carry blood under low pressure, so a weak spot collapses inward
questions.why: Blood leaves the heart under high pressure, and the arteries take that pressure with every beat. A weakened area cannot resist it, so the wall stretches outward into a balloon-like bulge, and the thin bulge can rupture and bleed severely. Veins carry blood under low pressure, so their disorders tend to involve pooled blood and failed valves instead.
notes: Arteries have a thick tunica media of smooth muscle and elastic fibers, the thickest layer of their wall. A vessel without a tunica media is a capillary, which has only the tunica intima.
Correct. High arterial pressure stretches a weak spot into a bulge that can burst.
One-way valves are a feature of veins, not arteries away from the heart. Pick valves for a question about varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency.
Low pressure describes veins, not arteries, and a weak spot under pressure bulges outward rather than collapsing. This mixes up the two sides of the circulation.
questions.answerText: Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so a weak spot balloons and can burst

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Varicose veins develop when the one-way valves in leg veins fail. Using the valves' normal role, why does their failure make blood pool?
options: The valves normally stop backflow, so failure lets blood fall back and collect
The valves normally narrow the vein, so failure lets it widen slowly
The valves normally block arterial blood, so failure lets it leak in
The valves normally pump blood upward, so failure removes the pump
questions.why: Blood in the leg veins has to travel upward against gravity under low pressure. One-way valves divide each vein into short segments and close whenever blood starts to slip backward. When the valves fail, blood falls back down the vein and collects, stretching the superficial veins until they twist and bulge.
notes: Correct. The valves prevent backflow, so their failure lets blood fall back and pool.
Valves do not narrow the vein to control flow; smooth muscle in the vessel wall changes diameter. This mixes up the valves with the tunica media.
Arteries and veins are joined through capillary beds, not through valves. Vein valves only control the direction of venous blood, so their failure does not let arterial blood leak in.
Valves do not pump; they only keep blood from flowing backward. The squeezing that pushes venous blood upward comes from nearby skeletal muscles, the skeletal muscle pump.
questions.answerText: The valves normally stop backflow, so failure lets blood fall back and collect

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does a clot that breaks free from a deep leg vein end up in the lungs rather than in the brain?
options: Venous blood goes to the right heart, which pumps it into the lung arteries
The clot travels in the aorta, which sends its first branches to the lungs
Leg veins drain directly into the pulmonary veins
The left ventricle pumps venous blood from the legs straight to the lungs
questions.why: A loose clot follows the normal venous return. Blood from the legs travels up the inferior vena cava to the right atrium and right ventricle, which pumps it into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. The pulmonary arteries branch into smaller and smaller vessels in the lungs, and the clot lodges there long before it could reach the left heart and the arteries to the brain.
notes: Correct. Venous blood returns to the right heart and is pumped into the pulmonary arteries, where the clot lodges.

Venous blood does not enter the aorta until after it has passed through the lungs and the left heart. The aorta's first branches are the coronary arteries, which fit a question about blood supply to the heart wall.
Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium; leg veins never connect to them directly. Pick the pulmonary veins for a question about where blood goes after leaving the lungs.
The left ventricle pumps blood into the aorta and out to the body, not to the lungs. The right ventricle is the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs.
questions.answerText: Venous blood goes to the right heart, which pumps it into the lung arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Chronic hypertension makes the heart pump against higher pressure in the systemic arteries. Which chamber's wall is most likely to thicken over time?
options: The right atrium
The left ventricle
The left atrium
The right ventricle
questions.why: Hypertension is chronically high pressure in the arteries, and the systemic arteries are fed by the left ventricle through the aorta. Like any muscle that is made to work harder, the myocardium of the left ventricle thickens to generate the extra force. The left ventricle already has the thickest wall of the four chambers because it pumps blood to the whole body.
notes: The right atrium receives blood from the venae cavae and pushes it only into the right ventricle. Pick it for a question about where systemic venous blood returns to the heart.
Correct. The left ventricle pumps into the systemic arteries, so its wall thickens against chronically high pressure.
The left atrium receives blood from the pulmonary veins and pushes it only into the left ventricle. It fits a question about where oxygenated blood returns from the lungs.
The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary trunk. It would thicken if pressure in the pulmonary circuit stayed high, so choose it for a question about the pulmonary side.
questions.answerText: The left ventricle

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A piece of a clot breaks free from an artery wall and travels in the bloodstream until it lodges in a smaller vessel. What is the traveling clot called?
options: An atheroma
An embolus
An aneurysm
A thrombus
questions.why: An embolus is a clot or fragment that breaks free and travels through the bloodstream to lodge somewhere else. It usually starts as a thrombus, a clot fixed in place, often on the rough surface of a plaque or in a deep vein. Where the embolus lodges decides the disease, such as a pulmonary embolism in the lung or a stroke in the brain.
notes: An atheroma is a fatty plaque within the artery wall, not a clot. Choose it for a question about the lesion of atherosclerosis.
Correct. A traveling clot or fragment is an embolus.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall. It fits a question about a wall that could rupture, not a moving clot.
A thrombus is a clot that forms and stays in place inside a vessel. Pick it if the clot had not broken free, as in a clot sitting on a roughened plaque.
questions.answerText: An embolus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a cadaver, a round fibrous cord runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. Which fetal vessel was this cord?
options: The umbilical vein
The ductus venosus
The ductus arteriosus
An umbilical artery
questions.why: The cord is the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver. Before birth it was the umbilical vein, which carried oxygen-rich blood from the placenta through the umbilicus to the liver. Its path in the free edge of the falciform ligament traces exactly where the vein once ran.
notes: Correct. The cord in the free edge of the falciform ligament is the ligamentum teres, left by the umbilical vein.
The ductus venosus leaves the ligamentum venosum on the inferior surface of the liver, reaching the inferior vena cava. It fits a cord on the liver's underside, not one coming from the umbilicus.
The ductus arteriosus leaves the ligamentum arteriosum in the thorax, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Choose it for a cord found above the heart.

The umbilical arteries leave the medial umbilical ligaments, paired cords on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. Pick them for paired cords heading down from the umbilicus, not one running to the liver.
questions.answerText: The umbilical vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder is defined as chronically high pressure within the arteries?
options: Arteriosclerosis
Hypertension
Chronic venous insufficiency
Aneurysm
questions.why: Hypertension means chronically high blood pressure within the arteries. It does not have to narrow or bulge any single vessel, but over time it strains the heart and damages vessel walls throughout the body. That long-term strain is why hypertension raises the risk of stroke, aneurysm, and a thickened left ventricle.
notes: Arteriosclerosis is the stiffening and thickening of artery walls. It is a change in the wall rather than in the pressure, so pick it for a question about hardened arteries.
Correct. Chronically high arterial pressure is hypertension.
Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term failure of the leg vein valves, a problem on the low-pressure venous side. It fits a question about persistent lower leg swelling.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge of a weakened artery wall. High pressure can make one worse, but choose it for a question about a bulging wall that can rupture.
questions.answerText: Hypertension

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares arterial and venous disorders?
options: Arterial and venous disorders are the same, since both vessels carry blood at the same pressure
Arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall, while venous disorders involve failed valves and pooled blood
Arterial disorders affect only the brain, while venous disorders affect only the legs
Arterial disorders mostly involve failed valves, while venous disorders mostly involve plaque
questions.why: Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so their disorders tend to narrow the channel, as in atherosclerosis, or weaken the wall, as in an aneurysm. Veins carry blood under low pressure and depend on valves, so their disorders tend to involve failed valves and pooled or clotted blood, as in varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis. The pressure each vessel carries shapes what goes wrong with it.
notes: Arteries carry blood under much higher pressure than veins, which is exactly why their disorders differ. Students pick this when they forget that pressure drops as blood moves through the capillaries.
Correct. Arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall, and venous disorders involve failed valves and pooled blood.

Arterial disorders occur throughout the body, such as coronary artery disease in the heart and peripheral artery disease in the legs. Venous disorders also occur outside the legs, as hemorrhoids show.
This reverses the two sides. Valves are a feature of veins, and plaque builds up in arteries, so valve failure belongs to venous disorders and plaque to arterial ones.
questions.answerText: Arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall, while venous disorders involve failed valves and pooled blood

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Most fetal shunts close into fibrous cords, but the foramen ovale leaves a shallow depression instead. Why?
options: It stays partly open in every adult to help the newborn lungs
It was the largest shunt, so it shrinks down into a shallow pit
It was a hole in a wall, not a tube, so it seals into a depression
It was an artery, and arteries always close into shallow depressions
questions.why: The ductus venosus, the ductus arteriosus, and the umbilical vessels were all tubes, and a closed tube collapses into a fibrous cord, or ligament. The foramen ovale was different: it was a hole in the interatrial septum. When a hole in a wall seals, it leaves a shallow mark in that wall, the fossa ovalis, rather than a cord.
notes: A foramen ovale that stays open after birth is an abnormal condition called patent foramen ovale. Normally it seals, so this describes a defect rather than the reason for the depression.
The fossa ovalis is not explained by size. The shape of the remnant depends on whether the original was a hole or a tube.
Correct. Because the foramen ovale was a hole rather than a vessel, it leaves a depression.
The foramen ovale was not an artery; it was an opening between the atria. Arteries such as the umbilical arteries close into cords, the medial umbilical ligaments.
questions.answerText: It was a hole in a wall, not a tube, so it seals into a depression

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The medial umbilical ligaments on the inside of the anterior abdominal wall are the remnants of which fetal vessels?
options: The umbilical arteries
The ductus venosus
The ductus arteriosus
The umbilical vein
questions.why: Before birth, two umbilical arteries branch from the internal iliac arteries and carry blood from the fetus to the placenta. After birth they close, and their distal parts become fibrous cords called the medial umbilical ligaments, which run up the inner surface of the abdominal wall toward the navel.
notes: Correct. The medial umbilical ligaments are the closed umbilical arteries.
The ductus venosus let blood bypass the liver. It becomes the ligamentum venosum. Pick it for the remnant on the liver.
The ductus arteriosus connected the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Pick it for the remnant between the pulmonary trunk and aortic arch.
The umbilical vein carried oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. After birth it becomes the round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres). Pick it for that remnant.
questions.answerText: The umbilical arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The fossa ovalis is the adult remnant of which fetal structure?
options: The ductus arteriosus
The umbilical vein
The foramen ovale
The ductus venosus
questions.why: Before birth, the foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. After birth it closes, leaving a shallow depression called the fossa ovalis. It is the one fetal shunt that becomes a depression instead of a cord, because it was a hole and not a vessel.
notes: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta in the fetus and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Pick it for the remnant cord between the pulmonary trunk and aortic arch.
The umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta and becomes the round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres). Pick it for that liver remnant.
Correct. The foramen ovale closes to leave the fossa ovalis.
The ductus venosus carries blood past the liver in the fetus and becomes the ligamentum venosum. Pick it for the remnant on the liver.
questions.answerText: The foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Before birth, the foramen ovale let blood pass directly between which two chambers?
options: From the right ventricle to the aorta
From the right atrium to the left atrium
From the left atrium to the right atrium
From the right ventricle to the left ventricle
questions.why: The fetal lungs are not yet used for breathing, so most blood is routed around them. The foramen ovale, an opening in the interatrial septum, lets blood pass directly from the right atrium into the left atrium, bypassing the pulmonary circuit. After birth it closes, and its site remains as the fossa ovalis.
notes: The fetal shunt toward the aorta is the ductus arteriosus, which connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Pick it for the vessel that becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
Correct. The foramen ovale carried blood from the right atrium to the left atrium.
This reverses the direction. Fetal blood flows from right to left, because the shunt exists to send blood around the unused lungs.
There is no normal fetal opening between the ventricles. A hole there would be a ventricular septal defect.
questions.answerText: From the right atrium to the left atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: If the valves in the leg veins fail, what problem can develop?
options: Capillaries in the legs lose their tunica intima
The veins develop a thicker tunica media
Blood flows backward and pools, stretching the veins
Blood pressure in the arteries rises sharply
questions.why: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that keep low-pressure blood moving toward the heart. If they fail, blood slips backward and pools in the veins, especially in the legs where gravity pulls it down. Over time the pooled blood stretches the vein walls, producing swollen, twisted varicose veins.
notes: Capillaries keep their tunica intima regardless of what happens in the veins; it is their only layer. This choice links two unrelated structures.
Failed valves let veins stretch and become swollen and thin-walled, not thicker. A thick tunica media is a feature of arteries.
Correct. Failed valves let blood pool and stretch the veins.
Valve failure affects the low-pressure venous side, where blood is returning to the heart. It does not cause a sharp rise in arterial pressure.
questions.answerText: Blood flows backward and pools, stretching the veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The valves in a person's superficial leg veins fail over many years. Which condition is most likely to develop?
options: Varicose veins
Atherosclerosis
Aneurysm
Peripheral artery disease
questions.why: Leg veins carry low-pressure blood upward against gravity, and their valves keep that blood from sliding back. When the valves fail, blood flows backward and pools in the vein, stretching it. Over time the superficial veins become twisted, swollen, and visibly bulging, which is the condition called varicose veins.
notes: Correct. Failed valves in superficial leg veins let blood pool and produce varicose veins.
Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque buildup in artery walls, not a valve problem in veins. Choose it if the question asked what narrows arteries and leads to heart attack or stroke.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall, most often the aorta or brain arteries. Pick it if the question asked about an artery at risk of rupture.
Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually from plaque. It would be the answer if the person had leg pain on walking.
questions.answerText: Varicose veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient is diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis. Which kind of vessel holds the clot?
options: A deep vein of the leg
A superficial vein of the leg
An artery of the lung
A deep artery of the leg
questions.why: Thrombosis means the formation of a clot (a thrombus) inside a vessel. Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in one of the deep veins, usually in the leg, where slow, low-pressure blood flow makes clotting more likely. The danger is that the clot can break free and travel to the lungs.
notes: Correct. A deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein, most often in the leg.
Superficial veins near the skin are the ones affected by varicose veins and often by phlebitis. They would be the answer if the question asked about twisted, bulging veins.
A clot lodged in an artery of the lung is a pulmonary embolism, the dangerous result if a DVT breaks free. Choose it if the question asked where a traveling leg clot ends up.
Narrowing of a leg artery is peripheral artery disease, not DVT. Pick the leg artery if the question asked what causes pain on walking.
questions.answerText: A deep vein of the leg

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which route describes the pulmonary circuit?
options: Right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side
Left side of the heart to the body and back to the right side
Right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the right side
Digestive organs through the liver before reaching the heart
questions.why: The pulmonary circuit carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs. There the blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. The oxygen-rich blood then returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, ready to be pumped to the body.
notes: Correct. The pulmonary circuit runs from the right heart to the lungs and back to the left heart.
This describes the systemic circuit, which delivers oxygen-rich blood to the body. Pick it if the question asked which circuit starts at the left ventricle.
Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium, not the right side. Returning to the right side would skip the left heart entirely and leave no way for oxygen-rich blood to reach the body.
This describes the hepatic portal circulation, which routes blood from the digestive organs through the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked about a portal system.
questions.answerText: Right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which route describes the systemic circuit?
options: Left side of the heart to the body and back to the right side
Right side of the heart to the body and back to the left side
Left side of the heart to the lungs and back to the right side
Right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side
questions.why: The systemic circuit begins when the left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. The blood travels through arteries to capillary beds throughout the body, where it delivers oxygen and picks up carbon dioxide. Oxygen-poor blood then returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium.
notes: Correct. The systemic circuit runs from the left heart to the body and back to the right heart.
This reverses the systemic circuit. The right side of the heart receives oxygen-poor blood and sends it to the lungs, not to the body.
The left side of the heart sends blood to the body, not the lungs. This route mixes the starting point of the systemic circuit with the destination of the pulmonary circuit.
This is the pulmonary circuit, which sends blood to the lungs for gas exchange. Pick it if the question asked which circuit starts at the right ventricle.
questions.answerText: Left side of the heart to the body and back to the right side

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a portal system?
options: Blood flows straight from an artery into a vein without a capillary bed
Blood passes through two capillary beds in a row before reaching the heart
Blood flows from the heart to the lungs and back to the heart
Two vessels join so blood has an alternate route if one is blocked
questions.why: In most routes, blood passes through one capillary bed between artery and vein. In a portal system, the veins draining the first capillary bed lead into a second capillary bed before the blood heads back to the heart. This lets the second organ handle what the first bed picked up, as in the hepatic portal system, where blood from the digestive organs passes through the liver.
notes: This describes an arteriovenous anastomosis, which bypasses capillaries altogether. Pick it if the question asked about a direct artery-to-vein connection.
Correct. A portal system has two capillary beds in a row.
This describes the pulmonary circuit. Choose it if the question asked how blood reaches the lungs for gas exchange.
This describes an anastomosis, a junction of vessels that provides a backup route. It would be the answer if the question asked how tissue can stay supplied when one vessel is blocked.
questions.answerText: Blood passes through two capillary beds in a row before reaching the heart

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which of these is an example of a portal system?
options: Pulmonary circuit
Coronary circulation
Cerebral arterial circle
Hepatic portal system
questions.why: The hepatic portal system collects blood from the capillaries of the stomach, intestines, spleen, and pancreas and carries it through the hepatic portal vein into the liver's sinusoids, a second capillary bed. Only after the liver has processed this blood does it drain to the inferior vena cava and the heart. The hypophyseal portal system, between the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, is another example.
notes: The pulmonary circuit has a single capillary bed in the lungs between the heart and back again. Pick it if the question asked which route carries blood to the lungs.
The coronary circulation supplies the heart wall itself through one capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessels feed the myocardium.
The cerebral arterial circle is an arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain that provides backup routes. Choose it if the question asked for an example of an anastomosis.
Correct. The hepatic portal system passes blood through the digestive capillaries and then the liver sinusoids.
questions.answerText: Hepatic portal system

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is an arteriovenous anastomosis?
options: A direct artery-to-vein link that skips the capillaries
An opening between the right and left atria
A junction of two arteries that gives an alternate route
Two capillary beds connected in series by a vein
questions.why: An anastomosis is any place where vessels join. In an arteriovenous anastomosis, an artery connects directly to a vein, so blood can pass from the arterial side to the venous side without going through capillaries. Because capillaries are skipped, no exchange with the tissue happens along that route.
notes: Correct. An arteriovenous anastomosis links an artery directly to a vein.
An opening between the atria is the foramen ovale of the fetal heart. Choose it if the question asked about a fetal shunt that bypasses the lungs.
A junction of two arteries is an arterial anastomosis, which provides a backup route to a tissue. Pick it if the question asked how blood can still reach a tissue when one artery is blocked.
Two capillary beds in series describe a portal system. It would be the answer if the question asked about the hepatic portal system.
questions.answerText: A direct artery-to-vein link that skips the capillaries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which chamber starts each circuit?
options: Pulmonary starts at the right atrium, systemic at the left atrium
Both circuits start at the left ventricle
Pulmonary starts at the right ventricle, systemic at the left ventricle
Pulmonary starts at the left ventricle, systemic at the right ventricle
questions.why: Each circuit begins with the ventricle that pumps blood out into it. The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood into the pulmonary trunk, starting the pulmonary circuit to the lungs. The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta, starting the systemic circuit to the body.
notes: Atria receive blood returning to the heart; they do not start a circuit. Pick the atria if the question asked where each circuit ends.
The left ventricle starts only the systemic circuit. The pulmonary circuit needs its own pump, the right ventricle.
Correct. The right ventricle feeds the pulmonary circuit, and the left ventricle feeds the systemic circuit.
This swaps the two ventricles. The right side of the heart handles oxygen-poor blood headed to the lungs.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary starts at the right ventricle, systemic at the left ventricle

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which chamber receives the blood at the end of each circuit?
options: Both circuits return to the right atrium
Pulmonary returns to the right ventricle, systemic to the left ventricle
Pulmonary returns to the left atrium, systemic to the right atrium
Pulmonary returns to the right atrium, systemic to the left atrium
questions.why: Each circuit ends in an atrium on the opposite side of the heart from where it began. Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Oxygen-poor blood from the body returns through the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus to the right atrium.
notes: Only the systemic circuit returns to the right atrium. If the pulmonary circuit did too, oxygen-rich blood would never reach the left ventricle and the body.
Blood returns to the atria first, then passes through the AV valves into the ventricles. Pick the ventricles if the question asked where each circuit starts.
Correct. The lungs drain to the left atrium, and the body drains to the right atrium.
This swaps the two atria. Blood coming back from the lungs must reach the left side so it can be pumped to the body.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary returns to the left atrium, systemic to the right atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does a portal system include two capillary beds?
options: So blood can skip all exchange on its way back to the heart
So a second capillary bed can process blood from the first
So blood can pick up oxygen twice before reaching the body
So the heart can pump less blood with each beat
questions.why: In a portal system, blood picks up materials in the first capillary bed and then carries them straight to a second capillary bed. In the hepatic portal system, nutrients and other substances absorbed by the intestines go directly to the liver, which processes them before they enter the general circulation.
notes: Skipping exchange is what an arteriovenous anastomosis does. Pick that idea if the question asked about a direct artery-to-vein connection.
Correct. The second capillary bed lets another organ process what the first bed collected.
Blood picks up oxygen only in the lungs. Neither capillary bed in the hepatic portal system adds oxygen.
Portal systems do not change how much blood the heart pumps per beat. They change the route blood takes, not the heart's output.
questions.answerText: So a second capillary bed can process blood from the first

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does an anastomosis provide if one vessel path is blocked?
options: A direct path to a vein that skips exchange
A valve that stops blood from flowing backward
A backup route for blood to reach the tissue
A second capillary bed to process the blood
questions.why: An anastomosis is a place where two vessels join. If one path to a tissue becomes blocked, blood can travel through the joining vessel and still reach the tissue by another route. The cerebral arterial circle at the base of the brain and the palmar arches of the hand are examples.
notes: A direct path to a vein that skips exchange is an arteriovenous anastomosis. It would be the answer if the question asked which connection bypasses capillaries.
Valves stop backflow in veins and are not formed by anastomoses. Choose valves if the question asked what keeps blood moving toward the heart in the legs.
Correct. An anastomosis gives blood a backup route around a blockage.
