A second capillary bed in series describes a portal system. Pick it if the question asked about the hepatic portal system.
questions.answerText: A backup route for blood to reach the tissue

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares an arteriovenous anastomosis and a capillary bed?
options: Both carry blood away from the heart under high pressure
An arteriovenous anastomosis skips exchange, while a capillary bed is where exchange happens
An arteriovenous anastomosis is where exchange happens, while a capillary bed skips it
Both connect two capillary beds in series, as in a portal system
questions.why: In a capillary bed, blood passes through thin-walled capillaries where gases, nutrients, and wastes are exchanged with the tissue. An arteriovenous anastomosis connects an artery directly to a vein, so blood moving through it skips the capillaries and no exchange takes place. Arteriovenous anastomoses are common in places like the skin of the fingers.
notes: Capillary beds are low-pressure exchange areas, and an arteriovenous anastomosis carries blood toward a vein. High-pressure flow away from the heart describes arteries.
Correct. The anastomosis bypasses exchange, while the capillary bed performs it.
This reverses the two. Exchange needs the thin capillary wall, which an artery-to-vein shortcut does not have.
Two capillary beds in series describe a portal system, which is different from both of these. Pick a portal system if the question asked about blood passing through the intestines and then the liver.
questions.answerText: An arteriovenous anastomosis skips exchange, while a capillary bed is where exchange happens

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why are capillary beds positioned between arterioles and venules?
options: So valves can stop blood from flowing backward
So blood pressure rises before blood enters the veins
So exchange happens before blood heads back to the heart
So blood picks up oxygen before entering the arteries
questions.why: The vascular sequence runs from arteries to arterioles, then capillaries, then venules and veins. Arterioles deliver blood to the capillaries at a controlled rate, and the capillaries exchange oxygen, nutrients, and wastes with the tissue. Only after this exchange do venules collect the blood and start it back toward the heart.
notes: Capillaries have no valves. Valves are found in veins, the answer if the question asked what prevents backflow in the limbs.
Pressure falls, not rises, as blood moves through arterioles and capillaries. By the time blood reaches the veins, its pressure is low.
Correct. Capillary beds sit between the delivery side and the return side so exchange can happen.
Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, not in tissue capillary beds. Tissue capillaries give oxygen away to cells.
questions.answerText: So exchange happens before blood heads back to the heart

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Blood reaches a vein through an arteriovenous anastomosis instead of a capillary bed. What function is skipped?
options: Return of blood to the heart
Oxygenation of blood in the lungs
Propulsion of blood by elastic recoil
Exchange of materials with the tissue
questions.why: Capillaries are the only vessels with walls thin enough for exchange. An arteriovenous anastomosis connects an artery straight to a vein, so the blood never enters the capillaries of that tissue. It still returns to the heart, but it does so without delivering oxygen and nutrients or picking up wastes along the way.
notes: The blood still returns to the heart, because it ends up in a vein. Pick venous return if the question asked what veins and their valves accomplish.
Oxygenation happens in the pulmonary capillaries, not in systemic tissue beds. This would be the answer for a question about what the pulmonary circuit does.
Elastic recoil happens in the large elastic arteries near the heart, upstream of any anastomosis. Choose it if the question asked how the aorta keeps blood moving between beats.
Correct. Bypassing the capillaries means no exchange with that tissue.
questions.answerText: Exchange of materials with the tissue

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why can anastomoses reduce tissue damage when an artery is blocked?
options: They send blood through a second capillary bed for processing
They give blood a collateral route around the blockage
They dissolve the clot that caused the blockage
They raise pressure enough to push through the blockage
questions.why: A collateral route is a side path that runs alongside the main one. Where vessels join in an anastomosis, blood can detour through the connecting vessel and reach tissue beyond the blockage. Areas with many anastomoses, such as the hand with its palmar arches or the base of the brain with its cerebral arterial circle, are better protected when one vessel is blocked.
notes: Passing blood through a second capillary bed describes a portal system. Choose it if the question asked about the hepatic portal system.
Correct. Anastomoses supply a collateral, or side, route that keeps blood reaching the tissue.
Anastomoses are just vessel connections; they do not break down clots. Pick a clot-dissolving process if the question were about treating a blockage rather than routing around it.
Anastomoses route blood around a blockage, not through it. Raising pressure against a blocked vessel would not restore flow beyond the block.
questions.answerText: They give blood a collateral route around the blockage

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: An artery whose region has no anastomoses is suddenly blocked. What is most likely to happen?
options: Blood reroutes through a collateral vessel with no harm
The tissue begins drawing its blood from lymphatic vessels
Blood flows backward through veins to reach the tissue
The tissue it supplies loses blood flow and may die
questions.why: Without an anastomosis, the blocked artery is the only path to the tissue it supplies. Blood cannot detour around the block, so the downstream tissue is starved of oxygen. If the block lasts, the tissue dies, which is what happens to heart muscle in a heart attack or brain tissue in a stroke.
notes: Rerouting through a collateral vessel requires an anastomosis, which this region lacks. This would be the answer if the region had one, as the hand does with its palmar arches.
Lymphatic vessels carry lymph away from tissues and do not deliver blood. Pick lymphatic vessels if the question asked what drains excess tissue fluid.
Venous valves keep blood moving toward the heart, so veins cannot deliver blood backward to a tissue. Veins drain tissues; they do not supply them.
Correct. With no collateral route, the downstream tissue loses its blood supply.
questions.answerText: The tissue it supplies loses blood flow and may die

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence traces systemic blood from the left ventricle to a tissue capillary?
options: Left ventricle, aorta, artery, venule, capillary
Left ventricle, pulmonary trunk, artery, arteriole, capillary
Left ventricle, aorta, arteriole, artery, capillary
Left ventricle, aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta, the largest elastic artery. From there blood moves into smaller muscular arteries that serve each region, then into arterioles, which control how much enters each capillary bed. Vessels get smaller at each step on the way out to the tissues.
notes: Venules come after capillaries and carry blood toward the heart. They would appear in a sequence tracing blood from a capillary back to the right atrium.
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, not the left, and carries blood to the lungs. Pick it if the question traced blood from the right ventricle.
This places the arteriole before the artery. Arterioles are the smallest arteries and come last, right before the capillaries.
Correct. Blood moves from large to small: aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary.
questions.answerText: Left ventricle, aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence traces systemic blood from a tissue capillary back to the heart?
options: Capillary, venule, vein, pulmonary vein, left atrium
Capillary, vein, venule, vena cava, right atrium
Capillary, arteriole, vein, vena cava, right atrium
Capillary, venule, vein, vena cava, right atrium
questions.why: After exchange in the capillaries, blood drains into venules, the smallest veins. Venules merge into larger veins, which join the superior or inferior vena cava. The venae cavae empty oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium, finishing the systemic circuit.
notes: Pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. This path fits the end of the pulmonary circuit, not the systemic circuit.
Veins are larger than venules, so blood reaches venules first. Swapping them reverses the size order of the venous side.
Arterioles carry blood toward capillaries, not away from them. They would appear in a sequence from the left ventricle to a capillary.
Correct. Blood moves from small to large on the way back: capillary, venule, vein, vena cava, right atrium.
questions.answerText: Capillary, venule, vein, vena cava, right atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does the hepatic portal system send blood from the digestive organs through the liver before it reaches the heart?
options: So the liver can filter urine out of the blood
So the liver can process nutrients absorbed by the gut
So the liver can add oxygen to blood leaving the intestines
So blood can skip the digestive organs on its way back
questions.why: Blood leaving the stomach and intestines carries newly absorbed nutrients and other substances. The hepatic portal vein delivers this blood straight to the liver's sinusoids, where liver cells store, change, or remove many of those materials. Only then does the blood drain through the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava and the heart.
notes: Filtering urine is the job of the kidneys. Pick the kidneys if the question asked which organ filters blood to form urine.
Correct. The liver processes absorbed materials before they reach the rest of the body.
The liver does not add oxygen to blood; oxygen is added only in the lungs. The liver actually receives its oxygen from the hepatic artery.
The hepatic portal system collects blood from the digestive organs, so it does not skip them. Skipping the liver is what the fetal ductus venosus does.
questions.answerText: So the liver can process nutrients absorbed by the gut

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement best defines fetal circulation?
options: The adult circulatory plan that forms after the shunts close
The flow of the mother's blood through the body of the fetus
The flow of blood through the umbilical cord and nowhere else
A fetal circulatory plan that gets oxygen from the placenta
questions.why: Before birth, the fetal lungs are collapsed and do not exchange gases. Fetal blood picks up oxygen and nutrients at the placenta and returns to the fetus through the umbilical vein. Fetal circulation is arranged around this fact, with shunts that send much of the blood around the lungs and liver.
notes: After the shunts close at birth, the baby is on the adult plan, which is the opposite of fetal circulation. Pick this if the question asked what happens once the lungs inflate.
The mother's blood and the fetal blood normally stay separate; materials pass between them across the placenta. This misconception comes from thinking the two blood supplies mix.
The umbilical cord carries only part of the route. Fetal blood circulates through the whole fetal body, the heart, and the shunts as well.
Correct. Fetal circulation is built around the placenta as the source of oxygen.
questions.answerText: A fetal circulatory plan that gets oxygen from the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the placenta?
options: An opening in the fetal heart that lets blood bypass the lungs
The cord that connects the fetus to the mother's uterine wall
The organ where fetal blood exchanges gases, nutrients, and wastes
A shunt that carries fetal blood past the liver
questions.why: The placenta is the organ of exchange between mother and fetus. Fetal blood flows through it and picks up oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood while handing off carbon dioxide and other wastes, without the two blood supplies mixing. Before birth, the placenta does the jobs that the lungs, digestive tract, and kidneys will take over later.
notes: This describes the foramen ovale, an opening in the interatrial septum. It would be the answer if the question asked about the fetal shunt between the atria.
This describes the umbilical cord, which links the fetus to the placenta and carries the umbilical vessels. Pick it if the question asked what carries blood between the fetus and the placenta.
Correct. The placenta is where fetal blood exchanges materials with the mother's blood.
This describes the ductus venosus. Choose it if the question asked which fetal shunt bypasses the liver.
questions.answerText: The organ where fetal blood exchanges gases, nutrients, and wastes

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the umbilical cord?
options: A fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver
The cord linking the fetus to the placenta, holding the umbilical vessels
The organ where fetal blood exchanges materials with the mother's blood
A short vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
questions.why: The umbilical cord links the fetus to the placenta. It carries one umbilical vein, which brings oxygen-rich blood to the fetus, and two umbilical arteries, which take oxygen-poor blood back to the placenta. When the cord is cut at birth, these vessels close and later become ligaments.
notes: This describes the ligamentum venosum, the adult remnant of the ductus venosus. Choose it if the question asked what the ductus venosus becomes after birth.
Correct. The umbilical cord holds the umbilical vein and arteries.
This describes the placenta, the organ of exchange. Pick it if the question asked where fetal blood picks up oxygen.
This describes the ductus arteriosus, a fetal shunt. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel diverts blood away from the lungs.
questions.answerText: The cord linking the fetus to the placenta, holding the umbilical vessels

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is most fetal blood routed around the lungs?
options: The lungs already get oxygen from the amniotic fluid
The lungs receive oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical arteries
The lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange
The pulmonary trunk does not form until after birth
questions.why: Before birth, the fetal lungs are filled with fluid and collapsed, and the placenta handles gas exchange. Sending all the blood through the lungs would waste effort, so the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus route most of it around them. The lungs still receive a small flow, enough to supply their own developing tissue.
notes: The fetus does not get oxygen from amniotic fluid; all its oxygen comes through the placenta. This misconception comes from the fact that the fetal lungs contain fluid.
The umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the fetus to the placenta, not to the lungs. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels return fetal blood to the placenta.
Correct. Collapsed, nonfunctional lungs are the reason the fetus bypasses them.
The pulmonary trunk is present before birth; in fact the ductus arteriosus branches from it. The lungs are bypassed because they are not working, not because the vessels are missing.
questions.answerText: The lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does much fetal blood bypass the liver?
options: The ductus arteriosus carries liver blood to the aorta
The fetal liver is collapsed like the fetal lungs
The placenta does much of the liver's later work
The fetal liver has not formed yet
questions.why: Before birth, the fetus does not digest food, and the placenta takes care of much of the processing and filtering that the liver will handle after birth. So the ductus venosus, a shunt through the liver, lets most of the oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein pass straight toward the inferior vena cava. This gets that blood to the heart quickly.
notes: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta and bypasses the lungs, not the liver. The liver shunt is the ductus venosus.
Collapse applies to the lungs, which are filled with fluid and not used for gas exchange. Pick the lungs if the question asked which organ the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass.
Correct. The placenta covers much of the liver's later work, so much blood can skip the liver.
The fetal liver is present and large; it is bypassed, not missing. The shunt runs through the liver itself.
questions.answerText: The placenta does much of the liver's later work

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, what is a shunt?
options: A valve that keeps fetal blood from flowing backward
A special vessel or opening that routes blood around an organ
A capillary bed that exchanges materials with the mother
A ligament left behind after a fetal vessel closes
questions.why: A shunt is a detour. The fetus has three: the ductus venosus routes blood around the liver, and the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus route blood around the lungs. Each one is needed only before birth, while the placenta handles the jobs those organs will take on later.
notes: A valve blocks backflow, which is the job of heart valves and venous valves. Shunts are detours, not one-way gates.
Correct. A fetal shunt routes blood around an organ that is not yet in full use.
The capillaries that exchange materials with the mother are in the placenta. Choose the placenta if the question asked where fetal blood picks up oxygen.
A ligament left behind after closure is a remnant, such as the ligamentum arteriosum. Pick it if the question asked what a shunt becomes after birth.
questions.answerText: A special vessel or opening that routes blood around an organ

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which list names the three fetal shunts?
options: Foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and coronary sinus
Fossa ovalis, ligamentum arteriosum, and ligamentum venosum
Umbilical vein, umbilical arteries, and ductus venosus
Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus
questions.why: The fetus uses three shunts to send blood around organs that are not yet working fully. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver. The foramen ovale, an opening between the atria, and the ductus arteriosus, a vessel from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, both bypass the lungs.
notes: The coronary sinus is a normal vein on the back of the heart that drains the heart wall into the right atrium, not a fetal shunt. Choose it if the question asked where cardiac veins empty.
These are the adult remnants of the shunts. They would be the answer if the question asked what the shunts become after birth.
The umbilical vein and arteries are fetal vessels in the cord, not shunts. Pick this list if the question asked which vessels connect the fetus to the placenta.
Correct. These three are the fetal shunts.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does the umbilical vein carry?
options: Oxygen-poor blood from the placenta to the fetus
Oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta
Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
Oxygen-rich blood from the fetus to the placenta
questions.why: Veins are defined by direction: they carry blood toward the heart. The umbilical vein brings blood from the placenta toward the fetal heart, and because that blood has just picked up oxygen at the placenta, it is the most oxygen-rich blood in the fetus.
notes: This has the direction right but the oxygen wrong. Blood coming from the placenta has just been loaded with oxygen.
This describes the umbilical arteries, which return fetal blood to the placenta. Pick it if the question asked what the umbilical arteries carry.
Correct. The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.
This has the oxygen right but the direction backward. Blood leaving the fetus for the placenta has already given up its oxygen to fetal tissues.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the ductus venosus?
options: An opening in the interatrial septum
A short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and aorta
A vessel in the umbilical cord carrying blood to the fetus
A shunt that passes through the fetal liver
questions.why: The ductus venosus is a fetal shunt that runs through the liver. It carries most of the blood arriving from the umbilical vein past the liver tissue and on toward the inferior vena cava. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
notes: This is the foramen ovale, which lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. Pick it if the question asked which shunt is a hole in the heart.
This is the ductus arteriosus, which bypasses the lungs. It would be the answer if the question asked which shunt connects to the aorta.
This is the umbilical vein, which brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta. Choose it if the question asked which vessel carries the most oxygen-rich fetal blood.
Correct. The ductus venosus is the liver bypass of the fetus.
questions.answerText: A shunt that passes through the fetal liver

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Where does the ductus venosus send most of the blood that would otherwise pass through the fetal liver?
options: Into the arch of the aorta
Back through the umbilical arteries
Into the left atrium of the heart
Toward the inferior vena cava
questions.why: The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the liver. The ductus venosus lets most of this blood bypass the liver tissue and flow straight toward the inferior vena cava. From there it enters the right atrium, where much of it then crosses through the foramen ovale.
notes: Blood reaches the aorta from the pulmonary trunk through the ductus arteriosus, a different shunt. Pick the aorta if the question asked where the ductus arteriosus sends blood.
Blood returns to the placenta through the umbilical arteries. Choose the placenta if the question asked where the umbilical arteries go.
Blood reaches the left atrium from the right atrium through the foramen ovale. That would be the answer if the question asked where the foramen ovale sends blood.
Correct. The ductus venosus empties toward the inferior vena cava.
questions.answerText: Toward the inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the foramen ovale?
options: A short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and aorta
A shunt that passes through the fetal liver
An opening in the interventricular septum
An opening in the interatrial septum
questions.why: Foramen means opening, and the foramen ovale is an oval opening in the interatrial septum, the wall between the right and left atria. In the fetus it lets blood pass directly from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. After birth it closes and leaves a shallow depression called the fossa ovalis.
notes: This describes the ductus arteriosus, the other shunt that bypasses the lungs. Pick it if the question asked which shunt is a vessel rather than an opening.
This describes the ductus venosus. Choose it if the question asked which shunt bypasses the liver.
The interventricular septum separates the ventricles, and the fetus has no normal opening there. An opening in that wall would be a ventricular septal defect, a birth defect, not a fetal shunt.
Correct. The foramen ovale is an opening between the two atria.
questions.answerText: An opening in the interatrial septum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In the fetus, which way does blood move through the foramen ovale?
options: From the right ventricle to the left ventricle
From the left atrium to the right atrium
From the right atrium to the left atrium
From the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
questions.why: In the fetus, blood arriving from the inferior vena cava enters the right atrium. Instead of all of it going to the right ventricle and lungs, much of it passes through the foramen ovale into the left atrium. From there it goes to the left ventricle and out the aorta to the body, skipping the lungs.
notes: The foramen ovale connects the atria, not the ventricles. A right-to-left connection between ventricles is not a normal fetal shunt.
This reverses the direction. Right-to-left flow is what lets blood skip the lungs.
Correct. Fetal blood crosses the foramen ovale from right atrium to left atrium.
This is the route through the ductus arteriosus. Pick it if the question asked which way blood moves through the ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: From the right atrium to the left atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the ductus arteriosus?
options: One of the paired vessels carrying blood back to the placenta
A short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta
A shunt that passes through the fetal liver
An opening in the interatrial septum
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is a short fetal vessel that connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. It lets blood pumped by the right ventricle skip the collapsed lungs and enter the systemic circulation directly. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
notes: This describes the umbilical arteries. Choose them if the question asked which vessels carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus links the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
This is the ductus venosus, the liver bypass. It would be the answer if the question asked which shunt sends blood toward the inferior vena cava.
This is the foramen ovale, the lung bypass between the atria. Pick it if the question asked which shunt is a hole in the heart wall.
questions.answerText: A short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In the fetus, what does the ductus arteriosus do?
options: Shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta
Shunts blood from the umbilical vein toward the vena cava
Shunts blood from the aorta into the pulmonary trunk
Shunts blood from the right atrium into the left atrium
questions.why: In the fetus, the right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk, but the lungs are collapsed and resist flow. The ductus arteriosus provides an easier path, carrying most of this blood straight into the aorta. That way, blood that left the right ventricle still reaches the body without going through the lungs.
notes: Correct. The fetal ductus arteriosus carries blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
This is the route of the ductus venosus. Choose it if the question asked how fetal blood bypasses the liver.
This reverses the fetal direction. Before birth, blood moves from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, away from the lungs.
This is the route through the foramen ovale. Pick it if the question asked what the opening between the atria does.
questions.answerText: Shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What do the umbilical arteries carry?
options: Oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta
Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
Oxygen-poor blood from the placenta to the fetus
Oxygen-rich blood from the fetus to the placenta
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The two umbilical arteries branch from the fetal internal iliac arteries and carry blood away from the fetus to the placenta. That blood has already given up its oxygen to fetal tissues, so it is oxygen-poor and loaded with carbon dioxide and wastes for the placenta to remove.
notes: Correct. The umbilical arteries return oxygen-poor fetal blood to the placenta.
This describes the umbilical vein. Pick it if the question asked which umbilical vessel carries oxygen-rich blood.
This has the oxygen right but the direction backward. Blood from the placenta is freshly oxygenated and travels in the umbilical vein.
This has the direction right but the oxygen wrong. Blood leaving the fetus has already delivered its oxygen to fetal tissues.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does the umbilical vein become after birth?
options: Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum venosum
Medial umbilical ligament
Ligamentum teres
questions.why: After the umbilical cord is cut, the umbilical vein no longer carries blood and closes into a fibrous cord. This remnant is the ligamentum teres, also called the round ligament of the liver. It runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament toward the liver.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus. It would be the answer if the question asked what connects the pulmonary trunk and aorta in an adult.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus. Pick it if the question asked what the liver shunt becomes.
The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the umbilical arteries. Choose them if the question asked what the umbilical arteries become.
Correct. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum teres

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does the ductus venosus become after birth?
options: Fossa ovalis
Ligamentum venosum
Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum teres
questions.why: Once the placenta is cut off at birth, there is no longer a stream of umbilical blood to send past the liver. The ductus venosus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Its name keeps the venosus part of the original shunt.
notes: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale. Choose it if the question asked about the opening between the atria.
Correct. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
The ligamentum arteriosum comes from the ductus arteriosus. It would be the answer if the question asked about the lung bypass vessel.
The ligamentum teres comes from the umbilical vein. It is also on the liver, which makes it easy to mix up, so pick it if the question asked about the umbilical vein.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum venosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does the foramen ovale become after birth?
options: Fossa ovalis
Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum venosum
Ligamentum teres
questions.why: At birth, pressure in the left atrium rises as blood returns from the newly working lungs, pushing a flap against the foramen ovale and closing it. The opening seals over and leaves the fossa ovalis, a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum seen from the right atrium. It is the one remnant that becomes a depression rather than a ligament, because it was a hole rather than a vessel.
notes: Correct. The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus. Pick it if the question asked about the other lung bypass.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus. It would be the answer if the question asked about the liver bypass.
The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein. Choose it if the question asked what the vessel bringing blood from the placenta becomes.
questions.answerText: Fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What does the ductus arteriosus become after birth?
options: Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum venosum
Ligamentum teres
Medial umbilical ligament
questions.why: After birth the lungs inflate and blood flows easily into them, so the ductus arteriosus is no longer needed. It constricts and closes, becoming the ligamentum arteriosum, a short fibrous cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch. Its name keeps the arteriosus part of the original vessel.
notes: Correct. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
The ligamentum venosum comes from the ductus venosus, the liver bypass. Pick it if the question asked about the shunt through the liver.
The ligamentum teres comes from the umbilical vein. It would be the answer if the question asked about the vessel from the placenta.
The medial umbilical ligaments come from the umbilical arteries. Choose them if the question asked about the vessels returning blood to the placenta.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum arteriosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What do the umbilical arteries become after birth?
options: Median umbilical ligament
Ligamentum teres
Medial umbilical ligaments
Ligamentum arteriosum
questions.why: Once the cord is cut, the parts of the umbilical arteries that ran toward the umbilicus close into fibrous cords. These are the medial umbilical ligaments, paired cords on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. There are two of them because there were two umbilical arteries.
notes: The median umbilical ligament is a single midline cord that is the remnant of the urachus, a fetal canal from the bladder, not of a blood vessel. The names differ by one letter, so read carefully.
The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein. Pick it if the question asked about the vessel carrying blood from the placenta.
Correct. The paired umbilical arteries become the paired medial umbilical ligaments.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus. It would be the answer if the question asked about the cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
questions.answerText: Medial umbilical ligaments

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which single difference explains why fetal circulation is arranged differently from the adult plan?
options: Fetal arteries carry blood toward the heart instead of away
The fetus has no liver until shortly after birth
The fetal heart has only two chambers instead of four
The fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta rather than its lungs
questions.why: Every special feature of fetal circulation follows from where the oxygen comes from. Because the placenta, not the lungs, supplies oxygen, the umbilical vein carries the richest blood, and the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus send most blood past the nonworking lungs. Once the lungs take over at birth, these features are no longer needed.
notes: Arteries carry blood away from the heart in both the fetus and the adult. The umbilical arteries are unusual only because their blood is oxygen-poor.
The fetal liver is present and large before birth. Blood partly bypasses it through the ductus venosus, but the liver itself exists.
The fetal heart has four chambers, the same as the adult heart. The difference is the opening between the atria, the foramen ovale.
Correct. Relying on the placenta for oxygen is the reason for the whole fetal arrangement.
questions.answerText: The fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta rather than its lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the ductus venosus and the ductus arteriosus?
options: The ductus venosus joins the atria, while the ductus arteriosus joins the ventricles
The ductus venosus bypasses the liver, while the ductus arteriosus bypasses the lungs
The ductus venosus bypasses the lungs, while the ductus arteriosus bypasses the liver
Both bypass the lungs, one in the heart wall and one in the liver
questions.why: Both are fetal shunts named ductus, meaning duct. The ductus venosus is on the venous side, in the liver, carrying umbilical vein blood past the liver toward the inferior vena cava. The ductus arteriosus is on the arterial side, linking the pulmonary trunk to the aorta so blood skips the lungs.
notes: Neither ductus is in the heart wall. The atria are joined by the foramen ovale, the answer if the question asked about the opening between the atria.
Correct. Venosus bypasses the liver, and arteriosus bypasses the lungs.
This swaps the two. A helpful clue is that the ductus arteriosus joins two great arteries, the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
Only the ductus arteriosus bypasses the lungs. The ductus venosus is in the liver and bypasses the liver.
questions.answerText: The ductus venosus bypasses the liver, while the ductus arteriosus bypasses the lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus?
options: Both bypass the lungs, one joining the ventricles and the other joining the aorta to the vena cava
Both bypass the liver, one joining the atria and the other joining the umbilical vein to the vena cava
Both bypass the lungs, one joining the atria and the other joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
One bypasses the lungs and the other bypasses the liver, and both are openings in a septum
questions.why: The fetus has two lung bypasses that work at different levels. The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that moves blood from the right atrium to the left atrium. The ductus arteriosus is a vessel that moves blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Between them, most blood never passes through the collapsed lungs.
notes: The foramen ovale joins the atria, not the ventricles, and the ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, not to the vena cava.
Neither one bypasses the liver; that is the ductus venosus. A shunt from the umbilical vein toward the vena cava describes the ductus venosus.
Correct. Both are lung bypasses, one between the atria and one between the great arteries.
Both bypass the lungs, and only the foramen ovale is an opening in a septum. The ductus arteriosus is a vessel outside the heart.
questions.answerText: Both bypass the lungs, one joining the atria and the other joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is the umbilical vein unusual compared with most systemic veins?
options: It carries blood from the fetus to the placenta
It carries blood away from the heart, unlike other veins
It has no tunica intima, unlike other veins
It carries oxygen-rich blood, unlike most systemic veins
questions.why: Most systemic veins carry oxygen-poor blood back from the tissues. The umbilical vein is still a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, but that blood comes straight from the placenta and is full of oxygen. The pulmonary veins are the other well-known veins that carry oxygen-rich blood, for the same reason: they drain the organ of gas exchange.
notes: Blood traveling from the fetus to the placenta moves in the umbilical arteries. Pick them if the question asked which vessels return fetal blood to the placenta.
Veins are defined by carrying blood toward the heart, and the umbilical vein does that. A vessel carrying blood away from the heart would be an artery.
All veins have a tunica intima, the endothelial lining. Only the proportions of the media and externa vary between vessels.
Correct. The umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood, which is unusual for a vein.
questions.answerText: It carries oxygen-rich blood, unlike most systemic veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why are the umbilical arteries unusual compared with most systemic arteries?
options: They have valves along their length, like limb veins
They carry blood toward the heart, unlike other arteries
They carry oxygen-poor blood, unlike most systemic arteries
They carry blood from the placenta to the fetus
questions.why: Most systemic arteries carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the tissues. The umbilical arteries are still arteries because they carry blood away from the fetal heart, but that blood has already given its oxygen to fetal tissues and is heading to the placenta to be refreshed. The pulmonary arteries are the other arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood, since they also lead to the organ of gas exchange.
notes: Arteries do not have valves along their length. Valves are a feature of veins, especially in the limbs.
Arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart, and the umbilical arteries do exactly that. A vessel carrying blood toward the heart would be a vein.
Correct. The umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood, which is unusual for arteries.
Blood traveling from the placenta to the fetus moves in the umbilical vein. Pick it if the question asked which vessel carries oxygen-rich blood into the fetus.
questions.answerText: They carry oxygen-poor blood, unlike most systemic arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the purpose of moving blood from the right atrium to the left atrium through the foramen ovale?
options: It returns oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the right heart
It sends blood to the left heart without passing through the lungs
It lets blood skip the liver on its way to the heart
It sends oxygen-poor blood back to the placenta
questions.why: Blood normally reaches the left atrium only after passing from the right ventricle through the lungs. In the fetus the lungs are collapsed and not exchanging gases, so the foramen ovale offers a shortcut. Blood crosses directly from the right atrium to the left atrium and then goes out the aorta to the body, saving a trip through the lungs.
notes: Blood returning from working lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, not the right heart. That route belongs to the adult pulmonary circuit.
Correct. The foramen ovale lets blood reach the left heart while skipping the lungs.
Skipping the liver is the job of the ductus venosus. It would be the answer if the question asked about the liver bypass.
Returning oxygen-poor blood to the placenta is the job of the umbilical arteries. Pick them if the question asked which vessels carry blood back to the placenta.
questions.answerText: It sends blood to the left heart without passing through the lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does the fetal ductus arteriosus connect the pulmonary trunk to the aorta?
options: It diverts blood from the pulmonary trunk away from the collapsed lungs
It moves blood between the atria without entering the ventricles
It lets blood from the placenta skip the liver
It sends blood from the aorta to the lungs to pick up oxygen
questions.why: Before birth, the right ventricle still pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk, but the collapsed, fluid-filled lungs resist flow. The ductus arteriosus gives that blood an easier path into the aorta, so it reaches the body instead of the lungs. Only a small share of blood continues into the pulmonary arteries to nourish the developing lung tissue.
notes: Correct. The ductus arteriosus moves blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, away from the lungs.
Moving blood between the atria is the job of the foramen ovale. It would be the answer if the question asked about the opening in the interatrial septum.
Skipping the liver is the job of the ductus venosus. Pick it if the question asked about the liver bypass.
The fetal lungs do not oxygenate blood, so sending blood to them for oxygen would not help. Oxygen comes from the placenta through the umbilical vein.
questions.answerText: It diverts blood from the pulmonary trunk away from the collapsed lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is the advantage of routing umbilical vein blood through the ductus venosus?
options: Blood from the liver is sent straight into the aorta
Blood skips the lungs by moving between the atria
Oxygen-poor fetal blood reaches the placenta faster
Oxygen-rich blood skips the liver on its way to the heart
questions.why: The umbilical vein carries the most oxygen-rich blood in the fetus. If all of it passed through the liver's sinusoids, liver tissue would use some of that oxygen and slow the trip. The ductus venosus lets most of it travel straight toward the inferior vena cava and on to the heart, so well-oxygenated blood reaches the body quickly.
notes: Blood reaches the aorta from the pulmonary trunk through the ductus arteriosus, not from the liver. The ductus venosus empties toward the inferior vena cava.
Moving between the atria is the job of the foramen ovale, a lung bypass. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood skips the lungs inside the heart.
Oxygen-poor blood returns to the placenta through the umbilical arteries, which do not pass through the liver. Pick them if the question asked how fetal blood gets back to the placenta.
Correct. The ductus venosus speeds oxygen-rich blood past the liver to the vena cava.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-rich blood skips the liver on its way to the heart

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In an adult heart, the fossa ovalis is the remnant of which fetal structure?
options: Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
Umbilical vein
Foramen ovale
questions.why: The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum, seen from inside the right atrium. It marks the spot where the foramen ovale, the fetal opening between the atria, sealed shut after birth. Fossa means a shallow pit, which fits because the old opening is now covered but still visible.
notes: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum on the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked about the liver shunt's remnant.
The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the question asked about that ligament.
The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver. Choose it if the question asked about the round ligament of the liver.
Correct. The fossa ovalis marks where the foramen ovale closed.
questions.answerText: Foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ligamentum arteriosum is a short fibrous cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch. Which fetal structure did it come from?
options: Ductus venosus
Umbilical arteries
Foramen ovale
Ductus arteriosus
questions.why: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus carried blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta to bypass the lungs. After birth it closes and shrinks into the ligamentum arteriosum, which still connects the same two vessels. The name keeps the arteriosus part of the original shunt.
notes: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum on the inferior surface of the liver. Pick it if the question asked about a ligament on the liver.
The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments on the anterior abdominal wall. Choose them if the question asked about remnants on the abdominal wall.
The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis, a depression rather than a cord. It would be the answer if the question asked about the interatrial septum.
Correct. The ligamentum arteriosum is the closed ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: Ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ligamentum teres runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament of the liver. Which fetal vessel did it come from?
options: Ductus venosus
Umbilical vein
Ductus arteriosus
Umbilical arteries
questions.why: In the fetus, the umbilical vein carried oxygen-rich blood from the placenta through the umbilicus to the liver. After the cord is cut, the vessel closes into a fibrous cord, the ligamentum teres or round ligament of the liver. It still runs from the umbilicus to the liver, following the old path of the vein.
notes: The ductus venosus also involves the liver, which makes it a tempting choice, but it becomes the ligamentum venosum. Pick it if the question asked about the fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver.
Correct. The ligamentum teres is the closed umbilical vein.
The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum near the heart. Choose it if the question asked about the cord between the pulmonary trunk and aorta.
The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments. They would be the answer if the question asked about cords on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.answerText: Umbilical vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ligamentum venosum is a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Which fetal structure did it come from?
options: Foramen ovale
Umbilical vein
Ductus arteriosus
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The ductus venosus was the fetal shunt through the liver that carried umbilical vein blood toward the inferior vena cava. After birth, with no placental blood arriving, it closes into the ligamentum venosum. Its name keeps the venosus part of the original shunt.
notes: The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis in the heart. Choose it if the question asked about the depression in the interatrial septum.
The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, another liver remnant. Pick it if the question asked about the round ligament of the liver.
The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum near the heart. It would be the answer if the question asked about a cord between the pulmonary trunk and aorta.
Correct. The ligamentum venosum is the closed ductus venosus.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The medial umbilical ligaments lie on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. Which fetal vessels did they come from?
options: Umbilical vein
Ductus arteriosus
Umbilical arteries
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The two umbilical arteries carried oxygen-poor blood from the fetus out through the umbilicus to the placenta. After the cord is cut, the parts of these arteries running up the inside of the abdominal wall close into fibrous cords, the medial umbilical ligaments. There are two of them, one for each umbilical artery.
notes: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, which runs to the liver. Pick it if the question asked about the round ligament of the liver.
The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum near the heart. Choose it if the question asked about the lung bypass vessel.
Correct. The medial umbilical ligaments are the closed umbilical arteries.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum on the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked about the liver shunt.
questions.answerText: Umbilical arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which changes at birth make the fetal shunts unnecessary?
options: The lungs inflate and the placenta is cut off
The liver starts working and the heart gains a chamber
The lungs collapse and the placenta takes over
The umbilical cord lengthens and the foramen ovale widens
questions.why: With the first breaths, the lungs fill with air and blood can flow through them easily, so there is no reason to route blood around them. At the same time, cutting the umbilical cord ends placental flow, so there is no stream of umbilical blood for the ductus venosus to carry past the liver. Each shunt then closes and leaves behind a ligament or remnant.
notes: Correct. Inflated lungs and the loss of the placenta remove the need for the shunts.
The heart already has four chambers before birth, and the liver is present. The change at birth is in where oxygen comes from, not in the number of chambers.
This is the reverse of what happens. The lungs inflate at birth, and the placenta stops working once the cord is cut.
The cord is cut at birth, and the foramen ovale closes rather than widens. A widening foramen ovale would keep blood bypassing the lungs.
questions.answerText: The lungs inflate and the placenta is cut off

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a patent ductus arteriosus?
options: A foramen ovale that stays open after birth
A ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth
A ductus venosus that stays open after birth
A ductus arteriosus that closes before birth
questions.why: Patent means open. Normally the ductus arteriosus closes in the first days after birth and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. If it stays open, a patent ductus arteriosus leaves an abnormal connection between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, linking the systemic and pulmonary sides of the circulation.
notes: An open foramen ovale is a patent foramen ovale. Pick it if the question described a lasting connection between the atria.
Correct. A patent ductus arteriosus is a ductus arteriosus that fails to close.

The ductus venosus is the liver shunt, and the term patent ductus arteriosus refers only to the shunt between the pulmonary trunk and aorta. A lasting open ductus venosus would be named for the ductus venosus.
Closing early is the opposite of patent. Patent always means remaining open.
questions.answerText: A ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a patent foramen ovale?
options: A foramen ovale that stays open after birth
A ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth
An opening between the ventricles present at birth
A foramen ovale that seals into the fossa ovalis on schedule
questions.why: Patent means open. Normally the foramen ovale closes soon after birth and leaves the fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum. When it stays open, a patent foramen ovale leaves an abnormal connection between the right and left atria.
notes: Correct. A patent foramen ovale is a foramen ovale that fails to seal.
An open ductus arteriosus is a patent ductus arteriosus. Pick it if the question described a lasting connection between the pulmonary trunk and aorta.
An opening between the ventricles is a ventricular septal defect, a different birth defect. The foramen ovale is between the atria, not the ventricles.
Sealing on schedule into the fossa ovalis is normal closure, the opposite of patent. This would be the answer if the question asked what normally happens to the foramen ovale.
questions.answerText: A foramen ovale that stays open after birth

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is a fetal shunt that stays open after birth considered abnormal?
options: It makes the umbilical vessels reopen after the cord is cut
It links two circuits that should be separate after birth
It turns the shunt into a ligament much too early
It blocks all blood from reaching the lungs after birth
questions.why: After birth the pulmonary and systemic circuits are meant to be separate, with the right heart serving the lungs and the left heart serving the body. A shunt that stays open, such as a patent ductus arteriosus or a patent foramen ovale, links these two circuits where they should be sealed apart. That abnormal connection lets blood cross between sides that should no longer mix.
notes: The umbilical vessels close once the cord is cut, and an open heart shunt does not reopen them. Their closure produces the ligamentum teres and the medial umbilical ligaments.
Correct. An open shunt connects circuits that should be separate after birth.
Becoming a ligament is the normal, healthy outcome. A patent shunt is a problem because it fails to close, not because it closes too soon.
An open shunt diverts some blood, but it does not stop all blood from reaching the lungs. The lungs still receive blood through the pulmonary arteries.
questions.answerText: It links two circuits that should be separate after birth

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A newborn still has an open vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Which fetal structure failed to close?
options: Foramen ovale
Umbilical vein
Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is the fetal vessel joining the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. It normally closes shortly after birth and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. When it stays open, the condition is a patent ductus arteriosus, named for the structure that failed to seal.
notes: The foramen ovale is an opening between the atria, not a vessel between the great arteries. Pick it if the newborn had a lasting connection between the atria.
The umbilical vein runs from the umbilicus to the liver and closes into the ligamentum teres. Choose it if the question asked about the vessel that carried blood from the placenta.
The ductus venosus is in the liver and connects to the inferior vena cava side. It would be the answer if the question described a shunt through the liver.
Correct. An open vessel between the pulmonary trunk and aorta is a patent ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: Ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A newborn has a persistent opening between the right and left atria. Which fetal structure stayed open?
options: Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
Ductus venosus
Fossa ovalis
questions.why: The foramen ovale is the fetal opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium. It normally seals after birth and leaves the fossa ovalis. An opening that persists between the atria is a patent foramen ovale.
notes: The ductus arteriosus is a vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, outside the atria. Pick it if the newborn had an open connection between those two great arteries.
Correct. A lasting opening between the atria is a patent foramen ovale.
The ductus venosus is the liver bypass and is not part of the heart. It would be the answer if the question described a shunt through the liver.
The fossa ovalis is what remains after the foramen ovale closes normally, so it is a sealed depression, not an opening. Choose it if the question asked what the foramen ovale becomes.
questions.answerText: Foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: If the ductus venosus failed to form, which organ would fetal blood no longer bypass efficiently?
options: Liver
Kidneys
Lungs
Heart
questions.why: The ductus venosus is the shunt that carries umbilical vein blood through the liver and toward the inferior vena cava without passing through the liver's sinusoids. Without it, much more of this blood would have to pass through the liver tissue itself. The lung bypasses, the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, would be unaffected.
notes: Correct. The ductus venosus is the liver bypass.
The fetus has no shunt that bypasses the kidneys. Kidneys would not be the answer for any of the fetal shunts.
The lungs are bypassed by the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. Pick the lungs if the question asked about either of those shunts.
Blood still passes through the heart in every fetal route; the shunts change which chambers and vessels it uses. The heart would not be the bypassed organ.
questions.answerText: Liver

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: If the foramen ovale failed to form, which fetal bypass route would be lost?
options: Liver bypass toward the inferior vena cava
Return of fetal blood to the placenta
Lung bypass between the atria
Lung bypass from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood move from the right atrium to the left atrium without going through the lungs. Without it, that atrial-level lung bypass would be gone. The ductus arteriosus would still provide the second lung bypass between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
notes: The liver bypass is the ductus venosus, which would still be present. Pick it if the question asked what the ductus venosus does.
Return to the placenta happens through the umbilical arteries, not the foramen ovale. Choose it if the question asked what the umbilical arteries do.
Correct. The foramen ovale is the lung bypass between the atria.
The pulmonary trunk to aorta route is the ductus arteriosus, a separate shunt that would still work. It would be the answer if the ductus arteriosus were missing.
questions.answerText: Lung bypass between the atria

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: If the ductus arteriosus failed to form, which fetal bypass route would be lost?
options: Lung bypass from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
Return of fetal blood to the placenta
Liver bypass toward the inferior vena cava
Lung bypass between the atria
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is the short vessel that carries blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, sending blood from the right ventricle past the lungs. Without it, that route would be lost, and more blood leaving the right ventricle would be pushed toward the collapsed lungs. The foramen ovale would still provide the atrial-level bypass.
notes: Correct. The ductus arteriosus is the lung bypass between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
Return to the placenta happens through the umbilical arteries. Choose it if the question asked which vessels carry oxygen-poor blood away from the fetus.
The liver bypass is the ductus venosus. It would be the answer if the question asked which shunt runs through the liver.
The bypass between the atria is the foramen ovale, which would still be present. Pick it if the foramen ovale were missing.
questions.answerText: Lung bypass from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does the umbilical vein carry the most oxygen-rich blood in the fetus?
options: Its blood has mixed with blood returning from the lower body
Its blood has just passed through the fetal lungs
Its blood has just picked up oxygen at the placenta
Its blood has just left the left ventricle
questions.why: The placenta is where fetal blood picks up oxygen, and the umbilical vein is the first vessel the blood enters after leaving it. Once this blood reaches the fetal body, it starts to mix with oxygen-poor blood, for example in the inferior vena cava and the right atrium. So the umbilical vein holds the richest blood before any mixing happens.
notes: Mixing with returning blood lowers oxygen content rather than raising it. This happens in the inferior vena cava, after the umbilical vein blood has arrived.
The fetal lungs are collapsed and do not add oxygen. In the adult, freshly oxygenated blood would come from the lungs through the pulmonary veins.
Correct. The umbilical vein carries blood fresh from the placenta.

Blood leaving the left ventricle has already mixed with less oxygenated blood in the fetal heart. In the adult, the left ventricle would be the source of the most oxygen-rich blood pumped to the body.
questions.answerText: Its blood has just picked up oxygen at the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why do the umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the fetus?
options: They take used fetal blood to the placenta for exchange
They carry blood to the fetal liver for processing
They return blood to the fetal right atrium
They carry blood to the fetal lungs to pick up oxygen
questions.why: By the time blood reaches the umbilical arteries, it has already delivered oxygen to fetal tissues and picked up carbon dioxide and other wastes. The umbilical arteries carry this used blood out through the cord to the placenta, where wastes pass to the mother's blood and fresh oxygen is picked up. The refreshed blood then returns in the umbilical vein.
notes: Correct. The umbilical arteries take used blood to the placenta for exchange.
The liver receives blood from the umbilical vein, partly bypassed by the ductus venosus. It would be the answer if the question asked which organ the ductus venosus routes blood past.
Blood returns to the right atrium through the venae cavae, not the umbilical arteries. Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
The fetal lungs do not exchange gases before birth. Pick the lungs if the question asked about gas exchange after birth.
questions.answerText: They take used fetal blood to the placenta for exchange

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sentence best summarizes how fetal circulation works?
options: Placental blood passes fully through the liver and lungs before reaching the body
Oxygen-poor blood from the placenta enters the fetus and picks up oxygen in the fetal liver
Placental oxygen-rich blood enters, and shunts route much of it past the liver and lungs
Oxygen-rich blood from the fetal lungs is pumped to the placenta for storage
questions.why: The fetus depends on the placenta for oxygen and nutrients. Oxygen-rich blood enters through the umbilical vein, the ductus venosus carries much of it past the liver, and the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus carry much of it past the collapsed lungs. Used blood returns to the placenta through the umbilical arteries, and the shunts close once the lungs take over at birth.
notes: Sending all placental blood through the liver and lungs is exactly what the shunts prevent. This describes a route without any shunts.
Blood coming from the placenta is already oxygen-rich, and the liver does not add oxygen. Only the placenta before birth, and the lungs after birth, load blood with oxygen.
Correct. Placental oxygen plus three shunts around the liver and lungs sums up fetal circulation.
The fetal lungs do not oxygenate blood, and the placenta is an exchange organ, not a storage site. This reverses the direction of oxygen supply.
questions.answerText: Placental oxygen-rich blood enters, and shunts route much of it past the liver and lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which features describe a healthy blood vessel?
options: A lining with fatty deposits and a narrowed lumen
A smooth lining and a wall that stretches and recoils
A smooth lining and a thin wall bulging outward
A rough, damaged lining and a thick, stiff wall
questions.why: A healthy vessel has an intact, smooth endothelium lining its tunica intima, which lets blood flow without sticking or clotting. Its wall, especially in arteries, can stretch with each pulse of blood and then recoil. Most vascular disorders damage one of these two features, either roughening the lining or stiffening and weakening the wall.
notes: Fatty deposits and a narrowed lumen describe atherosclerosis. Choose this if the question asked how plaque changes an artery.
Correct. A smooth lining and an elastic wall mark a healthy vessel.
An outward bulge describes an aneurysm, a weakened wall that can rupture. It would be the answer if the question asked about a balloon-like swelling of an artery.
A rough lining and a stiff, thick wall describe a diseased artery, as in arteriosclerosis. Pick this if the question asked about general stiffening of artery walls.
questions.answerText: A smooth lining and a wall that stretches and recoils

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a vascular disorder?
options: A disease of the heart valves that lets blood leak backward
A vessel disease that narrows, weakens, or lets blood pool
A blockage of lymphatic vessels that causes tissue swelling
A shortage of red blood cells or hemoglobin in the blood
questions.why: Vascular means relating to blood vessels. A vascular disorder is a disease of the vessel itself, and most of them change the vessel in one of three ways: they narrow the lumen, as atherosclerosis does; they weaken the wall, as in an aneurysm; or they let blood pool, as in varicose veins.
notes: Leaky heart valves are a heart disorder, involving valves inside the heart. This would be the answer if the question asked about valve problems of the heart.
Correct. Vascular disorders narrow, weaken, or let blood pool in vessels.
Blocked lymphatic vessels cause lymphedema, a lymphatic disorder. Choose it if the question asked about swelling from poor lymph drainage.
A shortage of red blood cells or hemoglobin is anemia, a blood disorder rather than a vessel disorder. Pick it if the question asked about the blood's oxygen-carrying ability.
questions.answerText: A vessel disease that narrows, weakens, or lets blood pool

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which layer of an artery wall is damaged at the start of plaque formation?
options: Tunica externa
Tunica media
Tunica intima
External elastic lamina
questions.why: Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the endothelium, the smooth lining of the tunica intima. Once this lining is damaged, fatty material, cells, and debris start to collect in the wall at that spot, forming a plaque. Because the plaque starts in the innermost layer, it bulges into the lumen as it grows.
notes: The tunica externa is the outer collagen layer that anchors the vessel. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer is thickest in a vein.
The tunica media is the middle smooth muscle and elastic layer. Pick it if the question asked which layer is thickest in an artery.
Correct. Plaque starts with damage to the endothelium of the tunica intima.
The external elastic lamina separates the media from the externa, well away from the lining. Choose it if the question asked about the boundary between the middle and outer layers.
questions.answerText: Tunica intima

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is an atheroma?
options: A balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall
A clot that forms on the surface of a roughened plaque
A clot or fragment that breaks free and travels in the blood
A plaque of fatty material, cells, and debris in an artery wall
questions.why: An atheroma, also called a plaque, is the deposit that builds up in atherosclerosis. It forms in the artery wall after injury to the endothelium and contains fatty material, cells, and debris. As it grows, it bulges into the lumen and narrows the channel that blood flows through.
notes: A balloon-like bulge is an aneurysm. Choose it if the question asked about a weakened artery wall at risk of rupture.
A clot on a roughened plaque is a thrombus. Pick it if the question asked what can suddenly block an artery that already has a plaque.
A clot or fragment that travels is an embolus. It would be the answer if the question asked what lodges in a lung artery in a pulmonary embolism.
Correct. An atheroma is the fatty plaque within an artery wall.
questions.answerText: A plaque of fatty material, cells, and debris in an artery wall

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What happens to the lumen of an artery as an atheroma grows?
options: It widens as the plaque pushes the wall outward
It narrows as the plaque bulges inward
It fills with fluid that leaks from the plaque
It stays the same because the plaque grows outward
questions.why: A plaque forms in the tunica intima, the innermost layer of the artery wall. As it enlarges, it bulges into the lumen, the hollow channel where blood flows. The narrower channel lets less blood through to the tissues downstream.
notes: A widened vessel with an outward bulge describes an aneurysm. Pick it if the question asked about a weakened artery wall that balloons out.
Correct. A growing plaque bulges inward and narrows the lumen.
The lumen narrows because of the solid plaque, not because of fluid leaking out of it. Leaking fluid is not part of how a plaque narrows an artery.
Because the plaque starts in the innermost layer, it pushes into the channel rather than away from it. A plaque that left the lumen unchanged would not reduce blood flow.
questions.answerText: It narrows as the plaque bulges inward

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is arteriosclerosis?
options: General stiffening and thickening of artery walls
A blood clot in a deep vein of the leg
A balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall
Inflammation of a vein, causing redness and pain
questions.why: Sclerosis means hardening, so arteriosclerosis literally means hardening of the arteries. It is a general term for artery walls that become thick and stiff and lose their ability to stretch and recoil. Atherosclerosis, caused by fatty plaques, is its most common form.
notes: Correct. Arteriosclerosis is the general stiffening and thickening of artery walls.
A clot in a deep leg vein is a deep vein thrombosis. Choose it if the question asked about a clot that can travel to the lungs.
A balloon-like bulge is an aneurysm. Pick it if the question asked which disorder can rupture in the aorta or brain.
Inflammation of a vein is phlebitis. It would be the answer if the question asked what causes pain, redness, and tenderness along a vein.
questions.answerText: General stiffening and thickening of artery walls

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How is atherosclerosis related to arteriosclerosis?
options: Atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis
They are unrelated, since one affects arteries and the other veins
Arteriosclerosis is the most common form of atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis is the healed stage that follows arteriosclerosis
questions.why: Arteriosclerosis is the broad term for stiff, thickened artery walls. Atherosclerosis is one specific kind, in which the stiffening comes from fatty plaques (atheromas) building up in the wall. Because it is by far the most frequent cause, atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis.
notes: Correct. Atherosclerosis is one type, and the most common type, of arteriosclerosis.
Both terms describe arteries, as the word root arterio tells you. Neither one is a vein disorder.
This flips the relationship. Arteriosclerosis is the broad category, and atherosclerosis is the specific plaque-driven type within it.
Atherosclerosis is not a healed stage; it is an ongoing disease that worsens as plaque grows. This misconception treats the two names as steps in time instead of a category and a type.
questions.answerText: Atherosclerosis is the most common form of arteriosclerosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Where are aneurysms most common?
options: The superficial veins of the legs
The aorta and the arteries of the brain
The deep veins of the legs
The veins of the rectal and anal region
questions.why: An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall. They are most common in the aorta, the largest artery carrying blood under high pressure, and in the arteries of the brain. Both locations are dangerous because a rupture can cause severe bleeding.
notes: The superficial leg veins are the usual site of varicose veins. They would be the answer if the question asked where twisted, swollen veins appear.
Correct. Aneurysms most often form in the aorta and brain arteries.
The deep leg veins are the usual site of deep vein thrombosis, a clot rather than a bulging wall. Pick them if the question asked where DVT forms.
The rectal and anal veins are the site of hemorrhoids. Choose them if the question asked which varicose veins are found in the anal region.
questions.answerText: The aorta and the arteries of the brain

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does an aneurysm matter clinically?
options: It lets blood pool behind failed valves
It forms clots that travel to the lungs
It can rupture and bleed
It narrows the lumen with fatty plaque
questions.why: An aneurysm is a weakened section of artery wall that has ballooned outward. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, and a thin, stretched wall may not hold it. If the aneurysm ruptures, blood escapes rapidly from the artery, which can be life-threatening, especially in the aorta or the brain.
notes: Pooling behind failed valves describes varicose veins, a venous disorder. It would be the answer if the question asked about twisted, swollen leg veins.
Clots that travel to the lungs come from deep vein thrombosis. Choose that if the question asked what causes a pulmonary embolism.
Correct. The main danger of an aneurysm is rupture.
Narrowing by fatty plaque is atherosclerosis. Pick it if the question asked what causes coronary artery disease or peripheral artery disease.
questions.answerText: It can rupture and bleed

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is coronary artery disease?
options: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart wall
Loss of blood supply to part of the brain
Narrowing of the arteries of the limbs
Chronically high pressure within the arteries
questions.why: The coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta and supply the myocardium, the muscle of the heart wall. In coronary artery disease, usually caused by atherosclerosis, these arteries become narrowed. The heart muscle then receives less blood than it needs, especially when it is working hard.
notes: Correct. Coronary artery disease is narrowing of the arteries that feed the heart wall.
Loss of blood supply to the brain is a stroke. It would be the answer if the question asked about a blocked or burst brain artery.
Narrowing of limb arteries is peripheral artery disease. Pick it if the question asked about leg pain on walking.
Chronically high arterial pressure is hypertension. Choose it if the question asked which condition strains the heart and damages vessel walls over time.
questions.answerText: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart wall

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What can coronary artery disease cause?
