options: Lower-leg swelling and skin changes
Leg pain that comes on with walking
Myocardial ischemia and a heart attack
A stroke from a blocked brain artery
questions.why: Ischemia means a tissue is not getting enough blood. When narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough blood to the myocardium, the heart muscle becomes ischemic. If a coronary artery becomes blocked completely, the heart muscle it supplies begins to die, which is a heart attack (myocardial infarction).
notes: Lower-leg swelling and skin changes come from chronic venous insufficiency, a vein problem. Choose it if the question asked about long-term failure of leg vein valves.
Leg pain on walking is the classic symptom of peripheral artery disease. It would be the answer if the plaque were in a leg artery.
Correct. Narrowed coronary arteries can starve the myocardium and cause a heart attack.
A stroke comes from a blocked or burst artery in the brain, not the coronary arteries. Pick it if the question asked what happens when a brain artery loses flow.
questions.answerText: Myocardial ischemia and a heart attack

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is peripheral artery disease?
options: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart wall
A blood clot in a deep vein of the leg
Long-term failure of the valves of the leg veins
Narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs
questions.why: Peripheral means away from the center of the body. Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries that supply the limbs, most often the legs, usually because of atherosclerosis. The narrowed arteries cannot deliver enough blood to the muscles, especially during activity.
notes: Narrowing of the arteries to the heart wall is coronary artery disease. Choose it if the question asked what can lead to a heart attack.
A clot in a deep leg vein is deep vein thrombosis. It would be the answer if the question asked about a clot that could travel to the lungs.
Long-term valve failure in leg veins is chronic venous insufficiency. Pick it if the question asked what causes persistent lower-leg swelling and skin changes.
Correct. Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of limb arteries, most often in the legs.
questions.answerText: Narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which symptom is typical of peripheral artery disease?
options: Redness and tenderness along a vein
Twisted, bulging veins under the skin
Sudden weakness on one side of the body
Leg pain that comes on with walking
questions.why: In peripheral artery disease, the arteries of the legs are narrowed. At rest, enough blood may still get through, but walking increases the muscles' need for oxygen. The narrowed arteries cannot keep up, so the muscles are starved of blood and become painful until the person rests.
notes: Redness and tenderness along a vein are signs of phlebitis, inflammation of a vein. Choose it if the question asked about an inflamed vein.
Twisted, bulging veins are varicose veins, caused by failed venous valves. Pick them if the question asked about pooling in superficial leg veins.
Sudden weakness on one side of the body is a warning sign of stroke. It would be the answer if the question asked about a blocked or burst brain artery.
Correct. Pain with walking is the classic sign of peripheral artery disease.
questions.answerText: Leg pain that comes on with walking

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is hypertension?
options: Chronically high pressure within the arteries
A balloon-like bulge in an artery wall
Narrowing of the coronary arteries
Stiffening and thickening of artery walls
questions.why: Hyper means above normal and tension refers to pressure, so hypertension is high blood pressure. It means the pressure inside the arteries stays above normal over a long period, not just briefly during exercise or stress. This constant extra force strains the heart and wears on the vessel walls.
notes: Correct. Hypertension is chronically high arterial pressure.
A balloon-like bulge is an aneurysm. Pick it if the question asked which disorder is common in the aorta and brain arteries and can rupture.
Narrowed coronary arteries describe coronary artery disease. It would be the answer if the question asked what reduces blood supply to the heart wall.
Stiff, thick artery walls describe arteriosclerosis. Choose it if the question asked about general hardening of the arteries.
questions.answerText: Chronically high pressure within the arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does hypertension matter for health?
options: It causes brain tissue to die within minutes
It forms clots that travel straight to the lungs
It makes blood pool behind failed valves in the legs
It strains the heart and damages vessel walls over time
questions.why: When arterial pressure stays high, the heart must work harder with every beat to push blood out. At the same time, the constant extra force injures the walls of the arteries, damaging the endothelium where plaques can then begin. Over years, this raises the risk of heart disease, stroke, and other vessel problems.
notes: Brain tissue dying within minutes describes a stroke, a sudden event. Choose it if the question asked why a stroke is an emergency.
Clots traveling to the lungs come from deep vein thrombosis and cause a pulmonary embolism. That would be the answer if the question asked why a DVT is dangerous.
Pooling behind failed valves describes varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency, which are low-pressure vein problems. Pick that if the question asked about swollen leg veins.
Correct. Long-term high pressure strains the heart and harms vessel walls.
questions.answerText: It strains the heart and damages vessel walls over time

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a stroke?
options: Loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery
A clot that lodges in an artery of the lung
A bulge in the wall of a brain artery that has not ruptured
Loss of blood supply to the heart wall from a narrowed coronary artery
questions.why: A stroke happens when part of the brain stops receiving blood. This can occur because an artery is blocked, often by a plaque or a clot, or because an artery bursts and bleeds. Either way, the brain tissue supplied by that artery is cut off from oxygen.
notes: Correct. A stroke is loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery.
A clot in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism. It would be the answer if the question asked where a traveling DVT clot lodges.

An unruptured bulge in a brain artery is an aneurysm. It can cause a stroke if it bursts, but the bulge alone has not cut off blood supply. Choose it if the question asked about a weakened artery wall.
Loss of blood to the heart wall is a heart attack, from coronary artery disease. Pick it if the question asked about the myocardium.
questions.answerText: Loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is a stroke treated as an emergency?
options: Brain tissue begins to die within minutes without blood
The brain can store a full day's oxygen supply
Leg muscles lose their blood supply at the same time
The clot always travels on to the lungs next
questions.why: Neurons use a lot of oxygen and have almost no reserve. When blood flow to part of the brain stops, those neurons begin to die within minutes. The faster blood flow is restored, the more brain tissue can be saved.
notes: Correct. Brain tissue dies within minutes without blood flow.
The brain stores very little oxygen, which is exactly why a stroke is so urgent. This misconception reverses the reason for the emergency.
A stroke affects the brain's blood supply, not the legs. Loss of blood to the leg muscles describes peripheral artery disease.
A clot that blocks a brain artery stays in the brain; it does not move on to the lungs. Clots reach the lungs when they come from the deep veins, as in a pulmonary embolism.
questions.answerText: Brain tissue begins to die within minutes without blood

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Where do varicose veins most often occur?
options: Superficial veins of the legs
Coronary arteries of the heart
Arteries at the base of the brain
Pulmonary arteries of the lungs
questions.why: Varicose veins are superficial veins that have become twisted and swollen because their valves have failed. They are most common in the legs, where veins carry low-pressure blood upward against gravity. When the valves fail, blood pools and stretches the veins until they bulge visibly under the skin.
notes: Correct. Varicose veins are most common in the superficial veins of the legs.
The coronary arteries are the site of coronary artery disease. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels narrow in a heart attack.
The arteries of the brain are a common site of aneurysms. Pick them if the question asked where a weakened, bulging artery might rupture.
The pulmonary arteries are where a pulmonary embolism lodges. Choose them if the question asked where a clot from a deep vein ends up.
questions.answerText: Superficial veins of the legs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is deep vein thrombosis?
options: A clot lodged in an artery of the lung
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg
Twisted, swollen veins just under the skin
Inflammation of a vein, with redness and pain
questions.why: A thrombus is a clot that forms inside a vessel. Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is a thrombus in one of the deep veins, most often in the leg, where blood flows slowly under low pressure. The clot can break free and travel through the venous return to the lungs.
notes: A clot lodged in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism, which can result when a DVT breaks loose. Pick it if the question asked where a traveling leg clot ends up.
Correct. DVT is a clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg.
Twisted, swollen superficial veins are varicose veins. Choose them if the question asked about failed valves in surface leg veins.
Inflammation of a vein is phlebitis. It would be the answer if the question asked what causes pain, redness, and tenderness along a vein.
questions.answerText: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is a pulmonary embolism?
options: A plaque that narrows the pulmonary veins
A ruptured bulge in the wall of the aorta
A clot, often from a deep vein, that lodges in a lung artery
A clot that forms and stays in a deep vein of the leg
questions.why: An embolus is a clot or fragment that breaks free and travels in the bloodstream. A pulmonary embolism is an embolus that lodges in an artery of the lung, most often a clot that started as a deep vein thrombosis in the leg. It blocks blood flow to part of the lung and is a life-threatening emergency.
notes: Plaque in vessels is atherosclerosis, which affects arteries, and a pulmonary embolism is a clot rather than a plaque. Plaque narrowing would fit a question about coronary artery disease.
A ruptured bulge in the aorta is a ruptured aortic aneurysm. Choose it if the question asked about massive bleeding from the body's largest artery.
Correct. A pulmonary embolism is a traveling clot stuck in a lung artery.
A clot that stays in the leg vein is a deep vein thrombosis. Pick it if the question asked about a clot that has not moved yet.
questions.answerText: A clot, often from a deep vein, that lodges in a lung artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is a pulmonary embolism dangerous?
options: It makes blood pool in the leg veins
It weakens the aortic wall until it ruptures
It blocks blood flow to part of the lung
It blocks blood flow out of the brain
questions.why: All the blood returning from the body must pass through the pulmonary arteries to reach the lungs. A clot lodged in one of these arteries blocks that flow, so part of the lung receives no blood and the blood cannot pick up oxygen there. A large embolism can be fatal, which is why it is treated as an emergency.
notes: Pooling in leg veins describes varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency. Pick that if the question asked about failed valves in the legs.
Weakening of the aortic wall describes an aortic aneurysm. It would be the answer if the question asked about a bulge in the aorta that could rupture.
Correct. A pulmonary embolism blocks blood flow into the lung.
A clot in a pulmonary artery affects the lungs, not the brain. Loss of blood supply to brain tissue describes a stroke.
questions.answerText: It blocks blood flow to part of the lung

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which symptoms are typical of phlebitis?
options: Pain, redness, and tenderness along a vein
Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath
Leg pain that comes on only with walking
Sudden weakness on one side of the body
questions.why: Phleb refers to a vein and itis means inflammation, so phlebitis is inflammation of a vein. Like inflammation anywhere, it produces pain, redness, and tenderness, and these follow the course of the affected vein under the skin.
notes: Correct. Phlebitis causes pain, redness, and tenderness along the vein.
Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath are warning signs of a pulmonary embolism. Choose them if the question asked what happens when a clot lodges in a lung artery.
Pain with walking is typical of peripheral artery disease, where narrowed leg arteries starve the muscles. Pick it if the question asked about narrowed limb arteries.
Sudden one-sided weakness is a warning sign of stroke. It would be the answer if the question asked about loss of blood supply to the brain.
questions.answerText: Pain, redness, and tenderness along a vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What is chronic venous insufficiency?
options: A single clot in a deep vein of the leg
Long-term valve failure in the leg veins
Inflammation of a vein near the skin
Narrowing of the arteries of the legs
questions.why: Chronic means long-lasting, and venous insufficiency means the veins are not returning blood well. In chronic venous insufficiency, the valves of the leg veins have failed over a long period. Blood is not moved effectively back toward the heart, so it collects in the lower legs.
notes: A single clot in a deep leg vein is deep vein thrombosis. Pick it if the question asked about a clot that could travel to the lungs.
Correct. Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term valve failure in the leg veins.
Inflammation of a vein is phlebitis. Choose it if the question asked what causes redness and tenderness along a vein.
Narrowed leg arteries describe peripheral artery disease. It would be the answer if the question asked about pain on walking.
questions.answerText: Long-term valve failure in the leg veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What can chronic venous insufficiency cause?
options: Loss of blood supply to part of the brain
Leg pain that comes on with walking
Persistent lower-leg swelling and skin changes
Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath
questions.why: When the valves of the leg veins fail over a long time, blood pools in the lower legs and pressure in those veins stays high. Fluid is pushed out into the surrounding tissue, causing persistent swelling. Over months and years, the skin of the lower leg also changes in appearance from this constant congestion.
notes: Loss of blood to part of the brain is a stroke. Choose it if the question asked about a blocked or burst brain artery.
Pain on walking comes from peripheral artery disease, an artery problem. Pick it if the question asked about narrowed leg arteries.
Correct. Long-term valve failure causes lasting lower-leg swelling and skin changes.
Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath suggest a pulmonary embolism. It would be the answer if the question asked about a clot lodged in a lung artery.
questions.answerText: Persistent lower-leg swelling and skin changes

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis?
options: Arteriosclerosis affects veins, while atherosclerosis affects arteries
Atherosclerosis is general artery stiffening, and arteriosclerosis is its plaque-forming type
Arteriosclerosis is general artery stiffening, and atherosclerosis is its plaque-forming type
Both terms describe a weakened artery wall that bulges outward
questions.why: Arteriosclerosis is the broad term for thick, stiff artery walls. Atherosclerosis is a specific type in which the stiffening and narrowing come from fatty plaques, called atheromas, building up in the wall. The athero part of the name, which refers to the fatty plaque, is the clue to which term is the specific one.
notes: Both terms describe arteries, as the arterio root shows. Vein disorders include varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis.
This swaps the two terms. The word athero points to fatty plaque, so atherosclerosis is the specific, plaque-forming type.
Correct. Arteriosclerosis is the general category, and atherosclerosis is the plaque-forming type.
A weakened wall that bulges outward is an aneurysm. Pick it if the question asked about an artery at risk of rupture.
questions.answerText: Arteriosclerosis is general artery stiffening, and atherosclerosis is its plaque-forming type

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How does injury to the endothelium contribute to plaque formation?
options: It relaxes the tunica media so the vessel widens
It weakens the tunica externa so the wall bulges outward
It roughens the intima and gives plaque a place to start
It breaks the venous valves so blood pools in the legs
questions.why: The endothelium is the smooth inner lining of the tunica intima. When it is injured, by high blood pressure for example, that spot is no longer smooth and protected. Fatty material, cells, and debris begin to collect in the wall there, and the deposit grows into an atheroma, or plaque.
notes: Relaxing the smooth muscle of the media is vasodilation, a normal way to increase flow. It would be the answer if the question asked how a vessel widens.
A wall that bulges outward describes an aneurysm, which involves weakening of the wall rather than plaque. Pick that if the question asked how an aneurysm forms.
Correct. Endothelial injury is where a plaque begins.
Broken venous valves cause varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency, not arterial plaque. Choose that if the question asked about pooling in leg veins.
questions.answerText: It roughens the intima and gives plaque a place to start

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does a growing plaque reduce blood flow through an artery?
options: It bulges into the lumen and narrows the channel
It thins the wall so blood leaks out of the artery
It closes the artery's valves against forward flow
It widens the lumen so blood slows and pools
questions.why: A plaque grows in the innermost layer of the artery wall, so as it enlarges it pushes into the lumen. A narrower channel lets less blood pass at a time, so the tissue downstream receives less blood. The more the plaque grows, the greater the reduction in flow.
notes: Correct. The plaque narrows the lumen, so less blood gets through.
Plaque thickens and stiffens the wall rather than thinning it, and blood does not leak out through it. A thin, weakened wall that can burst describes an aneurysm.
Arteries do not have valves along their length. Valves are found in veins, the answer if the question asked what prevents backflow in the legs.
A plaque narrows the lumen rather than widening it. Widened, pooling vessels describe varicose veins.
questions.answerText: It bulges into the lumen and narrows the channel

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why can a roughened plaque suddenly make blood flow much worse?
options: It can turn into an aneurysm and widen the lumen
It can cause nearby valves to fail and allow backflow
It can dissolve quickly and release fat into the lumen
A thrombus can form on it and suddenly block the vessel
questions.why: A plaque that has a rough or broken surface no longer has smooth endothelium covering it. Platelets and clotting factors collect on the rough spot and form a thrombus, a clot attached to the vessel wall. Because the lumen is already narrowed by the plaque, a clot on top of it can block the vessel suddenly, triggering a heart attack or stroke.
notes: An aneurysm is a bulging, weakened wall and would widen the lumen rather than block it. Pick it if the question asked about a wall at risk of rupture.
Arteries do not have valves along their length, so valve failure is not part of this process. Failed valves describe varicose veins.
Plaques do not simply dissolve and release fat; they tend to grow over time. A sudden worsening comes from a clot forming on the plaque.
Correct. A clot on a roughened plaque can suddenly close an already narrowed artery.
questions.answerText: A thrombus can form on it and suddenly block the vessel

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares an aneurysm and atherosclerosis?
options: An aneurysm is a weak wall that bulges outward, while atherosclerosis is plaque that narrows the lumen
Both are vein disorders caused by failed valves in the legs
An aneurysm is plaque that narrows the lumen, while atherosclerosis is a weak wall that bulges outward
An aneurysm narrows the lumen, while atherosclerosis widens it
questions.why: Both are artery disorders, but they change the wall in opposite directions. In an aneurysm, a weakened section of wall balloons outward, and the danger is rupture. In atherosclerosis, plaque builds up inside the wall and bulges inward, and the danger is reduced or blocked blood flow.
notes: Correct. An aneurysm bulges outward, while atherosclerosis narrows the lumen.
Both are artery disorders, not vein disorders. Failed valves in the legs cause varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency.
This swaps the two disorders. The plaque belongs to atherosclerosis, and the outward bulge belongs to an aneurysm.
This reverses the effect on the lumen. An aneurysm enlarges the vessel, and atherosclerosis narrows it.
questions.answerText: An aneurysm is a weak wall that bulges outward, while atherosclerosis is plaque that narrows the lumen

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why do arterial disorders usually involve narrowing of the channel or weakening of the wall?
options: Arteries depend on valves that can fail and let blood pool
Arteries carry blood at low pressure, so it tends to clot
Arteries have walls only one cell thick that tear easily
Arteries carry blood under high pressure, which strains the wall
questions.why: Arteries receive blood directly from the heart under high pressure. Over time that pressure can injure the lining, which starts plaque formation and narrowing, or it can weaken a section of wall until it bulges into an aneurysm. So the problems typical of arteries come from the force they must handle.
notes: Arteries do not have valves along their length. Valve failure and pooling describe vein disorders, the answer if the question asked about varicose veins.
Low pressure and slow flow describe veins, where clots such as DVT form more easily. Pick that idea if the question asked why venous disorders involve pooling or clotting.
Walls one cell thick belong to capillaries. Arteries have the thickest walls of any vessel, built to resist high pressure.
Correct. High pressure explains why arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall.
questions.answerText: Arteries carry blood under high pressure, which strains the wall

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why do venous disorders usually involve pooled or clotted blood?
options: Veins carry low-pressure blood and depend on valves
Veins have thick, stiff walls that cannot stretch
Veins carry blood under the highest pressure in the body
Veins lack a tunica intima to keep blood moving
questions.why: By the time blood reaches the veins, its pressure is low, so it depends on valves and the squeezing of skeletal muscles to keep moving toward the heart. When valves fail or muscles are inactive for long periods, blood slows and collects. Slow, pooled blood stretches the veins, as in varicose veins, and is more likely to clot, as in deep vein thrombosis.
notes: Correct. Low pressure and dependence on valves make veins prone to pooling and clotting.
Veins have thin walls that stretch easily, which is why pooled blood can make them bulge. Thick, stiff walls describe arteriosclerosis in arteries.
The highest pressure is in the arteries near the heart, not the veins. High pressure explains arterial disorders such as aneurysms.
Veins do have a tunica intima, and their valves are made from it. The lining itself does not push blood forward.
questions.answerText: Veins carry low-pressure blood and depend on valves

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How does valve failure lead to varicose veins?
options: Failed valves let blood fall back, pool, and stretch the vein
Failed valves raise the pressure in the arteries of the leg
Failed valves let fatty plaque build up inside the vein wall
Failed valves let blood escape from the vein into nearby arteries
questions.why: Healthy valves in the leg veins let blood move only toward the heart. When they fail, gravity pulls blood back down, and it collects in the superficial veins. The extra blood stretches the thin vein walls until the veins become twisted, swollen, and visible under the skin.
notes: Correct. Backflow through failed valves makes blood pool and the veins bulge.
Venous valve failure affects the veins, not arterial pressure. Chronically high arterial pressure is hypertension.
Fatty plaque buildup is atherosclerosis, which affects arteries rather than veins. Pick it if the question asked what narrows the coronary or leg arteries.
Veins and arteries are not directly connected by valves, and blood does not escape into arteries. A direct artery-to-vein connection is an arteriovenous anastomosis.
questions.answerText: Failed valves let blood fall back, pool, and stretch the vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot breaks free from a deep vein in the leg. Which path does it follow to reach the lung?
options: Leg vein, femoral artery, aorta, left ventricle, pulmonary trunk
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, left atrium, pulmonary vein
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
questions.why: A clot that breaks loose from a deep leg vein simply follows normal venous return. It travels up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and is pumped into the pulmonary trunk and then a pulmonary artery. The pulmonary arteries branch into smaller and smaller vessels, so the clot eventually lodges in one, causing a pulmonary embolism.
notes: A clot in a vein cannot jump into an artery; veins return blood to the heart. The femoral artery carries blood down the leg, away from the heart.
Correct. The clot follows venous return through the right heart to the pulmonary arteries.

Blood does not normally pass from the right atrium to the left atrium after birth, and the pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the heart. Right-to-left atrial flow is the fetal route through the foramen ovale.
Blood from the body enters the right side of the heart, not the left. This route skips the lungs entirely, which is why it does not explain a pulmonary embolism.
questions.answerText: Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism?
options: A DVT is a clot in a leg artery, while a pulmonary embolism is a clot in a lung vein
Both are clots that form and stay in the right atrium
A DVT is a clot in a deep vein, while a pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in a lung artery
A DVT is a clot lodged in a lung artery, while a pulmonary embolism is a clot in a deep vein
questions.why: A deep vein thrombosis is a clot that forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg. If part of it breaks free, it becomes an embolus and travels through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries. When it lodges there, the condition is a pulmonary embolism. The two are often stages of the same event.
notes: DVT is in a vein, not an artery, and a pulmonary embolism lodges in a pulmonary artery, not a vein. Pick a leg artery if the question asked about peripheral artery disease.
Neither condition is defined as a clot staying in the heart. The right atrium is only a stop along the route from the leg veins to the lungs.
Correct. DVT is where the clot forms, and pulmonary embolism is where it can end up.
This swaps the two. The word pulmonary refers to the lung, so the pulmonary embolism is the one in the lung.
questions.answerText: A DVT is a clot in a deep vein, while a pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in a lung artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How can the same atherosclerotic process cause coronary artery disease, stroke, or peripheral artery disease?
options: The disease depends only on how fast the heart is beating
The location of the plaque determines which disease results
Each disease comes from a different kind of plaque material
Plaque in veins causes stroke, and plaque in arteries causes heart attack
questions.why: Atherosclerosis is the same wall change wherever it happens: plaque builds up and narrows an artery. What differs is which tissue loses blood. Plaque in a coronary artery starves the heart muscle and can cause a heart attack, plaque in a brain artery can cause a stroke, and plaque in a leg artery causes peripheral artery disease.
notes: Heart rate does not decide which disease a plaque causes. The disease is named for the tissue that loses its blood supply.
Correct. The same plaque produces different diseases depending on which artery it affects.
The plaque material is basically the same in each case: fatty material, cells, and debris. The difference is the artery involved, not the plaque type.
Atherosclerosis affects arteries, not veins. A stroke happens when a brain artery is blocked or bursts.
questions.answerText: The location of the plaque determines which disease results

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How does coronary artery disease lead to a myocardial infarction?
options: Narrowed coronary arteries starve the myocardium of oxygen
Narrowed coronary veins stop blood returning to the right atrium
Narrowed pulmonary arteries stop the heart from receiving blood
Narrowed coronary arteries block blood leaving the ventricles
questions.why: A myocardial infarction, or heart attack, is the death of a region of heart muscle. The myocardium gets its own blood from the coronary arteries, not from the blood passing through the chambers. When these arteries are narrowed or blocked, the muscle they supply is starved of oxygen, and if the blockage lasts, that muscle dies.
notes: Correct. Without enough coronary blood flow, heart muscle is starved of oxygen and can die.
Coronary artery disease involves arteries, not cardiac veins. The cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, the answer if the question asked how blood leaves the heart wall.
The pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs. Blocking them describes a pulmonary embolism, not a heart attack.
The coronary arteries feed the heart wall; they do not control blood leaving the ventricles. Blood leaves through the aortic and pulmonary valves.
questions.answerText: Narrowed coronary arteries starve the myocardium of oxygen

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does peripheral artery disease cause pain during walking but often not at rest?
options: Walking makes blood pool in the leg veins and stretch them
Working muscles need more blood than narrowed arteries supply
Walking inflames the leg veins and presses on the muscles
Walking loosens clots that travel from the leg to the lungs
questions.why: At rest, leg muscles need only a modest blood supply, and a narrowed artery may still deliver enough. During walking, the muscles work harder and need much more oxygen. The narrowed arteries cannot increase flow to match, so the muscles become starved of blood and painful until the person stops and rests.
notes: Pooling in leg veins describes varicose veins or chronic venous insufficiency. Walking actually helps venous return through the skeletal muscle pump.
Correct. The gap between muscle demand and limited supply causes the pain.
Inflamed veins describe phlebitis. It would be the answer if the question asked about redness and tenderness along a vein.
Clots traveling to the lungs come from deep vein thrombosis, a venous problem. Pick that if the question asked how a pulmonary embolism forms.
questions.answerText: Working muscles need more blood than narrowed arteries supply

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How does hypertension damage blood vessels over time?
options: Low pressure lets blood pool and clot in the arteries
High pressure makes venous valves close for good
High pressure widens every vessel and keeps walls healthy
Constant high pressure strains and injures the vessel walls
questions.why: In hypertension, blood presses harder than normal against the artery walls with every heartbeat, year after year. That steady extra force injures the endothelium and strains the wall. An injured lining is where plaques can start, so hypertension also raises the risk of atherosclerosis, heart disease, and stroke.
notes: Hypertension is high pressure, not low. Low-pressure pooling and clotting describe veins, as in deep vein thrombosis.
Hypertension affects the arteries and does not close venous valves. Failed or damaged venous valves describe varicose veins.
High pressure harms vessel walls rather than keeping them healthy. This misconception treats more pressure as better flow.
Correct. Long-term high pressure strains and injures the walls.
questions.answerText: Constant high pressure strains and injures the vessel walls

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a blocked-artery stroke and a burst-artery stroke?
options: Both are caused by clots that travel up from the leg veins
A blocked-artery stroke affects the heart, while a burst-artery stroke affects the brain
A blocked-artery stroke affects veins, while a burst-artery stroke affects arteries
Both cut off brain blood supply, one by a blockage and the other by a rupture that bleeds
questions.why: Every stroke means part of the brain has lost its blood supply. In one type, an artery is blocked, often by a plaque or a clot, and blood cannot get through. In the other, a weakened artery, such as one with an aneurysm, bursts and bleeds, so the tissue beyond it loses its supply and blood leaks into or around the brain.
notes: A burst artery bleeds; it is not caused by a clot. Clots from the leg veins normally lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.
Both kinds of stroke affect the brain. Loss of blood to the heart muscle is a heart attack.
Both kinds of stroke involve arteries supplying the brain. Veins are not the vessels at fault in either one.
Correct. Both types cut off brain blood supply, by blockage or by rupture.
questions.answerText: Both cut off brain blood supply, one by a blockage and the other by a rupture that bleeds

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A plaque gradually narrows one of a patient's coronary arteries. Which disease process does this describe, and what can it lead to?
options: Stroke, from loss of blood supply to the brain
Peripheral artery disease, which causes leg pain on walking
Deep vein thrombosis, from a clot in a leg vein
Coronary artery disease, which can lead to a heart attack
questions.why: The coronary arteries supply the myocardium, the muscle of the heart wall. When atherosclerotic plaque narrows them, the condition is coronary artery disease. If the narrowing becomes severe or a clot forms on the plaque, the heart muscle downstream can be starved of oxygen and die, which is a myocardial infarction.
notes: A stroke involves loss of blood to the brain. It would be the answer if the plaque were in a brain artery.
Peripheral artery disease involves the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs. Pick it if the plaque were in a leg artery.
Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a vein, not plaque in an artery. Choose it if the question described a clot in a deep leg vein.
Correct. A narrowed coronary artery is coronary artery disease, which can lead to a heart attack.
questions.answerText: Coronary artery disease, which can lead to a heart attack

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A plaque narrows an artery in a patient's leg. Which disorder does this suggest?
options: Deep vein thrombosis
Chronic venous insufficiency
Peripheral artery disease
Varicose veins
questions.why: Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs, and atherosclerotic plaque is the usual cause. The narrowed artery delivers less blood to the leg muscles, which typically causes pain on walking.
notes: Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep leg vein. It would be the answer if the question described a clot rather than a plaque.
Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term failure of the leg vein valves. Choose it if the question described persistent lower-leg swelling and skin changes.
Correct. Plaque narrowing a leg artery is peripheral artery disease.
Varicose veins come from failed valves in superficial leg veins, not plaque in an artery. Pick them if the question described twisted, bulging surface veins.
questions.answerText: Peripheral artery disease

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A plaque blocks an artery supplying part of a patient's brain, and that tissue loses its blood supply. What event has occurred?
options: Heart attack
Stroke
Peripheral artery disease
Pulmonary embolism
questions.why: A stroke is the loss of blood supply to part of the brain, caused by a blocked or burst artery. Here the artery is blocked by plaque, so the brain tissue it supplies is starved of oxygen. Because neurons begin to die within minutes, a stroke is a medical emergency.
notes: A heart attack is the death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery. Pick it if the plaque were in a coronary artery.
Correct. Loss of blood supply to brain tissue is a stroke.
Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the limb arteries. Choose it if the plaque were in a leg artery.
A pulmonary embolism is a clot lodged in a lung artery, usually from a deep vein. It would be the answer if the blockage were in the lungs.
questions.answerText: Stroke

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why can a ruptured aortic aneurysm be catastrophic?
options: The aorta has valves along its length that fail when it bulges
The aorta carries high-pressure blood, so a rupture bleeds massively
An aortic aneurysm sends clots directly into the lungs
The aorta carries low-pressure blood that pools inside the bulge
questions.why: The aorta is the largest artery in the body and receives blood directly from the left ventricle under high pressure. When a weakened, bulging section of its wall tears open, blood pours out very quickly. This rapid, massive blood loss can be fatal within a short time.
notes: The aorta has no valves along its length. The aortic valve sits at the junction of the left ventricle and the aorta, and it would be the answer if the question asked what prevents backflow into the left ventricle.
Correct. High pressure in the aorta means a rupture causes massive bleeding.
Clots that travel to the lungs come from the deep veins and pass through the right heart. Blood leaving the aorta goes to the body, not the lungs.
The aorta carries the highest-pressure blood in the body, not low-pressure blood. Low-pressure pooling describes veins, as in varicose veins.
questions.answerText: The aorta carries high-pressure blood, so a rupture bleeds massively

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why can a ruptured brain aneurysm cause sudden damage to the nervous system?
options: Rupture causes plaque to form in the coronary arteries
Blood escapes into or around the brain and tissue loses supply
Rupture stops the heart's chambers from filling with blood
Rupture blocks venous blood returning from the lower limbs
questions.why: A brain aneurysm is a weakened, bulging section of an artery that supplies the brain. When it ruptures, blood escapes into or around the brain, and the tissue that artery supplied loses its blood. Both the bleeding and the lost supply can damage neurons quickly, which is why the effects are sudden.
notes: A ruptured brain aneurysm does not create plaque elsewhere. Plaque in the coronary arteries is coronary artery disease.
Correct. Bleeding plus lost blood supply quickly damages brain tissue.
A brain artery does not control filling of the heart. The heart fills with blood returning through the venae cavae and pulmonary veins.
Venous return from the legs travels through the inferior vena cava, far from the brain arteries. Problems with leg venous return describe chronic venous insufficiency.
questions.answerText: Blood escapes into or around the brain and tissue loses supply

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient has a superficial leg vein that is swollen and twisted. Which valve problem explains this?
options: Failed valves let blood flow backward and pool
Overactive valves block blood from leaving the vein
Valves in the leg arteries have closed too tightly
Valves in the vein have hardened with fatty plaque
questions.why: Valves in leg veins normally keep blood moving upward toward the heart. When they fail, blood slips back and collects in the superficial veins. The extra volume stretches the thin walls, and over time the veins become swollen and twisted, which are varicose veins.
notes: Correct. Valve failure causes backflow and pooling, producing varicose veins.
Valves do not become overactive and trap blood; the problem is valves that no longer close. A blockage in a vein would more likely come from a clot, as in deep vein thrombosis.
Arteries do not have valves along their length. Narrowed leg arteries are peripheral artery disease, the answer if the patient had pain on walking.
Fatty plaque forms in artery walls, not in venous valves. Plaque in an artery describes atherosclerosis.
questions.answerText: Failed valves let blood flow backward and pool

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot breaks loose from a deep leg vein. Which side of the heart does it pass through before reaching the lung?
options: Right side of the heart
Both sides equally
Neither side, since it travels straight to the lung
Left side of the heart
questions.why: Blood from the legs returns through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium, then flows into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs. A clot riding in that blood follows the same path. This is why a deep vein clot ends up in a lung artery rather than in the brain or heart wall.
notes: Correct. Venous blood, and any clot in it, passes through the right heart on its way to the lungs.
After birth, the two sides of the heart are separated, so the clot does not pass through both. Normal venous return goes only through the right side before the lungs.
Every vessel carrying blood from the body to the lungs passes through the right side of the heart first. There is no direct path from the vena cava to the lungs.
The left side of the heart receives blood after it has passed through the lungs. A clot from a leg vein normally lodges in the lungs before ever reaching the left side.
questions.answerText: Right side of the heart

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does a deep vein thrombosis become dangerous when the clot breaks free?
options: It can block a leg artery and cause peripheral artery disease
It can settle in a superficial vein and cause varicose veins
It can enter the hepatic portal vein and block the liver
It can lodge in a pulmonary artery as a pulmonary embolism
questions.why: While a DVT stays in place, it mainly affects the leg vein it sits in. Once it breaks free, it becomes an embolus and is carried by normal venous return up the inferior vena cava and through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries. There it lodges and blocks blood flow to part of the lung, a life-threatening pulmonary embolism.
notes: Venous clots travel toward the heart, not into leg arteries. Peripheral artery disease is plaque narrowing a limb artery.
Clots in deep veins travel toward the heart, not back out to superficial veins. Varicose veins come from failed valves in superficial veins.
The hepatic portal vein drains the digestive organs, not the legs. Blood from a leg vein enters the inferior vena cava instead.
Correct. A traveling DVT can become a pulmonary embolism.
questions.answerText: It can lodge in a pulmonary artery as a pulmonary embolism

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why are hemorrhoids grouped with varicose veins?
options: They are plaques in the arteries of the colon
They are aneurysms of the rectal arteries
They are clots lodged in the deep pelvic veins
They are varicose veins of the rectal and anal region
questions.why: Varicose veins are veins that have become swollen and twisted as blood pools in them. Hemorrhoids are the same kind of change in the veins of the rectal and anal region. They are a common cause of rectal discomfort and bleeding.
notes: Plaque in arteries is atherosclerosis. It would be the answer if the question asked what narrows arteries over time.
An aneurysm is a bulge in a weakened artery wall, common in the aorta and brain. Hemorrhoids involve veins, not arteries.
A clot in a deep vein is a deep vein thrombosis, most often in the leg. Pick it if the question asked about a clot that could travel to the lungs.
Correct. Hemorrhoids are varicose veins in the rectal and anal region.
questions.answerText: They are varicose veins of the rectal and anal region

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does chronic venous insufficiency produce lasting swelling of the lower legs?
options: Failed vein valves let blood and fluid pool in the lower legs
Narrowed leg arteries deliver too little blood to the legs
A ruptured artery bleeds into the tissues of the leg
Clots from the legs travel to the lungs and back
questions.why: In chronic venous insufficiency, the valves of the leg veins have failed over a long time, so blood is not returned effectively to the heart. Blood collects in the lower leg veins, and the raised pressure pushes fluid out into the surrounding tissue. Because the valve failure is long-term, the swelling persists rather than coming and going.
notes: Correct. Long-term valve failure lets blood and fluid pool, causing lasting swelling.
Narrowed leg arteries describe peripheral artery disease, which causes pain on walking rather than swelling. Pick it if the question asked about too little blood reaching the leg muscles.
A ruptured artery causes sudden bleeding, not slow, lasting swelling. Rupture is the main danger of an aneurysm.
Clots that leave the legs lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism; they do not travel back. That would be the answer if the question asked about sudden chest pain and breathlessness.
questions.answerText: Failed vein valves let blood and fluid pool in the lower legs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Besides the hepatic portal system, which portal system is named in the course notes?
options: Cerebral arterial circle
Coronary sinus
Palmar arterial arches
Hypophyseal portal system
questions.why: A portal system passes blood through two capillary beds in series before it returns to the heart. In the hypophyseal portal system, blood picks up substances in a capillary bed in the hypothalamus and carries them through portal veins to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary. This lets the hypothalamus send chemical signals straight to the pituitary.
notes: The cerebral arterial circle is an arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain, giving alternate routes if one artery is blocked. Pick it if the question asked for an example of an anastomosis.
The coronary sinus is a vein on the back of the heart that drains the cardiac veins into the right atrium. Choose it if the question asked where blood from the heart wall returns.

The palmar arches are arterial anastomoses in the hand formed by the radial and ulnar arteries. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood still reaches the fingers when one forearm artery is blocked.
Correct. The hypophyseal portal system links the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary through two capillary beds.
questions.answerText: Hypophyseal portal system

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a thrombus and an embolus?
options: A thrombus is a fatty plaque, while an embolus is a bulging artery wall
Both are bulges in a weakened vessel wall that can rupture
An embolus stays where it formed, while a thrombus breaks free and travels
A thrombus stays where it formed, while an embolus breaks free and travels
questions.why: A thrombus is a clot that forms inside a vessel and stays attached there, for example on a roughened plaque or in a deep leg vein. If a thrombus, or a piece of it, breaks loose and is carried in the blood, it becomes an embolus. An embolus lodges wherever the vessel becomes too narrow, as in a pulmonary embolism.
notes: A fatty plaque is an atheroma, and a bulging wall is an aneurysm. Pick those terms if the question asked about atherosclerosis or an artery at risk of rupture.
A bulge in a weakened wall is an aneurysm, not a clot. Choose it if the question asked which disorder is common in the aorta and brain arteries.
This swaps the two terms. Embolism always describes something that has moved, as in a pulmonary embolism from a leg clot.
Correct. A thrombus is stationary, and an embolus travels.
questions.answerText: A thrombus stays where it formed, while an embolus breaks free and travels

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Blood leaves a capillary bed in the forearm and returns to the heart. Which sequence does it follow?
options: Capillary, venule, vein, superior vena cava, right atrium
Capillary, venule, vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium
Capillary, arteriole, artery, superior vena cava, right atrium
Capillary, venule, vein, pulmonary veins, left atrium
questions.why: Capillaries drain into venules, the smallest veins, which merge into larger veins. Veins of the upper limb drain toward the superior vena cava, which returns blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs to the right atrium. Arteries and arterioles carry blood away from the heart, so they are never part of the return trip.
notes: Correct. Forearm blood drains through venules and veins into the superior vena cava and then the right atrium.
The inferior vena cava drains the trunk and lower limbs. This sequence would be right if the capillary bed were in the leg instead of the forearm.
Arterioles and arteries carry blood away from the heart toward the capillaries. They would be the answer for the trip from the aorta down to a capillary bed, which runs in the opposite direction.
The pulmonary veins and left atrium receive blood only from the lungs. This ending would be right for blood leaving a lung capillary bed, not a capillary bed in the forearm.
questions.answerText: Capillary, venule, vein, superior vena cava, right atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot breaks free from a deep vein in the leg. Which route does it follow to reach the lung?
options: Inferior vena cava, right atrium, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, pulmonary artery
Inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary veins, pulmonary artery
Superior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, pulmonary artery
questions.why: A clot that breaks loose from a deep vein of the leg simply rides the normal venous return. Leg veins drain into the inferior vena cava, which empties into the right atrium. The clot passes into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the pulmonary trunk and a pulmonary artery, where it lodges as a pulmonary embolism.
notes: This route crosses from the right atrium to the left atrium, which does not happen in a normal adult heart because the interatrial septum is closed. The left atrium, left ventricle, and aorta would be the route for blood that has already returned from the lungs.
Correct. A leg clot follows venous return through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries.

This route puts the pulmonary veins between the pulmonary trunk and the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary veins actually carry blood out of the lungs to the left atrium, so they come after the lungs, not before.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs. This route would be right for a clot that started in an arm vein, not a leg vein.
questions.answerText: Inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, pulmonary artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, which sequence carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the inferior vena cava?
options: Placenta, umbilical vein, ductus venosus, inferior vena cava
Placenta, umbilical vein, foramen ovale, inferior vena cava
Placenta, umbilical vein, ductus arteriosus, inferior vena cava
Placenta, umbilical arteries, ductus venosus, inferior vena cava
questions.why: A fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta, not its lungs. Oxygen-rich blood travels from the placenta to the fetus in the single umbilical vein. Most of it then passes through the ductus venosus, a shunt through the liver, which delivers it straight into the inferior vena cava.
notes: Correct. The umbilical vein and ductus venosus carry placental blood into the inferior vena cava.
The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum between the right and left atria. It would fit a trace from the right atrium to the left atrium, which happens after blood reaches the heart.

The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta that lets blood bypass the lungs. It would fit a trace from the right ventricle to the aorta, not from the umbilical vein.
The umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus back to the placenta, the opposite direction. They would be the answer if the question asked how fetal blood returns to the placenta.
questions.answerText: Placenta, umbilical vein, ductus venosus, inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, blood in the right atrium can bypass the lungs by passing through the foramen ovale. Which chamber does it enter?
options: Left atrium
Pulmonary trunk
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum, the wall between the two atria. In the fetus it lets blood pass directly from the right atrium into the left atrium, skipping the right ventricle and the collapsed lungs. From the left atrium the blood goes on to the left ventricle and out the aorta.
notes: Correct. The foramen ovale connects the right atrium to the left atrium.
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, so blood reaches it only by the ordinary route. It would be the starting point of the other lung bypass, the ductus arteriosus.
The left ventricle is one step beyond the left atrium, reached through the mitral valve. It would be the answer if the question asked where the blood goes after the left atrium.

The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve, which is the normal route and does not bypass the lungs. It would be the answer if the blood took the tricuspid valve instead of the foramen ovale.
questions.answerText: Left atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, blood from the right ventricle enters the pulmonary trunk and then crosses the ductus arteriosus. Which vessel does it enter at the far end of that shunt?
options: Aorta
Pulmonary veins
Inferior vena cava
Left pulmonary artery
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Because the fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange, most blood pumped into the pulmonary trunk is shunted through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta instead of going to the lungs.
notes: Correct. The ductus arteriosus empties into the aorta.
The pulmonary veins drain the lungs into the left atrium. They are on the far side of the lungs, so blood that bypasses the lungs never enters them first.
The inferior vena cava is where the ductus venosus empties, carrying placental blood past the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked about the liver bypass.

The left pulmonary artery is a branch of the pulmonary trunk that leads into the left lung. Blood going there is not bypassing the lungs, so it would be the answer for the normal adult route, not for the ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: Aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, oxygen-poor blood returns from the fetus to the placenta through which vessels?
options: Pulmonary arteries
Umbilical arteries
Ductus venosus
Umbilical vein
questions.why: After circulating through the fetal body, oxygen-poor blood leaves through the two umbilical arteries, which run in the umbilical cord back to the placenta. They are called arteries because they carry blood away from the fetal heart, even though the blood is low in oxygen. At the placenta the blood unloads wastes and picks up oxygen again.
notes: The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the pulmonary trunk to the lungs. In an adult they send oxygen-poor blood to be refreshed, but in a fetus that job belongs to the placenta, not the lungs.
Correct. The umbilical arteries return oxygen-poor blood to the placenta.

The ductus venosus is a shunt inside the fetal liver that passes blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava. It would be the answer if the question asked how fetal blood bypasses the liver.
The umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood the other way, from the placenta to the fetus. It would be the answer if the question asked how oxygen reaches the fetus.
questions.answerText: Umbilical arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, most of the blood pumped into the pulmonary trunk enters which structure next?
options: Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
Ductus venosus
Right and left pulmonary arteries
questions.why: The fetal lungs are collapsed and do not exchange gases, so most blood in the pulmonary trunk is diverted away from them. It passes through the ductus arteriosus, a short vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Only a small share continues into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs.
notes: Correct. Most fetal blood leaves the pulmonary trunk through the ductus arteriosus.
The foramen ovale is the opening between the right and left atria, the other lung bypass. It would be the answer if the question started in the right atrium.
The ductus venosus is the shunt through the fetal liver, carrying blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava. It would be the answer if the question started at the umbilical vein.
The right and left pulmonary arteries are where blood goes after the pulmonary trunk in an adult. In a fetus only a small share goes this way, because the lungs are not yet used for gas exchange.
questions.answerText: Ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, oxygen-rich blood in the umbilical vein bypasses the liver by passing through which shunt?
options: Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
Umbilical arteries
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The ductus venosus is a shunt that runs through the fetal liver. It lets most of the oxygen-rich blood arriving in the umbilical vein skip the liver tissue and flow straight toward the inferior vena cava. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
notes: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta and is a lung bypass. It would be the answer if the question started at the pulmonary trunk.

The foramen ovale is the opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood skip the lungs, not the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked how blood passes from the right atrium to the left atrium.
The umbilical arteries are vessels in the cord, not a shunt, and they carry oxygen-poor blood back to the placenta. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood returns to the placenta.
Correct. The ductus venosus carries umbilical vein blood past the liver.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, blood that leaves the ductus venosus flows next into which vessel?
options: Inferior vena cava
Umbilical arteries
Superior vena cava
Aorta
questions.why: The ductus venosus carries blood from the umbilical vein through the liver and delivers it to the inferior vena cava. From there the blood enters the right atrium. Because this placental blood is oxygen-rich, the inferior vena cava of a fetus carries a mix of oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood.
notes: Correct. The ductus venosus empties into the inferior vena cava.
The umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus back to the placenta at the end of the fetal route. They would be the answer if the question asked how blood returns to the placenta.
The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs and enters the right atrium from above. It would be the answer if the question asked about venous return from the upper body.
The aorta is where the ductus arteriosus empties, not the ductus venosus. It would be the answer if the question started at the ductus arteriosus.
questions.answerText: Inferior vena cava

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: One artery supplying a region is blocked, yet the tissue still receives blood through a connection with a neighboring artery. What structure explains this?
options: Venous valve
Precapillary sphincter
Anastomosis
Portal system
questions.why: An anastomosis is a place where two vessels join. When arteries supplying the same region are connected this way, blood can take an alternate route if one path is blocked. That backup route is why some tissues survive a blocked artery while tissues supplied by a single artery are more vulnerable.
notes: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima that keep blood in veins from flowing backward. They would be the answer if the question asked why blood in leg veins does not pool.

A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle that opens or closes the entrance to a single capillary. It would be the answer if the question asked what controls flow into an individual capillary.
Correct. An anastomosis gives blood an alternate route around a blockage.

A portal system sends blood through two capillary beds in a row before it returns to the heart, as in the hepatic portal circulation. It would be the answer if the question described blood passing through the intestines and then the liver.
questions.answerText: Anastomosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In some tissues, blood flows from a small artery directly into a vein without passing through any capillaries. What is this direct connection called?
options: Postcapillary venule
Arteriovenous anastomosis
Portal system
Precapillary sphincter
questions.why: An arteriovenous anastomosis is a direct connection from an artery to a vein that bypasses the capillaries. The name tells you what it joins: arterio for the artery side and venous for the vein side. Because the blood skips the capillary bed, little exchange with the tissue happens along this route.
notes: A postcapillary venule is the first venule to receive blood from the capillaries, so blood reaching it has already passed through a capillary bed. It would be the answer if the question asked which vessel drains a capillary bed.
Correct. An arteriovenous anastomosis links an artery directly to a vein.

A portal system is the opposite arrangement, with blood passing through two capillary beds in series instead of none. It would be the answer if the question described blood flowing from the intestines to the liver.
A precapillary sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle that opens or closes the entrance to a capillary. It controls flow into capillaries rather than connecting an artery to a vein.
questions.answerText: Arteriovenous anastomosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces systemic blood from the left ventricle to a capillary bed?
options: Left ventricle, pulmonary valve, aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary bed
Left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, arteriole, artery, capillary bed
Left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, artery, venule, capillary bed
Left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary bed
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. The aorta branches into smaller arteries, which branch into arterioles, the smallest arteries. Arterioles control how much blood enters each capillary bed, where exchange with the tissue takes place.
notes: The pulmonary valve is the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk. It would belong in a trace from the right ventricle to the lungs, not from the left ventricle to the aorta.
This sequence puts arterioles before arteries. Vessels get smaller as blood moves away from the heart, so the larger arteries come first and branch into the smaller arterioles.
Venules carry blood away from capillaries toward the heart, so they come after a capillary bed. This sequence puts a venous vessel on the arterial side of the route.
Correct. This is the systemic route from the left ventricle down to a capillary bed.
questions.answerText: Left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, artery, arteriole, capillary bed

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Where is the foramen ovale, one of the fetal lung bypasses, located?
options: In the interventricular septum
Within the fetal liver
In the interatrial septum
Between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum, the wall between the right and left atria. In the fetus it lets blood pass from the right atrium into the left atrium so it can skip the lungs. After birth it closes, leaving a shallow depression called the fossa ovalis.
notes: The interventricular septum is the thick wall between the two ventricles, and it has no fetal shunt. An opening there would be an abnormal defect, not the foramen ovale. It would be the answer if the question asked where the AV bundle and bundle branches run.
The shunt within the fetal liver is the ductus venosus, which bypasses the liver rather than the lungs. It would be the answer if the question asked where the ductus venosus is.
Correct. The foramen ovale is an opening in the wall between the two atria.
The connection between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta is the ductus arteriosus, the other fetal lung bypass. It would be the answer if the question asked where the ductus arteriosus is.
questions.answerText: In the interatrial septum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus connects which two vessels?
options: Pulmonary veins and pulmonary trunk
Superior vena cava and aorta
Umbilical vein and inferior vena cava
Pulmonary trunk and aorta
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel running from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Because the fetal lungs are not used for gas exchange, it diverts most of the blood leaving the right ventricle into the aorta instead. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
notes: The pulmonary veins carry blood out of the lungs to the left atrium and are not joined to the pulmonary trunk by any shunt. This pairing mixes the vessels on the two ends of the lungs.

The superior vena cava returns blood to the right atrium and is not connected to the aorta by any fetal shunt. Students may pick this because both vessels sit at the base of the heart, but no fetal shunt joins them.
The umbilical vein and inferior vena cava are joined by the ductus venosus, the liver bypass. That pair would be the answer if the question asked about the ductus venosus.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary trunk and aorta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The ductus venosus is a fetal shunt that passes through which organ?
options: Liver
Heart
Placenta
Lungs
questions.why: The ductus venosus runs through the fetal liver. It carries most of the oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein past the liver tissue and into the inferior vena cava. The fetus can skip much of the liver because the placenta handles that filtering before birth.
notes: Correct. The ductus venosus is the shunt through the liver.
The heart holds the foramen ovale, the opening in the interatrial septum. The heart would be the answer if the question asked where the foramen ovale is.

The placenta is where fetal blood picks up oxygen and gives up wastes. It connects to the fetus through the umbilical cord, so it would be the answer if the question asked where the umbilical vessels lead.

The lungs are bypassed by the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus, but no shunt passes through the lungs themselves. They would be the answer if the question asked which organ those two shunts bypass.
questions.answerText: Liver

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement about the umbilical vessels in fetal circulation is correct?
options: Two umbilical veins carry oxygen-poor blood to the placenta
Two umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the placenta
Two umbilical arteries carry oxygen-rich blood to the fetus
One umbilical vein carries oxygen-poor blood to the placenta
questions.why: The umbilical cord holds three vessels: one umbilical vein and two umbilical arteries. The two arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the fetus to the placenta, and the single vein brings oxygen-rich blood back. As with the pulmonary vessels, artery and vein are named by direction relative to the heart, not by oxygen content.
notes: There is only one umbilical vein, and it carries oxygen-rich blood toward the fetus. This choice mixes up both the number of veins and their direction.
Correct. The two umbilical arteries return oxygen-poor blood to the placenta.
This reverses the job of the umbilical arteries. Blood moving toward the fetus with oxygen from the placenta travels in the umbilical vein, so that would be the true statement about the vein.
The number is right, since there is one umbilical vein, but the direction and oxygen content are reversed. The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus.
questions.answerText: Two umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta and returns to the right atrium through the venae cavae. In what order does it pass through the vessel types in between?
options: Arteries, arterioles, venules, capillaries, veins
Arterioles, arteries, capillaries, veins, venules
Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins
Arteries, venules, capillaries, arterioles, veins
questions.why: The systemic circuit follows a fixed vascular sequence. Arteries branch into arterioles, which feed capillaries, where exchange happens. Capillaries merge into venules, which merge into veins, and the veins finally drain into the superior and inferior venae cavae.
notes: This places venules before capillaries. Venules collect blood after it leaves the capillaries, so the capillaries come first.
This reverses the size order on both sides. Large arteries branch into small arterioles, and small venules merge into larger veins, so arteries come first and veins come last.
Correct. This is the standard vascular sequence from artery to vein.
This puts venules and arterioles on the wrong sides of the capillaries. Arterioles deliver blood to capillaries and venules drain it away, so the arterioles must come before the capillaries.
questions.answerText: Arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence describes the route blood takes through a portal system, such as the hepatic portal circulation?
options: Artery, directly into a vein, back to the heart
First capillary bed, artery, second capillary bed, veins back to the heart
Artery, capillary bed, vein, back to the heart
First capillary bed, portal vein, second capillary bed, veins back to the heart
questions.why: A portal system passes blood through two capillary beds in a row before it returns to the heart. A portal vein links the two beds. In the hepatic portal circulation, blood from the capillaries of the digestive organs travels in the hepatic portal vein to a second set of capillaries in the liver, then drains toward the inferior vena cava.
notes: A direct artery-to-vein connection with no capillaries is an arteriovenous anastomosis. It would be the answer if the question asked about blood bypassing a capillary bed.

The vessel linking the two capillary beds is a vein, because it collects blood from the first capillary bed. An artery carries blood away from the heart toward capillaries, so it would not drain a capillary bed.
This is the ordinary route with only one capillary bed. It describes most of the systemic circuit, not a portal system.
Correct. A portal vein links two capillary beds in series.
questions.answerText: First capillary bed, portal vein, second capillary bed, veins back to the heart

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A deep vein thrombosis in the leg breaks free. Why does it usually end up as a pulmonary embolism in the lung rather than blocking an artery in the brain?
options: The left ventricle pumps venous blood to the lungs before sending it to the brain
Venous blood from the leg returns to the right heart, which pumps it only to the lungs
The clot crosses the interatrial septum and is pumped into the pulmonary trunk
Leg veins drain directly into the pulmonary veins, which carry it to the lungs
questions.why: A clot that leaves a leg vein rides the normal venous return: up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium and right ventricle. The right ventricle sends its blood only into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries. As those arteries branch and narrow in the lung, the clot lodges there before it could ever reach the left heart and the arteries of the brain.
notes: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta for the body, not to the lungs. Pumping to the lungs is the job of the right ventricle.
Correct. The right heart sends venous return only to the lungs, so the clot lodges there.

In a normal adult the interatrial septum is closed, so a clot cannot cross it. Crossing would take it to the left side and away from the pulmonary trunk, which is the opposite of what this choice claims.
The pulmonary veins carry blood out of the lungs to the left atrium and receive nothing from the legs. Leg veins drain into the inferior vena cava, which empties into the right atrium.
questions.answerText: Venous blood from the leg returns to the right heart, which pumps it only to the lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence explains how coronary artery disease leads to a myocardial infarction (heart attack)?
options: Plaque narrows a brain artery, a clot blocks it, and brain tissue beyond it dies
Plaque narrows a leg artery, and the leg muscles hurt during walking
A clot from a leg vein blocks a pulmonary artery, and blood flow to the lung stops
Plaque narrows a coronary artery, a clot blocks it, and the myocardium beyond it dies
questions.why: Coronary artery disease is atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries, the narrow vessels that supply the heart wall. A fatty plaque narrows the artery, and a clot (thrombus) can form on the rough plaque and suddenly block it. The patch of myocardium beyond the block is starved of oxygen and begins to die, which is a myocardial infarction.
notes: This is the same plaque-and-clot process in an artery of the brain, which causes a stroke. Pick it if the question asked how atherosclerosis leads to a stroke.
Plaque narrowing the arteries of the legs is peripheral artery disease, which causes pain on walking. It would be the answer if the question asked about leg pain from narrowed arteries.
