A clot traveling from a leg vein into a pulmonary artery is a pulmonary embolism. It would be the answer if the question asked how a deep vein thrombosis becomes dangerous.
Correct. A blocked coronary artery starves the myocardium beyond it, causing an infarction.
questions.answerText: Plaque narrows a coronary artery, a clot blocks it, and the myocardium beyond it dies

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which sequence explains how failing valves in leg veins lead to varicose veins?
options: Valves fail, blood flows backward and pools, and the superficial veins swell and twist
Plaque builds up in the vessel wall, the lumen narrows, and blood flow drops
A clot forms in a deep vein, breaks free, and travels to the lung
An artery wall weakens, the wall bulges outward, and the bulge may rupture
questions.why: Veins carry blood under low pressure, so they depend on valves (flaps of the tunica intima) to keep blood moving toward the heart. When the valves in superficial leg veins fail, blood slips backward and pools. The pooled blood stretches the vein walls until the veins become swollen, twisted, and visible under the skin.
notes: Correct. Failed valves let blood pool and stretch the superficial veins.
Plaque buildup that narrows a vessel is atherosclerosis, which affects arteries rather than veins. It would be the answer if the question asked how an artery becomes narrowed.
A clot in a deep vein that travels to the lung is a deep vein thrombosis becoming a pulmonary embolism. It would be the answer if the question asked about a clot, not about failed valves.
A weakened artery wall that bulges outward is an aneurysm, an arterial disorder. It would be the answer if the question asked how an aneurysm forms.
questions.answerText: Valves fail, blood flows backward and pools, and the superficial veins swell and twist

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: After birth the fetal shunts close and leave remnants. Which pairing of fetal structure and adult remnant is correct?
options: Ductus arteriosus and ligamentum venosum
Ductus venosus and ligamentum arteriosum
Foramen ovale and fossa ovalis
Umbilical vein and medial umbilical ligament
questions.why: When the lungs inflate at birth and the placenta is cut off, the fetal shunts close. The foramen ovale, a hole in the interatrial septum, seals to leave a shallow depression called the fossa ovalis. The others become cords: the ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, and the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
notes: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, and the ligamentum venosum comes from the ductus venosus. Each remnant keeps part of its original name, so matching the names catches this swap.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, not the ligamentum arteriosum. The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
Correct. The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.
The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver. The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the two umbilical arteries.
questions.answerText: Foramen ovale and fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: After birth, the umbilical vein closes and becomes which structure?
options: Medial umbilical ligaments
Ligamentum teres
Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum venosum
questions.why: The umbilical vein carried oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver, which runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament. The two umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments on the inner anterior abdominal wall.
notes: The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the two umbilical arteries, not the vein. They would be the answer if the question asked what the umbilical arteries become.
Correct. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. It would be the answer if the question asked what the ductus arteriosus becomes.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, the shunt through the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked what the ductus venosus becomes.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum teres

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder develops when the valves of superficial veins fail, so blood pools and the veins become twisted and swollen, most often in the legs?
options: Varicose veins
Phlebitis
Deep vein thrombosis
Aneurysm
questions.why: Varicose veins form when the valves in superficial veins stop closing properly. Blood that should move up toward the heart slides back and pools, stretching the vein walls until the veins bulge and twist under the skin. The legs are most often affected because blood there has to climb against gravity.
notes: Correct. Failed valves in superficial veins cause varicose veins.
Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, causing pain, redness, and tenderness along it. Choose it if the question described an inflamed, tender vein rather than one swollen from pooled blood.
Deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, not a stretched superficial vein. Pick it if the question asked about a clot that could break free and travel to the lungs.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall, not a vein. It would be the answer if the question asked about a bulging artery that could rupture, such as in the aorta or brain.
questions.answerText: Varicose veins

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg?
options: Deep vein thrombosis
Varicose veins
Pulmonary embolism
Atherosclerosis
questions.why: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a clot, or thrombus, that forms in a deep vein, most often in the leg. It is dangerous because of where the clot can go. If a piece breaks free, it rides the normal venous return up the inferior vena cava, through the right side of the heart, and into the lungs.
notes: Correct. A deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg.

Varicose veins are superficial veins that swell and twist when their valves fail, without a clot being the defining problem. Pick them if the question asked about bulging veins under the skin of the legs.
A pulmonary embolism is what happens when a clot, often from a DVT, lodges in an artery of the lung. It would be the answer if the question asked where a traveling leg clot ends up.
Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque building up in artery walls, not a clot in a vein. Choose it if the question asked about the disease behind most heart attacks and strokes.
questions.answerText: Deep vein thrombosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder occurs when a clot, often from a deep leg vein, lodges in an artery of the lung?
options: Pulmonary embolism
Stroke
Pneumothorax
Deep vein thrombosis
questions.why: A pulmonary embolism is a blockage of a lung artery by an embolus, a clot or fragment that has traveled through the bloodstream. Most start as a deep vein thrombosis in the leg, then travel up the venae cavae, through the right atrium and right ventricle, and out the pulmonary trunk until they wedge in a pulmonary artery branch. It blocks blood flow to part of the lung and is a medical emergency.
notes: Correct. A clot lodged in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism.
A stroke is loss of blood supply to part of the brain from a blocked or burst artery. Choose it if the clot had lodged in an artery of the brain instead of the lung.
A pneumothorax is air in the pleural cavity that lets the lung collapse, not a blocked vessel. It would be the answer if the question described a punctured chest wall and a collapsed lung.
A deep vein thrombosis is the clot while it is still sitting in a deep leg vein, before it travels. Pick it if the question asked about the original clot in the leg.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary embolism

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disease is the buildup of fatty plaques within the walls of arteries, narrowing the lumen?
options: Atherosclerosis
Varicose veins
Hypertension
Aneurysm
questions.why: Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the tunica intima, the smooth inner lining of an artery. Fatty material, cells, and debris then collect in the wall as a plaque (atheroma), which bulges inward and narrows the channel. A clot can also form on the rough plaque and suddenly block the artery, which is why atherosclerosis is behind most heart attacks and strokes.
notes: Correct. Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque buildup in artery walls.
Varicose veins are swollen superficial veins caused by failed valves, a venous problem rather than an arterial one. Choose them if the question asked about twisted, bulging leg veins.

Hypertension is chronically high pressure inside the arteries, not a plaque in the wall, though it can damage the wall over time. It would be the answer if the question asked about long-term high blood pressure.
An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall, which widens rather than narrows the vessel. Pick it if the question asked about an artery wall that balloons outward and may rupture.
questions.answerText: Atherosclerosis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall?
options: Deep vein thrombosis
Varicose veins
Atherosclerosis
Aneurysm
questions.why: An aneurysm is a weak spot in an artery wall that balloons outward under the high pressure inside the vessel. The thinned wall can rupture and cause severe bleeding. Aneurysms are most common in the aorta and in the arteries of the brain.
notes: A deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg. Choose it if the question asked about a clot that could travel to the lungs.
Varicose veins are swollen, twisted superficial veins caused by failed valves. They would be the answer if the question asked about bulging veins in the legs instead of a bulging artery.
Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque that builds up inside an artery wall and narrows the lumen. Pick it if the question asked about a narrowed artery rather than a bulging one.
Correct. An aneurysm is a bulge in a weakened artery wall.
questions.answerText: Aneurysm

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which disorder is chronically high pressure within the arteries, which strains the heart and damages vessel walls over time?
options: Atherosclerosis
Hypertension
Peripheral artery disease
Aneurysm
questions.why: Hypertension means blood pressure in the arteries stays high over a long period. The heart has to work harder to push blood against that pressure, and the constant force wears on the artery walls. Over time this damage can contribute to other vessel disorders, which is why it is described as a disorder of pressure rather than of one specific structure.
notes: Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque buildup within the artery wall that narrows the lumen. It would be the answer if the question asked about plaques rather than the pressure itself.
Correct. Hypertension is chronically high arterial pressure.
Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs, causing pain on walking. Choose it if the question described leg pain from muscles starved of blood.
An aneurysm is a specific balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall. Pick it if the question described a bulging artery that could rupture.
questions.answerText: Hypertension

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, which vessel carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus?
options: Umbilical arteries
Ductus arteriosus
Umbilical vein
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta, not its own lungs. The single umbilical vein runs through the umbilical cord and carries oxygen-rich, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta toward the fetal liver and heart. It is a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, even though its blood is the most oxygen-rich in the fetus.
notes: The umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood the other way, from the fetus back to the placenta. Pick them if the question asked which vessels return blood to the placenta.

The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel that shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs. Choose it if the question asked which fetal vessel connects those two great arteries.
Correct. The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta.
The ductus venosus is the shunt that lets blood from the umbilical vein bypass most of the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked how fetal blood skips the liver.
questions.answerText: Umbilical vein

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In fetal circulation, which vessels carry oxygen-poor blood from the fetus back to the placenta?
options: Umbilical arteries
Pulmonary veins
Umbilical vein
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The two umbilical arteries run through the umbilical cord and carry oxygen-poor blood and wastes from the fetus back to the placenta. They are arteries because they carry blood away from the fetal heart. After birth they close and become the medial umbilical ligaments on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall.
notes: Correct. The two umbilical arteries return oxygen-poor blood to the placenta.

The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the fetal lungs are not yet used for gas exchange. They would be the answer if the question asked which vessels bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs after birth.
The umbilical vein carries oxygen-rich blood the opposite direction, from the placenta to the fetus. Pick it if the question asked which vessel delivers oxygen to the fetus.
The ductus venosus is a shunt inside the fetal liver that lets blood bypass the liver tissue. Choose it if the question asked how umbilical vein blood skips the liver.
questions.answerText: Umbilical arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which fetal shunt lets most blood from the umbilical vein bypass the liver and flow toward the inferior vena cava?
options: Ligamentum venosum
Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
questions.why: Before birth, the placenta handles much of the work the liver will later do, so most fetal blood does not need to pass through the liver tissue. The ductus venosus is a shunt through the fetal liver that carries blood from the umbilical vein straight toward the inferior vena cava. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
notes: The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous cord the ductus venosus becomes after birth, so it carries no blood. Choose it if the question asked for the adult remnant of this shunt.
Correct. The ductus venosus carries blood past the liver.
The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, bypassing the lungs, not the liver. Pick it if the question asked which shunt connects the two great arteries.

The foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. It would be the answer if the question asked about the shunt inside the heart.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which fetal shunt is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs?
options: Fossa ovalis
Ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus
Foramen ovale
questions.why: The foramen ovale is an opening in the wall between the two atria of the fetal heart. Because the fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange, much of the blood entering the right atrium passes straight through this opening into the left atrium and out to the body. After birth the opening seals, leaving the fossa ovalis.
notes: The fossa ovalis is the shallow depression left after the foramen ovale closes, so no blood passes through it. It would be the answer if the question asked for the adult remnant of this opening.
The ductus venosus is the shunt that lets blood bypass the liver, not the lungs. Choose it if the question asked how umbilical vein blood skips the liver.

The ductus arteriosus also bypasses the lungs, but it is a vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, outside the atria. Pick it if the question asked about the shunt between the two great arteries.
Correct. The foramen ovale lets blood pass from the right atrium to the left atrium.
questions.answerText: Foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which fetal shunt is a short vessel that carries blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, bypassing the lungs?
options: Foramen ovale
Ligamentum arteriosum
Ductus arteriosus
Ductus venosus
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aorta in the fetus. Blood that the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk mostly crosses this shunt into the aorta instead of going to the collapsed fetal lungs. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; if it stays open, the condition is called patent ductus arteriosus.
notes: The foramen ovale also bypasses the lungs, but it is an opening between the right and left atria, not a vessel between arteries. Pick it if the question asked about the shunt in the interatrial septum.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous cord the ductus arteriosus becomes after birth, so it no longer carries blood. Choose it if the question asked for the adult remnant of this shunt.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.

The ductus venosus is the shunt that lets blood bypass the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked how umbilical vein blood reaches the inferior vena cava without passing through liver tissue.
questions.answerText: Ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: After birth, which structure is the adult remnant of the foramen ovale?
options: Ligamentum arteriosum
Fossa ovalis
Ligamentum teres
Ligamentum venosum
questions.why: At birth the lungs inflate and the foramen ovale seals shut. What remains is the fossa ovalis, a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum. It is the one fetal shunt that becomes a depression instead of a ligament, because it was a hole rather than a vessel.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, a cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the question asked what the ductus arteriosus becomes.
Correct. The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.
The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein, also called the round ligament of the liver. Choose it if the question asked what the umbilical vein becomes.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked what the liver shunt becomes.
questions.answerText: Fossa ovalis

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which adult structure is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus?
options: Ligamentum teres
Ligamentum venosum
Ligamentum arteriosum
Medial umbilical ligament
questions.why: After birth the lungs begin working, so the ductus arteriosus is no longer needed and it closes. It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, a short fibrous cord between the pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch. The name keeps a piece of the original, which makes the pair easy to match.
notes: The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein, the round ligament of the liver. It would be the answer if the question asked what the umbilical vein becomes.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, found on the inferior surface of the liver. Pick it if the question asked what the liver shunt becomes.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the umbilical arteries on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall. Choose them if the question asked what the umbilical arteries become.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum arteriosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which adult structure is the remnant of the ductus venosus?
options: Ligamentum teres
Ligamentum venosum
Fossa ovalis
Ligamentum arteriosum
questions.why: The ductus venosus carried fetal blood through the liver and past its tissue. Once the umbilical cord is cut, no blood flows through it and it closes into the ligamentum venosum, a fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver. Like the ductus arteriosus, its adult name keeps part of the fetal name.
notes: The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the umbilical vein, which also ends up on the liver. Choose it if the question asked which liver ligament runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament.
Correct. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, a depression in the interatrial septum. It would be the answer if the question asked what the opening between the atria becomes.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, lying between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it if the question asked what the shunt between the great arteries becomes.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum venosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which adult structure is the remnant of the umbilical vein?
options: Medial umbilical ligaments
Ligamentum arteriosum
Ligamentum teres
Ligamentum venosum
questions.why: After birth the umbilical vein no longer carries blood from the placenta, so it closes into a fibrous cord called the ligamentum teres, or round ligament of the liver. It runs from the umbilicus to the liver in the free edge of the falciform ligament. Its name does not echo the fetal vessel the way ligamentum venosum and ligamentum arteriosum do, so it has to be learned on its own.
notes: The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the two umbilical arteries, not the single umbilical vein. They would be the answer if the question asked what the umbilical arteries become.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Choose it if the question asked what the shunt between the great arteries becomes.
Correct. The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres.
The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, the shunt that passed through the liver. Pick it if the question asked what the liver shunt becomes.
questions.answerText: Ligamentum teres

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: An atherosclerotic plaque narrows the lumen of an artery. What happens to the tissue downstream of the narrowing?
options: It receives more blood because pressure rises
Its blood flow reverses direction
It receives less blood and oxygen
It is unaffected because its veins supply it instead
questions.why: Atherosclerosis is a buildup of fatty plaque (an atheroma) within the artery wall. As the plaque grows, it bulges inward and narrows the lumen, the channel the blood flows through. A narrower channel lets less blood through, so the tissue beyond the narrowing receives less blood and less oxygen. Depending on the artery, this shows up as chest pain, leg pain on walking, or a stroke.
notes: This mixes up pressure with flow. Pressure may build behind a narrowing, but the smaller channel lets less blood through, so the tissue downstream gets less, not more.

Blood in an artery keeps flowing away from the heart even when the vessel narrows; it simply flows in a smaller amount. Backward flow is a problem of failed valves in veins or the heart, as in varicose veins or regurgitation.
Correct. The narrowed lumen lets less blood through, so the tissue beyond it gets less blood and oxygen.
Veins carry blood away from a tissue and back to the heart, so they cannot deliver fresh oxygen-rich blood to it. Students choose this when they forget the direction of flow in veins.
questions.answerText: It receives less blood and oxygen

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient with a slowly growing plaque in a coronary artery suddenly has much worse chest pain, and a clot is found on the plaque. Why did symptoms worsen so suddenly?
options: The clot can block the narrowed vessel all at once
The artery's valves closed and stopped the flow
The clot dissolved the plaque and widened the vessel
The plaque suddenly turned into an aneurysm
questions.why: A plaque roughens the smooth tunica intima, and a clot, called a thrombus, can form on that rough surface. The plaque grew over years, but a thrombus can form in minutes, and because the lumen was already narrowed, the added clot can block it completely. Blood flow to the tissue beyond stops suddenly, which can cause a heart attack in a coronary artery or a stroke in a brain artery.
notes: Correct. A thrombus on top of a plaque can close an already narrowed lumen in minutes.
Arteries do not have valves; valves are found in veins and in the heart. This choice comes from mixing up arteries with veins, where failed valves cause varicose veins.
A clot adds material to the lumen; it does not break down the plaque or widen the channel. Choosing this reverses what a thrombus does.

An aneurysm is a bulge in a weakened artery wall that pushes outward and may rupture. It widens the vessel rather than closing it, so pick it for a question about a ballooning wall, not a sudden blockage.
questions.answerText: The clot can block the narrowed vessel all at once

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A weakened section of the aortic wall balloons outward. What is this disorder called?
options: Aneurysm
Varicose vein
Embolus
Atherosclerosis
questions.why: An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened artery wall. The weak section can no longer hold its shape against the high pressure inside the artery, so it stretches outward. Aneurysms are most common in the aorta and in the arteries of the brain, and the main danger is that the thinned wall can rupture.
notes: Correct. An aneurysm is an outward bulge in a weakened artery wall, common in the aorta.

A varicose vein is a superficial vein, usually in the leg, that becomes twisted and swollen when its valves fail. It also bulges, but it is a low-pressure vein, so pick it when the question describes a vein rather than the aorta.

An embolus is a clot or fragment that breaks free and travels through the bloodstream until it lodges in a smaller vessel. Choose it for a question about something traveling and blocking a distant vessel, like a pulmonary embolism.

Atherosclerosis is fatty plaque building up inside the artery wall and narrowing the lumen. It is the answer when the channel narrows; the disorder named for an outward bulge of the wall is an aneurysm.
questions.answerText: Aneurysm

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A patient gets cramping pain in the calves while walking that eases with rest. The arteries of the legs are narrowed by plaque. Which disorder fits?
options: Varicose veins
Peripheral artery disease
Coronary artery disease
Deep vein thrombosis
questions.why: Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries of the limbs, usually the legs, most often by atherosclerotic plaque. At rest the narrowed arteries can deliver enough blood, but during walking the leg muscles need more than can get through. The muscles are starved of blood and hurt, and the pain fades once they rest.
notes: Varicose veins are swollen, twisted superficial veins caused by failed valves. They involve veins and pooled blood, not narrowed arteries starving the muscles.
Correct. Narrowed limb arteries starve the leg muscles during walking, which causes the pain.

Coronary artery disease is the same narrowing process in the coronary arteries that supply the heart wall. It would be the answer if the pain were in the chest during exertion rather than in the legs.
Deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep vein of the leg, a problem on the venous side. Pick it when a question describes a clot in a leg vein that could break free and travel to the lungs.
questions.answerText: Peripheral artery disease

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot forms in a deep vein of the calf, breaks free, and lodges in an artery of the lung. What has happened?
options: A varicose vein from a failed valve
A pulmonary embolism from a DVT
A stroke from a blocked brain artery
A myocardial infarction from a coronary thrombus
questions.why: A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg. If part of it breaks free, it becomes an embolus, a traveling clot, and it follows the normal path of venous return: up the inferior vena cava, into the right atrium and right ventricle, and out the pulmonary trunk into a pulmonary artery. When it lodges there and blocks blood flow to part of the lung, it is called a pulmonary embolism.
notes: A varicose vein is a swollen superficial vein whose valves have failed, so blood pools in it. Choose it for a bulging leg vein, since it does not involve a clot traveling to another organ.
Correct. A clot from a deep leg vein that lodges in a lung artery is a pulmonary embolism.
A stroke is loss of blood supply to part of the brain. It would be the answer if the clot lodged in a brain artery rather than a lung artery.

A myocardial infarction is death of heart muscle when a coronary artery is blocked. A clot from a leg vein does not reach the coronary arteries by the normal venous route, so pick this only when the blocked vessel feeds the heart wall.
questions.answerText: A pulmonary embolism from a DVT

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A superficial vein in the leg becomes twisted and bulging because blood flows backward and pools in it. Which structure has failed?
options: The capillary endothelium
The venous valves
The precapillary sphincters
The semilunar valves of the heart
questions.why: Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima, common in the veins of the limbs, that let blood move only toward the heart. In the legs, blood must travel upward against gravity at low pressure, so the valves keep it from sliding back down. When they fail, blood flows backward and pools, and the superficial vein stretches into a twisted, swollen varicose vein.
notes: The capillary endothelium is the single cell layer that forms a capillary wall and allows exchange. Damage to it does not cause backward flow in a vein, so it fits questions about exchange instead.
Correct. Failed venous valves let blood fall back and pool, producing a varicose vein.

Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle that open or close the entrance to a capillary bed. They would be the answer for a question about directing blood into a tissue, not about backflow in veins.

The semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves at the exits of the ventricles. They prevent backflow into the heart, so pick them for a question about blood leaking back into a ventricle, not about a leg vein.
questions.answerText: The venous valves

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Over many years, the valves of a patient's leg veins fail, leading to persistent swelling and skin changes in the lower leg. Which disorder fits?
options: Phlebitis
Chronic venous insufficiency
Deep vein thrombosis
Peripheral artery disease
questions.why: Chronic venous insufficiency is long-term failure of the valves in the leg veins. Without working valves, blood is not moved efficiently back toward the heart and pools in the lower leg. Over time the pooling leads to persistent swelling and changes in the skin of the lower leg. Chronic signals a long-lasting condition, and insufficiency signals that the valves are no longer doing enough.
notes: Phlebitis is inflammation of a vein, which causes pain, redness, and tenderness along the vein. It would be the answer for an inflamed, tender vein rather than years of valve failure.
Correct. Long-term valve failure in the leg veins causes swelling and skin changes.
A deep vein thrombosis is a clot in a deep leg vein, a sudden event that can break free and travel to the lungs. Choose it when the question describes a clot, not long-term failing valves.

Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the leg arteries, which starves the muscles and causes pain on walking. It is an arterial problem, so pick it when too little blood reaches the leg, not when blood pools in it.
questions.answerText: Chronic venous insufficiency

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The opening in the fetal interatrial septum fails to seal after birth. What is this defect called?
options: Ligamentum arteriosum
Patent foramen ovale
Patent ductus arteriosus
Fossa ovalis
questions.why: Before birth, the foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that lets blood pass straight from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. Normally it seals after birth and leaves a shallow depression, the fossa ovalis. If it stays open, the defect is called a patent foramen ovale, since patent means open.
notes: The ligamentum arteriosum is the normal adult cord left when the ductus arteriosus closes. It would be the answer for the remnant between the pulmonary trunk and aorta, not for a defect.
Correct. A foramen ovale that stays open after birth is a patent foramen ovale.

A patent ductus arteriosus is the other common shunt defect, an open vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Pick it when the question describes a vessel outside the heart, not an opening in the atrial wall.
The fossa ovalis is the normal shallow depression left when the foramen ovale closes properly. Choose it for the adult remnant, not for an opening that failed to seal.
questions.answerText: Patent foramen ovale

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: The fetal vessel that connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta stays open after birth. What is this defect called?
options: Ligamentum venosum
Patent foramen ovale
Patent ductus arteriosus
Ligamentum arteriosum
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus is a short fetal vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. Before birth it shunts blood away from the collapsed lungs and into the aorta. It should close after birth and become the ligamentum arteriosum, and when it stays open the defect is called a patent ductus arteriosus.
notes: The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus, the fetal shunt through the liver. Choose it for the fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver.
A patent foramen ovale is an opening in the interatrial septum that did not seal. Pick it when the leftover connection is between the two atria, inside the heart.
Correct. A ductus arteriosus that stays open after birth is a patent ductus arteriosus.
The ligamentum arteriosum is the normal fibrous cord the ductus arteriosus becomes after it closes. It is the answer for the adult remnant, not for a vessel that stayed open.
questions.answerText: Patent ductus arteriosus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a fetus, why does the umbilical vein carry oxygen-rich blood?
options: It carries blood from the fetus to the placenta
It carries blood from the fetal lungs to the heart
It carries blood from the placenta to the fetus
It carries blood from the fetal liver to the heart
questions.why: Before birth, the fetal lungs are collapsed and do not exchange gases, so the fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta. The umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta, where it has just picked up oxygen and nutrients, through the umbilical cord to the fetus. It is a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, and it is oxygen-rich because of where it comes from.
notes: Blood traveling from the fetus to the placenta is carried by the two umbilical arteries, and it is oxygen-poor. Pick this direction for a question about the umbilical arteries.

The fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange, so they are not the source of oxygen before birth. After birth, the pulmonary veins would be the answer for oxygen-rich blood coming from the lungs.
Correct. The umbilical vein brings freshly oxygenated blood from the placenta.

Blood leaving the liver does flow on toward the heart, but the liver is not where fetal blood gets its oxygen. The ductus venosus, which lets umbilical blood bypass the liver, would be the answer for a question about that route.
questions.answerText: It carries blood from the placenta to the fetus

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: In a fetus, why do the umbilical arteries carry oxygen-poor blood?
options: They carry blood from the fetal lungs
They carry blood from the placenta to the fetus
They carry blood through the ductus arteriosus
They carry fetal blood back to the placenta
questions.why: The two umbilical arteries carry blood away from the fetus, which is why they are called arteries. That blood has already circulated through the fetal body, delivering oxygen and picking up wastes, so it is oxygen-poor. It travels through the umbilical cord to the placenta, where it gives up wastes and picks up a fresh supply of oxygen.
notes: The fetal lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange, and blood does not travel from them to the umbilical cord. Choose the lungs for a question about what the fetal shunts bypass.
Blood from the placenta to the fetus travels in the umbilical vein, which is oxygen-rich. Pick this for a question about the umbilical vein.

The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel shunting blood from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta to bypass the lungs. It would be the answer for a question about the lung bypass, not the vessels in the umbilical cord.
Correct. The umbilical arteries return used, oxygen-poor fetal blood to the placenta.
questions.answerText: They carry fetal blood back to the placenta

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why do the fetal shunts close after birth?
options: The coronary arteries open for the first time
The heart begins beating for the first time
The lungs inflate and the placental supply ends
The umbilical vein reverses its direction of flow
questions.why: Before birth, oxygen comes from the placenta and the collapsed lungs are bypassed, so the shunts route blood around the lungs and liver. At birth the lungs inflate and begin exchanging gases, and cutting the umbilical cord ends the placental supply. The detours are no longer needed, so the ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus close, leaving ligaments or, for the foramen ovale, the fossa ovalis.
notes: The coronary arteries supply the fetal heart wall before birth, just as they do after. Nothing about them changes at birth, so this choice confuses the heart's own supply with the fetal shunts.
The fetal heart beats long before birth; it is what pushes blood through the shunts. Students choose this when they assume the heart starts working at birth.
Correct. Once the lungs work and the placenta is cut off, the detours are no longer needed.

The umbilical vein does not reverse; it stops carrying blood once the cord is cut and later becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver. Pick the umbilical vein for a question about which remnant runs in the falciform ligament.
questions.answerText: The lungs inflate and the placental supply ends

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A clot breaks free from a deep vein in the leg. Which route does it follow to become a pulmonary embolism?
options: Inferior vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Superior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, aorta
Inferior vena cava, right atrium, left atrium, pulmonary veins
Inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk
questions.why: A clot from a leg vein follows the normal path of venous return. It travels up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and out through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk. The pulmonary arteries branch into smaller and smaller vessels inside the lung, so the clot eventually lodges in one and blocks blood flow to part of the lung. That blockage is a pulmonary embolism.
notes: The inferior vena cava empties into the right atrium, not the left. A clot in the left heart would be pumped out the aorta to the body, which is how a clot can cause a stroke.

The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, and upper limbs, not the legs, and the right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta. Students choose this when they mix up which great vessel leaves each ventricle.

The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium, so a clot cannot travel through them toward the lungs. Pick the pulmonary veins for a question about where oxygen-rich blood enters the heart.
Correct. The clot rides normal venous return through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries.
questions.answerText: Inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: What makes a portal system, such as the hepatic portal system, different from the usual circulatory route?
options: Blood flows from the right heart to the lungs and back
Blood skips the capillaries and flows from artery to vein
Two arteries join so blood has an alternate route
Blood passes through two capillary beds in a row
questions.why: In most of the body, blood goes from an artery to one capillary bed and then into veins headed back to the heart. In a portal system, blood passes through a capillary bed, collects into a portal vein, and then passes through a second capillary bed before returning to the heart. In the hepatic portal system, blood from the digestive organs goes to the liver's capillaries next, so the liver can process absorbed nutrients and remove harmful substances before that blood reaches the rest of the body.
notes: Right heart to lungs to left heart is the pulmonary circuit. It is the answer for a question about the loop that carries blood to the lungs for gas exchange.
A direct artery-to-vein connection that skips the capillaries is an arteriovenous anastomosis. Pick it for a question about blood bypassing a capillary bed.
Two vessels joining to give an alternate route is an anastomosis. Choose it for a question about what protects tissue when one vessel is blocked.
Correct. A portal system sends blood through two capillary beds in series before it returns to the heart.
questions.answerText: Blood passes through two capillary beds in a row

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does an anastomosis between two arteries help protect the tissue they supply?
options: It lets blood skip the capillaries entirely
It keeps blood from flowing backward
It sends blood through two capillary beds in a row
It gives blood a second route if one is blocked
questions.why: An anastomosis is a place where two vessels join. When two arteries supplying the same region connect, blood can reach the tissue through either one. If one path is blocked, blood can still arrive by the other route, which protects the tissue from losing its blood supply. The cerebral arterial circle at the base of the brain is a well-known example.
notes: Skipping the capillaries describes an arteriovenous anastomosis, a direct artery-to-vein connection. It routes blood away from the tissue's capillaries, so it would not protect the tissue's supply.
Preventing backward flow is the job of valves, which are found in veins and the heart. Choose valves for a question about one-way flow.
Passing through two capillary beds in a row describes a portal system, like the hepatic portal system. Pick it for a question about blood going from the digestive organs to the liver.
Correct. Joined arteries let blood reach the tissue by a second path.
questions.answerText: It gives blood a second route if one is blocked

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does the ductus arteriosus route fetal blood around the lungs?
options: The pulmonary trunk is too narrow to carry blood
The fetal lungs are collapsed and not yet in use
The fetal liver needs the blood instead
The fetal lungs are already full of oxygen-rich blood
questions.why: Before birth, the fetus gets its oxygen from the placenta, and its lungs are collapsed and not used for gas exchange. Sending all the blood through them would be wasted effort. The ductus arteriosus is a short vessel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta, so it shunts most of the blood leaving the right ventricle into the aorta and out to the body instead.
notes: The pulmonary trunk is a large vessel, and it actually feeds the ductus arteriosus. Students choose this when they think the shunt exists because of a blocked vessel rather than unused lungs.
Correct. With the lungs not yet working, blood is shunted past them into the aorta.
The ductus arteriosus empties into the aorta, not the liver. A question about blood bypassing the liver would point to the ductus venosus instead.
The fetal lungs do not oxygenate blood before birth; the placenta does. This choice comes from assuming the fetus breathes the way it will after birth.
questions.answerText: The fetal lungs are collapsed and not yet in use

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why does the ductus venosus route much fetal blood around the liver?
options: The ductus venosus carries blood to the lungs
The fetal liver has no blood supply
The fetal liver is collapsed like the lungs
The placenta handles most filtering before birth
questions.why: In the fetus, oxygen-rich blood arrives from the placenta in the umbilical vein. Because the placenta handles much of the filtering that the liver will do after birth, most of that blood does not need to pass through the liver. The ductus venosus is a shunt through the liver that lets this blood flow straight toward the inferior vena cava and on to the heart.
notes: The ductus venosus leads toward the inferior vena cava, not the lungs. The shunts that bypass the lungs are the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus.
The fetal liver does receive blood; only part of the umbilical blood bypasses it. Students choose this when they think bypassed means completely cut off.
Only the fetal lungs are collapsed; the liver is a working organ before birth. This choice borrows the reason the lungs are bypassed and applies it to the wrong organ.
Correct. With the placenta doing much of the filtering, most umbilical blood can skip the liver.
questions.answerText: The placenta handles most filtering before birth

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why can atherosclerosis cause coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, or a stroke?
options: Each disease comes from a different kind of plaque
The same plaque forms in different arteries
Plaques form in veins and travel to each artery
Plaque forms in the heart and spreads outward
questions.why: Atherosclerosis is the buildup of fatty plaque within artery walls, and it can occur in arteries throughout the body. The disease a patient develops depends on which artery the plaque narrows. In the coronary arteries it causes coronary artery disease and heart attacks, in a brain artery it can cause a stroke, and in the leg arteries it causes peripheral artery disease.
notes: The same process, fatty deposits in the artery wall, underlies all three diseases. Only the location differs, so this choice overcomplicates what is one disease in different places.
Correct. One plaque process produces different diseases depending on which artery it affects.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of arteries, not veins. Clots that start in veins, like a deep vein thrombosis, travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism instead.
Plaque forms locally in the wall of each affected artery; it does not start in the heart and spread. Students choose this when they picture the disease as one growing mass.
questions.answerText: The same plaque forms in different arteries

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is an aneurysm in a large artery such as the aorta so dangerous?
options: The weak wall can burst under high pressure
The bulge makes the wall too thick to stretch
The bulge sends clots into the veins
The bulge blocks the artery completely
questions.why: An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in a weakened section of artery wall. Arteries carry blood under high pressure, and the thinned, stretched wall of the bulge has less and less strength to resist it. If the wall gives way, the aneurysm ruptures and blood escapes rapidly, which can be fatal in a large artery like the aorta or in an artery of the brain.
notes: Correct. The thinned wall of an aneurysm can rupture under arterial pressure.
An aneurysm thins and stretches the wall rather than thickening it. A thickened, stiffened artery wall describes arteriosclerosis instead.
Material leaving an artery travels onward in arteries, away from the heart, not into the veins. Students choose this when they mix up an aneurysm with a deep vein thrombosis.
An aneurysm widens the vessel outward rather than closing it. Complete blockage describes a thrombus forming on a plaque, which can trigger a heart attack or stroke.
questions.answerText: The weak wall can burst under high pressure

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Why is a stroke treated as a time-sensitive emergency?
options: Brain tissue starts dying within minutes
The heart stops beating soon after a stroke
Brain tissue can survive for days without blood
The blocked artery always reopens within an hour
questions.why: A stroke is a loss of blood supply to part of the brain, caused by a blocked or burst artery. Brain tissue depends on a constant flow of oxygen-rich blood, and it begins to die within minutes once that supply is lost. The faster blood flow is restored, the less brain tissue is lost, which is why every minute counts.
notes: Correct. Brain tissue starts to die within minutes of losing its blood supply.
A stroke affects the brain's blood supply, not the heart's pumping. Pick the heart for a question about ventricular fibrillation or a myocardial infarction.
Brain tissue has almost no tolerance for lost blood supply, so it cannot wait days. This choice underestimates how quickly brain cells are damaged.
A blocked brain artery does not reliably reopen on its own, which is why treatment aims to restore flow quickly. Students choose this when they confuse a stroke with a brief, passing symptom.
questions.answerText: Brain tissue starts dying within minutes

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how the heart, blood vessels, and lungs work together to deliver oxygen to the body?
options: The lungs add oxygen in the arteries, and the capillaries pump it to the body
The left heart sends blood to the lungs, and the right heart pumps it to the body
The right heart sends blood to the lungs, and the left heart pumps it to the body
The heart adds oxygen to the blood, and the lungs pump it through the vessels
questions.why: Oxygen-poor blood returning from the body enters the right atrium and is pumped by the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs. In the lungs, blood in the pulmonary capillaries picks up oxygen from the air in the alveoli and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left ventricle then pumps this oxygen-rich blood into the aorta, and the arteries carry it to capillaries throughout the body, where oxygen moves into the tissues.
notes: Oxygen is loaded in the pulmonary capillaries around the alveoli, not in arteries, and capillaries do not pump. Pick capillaries for a question about where exchange with the tissues happens.
This reverses the two sides. The right ventricle drives the pulmonary circuit to the lungs, and the left ventricle, with its thicker wall, drives the systemic circuit to the body.
Correct. The right side drives the pulmonary circuit and the left side drives the systemic circuit.
The heart is a pump and does not add oxygen to blood; oxygen is picked up at the alveoli. Students choose this when they mix up the job of the pump with the job of the exchange surface.
questions.answerText: The right heart sends blood to the lungs, and the left heart pumps it to the body

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the pulmonary and systemic circuits?
options: Pulmonary supplies the heart wall; systemic supplies the lungs and the rest of the body
Pulmonary goes to the lungs and returns to the right atrium; systemic goes to the body and returns to the left atrium
Pulmonary goes to the lungs and returns to the left atrium; systemic goes to the body and returns to the right atrium
Pulmonary goes to the body and returns to the left atrium; systemic goes to the lungs and returns to the right atrium
questions.why: The pulmonary circuit starts at the right ventricle, carries blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and returns it through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The systemic circuit starts at the left ventricle, carries blood through the aorta to the body tissues, and returns it through the venae cavae to the right atrium. Each circuit ends on the opposite side of the heart from where it began, which links the two into one continuous loop.
notes: The heart wall is supplied by the coronary arteries, which branch from the aorta and are part of the systemic circuit. Students pick this when they treat the coronary vessels as a separate circuit; choose a coronary answer for a question about how the myocardium gets its blood.

This swaps the return chambers. Blood coming back from the lungs enters the left atrium so it can be pumped out to the body, and blood from the body enters the right atrium so it can be sent to the lungs.
Correct. Each circuit returns to the side of the heart that pumps the other circuit.
This swaps where the two circuits go. Pulmonary refers to the lungs, so the pulmonary circuit is the one that carries blood to them.
questions.answerText: Pulmonary goes to the lungs and returns to the left atrium; systemic goes to the body and returns to the right atrium

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: How do arterial disorders differ from venous disorders in what tends to go wrong?
options: Arterial disorders affect only the tunica externa; venous disorders affect only the tunica intima
Arterial disorders involve failed valves and pooled blood; venous disorders narrow or weaken the wall
Arterial disorders come from low pressure; venous disorders come from high pressure
Arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall; venous disorders involve failed valves and pooled or clotted blood
questions.why: Arteries carry blood under high pressure, so their disorders tend to narrow the channel, as in atherosclerosis, or weaken the wall until it bulges, as in an aneurysm. Veins carry blood under low pressure and depend on valves, so their disorders tend to involve failed valves and pooled blood, as in varicose veins, or clots, as in deep vein thrombosis. The wall each vessel has, and the pressure it carries, predict how it tends to fail.
notes: Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the tunica intima of an artery, so arterial disease is not limited to the outer layer. Students choose this when they try to tie each group of disorders to a single tunic.
This swaps the two groups. Valves are a feature of veins, especially in the limbs, so valve failure and pooling belong to venous disorders like varicose veins.
This reverses the pressures. Arteries are the high-pressure vessels, and chronically high arterial pressure (hypertension) is itself an arterial disorder that strains vessel walls.
Correct. High-pressure arteries narrow or weaken, and low-pressure veins pool or clot.
questions.answerText: Arterial disorders narrow or weaken the wall; venous disorders involve failed valves and pooled or clotted blood

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: A deep vein thrombosis (a clot in a deep leg vein) breaks free. Which route does the clot follow to become a pulmonary embolism?
options: Leg artery, aorta, left ventricle, left atrium, pulmonary veins, lung artery
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, aorta, brain artery
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, lung artery
Leg vein, inferior vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta, lung artery
questions.why: A clot that breaks free from a deep leg vein simply follows normal venous return. It travels up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, through the right ventricle, and out the pulmonary trunk into the pulmonary arteries. As those arteries branch and narrow, the clot lodges in one, blocking blood flow to part of the lung.
notes: A deep vein thrombosis forms in a vein, not an artery, and blood does not flow backward from the aorta into the left ventricle. This route runs against the normal direction of flow.

The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta, so a clot from a leg vein heads to the lungs. Pick a route through the left heart and aorta for a question about how a clot reaches a brain artery and causes a stroke.
Correct. The clot follows the normal route of venous blood back through the right heart to the lungs.
Venous blood from the body returns to the right side of the heart, not the left. The left atrium receives only the pulmonary veins, so a clot from a leg vein cannot reach it first.
questions.answerText: Leg vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary trunk, lung artery

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches each fetal shunt to the organ it lets blood bypass?
options: Ductus venosus bypasses the liver; foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs
Ductus arteriosus bypasses the liver; ductus venosus and foramen ovale bypass the lungs
Ductus venosus bypasses the lungs; foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the liver
All three shunts bypass the lungs, since the fetal lungs are not yet in use
questions.why: Before birth, the placenta handles gas exchange and much of the filtering, so the fetal lungs and liver are largely bypassed. The ductus venosus passes through the liver and lets most blood from the umbilical vein skip it on the way to the inferior vena cava. The foramen ovale (an opening between the atria) and the ductus arteriosus (a vessel from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta) both route blood around the lungs.
notes: Correct. One shunt skips the liver and two skip the lungs.

The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, so it bypasses the lungs, not the liver. Students choose this when they mix up the two ductus names; venosus goes with the venous side and the liver.

This swaps the two organs. The ductus venosus runs through the fetal liver toward the inferior vena cava, and the other two shunts sit at the heart and great vessels, where they route blood around the lungs.
Two shunts do bypass the lungs, but the ductus venosus bypasses the liver. Students pick this when they focus on the collapsed fetal lungs and forget that the liver is also largely skipped.
questions.answerText: Ductus venosus bypasses the liver; foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Which pairing of a fetal structure with its adult remnant is correct?
options: Umbilical vein becomes the medial umbilical ligaments
Foramen ovale becomes the ligamentum venosum
Ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum
Ductus venosus becomes the fossa ovalis
questions.why: After birth, each fetal shunt closes and leaves a remnant whose name often echoes the original. The ductus arteriosus, which linked the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, becomes the ligamentum arteriosum, a short cord between those same two vessels. The foramen ovale, which was a hole rather than a vessel, becomes a depression instead of a cord: the fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum.
notes: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, the round ligament of the liver. The medial umbilical ligaments are the remnants of the two umbilical arteries, on the inner surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

The foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis, a depression in the interatrial septum. The ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus; pick it for the fibrous cord on the inferior surface of the liver.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus closes into the ligamentum arteriosum between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum on the liver. The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, so choose it for the depression in the wall between the atria.
questions.answerText: Ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum

questions.topic: Circulatory routes, fetal circulation and vessel disorders
questions.q: Varicose veins form when a structure inside superficial leg veins fails. Which structure is it, and which tunic of the vein wall forms it?
options: The venous valves, formed by the tunica media
The internal elastic lamina, in the tunica media
The vasa vasorum, found in the tunica externa
The venous valves, formed by the tunica intima
questions.why: Varicose veins are superficial veins that become twisted and swollen when their valves fail, so blood pools in them. Venous valves are flaps of the tunica intima, common in the limb veins, that keep blood from flowing backward. When the flaps no longer close, blood slips back and the vein swells.
notes: The structure is right, but venous valves are flaps of the innermost tunic, the tunica intima. The tunica media is the smooth muscle layer.
The internal elastic lamina is a sheet of elastic fibers at the boundary between the tunica intima and the tunica media. It is not a flap and does not stop backflow.
The vasa vasorum are small vessels in the tunica externa that supply the wall of a large vessel. Their failure is not what lets blood pool in varicose veins.
Correct. Varicose veins follow failure of the venous valves, which are flaps of the tunica intima.
questions.answerText: The venous valves, formed by the tunica intima

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces the main artery of the upper limb from the axilla into the forearm?
options: Axillary artery, brachial artery, then the cephalic and basilic arteries
Axillary artery, brachial artery, then the radial and ulnar arteries
Axillary artery, radial artery, then the brachial and ulnar arteries
Brachial artery, axillary artery, then the radial and ulnar arteries
questions.why: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib, and the axillary becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major. The brachial artery runs down the medial arm and, in the cubital fossa, divides into the radial artery on the thumb side and the ulnar artery on the little finger side. One vessel simply changes its name as it passes each landmark.
notes: The cephalic and basilic are superficial veins of the upper limb, not arteries. Pick them if the question asked which superficial veins run up the lateral and medial arm.
Correct. Axillary, then brachial, then the radial and ulnar branches in the forearm.
The radial artery is a forearm branch of the brachial artery, so it cannot come before the brachial. Students pick this when they lose track of where the brachial artery divides.
This puts the brachial artery before the axillary. The axillary artery lies in the armpit and becomes the brachial artery in the arm, so the order is reversed.
questions.answerText: Axillary artery, brachial artery, then the radial and ulnar arteries

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which group lists the superficial veins of the upper limb that are commonly used for blood draws?
options: The cephalic, basilic, and great saphenous veins
The axillary, subclavian, and brachiocephalic veins
The brachial, radial, and ulnar veins
The cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins
questions.why: The superficial veins of the upper limb run in the subcutaneous tissue, where they can be seen and reached with a needle. The cephalic vein ascends the lateral side, the basilic vein ascends the medial side, and the median cubital vein connects them across the front of the elbow. The median cubital vein is the usual site for drawing blood.
notes: The cephalic and basilic are correct, but the great saphenous vein is a superficial vein of the lower limb, running up the medial leg and thigh. Choose it if the question asked about the longest superficial vein of the leg.

These are deep veins of the shoulder and root of the neck that carry blood toward the superior vena cava. They would be the answer if the question traced venous return from the upper limb to the heart.

The brachial, radial, and ulnar veins are deep veins that travel alongside the arteries of the same names. Pick them if the question asked which veins accompany the brachial, radial, and ulnar arteries.
Correct. The cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins are the superficial veins used for blood draws.
questions.answerText: The cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which superficial vein crosses the cubital fossa to connect the cephalic and basilic veins, making it the usual site for a blood draw?
options: The basilic vein
The median antebrachial vein
The median cubital vein
The cephalic vein
questions.why: The median cubital vein runs diagonally across the front of the elbow, linking the cephalic vein on the lateral side to the basilic vein on the medial side. It is large, close to the surface, and fairly well anchored, which makes it easy to reach with a needle. The bicipital aponeurosis lies just deep to it, separating it from the brachial artery and median nerve.
notes: The basilic vein ascends the medial forearm and arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein. It would be the answer for the superficial vein on the little finger side.

The median antebrachial vein ascends the middle of the anterior forearm, below the elbow rather than across it. Choose it if the question asked which superficial vein runs up the center of the forearm.
Correct. The median cubital vein bridges the cephalic and basilic veins in the cubital fossa.
The cephalic vein ascends the lateral forearm and arm and joins the axillary vein at the deltopectoral groove. Pick it if the question asked which superficial vein runs up the thumb side of the limb.
questions.answerText: The median cubital vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which artery is the first and largest branch to leave the aortic arch?
options: Right subclavian artery
Left subclavian artery
Brachiocephalic trunk
Left common carotid artery
questions.why: The aortic arch gives off three branches, and the brachiocephalic trunk is the first one, on the right, and the largest. It is a short shared stem that serves the right side of the head and neck and the right upper limb. It soon divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
notes: The right subclavian artery does not come off the arch at all. It is one of the two vessels the brachiocephalic trunk divides into, so pick it for a question about what the trunk splits into.
The left subclavian artery is the third and last branch of the arch. It would be the answer if the question asked which arch branch supplies the left upper limb.
Correct. The brachiocephalic trunk leaves the arch first and is the largest of the three branches.

The left common carotid artery is the second branch of the arch, arising directly from it between the other two. Pick it if the question asked for the middle branch of the arch or the artery to the left side of the head and neck.
questions.answerText: Brachiocephalic trunk

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Moving from the right side of the body to the left, what is the correct order of the branches of the aortic arch?
options: Left subclavian artery, left common carotid artery, brachiocephalic trunk
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery
Right common carotid artery, brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian artery
Brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian artery, left common carotid artery
questions.why: As the arch curves from right to left over the heart, it gives off the brachiocephalic trunk first, then the left common carotid artery, then the left subclavian artery. The right side gets one shared stem while the left side gets two separate arteries, which is why the branches are not symmetrical.
notes: This is the correct list read backward, from left to right. Students choose it when they lose track of which direction the question asked for.
Correct. Brachiocephalic trunk, then left common carotid, then left subclavian is the right to left order.

The right common carotid artery is not an arch branch. It comes from the brachiocephalic trunk, so placing it on the arch is the mix-up of treating the right side as if it had separate branches like the left.
This order swaps the two left-sided branches. The left common carotid leaves the arch before the left subclavian, because the carotid sits closer to the midline.
questions.answerText: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The brachiocephalic trunk divides into which two arteries?
options: Right vertebral and right internal thoracic arteries
Right internal and right external carotid arteries
Right common carotid and right subclavian arteries
Left common carotid and left subclavian arteries
questions.why: The brachiocephalic trunk exists only on the right side. It runs up and to the right from the arch and divides into the right common carotid artery, which heads up the neck, and the right subclavian artery, which heads toward the right upper limb. Its name reflects that job: brachio means arm and cephalic means head.
notes: The vertebral and internal thoracic arteries are branches of the subclavian artery, not of the trunk. They would be the answer for a question about branches of the subclavian.

The internal and external carotid arteries are formed when the common carotid artery divides in the neck, one level beyond the trunk. Pick them if the question asked what the right common carotid splits into.
Correct. The trunk splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise separately and directly from the aortic arch. They would be the answer if the question asked which two arteries leave the arch on the left side.
questions.answerText: Right common carotid and right subclavian arteries

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Where does the left subclavian artery arise?
options: From the descending thoracic aorta
From the left common carotid artery
From the brachiocephalic trunk
Directly from the aortic arch
questions.why: The left subclavian artery is the third branch of the aortic arch and comes straight off the arch. On the right, the subclavian comes from the brachiocephalic trunk instead. This difference in origin is the asymmetry of the arch, since there is no left brachiocephalic trunk.
notes: The descending thoracic aorta begins after the arch and gives off branches such as the posterior intercostal, bronchial, and esophageal arteries. Pick it for those vessels, not for any upper limb artery.

The left common carotid is a separate arch branch that runs up the neck and does not give off the subclavian. It would be the answer only for the origin of the left internal and external carotid arteries.
The brachiocephalic trunk gives rise to the right subclavian artery, not the left. This would be the answer if the question asked about the origin of the right subclavian artery.
Correct. The left subclavian is the last of the three branches leaving the arch.
questions.answerText: Directly from the aortic arch

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: At which landmark does the subclavian artery change its name to the axillary artery?
options: The lower border of teres major
The sternoclavicular joint
The cubital fossa
The lateral border of the first rib
questions.why: The artery to the upper limb is one continuous vessel that changes name at landmarks. It is called the subclavian artery until it crosses the lateral (outer) border of the first rib, and from there through the armpit it is the axillary artery. Learning the landmark is what lets you name the segment you are looking at.
notes: The lower border of teres major is the next landmark down the limb, where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery. Pick it if the question asked where the brachial artery begins.

The right sternoclavicular joint is roughly where the brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. It marks where the right subclavian begins, not where it ends.
The cubital fossa, the hollow at the front of the elbow, is where the brachial artery divides into the radial and ulnar arteries. It would be the answer for where the brachial artery ends.
Correct. The subclavian becomes the axillary at the lateral border of the first rib.
questions.answerText: The lateral border of the first rib

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: At which landmark does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
options: The lower border of teres major
The lateral border of the first rib
The surgical neck of the humerus
The cubital fossa
questions.why: The axillary artery runs through the armpit and is renamed the brachial artery once it passes the lower (inferior) border of the teres major muscle. From there the brachial artery travels down the medial side of the arm to the elbow. Teres major is the muscle landmark that separates the armpit segment from the arm segment.
notes: Correct. The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major.
The lateral border of the first rib is where the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery, one step earlier along the vessel. Pick it if the question asked where the axillary artery begins.

The surgical neck of the humerus is a bony landmark that the circumflex humeral arteries wrap around. It does not mark a name change for the main artery, so it fits a question about where the circumflex humeral arteries run.
The cubital fossa is where the brachial artery ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries. It would be correct for the end of the brachial artery, not its start.
questions.answerText: The lower border of teres major

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Where does the brachial artery divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?
options: In the radial groove of the humerus
At the wrist, just above the carpal bones
In the cubital fossa, just below the elbow
In the axilla
questions.why: The brachial artery runs down the medial arm and enters the cubital fossa, the triangular hollow at the front of the elbow. Just below the elbow it divides into the radial artery on the thumb side of the forearm and the ulnar artery on the little finger side. These two arteries then carry blood down the forearm to the hand.
notes: The radial groove on the back of the humerus holds the deep brachial artery and the radial nerve, not the division of the brachial artery. Students pick it because of the look-alike word radial.

At the wrist the radial and ulnar arteries already exist as separate vessels and are heading into the hand to form the palmar arches. The wrist would fit a question about where the radial pulse is felt.
Correct. The brachial artery splits in the cubital fossa just below the elbow.
The axilla, or armpit, is the region of the axillary artery, which has not yet become the brachial artery. Pick the axilla for questions about the axillary artery or the cords of the brachial plexus.
questions.answerText: In the cubital fossa, just below the elbow

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: When a blood pressure cuff is inflated around the upper arm, which artery does it compress?
options: Deep brachial artery
Brachial artery
Axillary artery
Radial artery
questions.why: The brachial artery is the main artery of the arm, running from the lower border of teres major down to the cubital fossa. A cuff wrapped around the upper arm squeezes it against the humerus, and the sounds are listened for over the artery at the front of the elbow. That is why blood pressure readings are taken on the arm.
notes: The deep brachial artery is a branch that runs on the back of the humerus in the radial groove with the radial nerve. It is not the vessel used to read blood pressure, so pick it only for questions about the radial groove.
Correct. The cuff compresses the brachial artery in the arm.
The axillary artery lies up in the armpit, above where a cuff sits. It would be the answer for the artery between the first rib and teres major.
The radial artery runs on the thumb side of the forearm and is used for the pulse at the wrist. Pick it for a question about taking a pulse at the wrist, not about a cuff on the upper arm.
questions.answerText: Brachial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
