questions.q: A pulse is felt on the anterior wrist, on the thumb side. Which artery is being felt?
options: Radial artery
Ulnar artery
Common interosseous artery
Brachial artery
questions.why: The radial artery runs down the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm and lies close to the surface at the front of the wrist. It can be pressed against the radius there, which is why it is the standard site for taking a pulse. The ulnar artery runs on the opposite, little finger side.
notes: Correct. The radial artery is felt on the thumb side of the anterior wrist.
The ulnar artery runs on the medial (little finger) side of the forearm, so it would be felt on the opposite side of the wrist. Pick it if the question described the little finger side.
The common interosseous artery is a short branch of the ulnar artery deep in the upper forearm. It lies too deep to be felt and does not reach the wrist as a named pulse.
The brachial artery ends at the elbow, so it cannot be felt at the wrist. It is the pulse felt at the front of the elbow or the artery compressed by a blood pressure cuff.
questions.answerText: Radial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which is the largest branch of the axillary artery?
options: Subscapular artery
Anterior circumflex humeral artery
Thoracoacromial artery
Lateral thoracic artery
questions.why: The axillary artery gives off several named branches in the armpit, and the subscapular artery is the largest of them. It runs down along the lateral border of the scapula toward the muscles on the back of the shoulder. The other branches are smaller and supply the chest wall, the shoulder, and the area around the humerus.
notes: Correct. The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery.

The anterior circumflex humeral artery is a small vessel that wraps the front of the surgical neck of the humerus. It fits a question about arteries around the neck of the humerus, not the largest branch.
The thoracoacromial artery is a short axillary branch that supplies the pectoral region and the deltoid. It would be the answer for the branch to the front of the shoulder and chest muscles.
The lateral thoracic artery runs down the lateral chest wall alongside the long thoracic nerve. Pick it if the question asked which axillary branch follows the side of the chest wall.
questions.answerText: Subscapular artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which artery travels with the radial nerve in the radial groove on the back of the humerus?
options: Deep brachial artery
Brachial artery
Radial artery
Posterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.why: The deep brachial artery is a branch of the brachial artery that swings around the back of the humerus. It runs in the radial groove, an oblique groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus, together with the radial nerve. A nerve and artery that share a path like this are often injured together.
notes: Correct. The deep brachial artery runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove.
The brachial artery itself runs down the medial side of the arm with the median nerve, not in the groove on the back of the bone. It would be the answer for the main artery of the arm.
The radial artery is in the forearm on the thumb side, below the elbow, and has nothing to do with the radial groove of the humerus. Students choose it because of the shared word radial.
The posterior circumflex humeral artery wraps around the back of the surgical neck of the humerus with the axillary nerve. Pick it if the question asked which artery travels with the axillary nerve.
questions.answerText: Deep brachial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The superficial palmar arch is supplied chiefly by which artery?
options: Radial artery
Brachial artery
Ulnar artery
Common interosseous artery
questions.why: In the hand, the radial and ulnar arteries join each other to form two arches across the palm. The superficial palmar arch, the more distal of the two, is formed mainly by the ulnar artery. The deep palmar arch, the more proximal one, is formed mainly by the radial artery.
notes: The radial artery is the chief supply of the deep palmar arch, the more proximal arch. Pick it if the question asked about the deep arch.
The brachial artery ends at the elbow by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries, so it never reaches the hand. It would be the answer for the artery compressed by a blood pressure cuff.
Correct. The superficial palmar arch is chiefly a continuation of the ulnar artery.
The common interosseous artery is a short branch of the ulnar artery in the upper forearm that splits into anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. It does not form either palmar arch.
questions.answerText: Ulnar artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The vertebral artery, the internal thoracic artery, the thyrocervical trunk, and the costocervical trunk all branch from which artery?
options: Common carotid artery
Axillary artery
Subclavian artery
Descending thoracic aorta
questions.why: Before it crosses the first rib, the subclavian artery gives off several branches to the neck, brain, and chest wall. The vertebral artery climbs to the brain, the internal thoracic artery runs down the inside of the front chest wall, and the thyrocervical and costocervical trunks supply the neck and upper chest. All of them leave the subclavian before it becomes the axillary artery.
notes: The common carotid artery runs up the neck and divides into the internal and external carotid arteries, with no branches to the chest wall. Pick it for the arteries that supply the face and the front of the brain.
The axillary artery begins at the first rib, after these branches have already left. Its own branches include the thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular, and circumflex humeral arteries.
Correct. All four vessels are branches of the subclavian artery.

The descending thoracic aorta gives off the posterior intercostal, bronchial, and esophageal arteries. It would be the answer for those vessels, which supply the chest wall from behind and the organs of the thorax.
questions.answerText: Subclavian artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: As the vertebral artery ascends the neck toward the brain, which openings does it pass through?
options: Carotid canals of the temporal bones
Transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae
Intervertebral foramina
Vertebral foramina
questions.why: The vertebral artery leaves the subclavian artery and climbs the neck through the transverse foramina, the small holes in the transverse processes that are found only in cervical vertebrae. It then enters the skull through the foramen magnum to help supply the brain. The transverse foramina are the feature that identifies a cervical vertebra.
notes: The carotid canals are openings in the temporal bones that carry the internal carotid arteries into the skull. Choose them for the internal carotid artery, not the vertebral artery.
Correct. The vertebral artery rises through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae.
The intervertebral foramina are the openings between neighboring vertebrae where spinal nerves exit. Pick them if the question asked where spinal nerves leave the vertebral column.
The vertebral foramina line up to form the vertebral canal, which holds the spinal cord. They would be the answer for the passage of the spinal cord, not an artery.
questions.answerText: Transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which superficial vein ascends the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm and arm and passes through the deltopectoral groove to join the axillary vein?
options: Cephalic vein
Median antebrachial vein
Basilic vein
Median cubital vein
questions.why: The cephalic vein starts on the back of the hand and climbs the lateral side of the forearm and arm just under the skin. Near the shoulder it runs in the deltopectoral groove, the furrow between the deltoid and pectoralis major, and then dives deep to join the axillary vein. Its lateral course is what tells it apart from the basilic vein.
notes: Correct. The cephalic vein runs up the lateral side and through the deltopectoral groove.
The median antebrachial vein runs up the middle of the anterior forearm and stays below the elbow. It would be the answer for the vein along the center of the front of the forearm.
The basilic vein ascends the medial (little finger) side of the forearm and arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein. Pick it if the question described the medial side.
The median cubital vein is a short connecting vein that crosses the front of the elbow between the cephalic and basilic veins. It is the usual blood draw site, not a vein that climbs to the shoulder.
questions.answerText: Cephalic vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which superficial vein ascends the medial side of the forearm and arm and then joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein?
options: Median cubital vein
Cephalic vein
Subclavian vein
Basilic vein
questions.why: The basilic vein runs up the medial (little finger) side of the forearm and arm. Partway up the arm it passes deep and joins the paired brachial veins, and together they form the axillary vein. The cephalic vein is its mirror image on the lateral side.
notes: The median cubital vein is the short link between the cephalic and basilic veins at the front of the elbow. It would be the answer for the usual site of a blood draw.
The cephalic vein is the lateral superficial vein that passes through the deltopectoral groove to reach the axillary vein. Pick it if the question described the thumb side.
The subclavian vein is a deep vein near the clavicle, formed when the axillary vein crosses the first rib. It fits a question about the vein that joins the internal jugular vein.
Correct. The basilic vein ascends medially and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
questions.answerText: Basilic vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The median cubital vein connects which two veins across the front of the elbow?
options: The cephalic and basilic veins
The radial and ulnar veins
The subclavian and internal jugular veins
The brachial and axillary veins
questions.why: The median cubital vein is a short superficial vein that runs diagonally across the cubital fossa, the hollow at the front of the elbow. It links the cephalic vein on the lateral side to the basilic vein on the medial side. Because it is large and close to the skin, it is the usual site for drawing blood.
notes: Correct. The median cubital vein links the cephalic and basilic veins.
The radial and ulnar veins are deep, paired veins that travel beside the arteries of the same names in the forearm. Pick them for a question about deep veins of the forearm.
The subclavian and internal jugular veins join near the clavicle to form the brachiocephalic vein. They would be the answer for a question about how a brachiocephalic vein forms.
The brachial veins join the basilic vein to form the axillary vein, so they are connected in series, not by a crossing vein. This pair fits a question about how the axillary vein forms.
questions.answerText: The cephalic and basilic veins

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Each brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of which two veins?
options: Subclavian and internal jugular veins
Azygos and hemiazygos veins
Basilic and brachial veins
Axillary and cephalic veins
questions.why: Behind each sternoclavicular joint, the subclavian vein from the upper limb meets the internal jugular vein from the head and neck. Their union forms the brachiocephalic vein on that side. This happens on both the right and the left, so there are two brachiocephalic veins.
notes: Correct. The subclavian and internal jugular veins unite to form each brachiocephalic vein.
The hemiazygos vein crosses the midline to drain into the azygos vein, which then empties into the superior vena cava. Pick this pair for a question about veins draining the posterior thoracic wall.
The basilic vein and the brachial veins join to form the axillary vein, two steps before the brachiocephalic vein. They would be the answer for how the axillary vein forms.
The cephalic vein empties into the axillary vein, and the axillary then continues as the subclavian vein. This pair fits a question about where the cephalic vein ends.
questions.answerText: Subclavian and internal jugular veins

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The right and left brachiocephalic veins join to form which vessel?
options: Inferior vena cava
Pulmonary trunk
Azygos vein
Superior vena cava
questions.why: The two brachiocephalic veins meet behind the right side of the sternum to form the superior vena cava. The superior vena cava carries blood from the head, neck, upper limbs, and chest wall down into the right atrium. It is the final step for venous blood returning from the upper limb.
notes: The inferior vena cava drains the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdomen and enters the right atrium from below. Pick it if the question asked about blood returning from below the diaphragm.
The pulmonary trunk carries blood out of the right ventricle to the lungs. It is an artery leaving the heart, so it would fit a question about the vessel leaving the right ventricle.
The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic wall and empties into the superior vena cava, so it is a tributary, not the vessel formed by the brachiocephalic veins.
Correct. The two brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava.
questions.answerText: Superior vena cava

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which arteries, branching from the thoracic aorta, supply the tissue of the lungs themselves rather than carrying blood for gas exchange?
options: Posterior intercostal arteries
Esophageal arteries
Pulmonary arteries
Bronchial arteries
questions.why: Lung tissue needs its own oxygen-rich supply, just like any other organ. The bronchial arteries branch from the thoracic aorta and feed the walls of the bronchi and the supporting tissue of the lungs. The pulmonary arteries carry blood to the alveoli for gas exchange, which is a separate job.
notes: The posterior intercostal arteries leave the thoracic aorta to run in the intercostal spaces with the intercostal nerve and vein. Pick them for the blood supply of the chest wall between the ribs.
The esophageal arteries also branch from the thoracic aorta, but they supply the esophagus. They would be the answer for the blood supply of the esophagus in the thorax.

The pulmonary arteries come from the pulmonary trunk and carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs for gas exchange. Pick them if the question asked which vessels bring blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
Correct. The bronchial arteries supply the lung tissue itself.
questions.answerText: Bronchial arteries

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which vein ascends along the right side of the vertebral column, drains the posterior thoracic wall, and empties into the superior vena cava?
options: Internal thoracic vein
Azygos vein
Left brachiocephalic vein
Hemiazygos vein
questions.why: The azygos vein runs up the right side of the vertebral bodies in the posterior thorax, collecting blood from the posterior intercostal veins. At the top it arches forward over the root of the right lung and empties into the superior vena cava. It is the main drain of the back of the chest wall.
notes: The internal thoracic vein runs down the inside of the anterior chest wall beside the internal thoracic artery. It would fit a question about veins of the front of the chest wall.
Correct. The azygos vein runs on the right and empties into the superior vena cava.

The left brachiocephalic vein crosses the upper chest from left to right in front of the arch branches, carrying blood from the left head and upper limb. Pick it for a question about the vein that crosses the midline to help form the superior vena cava.
The hemiazygos vein runs on the left side of the vertebral column and crosses the midline to empty into the azygos vein. Pick it if the question described the left side.
questions.answerText: Azygos vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly explains why there is one brachiocephalic artery but two brachiocephalic veins?
options: The brachiocephalic artery serves both upper limbs, so only one is needed, while each vein drains only one side
Arteries always occur singly in the midline, while veins always occur in pairs, so every artery has two matching veins
The left upper limb is fed by the thoracic aorta instead, while each side drains through its own brachiocephalic vein
The left upper limb and left head get separate arteries off the arch, but both sides form their own brachiocephalic vein
questions.why: On the arterial side, the arch gives the right side one shared stem, the brachiocephalic trunk, while the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries leave the arch separately, so there is no left trunk. On the venous side, both the right and the left subclavian veins meet their internal jugular veins to form a brachiocephalic vein. The asymmetry of the arch shows up as one artery against two veins.
notes: The brachiocephalic trunk supplies only the right upper limb and the right side of the head and neck. Students pick this when they forget that the left upper limb has its own subclavian artery.
This is an overgeneralization. Many arteries are paired, such as the two subclavian and two common carotid arteries, so the rule does not exist.

The left upper limb is supplied by the left subclavian artery from the arch, not by the thoracic aorta. This option gets the venous half right but invents the wrong arterial source, which is the descending aorta mix-up.
Correct. The left side has separate arterial branches, but both sides build a brachiocephalic vein.
questions.answerText: The left upper limb and left head get separate arteries off the arch, but both sides form their own brachiocephalic vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Blood travels from the aortic arch to the left radial artery. Which sequence of arteries does it pass through?
options: Left subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial
Left common carotid, left subclavian, axillary, radial
Brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial
Left subclavian, brachial, axillary, radial
questions.why: On the left, the subclavian artery leaves the aortic arch directly, so there is no brachiocephalic step. The vessel is renamed axillary at the lateral border of the first rib and brachial at the lower border of teres major, and the brachial artery then divides in the cubital fossa into the radial and ulnar arteries.
notes: Correct. Left subclavian, axillary, brachial, then radial is the left side route.
The left common carotid artery runs up the neck and does not give rise to the subclavian. This sequence also skips the brachial artery, which every route to the forearm must pass through.
The brachiocephalic trunk exists only on the right. This sequence would be correct for blood heading to the right upper limb, where the subclavian comes from the trunk.
This puts brachial before axillary, which reverses the order. The axillary artery is in the armpit and comes first, then the brachial artery in the arm.
questions.answerText: Left subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Blood travels from the aortic arch to the right ulnar artery. Which sequence of arteries does it pass through?
options: Brachiocephalic trunk, right common carotid, axillary, brachial, ulnar
Brachiocephalic trunk, right subclavian, axillary, brachial, ulnar
Brachiocephalic trunk, right subclavian, brachial, axillary, ulnar
Right subclavian, axillary, brachial, ulnar
questions.why: On the right, blood first enters the brachiocephalic trunk, which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The subclavian becomes the axillary at the first rib and the brachial at teres major, and the brachial divides below the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries. The right side has one more named step than the left because of the trunk.
notes: The right common carotid artery goes up the neck to the head, not to the upper limb. Pick it only for a route from the arch to the right side of the face or brain.
Correct. Brachiocephalic trunk, right subclavian, axillary, brachial, then ulnar is the right side route.
This reverses axillary and brachial. The axillary artery lies in the armpit and comes before the brachial artery of the arm.
This sequence leaves out the brachiocephalic trunk. It would be correct for the left side, where the subclavian artery comes straight off the arch.
questions.answerText: Brachiocephalic trunk, right subclavian, axillary, brachial, ulnar

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: In the lab you point to the segment of the main upper limb artery that lies between the lateral border of the first rib and the lower border of teres major. What is this segment called?
options: Axillary artery
Subclavian artery
Deep brachial artery
Brachial artery
questions.why: The name of the main artery of the upper limb depends on where you are along it. Between the lateral border of the first rib and the lower border of teres major, it passes through the axilla (armpit) and is called the axillary artery. Above that segment it is the subclavian artery, and below it is the brachial artery.
notes: Correct. Between the first rib and teres major the vessel is the axillary artery.
The subclavian artery is the segment before the first rib, arching over the rib behind the clavicle. Pick it for the part of the vessel medial to the first rib.
The deep brachial artery is a branch of the brachial artery that runs in the radial groove. It is a side branch, not a segment of the main vessel, so it fits a question about the radial groove.
The brachial artery begins at the lower border of teres major and runs down the arm. It would be the answer for the segment between teres major and the cubital fossa.
questions.answerText: Axillary artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the superficial and deep palmar arches?
options: The superficial arch lies on the back of the hand, and the deep arch lies in the palm
The superficial arch is more distal and mainly ulnar; the deep arch is more proximal and mainly radial
Both arches are formed only by the ulnar artery, one lying on top of the other
The superficial arch is more proximal and mainly radial; the deep arch is more distal and mainly ulnar
questions.why: Both palmar arches are joins between the radial and ulnar arteries in the palm. The superficial palmar arch lies nearer the fingers (more distal) and is formed mainly by the ulnar artery. The deep palmar arch lies nearer the wrist (more proximal) and is formed mainly by the radial artery.
notes: Both arches are in the palm, as their name palmar says. The back of the hand drains through the dorsal venous network, which would fit a question about superficial veins of the hand.
Correct. The superficial arch is distal and mainly ulnar, and the deep arch is proximal and mainly radial.
Both arches are formed by the radial and ulnar arteries together, which is the whole point of an arch. This option misses that each arch is a connection between the two arteries.
This statement swaps every feature of the two arches. Students pick it when they try to match radial with superficial because the radial pulse is superficial at the wrist.
questions.answerText: The superficial arch is more distal and mainly ulnar; the deep arch is more proximal and mainly radial

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the superficial and deep veins of the upper limb?
options: Superficial veins carry blood away from the heart, while deep veins carry blood back toward the heart
Superficial veins take their own paths under the skin, while deep veins are paired beside the arteries of the same names
Superficial veins travel deep beside the arteries of the same names, while the deep veins run alone just under the skin
The upper limb has only deep veins, because large superficial veins are found only in the lower limb
questions.why: The superficial veins of the upper limb, such as the cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins, run in the tissue just under the skin and follow their own routes. The deep veins, such as the radial, ulnar, and brachial veins, are paired and travel alongside the artery with the same name. In the upper limb the superficial veins are the large, visible ones, which is the reverse of the lower limb.
notes: All veins carry blood toward the heart; carrying blood away from the heart is what arteries do. This is the mix-up of thinking depth decides direction of flow.
Correct. Superficial veins take their own paths, and deep veins are paired beside arteries of the same name.
This statement reverses the two systems. The deep veins are the ones that accompany named arteries, while the cephalic and basilic veins take their own paths under the skin.
The upper limb has well developed superficial veins, including the cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins. They are in fact the large veins used for blood draws.
questions.answerText: Superficial veins take their own paths under the skin, while deep veins are paired beside the arteries of the same names

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Blood in the cephalic vein of the arm returns to the heart. Which sequence of veins does it follow?
options: Cephalic, basilic, brachial, axillary, superior vena cava
Cephalic, axillary, subclavian, internal jugular, superior vena cava
Cephalic, axillary, subclavian, brachiocephalic, superior vena cava
Cephalic, subclavian, axillary, brachiocephalic, superior vena cava
questions.why: The cephalic vein passes through the deltopectoral groove and empties into the axillary vein. The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein at the first rib, the subclavian joins the internal jugular to form the brachiocephalic vein, and the two brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava, which enters the right atrium.
notes: The cephalic vein does not drain into the basilic or brachial veins on its way up; it joins the axillary vein directly. This route also skips the subclavian and brachiocephalic veins.

The internal jugular vein carries blood down from the head and meets the subclavian vein, so blood from the arm does not flow into it. The vessel formed at that meeting, the brachiocephalic vein, is the correct next step.
Correct. Cephalic, axillary, subclavian, brachiocephalic, then superior vena cava.
This swaps the axillary and subclavian veins. The axillary vein lies in the armpit and comes first, then the subclavian vein near the clavicle.
questions.answerText: Cephalic, axillary, subclavian, brachiocephalic, superior vena cava

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A medication is injected into the basilic vein in the arm. As the blood rises toward the shoulder, which named vein does it enter next?
options: Subclavian vein
Cephalic vein
Axillary vein
Internal jugular vein
questions.why: The basilic vein runs up the medial arm and joins the paired brachial veins, and their union forms the axillary vein. So the next named vein after the basilic is the axillary vein, which then becomes the subclavian vein at the first rib.
notes: The subclavian vein comes one step later, after the axillary vein crosses the first rib. It would be the answer if the question asked where blood goes after the axillary vein.

The cephalic vein is the other superficial vein, on the lateral side of the arm, and the basilic vein does not drain into it. Pick it for the lateral vein that passes through the deltopectoral groove to reach the axillary vein.
Correct. The basilic vein joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
The internal jugular vein drains the head and neck downward and meets the subclavian vein. It would fit a question about which vein joins the subclavian to form the brachiocephalic vein.
questions.answerText: Axillary vein

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. Where does the axillary vein become the subclavian vein?
options: At the lower border of teres major
At the deltopectoral groove
At the sternoclavicular joint
At the lateral border of the first rib
questions.why: The deep veins follow the arteries, so the same landmark changes the name of both vessels. The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein as it crosses the lateral border of the first rib, just as the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery there. The only difference is direction: blood in the vein is flowing toward the heart.
notes: The lower border of teres major is where the brachial veins and basilic vein become the axillary vein, and where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery. Pick it for the lower end of the axillary vessels.
The deltopectoral groove is where the cephalic vein runs before it dives to join the axillary vein. It would be the answer for the path of the cephalic vein.
The sternoclavicular joint is roughly where the subclavian vein joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. It marks the end of the subclavian vein, not its start.
Correct. The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.
questions.answerText: At the lateral border of the first rib

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the anterior and posterior intercostal arteries?
options: Both sets branch from the subclavian artery before it crosses the first rib
Both sets branch from the axillary artery as it passes through the armpit
The anterior intercostals branch from the internal thoracic artery, and the posterior intercostals branch from the thoracic aorta
The anterior intercostals branch from the thoracic aorta, and the posterior intercostals branch from the internal thoracic artery
questions.why: Each intercostal space gets blood from both ends. The anterior intercostal arteries come from the internal thoracic artery, which runs down the inside of the front chest wall beside the sternum. The posterior intercostal arteries come from the thoracic aorta, which lies against the vertebral column at the back, and they run in the intercostal space with the intercostal nerve and vein.
notes: The subclavian artery gives rise to the internal thoracic artery, so it is only the indirect source of the anterior set. This option is the mix-up of naming the parent vessel instead of the direct branch.

The axillary artery supplies the shoulder, the lateral chest wall, and the pectoral region through branches like the lateral thoracic artery. It would fit a question about the arteries of the armpit, not the intercostal spaces.
Correct. Anterior intercostals come from the internal thoracic artery, and posterior intercostals come from the thoracic aorta.
This statement swaps the two sources. Think about location: the internal thoracic artery runs down the front of the chest, so it feeds the front ends of the spaces, and the aorta lies at the back.
questions.answerText: The anterior intercostals branch from the internal thoracic artery, and the posterior intercostals branch from the thoracic aorta

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A cardiac surgeon needs an artery that runs down the inside of the anterior chest wall, just beside the sternum, to use as a coronary bypass graft. Which artery is it?
options: Posterior intercostal artery
Internal thoracic artery
Lateral thoracic artery
Thoracoacromial artery
questions.why: The internal thoracic artery branches from the subclavian artery and runs down the deep surface of the anterior chest wall, just lateral to the sternum. Because it lies so close to the heart, surgeons can redirect it to carry blood past a blocked coronary artery. It also gives off the anterior intercostal arteries along the way.
notes: The posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta at the back of the chest and run in the intercostal spaces. They would fit a question about the arteries that run with the intercostal nerve from behind.
Correct. The internal thoracic artery runs beside the sternum and is used as a bypass graft.
The lateral thoracic artery is a branch of the axillary artery that runs down the side of the chest wall with the long thoracic nerve. Pick it if the question described the lateral chest wall.
The thoracoacromial artery is a short branch of the axillary artery that supplies the pectoral region and the deltoid. It lies near the shoulder, not along the sternum.
questions.answerText: Internal thoracic artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement best explains why the median cubital vein is the usual site for drawing blood?
options: It is a deep vein, so it is protected from bruising after the needle is removed
It has no structures beneath it, so the needle cannot hit anything if it goes too deep
It is a large superficial vein over the cubital fossa, easy to see and reach
It carries oxygen-rich blood straight from the heart, so the sample is fresher
questions.why: The median cubital vein crosses the front of the elbow just under the skin, linking the cephalic and basilic veins. It is large, easy to see and feel, and sits over the cubital fossa where the arm can be held straight and still. The brachial artery and median nerve lie just deep to it, separated only by the bicipital aponeurosis, a flat sheet of tendon, so the draw is done carefully.
notes: The median cubital vein is superficial, not deep. A deep vein would be hard to find through the skin, which is the opposite of what a blood draw needs.
The brachial artery and median nerve lie just deep to the vein, separated only by the bicipital aponeurosis. That is exactly why the needle must not go too deep.
Correct. It is large, superficial, and easy to reach over the cubital fossa.
Veins carry blood toward the heart, and blood in the arm veins has already given up oxygen to the tissues. This is the mix-up of thinking a blood draw samples an artery.
questions.answerText: It is a large superficial vein over the cubital fossa, easy to see and reach

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the right and left brachiocephalic veins?
options: Both are the same length and join in the exact midline to form the inferior vena cava
The left one is longer because it must cross the midline to reach the superior vena cava
Only the right side has a brachiocephalic vein, matching the single brachiocephalic artery
The right one is longer because it must cross the midline to reach the heart
questions.why: The superior vena cava lies on the right side of the upper chest. The right brachiocephalic vein is short and runs almost straight down into it, while the left brachiocephalic vein must cross the midline from left to right to reach it, so the left one is longer. Both are formed by a subclavian vein joining an internal jugular vein.
notes: The brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava, not the inferior vena cava, which drains the body below the diaphragm. They also differ in length, because the superior vena cava sits to the right of the midline.
Correct. The left brachiocephalic vein is longer because it crosses the midline.
There are two brachiocephalic veins, one on each side, even though there is only one brachiocephalic artery. This is the mix-up of assuming the veins copy the arterial asymmetry.
The superior vena cava is on the right, so it is the left vein that has to cross the midline. This option reverses the sides.
questions.answerText: The left one is longer because it must cross the midline to reach the superior vena cava

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the azygos and hemiazygos veins?
options: The azygos runs on the right into the superior vena cava; the hemiazygos crosses from the left to join it
Both veins run along the front of the sternum and drain the breast
The azygos runs on the left and empties into the inferior vena cava; the hemiazygos runs on the right
Both veins drain the upper limb and empty into the axillary vein near the first rib
questions.why: Both veins drain the posterior thoracic wall through the posterior intercostal veins. The azygos vein runs up the right side of the vertebral column and arches forward to empty into the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos vein runs on the left side and crosses the midline behind the aorta to drain into the azygos.
notes: Correct. The azygos is on the right and ends in the superior vena cava, and the hemiazygos crosses from the left to join it.
The vein running down the inside of the front chest wall beside the sternum is the internal thoracic vein. Pick it if the question described the anterior chest wall.
This reverses the sides and sends the azygos to the wrong vena cava. The azygos is on the right and ends in the superior vena cava.
Veins from the upper limb, such as the cephalic and basilic veins, drain into the axillary vein. The azygos system drains the back of the chest wall instead.
questions.answerText: The azygos runs on the right into the superior vena cava; the hemiazygos crosses from the left to join it

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: Tracing the ulnar artery just below the cubital fossa, you find a short branch that soon splits into anterior and posterior interosseous arteries. What is this short branch?
options: Radial artery
Posterior circumflex humeral artery
Deep brachial artery
Common interosseous artery
questions.why: The common interosseous artery is a short branch of the ulnar artery in the upper forearm. It quickly divides into an anterior interosseous artery and a posterior interosseous artery, which run on either side of the interosseous membrane, the sheet of connective tissue between the radius and ulna. The name interosseous means between bones.
notes: The radial artery is the other terminal branch of the brachial artery, not a branch of the ulnar artery. Pick it for the artery on the thumb side of the forearm.
The posterior circumflex humeral artery is a branch of the axillary artery that wraps the surgical neck of the humerus. It is far above the forearm, so it fits only a question about the shoulder.
The deep brachial artery branches from the brachial artery in the arm and runs in the radial groove of the humerus. It would fit a question about the artery traveling with the radial nerve.
Correct. The common interosseous artery branches from the ulnar artery and splits into anterior and posterior interosseous arteries.
questions.answerText: Common interosseous artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: While taking a blood pressure, a nurse places the stethoscope in the cubital fossa just medial to the biceps brachii tendon, below the cuff. Which artery is the nurse listening over?
options: Axillary artery
Ulnar artery
Radial artery
Brachial artery
questions.why: The brachial artery runs down the medial side of the arm and enters the cubital fossa just medial to the biceps tendon, before it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries. That is where the stethoscope is placed, below the cuff that compresses the same artery higher up the arm. Knowing that the brachial artery has not yet divided at this point is what makes it the answer.
notes: The axillary artery is in the armpit, above the cuff and far from the elbow. Pick it for the segment between the first rib and teres major.
The ulnar artery also begins below the elbow and runs on the little finger side of the forearm. It would fit a question about the main supply of the superficial palmar arch.
The radial artery begins below the elbow and is felt at the thumb side of the wrist. Pick it if the question described a pulse taken at the wrist.
Correct. The stethoscope sits over the brachial artery medial to the biceps tendon.
questions.answerText: Brachial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A person cuts the anterior wrist on the thumb side with broken glass, and bright red blood spurts in rhythm with the heartbeat. Which artery has most likely been cut?
options: Radial artery
Median cubital vein
Ulnar artery
Cephalic vein
questions.why: Bright red blood that spurts with each heartbeat comes from an artery, not a vein. On the anterior wrist, the artery on the thumb side is the radial artery, the same vessel used to take the pulse. It lies close to the surface there, which is why it can be felt easily and also cut easily.
notes: Correct. The radial artery lies near the surface on the thumb side of the anterior wrist.
The median cubital vein is at the front of the elbow, not the wrist, and it is a vein. Pick it for a question about the usual blood draw site.
The ulnar artery is on the little finger side of the wrist. It would be the answer if the cut were on the opposite side of the wrist.
The cephalic vein does start on the thumb side, but blood from a cut vein is darker and flows steadily rather than spurting. Pick it if the wound oozed dark blood on the lateral forearm.
questions.answerText: Radial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A catheter is placed in a patient's radial artery at the wrist, and the vessel becomes temporarily blocked. Why does the hand still receive blood?
options: The deep brachial artery takes over and runs directly down into the hand
The cephalic vein reverses direction and carries blood into the hand
The hand receives its blood from the anterior intercostal arteries
The ulnar artery still feeds the palmar arches, which connect to the radial side
questions.why: The radial and ulnar arteries join each other in the palm to form the superficial and deep palmar arches. A connection like this between two arteries is called an anastomosis, and it means each artery can fill the arches if the other is blocked. This second supply from the ulnar side is why the radial artery can be used for a catheter fairly safely.
notes: The deep brachial artery stays in the arm, running in the radial groove of the humerus. It does not reach the hand, so it fits a question about the radial groove.
Veins carry blood toward the heart and have valves that prevent backward flow, so the cephalic vein cannot deliver blood to the hand. This is the mix-up of thinking a vein can stand in for an artery.
The anterior intercostal arteries supply the front of the intercostal spaces in the chest wall. They would fit a question about the branches of the internal thoracic artery.
Correct. The ulnar artery keeps feeding the hand through the palmar arches.
questions.answerText: The ulnar artery still feeds the palmar arches, which connect to the radial side

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A fall fractures the surgical neck of the humerus. Which artery, wrapping around the back of that neck with the axillary nerve, is most at risk?
options: Deep brachial artery
Subscapular artery
Posterior circumflex humeral artery
Anterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.why: The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries are branches of the axillary artery that circle the surgical neck, the narrowing just below the tubercles of the humerus. The posterior circumflex humeral artery travels around the back of the neck together with the axillary nerve. A fracture at this site can injure both the artery and the nerve that run with it.
notes: The deep brachial artery runs in the radial groove along the middle of the humeral shaft. It would be the vessel at risk in a mid-shaft fracture, not a fracture of the surgical neck.
The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery and runs down along the scapula. It does not wrap the humerus, so it fits a question about the largest axillary branch.
Correct. The posterior circumflex humeral artery wraps the surgical neck with the axillary nerve.

The anterior circumflex humeral artery is the smaller vessel that wraps the front of the surgical neck. It does not travel with the axillary nerve around the back, so pick it if the question asked about the artery on the front of the neck.
questions.answerText: Posterior circumflex humeral artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A fracture through the middle of the humeral shaft damages the radial nerve in the radial groove. Which artery, running in the same groove, could be torn as well?
options: Posterior circumflex humeral artery
Deep brachial artery
Axillary artery
Radial artery
questions.why: The deep brachial artery branches from the brachial artery and spirals around the back of the humerus in the radial groove, right beside the radial nerve. Both lie pressed against the bone at mid-shaft, so a fracture line there can injure the artery and the nerve together. Structures that share a groove share the same risk.
notes: The posterior circumflex humeral artery wraps the surgical neck higher up the bone, with the axillary nerve. Pick it for a fracture of the surgical neck.
Correct. The deep brachial artery runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove.
The axillary artery lies in the armpit above the humeral shaft. It would fit a question about the segment of the main artery between the first rib and teres major.
The radial artery is in the forearm on the thumb side and is not in the radial groove of the humerus. Students choose it because it shares the word radial with the nerve and the groove.
questions.answerText: Deep brachial artery

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A medication is injected into the cephalic vein on the forearm. Which great vein will deliver it into the right atrium?
options: Pulmonary vein
Superior vena cava
Inferior vena cava
Coronary sinus
questions.why: The cephalic vein drains into the axillary vein, which becomes the subclavian vein, which joins the internal jugular to form the brachiocephalic vein. The two brachiocephalic veins form the superior vena cava, which empties into the right atrium. Everything from the upper limbs, head, and neck returns to the heart this way.
notes: The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium. They would be the answer for blood returning from the lungs, not from the arm.
Correct. Blood from the upper limb reaches the right atrium through the superior vena cava.
The inferior vena cava returns blood from the body below the diaphragm. It would be the answer for a medication injected into a vein of the leg.
The coronary sinus drains the heart wall itself into the right atrium. Pick it for a question about where the cardiac veins empty.
questions.answerText: Superior vena cava

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A clot blocks the brachiocephalic trunk near its origin. Which regions lose much of their arterial supply?
options: The left upper limb and the left side of the head and neck
Both upper limbs, but not the head and neck
The left side of the head and neck only
The right upper limb and the right side of the head and neck
questions.why: The brachiocephalic trunk is the shared stem for the right side only, dividing into the right common carotid artery to the head and neck and the right subclavian artery to the upper limb. A block at its origin cuts off both of those branches. The left side is unaffected because the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries leave the arch on their own.
notes: The left side of the head, neck, and upper limb is fed by the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries straight off the arch. This option would be right if the question described blocks in both of those arteries.
The left upper limb has its own subclavian artery from the arch, and the trunk does feed the right head and neck. This is the mix-up of thinking the trunk serves both arms.
The left side of the head and neck is fed by the left common carotid artery. Pick this option for a block in the left common carotid artery.
Correct. The trunk serves the right upper limb and the right side of the head and neck.
questions.answerText: The right upper limb and the right side of the head and neck

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: During a blood draw from the median cubital vein, the needle goes too deep. Which structures lie just beneath the vein and are at risk?
options: The radial artery and the radial nerve
The brachial artery and the median nerve
The deep brachial artery and the axillary nerve
The ulnar artery and the ulnar nerve
questions.why: In the cubital fossa, the brachial artery and the median nerve lie immediately deep to the median cubital vein. The only thing separating them is the bicipital aponeurosis, a flat sheet of tendon from the biceps. That is why a blood draw is taken at this site, and why it is taken carefully.
notes: The radial artery begins below the cubital fossa and runs down the thumb side of the forearm, and the radial nerve lies on the lateral side of the elbow. Pick this pair for a deep cut on the lateral side.
Correct. The brachial artery and median nerve lie just deep to the vein.
The deep brachial artery is on the back of the humerus in the radial groove, and the axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck. Neither is in the cubital fossa.
The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle, not in front of the elbow under the vein. This pair fits a question about an injury on the medial side of the elbow.
questions.answerText: The brachial artery and the median nerve

questions.topic: Arteries and veins of the thorax and upper limb
questions.q: A stab wound on the medial side of the middle of the arm produces bright red, pulsing bleeding. Which artery is most likely injured?
options: Brachial artery
Deep brachial artery
Cephalic vein
Axillary artery
questions.why: Pulsing, bright red blood means an artery has been cut. The main artery of the arm, the brachial artery, runs down the medial side of the arm from the lower border of teres major to the cubital fossa, alongside the median nerve. A wound at mid-arm on the medial side is right over its path.
notes: Correct. The brachial artery runs down the medial side of the arm.
The deep brachial artery winds around the back of the humerus in the radial groove. It would be the answer for a wound or fracture at the back of the mid-arm.
The cephalic vein runs up the lateral side of the arm, and bleeding from a vein is darker and steady rather than pulsing. Pick it for a superficial cut on the lateral arm with dark, oozing blood.
The axillary artery lies in the armpit, above the arm. It would fit a wound deep in the axilla, between the first rib and teres major.
questions.answerText: Brachial artery

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: To which of the four primary tissue types does blood belong?
options: Epithelial tissue
Nervous tissue
Muscle tissue
Connective tissue
questions.why: The four primary tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue. Blood is classified as connective tissue because, like all connective tissues, it is made of cells suspended in an extracellular matrix. In blood the matrix is a fluid, the plasma, which makes blood the only liquid tissue in the body.
notes: Epithelial tissue is made of tightly packed cells that cover surfaces and line cavities, with almost no matrix between them. It is the answer for tissue like the lining of blood vessels, not the blood inside.
Nervous tissue is made of neurons and neuroglia that carry and support electrical signals. It fits the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
Muscle tissue is made of cells that contract, such as cardiac muscle in the heart wall. Pick it if the question asked about the tissue that pumps the blood.
Correct. Blood is cells suspended in a matrix, plasma, so it is a connective tissue.
questions.answerText: Connective tissue

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Blood is classified as which specific kind of connective tissue?
options: Fluid connective tissue
Loose connective tissue
Supporting connective tissue
Dense connective tissue
questions.why: Connective tissues are sorted partly by the nature of their matrix. Blood has a liquid matrix, the plasma, in which the formed elements float, so it is called a fluid connective tissue. This sets it apart from connective tissue proper, cartilage, and bone, which have fibrous, firm, or hard matrices.
notes: Correct. Plasma is a liquid matrix, so blood is a fluid connective tissue.
Loose connective tissue, such as areolar tissue, has a soft, gel-like matrix with scattered fibers and lies beneath epithelia. Its matrix is not a flowing fluid.
Cartilage and bone are the supporting connective tissues, with firm or calcified matrices. They are the answer for tissues that hold the body up.
Dense connective tissue is packed with collagen fibers and forms tendons and ligaments. Choose it for a structure that resists pulling forces.
questions.answerText: Fluid connective tissue

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: About what percentage of whole blood is made up of formed elements?
options: About 7 percent
About 55 percent
About 45 percent
About 92 percent
questions.why: When a blood sample is spun in a centrifuge, it separates into layers. The formed elements, which are the cells and cell fragments, settle to the bottom and make up about 45 percent of the volume, most of it erythrocytes. The plasma above them makes up the remaining 55 percent.
notes: About 7 to 8 percent is the share of body weight made up by blood, or the share of plasma made up by proteins. It is not the formed element fraction.
About 55 percent is the plasma fraction of whole blood. Students often swap the two numbers, so match the larger number to the fluid.
Correct. Formed elements are just under half of whole blood.
About 92 percent is the water content of plasma. Pick it for a question about what plasma is mostly made of.
questions.answerText: About 45 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: About what percentage of whole blood is plasma?
options: About 45 percent
About 92 percent
About 8 percent
About 55 percent
questions.why: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, and it makes up a little more than half of the volume, about 55 percent. The formed elements make up the other 45 percent. In a spun tube, the plasma is the pale yellow layer at the top.
notes: About 45 percent is the formed element fraction, mostly erythrocytes. It is the answer when the question asks about the cells and cell fragments.
About 92 percent is the share of plasma that is water. That number describes what plasma contains, not how much of the blood it makes up.
About 8 percent is close to the share of body weight that is blood, and to the share of plasma that is protein. It does not describe the plasma fraction of blood.
Correct. Plasma is a little more than half of whole blood.
questions.answerText: About 55 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the two major fractions of whole blood?
options: Plasma about 92 percent, formed elements about 8 percent
Plasma about 55 percent, buffy coat about 45 percent
Plasma about 45 percent, formed elements about 55 percent
Plasma about 55 percent, formed elements about 45 percent
questions.why: Whole blood separates into two major fractions. Plasma, the fluid matrix, is about 55 percent of the volume, and the formed elements, the erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets, are about 45 percent. A thin buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets lies between them in a spun sample, but it is part of the formed elements.
notes: About 92 percent is the water content of plasma, and about 8 percent is roughly the solute share. These describe plasma itself, not whole blood.
The buffy coat is the thin layer of leukocytes and platelets, less than 1 percent of the sample. The 45 percent fraction is mostly erythrocytes.
This reverses the two numbers. Plasma is the larger fraction, so this is the mix-up to watch for.
Correct. The fluid is slightly more than half and the cells slightly less.
questions.answerText: Plasma about 55 percent, formed elements about 45 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What structural role does plasma play in blood?
options: It is the layer of leukocytes and platelets
It is the fluid left after blood clots
It is the cellular fraction of blood
It is the extracellular matrix of blood
questions.why: Every connective tissue is made of cells and an extracellular matrix, the material between the cells. In blood that matrix is plasma, a fluid in which the formed elements are suspended and carried. Calling plasma the matrix is what places blood among the connective tissues.
notes: The thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets in a spun sample is the buffy coat. Pick it for the middle layer of a centrifuged tube.
The fluid left after blood clots is serum, which is plasma with the clotting proteins removed. Choose serum when the clotting proteins are gone.
The cellular fraction is the formed elements: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. Plasma is a fluid with no cells in it.
Correct. Plasma is the fluid matrix in which the formed elements float.
questions.answerText: It is the extracellular matrix of blood

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the approximate blood volume of an average adult?
options: About 15 liters
About 1 liter
About 40 liters
About 5 liters
questions.why: An average adult has about 5 liters of blood, which is roughly 7 to 8 percent of body weight. This volume circulates continuously through the heart and vessels. Losing a large fraction of it quickly is life threatening, which is why blood volume matters in trauma care.
notes: About 15 liters is closer to the total amount of fluid outside the cells in an adult, which includes the fluid between cells as well as plasma. Blood is only a part of that.
One liter is far too little for an adult. It is closer to the blood volume of a small child.
About 40 liters is closer to the total water in an adult body. Students who choose it confuse blood volume with all body water.
Correct. An average adult carries about 5 liters of blood.
questions.answerText: About 5 liters

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Blood makes up approximately what percentage of total body weight?
options: About 1 to 2 percent
About 60 percent
About 45 percent
About 7 to 8 percent
questions.why: Blood accounts for about 7 to 8 percent of body weight. For an average adult, that works out to about 5 liters. It is a small share of the body, but it reaches every tissue through the vessels.
notes: About 1 to 2 percent is the share of circulating red cells that are reticulocytes. It is much too small for blood as a share of body weight.
About 60 percent is closer to the share of body weight made up of water. Blood is only a small part of that water.
About 45 percent is the share of whole blood made up of formed elements. It describes blood itself, not blood as a part of the body.
Correct. Blood is about 7 to 8 percent of body weight, about 5 liters in an adult.
questions.answerText: About 7 to 8 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the normal pH range of blood?
questions.why: Blood pH is held in a narrow range of 7.35 to 7.45. Because 7.0 is neutral, this range is slightly alkaline, meaning slightly basic. Values outside this range disturb how cells and proteins work, so the body regulates blood pH closely.
notes: A range from 6.8 to 7.0 is neutral to slightly acidic. Students who pick it assume body fluids are neutral, but blood is slightly alkaline.
A pH of 7.0 to 7.2 is lower than normal blood. Blood in this range would be too acidic.
Correct. Normal blood is held in this narrow, slightly alkaline range.
A pH of 7.8 to 8.2 is far more alkaline than normal blood. Students who choose it overstate how basic blood is.

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which description fits the pH of normal blood?
options: Slightly alkaline, about 7.35 to 7.45
Slightly acidic, about 6.5 to 6.9
Strongly alkaline, about 9 to 10
Exactly neutral, at 7.0
questions.why: On the pH scale, 7.0 is neutral, numbers below 7 are acidic, and numbers above 7 are alkaline (basic). Normal blood sits at 7.35 to 7.45, just above neutral, so it is slightly alkaline. Keeping blood in this narrow range is one of the regulatory functions of blood.
notes: Correct. Just above neutral means slightly alkaline.
Values below 7.0 are acidic, and blood normally stays above 7.0. This choice reverses the side of neutral that blood sits on.
A pH of 9 to 10 is strongly basic, more like a mild cleaning solution. Blood is only slightly alkaline.
A pH of exactly 7.0 is neutral, like pure water. Blood is a little more alkaline than water.
questions.answerText: Slightly alkaline, about 7.35 to 7.45

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the normal temperature of blood?
options: About 35°C (95°F)
About 40°C (104°F)
questions.why: Blood runs at about 38°C (100.4°F). Blood picks up heat from active organs and carries it around the body, which is part of its role in spreading heat evenly. When blood flows near the skin, it can give off that heat.
notes: About 42°C (107.6°F) is a dangerously high temperature, well above any normal reading. Blood this hot would signal a medical emergency.
About 35°C (95°F) is cooler than normal and is the threshold usually used for hypothermia. Blood is not normally this cool.
About 40°C (104°F) is a high fever. Blood at this temperature would signal illness, not normal function.
Correct. Blood runs at about 38°C (100.4°F).

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: About how many times more viscous than water is blood?
options: About the same as water
About 2 times
About 20 times
About 5 times
questions.why: Viscosity is how thick and resistant to flow a fluid is. Blood is about 5 times more viscous than water because it carries plasma proteins and a large number of formed elements. That thickness affects how hard the heart must work to push blood through the vessels.
notes: Plasma is mostly water, but whole blood also carries proteins and cells, so it is clearly thicker than water. This choice ignores the formed elements.
Two times understates the thickness of whole blood. It is closer to the viscosity of plasma alone, which lacks the formed elements.
Twenty times overstates the thickness of blood. Blood this thick would flow very poorly through capillaries.
Correct. Proteins and formed elements make blood about 5 times thicker than water.
questions.answerText: About 5 times

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which two components of blood are chiefly responsible for its high viscosity?
options: Water and dissolved gases
Proteins and formed elements
Urea and other wastes
Electrolytes and glucose
questions.why: Viscosity is the thickness of a fluid, its resistance to flowing. Water alone flows easily, so blood gets its extra thickness from what is carried in it: the plasma proteins dissolved in the plasma and the formed elements suspended in it. More red cells, as in polycythemia, make blood even thicker and slower.
notes: Water is the solvent that lets blood flow, and dissolved gases add little bulk. These parts make blood thinner, not thicker.
Correct. Proteins and cells are what make blood about 5 times thicker than water.
Urea, creatinine, and other wastes are dissolved in small amounts. They are carried in plasma for removal, not a major cause of viscosity.
Electrolytes such as Na+ and nutrients such as glucose are small dissolved solutes. They matter for chemistry but add little to the thickness of blood.
questions.answerText: Proteins and formed elements

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What color is oxygen-rich blood?
options: Blue
Dark red
Bright red
Pale yellow
questions.why: Blood gets its color from hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein in erythrocytes. When hemoglobin is loaded with oxygen, the blood is bright red, or scarlet. When it has given up much of its oxygen, the blood is a darker red.
notes: Blood is never blue. Veins can look bluish through the skin because of how light passes through tissue, which leads students to this mistake.
Dark red is the color of oxygen-poor blood, such as blood returning to the heart in the veins. Pick it for blood after the tissues have taken its oxygen.
Correct. Oxygen-loaded hemoglobin makes blood scarlet.
Pale yellow is the color of plasma once the cells are removed. It does not describe whole blood.
questions.answerText: Bright red

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What color is oxygen-poor blood?
options: Bright red
Blue
Dark red
Pale yellow
questions.why: Hemoglobin changes color depending on how much oxygen it holds. Oxygen-poor blood, such as the blood returning to the heart in the veins, is dark red. It is still red because hemoglobin is a red pigment whether or not oxygen is bound to it.
notes: Bright red, or scarlet, is the color of oxygen-rich blood, as in the arteries of the systemic circuit. It is the answer for blood just leaving the lungs.
Blood is not blue at any point. Veins only look bluish through the skin, which is an effect of light passing through tissue.
Correct. Hemoglobin that has released much of its oxygen gives blood a darker red color.
Pale yellow is the color of plasma after the cells are removed. Whole blood, with its erythrocytes, is always some shade of red.
questions.answerText: Dark red

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the most abundant component of plasma?
options: Electrolytes
Nutrients
Water
Plasma proteins
questions.why: Plasma is mostly water, about 92 percent of its volume. Water is the solvent that carries every other component in solution: the plasma proteins, nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, and gases. The plasma proteins are the most abundant of the dissolved solutes, but they are a small share compared with water.
notes: Electrolytes such as Na+, K+, and Cl- are important dissolved ions, but they make up only a tiny share of plasma by weight.
Nutrients such as glucose and amino acids are carried in plasma in small amounts. They are not close to the bulk of plasma.
Correct. About 92 percent of plasma is water.
Plasma proteins are the most abundant of the dissolved solutes, about 7 to 8 percent of plasma. Pick them if the question asked which solute is most abundant.
questions.answerText: Water

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: About what percentage of plasma is water?
options: About 8 percent
About 55 percent
About 92 percent
About 45 percent
questions.why: Plasma is roughly 92 percent water, with the rest made up of dissolved solutes. The water acts as a solvent, carrying proteins, nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, and gases. This is why plasma looks like a thin, pale yellow fluid.
notes: About 8 percent is close to the share of plasma made up of solutes, mostly proteins. It is the other part of plasma, not the water.
About 55 percent is the share of whole blood made up of plasma. It describes how much of the blood is plasma, not how much of the plasma is water.
Correct. Plasma is about 92 percent water.
About 45 percent is the formed element fraction of whole blood. It does not describe plasma at all.
questions.answerText: About 92 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Plasma proteins make up approximately what percentage of plasma?
options: About 7 to 8 percent
About 45 percent
About 92 percent
About 55 percent
questions.why: After water, the plasma proteins are the largest part of plasma, at about 7 to 8 percent. They include albumin, the globulins, and fibrinogen. Even though they are a small share by weight, they make up most of the dissolved solutes in plasma.
notes: Correct. Plasma proteins are about 7 to 8 percent of plasma.
About 45 percent is the formed element share of whole blood. It is not a plasma component.
About 92 percent is the water content of plasma. Pick it for the most abundant component of plasma.
About 55 percent is the plasma share of whole blood. Students who pick this mix up how much blood is plasma with how much plasma is protein.
questions.answerText: About 7 to 8 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which is the most abundant plasma protein?
options: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Hemoglobin
Globulins
questions.why: Albumin makes up about 60 percent of the plasma proteins, which makes it the most abundant. It is made by the liver. Albumin holds water in the blood by maintaining osmotic pressure and carries hormones, fatty acids, and drugs.
notes: Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein and the clotting protein, but it is only about 4 percent of plasma proteins. Pick it for a question about clotting.
Correct. Albumin is about 60 percent of the plasma proteins.
Hemoglobin is found inside erythrocytes, not dissolved in plasma. Students choose it because it is the best-known blood protein.
The globulins are about 35 percent of plasma proteins and include transport proteins and the antibodies. They are the second most abundant group.
questions.answerText: Albumin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Albumin makes up about what share of the plasma proteins?
options: About 4 percent
About 35 percent
About 60 percent
About 92 percent
questions.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, at about 60 percent of the total. The globulins make up about 35 percent and fibrinogen about 4 percent. Because albumin is so plentiful, it is the main protein holding water in the blood by osmotic pressure.
notes: About 4 percent is the share of fibrinogen, the clotting protein. It is the smallest of the three main groups.
About 35 percent is the share of the globulins. Pick it if the question asked about the group that includes the antibodies.
Correct. Albumin is about 60 percent of the plasma proteins.
About 92 percent is the water content of plasma, not a protein share. Students who pick it mix up the plasma table.
questions.answerText: About 60 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma protein group includes the antibodies, also called immunoglobulins?
options: Gamma globulins
Alpha globulins
Albumin
Fibrinogen
questions.why: The globulins are divided into alpha, beta, and gamma globulins. The gamma globulins are the antibodies, the proteins of immune defense, and they are made by plasma cells rather than the liver. Alpha and beta globulins are transport proteins.
notes: Correct. The gamma globulins are the antibodies.
Alpha globulins, along with beta globulins, are transport proteins. They carry substances in the plasma rather than defending against pathogens.
Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, a carrier and the main source of osmotic pressure. It is not an antibody.
Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that converts to fibrin threads. Pick it for a question about clot formation.
questions.answerText: Gamma globulins

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma protein is the largest and is converted to fibrin during clotting?
options: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Gamma globulin
Transferrin
questions.why: Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein and the clotting protein. During clotting it is converted to fibrin, which forms threads that make up the framework of a clot. It is made by the liver and makes up about 4 percent of plasma proteins.
notes: Correct. Fibrinogen becomes the fibrin threads of a clot.
Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, but not the largest, and it does not form clots. Choose it for osmotic pressure or carrying hormones and drugs.
Gamma globulins are the antibodies made by plasma cells. They act in immune defense, not clotting.
Transferrin is a globulin that carries iron through the plasma. Pick it for a question about iron transport.
questions.answerText: Fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which list puts the three major classes of plasma proteins in order from most to least abundant?
options: Albumin, fibrinogen, globulins
Globulins, albumin, fibrinogen
Fibrinogen, albumin, globulins
Albumin, globulins, fibrinogen
questions.why: Albumin makes up about 60 percent of the plasma proteins, the globulins about 35 percent, and fibrinogen about 4 percent. So the order from most to least abundant is albumin, then globulins, then fibrinogen. Fibrinogen is the largest single molecule but the smallest share.
notes: Albumin is correctly first, but fibrinogen at about 4 percent is far less abundant than the globulins at about 35 percent.
This puts the globulins first, but at about 35 percent they rank behind albumin at about 60 percent.
Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein molecule, which leads some students to rank it first. By amount it is the least abundant of the three.
Correct. About 60, 35, and 4 percent.
questions.answerText: Albumin, globulins, fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Fibrinogen makes up approximately what share of the plasma proteins?
options: About 60 percent
About 4 percent
About 35 percent
About 92 percent
questions.why: Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein, but it is the smallest of the three main groups by amount, about 4 percent of plasma proteins. Albumin makes up about 60 percent and the globulins about 35 percent. A small amount of fibrinogen is enough because it only needs to form the fibrin framework of a clot when a vessel is injured.
notes: About 60 percent is the share of albumin, the most abundant plasma protein. Pick it for a question about the protein that holds water in the blood.
Correct. Fibrinogen is a small share even though it is the largest molecule.
About 35 percent is the share of the globulins, which include the transport proteins and the antibodies.
About 92 percent is the water content of plasma, not a share of the proteins. Students who pick it are reading from the wrong row of the plasma table.
questions.answerText: About 4 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The globulins make up approximately what share of the plasma proteins?
options: About 35 percent
About 55 percent
About 4 percent
About 60 percent
questions.why: The globulins are the second most abundant group of plasma proteins, at about 35 percent. Alpha and beta globulins are transport proteins, and gamma globulins are the antibodies. Albumin makes up about 60 percent and fibrinogen about 4 percent.
notes: Correct. The globulins are about a third of the plasma proteins.
About 55 percent is the share of whole blood that is plasma. It describes blood volume, not the protein mix inside plasma.
About 4 percent is fibrinogen, the clotting protein. It is the smallest of the three main groups.
About 60 percent is albumin, the most abundant plasma protein. Choose it for the protein that maintains osmotic pressure.
questions.answerText: About 35 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Where are all the plasma proteins made, except for the gamma globulins?
options: In the liver
In the spleen
In the kidney
In the red bone marrow
questions.why: The liver makes albumin, fibrinogen, and the alpha and beta globulins, so it produces most of the plasma proteins. The one exception is the gamma globulins, the antibodies, which are made by plasma cells of the immune system. This is why serious liver disease lowers most plasma protein levels.
notes: Correct. The liver makes every major plasma protein except the antibodies.
The spleen, along with the liver, breaks down worn-out erythrocytes. It is the answer for removing old red cells, not making plasma proteins.
The kidney is the main source of erythropoietin, the hormone that stimulates red cell production. It does not make the plasma proteins.
Red bone marrow is where the formed elements are made by hematopoiesis. Pick it for a question about where blood cells form.
questions.answerText: In the liver

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma proteins are not made in the liver, and which cells make them?
options: Gamma globulins, made by plasma cells
Fibrinogen, made by platelets
Albumin, made by plasma cells
Alpha globulins, made by macrophages
questions.why: The gamma globulins are the antibodies, the proteins of immune defense. They are made by plasma cells, which develop from activated B lymphocytes. All the other major plasma proteins, albumin, fibrinogen, and the alpha and beta globulins, come from the liver.
notes: Correct. Antibodies come from plasma cells, not the liver.
Fibrinogen is made by the liver. Platelets work alongside fibrinogen in clotting, which is why the two get linked, but platelets do not make it.
Albumin is made by the liver. Students who pick this attach the right cell to the wrong protein.
Alpha globulins are transport proteins made by the liver. Macrophages develop from monocytes and engulf debris and pathogens.
questions.answerText: Gamma globulins, made by plasma cells

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which globulins act as transport proteins, carrying substances such as iron and lipids in the plasma?
options: Alpha and beta globulins
Hemoglobin
