The gamma globulins
Fibrinogen, the clotting protein
questions.why: The globulins fall into three groups. The alpha and beta globulins are transport proteins that carry substances through the plasma; transferrin, which carries iron, is one of them. The gamma globulins are a different job entirely, since they are the antibodies.
notes: Correct. These globulins carry substances such as iron and lipids.
Hemoglobin transports oxygen, but it stays inside erythrocytes rather than circulating free in the plasma. It is not a plasma globulin.
The gamma globulins are the antibodies of immune defense, made by plasma cells. Pick them for a question about immunity.
Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that converts to fibrin threads. It is not a globulin and is not a transporter.
questions.answerText: Alpha and beta globulins

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma protein is the main carrier for hormones, fatty acids, and many drugs, and the main protein maintaining the osmotic pressure that holds water in the blood?
options: Albumin
Gamma globulin
Fibrinogen
Transferrin
questions.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, about 60 percent of the total. Because there is so much of it, it creates most of the osmotic pressure that pulls water into the blood and keeps it there. It also binds and carries hormones, fatty acids, and many drugs through the plasma.
notes: Correct. Albumin is both the main carrier and the main source of osmotic pressure.
Gamma globulins are the antibodies made by plasma cells. They defend against pathogens rather than carrying hormones or holding water in the blood.
Fibrinogen is the largest plasma protein and the clotting protein. Pick it when the question asks about building a clot.
Transferrin is a transport globulin, but it carries iron specifically. It is too narrow in its job to be the main carrier or the source of osmotic pressure.
questions.answerText: Albumin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab report lists the solutes found in a plasma sample. Which pair shows one nutrient and one nitrogenous waste?
options: Albumin and fibrinogen
Glucose and urea
Na+ and Cl-
O2 and CO2
questions.why: Plasma carries many dissolved solutes besides proteins. Nutrients include glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, and vitamins, which are delivered to cells. Wastes include urea, creatinine, bilirubin, and ammonia, which contain nitrogen and are carried to the liver or kidneys for removal. Glucose and urea give one of each.
notes: Albumin and fibrinogen are both plasma proteins. Pick this pair for a question about the main proteins made by the liver.
Correct. Glucose is a nutrient and urea is a nitrogenous waste.
Na+ and Cl- are both electrolytes, dissolved ions in plasma. They would answer a question about electrolytes.
O2 and CO2 are both dissolved gases. CO2 is a waste, but neither is a nutrient, and neither is a nitrogenous waste.
questions.answerText: Glucose and urea

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which of the following is a major electrolyte dissolved in plasma?
options: Glucose
Urea
Albumin
Na+
questions.why: Electrolytes are dissolved ions that carry an electrical charge. The major electrolytes in plasma are sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), calcium (Ca2+), chloride (Cl-), and bicarbonate. Sodium is the most abundant positive ion in plasma.
notes: Glucose is a nutrient carried in plasma. It dissolves but does not carry a charge, so it is not an electrolyte.
Urea is a nitrogenous waste carried to the kidneys. It is not an ion, so it is not an electrolyte.
Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein. Pick it for a question about proteins or osmotic pressure.
Correct. Sodium is a charged ion, a major plasma electrolyte.
questions.answerText: Na+

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which list contains only electrolytes normally dissolved in plasma?
options: Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl-
Albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, transferrin
Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins
Urea, creatinine, bilirubin, ammonia
questions.why: Electrolytes are charged ions dissolved in a fluid. Plasma carries sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), calcium (Ca2+), chloride (Cl-), and bicarbonate as its main electrolytes. Plasma also carries nutrients, wastes, gases, and proteins, but those are separate categories.
notes: Correct. All four are charged ions.
These are plasma proteins. They answer a question about the proteins, not the ions.
These are the nutrients carried in plasma. Pick this list for a question about what plasma delivers to cells for fuel and building.
These are the wastes carried in plasma. Choose this list for a question about what plasma carries away for removal.
questions.answerText: Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl-

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the liquid extracellular matrix of blood called?
options: Lymph
Plasma
Buffy coat
Serum
questions.why: Blood is a connective tissue, so it has cells suspended in a matrix. Its matrix is plasma, a pale yellow fluid that is about 92 percent water and carries proteins, nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, and gases. Plasma makes up about 55 percent of whole blood.
notes: Lymph is the fluid inside lymphatic vessels, drained from the spaces around cells. It is a separate fluid, not the matrix of blood.
Correct. Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood.
The buffy coat is the thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets in a spun sample. It is made of cells, not matrix.
Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins removed, the fluid left after blood clots. It is not the matrix of circulating blood.
questions.answerText: Plasma

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which waste product in plasma travels bound to albumin on its way to the liver?
options: Creatinine
Urea
Glucose
Bilirubin
questions.why: Bilirubin is the yellow pigment made when the heme from worn-out red cells is broken down. It does not dissolve well in water, so it rides through the plasma attached to albumin until it reaches the liver. The liver then processes it and releases it in bile.
notes: Creatinine is a waste from muscle that travels dissolved in plasma to the kidneys for excretion. It does not need albumin to carry it.
Urea is a nitrogenous waste made by the liver and carried dissolved in plasma to the kidneys. It travels toward the kidneys, not toward the liver on albumin.
Glucose is a nutrient, not a waste, and it dissolves freely in plasma. It is the answer for a fuel carried to cells.
Correct. Bilirubin from heme breakdown is carried on albumin to the liver.
questions.answerText: Bilirubin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A blood component is a fluid that forms about 55 percent of whole blood, is about 92 percent water, and carries dissolved proteins, nutrients, and electrolytes. What is it?
options: Formed elements
Buffy coat
Plasma
Serum
questions.why: Each clue points to plasma. It is the fluid part of blood, it makes up about 55 percent of whole blood, it is about 92 percent water, and the rest is dissolved solutes such as proteins, nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, and gases. In a spun tube it forms the pale yellow top layer.
notes: The formed elements are the cells and cell fragments, about 45 percent of whole blood. Pick them when the clues describe cells rather than fluid.
The buffy coat is a thin layer of leukocytes and platelets, less than 1 percent of a spun sample. It is cells, not a watery fluid.
Correct. Every clue matches plasma.
Serum is plasma after clotting, with the clotting proteins removed. It is not a fraction of circulating whole blood, so it does not match the 55 percent clue.
questions.answerText: Plasma

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient has severe liver failure, so the liver can no longer make proteins normally. Which group of plasma proteins is least directly affected?
options: The alpha and beta globulins
Albumin
Fibrinogen
The gamma globulins
questions.why: The liver makes albumin, fibrinogen, and the alpha and beta globulins, so all of these fall when the liver fails. The gamma globulins, the antibodies, are made by plasma cells of the immune system instead. Because their source is outside the liver, they are the group least directly affected.
notes: The alpha and beta globulins are transport proteins made by the liver. They fall in liver failure along with albumin and fibrinogen.
Albumin is made by the liver, so it drops in liver failure. Because it is the most abundant plasma protein, its loss is often the most noticeable.
Fibrinogen is made by the liver, so liver failure lowers it and slows clotting. Pick it for a question about why a patient with liver disease bleeds easily.
Correct. Antibodies come from plasma cells, not the liver.
questions.answerText: The gamma globulins

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A protein group makes up about 35 percent of the plasma proteins and includes both transport proteins and the antibodies. Name the group.
options: The clotting factors
The globulins
Albumin
Fibrinogen
questions.why: The globulins are the only plasma protein group with both jobs. Alpha and beta globulins transport substances such as iron and lipids, and gamma globulins are the antibodies. Together they make up about 35 percent of the plasma proteins.
notes: Clotting factors are proteins that work in clot formation, such as the one missing in hemophilia. They are not the group that includes antibodies and transporters.
Correct. Alpha and beta globulins transport, and gamma globulins are antibodies.
Albumin is about 60 percent of plasma proteins. It is a carrier, but it does not include the antibodies.
Fibrinogen is about 4 percent of plasma proteins and is the clotting protein. Pick it for a question about clot formation.
questions.answerText: The globulins

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What red, iron-containing protein fills the erythrocyte?
options: Myoglobin
Ferritin
Hemoglobin
Transferrin
questions.why: Hemoglobin is the red, iron-containing protein that fills the erythrocyte and binds oxygen for transport. Each molecule has four subunits, and each subunit carries a heme group that holds one iron. Hemoglobin is also what gives blood its red color.
notes: Myoglobin is a related oxygen-binding protein found in muscle cells, not in red blood cells. Pick it for a question about oxygen storage in muscle.
Ferritin is the protein that stores iron in tissues such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It holds iron but is not found filling red cells.
Correct. Hemoglobin packs the red cell and carries oxygen.
Transferrin is the plasma protein that carries iron to the bone marrow. It moves iron through the plasma rather than filling red cells.
questions.answerText: Hemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which polypeptide chains make up one molecule of normal adult hemoglobin?
options: Four alpha chains
One alpha and one beta chain
Two alpha and two beta chains
Three alpha and one beta chain
questions.why: Normal adult hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains: two alpha chains and two beta chains. Each chain holds one heme group with an iron at its center. Because the beta chains are part of the molecule, a change in the beta chain, as in sickle cell disease, changes the whole hemoglobin.
notes: Hemoglobin does have alpha chains, but only two. Students who pick this forget that the molecule pairs two kinds of chain.
This gives only two chains. Hemoglobin has four subunits, so it needs two of each kind.
Correct. Adult hemoglobin has two of each.
This adds up to four but in the wrong mix. The chains come in matched pairs, two alpha and two beta.
questions.answerText: Two alpha and two beta chains

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: How many heme groups does one hemoglobin molecule contain?
options: One
Four
Two
Eight
questions.why: Hemoglobin has four polypeptide subunits, and each subunit carries one heme group. So one hemoglobin molecule has four heme groups. Each heme holds one iron, and each iron can bind one oxygen molecule.
notes: One heme group would mean one subunit. Myoglobin in muscle has a single heme, which may be the source of this mix-up.
Correct. One heme group per subunit gives four.
Two matches the number of alpha chains, or the number of beta chains, but not the total. Each of the four chains has its own heme.
Eight would be two hemes per chain. Each chain carries only one heme group.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Each heme group in hemoglobin holds one ion of which element at its center?
options: Calcium
Magnesium
Iron
Sodium
questions.why: A heme group is a ring-shaped structure with a single iron ion at its center. The iron is the part that actually binds oxygen. This is why iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin and can cause anemia.
notes: Calcium is an important plasma electrolyte and is needed for clotting and muscle contraction. It is not part of heme.
Magnesium sits at the center of chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants, which has a ring similar to heme. Human heme uses iron instead.
Correct. Each heme holds one iron, which binds oxygen.
Sodium is the main positive electrolyte in plasma. It is dissolved in the fluid, not bound inside hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: Iron

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Based on its structure, what is the greatest number of oxygen molecules one hemoglobin molecule can carry?
options: Two
Four
Eight
One
questions.why: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with one heme group, and each heme holds one iron that can bind one oxygen molecule. So one hemoglobin molecule can carry up to four oxygen molecules. A single red cell holds millions of hemoglobin molecules, which is why red cells carry so much oxygen.
notes: Two matches the number of alpha chains or beta chains, not the total. Each of the four chains can bind oxygen.
Correct. Four hemes give four oxygen-binding sites.
Eight would require two binding sites per heme. Each heme iron binds only one oxygen molecule.
One oxygen would mean one heme. Students who pick this treat the whole molecule as a single binding site.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is hemoglobin called when it is bound to oxygen?
options: Oxyhemoglobin
Carboxyhemoglobin
Methemoglobin
Deoxyhemoglobin
questions.why: Hemoglobin is named by what is attached to it. When oxygen is bound to the heme iron, it is called oxyhemoglobin, and the blood is bright red. When the oxygen has been released to the tissues, it is called deoxyhemoglobin.
notes: Correct. Oxygen-bound hemoglobin is oxyhemoglobin.
Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide, the dangerous form in carbon monoxide poisoning.
Methemoglobin has its iron oxidized to Fe3+ and cannot carry oxygen. It is the answer for that abnormal form.
Deoxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin that has released its oxygen. Pick it for blood returning from the tissues.
questions.answerText: Oxyhemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is hemoglobin called after it has released its oxygen?
options: Deoxyhemoglobin
Methemoglobin
Carboxyhemoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin
questions.why: Hemoglobin loads oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Once the oxygen has been given up, the molecule is called deoxyhemoglobin, and the blood is a darker red. Its iron is still Fe2+, so it can pick up oxygen again on its next pass through the lungs.
notes: Correct. Hemoglobin that has given up its oxygen is deoxyhemoglobin.
Methemoglobin has iron oxidized to Fe3+, so it cannot bind oxygen at all. Deoxyhemoglobin, by contrast, can still reload oxygen.
Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide. Pick it for carbon monoxide poisoning, not for normal oxygen release.
Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin with oxygen bound, the bright red form leaving the lungs. It is the form before oxygen is released.
questions.answerText: Deoxyhemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is hemoglobin called when it is bound to carbon monoxide?
options: Carboxyhemoglobin
Deoxyhemoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin
Methemoglobin
questions.why: Carbon monoxide binds to the heme iron in hemoglobin much more tightly than oxygen does. Hemoglobin with carbon monoxide attached is called carboxyhemoglobin. Because those binding sites are blocked, the blood carries less oxygen, which is why carbon monoxide is so dangerous.
notes: Correct. Carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin forms carboxyhemoglobin.
Deoxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin that has released its oxygen. It has nothing bound to its heme sites.
Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to oxygen, the normal loaded form. Pick it for blood leaving the lungs.
Methemoglobin is defined by its iron being oxidized to Fe3+, not by carbon monoxide. Choose it for the Fe3+ form.
questions.answerText: Carboxyhemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which list names four forms of hemoglobin?
options: Proerythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte
Ferritin, transferrin, bilirubin, heme
Oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin, carbaminohemoglobin
Albumin, globulin, fibrinogen, transferrin
questions.why: Hemoglobin is named by what is bound to it. Oxyhemoglobin carries oxygen, deoxyhemoglobin has released its oxygen, carboxyhemoglobin carries carbon monoxide, and carbaminohemoglobin carries carbon dioxide. All four are the same protein carrying different cargo.
notes: These are stages in red cell development, not forms of hemoglobin. Choose this list for a question about erythropoiesis.
These are substances in iron handling and red cell breakdown. Ferritin stores iron, transferrin carries it, and bilirubin comes from broken-down heme.
Correct. These four are named forms of hemoglobin.
These are plasma proteins, dissolved in the plasma rather than packed inside red cells. Pick this list for a question about plasma proteins.
questions.answerText: Oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin, carbaminohemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which two forms of hemoglobin differ only in whether oxygen is bound to them?
options: Carboxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin and carboxyhemoglobin
Carbaminohemoglobin and carboxyhemoglobin
questions.why: Oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin are the normal working pair. Oxyhemoglobin has oxygen bound as blood leaves the lungs, and deoxyhemoglobin is the same molecule after it has released that oxygen in the tissues. Hemoglobin switches back and forth between these two forms on every trip around the body.
notes: Carboxyhemoglobin has carbon monoxide bound, while deoxyhemoglobin has released its oxygen and carries nothing on its heme. The difference is carbon monoxide, so pick this pair for a question about carbon monoxide poisoning.
Correct. Oxyhemoglobin has oxygen bound and deoxyhemoglobin has released it.

Oxyhemoglobin carries oxygen and carboxyhemoglobin carries carbon monoxide in the same binding sites, so they differ by which gas is bound. Pick this pair for a question about carbon monoxide taking the place of oxygen.
Carbaminohemoglobin carries carbon dioxide and carboxyhemoglobin carries carbon monoxide. Neither is defined by oxygen, so this pair fits a question about the two forms named for carbon gases.
questions.answerText: Oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Roughly what is the normal hemoglobin level in the blood of an adult man?
options: About 13 to 18 g/dL
About 42 to 52 g/dL
About 150 to 400 g/dL
About 4 to 11 g/dL
questions.why: Hemoglobin is measured in grams per deciliter (g/dL) of blood. A normal adult man runs roughly 13 to 18 g/dL, and an adult woman runs a little lower. A level well below the normal range points toward anemia, meaning the blood carries less oxygen.
notes: Correct. Adult men run roughly 13 to 18 grams of hemoglobin per deciliter.
The numbers 42 to 52 are the normal hematocrit for men, given as a percentage of blood volume. Students who pick this mix up hematocrit with hemoglobin.
The numbers 150 to 400 match the normal platelet count, in thousands per microliter. They are far too high for hemoglobin.
The numbers 4 to 11 match the normal white cell count, in thousands per microliter. A hemoglobin level in this range would mean anemia.
questions.answerText: About 13 to 18 g/dL

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares normal hemoglobin levels in adult women and men?
options: Women and men have exactly the same range
Women run slightly higher, about 13 to 18 versus 12 to 16 g/dL
Women run slightly lower, about 12 to 16 versus 13 to 18 g/dL
Women run about half the level of men
questions.why: Normal hemoglobin ranges differ a little between the sexes. Adult women typically run about 12 to 16 g/dL and adult men about 13 to 18 g/dL. The ranges overlap, but the female range sits slightly lower, so a lab result has to be read against the right range.
notes: The ranges overlap but are not identical. Treating them as the same can make a normal value look abnormal.
This swaps the two ranges. The higher range belongs to men.
Correct. The female range sits a little below the male range.
The difference is small, about 1 to 2 g/dL. A level half of the male range would be severe anemia.
questions.answerText: Women run slightly lower, about 12 to 16 versus 13 to 18 g/dL

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Roughly what is the normal hematocrit for an adult man?
options: About 42 to 52 percent
About 13 to 18 percent
About 55 to 65 percent
About 1 to 2 percent
questions.why: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes, measured by spinning a blood sample. In adult men it is roughly 42 to 52 percent, which matches the formed elements being a little under half of whole blood. Women run a few points lower.
notes: Correct. Red cells make up a little under half of a man's blood volume.
The numbers 13 to 18 are the normal hemoglobin range for men in g/dL. Students who pick this mix up hemoglobin with hematocrit.
About 55 percent is the share of blood made up of plasma, not red cells. A hematocrit this high would suggest polycythemia.
About 1 to 2 percent is the share of red cells that are reticulocytes. It is much too small for the whole red cell fraction.
questions.answerText: About 42 to 52 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Roughly what is the normal hematocrit for an adult woman?
options: About 60 to 70 percent
About 20 to 30 percent
About 7 to 8 percent
About 37 to 47 percent
questions.why: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume that is erythrocytes. In adult women it is roughly 37 to 47 percent, a few points lower than in men. A hematocrit well below this range is one sign of anemia.
notes: About 60 to 70 percent is close to the share of leukocytes that are neutrophils. A hematocrit this high would be abnormal.
A hematocrit this low would point to anemia. The numbers 20 to 30 are close to the lymphocyte share of leukocytes.
About 7 to 8 percent is the share of body weight made up of blood. It is far too low for a hematocrit.
Correct. Women run a few points below the male range.
questions.answerText: About 37 to 47 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The hematocrit measures the percentage of blood volume made up of which component?
options: Leukocytes
Platelets
Plasma
Erythrocytes
questions.why: When blood is spun in a tube, the heavy erythrocytes pack at the bottom, the plasma rises to the top, and a thin buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets lies between. The hematocrit is the height of the red cell layer as a percentage of the whole column. It gives a quick check on whether the blood has too few or too many red cells.
notes: Leukocytes form part of the thin buffy coat, less than 1 percent of the sample. A white cell count, not the hematocrit, measures them.
Platelets also sit in the thin buffy coat. They are counted separately as the platelet count.
Plasma is the fluid fraction, about 55 percent. It makes up the rest of the tube, but the hematocrit reports the red cells.
Correct. Hematocrit is the red cell fraction of blood volume.
questions.answerText: Erythrocytes

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: When worn-out erythrocytes are broken down, which protein stores the recovered iron, and where?
options: Transferrin, circulating in the plasma
Albumin, circulating in the plasma
Fibrinogen, in the red bone marrow
Ferritin, in liver, spleen, and marrow
questions.why: Iron from broken-down hemoglobin is too valuable to lose, so the body saves it. Ferritin is the storage protein that holds iron in tissues such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. When the marrow needs iron to build new hemoglobin, it is released and carried there through the plasma.
notes: Transferrin carries iron through the plasma rather than storing it. Pick it for the protein that moves iron to the marrow.
Albumin is a general carrier and the main osmotic protein. It carries bilirubin but is not the iron storage protein.
Fibrinogen is the clotting protein made by the liver. It plays no part in storing iron.
Correct. Ferritin is the iron storage protein in tissues.
questions.answerText: Ferritin, in liver, spleen, and marrow

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which protein transports iron through the plasma?
options: Albumin
Ferritin
Hemoglobin
Transferrin
questions.why: Iron does not travel freely in the blood. Transferrin, one of the transport globulins, binds iron and carries it through the plasma to the red bone marrow, where it is used to build new hemoglobin. Ferritin, by contrast, holds iron in storage inside tissues.
notes: Albumin carries hormones, fatty acids, drugs, and bilirubin, but iron has its own carrier. Pick albumin for the general carrier protein.
Ferritin stores iron in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Choose it for a question about iron storage.
Hemoglobin contains iron, but it stays inside erythrocytes and carries oxygen. It does not deliver iron through the plasma.
Correct. Transferrin carries iron through the plasma.
questions.answerText: Transferrin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: How do ferritin and transferrin differ in function?
options: Both store iron, in different organs
Ferritin stores iron; transferrin transports it in plasma
Both transport iron, in different fluids
Ferritin transports iron in plasma; transferrin stores it
questions.why: The body handles iron with two different proteins. Ferritin stores iron inside tissues such as the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Transferrin carries iron through the plasma to where it is needed, mainly the red bone marrow for building hemoglobin.
notes: Only ferritin is a storage protein. Transferrin moves iron through the plasma.
Correct. Storage and transport are separate jobs.
Only transferrin is a transport protein. Ferritin holds iron in place inside tissues.
This swaps the two roles. A memory cue is that transferrin transfers iron from place to place.
questions.answerText: Ferritin stores iron; transferrin transports it in plasma

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which pair of organs breaks down most worn-out erythrocytes?
options: The heart and the lungs
The thymus and the lymph nodes
The kidney and the pancreas
The spleen and the liver
questions.why: After about 120 days, erythrocytes become stiff and fragile. As they pass through the spleen and liver, macrophages in these organs engulf the worn cells and break them down. The iron is saved, the globin is recycled into amino acids, and the heme is converted to bilirubin.
notes: The heart pumps blood and the lungs load it with oxygen. Red cells pass through them constantly but are not broken down there.
The thymus is where T lymphocytes mature, and lymph nodes filter lymph. Neither is the main site for breaking down red cells.
The kidney makes erythropoietin, which stimulates red cell production, so it is involved in making red cells, not removing them. The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine gland.
Correct. Macrophages in these organs remove worn red cells.
questions.answerText: The spleen and the liver

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which cells engulf and break down aged erythrocytes?
options: Neutrophils
Plasma cells
Macrophages
Platelets
questions.why: Macrophages are large phagocytic cells, meaning cells that engulf and digest particles. They develop from monocytes that leave the blood. Macrophages in the spleen and liver recognize old, stiff red cells and engulf them, then break down their hemoglobin.
notes: Neutrophils are phagocytes too, but they are the first responders to bacterial infection. They are not the cells that clear old red cells.
Plasma cells develop from B lymphocytes and make antibodies. They do not engulf cells.
Correct. Macrophages engulf worn-out red cells.
Platelets are cell fragments that plug vessel injuries and help form clots. They cannot engulf other cells.
questions.answerText: Macrophages

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: When hemoglobin is broken down, which two main parts is it first split into?
options: Ferritin and transferrin
Bilirubin and urea
Heme and globin
Iron and albumin
questions.why: Hemoglobin is made of a protein part, globin, and the iron-holding heme groups. When macrophages break hemoglobin down, they first split it into these two parts. The globin goes on to become amino acids, while the heme gives up its iron and the rest becomes bilirubin.
notes: Ferritin and transferrin are proteins that store and carry iron after it is released. They are not pieces of hemoglobin.
Bilirubin is made later from the heme ring, and urea is a nitrogenous waste from protein breakdown in the liver. Neither is a first split product.
Correct. Hemoglobin separates into its heme groups and its globin chains.
Iron is released from heme later in the process, and albumin is a plasma protein that is not part of hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: Heme and globin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: After hemoglobin is broken down, what happens to the globin chains?
options: They are stored as ferritin
They are recycled as amino acids
They are excreted unchanged in urine
They are converted to bilirubin
questions.why: Globin is the protein portion of hemoglobin. Like any protein, it can be broken down into its building blocks, the amino acids. These amino acids return to the blood and are reused to build new proteins.
notes: Ferritin stores the iron from heme, not the globin. Pick ferritin for what happens to the iron.
Correct. The protein part is reduced to reusable amino acids.
Intact globin chains are not passed in urine. The body breaks them down and reuses the amino acids.
Bilirubin comes from the heme ring, not the globin. Choose bilirubin for the fate of the heme.
questions.answerText: They are recycled as amino acids

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: When the heme ring is broken down after iron is removed, which yellow pigment is formed and carried to the liver?
options: Bilirubin
Urea
Fibrin
Ferritin
questions.why: Once the iron is removed from heme, the remaining ring is converted to bilirubin, a yellow pigment. Bilirubin travels through the plasma bound to albumin to the liver, which secretes it in bile. When bilirubin builds up in the blood, the skin and eyes can turn yellow, a sign called jaundice.
notes: Correct. Heme breakdown produces the yellow pigment bilirubin.
Urea is a nitrogenous waste made in the liver from amino acid breakdown. It is carried to the kidneys, not made from heme.
Fibrin is the threadlike protein formed from fibrinogen during clotting. It has nothing to do with heme breakdown.
Ferritin is the protein that stores the iron removed from heme. It is not a pigment made from the ring.
questions.answerText: Bilirubin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the general name for the formation of all the formed elements of blood?
options: Erythropoiesis
Hemostasis
Hematopoiesis
Phagocytosis
questions.why: Hematopoiesis is the formation of all the formed elements: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. In adults it takes place in red bone marrow, starting from one kind of stem cell. More specific terms name the formation of each cell type, such as erythropoiesis for red cells.
notes: Erythropoiesis is the formation of red blood cells only. It is one branch of hematopoiesis.
Hemostasis is the stopping of bleeding, through vessel spasm, a platelet plug, and clotting. Pick it for a question about controlling blood loss.
Correct. Hematopoiesis covers the formation of every formed element.
Phagocytosis is the engulfing of particles by cells such as macrophages and neutrophils. It describes destroying cells, not forming them.
questions.answerText: Hematopoiesis

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Where does hematopoiesis take place in an adult?
options: In the liver
In yellow bone marrow
In red bone marrow
In the spleen
questions.why: In adults, blood cells are formed in red bone marrow, found in the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and the proximal ends of limb bones such as the femur and humerus. This is why a marrow sample to examine blood formation is taken from the iliac crest or sternum.
notes: The liver forms blood cells in the fetus, but not in a healthy adult. In adults it makes plasma proteins and helps remove old red cells.
Yellow marrow is mostly fat and fills the medullary cavity of adult long bones. It does not normally form blood cells.
Correct. Red marrow in spongy bone is the adult blood-forming tissue.
The spleen removes worn-out red cells and is a lymphatic organ. It is not the normal adult site of blood cell formation.
questions.answerText: In red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the name of the stem cell from which every formed element arises?
options: The myeloid stem cell
The lymphoid stem cell
The hemocytoblast
The megakaryocyte
questions.why: The hemocytoblast is the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, meaning it can give rise to every type of formed element. It lives in red bone marrow and divides to produce the myeloid and lymphoid stem cells. Those committed lines then produce red cells, platelets, and the five kinds of leukocytes.
notes: The myeloid stem cell comes from the hemocytoblast and gives rise to every formed element except lymphocytes. It is one step down the tree.
The lymphoid stem cell comes from the hemocytoblast and gives rise only to lymphocytes. Pick it for the lymphocyte line.
Correct. The hemocytoblast is the stem cell at the top of the blood cell family tree.
The megakaryocyte is the giant marrow cell whose cytoplasm breaks into platelets. It is far down one branch, not the common ancestor.
questions.answerText: The hemocytoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The hemocytoblast divides to produce which two committed stem cell lines?
options: Erythroid and megakaryocyte stem cells
Myeloid and lymphoid stem cells
Granulocyte and agranulocyte stem cells
B cell and T cell stem cells
questions.why: Just below the hemocytoblast, the blood cell family tree splits into two lines. The myeloid line produces erythrocytes, platelets, and all leukocytes except lymphocytes. The lymphoid line produces the lymphocytes.
notes: The red cell and platelet lineages both branch from the myeloid line further down. They are not the first split.
Correct. These are the two lines that branch from the hemocytoblast.
Granulocyte and agranulocyte are the two groups of leukocytes sorted by visible granules, not the two stem cell lines. Monocytes are agranulocytes but come from the myeloid line.
B and T cells are both lymphocytes and come from the lymphoid line. They are products of one branch, not the two branches.
questions.answerText: Myeloid and lymphoid stem cells

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which stem cell line gives rise to the lymphocytes?
options: The lymphoid line
The myeloid line
The megakaryocyte line
The erythroid line
questions.why: The hemocytoblast produces two committed lines. The lymphoid line gives rise to the lymphocytes, which include the B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Every other formed element comes from the myeloid line.
notes: Correct. Lymphocytes come from the lymphoid stem cell.
The myeloid line produces erythrocytes, platelets, and the other leukocytes, everything except lymphocytes. It is the answer for neutrophils or monocytes.
The megakaryocyte line produces platelets. It is also a branch of the myeloid line.
The erythroid line produces red blood cells through the proerythroblast and reticulocyte stages. It is a branch of the myeloid line.
questions.answerText: The lymphoid line

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The myeloid stem cell gives rise to every formed element except which one?
options: The monocyte
The platelet
The lymphocyte
The erythrocyte
questions.why: The myeloid line produces erythrocytes, platelets, and the leukocytes, with one exception. Lymphocytes come from the separate lymphoid line. So neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes are myeloid, while lymphocytes are lymphoid.
notes: Monocytes are agranulocytes like lymphocytes, which can mislead students, but monocytes come from the myeloid line through the monoblast.
Platelets come from the myeloid line through megakaryocytes. They are a myeloid product.
Correct. Lymphocytes come from the lymphoid line instead.
Erythrocytes come from the myeloid line through the proerythroblast. They are a myeloid product.
questions.answerText: The lymphocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which lineage branches from the myeloid stem cell?
options: The T lymphocyte lineage
The megakaryocyte lineage
The natural killer cell lineage
The B lymphocyte lineage
questions.why: The myeloid stem cell gives rise to several lineages: the red cell line, the granulocyte line, the monocyte line, and the megakaryocyte line that produces platelets. The lymphocytes, including B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells, all come from the separate lymphoid line.
notes: T lymphocytes come from the lymphoid line and mature in the thymus. They are not myeloid.
Correct. Platelet-forming megakaryocytes come from the myeloid line.
Natural killer cells are lymphocytes, so they come from the lymphoid line. They are not myeloid.
B lymphocytes come from the lymphoid line. Pick this for a question about the cells that become antibody-making plasma cells.
questions.answerText: The megakaryocyte lineage

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the specific name for the formation of red blood cells?
options: Hematopoiesis
Erythropoiesis
Thrombopoiesis
Leukopoiesis
questions.why: Erythro means red and poiesis means making, so erythropoiesis is the formation of red blood cells. It is one branch of hematopoiesis, the formation of all blood cells. Erythropoiesis is stimulated by erythropoietin, a hormone made mainly by the kidney.
notes: Hematopoiesis is the general term for forming all blood cells. It includes erythropoiesis but is broader.
Correct. Erythropoiesis is red cell formation.
Thrombopoiesis is the formation of platelets, also called thrombocytes. Pick it for platelet production.
Leukopoiesis is the formation of white blood cells. Pick it for leukocyte production.
questions.answerText: Erythropoiesis

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: In erythropoiesis, which cell is the first one committed to becoming a red blood cell?
options: The monoblast
The megakaryoblast
The proerythroblast
The myeloblast
questions.why: The myeloid stem cell can produce several kinds of blood cells. Once it gives rise to a proerythroblast, that cell is committed to the red cell line and will only become an erythrocyte. Each of the other myeloid lines has its own committed blast cell.
notes: The monoblast is the committed cell of the monocyte line. Pick it for the precursor of monocytes and macrophages.
The megakaryoblast is the committed cell of the platelet line. It develops into a megakaryocyte, which breaks into platelets.
Correct. The proerythroblast is the first cell committed to the red cell line.
The myeloblast is the committed cell of the granulocyte line, which produces neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
questions.answerText: The proerythroblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces erythropoiesis from the stem cell to the mature red cell?
options: Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, normoblast, erythroblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte
Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, erythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte
Hemocytoblast, lymphoid stem cell, proerythroblast, erythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte
Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, erythroblast, reticulocyte, normoblast, erythrocyte
questions.why: Red cell development starts with the hemocytoblast, the stem cell for all formed elements, and passes to the myeloid stem cell. The proerythroblast is the first committed red cell precursor, followed by the erythroblast stages as hemoglobin builds up. The normoblast ejects its nucleus, the reticulocyte still holds ribosome remnants, and the erythrocyte is the mature cell.
notes: This swaps the erythroblast and normoblast. The erythroblast comes first and builds hemoglobin, and the normoblast follows and ejects the nucleus.
Correct. This is the full red cell pathway in order.
Red cells come from the myeloid line, not the lymphoid line. The lymphoid stem cell would start a pathway that ends in lymphocytes.
This puts the reticulocyte before the normoblast. The nucleus is ejected at the normoblast stage, so the nucleus-free reticulocyte must come after it.
questions.answerText: Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, erythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: At which stage of erythropoiesis is the nucleus ejected as hemoglobin accumulates?
options: The reticulocyte
The normoblast
The hemocytoblast
The proerythroblast
questions.why: As a developing red cell fills with hemoglobin, it reaches the normoblast stage and ejects its nucleus. Losing the nucleus makes room for more hemoglobin and produces a reticulocyte, which still carries ribosome remnants. The reticulocyte then matures into an erythrocyte.
notes: The reticulocyte comes after nucleus ejection. It has no nucleus, only ribosome remnants.
Correct. The normoblast is the stage that ejects the nucleus.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell at the top of the blood cell tree. It keeps its nucleus and divides to make new cells.
The proerythroblast is the first committed red cell precursor. It still has its nucleus and has barely begun making hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: The normoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the last immature stage before a fully mature erythrocyte?
options: The reticulocyte
The proerythroblast
The normoblast
The hemocytoblast
questions.why: The reticulocyte is the final immature stage of the red cell line. It has already ejected its nucleus but still contains ribosome remnants. It enters the blood and matures into an erythrocyte within a day or two as those remnants disappear.
notes: Correct. The reticulocyte is the step right before the mature erythrocyte.
The proerythroblast is the first committed red cell precursor, at the start of the line rather than the end.
The normoblast comes just before the reticulocyte and is the stage that ejects the nucleus. It is one step too early.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell that every formed element comes from. It is at the very top of the tree.
questions.answerText: The reticulocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What does a reticulocyte still contain that a mature erythrocyte lacks?
options: A small nucleus
Ribosome remnants
Visible cytoplasmic granules
Hemoglobin
questions.why: A reticulocyte is an immature red cell that has already ejected its nucleus. It still holds remnants of its ribosomes, which can be stained to show a fine network, and that network gives the cell its name. Once these remnants are lost, the cell is a mature erythrocyte.
notes: The nucleus is ejected at the normoblast stage, before the reticulocyte. A cell that still has a nucleus is an earlier stage.
Correct. Leftover ribosomes are what mark a reticulocyte.
Visible cytoplasmic granules are the mark of granulocytes, the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. They are not found in the red cell line.
Both reticulocytes and mature erythrocytes contain hemoglobin. It is not something the mature cell lacks.
questions.answerText: Ribosome remnants

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: About what percentage of circulating red blood cells are normally reticulocytes?
options: About 1 to 2 percent
About 7 to 8 percent
About 45 percent
About 20 to 30 percent
questions.why: Normally about 1 to 2 percent of the red cells in circulation are reticulocytes. They enter the blood from the marrow and mature within a day or two, so only a small share is present at any time. This number gives a rough idea of how fast the marrow is making new red cells.
notes: Correct. Only a small share of circulating red cells are reticulocytes.
About 7 to 8 percent is the share of body weight that is blood. It is too high for the normal reticulocyte share.
About 45 percent is the share of whole blood made up of formed elements. It describes all the cells, not the young red cells.
This is close to the share of leukocytes that are lymphocytes. A reticulocyte count this high would be far above normal.
questions.answerText: About 1 to 2 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which is the first stage of erythropoiesis that has no nucleus?
options: The erythroblast
The proerythroblast
The reticulocyte
The normoblast
questions.why: The nucleus is ejected at the end of the normoblast stage. The cell that results, the reticulocyte, is the first stage with no nucleus. It still carries ribosome remnants until it matures into an erythrocyte.
notes: The erythroblast is an earlier stage that is building hemoglobin and still has its nucleus.
The proerythroblast is the first committed red cell precursor and has a nucleus.
Correct. The reticulocyte is the first stage after the nucleus is ejected.
The normoblast is the stage that ejects the nucleus, so it still has one until the end of that stage.
questions.answerText: The reticulocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which stage of erythropoiesis comes directly between the proerythroblast and the normoblast?
options: The reticulocyte
The megakaryoblast
The hemocytoblast
The erythroblast
questions.why: After the proerythroblast commits to the red cell line, it develops through the erythroblast stages, during which hemoglobin builds up in the cytoplasm. Next comes the normoblast, which ejects the nucleus. So the order is proerythroblast, erythroblast, normoblast.
notes: The reticulocyte comes after the normoblast, once the nucleus has been ejected. It is later in the sequence.
The megakaryoblast is on the platelet line, not the red cell line. Pick it for a question about platelet formation.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell at the very start of hematopoiesis. It comes before the proerythroblast.
Correct. The erythroblast stages lie between the proerythroblast and the normoblast.
questions.answerText: The erythroblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Erythropoietin is the hormone that stimulates red blood cell production. Which organ is its main source?
options: The spleen
The red bone marrow
The kidney
The liver
questions.why: Erythropoietin is made chiefly by the kidney. When tissues are short of oxygen, the kidney releases more erythropoietin, and the red bone marrow responds by making more erythrocytes. This is why people with failing kidneys often become anemic.
notes: The spleen removes worn-out red cells and is a lymphatic organ. It does not make erythropoietin.
Red bone marrow responds to erythropoietin by making red cells. It is the target of the hormone, not its source.
Correct. The kidney is the main source of erythropoietin.
The liver makes a small amount of erythropoietin, but the kidney is the main source. The liver is better known for making plasma proteins.
questions.answerText: The kidney

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which committed marrow cell develops into the megakaryocyte that produces platelets?
options: The monoblast
The megakaryoblast
The proerythroblast
The myeloblast
questions.why: Platelet formation, called thrombopoiesis, begins with a committed cell called the megakaryoblast. It grows into a megakaryocyte, a giant marrow cell, whose cytoplasm breaks into thousands of platelets. Each myeloid line has its own blast cell like this.
notes: The monoblast is the committed cell of the monocyte line, which leads to monocytes and then macrophages.
Correct. The megakaryoblast is the committed precursor of the platelet line.
The proerythroblast is the committed cell of the red cell line. Pick it for erythropoiesis.
The myeloblast is the committed cell of the granulocyte line, giving rise to neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
questions.answerText: The megakaryoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which blast cell of the myeloid line develops into the granulocytes?
options: The lymphoblast
The monoblast
The myeloblast
The megakaryoblast
questions.why: The granulocytes are the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, the leukocytes with visible cytoplasmic granules. All three develop from the myeloblast, a committed cell of the myeloid line. Monocytes, red cells, and platelets each have their own blast cell.
notes: The lymphoblast comes from the lymphoid line and gives rise to lymphocytes. It is not part of the myeloid line.
The monoblast gives rise to monocytes, which are agranulocytes. Pick it for the cell that becomes a macrophage.
Correct. The myeloblast gives rise to all three granulocytes.
The megakaryoblast gives rise to megakaryocytes and then platelets. It is the platelet line.
questions.answerText: The myeloblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which blast cell develops into monocytes?
options: The proerythroblast
The lymphoblast
The myeloblast
The monoblast
questions.why: Monocytes develop from the monoblast, a committed cell of the myeloid line. After a monocyte leaves the blood and enters a tissue, it matures into a macrophage. The name helps: the monoblast is the blast that makes monocytes.
notes: The proerythroblast produces red blood cells. Pick it for erythropoiesis.
The lymphoblast produces lymphocytes. Monocytes and lymphocytes are both agranulocytes, but they come from different lines.
The myeloblast produces the granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Monocytes have their own blast cell.
Correct. The monoblast leads to monocytes.
questions.answerText: The monoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: From which stem cell line do the lymphoblast and its products, the B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells, arise?
options: The myeloid line
The lymphoid line
The erythroid line
The megakaryocyte line
questions.why: The lymphoid stem cell produces the lymphoblast, which develops into the lymphocytes: B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. These are the only formed elements that come from the lymphoid line. Every other formed element comes from the myeloid line.
notes: The myeloid line produces red cells, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes, but not lymphocytes.
Correct. All lymphocytes come from the lymphoid stem cell.
The erythroid line is the red cell branch of the myeloid line. It produces erythrocytes.
The megakaryocyte line is the platelet branch of the myeloid line. It produces platelets.
questions.answerText: The lymphoid line

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which formed elements share the myeloid stem cell as a common ancestor?
options: Erythrocytes and lymphocytes only
Erythrocytes, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes
All five leukocytes, but not red cells or platelets
Lymphocytes only
questions.why: The myeloid stem cell gives rise to the red cell line, the platelet line, the granulocyte line, and the monocyte line. The only formed element it does not produce is the lymphocyte, which comes from the lymphoid line. So the myeloid family covers nearly everything in a blood smear except lymphocytes.
notes: Erythrocytes are myeloid, but lymphocytes are lymphoid. This list also leaves out platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes.
Correct. Everything except lymphocytes comes from the myeloid line.
This includes lymphocytes, which are lymphoid, and leaves out red cells and platelets, which are myeloid.
Lymphocytes are the one group that does not come from the myeloid line. They have their own lymphoid stem cell.
questions.answerText: Erythrocytes, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which cell is more primitive, meaning higher in the blood cell family tree: the hemocytoblast or the myeloid stem cell?
options: The myeloid stem cell
Neither, since both are mature cells
The hemocytoblast
They are the same cell
questions.why: The hemocytoblast is the pluripotent stem cell at the top of the tree, able to give rise to every formed element. The myeloid stem cell is one of its two committed descendants and can no longer produce lymphocytes. Moving down the tree, each cell becomes more limited in what it can become.
notes: The myeloid stem cell comes from the hemocytoblast and is already committed away from lymphocytes, so it is a step lower in the tree.
Both are stem cells, not mature cells. Mature cells such as erythrocytes and neutrophils sit at the bottom of the tree.
Correct. The hemocytoblast is the ancestor of the myeloid stem cell.
They are different cells. The hemocytoblast can make every formed element, while the myeloid stem cell cannot make lymphocytes.
questions.answerText: The hemocytoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which stage of erythropoiesis comes immediately before the reticulocyte?
options: The erythrocyte
The proerythroblast
The normoblast
The hemocytoblast
questions.why: The order of the later red cell stages is erythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte. The normoblast ejects its nucleus, and the nucleus-free cell that results is the reticulocyte. So the normoblast comes immediately before the reticulocyte.
notes: The erythrocyte is the mature cell that comes after the reticulocyte, not before it.
The proerythroblast is the first committed red cell precursor, several stages before the reticulocyte.
Correct. The normoblast ejects its nucleus and becomes a reticulocyte.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell at the start of hematopoiesis, far earlier in the sequence.
questions.answerText: The normoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The red cell lineage and the granulocyte lineage both branch from which shared stem cell?
options: The proerythroblast
The myeloid stem cell
The lymphoid stem cell
The megakaryoblast
questions.why: The myeloid stem cell is the common branch point for the red cell, granulocyte, monocyte, and platelet lineages. The red cell line passes through the proerythroblast and the granulocyte line through the myeloblast. Both trace back to the myeloid stem cell, which in turn comes from the hemocytoblast.
notes: The proerythroblast is already committed to the red cell line, so it cannot give rise to granulocytes.
Correct. Both lineages branch from the myeloid stem cell.
The lymphoid stem cell gives rise only to lymphocytes. Neither red cells nor granulocytes come from it.
The megakaryoblast is a committed cell of the platelet line, downstream of the branch point. It produces only platelets.
questions.answerText: The myeloid stem cell

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A bone marrow transplant is meant to restore a patient's ability to make every type of blood cell. Which cell must the donated marrow contain for this to work?
options: The reticulocyte
The proerythroblast
The myeloid stem cell
The hemocytoblast
questions.why: Only the hemocytoblast, the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, can give rise to every formed element. If donated marrow contains these stem cells, they settle in the patient's marrow and rebuild both the myeloid and lymphoid lines. A committed cell further down the tree could restore only one branch.
notes: The reticulocyte is an almost mature red cell with no nucleus. It cannot divide at all, so it could not rebuild any line.
The proerythroblast is committed to the red cell line and could only make erythrocytes.
The myeloid stem cell could restore red cells, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes, but not lymphocytes. It would leave the lymphoid line missing.
Correct. Only the pluripotent stem cell can rebuild every blood cell line.
questions.answerText: The hemocytoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A red cell precursor has no nucleus but still contains ribosome remnants, and it is the stage just before maturity. Which stage is it?
options: The reticulocyte
The erythroblast
The normoblast
The erythrocyte
questions.why: The reticulocyte is the stage after the normoblast has ejected its nucleus. It has no nucleus but still holds ribosome remnants, which can be stained to show a fine network. Within a day or two in the blood, these remnants disappear and the cell becomes a mature erythrocyte.
notes: Correct. No nucleus plus ribosome remnants identifies the reticulocyte.
The erythroblast is an earlier stage that still has its nucleus while it builds hemoglobin.
The normoblast is the stage that ejects the nucleus, so it still has a nucleus. It is the stage just before the reticulocyte.
The mature erythrocyte has lost its ribosome remnants too. The clue about remaining ribosomes rules it out.
questions.answerText: The reticulocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A cell sits one step below the hemocytoblast in the blood cell family tree and can no longer become a lymphocyte. Which cell is it?
options: The myeloid stem cell
The myeloblast
The lymphoid stem cell
The proerythroblast
questions.why: The hemocytoblast splits into two lines. The lymphoid stem cell makes lymphocytes, and the myeloid stem cell makes everything else. A cell one step below the hemocytoblast that cannot make lymphocytes must therefore be the myeloid stem cell.
notes: Correct. It is one step down and cannot produce lymphocytes.
The myeloblast cannot make lymphocytes, but it is a committed granulocyte precursor further down the myeloid line.
The lymphoid stem cell is also one step below the hemocytoblast, but it is the cell that does make lymphocytes.
The proerythroblast cannot make lymphocytes, but it sits further down the tree, committed to the red cell line.
questions.answerText: The myeloid stem cell

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which pair correctly names the formation of white blood cells and the formation of platelets?
options: Erythropoiesis for white cells, thrombopoiesis for platelets
Thrombopoiesis for white cells, leukopoiesis for platelets
Leukopoiesis for white cells, thrombopoiesis for platelets
Leukopoiesis for white cells, hemostasis for platelets
questions.why: Each branch of hematopoiesis is named for the cell it makes. Leuko means white, so leukopoiesis is the formation of leukocytes. Thrombo refers to the thrombocyte, another name for the platelet, so thrombopoiesis is platelet formation.
notes: Erythropoiesis is red cell formation, since erythro means red. It does not describe white cells.
This swaps the two terms. Leuko means white, so leukopoiesis must be the white cell term.
Correct. Each name follows the cell being made.
Hemostasis is the stopping of bleeding, which platelets help with. It is not the name for forming platelets.
questions.answerText: Leukopoiesis for white cells, thrombopoiesis for platelets

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which large marrow cell has cytoplasm that breaks into fragments to form platelets?
options: The megakaryocyte
The monocyte
The reticulocyte
The megakaryoblast
questions.why: The megakaryocyte is a giant cell in red bone marrow, with a very large, many-lobed nucleus that holds many copies of its DNA. Its cytoplasm breaks off into thousands of small fragments, and each fragment is a platelet. This is why platelets are cell fragments rather than whole cells.
notes: Correct. Platelets are fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm.
The monocyte is the largest leukocyte in the blood, which can lead to this mix-up. It becomes a macrophage, not platelets.
The reticulocyte is an immature red cell with ribosome remnants. It matures into an erythrocyte.
The megakaryoblast is the earlier committed cell that grows into the megakaryocyte. It does not fragment into platelets itself.
questions.answerText: The megakaryocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A blood test shows a higher than normal reticulocyte count. What does this most directly reflect?
options: An increase in plasma volume
Suppressed activity of the marrow
Stepped-up red cell production
An increase in stored iron
questions.why: Reticulocytes are newly released red cells that mature within a day or two. Normally they are only 1 to 2 percent of red cells, so a higher count means the marrow is releasing new red cells faster than usual. This is what happens when the marrow responds to blood loss or low oxygen by stepping up erythropoiesis.
notes: Plasma volume affects how concentrated the cells are, but the reticulocyte count reflects new red cell production, not fluid volume.
If the marrow were suppressed, fewer new red cells would be released, so the reticulocyte count would fall, not rise.
Correct. More reticulocytes means more new red cells are being released.
Stored iron is held by ferritin in tissues. A reticulocyte count does not measure iron stores.
questions.answerText: Stepped-up red cell production

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which set correctly matches each blast cell to the formed element it produces?
options: Myeloblast to platelets, monoblast to granulocytes, megakaryoblast to monocytes
Myeloblast to granulocytes, monoblast to monocytes, megakaryoblast to platelets
Myeloblast to lymphocytes, monoblast to monocytes, megakaryoblast to platelets
Myeloblast to monocytes, monoblast to platelets, megakaryoblast to granulocytes
questions.why: Each myeloid line has its own committed blast cell. The myeloblast produces the granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils), the monoblast produces monocytes, and the megakaryoblast produces the megakaryocyte that breaks into platelets. The names help: monoblast matches monocyte and megakaryoblast matches megakaryocyte.
notes: Every pairing here is scrambled. The myeloblast makes granulocytes, and the megakaryoblast makes platelets through the megakaryocyte.
Correct. Each blast is matched to its own line.
The last two pairings are right, but the myeloblast makes granulocytes. Lymphocytes come from the lymphoblast of the lymphoid line.
Every pairing here is shifted. The monoblast makes monocytes, as its name suggests, and the megakaryoblast makes platelets.
questions.answerText: Myeloblast to granulocytes, monoblast to monocytes, megakaryoblast to platelets

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A student traces a neutrophil back through its ancestry. Which sequence of cells is correct?
options: Hemocytoblast, lymphoid stem cell, myeloblast, neutrophil
Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, myeloblast, neutrophil
Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, proerythroblast, neutrophil
Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, monoblast, neutrophil
questions.why: A neutrophil is a granulocyte, so it comes from the granulocyte line of the myeloid branch. Its path runs from the hemocytoblast to the myeloid stem cell, then to the myeloblast, the committed granulocyte precursor, and finally to the mature neutrophil.
notes: The lymphoid stem cell makes only lymphocytes. Granulocytes such as the neutrophil come from the myeloid stem cell.
Correct. Neutrophils come through the myeloid line and the myeloblast.
The proerythroblast is the committed red cell precursor. It makes erythrocytes, not neutrophils.
The monoblast is the committed precursor of monocytes. Neutrophils come from the myeloblast instead.
questions.answerText: Hemocytoblast, myeloid stem cell, myeloblast, neutrophil

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: The antigens that determine a person's ABO blood type are located where?
options: On the outer surface of the erythrocyte plasma membrane
Inside the erythrocyte, attached to hemoglobin
Inside the nucleus of the erythrocyte
Dissolved in the plasma around the cells
questions.why: ABO blood type is named for the antigens a person carries on the outside of their red blood cells. An antigen is a molecule the immune system can recognize, and the A and B antigens are sugar chains sitting on the outer face of the erythrocyte plasma membrane. Because they face outward, antibodies in the plasma can find them, which is why a mismatched transfusion makes red cells clump.
notes: Correct. The A and B antigens sit on the outside of the red cell membrane, where plasma antibodies can reach them.

Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein inside the red cell that binds oxygen. It would be the answer for what carries oxygen in the erythrocyte, but blood type antigens are on the cell surface, not on hemoglobin.
A mature erythrocyte has no nucleus at all, since it ejects it to make room for hemoglobin. Students who choose this are picturing a typical cell rather than a red blood cell.
The plasma is where the ABO antibodies, anti-A and anti-B, are found, not the antigens. Pick the plasma if the question asked where the agglutinins of the ABO system circulate.
questions.answerText: On the outer surface of the erythrocyte plasma membrane

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is another name for the A and B surface antigens of the ABO system?
options: Gamma globulins
Fibrinogen
Agglutinins
Agglutinogens
questions.why: The A and B antigens on red cells are called agglutinogens because they are the molecules that trigger agglutination, the clumping of red cells when they meet a matching antibody. The ending -gen means producer, so an agglutinogen is the thing that produces clumping. The antibodies that bind them are the agglutinins.
notes: Gamma globulins are the plasma protein group that makes up the antibodies of immune defense. They would be the answer for which class of plasma proteins includes antibodies, but antigens on a red cell are not antibodies.
Fibrinogen is the large clotting protein made by the liver that converts to fibrin threads. Pick it for a question about which plasma protein forms the framework of a clot.

Agglutinins are the ABO antibodies dissolved in the plasma, such as anti-A and anti-B. Pick agglutinins if the question asked for the other name of the plasma antibodies rather than the surface antigens.
Correct. Agglutinogens are the A and B antigens on the red cell surface that cause clumping when matched by an antibody.
questions.answerText: Agglutinogens

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is another name for the anti-A and anti-B antibodies found in the plasma?
options: Agglutinogens
Fibrinogen
Agglutinins
Albumin
questions.why: The ABO antibodies in the plasma are called agglutinins because they cause agglutination, the clumping of red cells that carry the matching antigen. Each antibody can bind antigens on more than one red cell at once, linking the cells together into clumps. A useful way to keep the pair straight is that the agglutinogen generates the reaction and sits on the cell, while the agglutinin floats in the plasma.
notes: Agglutinogens are the A and B antigens on the surface of the red cells. Choose agglutinogens if the question asked about the surface antigens rather than the plasma antibodies.
Fibrinogen is the clotting protein of plasma, converted to fibrin threads at an injury. It would be correct for which plasma protein is removed when plasma becomes serum, not for an antibody.
Correct. Agglutinins are the ABO antibodies in the plasma that clump red cells carrying the matching antigen.

Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, made by the liver, and it holds water in the blood and carries hormones and drugs. It would be the answer for the main protein that maintains osmotic pressure, not for an antibody.
questions.answerText: Agglutinins

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which surface antigen or antigens does a person with type A blood carry on their red cells?
options: The A antigen only
Both the A and B antigens
The B antigen only
Neither the A nor the B antigen
questions.why: An ABO blood type is named directly for the antigens present on the red cells. A person with type A blood has the A antigen on their erythrocytes and lacks the B antigen. The name of the type always tells you the antigen, and type O is the special case meaning neither antigen is present.
notes: Correct. Type A red cells carry the A antigen and not the B antigen.
Carrying both antigens defines type AB blood, which is why that type gets both letters. Pick it for a type AB person.
Carrying the B antigen only defines type B blood. Pick this if the question asked about a person with type B.
Carrying neither antigen defines type O blood. Pick this if the question asked about a type O person.
questions.answerText: The A antigen only

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which surface antigen or antigens does a person with type AB blood carry on their red cells?
options: The A antigen only
Neither the A nor the B antigen
The B antigen only
Both the A and B antigens
questions.why: Type AB blood is named for having both antigens on the red cells, the A antigen and the B antigen together. Because both antigens are part of the person's own cells, the immune system treats both as self. That is also why a type AB person makes neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody.
notes: The A antigen alone defines type A blood. Choose it if the question asked about a person with type A.
Having neither antigen defines type O blood. Choose it for a type O person, whose red cells carry no A or B antigen.
The B antigen alone defines type B blood. Choose it if the question asked about a person with type B.
Correct. Type AB red cells carry both the A and B antigens.
questions.answerText: Both the A and B antigens

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which surface antigen or antigens does a person with type O blood carry on their red cells?
options: Neither the A nor the B antigen
The B antigen only
The A antigen only
Both the A and B antigens
questions.why: Type O blood has neither the A antigen nor the B antigen on its red cells. Students often read the O as a letter like A and B, but it is better to think of it as a zero, meaning no ABO antigen at all. Because type O cells lack both antigens, they do not trigger anti-A or anti-B antibodies in a recipient.
notes: Correct. Type O red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen.
The B antigen alone is found on type B red cells. Pick this if the question asked about a type B person.
The A antigen alone is found on type A red cells. Pick this if the question asked about a type A person.
Both antigens together define type AB, the opposite of type O. Pick this for a person with type AB blood.
questions.answerText: Neither the A nor the B antigen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which ABO antibody is present in the plasma of a person with type A blood?
options: Anti-B antibody only
Anti-A antibody only
Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Neither antibody
questions.why: A person makes antibodies only against the ABO antigen they do not have. Type A red cells carry the A antigen, so the body treats A as self and makes anti-B antibody in the plasma. A simple rule is that the plasma antibody is always the opposite letter of the antigen on the cells.
notes: Correct. Type A plasma carries anti-B, the antibody against the antigen this person lacks.
Anti-A antibody would attack the person's own type A red cells, so type A blood never carries it. Anti-A alone is the antibody found in type B plasma.
Both antibodies together are found in type O plasma, because type O cells carry neither antigen. Pick this for a type O person.
Having neither antibody describes type AB plasma, since both antigens are self for that person. Pick this for a type AB person.
questions.answerText: Anti-B antibody only

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which ABO antibody is present in the plasma of a person with type B blood?
options: Anti-B antibody only
Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Neither antibody
Anti-A antibody only
questions.why: Type B red cells carry the B antigen, so the immune system accepts B as self and makes antibody only against the missing A antigen. The plasma of a type B person therefore holds anti-A antibody. If type A blood were transfused into this person, the anti-A would bind the donor cells and clump them.
notes: Anti-B antibody would attack this person's own type B red cells, so it is never found in type B plasma. Anti-B alone is the antibody of type A plasma.
Both antibodies together are found in type O plasma, since type O cells carry no ABO antigen. Pick this for a type O person.
Having neither antibody describes type AB plasma, where both antigens are self. Pick this for a type AB person.
Correct. Type B plasma carries anti-A, the antibody against the antigen this person lacks.
questions.answerText: Anti-A antibody only

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which ABO antibodies are present in the plasma of a person with type O blood?
options: Neither antibody
Both anti-A and anti-B
Anti-B only
Anti-A only
questions.why: Type O red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen, so neither antigen is treated as self. The plasma of a type O person therefore holds both anti-A and anti-B antibodies. This is why a type O person can receive only type O red cells, since their antibodies would clump A, B, or AB cells.
notes: Having neither antibody describes type AB plasma, the mirror image of type O. Pick this for a type AB person.
Correct. Type O plasma carries both anti-A and anti-B, because type O cells have neither antigen.
Anti-B alone is the plasma antibody of a type A person, whose cells carry the A antigen. Pick this for type A blood.
Anti-A alone is the plasma antibody of a type B person, whose cells carry the B antigen. Pick this for type B blood.
questions.answerText: Both anti-A and anti-B

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which ABO antibodies are present in the plasma of a person with type AB blood?
options: Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody
Anti-B antibody only
Anti-A antibody only
questions.why: Type AB red cells carry both the A and B antigens, so the immune system treats both as self and makes neither antibody. With no anti-A or anti-B in the plasma, a type AB person will not clump donor red cells of any ABO type. Type AB is the mirror image of type O, which has neither antigen and both antibodies.
notes: Both antibodies together are found in type O plasma, the opposite of type AB. Pick this for a type O person.
Correct. Type AB plasma holds neither antibody, since both antigens are self.
Anti-B alone is the plasma antibody of type A blood. A type AB person cannot make it, because B is one of their own antigens.
Anti-A alone is the plasma antibody of type B blood. Pick it for a type B person, not a type AB person, who carries the A antigen on their own cells.
questions.answerText: Neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody
