questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly lists the plasma antibodies for all four ABO blood types?
options: Type A has anti-B, type B has anti-A, type AB has both, and type O has neither
Type A has anti-B, type B has anti-A, type AB has neither, and type O has both
Type A has anti-A, type B has anti-B, type AB has neither, and type O has both
Type A has anti-A, type B has anti-B, type AB has both, and type O has neither
questions.why: Each person makes antibodies only against the ABO antigens their own red cells lack. Type A lacks B, so it has anti-B; type B lacks A, so it has anti-A. Type AB lacks neither antigen and makes no antibody, while type O lacks both antigens and makes both antibodies.
notes: Types A and B are right here, but types AB and O are swapped. Students who choose this have mixed up antigens and antibodies for the last two types, since AB carries both antigens and O carries neither.
Correct. The antibody is always against the missing antigen, so AB has none and O has both.
Types AB and O are right here, but types A and B are matched to their own antigen. A type A person making anti-A would destroy their own red cells, so this cannot be correct.

This list gives each type the antigens it carries rather than its antibodies. Read as antibodies, it would make every person attack their own red cells, so pick it only if the question asked which antigens each type carries.
questions.answerText: Type A has anti-B, type B has anti-A, type AB has neither, and type O has both

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Whether a person is Rh positive or Rh negative depends on the presence or absence of which red cell antigen?
options: The H antigen
The A antigen
The B antigen
The D antigen
questions.why: The Rh blood group is a separate system from ABO, and Rh status is set by one antigen, the D antigen, on the red cell surface. A person whose red cells carry the D antigen is Rh positive, and a person whose cells lack it is Rh negative. Blood type is usually written with both systems together, such as A positive or O negative.
notes: The H antigen is the base sugar chain of the ABO system, the chain the A and B sugars are added onto. It would fit a question about type O cells, not about Rh status.
The A antigen belongs to the ABO system and decides whether a person is type A or AB. Pick it for a question about ABO type, not Rh status.
The B antigen belongs to the ABO system and decides whether a person is type B or AB. Pick it for a question about ABO type, not Rh.
Correct. The D antigen defines Rh status: present means Rh positive, absent means Rh negative.
questions.answerText: The D antigen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What does it mean for a person to be Rh positive?
options: The D antigen is absent from their red cells
Anti-D antibody is in their plasma from birth
Both the A and B antigens are on their red cells
The D antigen is present on their red cells
questions.why: Rh positive means the red cells carry the D antigen, the antigen that defines the Rh system. The positive sign simply reports that the antigen is present. Rh positive is the more common status, and a person who is Rh positive does not make anti-D antibody because the D antigen is part of their own cells.
notes: Red cells without the D antigen are Rh negative. Pick this if the question asked what Rh negative means.
Anti-D antibody is never present from birth. It forms only in an Rh negative person after exposure to Rh positive blood, such as a mismatched transfusion or a pregnancy with an Rh positive baby.
Carrying both the A and B antigens defines type AB in the ABO system. Students sometimes connect the plus sign with having more antigens, but ABO type and Rh status are separate.
Correct. Rh positive means the D antigen is present on the red cell surface.
questions.answerText: The D antigen is present on their red cells

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: In the United States, about what percentage of people are Rh positive?
options: About 50 percent
About 85 percent
About 15 percent
About 99 percent
questions.why: Most people carry the D antigen, so about 85 percent of people in the United States are Rh positive. That leaves about 15 percent who are Rh negative. Because Rh negative people are the minority, Rh negative blood is in shorter supply and matters most in transfusion and pregnancy.
notes: An even split is a guess that assumes the D antigen is equally likely to be present or absent. In reality the D antigen is present in a large majority of people.
Correct. About 85 percent of people are Rh positive.
About 15 percent is the share of people who are Rh negative. Pick it if the question asked how many people lack the D antigen.
Nearly everyone is not Rh positive. Roughly one person in seven lacks the D antigen, which is why Rh negative status is common enough to check before every transfusion.
questions.answerText: About 85 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: How do Rh antibodies differ from ABO antibodies in when they appear?
options: ABO antibodies form naturally in infancy, but Rh antibodies need prior exposure
Both appear in the plasma before birth
Both form only after a person receives a mismatched transfusion
Rh antibodies form naturally in infancy, while ABO antibodies form only after a transfusion
questions.why: Anti-A and anti-B antibodies appear on their own during the first months of life, without any transfusion. Anti-D antibody is different. An Rh negative person makes it only after being sensitized, meaning after Rh positive red cells enter their blood through a transfusion or a pregnancy. This is why a first mismatched Rh exposure usually causes no reaction, while a second one can.
notes: Correct. ABO antibodies are naturally occurring, while Rh antibodies require prior sensitization.
Neither type of antibody is a normal part of plasma before birth. ABO antibodies appear in the first months after birth, and Rh antibodies appear only after sensitization.
This fits Rh antibodies but not ABO antibodies. A type O person has anti-A and anti-B even if they have never had a transfusion.
This reverses the two systems. Pick the reverse statement, in which ABO antibodies are natural and Rh antibodies need exposure, because that is the correct pattern.
questions.answerText: ABO antibodies form naturally in infancy, but Rh antibodies need prior exposure

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab report shows that a donor's red cells carry the A antigen and that the donor's plasma contains anti-B antibody. What is the donor's ABO type?
options: Type AB
Type B
Type O
Type A
questions.why: The antigen on the red cells names the blood type, and the antibody in the plasma is against the missing antigen. Red cells with the A antigen and plasma with anti-B fit only type A. Reading both pieces of evidence together is a good habit, because they should always agree with each other.
notes: Type AB cells would carry both antigens, and the plasma would have no anti-A or anti-B. Pick type AB if both antigens appeared with no antibody.
Type B cells would carry the B antigen and the plasma would hold anti-A. Pick type B if the report showed the B antigen with anti-A antibody.
Type O cells would carry no ABO antigen, and the plasma would hold both antibodies. Pick type O if the report showed no antigen with both antibodies.
Correct. The A antigen with anti-B antibody is the pattern of type A blood.
questions.answerText: Type A

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab report shows no A or B antigen on a patient's red cells and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. What is the patient's ABO type?
options: Type B
Type AB
Type O
Type A
questions.why: Red cells with no ABO antigen belong to type O. Because neither antigen is part of the patient's own cells, the plasma makes antibodies against both, so anti-A and anti-B are both present. The two findings confirm each other and point clearly to type O.
notes: Type B would show the B antigen on the cells and anti-A alone in the plasma. Pick type B if the report showed that pattern.
Type AB is the mirror image of this report, with both antigens on the cells and no antibody in the plasma. Pick type AB for that pattern.
Correct. No antigens and both antibodies is the pattern of type O blood.
Type A would show the A antigen on the cells and anti-B alone in the plasma. Pick type A if the report showed that pattern.
questions.answerText: Type O

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab report shows both the A and B antigens on a patient's red cells and no anti-A or anti-B antibody in the plasma. What is the patient's ABO type?
options: Type A
Type O
Type B
Type AB
questions.why: Red cells that carry both the A and B antigens are type AB. Since both antigens are self for this patient, the immune system makes neither antibody, so the plasma has no anti-A or anti-B. The absence of both antibodies is what lets a type AB patient receive red cells of any ABO type.
notes: Type A would show only the A antigen and anti-B antibody in the plasma. Pick type A if the B antigen were missing and anti-B were present.
Type O is the opposite pattern, with no antigens on the cells and both antibodies in the plasma. Pick type O for that report.
Type B would show only the B antigen and anti-A antibody in the plasma. Pick type B if the A antigen were missing and anti-A were present.
Correct. Both antigens and no antibodies is the pattern of type AB blood.
questions.answerText: Type AB

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab report shows the B antigen on a patient's red cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma. What is the patient's ABO type?
options: Type O
Type AB
Type B
Type A
questions.why: The B antigen on the red cells names this as type B blood. Since the A antigen is missing, the plasma makes anti-A antibody, which matches the report. Whenever one antigen is present, expect the plasma to carry the antibody of the opposite letter.
notes: Type O would show no antigen on the cells and both antibodies in the plasma. Pick type O if neither antigen were present.
Type AB would show both antigens on the cells and no antibody in the plasma. Pick type AB if the A antigen were also present and anti-A were absent.
Correct. The B antigen with anti-A antibody is the pattern of type B blood.
Type A is the mirror of this report, with the A antigen on the cells and anti-B in the plasma. Pick type A for that pattern.
questions.answerText: Type B

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which description fits anemia?
options: The blood clots too slowly because a clotting factor is missing
The blood carries less oxygen because there are too few red cells or too little hemoglobin
The blood has too few platelets, so the risk of bleeding rises
The blood has too many red cells, so it thickens and flows slowly
questions.why: Anemia is a problem of the erythrocytes. Either there are too few red cells, or the red cells hold too little hemoglobin, and in both cases the blood carries less oxygen to the tissues. Because the cause can be a low count or low hemoglobin, anemia is described as a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity rather than simply a low red cell number.
notes: A missing clotting factor that slows clotting is hemophilia, a disorder of the plasma clotting proteins. Pick it for hemophilia.
Correct. Anemia is a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity from too few red cells or too little hemoglobin.
A low platelet count that raises bleeding risk is thrombocytopenia. Pick it if the question asked about a platelet disorder.
An excess of red cells that thickens the blood is polycythemia. Pick this description if the question asked about polycythemia.
questions.answerText: The blood carries less oxygen because there are too few red cells or too little hemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: In sickle cell disease, which part of the hemoglobin molecule carries the inherited change?
options: The beta-globin chain
The heme group
The alpha-globin chain
The red cell plasma membrane
questions.why: Hemoglobin is built from four protein chains, two alpha-globin and two beta-globin, each holding a heme group with one iron. Sickle cell disease is caused by a change in the gene for the beta-globin chain. The altered beta chains make the hemoglobin stick together when oxygen is low, which bends the red cell into a sickle shape.
notes: Correct. Sickle cell disease comes from a change in the beta-globin chain.
The heme group is the iron-holding ring that binds oxygen within each subunit. Pick heme for a question about where oxygen attaches, not for the sickle cell change.
The alpha-globin chain is the other type of chain in adult hemoglobin. Pick it if the question asked which chain is underproduced in alpha-thalassemia.
The plasma membrane is the outer surface of the red cell, where the ABO antigens sit. The sickle shape changes the membrane's outline, but the inherited defect is in hemoglobin inside the cell.
questions.answerText: The beta-globin chain

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the abnormal hemoglobin found in sickle cell disease called?
options: Hemoglobin A
Hemoglobin S
Hemoglobin F
Methemoglobin
questions.why: The abnormal hemoglobin of sickle cell disease is called hemoglobin S, with the S standing for sickle. It differs from normal adult hemoglobin by a change in its beta-globin chains. When oxygen levels drop, hemoglobin S molecules link into long stiff strands that bend the red cell into a crescent.
notes: Hemoglobin A is the normal adult hemoglobin. Pick it if the question asked which hemoglobin most adult red cells carry.
Correct. Hemoglobin S is the sickle hemoglobin.
Hemoglobin F is fetal hemoglobin, the form made before birth that holds oxygen more tightly. Pick it for a question about the hemoglobin of a fetus.
Methemoglobin is hemoglobin whose iron has been oxidized so it can no longer carry oxygen well. It is a different problem from the inherited sickle cell hemoglobin.
questions.answerText: Hemoglobin S

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What structural change to the erythrocytes gives sickle cell disease its name?
options: The red cells enlarge but keep their disc shape
The red cells shrink but keep their disc shape
The red cells swell into rigid spheres
The red cells become stiff, curved, and sickle-shaped
questions.why: In sickle cell disease, the abnormal hemoglobin links into long stiff strands when oxygen is low, and these strands bend the red cell into a curved crescent like a farm sickle. A normal red cell is a flexible biconcave disc that folds to squeeze through capillaries. The rigid sickled cell cannot fold, so it jams small vessels and causes pain and tissue damage downstream.
notes: Large red cells that keep a normal shape are the picture of a macrocytic anemia, such as vitamin B12 deficiency. Pick this for macrocytic anemia.
Small red cells that keep a normal shape are the picture of a microcytic anemia, such as iron deficiency. Pick this for microcytic anemia.
Rigid round red cells are spherocytes, seen in a different inherited disorder called hereditary spherocytosis. Pick this for a question about spherical red cells, not sickled ones.
Correct. The sickled cell is stiff and crescent-shaped, which is where the disease gets its name.
questions.answerText: The red cells become stiff, curved, and sickle-shaped

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A normal erythrocyte lasts about 120 days. About how long does a sickled erythrocyte survive in the circulation?
options: About 1 year
About 120 days
About 10 to 20 days
About 60 days
questions.why: Sickled red cells are stiff and easily damaged, so the spleen and liver remove them quickly. They survive only about 10 to 20 days instead of the normal 120. Because the bone marrow cannot replace cells that fast, people with sickle cell disease are chronically anemic.
notes: No red cell lasts a year. Students may be thinking of long-lived memory lymphocytes, which can persist for years, but erythrocytes are worn out within months even when healthy.
About 120 days is the lifespan of a normal, healthy red cell. Pick it if the question asked how long an ordinary erythrocyte lasts.
Correct. Sickled cells last only about 10 to 20 days, far shorter than normal red cells.
Sixty days is a guess at a moderate shortening. The real loss is much greater, because sickled cells are removed within a few weeks at most.
questions.answerText: About 10 to 20 days

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A child has painful episodes in which small blood vessels in the hands and feet become blocked. A blood smear shows many stiff, crescent-shaped red cells. Which disorder fits best?
options: Polycythemia
Iron-deficiency anemia
Beta-thalassemia
Sickle cell disease
questions.why: Crescent-shaped red cells are the signature of sickle cell disease. The abnormal hemoglobin S makes the cells rigid and curved, so they cannot fold through narrow capillaries and instead jam them. Blocked small vessels starve the tissue downstream of oxygen, which causes the painful episodes.
notes: Polycythemia is an excess of red cells that thickens the blood and slows flow, which can also block vessels. However, the cells keep their normal disc shape, so pick polycythemia if the smear showed too many normal-looking cells.
Iron-deficiency anemia gives small, pale red cells and fatigue, not crescent-shaped cells blocking vessels. Pick it for a microcytic anemia from low iron.
Beta-thalassemia is reduced production of the beta chain, which gives small, pale red cells rather than crescents. Pick it if the smear showed small cells and testing showed too little beta-globin.
Correct. Rigid crescent-shaped red cells that block small vessels are the hallmark of sickle cell disease.
questions.answerText: Sickle cell disease

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: In a lab test, a person's plasma clumps red cells that carry the B antigen but leaves red cells that carry only the A antigen alone. What is this person's ABO type, and which antibody explains the result?
options: Type O, because the plasma carries both antibodies
Type AB, because the plasma carries no antibody
Type A, because the plasma carries anti-B
Type B, because the plasma carries anti-A
questions.why: Clumping of B cells means the plasma holds anti-B, and leaving A cells alone means it lacks anti-A. Plasma with anti-B and no anti-A belongs to a type A person. A type A person cannot make anti-A, because the A antigen is on their own red cells.
notes: Type O plasma carries both antibodies, so it would clump the A cells as well as the B cells. Pick type O if both kinds of cells clumped.
Type AB plasma has no ABO antibody, so it would clump neither the A cells nor the B cells. Pick type AB if nothing clumped.
Correct. Anti-B without anti-A is the plasma of a type A person.
Type B plasma carries anti-A, which would clump the A cells and leave the B cells alone. Pick type B if the result were the reverse of this one.
questions.answerText: Type A, because the plasma carries anti-B

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What type of tissue is blood?
options: A nervous tissue
A muscle tissue
A fluid connective tissue
An epithelial tissue
questions.why: Blood is a connective tissue, the only one that is liquid. Like every connective tissue, it is made of cells suspended in an extracellular matrix, and in blood that matrix is a fluid called plasma. The cells and cell fragments in it are called the formed elements.
notes: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and neuroglia that carry and support electrical signals. It would be the answer for a question about the tissue of the brain and nerves.
Muscle tissue is made of cells specialized to contract, such as skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle. Choose muscle tissue for a question about the tunica media of an artery.
Correct. Blood is a fluid connective tissue, with plasma as its matrix.

Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines cavities, with cells packed tightly together on a basement membrane and very little matrix. Pick epithelium for a question about the lining of a blood vessel, the endothelium.
questions.answerText: A fluid connective tissue

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What are the cells and cell fragments suspended in plasma called?
options: The formed elements
The buffy coat
The plasma proteins
The solutes
questions.why: The formed elements are the cellular part of blood: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. Platelets are cell fragments rather than whole cells, which is why the term says cells and cell fragments. Together the formed elements make up about 45 percent of blood volume, and plasma makes up the other 55 percent.
notes: Correct. The cells and cell fragments of blood are the formed elements.
The buffy coat is the thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets in a spun sample, which is only part of the formed elements. Choose it for a question about the middle layer of a centrifuged tube.
Plasma proteins such as albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen are dissolved molecules in the plasma, not cells. Pick them for a question about the most abundant solutes in plasma.
Solutes are the substances dissolved in plasma, such as nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, and proteins. They would be the answer for what makes up the roughly 8 percent of plasma that is not water.
questions.answerText: The formed elements

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What does the hematocrit measure?
options: The amount of hemoglobin in each cell
The number of leukocytes in a sample
The percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes
The percentage of blood volume made up of plasma
questions.why: The hematocrit is the percentage of whole blood volume that is erythrocytes (red blood cells). It is measured by spinning a blood sample so the heavy red cells pack at the bottom of the tube, then comparing that red layer with the total height. A low hematocrit can point to anemia, and a high one to polycythemia.
notes: The hemoglobin content of red cells is a separate measurement in a blood count, not the hematocrit. Choose this for a question about how much oxygen-carrying protein is in the blood.
Counting leukocytes is the white blood cell count, part of a complete blood count. Pick this for a question about testing for infection or leukemia.
Correct. The hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes.

The plasma makes up the top layer of a spun sample, about 55 percent of blood. Students who choose this are reading the wrong layer of the tube; the hematocrit measures the packed red cells at the bottom.
questions.answerText: The percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the most abundant plasma protein?
options: Hemoglobin
Fibrinogen
Globulins
Albumin
questions.why: Albumin makes up about 60 percent of the plasma proteins, more than any other. It is made by the liver and helps hold water in the blood by maintaining osmotic pressure, the pull that keeps fluid from leaking out of the capillaries. It also carries hormones, fatty acids, and drugs.
notes: Hemoglobin is inside the red blood cells, not dissolved in the plasma. It would be the answer for the protein that binds oxygen inside erythrocytes.
Fibrinogen is only about 4 percent of the plasma proteins, though it is the largest. Pick it for a question about the protein that forms fibrin threads in a clot.
Globulins are about 35 percent of the plasma proteins, second to albumin. Choose them for a question about the plasma proteins that include the antibodies (gamma globulins).
Correct. Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein.
questions.answerText: Albumin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma protein converts into fibrin threads that form the framework of a clot?
options: Myoglobin
Globulins
Fibrinogen
Albumin
questions.why: Fibrinogen is the clotting protein of plasma, made by the liver. When a vessel is damaged, fibrinogen is converted into long fibrin threads that form a mesh, trapping blood cells to build the clot. Serum is what is left when fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins have been removed.
notes: Myoglobin is an oxygen-storing protein inside muscle fibers, not a plasma protein. It would be the answer for a question about what stores oxygen in skeletal muscle.
Globulins include transport proteins and the antibodies of immune defense. Choose them for a question about which plasma proteins are antibodies.
Correct. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin threads in a clot.
Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and holds water in the blood, but it does not form clots. Pick it for a question about plasma osmotic pressure.
questions.answerText: Fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which protein fills the erythrocyte and binds oxygen for transport?
options: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Myoglobin
Hemoglobin
questions.why: Hemoglobin is the red, iron-containing protein that fills each erythrocyte. It has four subunits, and each one holds a heme group with an iron atom that binds one oxygen molecule. Nearly everything about the red cell's structure, from its missing nucleus to its shape, serves to pack in and use this protein.
notes: Fibrinogen is a plasma protein that forms fibrin threads in a clot. Choose it for a question about clotting.
Albumin is a plasma protein dissolved outside the cells that holds water in the blood. Pick it for a question about the most abundant plasma protein.
Myoglobin is an oxygen-storing protein found inside muscle fibers, not red blood cells. It would be the answer for what stores oxygen in skeletal and cardiac muscle.
Correct. Hemoglobin fills the erythrocyte and carries oxygen.
questions.answerText: Hemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the formation of the blood's formed elements called?
options: Hematopoiesis
Hemolysis
Hematocrit
Hemostasis
questions.why: Hematopoiesis is the formation of blood cells, from hemato, meaning blood, and poiesis, meaning making. In adults it happens in red bone marrow, where hemocytoblasts give rise to every erythrocyte, leukocyte, and platelet. Several look-alike terms start with hem-, so the second half of the word is what tells them apart.
notes: Correct. Hematopoiesis is the formation of blood cells.
Hemolysis means the rupture of red blood cells, as in a mismatched transfusion. Choose hemolysis for a question about red cells bursting.
The hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes. It would be the answer for the measurement taken from a spun blood sample.
Hemostasis means stopping bleeding, through vessel spasm, a platelet plug, and clotting. Pick hemostasis for a question about how the body stops blood loss.
questions.answerText: Hematopoiesis

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: In a centrifuged blood sample, what is the thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets between the plasma and the erythrocytes called?
options: The plasma
The serum
The buffy coat
The colloid
questions.why: When blood is spun, it separates into three layers by weight. Heavy erythrocytes pack at the bottom, plasma rises to the top, and a thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets forms between them, called the buffy coat. It is thin because white cells and platelets make up only a tiny fraction of blood volume.
notes: Plasma is the straw-colored top layer of a spun sample, about 55 percent of blood volume. It would be the answer for the liquid matrix of blood.
Serum is the fluid left after blood has clotted, which is plasma without its clotting proteins. Pick serum for a question about the fluid above a clotted sample.
Correct. The buffy coat is the pale middle layer of leukocytes and platelets.
Colloid is the protein-rich material stored in the follicles of the thyroid gland, not a blood layer. Choose colloid for a question about thyroid histology.
questions.answerText: The buffy coat

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Where does hematopoiesis take place in adults?
options: In the yellow bone marrow
In the spleen
In the red bone marrow
In the liver
questions.why: In adults, all blood cells are formed in the red bone marrow, found in the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and the proximal ends of the limb bones. Hemocytoblasts there give rise to every formed element. Other organs such as the liver and spleen help make blood cells before birth, but not in a healthy adult.
notes: Yellow bone marrow is mostly fat and is not an active blood-forming tissue in adults. It would be the answer for what fills the medullary cavity of an adult long bone.
The spleen makes red blood cells in the fetus, and in adults it removes old ones instead. Choose the spleen for a question about filtering blood and storing platelets.
Correct. Adult hematopoiesis happens in red bone marrow.
The liver is an important site of blood cell formation in the fetus, but not in a healthy adult. Pick the liver for a question about where most plasma proteins are made.
questions.answerText: In the red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: From which single cell type do all the formed elements arise?
options: The reticulocyte
The hemocytoblast
The megakaryocyte
The monocyte
questions.why: The hemocytoblast is the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell of the red bone marrow. Pluripotent means it can become many different cell types, and its descendants split into the myeloid line and the lymphoid line. Every erythrocyte, leukocyte, and platelet traces back to it.
notes: The reticulocyte is an immature red blood cell, one step before a mature erythrocyte. Choose it for a question about the cell with ribosome remnants that makes up 1 to 2 percent of circulating red cells.
Correct. All formed elements arise from the hemocytoblast.
The megakaryocyte is a giant marrow cell that produces only platelets. Pick it for a question about where platelets come from.
The monocyte is a leukocyte that becomes a macrophage, far down one branch of the family tree. It would be the answer for the precursor of macrophages.
questions.answerText: The hemocytoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which giant bone marrow cell breaks apart to form thousands of platelets?
options: The monocyte
The megakaryocyte
The hemocytoblast
The reticulocyte
questions.why: A megakaryocyte is a giant cell in the red bone marrow, from mega, meaning large, and karyo, meaning nucleus. Its cytoplasm breaks into thousands of small membrane-bound fragments, and each fragment is a platelet. That is why platelets have no nucleus: the nucleus stays behind in the megakaryocyte.
notes: The monocyte is the largest circulating leukocyte and becomes a macrophage. Choose it for a question about the leukocyte with a kidney-shaped nucleus.
Correct. The megakaryocyte breaks apart into platelets.
The hemocytoblast is the stem cell that gives rise to all formed elements, including the megakaryocyte line. Pick it for a question about the single cell all blood cells come from.
The reticulocyte is an immature red blood cell, not a platelet producer. It would be the answer for the stage right before a mature erythrocyte.
questions.answerText: The megakaryocyte

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which statement correctly matches the two hematopoietic lines with what they produce?
options: The myeloid line makes only platelets; the lymphoid line makes red cells
The lymphoid line makes all leukocytes; the myeloid line makes red cells
The myeloid line makes lymphocytes; the lymphoid line makes the rest
The lymphoid line makes lymphocytes; the myeloid line makes the rest
questions.why: Hemocytoblasts split into two lines. The lymphoid line gives rise to the lymphocytes, which is easy to remember because the names match. The myeloid line gives rise to everything else: erythrocytes, platelets, and every leukocyte except lymphocytes, meaning neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes.
notes: The myeloid line makes platelets, but also red cells and most leukocytes, and the lymphoid line never makes red cells. This choice shrinks the myeloid line to a single product.
The lymphoid line makes only lymphocytes, not all leukocytes. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes come from the myeloid line along with the red cells.
This reverses the two lines. Use the shared root to keep them straight: the lymphoid line makes lymphocytes.
Correct. The lymphoid line makes lymphocytes, and the myeloid line makes everything else.
questions.answerText: The lymphoid line makes lymphocytes; the myeloid line makes the rest

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: After a blood sample has clotted, the fluid left behind has no clotting proteins. What is this fluid called?
options: Plasma
Buffy coat
Lymph
Serum
questions.why: Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins removed. When blood clots, fibrinogen is used up to form fibrin threads that trap the cells, and the fluid that remains is serum. Plasma, by contrast, still contains fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins.
notes: Plasma is the liquid part of unclotted blood, and it still contains fibrinogen. Pick plasma for a question about the top layer of a spun sample that was kept from clotting.
The buffy coat is the thin layer of leukocytes and platelets in a spun sample, not a cell-free fluid. Choose it for a question about the middle layer of a centrifuged tube.
Lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered a lymphatic vessel, not a product of clotted blood. It would be the answer for the fluid carried in lymphatic capillaries.
Correct. Serum is the fluid left after clotting, with no clotting proteins.
questions.answerText: Serum

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient's blood has too few erythrocytes and too little hemoglobin, so it carries less oxygen. What is this disorder?
options: Hemophilia
Leukemia
Polycythemia
Anemia
questions.why: Anemia is a shortage of erythrocytes or hemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen than the tissues need. It shows up as a low hematocrit or low hemoglobin on a blood count. The word means without blood, which reflects the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity rather than a lack of blood volume.
notes: Hemophilia is an inherited deficiency of a clotting factor, so the blood clots too slowly. It would be the answer for a question about prolonged bleeding with a normal platelet count.
Leukemia is a cancer of white blood cell formation that crowds the marrow with abnormal leukocytes. Choose it for a question about abnormal white cells filling the marrow.
Polycythemia is the opposite problem, an excess of erythrocytes that thickens the blood and slows its flow. Pick it for a question about a high hematocrit.
Correct. Too few red cells or too little hemoglobin is anemia.
questions.answerText: Anemia

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: An inherited abnormal hemoglobin distorts erythrocytes into a rigid curved shape that jams capillaries. Which disorder is this?
options: Polycythemia
Thrombocytopenia
Leukopenia
Sickle cell disease
questions.why: In sickle cell disease, a single abnormal hemoglobin makes red cells rigid and curved like a sickle. A normal red cell is a flexible biconcave disc that folds to pass through narrow capillaries, but a sickled cell cannot fold, so it blocks the capillary instead. This causes pain and tissue damage downstream.
notes: Polycythemia is an excess of erythrocytes that thickens the blood, but the cells keep their normal shape. It would be the answer for a question about a high red cell count.
Thrombocytopenia is an abnormally low platelet count, which raises the risk of bleeding. Pick it for a question about easy bruising from too few platelets.
Leukopenia is an abnormally low white blood cell count, which weakens defense against infection. Choose it for a question about frequent infections from too few leukocytes.
Correct. Rigid curved red cells from abnormal hemoglobin indicate sickle cell disease.
questions.answerText: Sickle cell disease

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient has a cancer of white blood cell formation that crowds the bone marrow with abnormal leukocytes. Which disorder is this?
options: Polycythemia
Hemophilia
Anemia
Leukemia
questions.why: Leukemia is a cancer of white blood cell formation in the red bone marrow. The abnormal leukocytes multiply and crowd out the normal blood-forming cells, so the patient can also develop anemia and bleeding problems. In leukemia the spleen may swell with abnormal white cells as well.
notes: Polycythemia is an excess of red cells that thickens the blood. It would be the answer for a question about a high hematocrit.
Hemophilia is an inherited clotting factor deficiency, not a cancer. Choose it for a question about blood that clots too slowly.

Anemia is a shortage of red cells or hemoglobin. It can follow leukemia when the marrow is crowded, but it is not the cancer itself, so pick anemia for a question about reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.
Correct. A cancer of white blood cell formation is leukemia.
questions.answerText: Leukemia

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient has an inherited deficiency of one clotting factor, so the blood clots too slowly even though the platelet count is normal. Which disorder is this?
options: Thrombocytopenia
Anemia
Hemophilia
Leukemia
questions.why: Hemophilia is an inherited deficiency of a clotting factor, one of the plasma proteins needed to build a clot. Platelets can still form a plug, but without the missing factor the fibrin mesh forms too slowly, so bleeding lasts much longer than normal. It is a disorder of the clotting proteins, not of any formed element.
notes: Thrombocytopenia also causes bleeding, but because of a low platelet count. This patient's platelet count is normal, so pick thrombocytopenia for a question about bleeding from too few platelets.
Anemia is a shortage of red cells or hemoglobin that reduces oxygen delivery. It would be the answer for fatigue from low oxygen-carrying capacity.
Correct. An inherited clotting factor deficiency is hemophilia.
Leukemia is a cancer of white blood cell formation. Choose it for a question about abnormal leukocytes crowding the marrow.
questions.answerText: Hemophilia

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient's blood count is abnormal, and the clinician needs to examine the blood-forming tissue itself. From which sites is a marrow sample typically drawn?
options: The phalanges or the metacarpals
The patella or the calcaneus
The femoral shaft or the radial shaft
The iliac crest or the sternum
questions.why: Red bone marrow in adults is found in the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and the limb girdles. The iliac crest of the hip bone and the sternum are rich in red marrow and sit close to the skin, so a needle can reach them easily. That is why marrow samples are drawn from these two sites.
notes: The phalanges and metacarpals are small bones of the hand that are not used for marrow sampling. They would be the answer for a question about the bones of the fingers and palm.
The patella and the calcaneus are bones of the knee and heel, not the standard red marrow sites. Choose the calcaneus for a question about the bone the calcaneal tendon attaches to.
The shafts of adult long bones contain mostly yellow marrow, which is fat, so they are poor sites for sampling blood-forming tissue. Pick the shaft for a question about where yellow marrow is stored.
Correct. Marrow samples are typically drawn from the iliac crest or the sternum.
questions.answerText: The iliac crest or the sternum

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Plasma is about 92 percent water. Why does that suit its job?
options: Water carries most of the blood's oxygen to the tissues
Water gives blood its deep red color in the vessels
Water forms the fibrous framework of a blood clot
Water dissolves and carries many substances as it flows
questions.why: Water is an excellent solvent, so plasma can dissolve and carry nutrients, wastes, electrolytes, gases, hormones, and proteins all at once. Because it is a liquid, it flows through the vessels and delivers this cargo to every tissue. This is why the notes describe water as the solvent that carries every other component of plasma.
notes: Most oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin inside red cells, with only a small amount dissolved in plasma. Pick hemoglobin for a question about how most oxygen is transported.
Blood's red color comes from the hemoglobin in erythrocytes, and plasma by itself is a pale straw color. This would be the answer for a question about hemoglobin.
The framework of a clot is made of fibrin threads formed from fibrinogen, a plasma protein. Choose fibrinogen for a question about clot formation.
Correct. Water dissolves and carries many substances and lets plasma flow.
questions.answerText: Water dissolves and carries many substances as it flows

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A person moves to a high altitude, where each breath brings in less oxygen, and gradually makes more red blood cells. Which change would show up on a blood test?
options: A higher hematocrit
A larger buffy coat
A lower hematocrit
A lower plasma albumin level
questions.why: When tissues are short of oxygen, the kidney releases erythropoietin, which signals the red bone marrow to make more erythrocytes. More red cells means a larger share of the blood volume is erythrocytes, so the hematocrit rises. The extra red cells carry more oxygen, which helps make up for the thinner air.
notes: Correct. More red cells raise the hematocrit.

The buffy coat holds leukocytes and platelets, which are not what the body increases in response to low oxygen. Choose a larger buffy coat for a question about a high white cell count, such as in infection or leukemia.
A lower hematocrit means fewer red cells, which is what happens in anemia. Pick it for a question about a patient with too few erythrocytes.
Albumin is a plasma protein made by the liver and is not the body's response to thin air. A low albumin level would fit a question about liver disease or fluid leaking out of the blood.
questions.answerText: A higher hematocrit

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Blood is typed as A, B, AB, or O based on antigens on the red cell surface. Why must donor and recipient blood be matched before a transfusion?
options: Mismatched blood carries much less oxygen to the tissues
Mismatched platelets cannot help form clots at an injury
Mismatched plasma contains too much water for the recipient
Mismatched red cells are attacked by the recipient's antibodies
questions.why: Each blood type is defined by antigens, which are marker molecules, on the surface of the red cells. A person's plasma contains antibodies against the ABO antigens they do not have. If mismatched blood is given, those antibodies bind the donor red cells and cause them to clump and burst, a dangerous transfusion reaction.
notes: All normal red cells carry oxygen the same way with hemoglobin, whatever their type. Students pick this because they assume blood types differ in function, but they differ only in surface antigens.
ABO typing is based on antigens on red cells, not on platelets. Choose platelets for a question about how a vessel is plugged after a cut.
Plasma is about 92 percent water in everyone, regardless of blood type. This choice confuses blood type with plasma composition.
Correct. The recipient's antibodies attack donor red cells with unfamiliar antigens.
questions.answerText: Mismatched red cells are attacked by the recipient's antibodies

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A person with anemia often feels tired and short of breath. Why do these symptoms follow from anemia?
options: Too few leukocytes leave the body open to infection
Too many red cells thicken the blood and slow flow
Too few platelets allow constant slow bleeding
Fewer red cells carry less oxygen to the tissues
questions.why: Anemia means too few red cells or too little hemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen. Muscles and other tissues then receive less oxygen than they need, which causes fatigue, and the body responds by breathing harder, which feels like shortness of breath. The symptoms follow directly from the red cell's job of carrying oxygen.
notes: Too few leukocytes is leukopenia, which weakens defense against infection. Choose it for a question about frequent infections.
Too many red cells is polycythemia, the opposite of anemia, which thickens the blood. It would be the answer for a question about a high hematocrit.
Too few platelets is thrombocytopenia, which causes bleeding and bruising rather than oxygen shortage. Pick it for a question about a low platelet count.
Correct. Anemia lowers oxygen delivery, causing fatigue and breathlessness.
questions.answerText: Fewer red cells carry less oxygen to the tissues

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What are the two main components of whole blood, and roughly what share of blood volume does each make up?
options: Plasma about 92 percent, formed elements about 8 percent
Plasma about 45 percent, formed elements about 55 percent
Plasma about 55 percent, formed elements about 45 percent
Plasma about 99 percent, formed elements about 1 percent
questions.why: When a tube of blood is spun, it separates into a pale yellow plasma layer on top, about 55 percent of the volume, and the formed elements below, about 45 percent. The formed elements are almost entirely erythrocytes, with a thin buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets between the two layers. Plasma is the liquid extracellular matrix that makes blood a fluid connective tissue.
notes: About 92 percent is the water content of plasma, not plasma's share of whole blood. Students pick this when they mix up what plasma is made of with how much of the blood it is.
This reverses the two numbers. Plasma is the larger share, which is why the plasma layer sits above a slightly smaller red cell layer in a spun tube.
Correct. Plasma is about 55 percent and formed elements about 45 percent of blood volume.

The leukocytes and platelets of the buffy coat make up only about 1 percent of blood, but the erythrocytes alone make up close to 45 percent. This choice forgets the red cells, the largest group of formed elements.
questions.answerText: Plasma about 55 percent, formed elements about 45 percent

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which list names the three main plasma proteins?
options: Albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen
Globulins, fibrinogen, and myoglobin
Albumin, globulins, and hemoglobin
Albumin, fibrinogen, and collagen
questions.why: The three main plasma proteins are albumin (about 60 percent), the globulins (about 35 percent), and fibrinogen (about 4 percent). Albumin helps hold water in the blood, globulins include transport proteins and antibodies, and fibrinogen is the clotting protein. All except the antibody-forming gamma globulins are made in the liver.
notes: Correct. Albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen are the three main plasma proteins.
Myoglobin is the oxygen-storing pigment in the sarcoplasm of muscle fibers, not a plasma protein. It would be the answer if the question asked what gives muscle its red color.
Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein packed inside erythrocytes, not a protein dissolved in plasma. Pick it if the question asked what fills a red blood cell.
Collagen is the strong fiber of connective tissue proper, cartilage, and bone. It is not dissolved in plasma, though students choose it because blood is classified as a connective tissue.
questions.answerText: Albumin, globulins, and fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant, and what is its main job?
options: Albumin, which helps hold water in the blood
Gamma globulins, which act as antibodies
Hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the plasma
Fibrinogen, which forms the framework of a blood clot
questions.why: Albumin makes up about 60 percent of plasma protein, more than any other. Because there is so much of it dissolved in the blood, it creates an osmotic pull (a tendency for water to move toward where more dissolved particles are) that keeps water inside the vessels instead of leaking into the tissues. It also carries hormones, fatty acids, and drugs.
notes: Correct. Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and helps keep water in the blood.
Gamma globulins are the antibodies of immune defense, made by plasma cells. They would be the answer if the question asked which plasma proteins fight infection.
Hemoglobin carries oxygen, but it stays inside erythrocytes rather than floating in plasma. Students pick it because it is the best known blood protein.
Fibrinogen is the clotting protein, but it is only about 4 percent of plasma protein. Pick it if the question asked which plasma protein becomes fibrin threads in a clot.
questions.answerText: Albumin, which helps hold water in the blood

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A lab tech lets a blood sample clot and then collects the fluid left behind, which is serum rather than plasma. What is missing from serum that was present in plasma?
options: Albumin
Water and electrolytes
The gamma globulins (antibodies)
The clotting proteins, such as fibrinogen
questions.why: Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins removed. When blood clots, fibrinogen is converted into fibrin threads that form the framework of the clot, so the fibrinogen is used up and stays behind in the clot. The fluid that remains still holds water, electrolytes, albumin, and antibodies.
notes: Albumin is not used in clotting, so it remains in serum. Pick albumin if the question asked which plasma protein is the most abundant.
Water and electrolytes stay in the fluid after clotting, since they play no part in forming the clot. Water is about 92 percent of plasma and is still the bulk of serum.
Antibodies stay in serum, which is why serum is used for many antibody tests. They would be the answer if the question asked which plasma proteins defend against infection.
Correct. The clotting proteins are used up in the clot, so serum lacks them.
questions.answerText: The clotting proteins, such as fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Where does hematopoiesis, the formation of blood cells, take place in an adult?
options: In yellow bone marrow
In red bone marrow
In the spleen
In the thymus
questions.why: In adults, all the formed elements are produced in red bone marrow, found in the spongy bone of the axial skeleton and the proximal ends of limb bones such as the humerus and femur. Every blood cell traces back to one stem cell type, the hemocytoblast, living in this marrow. That is why a marrow sample from the iliac crest or sternum is used to examine blood formation directly.
notes: Yellow bone marrow is mostly fat stored in the medullary cavity of adult long bones, and it does not make blood cells under normal conditions. Pick it if the question asked what fills the medullary cavity of an adult long bone.
Correct. Red bone marrow is the site of hematopoiesis in adults.
The spleen makes red blood cells in the fetus, but in adults it removes worn-out red cells and stores platelets. It would be the answer if the question asked where old red cells are broken down.
The thymus is where T cells finish maturing, but the T cell precursors are first formed in red bone marrow. Choose the thymus if the question asked where T cells mature.
questions.answerText: In red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is the stem cell that gives rise to every formed element of blood?
options: The reticulocyte
The hemocytoblast
The osteoprogenitor cell
The megakaryocyte
questions.why: The hemocytoblast is the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell in red bone marrow, meaning it can become any type of blood cell. It gives rise to the myeloid line, which produces erythrocytes, platelets, and all leukocytes except lymphocytes, and to the lymphoid line, which produces lymphocytes. Every formed element in circulation traces back to it.
notes: The reticulocyte is an immature erythrocyte released into the blood, near the end of red cell development rather than the start. It would be the answer if the question asked which young red cell still contains ribosome remnants.
Correct. The hemocytoblast is the stem cell for all formed elements.
The osteoprogenitor cell is the stem cell of bone tissue, which becomes osteoblasts. Students pick it because blood forms inside bone, but it makes bone cells, not blood cells.
The megakaryocyte is a giant marrow cell whose cytoplasm breaks into platelets, so it makes only one formed element. Pick it if the question asked which cell produces platelets.
questions.answerText: The hemocytoblast

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: What is anemia?
options: An inherited lack of a clotting factor, so blood clots too slowly
Too few erythrocytes or too little hemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen
An excess of erythrocytes that thickens the blood
An abnormally low platelet count that raises the risk of bleeding
questions.why: Anemia is a disorder of the erythrocytes: either there are too few of them or they hold too little hemoglobin. Since hemoglobin is the protein that carries oxygen, either problem lowers the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. A low hematocrit on a spun tube is one common sign.
notes: An inherited lack of a clotting factor is hemophilia, a disorder of the clotting proteins rather than the red cells. Choose it if the question asked which inherited disorder makes blood clot too slowly.
Correct. Anemia means reduced oxygen-carrying capacity from too few red cells or too little hemoglobin.
An excess of erythrocytes is polycythemia, which thickens the blood and slows its flow. Pick it if the question asked about the opposite of anemia.
A low platelet count is thrombocytopenia. It would be the answer if the question asked which disorder causes easy bruising and bleeding from too few platelets.
questions.answerText: Too few erythrocytes or too little hemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A tube of blood kept from clotting is spun and separates into a clear top layer, a thin pale middle layer, and a dark red bottom layer. A student draws off only the thin middle layer. What has the student collected, and which layer is read for the hematocrit?
options: Leukocytes and platelets; the dark red bottom layer
Plasma proteins such as fibrinogen; the clear top layer
Erythrocytes only; the thin pale middle layer
Leukocytes and platelets; the thin pale middle layer
questions.why: A spun tube of blood settles into plasma on top, the buffy coat in the middle, and the erythrocytes at the bottom. The buffy coat is the thin pale layer of leukocytes and platelets. The hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes, so it is read from the dark red bottom layer.
notes: Correct. The thin pale middle layer is the buffy coat, and the hematocrit is the share taken up by the red bottom layer.
Plasma and its proteins, including fibrinogen, make up the clear top layer, not the middle one. The hematocrit measures erythrocytes, not plasma.
Erythrocytes form the dark red bottom layer. The thin pale middle layer holds the leukocytes and platelets.
The middle layer is right, but the hematocrit measures erythrocytes, so it is read from the dark red bottom layer, not the buffy coat.
questions.answerText: Leukocytes and platelets; the dark red bottom layer

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A disease destroys the lymphoid line of hematopoiesis but leaves the myeloid line working. Which formed elements are still made normally?
options: Lymphocytes only, since they are the main leukocytes in tissues
Platelets and lymphocytes, but no erythrocytes or granulocytes
Erythrocytes, platelets, and every leukocyte except lymphocytes
No formed elements, since all of them come from the lymphoid line
questions.why: The hemocytoblast gives rise to two lines. The myeloid line produces erythrocytes, platelets, and every leukocyte except lymphocytes, and the lymphoid line produces only the lymphocytes. Losing the lymphoid line removes the lymphocytes, while everything the myeloid line makes is still produced.
notes: Lymphocytes are the one product of the lymphoid line, so they are exactly what this disease removes.
Erythrocytes and granulocytes come from the myeloid line, which still works, and lymphocytes come from the damaged lymphoid line. This answer has both lines backward.
Correct. The myeloid line still makes red cells, platelets, and all leukocytes but lymphocytes.
Every formed element comes from the hemocytoblast, not from the lymphoid line. The lymphoid line makes only lymphocytes.
questions.answerText: Erythrocytes, platelets, and every leukocyte except lymphocytes

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A giant bone marrow cell is seen breaking its cytoplasm into thousands of fragments. Which hematopoietic line does it belong to, and which formed element is it making?
options: The lymphoid line, making platelets
The myeloid line, making erythrocytes
The lymphoid line, making lymphocytes
The myeloid line, making platelets
questions.why: The giant marrow cell whose cytoplasm breaks into thousands of platelets is the megakaryocyte. Platelets are cell fragments, not whole cells, and they come from the myeloid line, which produces erythrocytes, platelets, and all leukocytes except lymphocytes.
notes: Platelets are right, but the lymphoid line makes only lymphocytes. Megakaryocytes belong to the myeloid line.
The line is right, but erythrocytes are whole cells that eject their nucleus as they mature, not fragments broken off a giant cell.
Lymphocytes are complete nucleated cells made by the lymphoid line. A cell breaking into thousands of fragments is making platelets.
Correct. The megakaryocyte belongs to the myeloid line and fragments into platelets.
questions.answerText: The myeloid line, making platelets

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Leukemia and leukopenia both affect the leukocytes. Which statement correctly compares them?
options: Leukemia is a low white cell count; leukopenia is a cancer of white cell formation.
Both are cancers of white cell formation that crowd the marrow with abnormal cells.
Leukemia affects the white cells; leukopenia affects the platelets and clotting.
Leukemia is a cancer of white cell formation; leukopenia is a low white cell count.
questions.why: Leukemia is a cancer of white blood cell formation that crowds the bone marrow with abnormal leukocytes. Leukopenia is an abnormally low white blood cell count, which weakens the body's defense. The first is a problem of abnormal cells, and the second is a problem of too few.
notes: This swaps the two. Leukopenia, like thrombocytopenia, names an abnormally low count, and leukemia is the cancer.
Only leukemia is a cancer. Leukopenia means too few white cells, not abnormal ones crowding the marrow.
Leukopenia affects leukocytes, as its name says. An abnormally low platelet count is thrombocytopenia.
Correct. Leukemia is the cancer, and leukopenia is the low count.
questions.answerText: Leukemia is a cancer of white cell formation; leukopenia is a low white cell count.

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: Thrombocytopenia and hemophilia both raise the risk of bleeding. Which statement correctly matches each one to the component it affects?
options: Thrombocytopenia affects the platelets; hemophilia affects a clotting factor.
Thrombocytopenia affects a clotting factor; hemophilia affects the platelets.
Both affect the platelets, one with too few and the other with abnormal ones.
Thrombocytopenia affects the erythrocytes; hemophilia affects the leukocytes.
questions.why: Thrombocytopenia is an abnormally low platelet count, so there are too few platelets to gather at a vessel injury and form a plug. Hemophilia is an inherited deficiency of a clotting factor, so the blood clots too slowly. Both lead to bleeding, but through different components of the blood.
notes: Correct. Thrombocytopenia is a platelet problem, and hemophilia is a clotting protein problem.
This swaps the two. Thrombocytopenia is the low platelet count, and hemophilia is the inherited lack of a clotting factor.
Only thrombocytopenia is a platelet disorder. Hemophilia is a deficiency of a clotting protein in the plasma.
Too few erythrocytes is anemia, and a low leukocyte count is leukopenia. This answer names the wrong component for both disorders.
questions.answerText: Thrombocytopenia affects the platelets; hemophilia affects a clotting factor.

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient bruises and bleeds easily. The blood count shows a very low number of the formed element that breaks off megakaryocytes. Which disorder fits, and which component is affected?
options: Thrombocytopenia, affecting the platelets
Hemophilia, affecting a clotting protein
Anemia, affecting the erythrocytes
Leukopenia, affecting the leukocytes
questions.why: Megakaryocytes are the giant marrow cells whose cytoplasm breaks into platelets, so the low count is a platelet count. An abnormally low platelet count is thrombocytopenia. It raises the risk of bleeding because platelets gather at a vessel injury to form a plug.
notes: Correct. Fragments of megakaryocytes are platelets, and too few of them is thrombocytopenia.
Hemophilia also causes bleeding, but it is a deficiency of a clotting factor, a plasma protein. It is not a low count of a formed element.
Anemia is too few erythrocytes or too little hemoglobin. Erythrocytes are whole cells, not fragments of megakaryocytes, and anemia lowers oxygen carrying rather than clotting.
Leukopenia is a low white cell count, which weakens defense. Leukocytes are complete cells, not fragments of megakaryocytes.
questions.answerText: Thrombocytopenia, affecting the platelets

questions.topic: Blood: composition, plasma, hematopoiesis, blood types and disorders
questions.q: A patient's hematocrit is well above normal, and the blood is thick and slow-moving. Which disorder fits, and which layer of a spun tube of this blood is larger than normal?
options: Polycythemia; the buffy coat
Polycythemia; the erythrocyte layer
Leukemia; the buffy coat
Anemia; the plasma layer
questions.why: The hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of erythrocytes, so a high hematocrit means extra red cells. An excess of erythrocytes that thickens the blood and slows its flow is polycythemia. In a spun tube the erythrocytes form the layer below the buffy coat, so that layer is larger.
notes: The disorder is right, but the buffy coat holds the leukocytes and platelets. Extra red cells enlarge the erythrocyte layer.
Correct. Polycythemia is an excess of erythrocytes, which enlarges the erythrocyte layer.
Leukemia crowds the marrow with abnormal white cells. It does not explain a high hematocrit, which measures red cells.
Anemia is too few erythrocytes, which would lower the hematocrit, not raise it.
questions.answerText: Polycythemia; the erythrocyte layer

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Tracing the main artery of the lower limb from the thigh into the leg, which artery comes between the femoral artery and the tibial arteries?
options: Fibular artery
External iliac artery
Popliteal artery
Deep femoral artery
questions.why: The femoral artery runs down the front and medial thigh and passes to the back of the knee, where it is renamed the popliteal artery as it crosses the popliteal fossa. Below the knee the popliteal artery gives rise to the anterior and posterior tibial arteries, which supply the leg and foot. So the order from the thigh to the leg is femoral, popliteal, then tibial.
notes: The fibular artery is a branch of the posterior tibial artery in the leg, so it comes after the tibial arteries, not before them. Pick it for the artery along the fibula.

The external iliac artery comes before the femoral artery, in the pelvis. It becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament, which is the answer for the vessel just above the femoral.
Correct. The popliteal artery behind the knee links the femoral artery to the tibial arteries.
The deep femoral artery is a large branch of the femoral artery high in the thigh that supplies the thigh muscles. It branches off the main channel rather than continuing it into the leg.
questions.answerText: Popliteal artery

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Which long superficial vein runs up the medial side of the leg and thigh and is often harvested for bypass grafts?
options: Great saphenous vein
Small saphenous vein
Popliteal vein
Femoral vein
questions.why: The great saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body. It begins on the medial side of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus, and runs up the medial leg and thigh just under the skin to drain into the femoral vein near the groin. Because it is long, superficial, and not essential for returning blood from the limb, surgeons often use pieces of it for coronary bypass grafts.
notes: Correct. The great saphenous vein runs up the medial leg and thigh and is used for grafts.
The small saphenous vein is also superficial, but it runs up the back of the calf and drains into the popliteal vein behind the knee. Pick it for the superficial vein of the posterior leg.
The popliteal vein is a deep vein behind the knee that continues upward as the femoral vein. It is the answer for the vein in the popliteal fossa that receives the small saphenous vein.
The femoral vein is a deep vein that travels with the femoral artery in the thigh. It receives the great saphenous vein near the groin and is the answer for the main deep vein of the thigh.
questions.answerText: Great saphenous vein

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Which sequence gives the main contents of the femoral triangle in order from lateral to medial?
options: Nerve, artery, vein
Nerve, vein, artery
Vein, artery, nerve
Artery, nerve, vein
questions.why: The femoral nerve enters the thigh lateral to the femoral vessels. The femoral artery sits in the middle, and the femoral vein lies medial to it. The memory tip NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics) follows this lateral to medial order, which lets a clinician find the artery for a pulse without hitting the vein or nerve.
notes: Correct. Lateral to medial, the order is nerve, artery, vein.
This places the vein in the middle, but the artery lies between the nerve and the vein. The vein is the most medial of the three.
This is the correct order read the wrong way, from medial to lateral. Pick it if the question asked for the order starting from the medial side.
This puts the artery on the outside, but the femoral nerve is the most lateral of the three. The artery sits between the nerve and the vein.
questions.answerText: Nerve, artery, vein

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Which skin nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs down the medial side of the leg alongside the great saphenous vein?
options: Sural nerve
Obturator nerve
Saphenous nerve
Tibial nerve
questions.why: The saphenous nerve is the longest branch of the femoral nerve and carries only sensation. It travels down the medial side of the knee, leg, and ankle, right beside the great saphenous vein. Both share the name because they run together.
notes: The sural nerve is a skin nerve on the back and lateral side of the calf that runs with the small saphenous vein. It is the companion of the other saphenous vein.
The obturator nerve serves the medial thigh but ends above the knee. Pick it for the nerve that passes through the obturator foramen.
Correct. The saphenous nerve accompanies the great saphenous vein on the medial leg.
The tibial nerve runs deep in the posterior leg with the posterior tibial vessels, not with a superficial vein.
questions.answerText: Saphenous nerve

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery when it passes which structure?
options: Popliteal fossa
Adductor hiatus
Inguinal ligament
Greater sciatic foramen
questions.why: The external iliac artery runs along the pelvic brim. Where it passes under the inguinal ligament into the thigh, it takes the name femoral artery. The vessel is continuous, and the name changes only because it has entered a new region.
notes: The popliteal fossa is behind the knee, where the popliteal artery runs. It lies two name changes further down the limb.

The adductor hiatus is the opening in the adductor magnus where the femoral artery passes to the back of the knee and becomes the popliteal artery. That is the next name change down the limb, not this one.
Correct. The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament.
The greater sciatic foramen is where the sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis at the back, toward the buttock. The external iliac artery stays in front and does not pass through it.
questions.answerText: Inguinal ligament

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Which branch of the femoral artery is the main supply to the muscles of the thigh?
options: External iliac artery
Popliteal artery
Anterior tibial artery
Deep femoral artery
questions.why: Shortly after entering the femoral triangle, the femoral artery gives off a large branch called the deep femoral artery, or deep artery of the thigh. It runs deep and sends branches around the femur and into the muscles of the thigh, while the main femoral artery continues down toward the knee.
notes: The external iliac artery is the vessel above the femoral artery, in the pelvis. It gives rise to the femoral artery rather than branching from it.
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee. Pick it for the artery in the popliteal fossa.
The anterior tibial artery is a branch of the popliteal artery that supplies the front of the leg. It lies below the knee, not in the thigh.
Correct. The deep femoral artery is the main supply to the thigh muscles.
questions.answerText: Deep femoral artery

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: The femoral artery passes through which opening to reach the back of the knee, where it becomes the popliteal artery?
options: Femoral triangle
Greater sciatic foramen
Obturator foramen
Adductor hiatus
questions.why: In the lower thigh, the femoral artery runs in a groove between the muscles called the adductor canal. At its end, the artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a gap in the tendon of the adductor magnus, and reaches the back of the knee. From that point it is called the popliteal artery.
notes: The femoral triangle is where the femoral artery first enters the thigh, just below the inguinal ligament. It is the start of the femoral artery, not where it becomes the popliteal artery.
The greater sciatic foramen is where the sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis for the buttock. The femoral artery never passes through it.
The obturator foramen is the opening in the hip bone that the obturator nerve uses to reach the medial thigh. It is at the hip, far above the knee.
Correct. The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the popliteal artery.
questions.answerText: Adductor hiatus

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: Where does the popliteal artery run?
options: Behind the medial malleolus
Behind the knee
On the top of the foot
In the femoral triangle
questions.why: The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery after it passes through the adductor hiatus. It runs through the popliteal fossa, the diamond-shaped space at the back of the knee, lying deep against the femur and knee joint. At the lower end of the fossa it divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
notes: Behind the medial malleolus is the path of the posterior tibial artery. It would be the answer for the artery that reaches the sole.
Correct. The popliteal artery runs behind the knee in the popliteal fossa.
The top of the foot is the path of the dorsalis pedis artery, the continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
The femoral triangle is in the upper front thigh and holds the femoral artery. Pick it for the artery just below the inguinal ligament.
questions.answerText: Behind the knee

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: In the popliteal fossa, which of these structures lies deepest, closest to the knee joint?
options: Popliteal artery
Tibial nerve
Popliteal vein
Small saphenous vein
questions.why: The main contents of the popliteal fossa are stacked from superficial to deep. The tibial nerve is the most superficial, the popliteal vein lies beneath it, and the popliteal artery is deepest, resting against the back of the femur and knee joint capsule. That is why the popliteal pulse is hard to feel unless the knee is slightly bent.
notes: Correct. The popliteal artery is the deepest of these structures in the fossa.
The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the three main contents. It would be the answer for the structure closest to the skin.
The popliteal vein lies between the nerve and the artery, in the middle layer. Pick it for the intermediate structure.
The small saphenous vein is a superficial vein that pierces the fascia to drain into the popliteal vein. It lies near the surface, not deep against the joint.
questions.answerText: Popliteal artery

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: The popliteal artery divides into which two arteries?
options: Anterior and posterior tibial
Medial and lateral plantar
Dorsalis pedis and fibular
Femoral and deep femoral
questions.why: At the lower edge of the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery, which passes forward into the front of the leg, and the posterior tibial artery, which continues down the back of the leg. These two vessels supply the leg and foot.
notes: Correct. The popliteal artery divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
The medial and lateral plantar arteries are the end branches of the posterior tibial artery in the sole. They are at the far end of the pathway.
The dorsalis pedis and fibular arteries come later. The dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial on the foot, and the fibular branches from the posterior tibial.
The femoral and deep femoral arteries are in the thigh, above the popliteal artery. The deep femoral is a branch of the femoral, one step earlier in the pathway.
questions.answerText: Anterior and posterior tibial

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: After branching from the popliteal artery, how does the anterior tibial artery reach the front of the leg?
options: Behind the medial malleolus
Around the neck of the fibula
Through a gap above the interosseous membrane
Under the inguinal ligament
questions.why: The anterior tibial artery starts on the back of the leg. It passes forward through a gap at the upper edge of the interosseous membrane, between the tibia and fibula, and then runs down the anterior compartment on the front of the membrane. At the ankle it continues onto the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery.
notes: Behind the medial malleolus is the path of the posterior tibial artery and tibial nerve on their way to the sole, not a route to the front of the leg.
Wrapping around the neck of the fibula is the course of the common fibular nerve, not an artery.
Correct. The anterior tibial artery passes forward through a gap above the interosseous membrane into the front of the leg.
The inguinal ligament is in the groin, where the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery. It is far above the leg.
questions.answerText: Through a gap above the interosseous membrane

questions.topic: Nerves and vessels of the lower limb
questions.q: On the top of the foot, the anterior tibial artery continues as which artery?
options: Posterior tibial artery
Fibular artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
Popliteal artery
questions.why: The anterior tibial artery runs down the front of the leg and crosses the front of the ankle. Once it reaches the dorsum, the top of the foot, it is renamed the dorsalis pedis artery. The name means artery of the back of the foot, since dorsum refers to the upper surface.
notes: The posterior tibial artery is the other branch of the popliteal artery. It runs down the back of the leg and passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole.
The fibular artery branches from the posterior tibial artery and runs along the fibula in the back of the leg. It does not reach the top of the foot as a main vessel.
Correct. The anterior tibial artery continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.
