questions.why: Physiology texts group everything blood does into transport of gases, nutrients and wastes, regulation of pH, temperature and fluid balance, and protection through clotting and immunity. Filtration, secretion and absorption are the operations of the kidney tubule and gut, not categories of blood function. Conduction and contraction belong to excitable tissues. Digestion, storage and excretion describe organ systems that blood serves rather than what blood itself does.
questions.answerText: Transport, regulation, and protection

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant by mass?
options: Transferrin
Albumin
Fibrinogen
Gamma globulin
questions.why: Albumin makes up roughly 60 percent of plasma protein, which is why it dominates colloid osmotic pressure. Fibrinogen is only about 4 percent even though it is essential for clotting. Gamma globulins are the antibody fraction and sit between the two in abundance. Transferrin is one specific beta globulin carrying iron, present in far smaller amounts.
questions.answerText: Albumin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the principal function of plasma albumin?
options: It binds and neutralizes bacterial toxins as an antibody
It carries oxygen when hemoglobin is saturated
It generates the colloid osmotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary
It forms the insoluble protein mesh that traps red cells and platelets in a clot
questions.why: Albumin is too large to cross the capillary wall easily, so it stays in plasma and pulls water back in by osmosis, opposing filtration. Forming the clot mesh is the job of fibrinogen once thrombin converts it to fibrin. Neutralizing toxins is an antibody function belonging to the gamma globulins. Albumin does carry fatty acids and drugs, but it has no heme and cannot carry oxygen.
questions.answerText: It generates the colloid osmotic pressure that holds fluid in the capillary

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which plasma protein is converted into the fibers that form the framework of a blood clot?
options: Albumin
Immunoglobulin G
Haptoglobin
Fibrinogen
questions.why: Thrombin cleaves soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that polymerize into the strands of the clot. Albumin holds fluid in the vessel and carries lipids and drugs but has no role in the mesh. Immunoglobulin G is an antibody and belongs to the protection category through immunity, not clotting. Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin released from lysed red cells.
questions.answerText: Fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Antibodies circulating in plasma belong to which class of plasma protein?
options: The gamma globulins
The albumins
The alpha globulins
The fibrinogens
questions.why: Immunoglobulins migrate in the gamma fraction when plasma proteins are separated, so antibody and gamma globulin describe the same molecules. Albumin is a single transport and osmotic protein, not an antibody family. Alpha globulins carry lipids, hormones and copper. Fibrinogen is a single clotting precursor and forms its own fraction.
questions.answerText: The gamma globulins

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: About what percentage of plasma is water?
options: About 55 percent
About 92 percent
About 45 percent
About 70 percent
questions.why: Plasma is roughly 92 percent water, with about 7 percent protein and 1 percent ions, nutrients, gases and wastes, which is why plasma behaves osmotically like a slightly protein rich salt solution. About 45 percent is the hematocrit, the red cell share of whole blood. About 55 percent is the share of whole blood that is plasma, not the water inside plasma. About 70 percent describes total body water as a fraction of lean mass.
questions.answerText: About 92 percent

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What distinguishes serum from plasma?
options: Serum is plasma with the albumin removed
Serum is plasma with all of the dissolved electrolytes and small solutes removed
Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins, including fibrinogen, removed
Serum is plasma with the red cells still suspended in it
questions.why: When blood is allowed to clot, fibrinogen is consumed into the fibrin mesh, and the straw colored fluid left behind is serum. Plasma with cells still in it is simply whole blood. Albumin and electrolytes remain in serum at nearly the same concentration as in plasma, so neither one is the difference. This is why a fibrinogen level cannot be measured on a serum sample.
questions.answerText: Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins, including fibrinogen, removed

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Blood carries heat from active muscle to the skin, where it can be lost. Which functional category does this belong to?
options: Transport
Protection
Secretion
Regulation
questions.why: Moving heat to keep core temperature near 37 C is homeostatic regulation, alongside buffering pH and holding fluid balance. Transport is the delivery of gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes to and from tissues, which is the vehicle for this effect but not the category it is filed under. Protection covers clotting and immune defense. Secretion is a cellular activity, not one of the three categories of blood function.
questions.answerText: Regulation

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with advanced liver disease has a plasma albumin of 2.0 g/dL instead of the normal 4.5 g/dL. What happens to fluid movement at the capillary?
options: Net filtration out of the capillary increases, so fluid accumulates in the tissue
Net reabsorption into the capillary increases, so the tissue dries out
Fluid movement is unchanged because hydrostatic pressure is normal
Filtration stops because there is too little protein to drive it
questions.why: Albumin supplies the colloid osmotic pressure that opposes filtration, so losing half of it weakens the pull back into the capillary and net filtration rises, producing edema. Reabsorption would increase only if colloid osmotic pressure went up, which is the opposite of what happened. Hydrostatic pressure being normal does not protect the balance, because the balance is the difference between the two forces. Filtration is driven by hydrostatic pressure, not by protein, so it does not stop.
questions.answerText: Net filtration out of the capillary increases, so fluid accumulates in the tissue

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Insulin travels from the pancreas through the blood to liver and muscle cells. Which functional category of blood does this illustrate?
options: Coagulation
Transport
Regulation
Protection
questions.why: Carrying a hormone from the gland that makes it to the tissue that responds is a delivery job, and delivery is transport. Regulation refers to blood stabilizing pH, temperature and fluid volume rather than to carrying a messenger. Protection covers clotting and immune defense. Coagulation is one specific mechanism inside protection, not a category of its own.
questions.answerText: Transport

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A tube of blood is allowed to clot and the fluid above the clot is analyzed. Which measurement will come back essentially zero?
options: Albumin
Glucose
Fibrinogen
Sodium
questions.why: Clotting converts fibrinogen into the fibrin strands of the clot, so the serum left above contains almost none of it. Sodium and glucose are small solutes that stay dissolved in the fluid regardless of clotting. Albumin is not consumed by the clotting reaction and remains at its usual concentration. If you need a fibrinogen level, the sample has to be drawn into an anticoagulant so that plasma, not serum, is obtained.
questions.answerText: Fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Transferrin carries iron and lipoproteins carry cholesterol through the plasma. What do these two proteins have in common functionally?
options: Both are albumins acting in the regulation category
Both are clotting factors acting in the protection category
Both are antibodies acting in the protection category
Both are globulins acting in the transport category
questions.why: Alpha and beta globulins are the carrier proteins of plasma, ferrying iron, lipids, hormones and metals that are poorly soluble on their own. Albumin is a separate protein, and neither of these is albumin, though albumin also carries fatty acids. Clotting factors act on the fibrin pathway rather than carrying cargo. Antibodies are gamma globulins and bind antigens rather than transporting nutrients.
questions.answerText: Both are globulins acting in the transport category

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Plasma bicarbonate takes up a hydrogen ion produced by exercising muscle, keeping arterial pH near 7.4. Which functional category of blood is this?
options: Regulation
Transport
Protection
Filtration
questions.why: Buffering hydrogen ions to hold pH in a narrow range is a homeostatic job, and homeostatic jobs of blood are filed under regulation. Transport would describe carrying the carbon dioxide that generated the hydrogen ion, a separate step. Protection covers clotting and immune defense against injury and pathogens. Filtration is a kidney process, not a category of blood function.
questions.answerText: Regulation

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An antibody in plasma binds to a bacterial toxin and prevents it from attaching to a host cell. Which functional category of blood does this belong to?
options: Buffering
Protection
Regulation
Transport
questions.why: Immune defense and clotting are both grouped under protection, because both defend the body against a threat. Regulation is about holding pH, temperature and fluid volume steady. Transport is the delivery of gases, nutrients and hormones. Buffering is one specific mechanism inside regulation, not a category.
questions.answerText: Protection

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Colloid osmotic pressure in a capillary falls from 25 mmHg to 15 mmHg while capillary hydrostatic pressure stays at 30 mmHg. What happens to net filtration pressure?
options: It stays the same because hydrostatic pressure did not change
It falls to zero because the two pressures now cancel
It rises by about 10 mmHg, favoring filtration
It falls by about 10 mmHg, favoring reabsorption
questions.why: Net filtration pressure is hydrostatic pressure minus colloid osmotic pressure, so it goes from 30 minus 25, or 5 mmHg, to 30 minus 15, or 15 mmHg, a rise of 10. It cannot fall, because the force opposing filtration is the one that shrank. Hydrostatic pressure staying constant does not hold the net constant, since the net is a difference. The two pressures would cancel only if colloid osmotic pressure had risen to 30 mmHg.
questions.answerText: It rises by about 10 mmHg, favoring filtration

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome loses large amounts of albumin into the urine. Predict the sequence in the capillary and the tissue.
options: Colloid osmotic pressure rises, net filtration falls, and the tissues become dehydrated
Colloid osmotic pressure falls, net reabsorption rises, and plasma volume expands
Colloid osmotic pressure is unchanged, and only urine volume increases
Colloid osmotic pressure falls, net filtration rises, and generalized edema develops
questions.why: Losing albumin in the urine drops plasma protein concentration, which drops the osmotic pull holding water inside the capillary, so more fluid filters into the interstitium at every capillary bed and swelling appears. Colloid osmotic pressure cannot rise when the protein generating it is being lost. Reabsorption falls rather than rises for the same reason, and plasma volume tends to shrink as fluid leaves the vessels. Urine volume alone would not explain the swelling, and the protein loss does change plasma composition.
questions.answerText: Colloid osmotic pressure falls, net filtration rises, and generalized edema develops

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with severe cirrhosis makes far less albumin and far less fibrinogen than normal. Predict the two consequences.
options: Edema from low colloid osmotic pressure and prolonged clotting from a shortage of fibrin
Dehydration from high colloid osmotic pressure and rapid clotting from excess fibrin
Edema from low colloid osmotic pressure and rapid clotting from excess platelet activity
Normal fluid balance and prolonged clotting, since albumin does not affect capillary fluid
questions.why: The liver is the source of nearly all plasma proteins, so cirrhosis hits both jobs at once: less albumin means weaker osmotic pull and fluid leaks into tissue and the abdomen, and less fibrinogen means less substrate for thrombin so the clot forms slowly and poorly. Colloid osmotic pressure falls rather than rises when protein synthesis fails. Platelet activity is not increased here, and low platelets are actually common in cirrhosis. Albumin is the main determinant of colloid osmotic pressure, so fluid balance is not spared.
questions.answerText: Edema from low colloid osmotic pressure and prolonged clotting from a shortage of fibrin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A laboratory needs both a fibrinogen level and a sodium level from one patient. Which sample handling gives valid results for both?
options: Either sample works, since clotting does not change plasma protein content
Draw into an anticoagulant tube and use plasma, since serum has lost its fibrinogen
Let the sample clot and use serum, since clotting concentrates fibrinogen
Let the sample clot and use serum, since sodium can only be measured after clotting
questions.why: Preventing clotting leaves fibrinogen dissolved in the plasma where it can be measured, and sodium is unaffected by anticoagulant, so one plasma sample serves both tests. Clotting consumes fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh rather than concentrating it, so serum would read near zero. Sodium is a small ion that measures the same in serum or plasma, so clotting is not required for it. Clotting does change protein content, which is exactly the difference between serum and plasma.
questions.answerText: Draw into an anticoagulant tube and use plasma, since serum has lost its fibrinogen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A hiker becomes dehydrated and loses 2 L of water from plasma without losing protein. Predict what happens to plasma protein concentration and to capillary fluid movement.
options: Protein concentration falls, colloid osmotic pressure falls, and filtration is favored
Protein concentration is unchanged, since protein and water are lost together
Protein concentration rises, colloid osmotic pressure rises, and reabsorption is favored
Protein concentration rises, colloid osmotic pressure falls, and filtration is favored
questions.why: Water left but protein stayed, so the same protein is dissolved in less volume and its concentration goes up, raising the osmotic pull that draws interstitial fluid back into the capillary. Colloid osmotic pressure tracks protein concentration directly, so it cannot fall while concentration rises. Concentration cannot fall when only the solvent is lost. Protein does not leave with sweat or exhaled water, so the two are not lost together.
questions.answerText: Protein concentration rises, colloid osmotic pressure rises, and reabsorption is favored

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does hematocrit measure?
options: The percentage of whole blood volume occupied by plasma
The mass of hemoglobin in a given volume of blood
The number of erythrocytes in a microliter of blood
The percentage of whole blood volume occupied by erythrocytes
questions.why: Hematocrit is a packed cell volume: spin the sample and read what fraction of the column is red cells. The plasma fraction is the remainder, roughly 55 percent, and is not what the number reports. Hemoglobin mass per volume is a separate measurement reported in g/dL. Red cell count per microliter is a third measurement, reported in millions per microliter, and it can move independently of hematocrit if cell size changes.
questions.answerText: The percentage of whole blood volume occupied by erythrocytes

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal hematocrit range for an adult male?
options: About 42 to 52 percent
About 30 to 38 percent
About 55 to 65 percent
About 12 to 18 percent
questions.why: Adult males run higher than females because testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis, giving a typical range in the low to mid forties. A value of 30 to 38 percent would be anemia in a male. A value of 55 to 65 percent would be polycythemia, from dehydration, chronic hypoxia or a marrow disorder. The 12 to 18 range is hemoglobin in g/dL, not hematocrit.
questions.answerText: About 42 to 52 percent

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal hematocrit range for an adult female?
options: About 50 to 60 percent
About 37 to 47 percent
About 42 to 52 percent
About 25 to 33 percent
questions.why: The female range sits a few points below the male range, in part because of menstrual iron loss and lower androgen drive on the marrow. The 42 to 52 range is the male reference range and would make a mildly anemic woman look normal. A value of 25 to 33 percent is clearly anemic. A value of 50 to 60 percent would be polycythemic for a woman.
questions.answerText: About 37 to 47 percent

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In a centrifuged blood sample, what is contained in the thin buffy coat?
options: Albumin and fibrinogen
Bilirubin and free hemoglobin
Leukocytes and platelets
Reticulocytes and young erythrocytes
questions.why: White cells and platelets are less dense than red cells but denser than plasma, so they settle into a narrow pale band at the interface, usually about 1 percent of the volume. Reticulocytes are young red cells and pack down with the rest of the red cell column. Albumin and fibrinogen are dissolved in the plasma above. Bilirubin and free hemoglobin, if present, also stay in the plasma and would tint it yellow or pink.
questions.answerText: Leukocytes and platelets

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In a normal centrifuged sample, about what fraction of whole blood volume is plasma?
options: About 45 percent
About 92 percent
About 1 percent
About 55 percent
questions.why: Plasma and formed elements split whole blood roughly 55 to 45, which is why a normal hematocrit sits in the forties. The 45 percent figure is the formed element fraction, the hematocrit itself. The 92 percent figure is the water content of plasma, a fraction of a fraction. The 1 percent figure is the buffy coat.
questions.answerText: About 55 percent

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is anemia?
options: A reduction in the oxygen carrying capacity of blood, from too few erythrocytes or too little hemoglobin
A reduction in the number of circulating leukocytes
A reduction in the number of circulating platelets
A reduction in the arterial partial pressure of oxygen, from poor ventilation or poor diffusion in the lung
questions.why: Anemia is defined by how much oxygen the blood can carry, so it can arise from fewer red cells, smaller red cells, or less hemoglobin per cell. Low leukocytes is leukopenia and affects defense, not oxygen delivery. Low platelets is thrombocytopenia and affects hemostasis. Low arterial PO2 is hypoxemia, a lung problem, and an anemic patient often has a perfectly normal PO2.
questions.answerText: A reduction in the oxygen carrying capacity of blood, from too few erythrocytes or too little hemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is polycythemia?
options: An abnormally high plasma protein concentration
An abnormally high erythrocyte count and hematocrit
An abnormally high leukocyte count
An abnormally low erythrocyte count
questions.why: Polycythemia means too many red cells, which raises hematocrit and blood viscosity and makes the heart work harder to move blood. A high white count is leukocytosis and reflects infection or a marrow disorder. A low red cell count is anemia, the opposite condition. High plasma protein is hyperproteinemia and is usually a sign of dehydration or a plasma cell disorder.
questions.answerText: An abnormally high erythrocyte count and hematocrit

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which change in blood makes it more viscous and harder for the heart to pump?
options: A fall in plasma sodium
A rise in plasma glucose
A rise in hematocrit
A fall in hematocrit
questions.why: Red cells are the main determinant of blood viscosity, so packing more of them into the same volume makes flow more resistant and increases cardiac workload. A falling hematocrit thins the blood, which is why severely anemic blood flows easily but carries little oxygen. Plasma sodium changes tonicity rather than viscosity in any meaningful way. Plasma glucose at physiological levels has a negligible effect on viscosity.
questions.answerText: A rise in hematocrit

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An adult male has a hematocrit of 30 percent. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is within the normal range for an adult male
It is above the normal range and indicates polycythemia
It is below normal and indicates dehydration
It is below the normal range and indicates anemia
questions.why: Thirty percent sits well under the 42 to 52 percent male range, so the blood is carrying fewer red cells than it should and oxygen capacity is reduced. It is not within the male range, and it is not even within the female range. Polycythemia would require a value well above the range, not below it. Dehydration concentrates the blood and raises hematocrit, so it moves the number in the opposite direction.
questions.answerText: It is below the normal range and indicates anemia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has had severe vomiting and diarrhea for two days. What happens to hematocrit and why?
options: It rises, because plasma volume is lost while red cell mass stays the same
It falls, because red cells are lost along with the fluid
It rises, because the marrow rapidly produces more red cells
It is unchanged, because dehydration removes cells and plasma equally
questions.why: Losing water shrinks the denominator of the ratio without changing the number of red cells, so the packed cell column takes up a larger share, a relative polycythemia. Red cells are not lost in vomit or diarrhea, so the cell mass is intact. Marrow cannot add meaningful red cell mass in two days, since a red cell takes several days to mature. Dehydration removes fluid selectively, so the two components do not fall together.
questions.answerText: It rises, because plasma volume is lost while red cell mass stays the same

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A person who has lived at 4,000 m for six months has a hematocrit of 60 percent. What best explains this?
options: Cold air has slowed the destruction of red cells in the spleen
Chronic hypoxia has raised erythropoietin, increasing true red cell mass
Chronic dehydration has concentrated the plasma without adding red cells
The low air pressure has physically compressed the red cells
questions.why: Low inspired oxygen lowers oxygen delivery to the kidney, which secretes more erythropoietin and drives the marrow to make more red cells over weeks, a genuine secondary polycythemia. Dehydration would raise hematocrit too, but it does not persist for six months as an adaptation and would not be the standard explanation for altitude. Air pressure does not compress cells inside the body, which stays at internal pressures. Temperature does not meaningfully change the rate of splenic removal.
questions.answerText: Chronic hypoxia has raised erythropoietin, increasing true red cell mass

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient receives 2 L of intravenous saline over an hour. What happens to hematocrit?
options: It falls, because saline destroys circulating red cells
It is unchanged, because saline is isotonic to plasma
It falls, because plasma volume increased while red cell number did not
It rises, because the added fluid shrinks the red cells and packs them more tightly
questions.why: Adding fluid enlarges the denominator of the ratio, so the same red cells now make up a smaller percentage, a dilutional drop sometimes called relative anemia. The cells do not shrink in isotonic saline, since there is no osmotic gradient across the membrane. Isotonic saline does not lyse red cells; that would require a hypotonic solution. Being isotonic prevents cell volume change but does nothing to prevent the change in plasma volume.
questions.answerText: It falls, because plasma volume increased while red cell number did not

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In the first ten minutes after a sudden large hemorrhage, what does the hematocrit usually show?
options: It falls immediately, because red cells are the first thing lost
It rises immediately, because plasma leaves the vessel faster than cells
It falls immediately, because the marrow stops producing red cells
It is close to normal, because whole blood was lost in its normal proportions
questions.why: Hemorrhage removes plasma and cells together, so the ratio between them is preserved and the hematocrit lags behind the actual loss until fluid shifts in from the interstitium over the next several hours. Red cells are not lost preferentially, so there is no immediate fall. Plasma does not escape faster than cells through a torn vessel. Marrow output changes over days, far too slowly to move the number in ten minutes.
questions.answerText: It is close to normal, because whole blood was lost in its normal proportions

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a hematocrit of 26 percent while well hydrated. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Reduced erythropoietin secretion, so the marrow makes fewer red cells
Excess plasma protein raising blood viscosity
Increased destruction of red cells as they pass through the damaged kidney
Dilution from an expanded plasma volume alone
questions.why: The kidney is the main source of erythropoietin, so damaged kidneys under stimulate the marrow and red cell mass falls, which is the classic anemia of chronic kidney disease. Plasma protein and viscosity do not determine how many red cells the marrow makes. The kidney is not the site of red cell destruction; senescent cells are removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Dilution alone is ruled out by the statement that the patient is well hydrated.
questions.answerText: Reduced erythropoietin secretion, so the marrow makes fewer red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Two blood samples are drawn from the same healthy donor, one before and one after a marathon in the heat with little fluid intake. How will the second hematocrit compare?
options: Unchanged, because hematocrit is fixed by the marrow
Higher, because sweating removed plasma water and concentrated the red cells
Lower, because running destroys red cells in the circulation faster than they are replaced
Lower, because exercise expands plasma volume during the run
questions.why: Heavy sweating without replacement pulls water out of plasma, shrinking the plasma fraction so the same red cells occupy a larger share of the column. Some mechanical destruction of red cells does occur with running, but it is far too small to reverse the concentrating effect of fluid loss. Plasma volume expands with training over weeks, not during a dehydrating race. Hematocrit is a ratio and moves with plasma volume, so the marrow does not fix it.
questions.answerText: Higher, because sweating removed plasma water and concentrated the red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A woman arrives dehydrated with a hematocrit of 55 percent. After 2 L of intravenous saline, her hematocrit reads 38 percent. What does this reveal?
options: The first value was accurate and the marrow suppressed production within hours
The second value is falsely low because saline is hypotonic and swelled the cells
The first value was falsely high from hemoconcentration, and she is actually mildly anemic
The saline destroyed about a third of her red cells
questions.why: Dehydration concentrates red cells into a small plasma volume, so the hematocrit overstates red cell mass and can hide anemia until volume is restored. Isotonic saline does not lyse red cells, so destruction cannot explain a 17 point drop in an hour. Marrow output cannot change red cell mass appreciably in hours, since maturation takes days. Isotonic saline causes no osmotic swelling, and swollen cells would raise, not lower, packed cell volume.
questions.answerText: The first value was falsely high from hemoconcentration, and she is actually mildly anemic

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An endurance cyclist uses injected erythropoietin until his hematocrit reaches 62 percent. Predict the effect on oxygen carrying capacity and on cardiac work.
options: Oxygen capacity rises and viscosity falls, so cardiac work decreases
Oxygen capacity is unchanged, because the hemoglobin content of each red cell is unchanged
Oxygen capacity falls because crowded cells cannot bind oxygen
Oxygen capacity rises, but viscosity rises steeply and the heart must work harder
questions.why: More red cells means more hemoglobin per liter and therefore more oxygen carried, but red cell concentration is the dominant driver of viscosity, so resistance climbs and the ventricle faces a larger workload, which is the danger of doping. Viscosity rises rather than falls when cells are packed more tightly. Capacity depends on total hemoglobin per volume, not on hemoglobin per cell alone, so it does change. Crowding does not impair oxygen binding at the heme group.
questions.answerText: Oxygen capacity rises, but viscosity rises steeply and the heart must work harder

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Six hours after a hemorrhage in which the initial hematocrit was normal, the value has fallen to 31 percent with no further bleeding. What happened?
options: Interstitial fluid shifted into the vessels, diluting the remaining red cells
The marrow destroyed the damaged red cells that survived the bleed
Erythropoietin fell, so the red cell count dropped within six hours
Additional red cells continued to leak slowly through intact capillary walls into the tissue
questions.why: After blood loss, lower capillary hydrostatic pressure lets interstitial fluid move into the plasma to defend blood volume, and that added fluid finally reveals the red cell deficit as a falling hematocrit. The marrow makes red cells and does not destroy them. Erythropoietin actually rises after hemorrhage in response to hypoxia, and in any case cannot change cell number in six hours. Intact capillaries do not leak red cells, which is why the loss stopped when bleeding stopped.
questions.answerText: Interstitial fluid shifted into the vessels, diluting the remaining red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Two adult male patients both have a hematocrit of 45 percent. One is well hydrated and one has lost 3 L of body water. What can you conclude?
options: Neither value can be interpreted because hematocrit is unrelated to hydration
The dehydrated patient has a lower true red cell mass, so his normal looking value is masking anemia
Both patients have identical red cell mass, since the hematocrit is identical
The dehydrated patient has a higher true red cell mass, since dehydration stimulates the marrow
questions.why: Hematocrit is a ratio, so a shrunken plasma volume props the number up; to read 45 percent on a small plasma volume the patient must have fewer red cells than someone reading 45 percent on a normal plasma volume. Identical ratios do not mean identical numerators when the denominators differ. Dehydration does not stimulate erythropoiesis; it only concentrates what is already there. Hematocrit is very much affected by hydration, which is exactly why the two cannot be compared directly.
questions.answerText: The dehydrated patient has a lower true red cell mass, so his normal looking value is masking anemia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: How many oxygen molecules can one fully saturated hemoglobin molecule carry?
options: Two
Eight
Four
One
questions.why: Hemoglobin has four globin chains, each holding one heme group with one iron atom, and each iron binds one oxygen molecule, giving four per hemoglobin. One is the number per heme group, not per hemoglobin. Two is the number of chains of each type, alpha and beta, not the oxygen count. Eight would require two oxygen molecules per iron, which the heme pocket cannot accommodate.
questions.answerText: Four

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which atom sits at the center of a heme group and binds oxygen?
options: Magnesium in the divalent state, Mg2+
Copper in the cupric state, Cu2+
Zinc in the divalent state, Zn2+
Iron in the ferrous state, Fe2+
questions.why: Each heme is a porphyrin ring holding one Fe2+, and oxygen binds reversibly to that ferrous iron without oxidizing it. Magnesium sits at the center of chlorophyll, not heme. Copper is the oxygen carrier metal in some invertebrate hemocyanins and a cofactor in cytochrome oxidase, but not in human hemoglobin. Zinc is a common enzyme cofactor, for example in carbonic anhydrase, but it does not bind oxygen in blood.
questions.answerText: Iron in the ferrous state, Fe2+

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What globin chains make up one molecule of normal adult hemoglobin?
options: Two alpha chains and two beta chains
Four identical alpha chains
Two alpha chains and two gamma chains
One alpha chain and three beta chains
questions.why: Adult hemoglobin, HbA, is a tetramer of two alpha and two beta globins, each carrying one heme. Four identical chains would not match the two gene families that produce hemoglobin. Two alpha and two gamma chains describe fetal hemoglobin, HbF, which has a higher oxygen affinity than the adult form. A one to three arrangement does not occur.
questions.answerText: Two alpha chains and two beta chains

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which structures does a mature circulating erythrocyte lack?
options: Glycolytic enzymes and glucose transporters
A nucleus and mitochondria
A plasma membrane and cytoskeleton
Hemoglobin and carbonic anhydrase
questions.why: The maturing red cell ejects its nucleus and degrades its organelles, which frees interior space for hemoglobin and prevents the cell from consuming the oxygen it carries. It certainly keeps its plasma membrane and a spectrin cytoskeleton, which give it its flexible biconcave shape. It is packed with hemoglobin and rich in carbonic anhydrase for carbon dioxide transport. It keeps glycolytic enzymes and glucose transporters because glycolysis is its only source of ATP.
questions.answerText: A nucleus and mitochondria

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: About how long does a circulating erythrocyte survive?
options: About 30 days
About 2 years
About 120 days
About 10 days
questions.why: Without a nucleus the red cell cannot make new proteins or repair damage, so its membrane wears out after roughly four months and macrophages remove it. About 10 days is the lifespan of a platelet. About 30 days is far shorter than observed red cell survival. Two years is far too long for a cell that cannot repair itself.
questions.answerText: About 120 days

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: How does a mature erythrocyte generate ATP?
options: By oxidative phosphorylation
By beta oxidation of fatty acids
By direct absorption of ATP from plasma
By anaerobic glycolysis
questions.why: With no mitochondria the red cell can only break glucose down to lactate, which yields a small amount of ATP but uses no oxygen, protecting its cargo. Oxidative phosphorylation requires mitochondria the cell has already discarded. Beta oxidation also runs in mitochondria and is unavailable. There is no plasma membrane transporter that imports usable ATP into the cell.
questions.answerText: By anaerobic glycolysis

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What shape is a mature erythrocyte?
options: A biconcave disc
A sphere
A flattened cube
A rod
questions.why: The dimpled disc shape gives a large surface area for the volume, so oxygen has a short diffusion distance to the center, and it lets the cell fold to pass through capillaries narrower than itself. A sphere has the least surface area per volume and is a sign of membrane disease, not the normal form. Cubes and rods do not occur among human red cells and would not deform well in capillaries.
questions.answerText: A biconcave disc

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is deoxyhemoglobin?
options: Hemoglobin that has lost its heme group
Hemoglobin that has released its oxygen
Hemoglobin whose iron has been oxidized to Fe3+
Hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide
questions.why: Deoxyhemoglobin simply means the oxygen binding sites are empty, which is the normal state in venous blood after tissues have taken their oxygen. Hemoglobin with Fe3+ is methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen at all. Hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide is carboxyhemoglobin, also unavailable for oxygen. Hemoglobin without heme would just be globin protein and could never carry oxygen.
questions.answerText: Hemoglobin that has released its oxygen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is the absence of mitochondria in the erythrocyte an advantage?
options: The cell can synthesize new hemoglobin as it ages
The cell becomes rigid enough to resist capillary pressure
The cell cannot consume the oxygen it is transporting
The cell can divide more rapidly in the circulation
questions.why: A red cell running oxidative phosphorylation would burn some of its own cargo on every trip; relying on glycolysis instead means every oxygen molecule it picks up is delivered. Mature red cells cannot divide at all, having lost the nucleus. They cannot synthesize hemoglobin either, for the same reason. Losing mitochondria makes the cell more deformable, not more rigid, and rigidity would be a disadvantage in capillaries.
questions.answerText: The cell cannot consume the oxygen it is transporting

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A capillary has an internal diameter of 5 micrometers and an erythrocyte is about 7.5 micrometers across. How does the cell get through?
options: It temporarily shrinks by pumping water out through its membrane aquaporins
It dissolves and reassembles on the far side
It is pushed through by a rise in plasma osmolarity
Its biconcave shape lets it fold and deform without tearing the membrane
questions.why: Excess membrane relative to volume, held by a flexible spectrin cytoskeleton, lets the disc bend into a bullet shape and squeeze single file through the capillary. Pumping out water would raise internal hemoglobin concentration and actually stiffen the cell. Cells do not dissolve and reassemble. Plasma osmolarity affects cell volume, not the propulsive force, which comes from blood pressure.
questions.answerText: Its biconcave shape lets it fold and deform without tearing the membrane

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In methemoglobinemia the heme iron is oxidized from Fe2+ to Fe3+. What is the consequence?
options: That heme group can no longer bind oxygen, lowering oxygen carrying capacity
That heme group binds oxygen so tightly it cannot release it in tissue
The globin chains separate and the molecule falls apart
The cell switches to carrying carbon dioxide instead
questions.why: Oxygen binds reversibly only to ferrous iron, so oxidation to the ferric state takes that site out of service and the blood carries less oxygen even though hemoglobin concentration looks normal. Excessively tight binding describes carbon monoxide poisoning, a different problem. The tetramer does not disassemble when iron is oxidized. Carbon dioxide is carried mostly as bicarbonate and on the globin chains, and that pathway is not a substitute for lost oxygen sites.
questions.answerText: That heme group can no longer bind oxygen, lowering oxygen carrying capacity

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Binding of the first oxygen molecule makes it easier for hemoglobin to bind the second and third. What is this property called and what does it do to the binding curve?
options: Allosteric inhibition, which shifts the curve to the right without changing its shape
Cooperative binding, which gives the curve its S shape
Competitive inhibition, which makes the curve linear
Saturation kinetics, which makes the curve a straight rise then a plateau
questions.why: Each oxygen bound changes the shape of the tetramer so the remaining hemes have higher affinity, producing the steep middle and sigmoid form of the oxygen dissociation curve. Competitive inhibition involves a rival molecule at the same site and does not describe positive interaction between sites. Simple saturation kinetics would give a hyperbola, which is what myoglobin with its single heme actually shows. Allosteric effects like the Bohr shift move the curve sideways but are a separate phenomenon from cooperativity.
questions.answerText: Cooperative binding, which gives the curve its S shape

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: If each gram of hemoglobin can carry 1.34 mL of oxygen and a patient has 15 g/dL of hemoglobin, what is the oxygen carrying capacity of 100 mL of blood?
options: About 200 mL of oxygen
About 10 mL of oxygen
About 20 mL of oxygen
About 2 mL of oxygen
questions.why: Multiply 15 g/dL by 1.34 mL per gram to get about 20.1 mL of oxygen per 100 mL of blood, the standard figure for a healthy adult. About 2 mL would be off by a factor of ten and is closer to the amount dissolved in plasma. About 200 mL is a factor of ten too large. About 10 mL would correspond to a hemoglobin of roughly 7.5 g/dL, that is, a markedly anemic patient.
questions.answerText: About 20 mL of oxygen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the physiological consequence of the erythrocyte having no nucleus?
options: It cannot bind oxygen properly without a fresh signal from the nucleus each cycle
It cannot maintain a membrane potential
It cannot pass through the spleen
It cannot synthesize new proteins to repair itself, which limits its lifespan
questions.why: No nucleus means no new messenger RNA, so damaged membrane proteins and enzymes cannot be replaced, and after about 120 days the worn cell is culled by macrophages. Oxygen binding is a chemical property of heme and needs no nuclear input. The cell does maintain ion gradients using ATP from glycolysis. Passing through the spleen depends on deformability, which the anucleate cell actually does better than a nucleated one.
questions.answerText: It cannot synthesize new proteins to repair itself, which limits its lifespan

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A hereditary membrane defect makes erythrocytes spherical rather than biconcave. Predict the consequence.
options: The stiff spheres cannot deform in narrow splenic channels and are removed early
The spheres carry more oxygen because a sphere holds more volume
The spheres live longer because a sphere exposes less surface area to mechanical damage
The spheres cannot bind oxygen because heme requires a flat cell
questions.why: Losing surface area relative to volume makes the cell rigid, and macrophages in the spleen trap and destroy cells that cannot squeeze through, producing a hemolytic anemia. The change does not add hemoglobin, so oxygen content per cell is not improved. Reduced surface makes the cell more fragile in transit, not more durable. Heme chemistry is unaffected by cell shape, so oxygen binding itself is normal.
questions.answerText: The stiff spheres cannot deform in narrow splenic channels and are removed early

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In sickle cell disease, deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes and distorts the cell into a rigid crescent. Predict the two main consequences.
options: The cells lose their heme groups, so hemoglobin concentration falls while lifespan is normal
The cells block small vessels and are destroyed early, causing pain crises and hemolytic anemia
The cells carry more oxygen per molecule but circulate more slowly
The cells cannot enter capillaries at all, so tissues rely on dissolved oxygen only
questions.why: A rigid crescent cannot fold to enter a capillary, so it lodges and obstructs flow, and the damaged membrane marks the cell for early removal, so the patient has both ischemic pain and chronic anemia. Oxygen carried per hemoglobin molecule is not increased; the abnormal beta chain changes solubility, not binding capacity. Some sickled cells do enter capillaries, and dissolved oxygen alone could not support tissue. Heme is not lost, and the defining feature of the disease is a shortened lifespan, not a normal one.
questions.answerText: The cells block small vessels and are destroyed early, causing pain crises and hemolytic anemia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL, an arterial PO2 of 95 mmHg, and an arterial oxygen saturation of 98 percent. Explain the oxygen status.
options: The lungs are failing, since low hemoglobin means low PO2
Oxygen content is high because hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly when scarce
Saturation and PO2 are normal but total oxygen content is about half normal
Oxygen content is normal because saturation is normal
questions.why: Saturation reports the percentage of available binding sites that are filled, and PO2 reports the oxygen dissolved in plasma, so both can be perfect while the number of sites is halved; content is hemoglobin times saturation times 1.34, so 7.5 g/dL yields about 10 mL per 100 mL instead of 20. Normal saturation does not guarantee normal content, which is the central point of this card. Hemoglobin concentration does not determine PO2, so the lungs are not implicated. Scarcity does not increase affinity in a way that could make up the deficit.
questions.answerText: Saturation and PO2 are normal but total oxygen content is about half normal

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Carbon monoxide binds heme with roughly 200 times the affinity of oxygen. Predict its effect on arterial PO2, on the number of usable binding sites, and on oxygen delivery.
options: PO2 falls, usable sites are unchanged, and delivery drops
PO2 stays normal, usable sites are unchanged, and delivery is normal
PO2 rises, usable sites rise, and delivery rises
PO2 stays normal, usable sites fall sharply, and delivery drops
questions.why: Carbon monoxide does not displace oxygen from plasma, so the dissolved gas measurement stays normal, but it occupies heme sites almost irreversibly, so far fewer sites are available for oxygen and tissue delivery collapses. PO2 does not fall, which is exactly why carbon monoxide poisoning can be missed by a blood gas alone. Sites are certainly affected, since that is where the gas binds. Nothing about the exposure increases oxygen delivery.
questions.answerText: PO2 stays normal, usable sites fall sharply, and delivery drops

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A reticulocyte still contains ribosomes and residual RNA when it leaves the marrow. What can it still do that a mature erythrocyte cannot, and what does a high reticulocyte count tell you?
options: It can still synthesize hemoglobin, and a high count means the marrow is producing red cells rapidly
It can still divide, and a high count means that red cells are actively dividing in the circulation
It can still use oxidative phosphorylation, and a high count means tissue oxygen is high
It can still bind carbon dioxide, and a high count means acidosis
questions.why: Retained ribosomes allow a day or two of continued globin synthesis, and because reticulocytes are the newest cells released, their share of circulating red cells is a direct readout of marrow output after hemorrhage or hemolysis. Red cells do not divide at any stage in the circulation, since the nucleus is already gone. A reticulocyte does retain some mitochondria briefly, but a high count signals marrow activity, not high tissue oxygen, which would suppress erythropoietin. All red cells carry carbon dioxide, so that is not a distinguishing feature.
questions.answerText: It can still synthesize hemoglobin, and a high count means the marrow is producing red cells rapidly

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which organ secretes most of the erythropoietin in an adult?
options: The spleen
The kidney
The liver
The red bone marrow
questions.why: Interstitial cells of the kidney sense oxygen delivery and release about 90 percent of circulating erythropoietin, which is why kidney disease causes anemia. The liver makes a small share in adults and is the main source in the fetus, but it cannot compensate for failed kidneys. The marrow is the target of erythropoietin, not its source. The spleen destroys old red cells rather than stimulating new ones.
questions.answerText: The kidney

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What stimulus triggers erythropoietin release?
options: A rise in arterial carbon dioxide
A fall in plasma potassium
Reduced oxygen delivery to the kidney
A rise in plasma iron concentration
questions.why: The kidney responds to hypoxia, whether from anemia, altitude, or lung disease, by increasing erythropoietin so that more oxygen carriers are built. Plasma iron is a raw material for hemoglobin and does not itself signal the kidney. Carbon dioxide drives ventilation through central and peripheral chemoreceptors, not erythropoietin release. Potassium regulates aldosterone secretion, a different loop entirely.
questions.answerText: Reduced oxygen delivery to the kidney

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the target tissue of erythropoietin?
options: The liver
The spleen
The kidney cortex
Red bone marrow
questions.why: Erythropoietin binds receptors on committed erythroid progenitors in red marrow, driving their proliferation and maturation into reticulocytes. The liver contributes some erythropoietin in adults but is not where the hormone acts. The spleen removes senescent red cells and does not respond to erythropoietin with production. The kidney cortex is the source of the hormone, not its target.
questions.answerText: Red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which three nutrients are specifically required in adequate supply for normal erythropoiesis?
options: Iron, vitamin B12, and folate
Calcium, vitamin D, and phosphate
Sodium, potassium, and chloride
Vitamin K, vitamin C, and magnesium
questions.why: Iron is built into heme, and B12 and folate are needed for the DNA synthesis that lets erythroid precursors divide, so a shortage of any one of the three limits red cell production. Calcium, vitamin D and phosphate govern bone mineral balance rather than red cell formation. The major electrolytes matter for fluid balance and excitability, not erythropoiesis. Vitamin K is required for clotting factor synthesis, and vitamin C helps iron absorption but is not one of the three classic requirements.
questions.answerText: Iron, vitamin B12, and folate

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Vitamin B12 absorption in the small intestine requires which substance?
options: Transferrin from the liver
Intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells
Bile salts from the gallbladder
Pepsinogen from gastric chief cells
questions.why: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds B12 and allows a specific receptor in the ileum to take it up, so stomach disease can cause a vitamin deficiency far downstream. Bile salts emulsify fats and are needed for fat soluble vitamins, not B12. Pepsinogen becomes pepsin and digests protein. Transferrin carries iron in the plasma and has nothing to do with B12 uptake.
questions.answerText: Intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Where does erythropoiesis take place in a healthy adult?
options: In the liver
In the yellow marrow of long bone shafts
In red bone marrow
In the spleen
questions.why: Red marrow in the flat bones and the ends of long bones houses the hematopoietic stem cells that generate red cells throughout adult life. The spleen and liver are fetal sites and can resume production only under extreme demand. Yellow marrow is fat storage and does not produce blood cells unless it converts back to red marrow under severe stimulus.
questions.answerText: In red bone marrow

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the name of the immature erythrocyte released into the blood shortly before it becomes fully mature?
options: A megakaryocyte
A myeloblast
A normoblast
A reticulocyte
questions.why: Reticulocytes have already ejected the nucleus but retain ribosomal RNA, and they finish maturing in the circulation over about a day. A megakaryocyte is the giant marrow cell that sheds platelets. A myeloblast is the precursor of the granulocytes, a different lineage. A normoblast is an earlier red cell stage that still has its nucleus and stays in the marrow.
questions.answerText: A reticulocyte

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What kind of molecule is erythropoietin?
options: A glycoprotein hormone
A steroid hormone
A fatty acid derivative
A mineral cofactor
questions.why: Erythropoietin is a protein with attached carbohydrate, so it acts at a surface receptor on marrow progenitors rather than entering the cell. Steroid hormones such as cortisol are lipid soluble and act on intracellular receptors, a different mechanism. Fatty acid derivatives describe the eicosanoids, such as thromboxane and prostacyclin. A mineral cofactor such as iron is a raw material, not a signal.
questions.answerText: A glycoprotein hormone

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has end stage kidney disease. Predict the effect on the erythropoietin loop.
options: Erythropoietin secretion falls, but red cell count is preserved by a longer red cell lifespan
Erythropoietin secretion falls, marrow output falls, and anemia develops despite tissue hypoxia
Erythropoietin secretion rises, because a damaged kidney senses more hypoxia
Erythropoietin secretion is unchanged, because the liver takes over fully
questions.why: The damaged kidney cannot produce the hormone even though the hypoxic stimulus is present, so the feedback loop is broken at the effector and the marrow never gets the message. Secretion cannot rise from tissue that has lost the cells that make it. The liver contributes only a small fraction and cannot substitute. Red cell lifespan actually tends to shorten in uremia, so it does not rescue the count.
questions.answerText: Erythropoietin secretion falls, marrow output falls, and anemia develops despite tissue hypoxia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An athlete moves from sea level to 3,000 m. Predict the sequence over the next three weeks.
options: Erythropoietin falls because breathing rate increases and restores oxygen
Reticulocytes fall as the marrow conserves iron for the new environment
Erythropoietin rises within days, then reticulocytes rise, then hematocrit rises
Hematocrit rises within hours, then erythropoietin rises, then reticulocytes rise
questions.why: The hormone signal comes first because the kidney responds to hypoxia quickly, then new cells appear in the blood as reticulocytes, and only after enough have accumulated does the packed cell volume climb. Hematocrit cannot lead the sequence, since cells must be built before they can be counted, although dehydration at altitude can raise it transiently. Increased ventilation helps but does not fully restore arterial oxygen at altitude, so the stimulus persists. Reticulocytes rise rather than fall when the marrow is being driven.
questions.answerText: Erythropoietin rises within days, then reticulocytes rise, then hematocrit rises

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with a dietary vitamin B12 deficiency develops anemia. What is characteristic of the red cells produced?
options: They are abnormally small, because there is far too little heme available to fill them out
They are normal in size but reduced in number only
They are spherical, because the membrane cannot be assembled
They are abnormally large, because DNA synthesis lags while the cytoplasm keeps growing
questions.why: B12 and folate are needed to make DNA, so precursors cannot divide on schedule while protein synthesis continues, producing few, oversized macrocytic cells. Small pale cells are the signature of iron deficiency, where heme rather than DNA is limiting. Cell size does change, which is the diagnostic clue that separates the two. Spherocytes come from inherited membrane protein defects, not from vitamin deficiency.
questions.answerText: They are abnormally large, because DNA synthesis lags while the cytoplasm keeps growing

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with chronic iron deficiency has anemia. What is characteristic of the red cells produced?
options: They are small and pale, because each cell contains less hemoglobin
They are large and deeply colored, because hemoglobin is concentrated
They are normal in size and color but shorter lived
They contain nuclei, because maturation is arrested
questions.why: Iron is the core of heme, so when it runs short the precursors divide an extra time while filling with less hemoglobin, giving microcytic hypochromic cells. Large deeply colored cells are not produced, since less hemoglobin means less color. Size and color both change, which is what distinguishes this from vitamin deficiency and from blood loss. Nucleated red cells appear in the blood only under extreme marrow stress and are not the defining feature here.
questions.answerText: They are small and pale, because each cell contains less hemoglobin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has had the stomach surgically removed. Predict the hematologic consequence and its mechanism.
options: Anemia from folate deficiency, because folate is absorbed only in the stomach
Anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency, because intrinsic factor is no longer secreted
Anemia from erythropoietin deficiency, because the stomach secretes erythropoietin
Polycythemia, because gastric acid normally destroys red cell precursors
questions.why: Parietal cells in the stomach make intrinsic factor, and without it B12 cannot be absorbed in the ileum, so a macrocytic anemia develops after liver stores are used up, often a year or more later. Erythropoietin comes from the kidney, not the stomach. Gastric acid does not regulate marrow output, so its loss does not raise red cell count. Folate is absorbed in the jejunum and does not need intrinsic factor.
questions.answerText: Anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency, because intrinsic factor is no longer secreted

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with anemia receives a transfusion that restores oxygen delivery to normal. What happens to erythropoietin?
options: It stays elevated for months, because the loop has no off signal
It rises briefly then falls, because transfused cells are recognized as foreign
It falls, because the hypoxic stimulus to the kidney has been removed
It rises, because more red cells demand more hormone to maintain
questions.why: This is the negative part of the negative feedback loop: once oxygen delivery is adequate, the kidney stops sensing hypoxia and hormone output drops back toward baseline. Erythropoietin is not needed to maintain cells already made, so more cells do not call for more hormone. The loop does have an off signal, namely restored oxygenation. Compatible transfused cells are not attacked, and immune recognition is not part of this regulatory loop.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the hypoxic stimulus to the kidney has been removed

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Two days after a significant hemorrhage, a patient's reticulocyte count is markedly elevated. What does this indicate?
options: The spleen is destroying circulating red cells much faster than the marrow can replace them
The kidney has stopped making erythropoietin
The patient is dehydrated rather than anemic
The marrow is responding to erythropoietin by releasing immature cells early
questions.why: A rising reticulocyte share means new cells are pouring out of the marrow, exactly what a healthy erythropoietin response to blood loss should produce. Splenic destruction removes cells and would not by itself increase the immature fraction released. Erythropoietin must be high, not absent, for the marrow to be pushed this hard. Dehydration raises hematocrit and would not create a wave of young cells.
questions.answerText: The marrow is responding to erythropoietin by releasing immature cells early

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Place the erythropoietin feedback loop in order after a significant hemorrhage.
options: Tissue hypoxia, kidney secretes erythropoietin, marrow increases red cell production, oxygen delivery improves, erythropoietin falls
Kidney secretes erythropoietin, tissue hypoxia develops, marrow increases red cell production, oxygen delivery improves, erythropoietin rises
Marrow increases production, tissue hypoxia develops, kidney secretes erythropoietin, oxygen delivery falls
Tissue hypoxia, marrow secretes erythropoietin, kidney increases red cell production, oxygen delivery improves
questions.why: The stimulus is the disturbance, the kidney is the sensor and endocrine effector, the marrow is the target, and restored oxygen delivery is what shuts the signal off, which is the definition of negative feedback. Hormone release cannot precede the hypoxia that triggers it. Production rising before any stimulus reverses cause and effect. The last option swaps the roles of kidney and marrow: the kidney secretes the hormone and the marrow makes the cells.
questions.answerText: Tissue hypoxia, kidney secretes erythropoietin, marrow increases red cell production, oxygen delivery improves, erythropoietin falls

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease is given erythropoietin but the hematocrit barely rises. Iron studies show depleted stores. Explain.
options: The marrow has no receptor for injected erythropoietin, only for the natural form
The hormone signal is now present, but without iron the marrow cannot build hemoglobin, so the raw material is limiting
Erythropoietin only works if the kidney is intact, so the injected hormone cannot reach the marrow receptors at all
Iron deficiency destroys erythropoietin in the plasma before it can act
questions.why: A feedback loop needs both a signal and the substrate to act on, so replacing the hormone alone still leaves production capped by the missing iron and the cells that are made are small and pale. Injected erythropoietin reaches marrow receptors regardless of kidney status, which is why it works as a therapy. Iron deficiency does not degrade the hormone. Marrow receptors respond to recombinant and natural erythropoietin alike.
questions.answerText: The hormone signal is now present, but without iron the marrow cannot build hemoglobin, so the raw material is limiting

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An athlete trains at altitude for four weeks and then returns to sea level. Predict what happens to erythropoietin and to hematocrit over the following days to weeks.
options: Erythropoietin stays high for weeks and hematocrit continues to rise
Erythropoietin rises at sea level because oxygen is more available
Erythropoietin falls quickly, while the elevated hematocrit declines slowly as existing cells age out
Erythropoietin falls quickly and the elevated hematocrit falls just as quickly, within about a day
questions.why: Restoring normal oxygen delivery removes the hypoxic stimulus within days, but the extra red cells already in circulation live out much of their 120 day lifespan, so the advantage persists for weeks even after the hormone has normalized. Hematocrit cannot fall in a day, because there is no mechanism to destroy healthy cells that fast. The stimulus is gone at sea level, so the hormone does not stay high. More available oxygen suppresses erythropoietin rather than raising it.
questions.answerText: Erythropoietin falls quickly, while the elevated hematocrit declines slowly as existing cells age out

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Two anemic patients are compared. Patient A has a high reticulocyte count and patient B has a very low one. What does this distinguish?
options: Patient A has a marrow that has completely failed, while patient B is steadily losing blood somewhere
Both patients have identical mechanisms, since both are anemic
Patient A is dehydrated and patient B is overhydrated
Patient A has a marrow responding to red cell loss, while patient B has a marrow production problem
questions.why: The reticulocyte count is a readout of marrow output, so a high value with anemia says the marrow is working hard against ongoing loss or hemolysis, and a low value with anemia says the marrow cannot answer the erythropoietin signal, as in aplasia, kidney disease, or nutrient deficiency. The interpretation is reversed in the second option: a failed marrow gives a low count. The two patterns point to different mechanisms, which is exactly why the test is ordered. Hydration status changes hematocrit, not the fraction of cells that are immature.
questions.answerText: Patient A has a marrow responding to red cell loss, while patient B has a marrow production problem

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Where are worn out erythrocytes removed from the circulation?
options: By macrophages in the spleen and liver
By filtration in the kidney glomerulus
By neutrophils in the capillary bed
By the red bone marrow that produced them
questions.why: Aged, stiff red cells fail to squeeze through narrow splenic channels and are engulfed by resident macrophages there and in the liver, which is why the spleen is sometimes called the red cell graveyard. The glomerulus does not filter whole cells, and hemoglobin in the urine is a sign that something has gone wrong. Neutrophils attack bacteria rather than clearing senescent host cells. The marrow builds red cells and does not destroy them under normal conditions.
questions.answerText: By macrophages in the spleen and liver

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: After a macrophage breaks down hemoglobin, what does the heme portion become, once the iron is removed?
options: Ferritin, which is stored in the liver
Biliverdin, which is then converted to bilirubin
Urea, which is excreted by the kidney
Amino acids, which are returned to the pool
questions.why: The porphyrin ring is opened to green biliverdin and quickly reduced to yellow bilirubin, the pigment that must then be handled by the liver. Urea comes from protein nitrogen metabolism, not from the heme ring. Amino acids come from the globin chains, the other half of the molecule. Ferritin is the storage protein for the iron that was pulled out before the ring was opened.
questions.answerText: Biliverdin, which is then converted to bilirubin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which plasma protein transports iron released from broken down hemoglobin?
options: Albumin
Haptoglobin
Transferrin
Ferritin
questions.why: Transferrin binds free iron in the plasma and delivers it to the marrow or to storage, keeping reactive iron from circulating unbound. Ferritin is the intracellular storage form, not the transport form. Albumin carries fatty acids, drugs and unconjugated bilirubin but not iron. Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin released when cells lyse inside vessels.
questions.answerText: Transferrin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In what form is iron stored inside liver and spleen cells?
options: As transferrin
As heme
As bilirubin
As ferritin
questions.why: Ferritin is a hollow protein shell that holds thousands of iron atoms in a safe, non reactive form and releases them when the marrow needs them. Transferrin is the plasma carrier that moves iron between sites. Heme is iron already built into a porphyrin ring inside hemoglobin. Bilirubin is the waste pigment left after the iron has been removed and contains no iron at all.
questions.answerText: As ferritin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What happens to the globin chains when hemoglobin is broken down?
options: They are digested to amino acids that reenter the body's amino acid pool
They are converted to bilirubin and excreted in bile
They are stored intact in the liver for reuse in the next generation of red cells
They are excreted unchanged in the urine
questions.why: Globin is ordinary protein, so it is hydrolyzed and the amino acids are recycled into whatever the body needs to build next. Bilirubin comes from the heme ring, not from the protein chains. Whole globin molecules are not warehoused for reuse. Intact protein is not excreted in urine in health, which is why proteinuria is a sign of glomerular damage.
questions.answerText: They are digested to amino acids that reenter the body's amino acid pool

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Where is bilirubin conjugated to make it water soluble?
options: In the small intestine
In the liver
In the spleen
In the kidney
questions.why: Hepatocytes attach glucuronic acid to bilirubin, converting the insoluble pigment into a form that can be secreted into bile. The spleen produces bilirubin from heme but cannot conjugate it. The kidney can excrete conjugated bilirubin once it is soluble, but it does not perform the conjugation. Intestinal bacteria act on bilirubin after it arrives in bile, further downstream.
questions.answerText: In the liver

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What gives normal feces its brown color?
options: Bile salts secreted into the duodenum by the gallbladder
Hemoglobin that escaped digestion
Pigments derived from bilirubin by intestinal bacteria
Undigested iron released from the heme ring
questions.why: Gut bacteria convert conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen and then to brown stercobilin, which is why blocked bile flow produces pale clay colored stools. Iron is largely reabsorbed or bound and is not the pigment. Bile salts emulsify fat and are not colored pigments. Intact hemoglobin in stool signals gastrointestinal bleeding and makes stool black or red, not normal brown.
questions.answerText: Pigments derived from bilirubin by intestinal bacteria

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is jaundice?
options: Bluish discoloration of the skin and lips from low oxygen saturation
Pale skin from a low circulating hemoglobin concentration
Reddening of the skin from increased blood flow
Yellowing of the skin and sclerae from accumulated bilirubin
questions.why: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment, and when production outruns clearance it deposits in tissues, showing first in the whites of the eyes. Bluish discoloration is cyanosis and reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin. Pallor accompanies anemia and comes from having too little hemoglobin. Flushing from vasodilation is a circulatory change unrelated to pigment accumulation.
questions.answerText: Yellowing of the skin and sclerae from accumulated bilirubin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble. How does it travel through plasma to the liver?
options: Bound to albumin
Dissolved freely in plasma water
Inside erythrocytes
Bound to transferrin
questions.why: Albumin has hydrophobic binding pockets that carry poorly soluble molecules such as unconjugated bilirubin, fatty acids and many drugs. Free dissolution is exactly what its insolubility prevents. It is not carried inside red cells, since it is produced after those cells have been destroyed. Transferrin is specific for iron and does not carry bilirubin.
questions.answerText: Bound to albumin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct. Predict what happens to plasma bilirubin and to stool color.
options: Bilirubin falls in plasma because it cannot be produced
Conjugated bilirubin rises in plasma and the stool becomes pale
Unconjugated bilirubin rises in plasma and the stool becomes pale
Conjugated bilirubin rises in plasma and the stool becomes darker than normal
questions.why: The liver still conjugates normally, but the soluble pigment cannot reach the intestine, so it backs up into the blood while the gut loses the raw material for brown stercobilin. Unconjugated bilirubin would rise if the liver could not process it, which is a different site of failure. Stool becomes lighter, not darker, when bile is obstructed. Production continues in the spleen regardless of what happens downstream.
questions.answerText: Conjugated bilirubin rises in plasma and the stool becomes pale

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In a patient with rapid intravascular hemolysis, which form of bilirubin rises first in plasma?
options: Neither, because hemolysis does not produce bilirubin
Both rise equally, because conjugation has unlimited capacity
Unconjugated bilirubin, because heme breakdown outpaces liver conjugation
Conjugated bilirubin, because the liver conjugates everything immediately
questions.why: A flood of heme delivers more bilirubin than the hepatocyte conjugating enzyme can handle, so the unprocessed insoluble form accumulates in plasma bound to albumin. The liver has a finite conjugating capacity, so it does not keep up instantly. Hemolysis is a major source of bilirubin, since every destroyed cell releases heme. Capacity is limited, which is why the two forms do not rise in step.
questions.answerText: Unconjugated bilirubin, because heme breakdown outpaces liver conjugation

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is mild jaundice common in newborns during the first week of life?
options: The newborn kidney cannot filter bilirubin from plasma
Newborns have no intestinal bacteria to make bilirubin
The newborn spleen is too small to remove worn out red cells at anything like a normal rate
The liver conjugating enzyme is still immature while red cell breakdown is rapid
questions.why: Two things coincide: a high turnover of fetal hemoglobin containing cells and a hepatic conjugating system that takes days to reach full activity, so unconjugated bilirubin transiently accumulates. The kidney does not clear unconjugated bilirubin in anyone, since it is albumin bound and insoluble. Gut bacteria consume bilirubin rather than producing it, and their absence contributes only indirectly. A small spleen would reduce, not increase, red cell breakdown.
questions.answerText: The liver conjugating enzyme is still immature while red cell breakdown is rapid

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In severe hepatocellular failure, why does jaundice develop?
options: The damaged hepatocytes cannot take up and conjugate bilirubin at a normal rate
The liver begins producing extra bilirubin from its own cells
The spleen doubles its rate of red cell destruction
Albumin binds bilirubin so tightly in the plasma that the liver can no longer take it up
questions.why: Bilirubin has only one route out of the body, through hepatic conjugation and biliary excretion, so losing hepatocyte function backs the pigment up into plasma. Dying liver cells do not manufacture bilirubin; it comes from heme. Splenic activity is not increased by liver failure. Albumin binding is normal physiology and is what delivers bilirubin to the liver rather than what prevents clearance.
questions.answerText: The damaged hepatocytes cannot take up and conjugate bilirubin at a normal rate

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has had chronic hemolysis for years. Predict what happens to body iron stores.
options: They fall, because iron is converted to bilirubin
They rise, because iron from destroyed cells is recycled rather than excreted
They fall, because iron is lost with each destroyed cell
They stay constant, because iron is excreted in bile with bilirubin
questions.why: The body has no regulated route for excreting iron, so macrophages return it to transferrin and ferritin, and with chronic accelerated turnover, especially with repeated transfusion, stores can build to harmful levels. Iron is not lost when a red cell is destroyed inside a macrophage; that is the whole point of recycling. Bilirubin leaves in bile without its iron, which was removed first. Iron is not chemically converted into bilirubin; only the porphyrin ring becomes pigment.
questions.answerText: They rise, because iron from destroyed cells is recycled rather than excreted

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with a stone obstructing the common bile duct has dark urine, pale stools, and yellow sclerae. Explain the pattern.
options: Bilirubin production has stopped, so both urine and stool lose their color
Iron accumulates in the urine, making it dark, while heme colors the sclerae
Conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood, enters the urine, and never reaches the gut to color the stool
Unconjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood, appears in the urine, and colors the stool unusually dark
questions.why: Solubility explains all three findings at once: conjugation makes bilirubin filterable, so obstruction sends it into urine and into tissues, while the gut is deprived of the pigment that bacteria convert to brown stercobilin. Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin bound and cannot be filtered, so it never darkens urine. Production continues normally in the spleen. Iron is not excreted in urine and heme itself does not stain the sclerae.
questions.answerText: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood, enters the urine, and never reaches the gut to color the stool

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with an inherited hemolytic anemia has a shortened red cell lifespan. Predict the bilirubin form, the reticulocyte count, and the spleen size.
options: Conjugated bilirubin high, reticulocytes low, spleen shrunken
Unconjugated bilirubin high, reticulocytes low, spleen normal
Conjugated bilirubin high, reticulocytes high, spleen normal
Unconjugated bilirubin high, reticulocytes high, spleen enlarged
questions.why: Accelerated destruction floods the liver with more bilirubin than it can conjugate, drives erythropoietin and marrow output so young cells pour into the blood, and enlarges the spleen because it is doing the extra work of removing defective cells. Conjugated bilirubin rises when the problem is in the liver or bile duct, not when it is upstream. A low reticulocyte count would mean the marrow is failing, which contradicts a hemolytic picture with an intact marrow. A normal sized spleen would be unusual when splenic macrophages are working overtime.
questions.answerText: Unconjugated bilirubin high, reticulocytes high, spleen enlarged

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A three day old newborn is jaundiced and is treated with blue light phototherapy. What does the light do?
options: It converts bilirubin in the skin into water soluble isomers that can be excreted directly
It destroys circulating red cells so less hemoglobin is available
It heats the liver so the conjugating enzyme works faster
It bleaches the yellow pigment permanently into a colorless compound circulating in the plasma
questions.why: Light energy changes the shape of the bilirubin molecule so that it becomes soluble enough to leave in bile and urine, bypassing the immature conjugating step that caused the problem. Destroying red cells would add more heme and make the jaundice worse. Warming the liver is not the mechanism, and the light does not penetrate to the liver. The change is a photochemical isomerization in the skin, not a bleaching reaction in the plasma.
questions.answerText: It converts bilirubin in the skin into water soluble isomers that can be excreted directly

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Trace one heme group from a 120 day old erythrocyte to its exit from the body, in order.
options: Liver, iron removed to ferritin, ring becomes urea, carried to kidney, excreted in urine
