Macrophage in spleen, iron removed to transferrin, ring becomes bilirubin, liver conjugation, bile, intestine, stercobilin in feces
Kidney glomerulus, filtered as heme, conjugated in the tubule, excreted as urobilin in urine
Macrophage in spleen, iron removed to ferritin, conjugated in the spleen, carried free in plasma, filtered by the kidney, excreted in urine
questions.why: Each step has a required order: destruction and iron salvage come first, the ring becomes pigment, the pigment needs a carrier because it is insoluble, and only the liver can make it excretable. The kidney does not filter heme or conjugate pigment, and heme in urine indicates abnormal intravascular hemolysis. The spleen has no conjugating enzyme, so nothing soluble leaves it. The heme ring becomes bilirubin, not urea, which is a nitrogen waste from amino acid metabolism.
questions.answerText: Macrophage in spleen, iron removed to transferrin, ring becomes bilirubin, liver conjugation, bile, intestine, stercobilin in feces

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the most abundant in normal blood?
options: The monocyte
The eosinophil
The neutrophil
The lymphocyte
questions.why: Neutrophils are roughly 60 to 70 percent of circulating white cells, matching their role as the first responders to bacterial invasion. Lymphocytes are second at about 25 percent. Monocytes are about 5 percent. Eosinophils are only 2 to 4 percent and rise mainly with parasites and allergy.
questions.answerText: The neutrophil

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which leukocyte leaves the blood and matures into a tissue macrophage?
options: The neutrophil
The basophil
The lymphocyte
The monocyte
questions.why: Monocytes circulate briefly and then enter tissue, where they enlarge into long lived macrophages that phagocytose debris and present antigen. Neutrophils also phagocytose but die at the site within a day or two and do not become macrophages. Basophils release histamine and heparin rather than transforming. Lymphocytes mediate specific immunity and do not become phagocytes.
questions.answerText: The monocyte

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which leukocyte releases histamine and heparin?
options: The basophil
The eosinophil
The neutrophil
The monocyte
questions.why: Basophil granules contain histamine, which dilates vessels and increases permeability, and heparin, which discourages clotting at the site of inflammation. Eosinophils release toxic proteins aimed at parasites and dampen allergic responses rather than driving them. Neutrophil granules hold lysozyme and other antibacterial enzymes. Monocytes are phagocytes and are not granule rich in this way.
questions.answerText: The basophil

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which leukocyte is the principal defense against parasitic worms?
options: The monocyte
The eosinophil
The basophil
The neutrophil
questions.why: Eosinophils attach to worms too large to swallow and release cytotoxic granule proteins onto their surface. Basophils act in immediate allergic responses by releasing histamine. Neutrophils are aimed at bacteria and fungi and phagocytose particles small enough to engulf. Monocytes become macrophages that clean up debris and chronic infections.
questions.answerText: The eosinophil

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which leukocyte gives rise to the plasma cells that secrete antibodies?
options: The eosinophil
The monocyte
The B lymphocyte
The neutrophil
questions.why: Activated B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which are dedicated antibody factories, giving lymphocytes their role in specific humoral immunity. Neutrophils phagocytose bacteria but make no antibody. Eosinophils attack parasites with granule proteins. Monocytes become macrophages, which present antigen to lymphocytes but do not secrete antibody themselves.
questions.answerText: The B lymphocyte

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which three leukocytes are classed as granulocytes?
options: Lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils
Monocytes, eosinophils, and lymphocytes
Basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes
Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils
questions.why: These three carry conspicuous cytoplasmic granules whose contents define their function, from antibacterial enzymes to antiparasitic proteins to histamine. Lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes with sparse granules and a large nucleus. Any grouping that includes a lymphocyte or a monocyte among the granulocytes mixes the two classes. The distinction matters because the granulocytes are short lived innate responders while the agranulocytes include the cells of specific immunity.
questions.answerText: Neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal total leukocyte count in an adult?
options: About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter
About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
About 4.5 to 5.5 million per microliter
About 500 to 1,000 per microliter
questions.why: White cells are far outnumbered by red cells, sitting in the thousands per microliter, so a count above 11,000 suggests infection and one below 4,500 suggests marrow suppression. The 150,000 to 400,000 range is the platelet count. The millions per microliter range is the erythrocyte count. A count of 500 to 1,000 would be severe leukopenia with a serious risk of infection.
questions.answerText: About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is leukopenia?
options: An abnormally low red blood cell count
An abnormally low white blood cell count
An abnormally high white blood cell count
An abnormally low platelet count
questions.why: Leukopenia means too few defensive cells, most often from marrow suppression by drugs or radiation, and it leaves the patient vulnerable to infection. A high count is leukocytosis and usually signals infection or a marrow disorder. A low platelet count is thrombocytopenia, which causes bleeding rather than infection. A low red cell count is anemia and reduces oxygen delivery.
questions.answerText: An abnormally low white blood cell count

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has acute appendicitis from a bacterial infection. Which leukocyte will be most elevated?
options: Basophils
Lymphocytes
Neutrophils
Eosinophils
questions.why: Neutrophils are recruited within hours to bacterial sites and the marrow releases its reserve pool, so acute bacterial infection typically shows neutrophilia. Eosinophils rise with parasites and allergy, not with ordinary bacterial infection. Basophils are few in number and rise mainly with allergic and some chronic conditions. Lymphocytes lead the response to viral infection instead.
questions.answerText: Neutrophils

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student has infectious mononucleosis, a viral illness. Which leukocyte pattern is expected?
options: Neutrophilia, an increase in neutrophils
Eosinophilia, an increase in eosinophils
Basophilia, an increase in basophils
Lymphocytosis, an increase in lymphocytes
questions.why: Viruses replicate inside host cells, so the response depends on lymphocytes that recognize infected cells and produce antibody, and their numbers climb. Neutrophils dominate bacterial infections and are often unremarkable or even reduced in viral illness. Eosinophils track parasites and allergy. Basophils are too scarce to define a response pattern.
questions.answerText: Lymphocytosis, an increase in lymphocytes

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with seasonal allergic rhinitis has a raised count of one leukocyte. Which one, and why?
options: Eosinophils, because they are recruited in allergic and hypersensitivity responses
Neutrophils, because allergens are treated as bacteria
Monocytes, because clearing allergens requires sustained phagocytosis by tissue macrophages
Lymphocytes, because allergens are viruses
questions.why: Eosinophils accumulate at sites of allergic inflammation, where they both contribute to and help limit the response, so an eosinophil count above the usual 2 to 4 percent points toward allergy or parasites. Allergens are not bacteria and do not drive a neutrophil response. Monocytes rise in chronic infections such as tuberculosis. Allergens are not viruses, so the lymphocyte pattern does not apply.
questions.answerText: Eosinophils, because they are recruited in allergic and hypersensitivity responses

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A traveler returns with an intestinal roundworm infection. Which leukocyte count rises?
options: The monocyte count
The eosinophil count
The basophil count
The neutrophil count
questions.why: Worms are far too large to phagocytose, so the body sends eosinophils to coat them and release destructive granule proteins onto their surface, and the blood count rises markedly. Basophils act in immediate allergic reactions by releasing histamine. Neutrophils engulf bacteria and small particles. Monocytes and their macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections and tissue debris.
questions.answerText: The eosinophil count

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with chronic tuberculosis has a persistently elevated count of one leukocyte type. Which one, and why?
options: Basophils, because chronic infection requires histamine release
Neutrophils, because chronic infection is simply prolonged acute infection
Monocytes, because macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections
Eosinophils, because mycobacteria are treated as parasites
questions.why: Mycobacteria survive inside cells, so the sustained response depends on monocytes entering tissue and becoming macrophages that wall the organism off in a granuloma, and blood monocytes rise. Mycobacteria are bacteria, not worms, so the eosinophil pathway does not apply. Histamine release is an immediate hypersensitivity mechanism, not a defense against chronic infection. Neutrophils dominate the first hours to days, but chronic infection recruits a different cell.
questions.answerText: Monocytes, because macrophages handle chronic intracellular infections

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy has a white cell count of 1,200 per microliter. Predict the consequence.
options: Excessive bleeding, because leukocytes are the cells that form the platelet plug and clot
Reduced oxygen delivery, because leukocytes carry oxygen
Jaundice, because leukocytes clear bilirubin
Marked vulnerability to infection, because too few defensive cells are available
questions.why: Chemotherapy suppresses rapidly dividing marrow precursors, and with the white count far below the normal 4,500 to 11,000 the patient cannot mount a normal response to bacteria or fungi. Bleeding comes from low platelets, which chemotherapy may also cause, but leukocytes themselves do not form the clot. Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin in red cells. Bilirubin is cleared by the liver, not by white cells.
questions.answerText: Marked vulnerability to infection, because too few defensive cells are available

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A differential count shows 88 percent neutrophils, many of them immature band forms, with a total white count of 19,000 per microliter. Interpret this.
options: An acute bacterial infection driving the marrow to release immature neutrophils early
A parasitic infection, since immature cells indicate worms
An allergic reaction, since a high total white cell count indicates a hypersensitivity response
A viral infection, since band forms are characteristic of viruses
questions.why: Two clues point the same way: the cell type is the bacterial responder, and the presence of immature bands means demand has outrun the mature reserve, a pattern often called a left shift. Parasitic infection would raise eosinophils rather than neutrophils. Allergy also raises eosinophils, and the total count alone does not identify a mechanism. Viral infection typically raises lymphocytes and does not produce a neutrophil left shift.
questions.answerText: An acute bacterial infection driving the marrow to release immature neutrophils early

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Minutes after a bee sting, a patient develops widespread hives, itching, and a fall in blood pressure. Which leukocyte mediator explains this and how?
options: Heparin from eosinophils, which prevents clotting in the skin
Histamine from basophils and mast cells, which dilates arterioles and leaks capillary fluid
Lysozyme from neutrophils, which digests bacterial cell walls
Antibody from plasma cells, which binds the venom but takes several days to be produced in quantity
questions.why: Histamine acts within minutes, widening arterioles so blood pressure falls and loosening capillary junctions so fluid leaks into skin as wheals, which matches the speed and the signs. Lysozyme is antibacterial and would not cause vasodilation. Antibody production does take days, so it cannot explain a reaction that begins in minutes, although preformed IgE is what triggered the release. Heparin comes from basophils and mast cells rather than eosinophils, and anticoagulation does not produce hives.
questions.answerText: Histamine from basophils and mast cells, which dilates arterioles and leaks capillary fluid

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Untreated HIV infection progressively destroys helper T lymphocytes. Predict the consequence for defense and explain why.
options: Anemia is the first consequence, because lymphocytes carry oxygen
Allergic reactions disappear, because all leukocyte function is lost
Opportunistic infections increase, because helper T cells coordinate antibody and cell mediated defense
Bleeding increases, because helper T lymphocytes are required for platelet plug formation and clotting
questions.why: Helper T cells sit at the center of specific immunity, activating B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so their loss disables far more than their own numbers suggest and organisms that a healthy person contains become dangerous. Platelet plug formation depends on platelets and von Willebrand factor, not on lymphocytes. Lymphocytes do not carry oxygen; that is the red cell's job. Other leukocyte lines persist, so defense is impaired selectively rather than abolished across the board.
questions.answerText: Opportunistic infections increase, because helper T cells coordinate antibody and cell mediated defense

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Two patients each have a total white count of 14,000 per microliter. Patient A has 82 percent neutrophils and patient B has 38 percent eosinophils. What does the differential add that the total does not?
options: It measures how severe the infection is, showing B is sicker than A
It shows which patient is anemic, since a high eosinophil share reduces hemoglobin production in the marrow
It adds nothing, since both totals are identical
It identifies the kind of threat, pointing to bacterial infection in A and to parasites or allergy in B
questions.why: The total says only that the immune system is mobilized, while the proportions say which arm is mobilized, and each cell line is tied to a characteristic class of threat. Severity is not read from the differential percentages, and a higher eosinophil share does not mean a sicker patient. Eosinophils have no effect on hemoglobin concentration. The two counts are identical, which is exactly why the differential is the informative test.
questions.answerText: It identifies the kind of threat, pointing to bacterial infection in A and to parasites or allergy in B

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the first phase of hemostasis after a vessel is cut?
options: Vascular spasm
Platelet plug formation
Coagulation
Fibrinolysis
questions.why: Injury makes the vessel wall smooth muscle contract immediately, narrowing the lumen and cutting blood loss before anything else has time to happen. Platelet plug formation comes second, once collagen is exposed and platelets can adhere. Coagulation is third and builds the fibrin mesh that stabilizes the plug. Fibrinolysis is the later removal of the clot, not part of the three phases of stopping bleeding.
questions.answerText: Vascular spasm

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the correct order of the three phases of hemostasis?
options: Vascular spasm, coagulation, platelet plug formation
Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, coagulation
Platelet plug formation, vascular spasm, coagulation
Coagulation, vascular spasm, platelet plug formation
questions.why: Each phase buys time for the next: spasm reduces flow in seconds, the platelet plug seals small breaks in a minute or two, and coagulation reinforces the plug with fibrin over several minutes. Starting with the platelet plug skips the immediate muscular response. Coagulation cannot come first because it needs a platelet surface and exposed tissue factor to get going. Putting coagulation before the platelet plug reverses the scaffold and the reinforcement.
questions.answerText: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation, coagulation

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does von Willebrand factor do?
options: It causes vascular smooth muscle to relax
It dissolves the fibrin strands of the clot once healing is complete
It bridges platelets to collagen exposed in the damaged vessel wall
It converts fibrinogen into fibrin
questions.why: Von Willebrand factor is a large adhesive protein that grips subendothelial collagen at one end and a platelet surface receptor at the other, making adhesion possible under flowing blood. Converting fibrinogen to fibrin is the job of thrombin. Relaxing vascular smooth muscle is the opposite of what injury calls for and describes nitric oxide. Dissolving fibrin is the work of plasmin during fibrinolysis.
questions.answerText: It bridges platelets to collagen exposed in the damaged vessel wall

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does thromboxane A2 released by activated platelets do?
options: It inhibits platelet aggregation and dilates the vessel
It converts prothrombin into thrombin
It cross links fibrin strands
It promotes platelet aggregation and constricts the vessel
questions.why: Thromboxane A2 is made from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase in the platelet and does two pro hemostatic jobs at once, recruiting more platelets and narrowing the vessel. Inhibiting aggregation and dilating the vessel describes prostacyclin, the endothelial counterpart that keeps the plug from spreading. Converting prothrombin to thrombin is done by factor Xa in the common pathway. Cross linking fibrin is the job of factor XIII.
questions.answerText: It promotes platelet aggregation and constricts the vessel

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Platelets are fragments shed from which marrow cell?
options: The megakaryocyte
The reticulocyte
The monocyte
The myeloblast
questions.why: Megakaryocytes are enormous multilobed marrow cells whose cytoplasm pinches off into thousands of anucleate platelets. A reticulocyte is a young red cell. A monocyte is a leukocyte that becomes a macrophage. A myeloblast is the granulocyte precursor and gives rise to neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
questions.answerText: The megakaryocyte

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal platelet count in an adult?
options: About 15,000 to 40,000 per microliter
About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter
About 4,500 to 11,000 per microliter
About 4.5 to 5.5 million per microliter
questions.why: Platelets are far more numerous than white cells but far fewer than red cells, and counts below about 50,000 begin to threaten hemostasis. The 4,500 to 11,000 range is the total leukocyte count. The millions per microliter range is the erythrocyte count. A count of 15,000 to 40,000 would be severe thrombocytopenia with a real risk of spontaneous bleeding.
questions.answerText: About 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which substance released from platelet granules recruits additional platelets to the growing plug?
options: Nitric oxide
Plasminogen
ADP
Prostacyclin
questions.why: Platelets release ADP from dense granules, and it activates passing platelets so they in turn release more, a positive feedback loop that builds the plug quickly. Prostacyclin comes from intact endothelium and inhibits aggregation. Nitric oxide also comes from endothelium and both dilates the vessel and discourages platelet adhesion. Plasminogen is the inactive precursor of the enzyme that later dissolves the clot.
questions.answerText: ADP

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does intact endothelium release to keep platelets from sticking where there is no injury?
options: Thromboxane A2 and ADP
Von Willebrand factor and collagen
Thrombin and fibrinogen
Prostacyclin and nitric oxide
questions.why: Healthy endothelium continuously produces these two inhibitors, so platelets glide past undamaged wall and the plug stays confined to the injury. Thromboxane A2 and ADP are the platelet derived signals that do the opposite, promoting aggregation. Von Willebrand factor and collagen are adhesive surfaces exposed by injury, not inhibitors. Thrombin and fibrinogen drive the coagulation phase.
questions.answerText: Prostacyclin and nitric oxide

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient inherits a deficiency of von Willebrand factor. Predict the effect on hemostasis.
options: Platelet adhesion to collagen fails, so the plug forms poorly and bleeding time is prolonged
Platelet count falls well below normal, so there are too few platelets left to form a plug at all
Fibrin cannot be cross linked, so the clot dissolves as soon as it forms
Vascular spasm fails, so the vessel cannot narrow after injury
questions.why: Without the bridging protein, platelets cannot grab exposed collagen against the shear of flowing blood, so the very first step of plug formation is defective even though the platelets themselves are normal. The platelet count is typically normal in this disorder, which is the clue that separates it from thrombocytopenia. Cross linking is factor XIII work and is unaffected. Vascular spasm depends on smooth muscle and does not require von Willebrand factor.
questions.answerText: Platelet adhesion to collagen fails, so the plug forms poorly and bleeding time is prolonged

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase in platelets. Predict the effect on hemostasis.
options: More von Willebrand factor is made, so adhesion increases
Less thromboxane A2 is made, so platelet aggregation is reduced and bleeding time lengthens
Less thrombin is made, so fibrin formation is reduced
Fewer platelets are produced in the marrow, so the circulating platelet count falls steadily
questions.why: Cyclooxygenase is the enzyme that makes thromboxane A2 from arachidonic acid, so blocking it removes one of the main recruitment signals and the plug builds more slowly. Thrombin generation belongs to the coagulation cascade and is not affected by aspirin, which is why prothrombin time stays normal. Aspirin acts on platelet function, not on marrow production, so the count is unchanged. Von Willebrand factor synthesis is endothelial and is not increased by aspirin.
questions.answerText: Less thromboxane A2 is made, so platelet aggregation is reduced and bleeding time lengthens

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is platelet plug formation described as a positive feedback process?
options: Thrombin destroys platelets, which limits the size of the plug
Each platelet divides once it adheres, doubling the number present
Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2, which activate still more platelets
The plug releases prostacyclin, which recruits still more platelets until the vessel is fully sealed
questions.why: The output of the process amplifies its own input, which is the definition of positive feedback and is why a plug forms explosively at the injury site. Prostacyclin does the opposite, inhibiting aggregation, and it comes from endothelium rather than the plug. Thrombin actually activates platelets rather than destroying them. Platelets are anucleate cell fragments and cannot divide.
questions.answerText: Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2, which activate still more platelets

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient's platelet count is 20,000 per microliter. What clinical sign would you expect?
options: Widespread clotting in small vessels, because fewer platelets clot faster
Prolonged vascular spasm, because platelets normally inhibit smooth muscle
No abnormality, because coagulation factors compensate fully
Pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, because tiny vessel breaks are not sealed
questions.why: Everyday minor capillary damage is normally patched by platelets alone, so when they are scarce the small leaks show up as petechiae and easy bruising. Fewer platelets cannot cause more clotting. Platelets promote vasoconstriction through thromboxane and serotonin, so losing them does not prolong spasm. Coagulation factors need a platelet surface to work efficiently and cannot substitute for the plug.
questions.answerText: Pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, because tiny vessel breaks are not sealed

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What exposed material in the vessel wall triggers platelet adhesion?
options: Subendothelial collagen
Prostacyclin
Fibrin
Elastin in the tunica media
questions.why: Endothelium normally hides the collagen underneath it, so a break uncovers a surface that von Willebrand factor and platelet receptors bind avidly, marking the exact site of injury. Prostacyclin is an endothelial inhibitor of adhesion, the opposite signal. Fibrin appears later, after coagulation has been triggered, so it is a consequence and not the trigger. Elastin gives the vessel recoil but is not the adhesion signal.
questions.answerText: Subendothelial collagen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: How does vascular spasm reduce blood loss?
options: Systemic blood pressure falls throughout the body, so much less blood reaches the wound
Smooth muscle contraction narrows the lumen, lowering flow through the injured segment
The endothelium secretes fibrin that plugs the tear directly
Blood viscosity rises sharply so flow slows
questions.why: Narrowing the vessel raises resistance locally, and because flow falls steeply as radius shrinks, even a modest constriction cuts loss substantially and gives platelets a slower stream to work in. Endothelium does not secrete fibrin; fibrin comes from plasma fibrinogen acted on by thrombin. Viscosity does not change appreciably in the seconds after injury. A systemic pressure drop would be a sign of serious blood loss rather than a local protective mechanism.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle contraction narrows the lumen, lowering flow through the injured segment

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is a platelet plug alone insufficient to stop bleeding from a larger vessel?
options: It dissolves immediately because plasmin is always active
It cannot form at all when flow velocity is high
It is loose and unreinforced, so it needs a fibrin mesh to withstand the pressure
It contains no platelets capable of adhering to the exposed collagen of a large vessel
questions.why: The plug is an aggregate of sticky cell fragments and can be washed away by the higher pressure and shear in a larger vessel until fibrin strands lock it in place, which is exactly why the third phase exists. The same adhesion machinery works in vessels of all sizes. Plasmin is generated locally and gradually rather than being constantly active enough to strip fresh plugs. Plugs do form under high shear; von Willebrand factor is specifically adapted for that condition.
questions.answerText: It is loose and unreinforced, so it needs a fibrin mesh to withstand the pressure

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient taking daily aspirin cuts a finger and it oozes for much longer than usual, but a laboratory test of the coagulation cascade is normal. Trace the mechanism.
options: Vitamin K is blocked, prothrombin falls, fibrin generation falls, and the platelet phase is left untouched
Von Willebrand factor is destroyed, adhesion fails, and the cascade is also impaired
Platelet production in the marrow is suppressed, so the count falls and the cascade slows
Cyclooxygenase is blocked, thromboxane A2 falls, platelet recruitment falls, and the plug forms slowly
questions.why: Aspirin acts only on the platelet arm, so the phase that seals small cuts is impaired while the enzymes that make fibrin work normally, which is why the cascade test comes back normal. Blocking vitamin K describes warfarin and would prolong the cascade test, contradicting the finding. Aspirin does not affect von Willebrand factor, and the cascade is specifically spared here. Aspirin does not suppress marrow production, so the platelet count is normal.
questions.answerText: Cyclooxygenase is blocked, thromboxane A2 falls, platelet recruitment falls, and the plug forms slowly

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with von Willebrand disease has a normal platelet count but prolonged bleeding after dental work, and a mildly prolonged cascade test as well. Explain both findings.
options: Adhesion fails because the bridging protein is missing, and factor VIII is less stable without it
Platelets are destroyed in the spleen, and the cascade slows because platelets are the source of all clotting factors
Fibrinogen is absent, so both the plug and the fibrin mesh fail
Vitamin K is deficient, so adhesion and the cascade both fail
questions.why: Von Willebrand factor has two jobs, gluing platelets to collagen and chaperoning factor VIII in the plasma, so a deficiency shows up in both the platelet phase and, more mildly, the intrinsic cascade. Splenic destruction would lower the platelet count, which is stated to be normal. Absent fibrinogen would cause a far more severe cascade defect and would not spare the count either. Vitamin K deficiency affects the cascade only and has no effect on platelet adhesion.
questions.answerText: Adhesion fails because the bridging protein is missing, and factor VIII is less stable without it

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Patient A has a platelet count of 15,000 per microliter. Patient B has normal platelets but a severe clotting factor deficiency. How do their bleeding patterns differ?
options: Neither bleeds abnormally, because vascular spasm compensates
Patient A shows petechiae and mucosal oozing, while patient B shows deep joint bleeding
Patient A shows deep bleeding into joints and muscles, while patient B shows petechiae and oozing
Both show identical patterns, since both phases end in the same clot
questions.why: Platelets patch the constant small capillary breaks in skin and mucosa, so losing them gives many tiny surface bleeds, while fibrin holds together the larger clots needed in deep tissue, so losing factors gives fewer but larger and deeper hemorrhages. The pattern is not reversed; joint bleeding is the hallmark of factor deficiency such as hemophilia. The two phases do different jobs, so the patterns differ. Vascular spasm lasts only seconds to minutes and cannot compensate for either defect.
questions.answerText: Patient A shows petechiae and mucosal oozing, while patient B shows deep joint bleeding

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Put the events after a small skin cut in the correct order: fibrin mesh traps cells, platelets adhere to collagen through von Willebrand factor, smooth muscle contracts, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets.
options: Fibrin mesh traps cells, smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
Smooth muscle contracts, fibrin mesh traps cells, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
Smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets, fibrin mesh traps cells
Platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, smooth muscle contracts, fibrin mesh traps cells, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets
questions.why: The sequence follows the three phases: an immediate muscular response, then adhesion, then amplification that builds the plug, and finally the fibrin reinforcement that turns the plug into a clot. Adhesion cannot precede the spasm, which begins within seconds of injury. Fibrin cannot come first, because coagulation requires the platelet surface and exposed tissue factor. Putting fibrin before adhesion places the reinforcement before the structure it reinforces.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle contracts, platelets adhere through von Willebrand factor, ADP and thromboxane recruit more platelets, fibrin mesh traps cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What initiates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation?
options: Contact of factor XII with the collagen exposed in the injured vessel wall
Thrombin acting on fibrinogen
Calcium binding to platelet membranes
Tissue factor released from damaged tissue outside the vessel
questions.why: Tissue factor, also called factor III, is a membrane protein of cells outside the bloodstream, so it meets blood only when tissue is injured, and it activates factor VII to start the fast pathway. Contact activation of factor XII starts the intrinsic pathway instead. Thrombin acting on fibrinogen is the end of the common pathway, not the beginning. Calcium is required at several steps but is not the initiating signal.
questions.answerText: Tissue factor released from damaged tissue outside the vessel

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What initiates the intrinsic pathway of coagulation?
options: Contact of factor XII with a negatively charged surface such as exposed collagen
Release of tissue factor from injured cells in the tissues just outside the vessel
Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin
Cross linking of fibrin by factor XIII
questions.why: The intrinsic pathway uses only components already present in blood, and it begins when factor XII contacts a charged surface such as collagen or glass, which is why blood clots in a plain glass tube. Tissue factor starts the extrinsic pathway, which requires something from outside the blood. Prothrombin conversion is a common pathway step downstream of both. Cross linking is the last step of all, after fibrin has already formed.
questions.answerText: Contact of factor XII with a negatively charged surface such as exposed collagen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: At which factor do the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge?
options: Factor XIII
Factor X
Factor VII
Factor XII
questions.why: Both pathways end by activating factor X, and from there a single common pathway runs to thrombin and fibrin. Factor VII belongs only to the extrinsic pathway. Factor XII belongs only to the intrinsic pathway. Factor XIII acts after fibrin has formed and is the final stabilizing step rather than the convergence point.
questions.answerText: Factor X

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What reaction does thrombin catalyze?
options: It converts plasminogen into plasmin
It converts factor X into tissue factor
It converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers
It converts prothrombin into fibrinogen in the plasma
questions.why: Thrombin is a protease that clips fibrinogen so the pieces polymerize into insoluble strands, which is the defining event of clot formation. Prothrombin is thrombin's own precursor, and fibrinogen is a separate protein made by the liver. Converting plasminogen to plasmin is done by tissue plasminogen activator during clot removal. Factor X is activated to Xa upstream of thrombin and is never converted into tissue factor.
questions.answerText: It converts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin monomers

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which clotting factor is prothrombin?
options: Factor I
Factor III
Factor X
Factor II
questions.why: Prothrombin is factor II, the circulating precursor that factor Xa cleaves into active thrombin. Factor I is fibrinogen, the substrate that thrombin acts on. Factor III is tissue factor, the trigger of the extrinsic pathway. Factor X is the convergence point whose active form generates thrombin.
questions.answerText: Factor II

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What role does calcium play in coagulation?
options: It is required as a cofactor at several steps of both pathways
It is the substrate that thrombin converts into fibrin
It dissolves the clot once healing is complete
It is the surface receptor that binds tissue factor
questions.why: Calcium, listed as factor IV, tethers vitamin K dependent factors to phospholipid surfaces so the reactions can proceed, which is why removing calcium from a blood sample prevents clotting. Fibrinogen, not calcium, is thrombin's substrate. Clot dissolution is performed by plasmin. Tissue factor is itself a membrane protein and does not need a calcium receptor to be recognized.
questions.answerText: It is required as a cofactor at several steps of both pathways

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which clotting factors require vitamin K for their synthesis in the liver?
options: Factors V, VI, VIII, and XI
Factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
Factors III, IV, XI, and XII
questions.why: Vitamin K is the cofactor for the enzyme that adds calcium binding sites to these four factors, plus the regulatory proteins C and S, so a deficiency cripples both pathways at once. Factor I is fibrinogen and factor XIII is the cross linker, and neither is vitamin K dependent. Factor III is tissue factor and factor IV is calcium, neither of which is synthesized as a vitamin K dependent protein. Factors V, VIII and XI are made in the liver but do not require vitamin K.
questions.answerText: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does factor XIII do?
options: It activates factor X in the common pathway
It digests fibrin during clot removal
It cross links fibrin strands to stabilize the clot
It converts prothrombin into thrombin
questions.why: Fibrin monomers first polymerize into a fragile mesh, and factor XIIIa forms covalent bonds between them so the clot resists mechanical stress and premature dissolution. Prothrombin conversion is carried out by factor Xa with factor V as cofactor. Factor X is activated by the ends of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. Digesting fibrin is the work of plasmin, which acts against factor XIII's product.
questions.answerText: It cross links fibrin strands to stabilize the clot

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which pathway generates fibrin faster after a traumatic injury, and why?
options: The intrinsic pathway, because it needs no external trigger
The extrinsic pathway, because it does not require calcium
The intrinsic pathway, because factor XII is the most abundant factor
The extrinsic pathway, because it takes fewer steps to reach factor X
questions.why: Tissue factor plus factor VII activates factor X almost directly, so fibrin appears in about fifteen seconds, while the intrinsic pathway needs a longer chain of activations and takes several minutes. Needing no external trigger does not make a pathway faster; it makes it slower here because more steps are involved. Both pathways require calcium. Abundance of a factor does not determine the speed of the sequence.
questions.answerText: The extrinsic pathway, because it takes fewer steps to reach factor X

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A blood sample is collected in a tube containing citrate, which binds calcium. Why does the sample not clot?
options: Calcium is required as a cofactor at multiple steps, so the cascade cannot proceed
Citrate destroys fibrinogen so there is no substrate for thrombin
Citrate blocks vitamin K, so no factors are synthesized in the tube
Citrate inactivates platelets, and platelets are the only source of clotting factors
questions.why: Chelating calcium removes the ion that anchors several factors to phospholipid surfaces, so both pathways stall, and adding calcium back lets the sample clot. Fibrinogen remains intact in a citrated tube, which is why fibrinogen can be measured from it. Vitamin K acts during synthesis in the liver, and no synthesis is happening in a collection tube. Platelets are affected by the lack of calcium too, but clotting factors are plasma proteins made by the liver, not by platelets.
questions.answerText: Calcium is required as a cofactor at multiple steps, so the cascade cannot proceed

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has a vitamin K deficiency from prolonged antibiotic use and poor diet. Predict the effect on coagulation.
options: Coagulation speeds up, because vitamin K normally inhibits the cascade
Both pathways slow, because four factors including prothrombin are made in nonfunctional form
Only the intrinsic pathway slows, because vitamin K acts on factor XII
Only fibrin cross linking fails, because vitamin K is required for the activity of factor XIII
questions.why: Factors II, VII, IX and X span the extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways, so a vitamin K shortage lengthens both routes to fibrin. Factor XII is not vitamin K dependent, so the effect is not limited to the intrinsic side. Factor XIII does not require vitamin K either. Vitamin K enables rather than inhibits factor synthesis, so its absence slows clotting rather than speeding it.
questions.answerText: Both pathways slow, because four factors including prothrombin are made in nonfunctional form

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Thrombin activates factors V, VIII, and XI in addition to cleaving fibrinogen. What does this accomplish?
options: It converts the intrinsic pathway into the extrinsic pathway
It replaces the need for calcium in the common pathway
It creates positive feedback that accelerates its own production once clotting has begun
It creates negative feedback that shuts the whole cascade down long before fibrin can form
questions.why: Thrombin amplifying the steps that make more thrombin is a classic positive feedback loop and explains why fibrin formation accelerates sharply once it starts. Negative feedback would slow the cascade, which is instead the job of antithrombin and protein C. Thrombin does not convert one pathway into another; the two pathways keep their own triggers. Calcium remains necessary regardless of thrombin's amplifying actions.
questions.answerText: It creates positive feedback that accelerates its own production once clotting has begun

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with advanced liver disease bleeds easily. What is the mechanism?
options: The liver stores platelets, so the platelet count falls to zero
The liver produces calcium for the cascade, so calcium falls
The liver secretes plasmin, so clots dissolve too fast
The liver synthesizes most clotting factors, so factor levels fall
questions.why: Fibrinogen, prothrombin and nearly every other factor are hepatocyte products, so failing liver tissue reduces the supply and the cascade runs short of substrate. The spleen, not the liver, sequesters platelets, and the count falls but not to zero. Plasma calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D, not by liver synthesis. Plasmin is generated from plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator, and the liver actually makes plasminogen rather than secreting active plasmin.
questions.answerText: The liver synthesizes most clotting factors, so factor levels fall

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which laboratory test evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways?
options: The prothrombin time
The activated partial thromboplastin time
The bleeding time
The platelet count
questions.why: Prothrombin time is run by adding tissue factor to plasma, so it measures how fast the extrinsic route reaches fibrin and is the test that responds to warfarin and to factor VII deficiency. The activated partial thromboplastin time uses a contact activator and tests the intrinsic and common pathways instead. Bleeding time assesses platelet function rather than the cascade. The platelet count is a number of cells and says nothing about factor activity.
questions.answerText: The prothrombin time

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of factor VIII. Which pathway is affected and what happens to the laboratory tests?
options: Neither pathway, so both tests are normal and only bleeding time is prolonged
The intrinsic pathway, so the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged while the prothrombin time is normal
The extrinsic pathway, so the prothrombin time is prolonged while the partial thromboplastin time is normal
The common pathway, so both tests are prolonged equally
questions.why: Factor VIII is the cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic route, so only the test that runs through that route is prolonged, and the pattern of one abnormal test localizes the defect. The extrinsic pathway does not use factor VIII, so prothrombin time is spared. A common pathway defect such as low factor X or prothrombin would prolong both. Bleeding time reflects platelet function, which is normal in hemophilia.
questions.answerText: The intrinsic pathway, so the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged while the prothrombin time is normal

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has a prolonged prothrombin time with a normal partial thromboplastin time. Where is the defect?
options: In the common pathway, most likely factor X
In platelet function, most likely von Willebrand factor
In the extrinsic pathway, most likely factor VII
In the intrinsic pathway, most likely factor VIII
questions.why: Only one test is abnormal, so the defect must lie in a factor unique to that pathway, and factor VII is the only factor tested exclusively by prothrombin time. A factor VIII problem would prolong the partial thromboplastin time instead, since factor VIII is unique to the intrinsic route. A common pathway defect would prolong both tests, because both routes pass through it. Platelet defects do not lengthen either cascade test.
questions.answerText: In the extrinsic pathway, most likely factor VII

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Newborns are given vitamin K at birth. Explain the physiology behind this.
options: Newborns have no platelets until the second week, so vitamin K substitutes for them
Newborn liver cannot make fibrinogen, and vitamin K is converted into fibrinogen
Vitamin K is needed to break down fetal hemoglobin, which otherwise blocks the clotting cascade completely
Vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly and the newborn gut is not yet colonized by bacteria that make it
questions.why: Two supply routes are missing at once, maternal transfer and gut bacterial synthesis, so the four vitamin K dependent factors are made in inactive form and bleeding risk is real until feeding establishes the gut flora. Newborns do have normal platelet counts, and vitamin K cannot substitute for platelets in any case. Fibrinogen is not made from vitamin K and is not vitamin K dependent. Fetal hemoglobin has no role in coagulation.
questions.answerText: Vitamin K crosses the placenta poorly and the newborn gut is not yet colonized by bacteria that make it

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Plasma from a citrated tube is warmed and calcium is added back. Predict what happens and why.
options: It clots, because the only missing element was calcium and all the factors are still present
It does not clot, because citrate permanently destroys the clotting factors
It does not clot, because plasma has no platelets and platelets make the factors
It clots only if vitamin K is also added, because vitamin K acts directly in the cascade reactions
questions.why: Citrate works by sequestering calcium, a reversible chemical effect, so restoring calcium restores the surface binding steps and the cascade proceeds, which is the basis of standard coagulation testing. Citrate does not damage the protein factors themselves. Clotting factors are plasma proteins made by the liver, so platelet free plasma still clots, though less efficiently without a platelet surface. Vitamin K acts during hepatic synthesis, not in the reaction tube.
questions.answerText: It clots, because the only missing element was calcium and all the factors are still present

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Trace the extrinsic pathway from injury to a stabilized clot in the correct order.
options: Prothrombin activates tissue factor, tissue factor activates factor X, factor Xa converts fibrin to fibrinogen, and factor XIIIa dissolves the finished clot
Tissue factor activates factor VII, factor VIIa activates factor X, factor Xa makes thrombin, thrombin makes fibrin, factor XIIIa cross links it
Factor XII activates factor VII, factor VIIa converts fibrinogen to thrombin, thrombin activates factor X, factor X cross links fibrin
Tissue factor converts fibrinogen to fibrin, fibrin activates factor X, factor Xa activates thrombin, thrombin cross links the clot
questions.why: The order follows the logic of a cascade: an external trigger, a short extrinsic segment, convergence at factor X, thrombin generation, fibrin formation, and finally stabilization. Factor XII belongs to the intrinsic pathway and does not activate factor VII. Tissue factor cannot act on fibrinogen directly, since only thrombin does that. The last option reverses several steps, including turning fibrin back into fibrinogen and having factor XIII dissolve rather than stabilize the clot.
questions.answerText: Tissue factor activates factor VII, factor VIIa activates factor X, factor Xa makes thrombin, thrombin makes fibrin, factor XIIIa cross links it

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which enzyme digests the fibrin mesh of a clot?
options: Factor XIIIa
Carbonic anhydrase
Plasmin
Thrombin
questions.why: Plasmin is a protease that cleaves fibrin into soluble fragments, gradually dismantling the clot as the vessel heals. Thrombin does the opposite, generating fibrin from fibrinogen. Factor XIIIa strengthens fibrin by cross linking it. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reaction between carbon dioxide and water and has no role in clotting.
questions.answerText: Plasmin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the inactive precursor of plasmin?
options: Prothrombin
Fibrinogen
Prekallikrein
Plasminogen
questions.why: Plasminogen circulates inactive and is trapped inside the clot as it forms, so the tool for taking the clot apart is built into the clot itself. Prothrombin is the precursor of thrombin, which builds the clot. Fibrinogen is the precursor of fibrin, the clot's structural protein. Prekallikrein participates in contact activation of the intrinsic pathway rather than in fibrinolysis.
questions.answerText: Plasminogen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What converts plasminogen into plasmin?
options: Tissue plasminogen activator
Thrombin acting alone
Factor XII acting alone
Antithrombin III bound to heparin
questions.why: Endothelial cells release tissue plasminogen activator, which cleaves plasminogen bound within the clot, keeping fibrinolysis local. Thrombin contributes indirectly to fibrinolysis but its main action is making fibrin, not plasmin. Factor XII has a minor role in activating the system but is not the principal activator. Antithrombin III inactivates thrombin and other proteases rather than generating plasmin.
questions.answerText: Tissue plasminogen activator

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does antithrombin III do?
options: It carries factor VIII through the plasma
It inactivates thrombin and several other activated clotting factors
It converts plasminogen into plasmin
It cross links the fibrin strands to stabilize and harden the finished clot
questions.why: Antithrombin III binds and neutralizes thrombin and factors such as Xa, keeping coagulation from spreading beyond the injury, and heparin accelerates its action dramatically. Generating plasmin is the job of tissue plasminogen activator. Cross linking fibrin is done by factor XIIIa. Carrying factor VIII is one of the functions of von Willebrand factor.
questions.answerText: It inactivates thrombin and several other activated clotting factors

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which cells are the natural source of heparin in the body?
options: Hepatocytes
Endothelial cells only
Basophils and mast cells
Platelets
questions.why: Heparin is stored in the granules of basophils and their tissue counterparts, mast cells, and released during inflammation to discourage clotting locally. Platelets release ADP, serotonin and thromboxane, which promote clotting rather than prevent it. The liver makes clotting factors and plasminogen, not heparin. Endothelium contributes heparan sulfate and other anticoagulant surfaces, but it is not the source usually named for heparin itself.
questions.answerText: Basophils and mast cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: How does warfarin reduce clotting?
options: It binds the calcium in the plasma so that the cascade reactions cannot proceed at all
It blocks cyclooxygenase so platelets cannot aggregate
It activates plasmin so existing clots are dissolved
It blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, and X are nonfunctional
questions.why: Warfarin inhibits the enzyme that regenerates active vitamin K, so newly synthesized factors lack their calcium binding sites and cannot work, which is why the effect takes days to appear. Binding calcium in plasma is how citrate works in a test tube, and it would be lethal in the body. Blocking cyclooxygenase describes aspirin, which acts on platelets rather than factors. Warfarin does not dissolve clots already present; that is the action of tissue plasminogen activator.
questions.answerText: It blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX, and X are nonfunctional

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is D-dimer?
options: A fibrin degradation fragment produced when plasmin digests a cross linked clot
The activated form of fibrinogen produced just before it polymerizes into strands
The complex of heparin and antithrombin III
The storage form of vitamin K in the liver
questions.why: Because it comes only from fibrin that was already cross linked by factor XIII, a raised D-dimer means a clot formed somewhere and is being broken down. Fibrinogen before polymerization is simply fibrinogen. The heparin and antithrombin complex is an anticoagulant mechanism and is not the measured fragment. Vitamin K is stored in the liver as the vitamin itself, unrelated to fibrin fragments.
questions.answerText: A fibrin degradation fragment produced when plasmin digests a cross linked clot

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What do activated protein C and protein S do?
options: They cross link fibrin to stabilize the clot
They inactivate factors V and VIII, slowing the cascade
They activate factors V and VIII, speeding the cascade
They convert plasminogen to plasmin
questions.why: Protein C, helped by protein S, degrades two key cofactors, which keeps thrombin generation confined to the site of injury. Activating those factors is what thrombin does as part of positive feedback, the opposite role. Plasminogen activation is the job of tissue plasminogen activator. Cross linking is factor XIIIa's function.
questions.answerText: They inactivate factors V and VIII, slowing the cascade

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient starts warfarin today. Why does the anticoagulant effect take two to three days to appear?
options: Warfarin acts only after existing clots have dissolved
Warfarin is stored in fat and must saturate the tissues first
Factors already in the circulation stay active until they are cleared and replaced
Warfarin must first be converted to its active form by intestinal bacteria in the gut
questions.why: Blocking vitamin K recycling stops the production line but does nothing to the stock already in the plasma, so clotting stays near normal until those factors are degraded over their natural half lives. Warfarin is absorbed and active without bacterial conversion. Existing clots are irrelevant to the timing, since warfarin does not act on them at all. Tissue saturation is not the reason for the delay.
questions.answerText: Factors already in the circulation stay active until they are cleared and replaced

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why does heparin prevent clotting in a test tube while warfarin does not?
options: Heparin binds calcium in the sample, while warfarin binds fibrinogen
Heparin destroys platelets in the tube, while warfarin destroys red cells
Heparin is a large protein and warfarin is a simple ion, so only heparin can work outside the body
Heparin acts directly on circulating antithrombin III, while warfarin acts on liver synthesis
questions.why: Heparin needs only plasma components that are already in the tube, so it works immediately anywhere, while warfarin needs a functioning liver making new factors, which a test tube does not have. Calcium binding is how citrate and EDTA work, not heparin. Neither drug works by destroying cells. Heparin is a polysaccharide rather than a protein, and warfarin is a small organic molecule rather than an ion.
questions.answerText: Heparin acts directly on circulating antithrombin III, while warfarin acts on liver synthesis

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient takes daily low dose aspirin. Predict the pattern of laboratory results.
options: Bleeding time is prolonged while both cascade tests stay entirely normal
Prothrombin time is prolonged while bleeding time stays normal
Both cascade tests are prolonged while the bleeding time stays entirely normal
All three tests are prolonged equally
questions.why: Aspirin blocks thromboxane synthesis in platelets, so the platelet phase is impaired while the plasma cascade is untouched, and only the test that measures platelet function changes. A prolonged prothrombin time with normal bleeding time is the warfarin pattern. Both cascade tests prolonged would indicate a common pathway or vitamin K problem. Nothing about aspirin affects all three tests.
questions.answerText: Bleeding time is prolonged while both cascade tests stay entirely normal

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Tissue plasminogen activator is given to a patient with a fresh clot. How does its action differ from that of heparin?
options: Neither affects existing clots; both act only on new fibrin
It dissolves fibrin already formed, while heparin only prevents further clot growth
It prevents the formation of new clots, while heparin dissolves clots already present
Both dissolve existing clots, but heparin acts faster
questions.why: Tissue plasminogen activator generates plasmin, which cuts fibrin apart, so it is a thrombolytic, whereas heparin accelerates antithrombin and simply stops more thrombin from acting. The roles are not reversed; heparin has no fibrin digesting ability. Heparin does not dissolve clots at any speed. Tissue plasminogen activator definitely affects existing fibrin, which is the point of giving it.
questions.answerText: It dissolves fibrin already formed, while heparin only prevents further clot growth

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has a markedly elevated D-dimer. What does this indicate?
options: Platelet count is elevated
Vitamin K stores are depleted
A clot has formed somewhere and plasmin is breaking it down
The patient cannot form clots at all, anywhere in the circulation
questions.why: D-dimer is released only when cross linked fibrin is digested, so its presence proves both that clotting occurred and that fibrinolysis is under way. An inability to clot would produce no fibrin and therefore no degradation fragments. Platelet count is measured separately and is not reflected in this fragment. Vitamin K status is assessed through the prothrombin time, not through fibrin fragments.
questions.answerText: A clot has formed somewhere and plasmin is breaking it down

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient on warfarin has excessive bleeding. What is the physiological rationale for giving vitamin K?
options: Vitamin K binds warfarin in the plasma and inactivates it
Vitamin K directly cross links the fibrin strands at each bleeding site in the body
Vitamin K stimulates the marrow to make more platelets
Supplying vitamin K lets the liver make functional factors II, VII, IX, and X again
questions.why: Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so flooding the system with the vitamin lets the liver resume adding calcium binding sites to those four factors, though the effect takes hours because new protein must be synthesized. Vitamin K does not chemically neutralize warfarin in the plasma. Cross linking fibrin is factor XIIIa's job and requires no vitamin K. Platelet production is driven by thrombopoietin, not by vitamin K.
questions.answerText: Supplying vitamin K lets the liver make functional factors II, VII, IX, and X again

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient stabilized on warfarin greatly increases their intake of leafy green vegetables, which are rich in vitamin K. Predict the effect on clotting.
options: Clotting speeds up, because more vitamin K competes with the drug at the same enzyme
Clotting slows further, because vitamin K adds to the anticoagulant effect
Clotting is unchanged, because dietary vitamin K is not absorbed
Clotting speeds up, because the extra vitamin K directly activates thrombin in the plasma
questions.why: Warfarin and vitamin K work against each other at the same enzyme, so raising vitamin K supply partly overcomes the block and the liver produces more working factors, shortening clotting times. Vitamin K opposes warfarin rather than adding to it. Dietary vitamin K is absorbed with fats and does reach the liver. The vitamin acts during hepatic synthesis, not by activating thrombin already in the plasma.
questions.answerText: Clotting speeds up, because more vitamin K competes with the drug at the same enzyme

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A hospitalized patient is receiving both heparin and aspirin. Which laboratory findings would you expect?
options: A prolonged bleeding time from the heparin and a prolonged prothrombin time from the aspirin
A prolonged partial thromboplastin time from the heparin and a prolonged bleeding time from the aspirin
A prolonged prothrombin time from the heparin and a normal bleeding time despite the aspirin
A normal partial thromboplastin time, since heparin acts only on platelets
questions.why: The two drugs act on different arms of hemostasis, so each shows up in the test that examines its arm: heparin boosts antithrombin and slows the intrinsic and common pathways, while aspirin blocks thromboxane and slows platelet plug formation. Heparin's main effect is on the partial thromboplastin time rather than the prothrombin time. Heparin acts on plasma proteases, not on platelets, so it certainly changes a cascade test. The last option assigns each drug the other's effect.
questions.answerText: A prolonged partial thromboplastin time from the heparin and a prolonged bleeding time from the aspirin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient with a deep vein clot is given tissue plasminogen activator. Trace what happens in the clot.
options: Factor XIII is activated, fibrin is cross linked further, and the clot hardens
Vitamin K is blocked, the new factors are nonfunctional, and the existing clot slowly shrinks away
Plasminogen in the clot becomes plasmin, plasmin digests fibrin, and D-dimer appears in the blood
Thrombin is inactivated, fibrinogen levels rise, and no fragments are released
questions.why: The drug activates the enzyme system already built into the clot, and the debris from cross linked fibrin is what the D-dimer test detects, so the sequence has a measurable endpoint. Inactivating thrombin describes heparin's action and would not release fibrin fragments. Activating factor XIII would strengthen the clot rather than remove it. Blocking vitamin K describes warfarin and does not dismantle fibrin that already exists.
questions.answerText: Plasminogen in the clot becomes plasmin, plasmin digests fibrin, and D-dimer appears in the blood

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient has an inherited deficiency of antithrombin III. Predict the clotting tendency and the response to heparin.
options: An increased tendency to bleed, and an exaggerated response to heparin
An increased tendency to form clots, and a greatly exaggerated response to heparin treatment
No change in clotting, but a reduced response to warfarin
An increased tendency to form clots, and a reduced response to heparin
questions.why: Antithrombin III is the main brake on thrombin, so having too little leaves clotting unchecked, and because heparin acts by accelerating that same brake, the drug has little to accelerate. The tendency is toward clotting rather than bleeding, since the missing protein is an anticoagulant. The response to heparin is reduced rather than exaggerated, for the same mechanistic reason. Clotting is definitely changed, and warfarin acts through vitamin K rather than through antithrombin III.
questions.answerText: An increased tendency to form clots, and a reduced response to heparin

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A person with type A blood has which antigen on their erythrocytes and which antibody in their plasma?
options: A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
A antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
No antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
questions.why: The rule is that you carry antibodies against the ABO antigen you lack, so a type A person makes anti-B and tolerates A. Having anti-A along with A antigen would mean attacking your own cells, which does not happen in a healthy person. B antigen with anti-A describes type B, not type A. No antigen with anti-B alone matches no ABO type, since a person lacking both antigens has both antibodies.
questions.answerText: A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A person with type B blood has which antigen and which antibody?
options: B antigen on the cells and no ABO antibody
B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma
B antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
A antigen on the cells and anti-B antibody in the plasma
questions.why: You make antibodies against the antigen you do not have, so type B carries anti-A. Carrying anti-B with B antigen would mean self attack and does not occur. A antigen with anti-B is the type A pattern. Having no ABO antibody at all is the type AB pattern, which requires both antigens to be present.
questions.answerText: B antigen on the cells and anti-A antibody in the plasma

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A person with type AB blood has which antigens and which antibodies?
options: Neither A nor B antigen, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and both anti-A and anti-B
questions.why: Because a type AB person carries both antigens, they can make antibodies against neither, which is why AB is the universal recipient for ABO purposes. Having both antibodies alongside both antigens would destroy their own cells. Having neither antigen is the type O pattern, not AB. Neither antigen with both antibodies is exactly type O, the opposite of AB.
questions.answerText: Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A person with type O blood has which antigens and which antibodies?
options: Neither A nor B antigen, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Both A and B antigens, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
Both A and B antigens, and neither anti-A nor anti-B
Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies
questions.why: Type O cells carry no A or B antigen, so the plasma is free to contain antibodies against both, which makes type O red cells safe to give but type O plasma the most reactive. Having no antigen and no antibody is not a natural ABO type. Both antigens with both antibodies would mean self destruction. Both antigens with no antibody is type AB, the mirror image of type O.
questions.answerText: Neither A nor B antigen, and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which blood type is the universal red cell donor?
options: Type O negative
Type AB positive
Type A negative
Type O positive
questions.why: O negative cells display neither A nor B antigen nor the D antigen, so there is nothing on their surface for a recipient's antibodies to attack. AB positive is the universal recipient, not the universal donor, because its cells carry every common antigen. A negative cells still carry the A antigen and would be attacked by anti-A. O positive cells are safe for ABO but carry D and can sensitize an Rh negative recipient.
questions.answerText: Type O negative

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which blood type is the universal recipient of red cells?
options: Type O positive
Type AB positive
Type O negative
Type AB negative
questions.why: An AB positive person makes neither anti-A nor anti-B and already has the D antigen, so no common donor red cell carries an antigen their plasma will attack. O negative is the universal donor, the opposite role. AB negative lacks D, so it can still react to Rh positive cells if the person has been sensitized. O positive plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, making it a poor recipient of A, B, or AB cells.
questions.answerText: Type AB positive

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: The naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies are mostly which immunoglobulin class, and what does that mean for the placenta?
options: IgE, which crosses the placenta readily
IgA, which is secreted into the amniotic fluid
IgM, which is too large to cross the placenta
IgG, which crosses the placenta readily
questions.why: ABO antibodies arise without deliberate immunization and are predominantly pentameric IgM, so they stay in the maternal circulation and rarely cause severe fetal disease. IgG is the class that does cross, and anti-D is IgG, which is precisely why Rh incompatibility is the classic cause of hemolytic disease of the newborn. IgE mediates allergy and does not cross the placenta. IgA is the secretory antibody of mucosal surfaces and is not the ABO antibody class.
questions.answerText: IgM, which is too large to cross the placenta

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: When does an Rh negative person develop anti-D antibodies?
options: From birth, in the same way as anti-A and anti-B
Whenever plasma D antigen concentration falls
Only if they also lack both A and B antigens
Only after exposure to Rh positive red cells
questions.why: Anti-D is not naturally occurring; the immune system must first meet the D antigen through transfusion or through fetal cells entering the maternal circulation, and only then does it produce antibody. ABO antibodies are present from infancy without deliberate exposure, which is the key difference between the two systems. There is no plasma D antigen level to sense. ABO type has no bearing on whether a person can become sensitized to D.
questions.answerText: Only after exposure to Rh positive red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Type A red cells are transfused into a type B recipient. What happens and why?
options: Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor A antigens
No reaction, because the donor cells carry no antigen the recipient can attack
Agglutination, because the donor's anti-B antibodies attack the recipient's cells
No reaction, because A and B antigens are compatible with each other
questions.why: A type B recipient carries anti-A, and the incoming cells display A, so the antibodies bridge the donor cells into clumps and hemolysis follows. There certainly is an antigen present, namely A, so the second option misstates the donor cells. The donor's own antibodies are diluted in the recipient's much larger plasma volume and are not the main problem, so the reaction is driven by recipient antibody against donor antigen. A and B are not compatible; each is the target of the other's antibody.
questions.answerText: Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-A antibodies bind the donor A antigens

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Type O red cells are transfused into a type A recipient. What happens and why?
options: No agglutination, because type A recipients have no antibodies
No agglutination, because the donor cells carry neither A nor B antigen
Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-B attacks the donor cells
Agglutination, because type O cells carry both A and B antigens
questions.why: The recipient's anti-B has nothing to bind on a type O cell, since those cells display no A or B antigen, which is what makes O the universal red cell donor. Anti-B is present in the type A recipient, but it needs a B antigen to attack and there is none. Type O cells lack both antigens rather than carrying both. Type A recipients do have an antibody, anti-B, so the last option is wrong about the mechanism even though the outcome is right.
questions.answerText: No agglutination, because the donor cells carry neither A nor B antigen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why can a type AB recipient safely receive red cells of any ABO type?
options: Their plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, which neutralize each other before they can act on donor cells
Their red cells carry the D antigen, which suppresses ABO reactions
Their plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so no antibody can attack the donor cells
Their red cells carry no antigens, so nothing can be recognized
questions.why: Compatibility in a red cell transfusion is decided by what antibodies the recipient has, and an AB person has no ABO antibodies at all, so any donor red cell passes unchallenged. Their cells carry both antigens rather than none; it is the antibody side that makes them universal recipients. They do not have both antibodies, and antibodies against different antigens would not neutralize each other anyway. The D antigen belongs to a separate system and does not suppress ABO reactions.
questions.answerText: Their plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so no antibody can attack the donor cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An Rh negative person with no prior exposure receives Rh positive red cells for the first time. What is the immediate result?
options: Immediate severe agglutination, because anti-D is present from birth
No reaction and no sensitization, because D is not immunogenic
Immediate agglutination, because the donor plasma anti-D attacks the recipient's own cells
Usually no immediate reaction, but the person becomes sensitized and makes anti-D later
questions.why: Anti-D is not naturally present, so the first exposure has nothing to react with, but it primes the immune system and antibody appears afterward, setting up trouble on a later exposure. Anti-D is not present from birth, which is the central difference from the ABO antibodies. The D antigen is strongly immunogenic, so sensitization does occur. An Rh positive donor has no anti-D to give, since a person does not make antibody against their own antigen.
questions.answerText: Usually no immediate reaction, but the person becomes sensitized and makes anti-D later

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A previously sensitized Rh negative patient receives Rh positive red cells. Predict the outcome.
options: The existing anti-D binds the donor cells and causes agglutination and hemolysis
No reaction, because sensitization only affects pregnancy
No reaction, because anti-D disappears from the plasma within a few days of forming
The donor cells lose the D antigen and are tolerated
questions.why: Once anti-D exists, any D positive cell entering the circulation is a target, so the second exposure produces the reaction that the first one did not. Sensitization is not limited to pregnancy; a transfusion can sensitize a person just as fetal cells can. Antibody and memory cells persist for years, so the response does not fade in days. Red cells do not shed their antigens to escape recognition.
questions.answerText: The existing anti-D binds the donor cells and causes agglutination and hemolysis

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient's plasma agglutinates both type A and type B test cells. What is the patient's ABO type?
options: Type B
Type O
Type AB
Type A
questions.why: Agglutinating both means the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, and only a type O person carries both, because they carry neither antigen. Type AB plasma has no ABO antibody and would agglutinate neither. Type A plasma has only anti-B and would agglutinate B cells alone. Type B plasma has only anti-A and would agglutinate A cells alone.
questions.answerText: Type O

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Type B red cells are transfused into a type AB recipient. Predict the outcome.
options: Agglutination, because the donor's anti-A binds the recipient's A antigen
No agglutination, because the donor cells carry no antigen at all
No agglutination, because the recipient has no anti-B to attack the donor B antigen
Agglutination, because the recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigen
questions.why: An AB recipient makes neither ABO antibody, so donor B cells are not recognized and the transfusion is compatible. The recipient does not have anti-B, since they carry the B antigen themselves. The donor plasma anti-A is present in only a small volume in a red cell unit and is not the deciding factor in red cell compatibility. Type B cells do carry an antigen, namely B, so the last option misstates the donor.
questions.answerText: No agglutination, because the recipient has no anti-B to attack the donor B antigen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An Rh negative woman carries an Rh positive fetus. Why is the first such pregnancy usually unaffected while a later one is at risk?
options: Anti-D is present from birth in every Rh negative woman, so the very first Rh positive fetus is attacked most severely
The first fetus is protected because IgM antibodies cross the placenta easily and dilute the response
The second fetus is at risk only if it is Rh negative, since D antigen accumulates over pregnancies
Fetal cells usually enter the maternal circulation at delivery, so anti-D is made only after the first birth
questions.why: The timing is everything: the mother is exposed near the end of the first pregnancy, so her anti-D appears after that fetus is already delivered, and it is the IgG anti-D crossing the placenta in a later Rh positive pregnancy that destroys fetal red cells. Anti-D is never naturally present before exposure, which is why the first pregnancy is generally safe. IgM does not cross the placenta at all, and it would not be protective if it did. Only an Rh positive fetus carries the D antigen, so an Rh negative fetus is not a target.
questions.answerText: Fetal cells usually enter the maternal circulation at delivery, so anti-D is made only after the first birth

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An Rh negative pregnant woman is given anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks and again after delivery. How does this prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn?
options: The injected antibody clears fetal Rh positive cells before the mother is sensitized
It converts the fetus from Rh positive to Rh negative
It blocks the placenta so no maternal antibody can cross
It destroys the mother's existing anti-D antibodies left over from her earlier pregnancies
questions.why: Passive antibody removes the fetal cells from the maternal circulation quickly, so her B lymphocytes never mount a primary response and no memory is established for the next pregnancy.
