Nothing can change the fetal genotype, so conversion is impossible. The placenta is not blocked; IgG transfer continues normally for all other antibodies. The treatment prevents sensitization rather than reversing it, which is why it is useless once a woman has already made her own anti-D.
questions.answerText: The injected antibody clears fetal Rh positive cells before the mother is sensitized

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A trauma patient arrives unconscious with unknown blood type and needs red cells immediately. Why is O negative the safest choice?
options: O negative cells are the only ones that carry the D antigen, which suppresses agglutination
O negative cells lack A, B, and D antigens, so no antibody the recipient could have will find a target
O negative plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B, which protect the recipient's own cells
O negative cells carry all three antigens, so they match any recipient
questions.why: Compatibility depends on whether the recipient's antibodies can bind something on the donor cell, and an O negative cell presents none of the three common antigens, so the reaction cannot start. O negative plasma does contain both antibodies, but that is a hazard rather than a protection, which is why red cells are given with most of the plasma removed. O negative cells lack antigens rather than carrying all of them. O negative means D is absent, so the last option contradicts itself.
questions.answerText: O negative cells lack A, B, and D antigens, so no antibody the recipient could have will find a target

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient types as A negative. Which donor red cell units are safe, and why?
options: AB negative and B negative, because those units lack the A antigen the patient already has
Any negative unit, because Rh negative blood is compatible with every ABO type
A negative and O negative, because the patient has anti-B and could be sensitized to D
A positive and O positive, because the D antigen is harmless in ABO matched blood
questions.why: Two rules run at once: the recipient's anti-B rules out any unit carrying B, and the absence of D means Rh positive cells could sensitize the patient, so only A negative and O negative units satisfy both. Rh positive units are not harmless to an Rh negative recipient, since D is strongly immunogenic. AB negative and B negative units both carry the B antigen that the patient's anti-B will attack. Being Rh negative does not make a unit ABO compatible; a B negative unit still has B antigen.
questions.answerText: A negative and O negative, because the patient has anti-B and could be sensitized to D

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In what units is hematocrit reported?
options: In grams per deciliter
In cells per microliter
In millimeters of packed column
As a percentage of total blood volume
questions.why: Hematocrit is a ratio of the packed red cell column to the whole column, so it is expressed as a percent and has no mass or count units. Grams per deciliter is the unit for hemoglobin concentration. Cells per microliter is the unit for a red cell count. Column length in millimeters is what you measure, but you must divide it by the total length to get the reported value.
questions.answerText: As a percentage of total blood volume

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does the microhematocrit centrifuge do to a blood sample?
options: It separates the components by density, packing red cells at the bottom of the tube
It lyses the red cells so that the hemoglobin they contain can be measured directly in the plasma
It removes the anticoagulant so the sample can clot
It warms the sample so plasma proteins dissolve
questions.why: High speed spinning drives the densest elements, the red cells, to the closed end, with the buffy coat above them and plasma on top, and the relative lengths of those layers give the hematocrit. Lysing cells is what a hemoglobin assay does chemically, not what the centrifuge does. The anticoagulant remains in the sample throughout. Warming is not part of the procedure and plasma proteins are already dissolved.
questions.answerText: It separates the components by density, packing red cells at the bottom of the tube

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is the capillary tube used for a microhematocrit coated with heparin?
options: To bind hemoglobin so it can be measured on the same tube
To prevent the sample from clotting before it can be spun
To lyse the white cells so the buffy coat disappears
To make the red cells denser so they pack faster
questions.why: A clotted sample cannot be separated into layers, so the tube carries an anticoagulant that keeps the cells suspended until centrifugation. Heparin does not lyse white cells, and the buffy coat should still be visible. It does not change red cell density. Hemoglobin is measured by a separate method on a separate portion of sample.
questions.answerText: To prevent the sample from clotting before it can be spun

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Why is one end of the filled capillary tube sealed with clay before spinning?
options: To mark which end contains the plasma
To absorb the plasma so only cells remain
To keep the sample from being thrown out of the tube during centrifugation
To provide the calcium that the red cells need in order to pack down tightly
questions.why: Spinning generates a large outward force, and an unsealed tube would lose sample, giving an inaccurate and messy result. The clay is inert and supplies no reagent to the reaction. Layer identification comes from the visible color boundaries, not from the seal. Nothing is absorbed by the clay; the plasma remains in the tube above the cells.
questions.answerText: To keep the sample from being thrown out of the tube during centrifugation

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In a spun microhematocrit tube, where is the buffy coat and what should you do with it when reading the result?
options: It lies at the sealed end below the red cells, and it is included in the red cell column
It lies at the top of the plasma, and it is included in the total column
It is dissolved in the plasma and cannot be seen
It lies between the packed red cells and the plasma, and it is excluded from the red cell column
questions.why: White cells and platelets are less dense than red cells but denser than plasma, so they form a thin pale band at the interface that is not part of the red cell measurement. Nothing packs below the red cells, which are the densest component. The buffy coat is not at the top, and the total column does include it as part of whole blood. It is visible as a distinct layer, usually about 1 percent of the column.
questions.answerText: It lies between the packed red cells and the plasma, and it is excluded from the red cell column

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for an adult male?
options: About 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL
About 42 to 52 g/dL
About 4.5 to 6.0 g/dL
About 30 to 40 g/dL
questions.why: Hemoglobin concentration in men runs in the mid teens in grams per deciliter, roughly one third of the hematocrit value. The 42 to 52 range is the male hematocrit in percent, not a hemoglobin in g/dL. A value of 4.5 to 6.0 g/dL would be a life threatening anemia. A value of 30 to 40 g/dL is far above anything physiologically possible.
questions.answerText: About 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for an adult female?
options: About 20 to 25 g/dL
About 12.0 to 16.0 g/dL
About 37 to 47 g/dL
About 6.0 to 8.0 g/dL
questions.why: Women run slightly lower than men, with a lower limit around 12 g/dL, below which anemia is diagnosed. The 37 to 47 range is the female hematocrit in percent. A value of 6.0 to 8.0 g/dL would be a severe anemia. A value of 20 to 25 g/dL is above any normal human value and would suggest an error.
questions.answerText: About 12.0 to 16.0 g/dL

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What is the rule of three that links hemoglobin and hematocrit?
options: Hematocrit plus hemoglobin equals 60 in a healthy adult
Hemoglobin equals hematocrit divided by ten
Hematocrit is approximately three times the hemoglobin in g/dL
Hemoglobin is approximately three times the hematocrit
questions.why: A hemoglobin of 15 g/dL corresponds to a hematocrit near 45 percent, so multiplying by three gives a quick internal check on whether two results agree. Reversing the relationship would predict a hemoglobin of 135 from a hematocrit of 45, which is impossible. Adding the two values has no physiological meaning. Dividing by ten would predict a hemoglobin of 4.5 from a hematocrit of 45, far below the normal range.
questions.answerText: Hematocrit is approximately three times the hemoglobin in g/dL

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student measures the packed red cell column as 21 mm and the total column of blood as 50 mm. What is the hematocrit?
options: 21 percent
50 percent
71 percent
42 percent
questions.why: Divide the red cell column by the total column and multiply by 100, so 21 divided by 50 is 0.42, or 42 percent, a normal adult value. Reporting 21 mistakes the raw length for the ratio. Reporting 50 gives the total column length rather than the fraction. Adding the two numbers gives 71 and has no meaning as a ratio.
questions.answerText: 42 percent

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student includes the buffy coat in the packed red cell column when reading the tube. What is the effect on the reported hematocrit?
options: It is slightly falsely high
It is slightly falsely low
It is unaffected
It is falsely high by about half
questions.why: Adding the white cell and platelet layer lengthens the numerator without changing the denominator, so the percentage comes out a point or so above the true value. It cannot be falsely low, since nothing was subtracted. It is not unaffected, because the numerator changed. The buffy coat is only about 1 percent of the column, so the error is small rather than enormous.
questions.answerText: It is slightly falsely high

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A capillary tube is inadequately sealed and some blood escapes during centrifugation, with cells lost preferentially from the packed end. What happens to the reported hematocrit?
options: It cannot be read at all, because the layers will not separate
It reads falsely low, because the red cell column is shortened
It reads falsely high, because plasma is lost first
It is unaffected, because the ratio is preserved
questions.why: Losing packed cells from the sealed end reduces the numerator relative to the total, so the calculated percentage falls below the true value. Plasma is not the fraction lost at the sealed end, so the error does not go upward for that reason. The ratio is not preserved when one component is selectively lost. Separation still occurs; it is the measurement that is wrong.
questions.answerText: It reads falsely low, because the red cell column is shortened

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample is spun for too short a time, leaving plasma trapped among the packed red cells. What happens to the reported hematocrit?
options: It is unaffected, because trapped plasma is part of blood anyway
It reads falsely low, because the buffy coat expands
It reads falsely high, because the red cell column includes trapped plasma
It reads falsely low, because some cells stay suspended in the plasma
questions.why: Incomplete packing leaves fluid between the cells, so the column measured as red cells is longer than the true cell volume and the percentage is overstated. Cells left suspended would also be a problem, but under spinning primarily leaves plasma trapped in a loosely packed column, pushing the value up. Trapped plasma is part of blood but it is not part of the red cell fraction being measured. The buffy coat does not expand with shorter spinning in a way that would lower the reading.
questions.answerText: It reads falsely high, because the red cell column includes trapped plasma

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient's hemoglobin is 10 g/dL. Using the rule of three, what hematocrit would you expect, and how would you interpret it?
options: About 30 percent, which sits comfortably within the normal reference range for an adult female
About 3 percent, which is incompatible with life
About 45 percent, which is normal for either sex
About 30 percent, which is below the normal range for either sex and indicates anemia
questions.why: Multiplying 10 by three predicts a hematocrit near 30 percent, well under the female range of 37 to 47 and the male range of 42 to 52, so the patient is anemic. Thirty percent is not within the female range, which starts at about 37. Three percent would come from dividing rather than multiplying and is not compatible with life. Forty five percent would correspond to a hemoglobin of about 15 g/dL, not 10.
questions.answerText: About 30 percent, which is below the normal range for either sex and indicates anemia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: An adult female's hematocrit measures 49 percent on a properly performed test. How should this be interpreted?
options: Above the female reference range, which should prompt a look at hydration status
Within the female reference range and entirely expected
Below the female reference range, indicating anemia
Impossible, since the hematocrit of any healthy adult cannot exceed 47 percent by definition
questions.why: The female range tops out near 47 percent, so 49 is high and the common explanations are hemoconcentration from fluid loss or a true increase in red cell mass. It is not within the range, and calling it expected would miss a real finding. It is well above rather than below any anemia threshold. Hematocrit can certainly exceed 47 percent, reaching 60 or more in polycythemia.
questions.answerText: Above the female reference range, which should prompt a look at hydration status

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A blood sample is drawn from a severely dehydrated patient. How does this affect the hematocrit as a measure of red cell mass?
options: The hematocrit cannot be measured until fluids are given
The hematocrit overstates red cell mass, because plasma volume is reduced
The hematocrit understates red cell mass, because cells shrink when dehydrated
The hematocrit measures red cell mass accurately regardless of hydration
questions.why: Hematocrit is a ratio, so shrinking the plasma denominator raises the percentage even though the number of red cells has not changed, which is why a dehydrated patient can look falsely normal or falsely polycythemic. Red cells do not shrink appreciably with whole body dehydration, since plasma osmolarity changes only modestly. Hydration status matters greatly, so the measurement is not independent of it. The test can be performed at any time; the difficulty is in interpreting it.
questions.answerText: The hematocrit overstates red cell mass, because plasma volume is reduced

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student reports a hematocrit of 62 percent and a hemoglobin of 14 g/dL on the same sample. What should be concluded?
options: The results are consistent and indicate anemia
The results are consistent, because hemoglobin and hematocrit are unrelated measurements
The two results are inconsistent by the rule of three, so one measurement is in error
The results are consistent and indicate polycythemia
questions.why: A hemoglobin of 14 predicts a hematocrit near 42, so a reading of 62 is far outside the expected relationship and points to a technique problem such as under spinning or a misread column. True polycythemia would raise both values together, giving a hemoglobin near 20. Anemia would lower both. The two measurements are closely related because both reflect red cell content, which is exactly what makes the internal check useful.
questions.answerText: The two results are inconsistent by the rule of three, so one measurement is in error

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A 20 year old female runner has a hematocrit of 33 percent and a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL. Evaluate these results together.
options: They are internally inconsistent, so the sample must be repeated before any interpretation
They are consistent and both fall within the female reference range
They are consistent and indicate polycythemia from endurance training
They are internally consistent and both fall below the female reference range, indicating anemia
questions.why: Eleven times three is 33, so the pair passes the rule of three check, and both numbers sit under the female ranges of 12 to 16 g/dL and 37 to 47 percent, so the finding is a real anemia rather than a laboratory artifact. There is no inconsistency to force a repeat on technical grounds. Neither value is within the reference range. Polycythemia would mean values above the range, the opposite of what is shown.
questions.answerText: They are internally consistent and both fall below the female reference range, indicating anemia

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A dehydrated patient has a hematocrit of 54 percent on admission and 44 percent after 2 L of intravenous fluid. Which value better reflects red cell mass, and why?
options: The post fluid value, because restoring plasma volume removes the hemoconcentration
The admission value, because it was measured before any dilution by treatment
Neither, because intravenous fluid destroys red cells and invalidates both
Both equally, since the number of red cells did not change at all between the two draws
questions.why: The red cell count was the same for both draws, so the difference is entirely in the denominator, and the value obtained at a normal plasma volume is the one that represents red cell mass fairly. The admission value was measured on an abnormally small plasma volume, so being first does not make it more valid. Isotonic fluid does not destroy red cells. The cell number being constant is precisely why the two percentages cannot both be right about red cell mass.
questions.answerText: The post fluid value, because restoring plasma volume removes the hemoconcentration

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample leaks during centrifugation, losing packed red cells, and hemoglobin is measured on a separate uncompromised sample. Predict the pattern of results.
options: Both values normal, since a leak affects only the appearance of the tube
A falsely low hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails
A falsely high hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails
Both values falsely low, so the rule of three check still passes
questions.why: Only the spun tube was compromised, so the shortened red cell column drives the percentage down while the separately measured hemoglobin is unaffected, and the mismatch flags the error. Losing cells cannot raise the hematocrit. The hemoglobin sample was intact, so both values are not affected. The leak changes the measurement, not just the appearance, which is why the discrepancy appears.
questions.answerText: A falsely low hematocrit with a normal hemoglobin, so the rule of three check fails

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which three antisera are used in a standard ABO and Rh typing slide?
options: Anti-AB, anti-O, and anti-D
Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-fibrinogen
Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D
Anti-A, anti-O, and anti-Rh negative
questions.why: Each reagent contains antibody against one antigen, so three wells test for the A antigen, the B antigen, and the D antigen of the Rh system. There is no O antigen and therefore no anti-O reagent; type O is identified by the absence of reactions. Rh negative means the absence of D, so no reagent can test for it directly. Fibrinogen is a clotting protein and has nothing to do with blood group antigens.
questions.answerText: Anti-A, anti-B, and anti-D

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does agglutination in a typing well indicate?
options: The red cells have lysed and released hemoglobin
The sample has clotted because it was collected without any anticoagulant present
The antigen being tested for is absent
The antibody in that antiserum has bound its matching antigen on the red cells
questions.why: Each antibody has multiple binding sites, so it bridges neighboring cells into visible clumps, and clumping is therefore a positive result for that antigen. Hemolysis is a separate event that may follow in the body but is not what you read on the slide. Clotting is a fibrin reaction involving plasma proteins and looks different from agglutination. Absence of the antigen produces a smooth, evenly red suspension with no clumping.
questions.answerText: The antibody in that antiserum has bound its matching antigen on the red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-A but not with anti-B. What ABO type is it?
options: Type A
Type B
Type AB
Type O
questions.why: Clumping with anti-A means the A antigen is present, and no clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is absent, which is the definition of type A. Type B would clump with anti-B instead. Type AB would clump with both reagents. Type O would clump with neither.
questions.answerText: Type A

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample agglutinates with both anti-A and anti-B. What ABO type is it?
options: Type B
Type AB
Type O
Type A
questions.why: Reacting with both reagents means both the A and the B antigen are on the cells, which is type AB. Type O carries neither antigen and clumps with neither reagent. Type A clumps only with anti-A. Type B clumps only with anti-B.
questions.answerText: Type AB

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample shows no agglutination with anti-A, anti-B, or anti-D. What is the full type?
options: O positive
AB negative
O negative
AB positive
questions.why: No reaction anywhere means none of the three antigens is present, so the cells are type O and Rh negative, the universal red cell donor. AB positive would clump in all three wells. O positive would clump with anti-D only. AB negative would clump with anti-A and anti-B but not anti-D.
questions.answerText: O negative

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What antigen does the anti-D reagent detect?
options: The A antigen on type A cells
The fibrin present in a clotted sample
The antibody present in the patient's plasma
The D antigen, which determines Rh positive status
questions.why: The D antigen is the clinically important member of the Rh system, so its presence is what the label Rh positive reports. The A antigen is detected by the anti-A reagent in a different well. Fibrin is not a blood group antigen and would not be part of a typing panel. Forward typing examines antigens on the patient's red cells, not antibodies in their plasma.
questions.answerText: The D antigen, which determines Rh positive status

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In forward typing on a slide, what is being tested?
options: The antigens present on the patient's red cells
The antibodies present in the patient's plasma
The hemoglobin concentration of the sample
The number of platelets in the sample
questions.why: Forward typing mixes the patient's cells with known antibodies, so the result tells you which surface antigens are there. Testing the patient's plasma against known cells is reverse typing, the confirmatory step that runs in the opposite direction. Hemoglobin concentration requires a separate assay. Platelet counts are unrelated to blood group determination.
questions.answerText: The antigens present on the patient's red cells

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: What does a typing antiserum contain?
options: Anticoagulant that prevents clumping
Antibodies directed against one specific red cell antigen
Red cells collected from a donor whose ABO blood type is known
Purified antigen from a donor
questions.why: Anti-A serum contains anti-A antibody, and so on, so mixing it with unknown cells reveals whether that antigen is present. Known red cells are the reagent used in reverse typing, the mirror image of this test. Purified antigen would not clump cells, since clumping requires the bridging action of antibody. An anticoagulant prevents fibrin formation and would defeat the purpose of a test that depends on visible clumping.
questions.answerText: Antibodies directed against one specific red cell antigen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-B and anti-D but not with anti-A. What is the full type?
options: B negative
AB positive
B positive
A positive
questions.why: Clumping with anti-B places the B antigen on the cells, no clumping with anti-A rules out A, and clumping with anti-D makes it Rh positive. A positive would have required a reaction with anti-A instead. B negative would have shown no reaction in the anti-D well. AB positive would have clumped with anti-A as well.
questions.answerText: B positive

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample agglutinates with anti-A and anti-D but not with anti-B. Which donor red cell types are compatible for this patient?
options: A positive, B positive, AB positive, and O positive
A negative and O negative only
Only A positive, since the type must match exactly
A positive, A negative, O positive, and O negative
questions.why: The patient is A positive, so their plasma has anti-B and any unit carrying B is excluded, while their own D antigen means Rh positive units are also acceptable. Including B positive and AB positive units would supply the B antigen that anti-B will attack. Restricting to Rh negative units alone is safe but unnecessarily narrow for a patient who already has the D antigen. Requiring an exact match ignores the fact that O cells carry no A or B antigen and are therefore compatible.
questions.answerText: A positive, A negative, O positive, and O negative

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A sample shows no reaction with anti-A or anti-B but agglutinates with anti-D. What is the full type, and what does the plasma contain?
options: O positive, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma
O negative, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma
AB positive, with neither anti-A nor anti-B in the plasma
O positive, with anti-D in the plasma
questions.why: No ABO antigens plus the D antigen makes this O positive, and because the person lacks both A and B they carry antibodies against both. O negative would have shown no reaction with anti-D, which contradicts the result. AB positive would have clumped with both ABO reagents. An Rh positive person does not make anti-D, since D is their own antigen.
questions.answerText: O positive, with both anti-A and anti-B in the plasma

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient types as AB negative. Which donor red cell types are compatible?
options: Every type, since AB is the universal recipient
AB negative, A negative, B negative, and O negative
AB positive, A positive, B positive, and O positive
AB negative and O negative only
questions.why: Having no ABO antibodies opens every ABO type, but lacking the D antigen means only Rh negative units avoid the risk of sensitizing the patient to D. The positive units all carry D and are therefore not the safe choice for an Rh negative recipient. Limiting to AB negative and O negative leaves out A negative and B negative units that would not be attacked, since the patient has no ABO antibodies. The universal recipient label applies fully only to AB positive.
questions.answerText: AB negative, A negative, B negative, and O negative

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student's sample agglutinates in all three wells. What is the type and what does it mean for donating?
options: AB positive, which can donate to anyone because it carries all antigens
AB negative, since agglutination with anti-D indicates the absence of D
AB positive, which can receive from anyone but can donate only to AB positive recipients
O negative, which can donate red cells to anyone but can receive only from other O negative donors
questions.why: Carrying A, B and D means no recipient antibody can be present that would attack these cells in an AB positive person, but every other recipient has at least one antibody that would, so the donation range is narrow. O negative would have shown no reaction at all. Carrying all the antigens makes a poor donor, not a universal one; it is the absence of antigens that makes a universal donor. Agglutination with anti-D means D is present, so the last option reverses the reading.
questions.answerText: AB positive, which can receive from anyone but can donate only to AB positive recipients

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: In reverse typing, a patient's plasma is mixed with known type A cells and agglutination occurs. What does this tell you?
options: The plasma contains anti-B, so the patient is type A or type O
The patient's cells carry the A antigen, so the patient is type A or AB
The patient has no ABO antibodies, so the patient is type AB
The plasma contains anti-A, so the patient is type B or type O
questions.why: Clumping known A cells means the plasma holds anti-A, and only people who lack the A antigen carry that antibody, which narrows the type to B or O. Anti-B would be revealed by testing against known B cells, a different well. Reverse typing examines plasma antibodies, not the patient's own cell antigens. A patient with no ABO antibodies would produce no clumping in any reverse typing well.
questions.answerText: The plasma contains anti-A, so the patient is type B or type O

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Which blood type can donate red cells to the largest number of recipients, and why?
options: O negative, because its cells display neither A, nor B, nor D antigen
AB positive, because its plasma contains no ABO antibodies
O positive, because it is the most common type in the population
AB negative, because it carries both ABO antigens but not D
questions.why: Red cell compatibility depends on what the donor cell displays, and an O negative cell displays none of the three common antigens, so no recipient antibody has a target. Having no ABO antibodies makes AB positive the best recipient, not the best donor, because compatibility for receiving depends on plasma rather than cells. Frequency in the population affects supply but not compatibility. AB negative cells carry both ABO antigens and would be attacked by anti-A or anti-B in most recipients.
questions.answerText: O negative, because its cells display neither A, nor B, nor D antigen

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A unit labeled B positive is accidentally started in a patient typed A positive. Trace what happens.
options: Nothing happens, because both units are Rh positive and Rh alone determines compatibility here
The recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigens, agglutinating and hemolyzing them
The recipient's anti-A binds the donor A antigens, destroying the donor cells
The donor plasma anti-A destroys all of the recipient's red cells within seconds
questions.why: A type A recipient carries anti-B, the donor cells display B, and the antibody bridges them into clumps that are then lysed, releasing free hemoglobin. The recipient does not have anti-A, because they carry the A antigen themselves. Donor plasma antibodies are present in small volume and heavily diluted, so they are not the main event in a red cell transfusion reaction. Matching Rh does nothing to prevent an ABO mismatch, since the two systems are independent.
questions.answerText: The recipient's anti-B binds the donor B antigens, agglutinating and hemolyzing them

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: Forward typing shows agglutination with anti-A only, but reverse typing shows the patient's plasma agglutinating known type A cells. How should this be handled?
options: The patient is type O, since reverse typing always overrules forward typing
The patient is type AB, since reacting in two different tests means both antigens are present
The two results contradict each other, so the typing must be repeated before the result is trusted
The patient is type A, and the reverse result simply confirms it
questions.why: Forward typing says the A antigen is present, which means the plasma should contain anti-B and not anti-A, so plasma that attacks A cells is inconsistent and points to a labeling or technique error. Calling it a confirmation misreads reverse typing, which should have been negative against A cells. Reverse typing does not automatically overrule forward typing; a discrepancy is a signal to investigate. Reacting in two tests is not evidence of two antigens when the two tests examine opposite things.
questions.answerText: The two results contradict each other, so the typing must be repeated before the result is trusted

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A student records a sample as type O after seeing clumping with anti-B and no clumping with anti-A or anti-D. What is the error and the correct result?
options: No error, since type O cells clump with anti-B
The result should be O positive, since anti-B clumping indicates the D antigen
The result should be AB negative, since one positive well means both antigens
Clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is present, so the sample is B negative, not O
questions.why: Type O is defined by the absence of both A and B antigens, so any positive ABO well rules it out, and the lack of a reaction with anti-D makes the sample Rh negative. Type O cells carry no B antigen and cannot clump with anti-B. Anti-B detects the B antigen, not D, which has its own reagent. A single positive well shows one antigen, so AB cannot be concluded from an anti-A well that stayed negative.
questions.answerText: Clumping with anti-B means the B antigen is present, so the sample is B negative, not O

questions.topic: Blood
questions.q: A patient types as B negative and the only units on the shelf are B positive and O positive. Explain the ABO and Rh consequences of each option.
options: Neither would cause ABO agglutination, but both carry D and could sensitize this patient
Both would cause immediate ABO agglutination, because the patient has anti-B
The B positive unit would agglutinate immediately, but the O positive unit would only sensitize
Neither poses any risk, because Rh incompatibility affects only pregnancy
questions.why: A type B recipient carries anti-A only, so B cells and O cells both pass the ABO test, but the patient lacks D and has no anti-D yet, so the risk is a delayed immune response that would make future Rh positive exposures dangerous. The patient does not have anti-B, since they carry the B antigen. The B positive unit is ABO compatible, so it would not agglutinate on those grounds. Rh sensitization from transfusion is a real problem for future transfusions as well as future pregnancies.
questions.answerText: Neither would cause ABO agglutination, but both carry D and could sensitize this patient

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: During the early part of the sinoatrial node pacemaker potential, which ion moves into the cell through the funny channels?
options: Na+
K+
Ca2+
Cl-
questions.why: The funny current is a slow inward Na+ current through HCN channels, and it starts the drift away from the most negative point of the cycle back toward threshold. K+ moves out of a pacemaker cell during repolarization, so it cannot be the ion driving the membrane in the depolarizing direction. Ca2+ entry is real but comes later in the pacemaker potential, first through T-type and then through L-type channels. Cl- movement plays no part in the sinoatrial pacemaker sequence.
questions.answerText: Na+

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What opens the funny channels of a sinoatrial node cell?
options: Depolarization of the membrane to about -40 mV
Hyperpolarization after the last action potential
Ca2+ binding to the channel from inside the cell
Stretch of the nodal cell membrane during filling
questions.why: HCN channels are called funny because hyperpolarization opens them, the opposite of most voltage-gated channels, so the current switches on exactly when the cell is most negative near -60 mV. Depolarization to about -40 mV is threshold, which opens the L-type Ca2+ channels for the upstroke, not the funny channels. These channels are gated by voltage and tuned by cyclic AMP, not opened by intracellular Ca2+ binding, and they are not mechanically gated by stretch.
questions.answerText: Hyperpolarization after the last action potential

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which channels carry the final part of the pacemaker drift up to threshold, just before the L-type channels open?
options: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
Delayed rectifier K+ channels
T-type Ca2+ channels
ATP-sensitive K+ channels
questions.why: Once the funny current has brought the membrane part of the way up, transient (T-type) Ca2+ channels open and carry Ca2+ inward for the last stretch to threshold near -40 mV. Fast Na+ channels are essentially absent in nodal tissue and would be inactivated at these voltages anyway, which is why the nodal upstroke is slow. Delayed rectifier K+ channels carry the repolarizing current after the peak, and ATP-sensitive K+ channels open during metabolic stress rather than in the normal pacemaker cycle.
questions.answerText: T-type Ca2+ channels

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which ion movement produces the upstroke of the sinoatrial node action potential?
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels
Cl- moving into the cell
Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels
questions.why: At threshold the L-type Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ influx carries the upstroke, which is why the nodal action potential rises far more slowly than a ventricular one. Fast Na+ channels carry the upstroke in ventricular contractile cells, not in the node, and this is the single contrast most often collapsed. K+ efflux repolarizes the cell after the peak and moves the membrane in the opposite direction. Cl- currents are not part of the nodal action potential.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What repolarizes a sinoatrial node cell after the peak of its action potential?
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Na+ pumped out by the Na+/K+ ATPase
Ca2+ carried out by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
Cl- moving out of the cell
questions.why: Repolarization is K+ efflux through delayed rectifier K+ channels while the L-type Ca2+ channels close, the same ion and the same direction that repolarize every excitable cell you have studied. The Na+/K+ ATPase does export Na+, but it moves far too little charge per second to repolarize an action potential and it runs continuously rather than in a burst. The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger clears Ca2+ from the cytosol over many milliseconds and actually carries net positive charge inward, so it is depolarizing. Cl- efflux is not a feature of nodal repolarization.
questions.answerText: K+ moving out of the cell

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Roughly what membrane potential must a sinoatrial node cell reach before it fires an action potential?
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -40 mV
About 0 mV
questions.why: Threshold in the sinoatrial node is near -40 mV, the voltage at which enough L-type Ca2+ channels open to make the upstroke self-sustaining. About -90 mV is the stable resting potential of a ventricular contractile cell, which is a resting value and not a threshold. About -70 mV is the resting potential typical of a neuron. Zero mV is above the peak of the nodal action potential, so the cell would already have fired long before reaching it.
questions.answerText: About -40 mV

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the intrinsic firing rate of the sinoatrial node in an isolated heart with no autonomic input?
options: About 30 beats per minute
About 50 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 160 beats per minute
questions.why: Stripped of nerves, sinoatrial tissue depolarizes to threshold about 100 times a minute. A resting heart rate near 70 is lower than that because vagal tone continuously slows the node, so the resting rate is the intrinsic rate minus parasympathetic braking. About 50 per minute matches the atrioventricular node and about 30 matches Purkinje fibers, the slower backup pacemakers. About 160 is a rate the heart reaches only with strong sympathetic drive, not on its own.
questions.answerText: About 100 beats per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why does the sinoatrial node, rather than the atrioventricular node, normally set heart rate?
options: It is the only cardiac tissue capable of spontaneous depolarization
Its pacemaker cells reach threshold faster than any other pacemaker tissue
It is the only tissue that receives sympathetic innervation
It has the most negative threshold, so it needs the smallest stimulus
questions.why: Several regions can depolarize spontaneously, but the fastest one wins: the sinoatrial node reaches threshold first and its impulse depolarizes the slower pacemakers before they ever get there on their own. The atrioventricular node and Purkinje fibers also have unstable membrane potentials, so the node is not unique in that ability, only in its speed. Both nodes receive sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. Threshold is roughly similar across pacemaker tissues; it is the steepness of the drift, not the threshold value, that decides which one leads.
questions.answerText: Its pacemaker cells reach threshold faster than any other pacemaker tissue

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Norepinephrine binds beta-1 receptors on sinoatrial node cells and raises cyclic AMP. What happens to the pacemaker potential?
options: The slope becomes steeper, so threshold is reached sooner
The slope becomes shallower, so threshold is reached later
Threshold shifts to a more negative value with no change in slope
The maximum diastolic potential becomes more negative
questions.why: Cyclic AMP binds the HCN channels directly and increases the funny current, and it also increases Ca2+ entry, so the drift toward threshold is faster and the interval between beats is shorter. A shallower slope is exactly what parasympathetic stimulation produces, so that option describes the opposite arm of the autonomic nervous system. Sympathetic stimulation works mainly by changing the rate of drift, not by relocating threshold. A more negative maximum diastolic potential is also a parasympathetic effect, since it comes from opening K+ channels.
questions.answerText: The slope becomes steeper, so threshold is reached sooner

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Vagal release of acetylcholine opens K+ channels in sinoatrial node cells. Predict the effect on the maximum diastolic potential and on heart rate.
options: A less negative maximum diastolic potential and a faster rate
No change in maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate
A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate
A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a faster rate
questions.why: Opening K+ channels lets more K+ leave, driving the membrane closer to the K+ equilibrium potential, so the cell starts each drift from a more negative point and has further to travel to threshold. Extra distance plus a reduced funny current means a longer interval between beats and a slower heart rate. A more negative starting point cannot speed the cell up, so the option pairing hyperpolarization with a faster rate has the logic backwards. A less negative maximum diastolic potential with a faster rate describes what sympathetic stimulation does, not acetylcholine.
questions.answerText: A more negative maximum diastolic potential and a slower rate

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in the sinoatrial node. What happens to the upstroke of the nodal action potential?
options: It is unchanged, because the nodal upstroke is carried by Na+
It becomes slower and smaller, because that current is reduced
It becomes faster, because fast Na+ channels take over the job
It is replaced by a maintained plateau at the threshold voltage
questions.why: The nodal upstroke is Ca2+ influx through L-type channels, so blocking those channels directly reduces the current that produces it and both the rate of rise and the peak fall. The option claiming no change assumes a Na+ upstroke, which is true for ventricular contractile cells but not for nodal cells. Fast Na+ channels cannot compensate because they are inactivated at the depolarized voltages a nodal cell lives at. A plateau requires sustained Ca2+ entry, which is exactly what the drug has removed.
questions.answerText: It becomes slower and smaller, because that current is reduced

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug shifts the threshold of sinoatrial node cells from -40 mV to -30 mV without changing the slope of the pacemaker potential or the maximum diastolic potential. What happens to heart rate?
options: It rises, because the cell is now closer to zero millivolts
It is unchanged, because the slope of the drift was not altered
It rises, because less Ca2+ entry is needed to reach threshold
It falls, because the cell must drift further before it reaches threshold
questions.why: Firing rate is set by how long the drift takes, which depends on both the slope and the distance to be covered. Raising threshold from -40 to -30 mV adds 10 mV to that distance, so at unchanged slope each cycle takes longer and rate falls. The slope being unchanged does not protect the rate, because time to threshold is distance divided by slope. Being closer to zero is not an advantage; the cell has to reach threshold from below, and a higher threshold is further away.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the cell must drift further before it reaches threshold

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: The sinoatrial node stops firing entirely. Which tissue is most likely to take over, and at roughly what rate?
options: Purkinje fibers, at about 60 to 100 beats per minute
Ordinary atrial muscle, at about 70 beats per minute
The atrioventricular node, at 40 to 60 per minute
The bundle branches, at about 90 beats per minute
questions.why: The next fastest pacemaker takes over, and that is the atrioventricular junction, whose cells drift to threshold about 40 to 60 times a minute. Purkinje fibers can also pace, but far more slowly, at roughly 20 to 40 per minute, so the rate given in that option belongs to the sinoatrial node. Ordinary atrial and ventricular muscle have stable resting potentials and no funny current, so they cannot generate their own rhythm. Bundle branch tissue is part of the same slow His and Purkinje escape system and does not pace at 90.
questions.answerText: The atrioventricular node, at 40 to 60 per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why does the sinoatrial node action potential rise far more slowly than a ventricular action potential?
options: Nodal cells have a much larger diameter, so charge spreads more slowly through them
Nodal cells are hyperpolarized, so they start further away from threshold
Nodal cells contain more Na+/K+ ATPase working against the upstroke current
The upstroke uses L-type Ca2+ channels, which pass current more slowly
questions.why: Speed of an upstroke is set by the channel that carries it, and L-type Ca2+ channels have slower gating and smaller currents than the fast voltage-gated Na+ channels that drive the ventricular upstroke. Nodal cells are in fact relatively depolarized, near -60 mV rather than -90 mV, which is why their fast Na+ channels sit inactivated and unavailable. Nodal cells are small, not large, and cell size affects conduction along tissue rather than the rate of rise in a single cell. Pump activity is far too small a current to slow an upstroke.
questions.answerText: The upstroke uses L-type Ca2+ channels, which pass current more slowly

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which of these changes in a sinoatrial node cell would raise heart rate?
options: A more negative maximum diastolic potential
A steeper pacemaker potential
A threshold shifted toward zero
A longer nodal action potential
questions.why: Rate is the inverse of the time from one upstroke to the next, and a steeper drift covers the distance to threshold in less time, so beats come closer together. A more negative maximum diastolic potential lengthens the distance the drift has to cover and slows the rate. A threshold shifted toward zero also lengthens that distance and slows the rate. A longer action potential adds time to each cycle before the drift can even begin, which slows the rate as well.
questions.answerText: A steeper pacemaker potential

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A transplanted heart has no autonomic innervation. At rest its rate is close to 100 beats per minute, while a healthy person with the same fitness rests near 70. What accounts for the difference?
options: The transplanted node runs at its intrinsic rate because the vagal braking normally present is absent
The transplanted node has lost its sympathetic supply, and sympathetic withdrawal raises the rate
Denervation makes the pacemaker potential steeper by opening more L-type Ca2+ channels
Denervation raises threshold in the nodal cells, which shortens each cycle
questions.why: The intrinsic rate of the sinoatrial node is about 100 per minute, and a resting rate of 70 is the product of continuous vagal tone slowing that intrinsic rhythm. Remove the nerves and the brake goes with them, so the node reverts to its own pace. Losing sympathetic input would tend to lower rate rather than raise it, so sympathetic withdrawal cannot explain a faster heart. Denervation removes signals rather than adding L-type channels, and raising threshold would lengthen each cycle and slow the heart.
questions.answerText: The transplanted node runs at its intrinsic rate because the vagal braking normally present is absent

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A compound selectively blocks the funny current in the sinoatrial node. Trace the consequences in order.
options: Steeper pacemaker slope, shorter time to threshold, higher heart rate
Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, lower heart rate
Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, unchanged heart rate
Unchanged pacemaker slope, longer action potential, lower heart rate
questions.why: The funny current is the inward Na+ current that starts the drift, so removing it makes the early pacemaker potential shallower, the cell needs longer to climb from about -60 mV to threshold near -40 mV, and fewer beats fit into a minute. A steeper slope would follow from adding funny current, as sympathetic stimulation does, not from blocking it. Rate cannot stay unchanged when the time between upstrokes lengthens, since rate is simply the inverse of cycle length. The action potential itself is carried by Ca2+ and K+ currents and is not lengthened by an HCN blocker.
questions.answerText: Shallower pacemaker slope, longer time to threshold, lower heart rate

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Surgery destroys the sinoatrial node, and the atrioventricular junction takes over, pacing the heart at about 45 beats per minute. Why is the escape rate lower than the sinoatrial rate it replaced?
options: Atrioventricular pacemaker cells cannot depolarize spontaneously and must wait for atrial stretch
Atrioventricular pacemaker cells have a shallower pacemaker potential, so they take longer to reach threshold
Atrioventricular cells repolarize to a less negative potential, which delays the next upstroke
Atrioventricular cells lack L-type Ca2+ channels, so each upstroke fails several times before succeeding
questions.why: Every pacemaker tissue in the heart drifts spontaneously, but they do it at different speeds, and the junctional cells have the shallower drift, so each cycle takes longer and the escape rhythm is slower. They do not need stretch or any external trigger; that is what makes them a functioning escape pacemaker at all. Repolarizing to a less negative potential would shorten the distance to threshold and speed the cell up, which is the opposite of what is seen. L-type Ca2+ channels are present and carry the junctional upstroke, otherwise there would be no escape rhythm.
questions.answerText: Atrioventricular pacemaker cells have a shallower pacemaker potential, so they take longer to reach threshold

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A sinoatrial node cell fires at 60 beats per minute. Each cycle is an action potential lasting 300 ms plus a pacemaker potential lasting 700 ms. Sympathetic stimulation steepens the drift so the pacemaker potential now takes 200 ms, with no change in action potential duration. What is the new rate?
options: About 86 beats per minute
About 100 beats per minute
About 120 beats per minute
About 200 beats per minute
questions.why: The new cycle length is 300 ms plus 200 ms, which is 500 ms, and 60 seconds divided by 0.5 seconds per beat gives 120 beats per minute. About 200 comes from timing only the action potential and forgetting that the drift still occupies 200 ms of every cycle. About 86 comes from using the old 700 ms drift alone. About 100 would require a 600 ms cycle, which is what you get if you shorten the action potential instead of the pacemaker potential.
questions.answerText: About 120 beats per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the resting membrane potential of a ventricular contractile cell during phase 4?
options: About -90 mV
About -70 mV
About -60 mV
About -40 mV
questions.why: A ventricular contractile cell rests near -90 mV, held there by inward rectifier K+ channels that keep the membrane close to the K+ equilibrium potential, and unlike a nodal cell it stays there until an impulse arrives. About -70 mV is the resting value of a typical neuron. About -60 mV is the most negative point a sinoatrial node cell reaches, and it does not stay there because the funny current immediately starts the drift. About -40 mV is nodal threshold, not a resting potential.
questions.answerText: About -90 mV

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which ion movement produces phase 0, the rapid upstroke of the ventricular action potential?
options: Ca2+ moving in through L-type channels
Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels
K+ moving out through delayed rectifier channels
Na+ moving in through HCN funny channels
questions.why: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open in a fraction of a millisecond and let Na+ rush down its electrochemical gradient, which is why the ventricular upstroke is steep and the cell can conduct quickly to its neighbors. L-type Ca2+ entry does happen, but it sustains the plateau and is the upstroke current in the sinoatrial node rather than in a contractile cell. K+ efflux moves the membrane in the repolarizing direction, the opposite of an upstroke. HCN channels belong to pacemaker tissue and are not part of the contractile cell action potential.
questions.answerText: Na+ moving in through fast voltage-gated channels

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What produces phase 1, the small dip immediately after the peak of the ventricular action potential?
options: L-type Ca2+ channels close briefly and then open again
Cl- floods into the cell through open leak channels
Fast Na+ channels inactivate as a K+ current flows out
The Na+/K+ ATPase briefly runs in the reverse direction
questions.why: Phase 1 is a brief notch: the fast Na+ channels inactivate so the inward current stops, and at the same moment a transient outward K+ current carries positive charge out, dropping the membrane slightly before the plateau holds it. L-type Ca2+ channels are opening during this window, not closing and reopening. Cl- influx is not a significant current in the human ventricular action potential. The Na+/K+ ATPase runs steadily in one direction and moves far too little charge to cause a visible notch.
questions.answerText: Fast Na+ channels inactivate as a K+ current flows out

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which two ion movements balance each other during phase 2, the plateau of the ventricular action potential?
options: Na+ entering through fast channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and Cl- entering through Cl- channels
Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels
Na+ entering through HCN channels and Ca2+ leaving through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger
questions.why: The plateau exists because slow inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels nearly cancels the outward K+ current, so net charge movement is close to zero and the membrane hangs near 0 mV for roughly 200 ms. Fast Na+ channels are already inactivated by this point, so they contribute nothing to the plateau. Cl- entry is not a meaningful plateau current. HCN channels are pacemaker channels and are absent from contractile cells.
questions.answerText: Ca2+ entering through L-type channels and K+ leaving through K+ channels

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which ion movement produces phase 3, repolarization of the ventricular cell?
options: Ca2+ moving out of the cell through L-type channels
Na+ moving out of the cell through fast channels
Cl- moving into the cell
K+ moving out of the cell
questions.why: Phase 3 begins when the L-type Ca2+ channels finish closing while delayed rectifier K+ channels stay open, so the outward K+ current is no longer balanced and the membrane falls back toward -90 mV. Voltage-gated channels carry ions down their gradients, so Ca2+ and Na+ channels can only let those ions in, never out. Cl- influx is not the repolarizing current of cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: K+ moving out of the cell

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What holds the ventricular cell membrane at its resting potential during phase 4?
options: A steady inward funny current balanced against Ca2+ entry
Open K+ leak channels holding the membrane near -90 mV
Continuous Cl- entry that holds the membrane negative
Fast Na+ channels held slightly open at a low steady level
questions.why: Between beats the dominant conductance is K+ through inward rectifier leak channels, so the membrane sits close to the K+ equilibrium potential near -90 mV and stays stable until the next impulse arrives. A funny current is what makes nodal phase 4 unstable, and contractile cells do not have one, which is exactly why they do not pace themselves. Cl- distribution is close to equilibrium at rest and does not set the resting potential in cardiac muscle. Fast Na+ channels are closed at rest, not partly open.
questions.answerText: Open K+ leak channels holding the membrane near -90 mV

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How long does a ventricular action potential last, compared with a skeletal muscle action potential?
options: About 25 ms, compared with about 2 ms
About 250 ms, compared with about 2 ms
About 250 ms, compared with about 100 ms
About 1000 ms, compared with about 2 ms
questions.why: A ventricular action potential runs roughly 200 to 300 ms because of the plateau, while a skeletal muscle fiber finishes its action potential in a couple of milliseconds. That hundredfold difference is the whole reason cardiac muscle cannot be summed into tetanus. About 100 ms is closer to the length of a skeletal muscle twitch, which is the contraction, not the action potential. A full second would be longer than an entire cardiac cycle at a resting heart rate.
questions.answerText: About 250 ms, compared with about 2 ms

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which phase gives the ventricular action potential its unusually long duration?
options: Phase 0, the upstroke
Phase 1, the notch
Phase 2, the plateau
Phase 4, the resting potential
questions.why: The plateau holds the membrane depolarized for about 200 ms because inward Ca2+ current offsets outward K+ current, and that single phase accounts for nearly the whole duration of the action potential. The upstroke is over in a millisecond or two, and the notch is briefer still. Phase 4 is the interval between action potentials rather than a part of one, and its length changes with heart rate.
questions.answerText: Phase 2, the plateau

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A toxin blocks fast voltage-gated Na+ channels in ventricular muscle. Predict the effect on phase 0.
options: The upstroke becomes slower and smaller, because less Na+ current flows
The upstroke becomes faster because K+ efflux is unopposed
The upstroke is unchanged because Ca2+ carries it
The upstroke reverses and becomes a hyperpolarization
questions.why: Phase 0 is Na+ influx through fast channels, so blocking them reduces the inward current available and the membrane rises more slowly and to a lower peak, which also slows conduction to neighboring cells. K+ efflux opposes depolarization, so removing an inward current cannot make the upstroke faster. Assuming Ca2+ carries the upstroke confuses the contractile cell with the sinoatrial node. A blocked channel simply passes less current; it does not drive the membrane in the opposite direction.
questions.answerText: The upstroke becomes slower and smaller, because less Na+ current flows

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in ventricular muscle. What happens to the action potential?
options: The upstroke slows, but the overall duration is unchanged
The plateau shortens, so the action potential is briefer
The plateau lengthens, because K+ efflux is also reduced
The resting potential becomes less negative than before
questions.why: The plateau is held up by inward Ca2+ current, so with less of it the outward K+ current wins sooner, repolarization starts earlier, and total action potential duration falls. The upstroke is a Na+ event and is not affected by an L-type blocker. Blocking Ca2+ channels does nothing to K+ channels, so there is no reason for the plateau to lengthen. Resting potential is set by K+ leak conductance and is not shifted by a Ca2+ channel blocker.
questions.answerText: The plateau shortens, so the action potential is briefer

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug blocks the delayed rectifier K+ channels of ventricular muscle. Predict the effect on the action potential.
options: Repolarization is slowed, so the action potential lasts longer
Repolarization is faster, so the action potential is shorter
The upstroke is slowed, so the peak is lower
The resting potential becomes more negative
questions.why: Phase 3 depends on outward K+ current, so reducing it means the membrane takes longer to fall back to -90 mV and the action potential, along with the QT interval on an ECG, is prolonged. Blocking a repolarizing current cannot speed repolarization up. The upstroke is a Na+ event, so its rate of rise is untouched. Less K+ conductance moves the resting membrane away from the K+ equilibrium potential, making it less negative rather than more.
questions.answerText: Repolarization is slowed, so the action potential lasts longer

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: During the plateau of the ventricular action potential, the membrane potential barely changes for about 200 ms. What does that tell you about the currents?
options: All voltage-gated channels are closed, so no current is flowing at all
Inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are nearly equal
The Na+/K+ ATPase is holding the membrane voltage constant
Membrane resistance has fallen to zero, so the voltage cannot change
questions.why: A flat voltage does not mean no current; it means the inward and outward currents cancel, and in the plateau that balance is Ca2+ entering through L-type channels against K+ leaving through K+ channels. If all channels were shut, the membrane would return to its resting potential rather than sitting near 0 mV. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves too little charge per second to clamp the voltage. Zero resistance would mean the membrane could not hold any potential at all, including the resting potential.
questions.answerText: Inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current are nearly equal

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why does a ventricular action potential last about a hundred times longer than a skeletal muscle action potential?
options: Cardiac cells are much larger, so it takes longer to move enough charge
Sustained Ca2+ entry holds the membrane depolarized in a plateau
Cardiac cells lack a Na+/K+ ATPase to restore the gradients quickly
Cardiac K+ channels open faster, which drags out repolarization
questions.why: The plateau is the difference: skeletal muscle repolarizes as soon as its Na+ channels inactivate, while cardiac muscle keeps an inward Ca2+ current running that opposes repolarization for roughly 200 ms. Cell size does not set action potential duration; single channels and their kinetics do, and cardiac cells are in fact smaller than skeletal fibers. Cardiac cells have plenty of Na+/K+ ATPase, and in any case the pump restores gradients over minutes rather than shaping a single action potential. Faster K+ channel opening would shorten repolarization, not lengthen it.
questions.answerText: Sustained Ca2+ entry holds the membrane depolarized in a plateau

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Extracellular K+ rises from 4 to 7 mEq/L. Which way does the resting membrane potential of a ventricular cell move?
options: It becomes more negative, moving away from threshold
It becomes less negative, moving toward threshold
It does not change, because the Na+/K+ ATPase compensates immediately
It becomes more negative, because more K+ leaves the cell
questions.why: Resting potential tracks the K+ equilibrium potential, and raising extracellular K+ reduces the gradient driving K+ out, so the equilibrium potential and the resting potential both shift toward zero. Less negative means closer to threshold, which is why moderate hyperkalemia first makes cardiac cells more excitable before inactivating Na+ channels and making them less excitable. A smaller outward gradient cannot drive more K+ out, so the option reasoning from increased efflux has the gradient backwards. The pump adjusts over minutes and cannot hold the membrane potential fixed against an acute change.
questions.answerText: It becomes less negative, moving toward threshold

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A ventricular cell is artificially held at -60 mV instead of -90 mV and then stimulated. What happens to the upstroke?
options: It is larger, because the cell starts out much closer to threshold
It is unchanged, because threshold is a fixed voltage value
It is smaller, because many fast Na+ channels are inactivated
It is faster, because less Na+ influx is needed to fire
questions.why: Fast Na+ channels inactivate when a cell sits depolarized, and they only recover once the membrane returns near -90 mV, so at -60 mV a large share of them are unavailable and the upstroke that follows is weak and slow. Starting closer to threshold makes the cell easier to trigger but does not give it more Na+ current to work with, so amplitude falls rather than rises. Threshold voltage is not the issue; availability of channels is. A weaker inward current always produces a slower rate of rise, never a faster one.
questions.answerText: It is smaller, because many fast Na+ channels are inactivated

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug reduces Ca2+ entry through L-type channels in ventricular muscle by half. Trace the consequences through to contraction.
options: Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, less Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, weaker contraction
Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, more Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, unchanged contraction
Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, slower upstroke, weaker contraction
Larger K+ current, longer plateau, stronger contraction
questions.why: The Ca2+ that enters during the plateau is the trigger for calcium induced calcium release, so halving it means the ryanodine receptors release less stored Ca2+, less Ca2+ reaches troponin, and the contraction is weaker. Release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum follows the trigger, so it cannot increase when the trigger falls. The upstroke belongs to fast Na+ channels and is not affected by an L-type blocker. Blocking an inward current shortens the plateau rather than lengthening it, and weakens rather than strengthens the beat.
questions.answerText: Smaller plateau Ca2+ current, less Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, weaker contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A toxin prevents fast Na+ channels in ventricular muscle from inactivating, so they stay open once triggered. Predict the effect on the action potential and the refractory period.
options: The action potential is shortened and the refractory period shortens with it
The action potential is prolonged and the refractory period lengthens with it
The upstroke disappears and the cell can no longer be excited
The plateau disappears but the total duration is unchanged
questions.why: Inactivation of the Na+ channels is what ends phase 0 and allows the notch and eventually repolarization, so if the channels stay open the inward current persists, the membrane is held depolarized far longer, and the action potential drags on. Because the refractory period lasts until the membrane repolarizes enough for Na+ channels to reset, it lengthens along with the action potential. The upstroke is not lost, since the channels still open normally; it is the switching off that fails. Losing inactivation adds inward current, which cannot shorten the action potential or abolish the plateau.
questions.answerText: The action potential is prolonged and the refractory period lengthens with it

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A recording from a ventricular cell shows a normal upstroke and normal resting potential, but the membrane stays near 0 mV for 500 ms instead of 200 ms before repolarizing. Which change best explains the tracing?
options: Fast Na+ channels are opening more slowly
Outward K+ current during the plateau is reduced
The resting K+ leak conductance is increased
The Na+/K+ ATPase has been blocked
questions.why: The plateau length is set by the balance between inward Ca2+ current and outward K+ current, so if K+ efflux is reduced the balance tips inward, repolarization is delayed, and the plateau stretches. Slower Na+ channel opening would change the upstroke, which the tracing says is normal. More resting K+ conductance would make the resting potential more negative and would speed repolarization, not delay it. Blocking the pump raises intracellular Na+ over minutes and does not directly hold a single plateau open.
questions.answerText: Outward K+ current during the plateau is reduced

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Both a sinoatrial node cell and a ventricular contractile cell are isolated in a dish with no stimulation. The nodal cell keeps firing and the ventricular cell stays silent. Which two differences explain this?
options: The ventricular cell lacks a funny current and its K+ conductance holds phase 4 stable
The ventricular cell lacks L-type Ca2+ channels and cannot generate an upstroke on its own
The ventricular cell has a lower threshold and so inactivates itself before firing
The ventricular cell lacks a Na+/K+ ATPase, so its gradients run down and it cannot fire
questions.why: Automaticity needs two things a contractile cell does not have: an inward current that starts at negative voltages, which is the funny current through HCN channels, and an unstable phase 4, which is impossible when inward rectifier K+ channels clamp the membrane near the K+ equilibrium potential. The ventricular cell has plenty of L-type Ca2+ channels; they run the plateau and would fire fine if the cell ever reached threshold. A lower threshold would make a cell easier to excite, not silent. Removing the pump would eventually stop the cell entirely rather than explain a quiet but excitable cell.
questions.answerText: The ventricular cell lacks a funny current and its K+ conductance holds phase 4 stable

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Where does a normal cardiac impulse begin?
options: In the sinoatrial node, high in the wall of the right atrium
In the atrioventricular node, in the floor of the right atrium
In the bundle of His, at the top of the interventricular septum
In the left atrium, near where the pulmonary veins enter
questions.why: The sinoatrial node sits high in the right atrial wall next to the superior vena cava, and because its cells drift to threshold fastest, that is where each normal beat starts. The atrioventricular node is downstream, in the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve, and only paces if the sinoatrial node fails. The bundle of His is further downstream still, carrying the impulse into the septum. The left atrium receives the impulse through internodal and interatrial pathways rather than generating it.
questions.answerText: In the sinoatrial node, high in the wall of the right atrium

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the correct order of the cardiac conduction pathway?
options: Sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, internodal pathways, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches, bundle of His
Sinoatrial node, bundle of His, atrioventricular node, internodal pathways, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
Atrioventricular node, sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers, bundle branches
Sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
questions.why: The impulse leaves the sinoatrial node, spreads across the atria through the internodal pathways to the atrioventricular node, is delayed there, then runs down the bundle of His into the two bundle branches and finally out through the Purkinje fibers to ventricular muscle. The versions that place the bundle of His before the atrioventricular node reverse the only electrical route between atria and ventricles. Putting Purkinje fibers before the bundle branches reverses the branching order, since Purkinje fibers are the terminal twigs. The sinoatrial node always precedes the atrioventricular node in a normal beat.
questions.answerText: Sinoatrial node, internodal pathways, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Where is the atrioventricular node located?
options: In the interventricular septum, just below the aortic valve
In the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve
In the roof of the left atrium, next to the mitral valve
In the apex of the right ventricle, at the base of the papillary muscles
questions.why: The atrioventricular node lies low in the interatrial septum, in the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve and coronary sinus, which places it right at the gateway between atria and ventricles where the delay is imposed. The interventricular septum carries the bundle of His and bundle branches, which are downstream of the node. The left atrium and the ventricular apex contain no nodal tissue; the apex is where Purkinje fibers first deliver the impulse to working muscle.
questions.answerText: In the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How long is the atrioventricular nodal delay in a normal heart?
options: About 0.01 second
About 0.1 second
About 0.5 second
About 1.0 second
questions.why: Conduction through the atrioventricular node takes roughly 100 ms, which is most of the normal PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 second. A delay of 0.01 second would be too brief to let the atria finish emptying. Half a second would be longer than the systole of an entire cardiac cycle at rest and would separate atrial from ventricular contraction badly. A full second is about the whole cardiac cycle at 60 beats per minute.
questions.answerText: About 0.1 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which structure is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles?
options: The internodal pathways
The coronary sinus
The bundle of His
The Purkinje network of the atria
questions.why: A ring of fibrous connective tissue insulates the atria from the ventricles, and the bundle of His is the single strand of conducting tissue that crosses it, which is why a block there can separate the two chambers completely. The internodal pathways run within the atria only, from the sinoatrial to the atrioventricular node. The coronary sinus is a vein returning blood from the heart wall and conducts nothing. Purkinje fibers are ventricular, not atrial.
questions.answerText: The bundle of His

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which part of the conduction system conducts most slowly?
options: The Purkinje fiber network
The bundle of His
The atrioventricular node
The bundle branches in the septum
questions.why: Atrioventricular nodal cells conduct at roughly 0.05 m/s, the slowest tissue in the heart, and that slowness is what creates the delay between atrial and ventricular contraction. Purkinje fibers are the fastest, at roughly 2 to 4 m/s, so the ventricles can be activated almost at once. The bundle of His and the bundle branches are also fast conducting tissue built for speed rather than delay.
questions.answerText: The atrioventricular node

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which fibers deliver the impulse from the bundle branches to ventricular muscle?
options: Internodal pathway fibers
Purkinje fibers
Chordae tendineae
Intercalated disc fibers
questions.why: Purkinje fibers are large, fast conducting cells that fan out from the ends of the bundle branches, beginning at the apex, and hand the impulse to working ventricular muscle. Internodal pathways carry the impulse across the atria, upstream of the atrioventricular node. Chordae tendineae are the tendinous cords anchoring the atrioventricular valve leaflets and carry no impulse. Intercalated discs are junctions between individual cardiac muscle cells, not a named conduction pathway.
questions.answerText: Purkinje fibers

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the purpose of the atrioventricular delay?
options: It gives the atria time to finish contracting before the ventricles contract
It allows the ventricles to repolarize fully before the next atrial beat
It lets the coronary arteries fill while the ventricles are depolarized
It prevents the sinoatrial node from firing more than 100 times per minute
questions.why: Holding the impulse for about 100 ms means atrial contraction is complete before ventricular contraction begins, so the ventricles receive the final portion of their filling volume rather than being squeezed shut on partly filled chambers. Ventricular repolarization is controlled by the length of the ventricular action potential and the refractory period, not by the nodal delay.
