Coronary filling happens mainly during ventricular relaxation, well after this delay. The nodal delay does not limit sinoatrial firing rate, which is set by the pacemaker potential.
questions.answerText: It gives the atria time to finish contracting before the ventricles contract

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why do atrioventricular nodal cells conduct so slowly?
options: They are wrapped in myelin, which slows the impulse between the nodes
They are small, poorly coupled, and use a slow Ca2+ upstroke
They lack a Na+/K+ ATPase, so their ion gradients are shallow
They are separated by synapses that add a chemical transmission delay
questions.why: Three features stack up: a narrow fiber offers high internal resistance, few gap junctions mean less current passes to the next cell, and a Ca2+ driven upstroke rises slowly compared with a Na+ driven one. Cardiac tissue has no myelin at all, which is a nervous system feature. Nodal cells have normal ion pumps and normal gradients. There are no synapses inside the conduction system; cardiac cells are electrically coupled directly through gap junctions.
questions.answerText: They are small, poorly coupled, and use a slow Ca2+ upstroke

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: If the atrioventricular delay were abolished so the impulse passed straight from atria to ventricles, what would happen to ventricular filling?
options: It would rise, because the two chambers would contract together and generate more pressure
It would fall, because the ventricles would contract while the atria are still emptying
It would be unchanged, because most filling is passive
It would rise, because diastole would be longer
questions.why: Atrial contraction tops off the ventricles at the end of diastole, so if the ventricles start contracting at the same moment the atrioventricular valves are pushed shut early and that final contribution is lost. Simultaneous contraction does not add pressure usefully; it makes the atria push against closed valves. Most filling is indeed passive, but the atrial contribution still matters, and it matters much more at high heart rates when passive filling time is short. Removing the delay shortens rather than lengthens the interval before ventricular systole.
questions.answerText: It would fall, because the ventricles would contract while the atria are still emptying

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A person has a block in the left bundle branch. How does the left ventricle become activated?
options: It is not activated at all and does not contract
By slow cell to cell spread from the right ventricle, so activation takes longer
By a direct atrial pathway that bypasses the ventricular conduction system
By the Purkinje fibers of the left ventricle firing spontaneously in time with the right
questions.why: Cardiac muscle cells are joined by gap junctions, so an impulse that cannot use the left bundle still reaches the left ventricle by spreading muscle cell to muscle cell, which is much slower than Purkinje conduction and widens the QRS complex. The ventricle is not silent, it is simply activated late and less uniformly. There is no normal accessory route from atria to ventricular muscle apart from the bundle of His. Purkinje fibers can pace when nothing else reaches them, but at 20 to 40 per minute and not synchronized to the other ventricle.
questions.answerText: By slow cell to cell spread from the right ventricle, so activation takes longer

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why does ventricular contraction begin at the apex and move toward the base?
options: The apex has thicker muscle, so it depolarizes at a lower threshold
Purkinje fibers reach the apex first, so blood is driven upward
The atrioventricular valves open at the apex and pull the impulse down
The base is insulated by the fibrous skeleton and cannot contract
questions.why: The bundle branches run down the interventricular septum to the apex before the Purkinje fibers fan out, so the apex depolarizes and contracts first and the wave of contraction wrings blood upward toward the aortic and pulmonary valves. Wall thickness does not change threshold; depolarization order is set by the conduction pathway. Valve movement is a consequence of pressure changes and does not steer the impulse. The fibrous skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles electrically, but the base of the ventricles is working muscle and contracts normally.
questions.answerText: Purkinje fibers reach the apex first, so blood is driven upward

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Sympathetic stimulation acts on the atrioventricular node. Predict the effect on conduction through it.
options: Conduction speeds up, so the delay is shorter
Conduction slows, so the delay is longer
Conduction is blocked entirely at high rates
Conduction is unaffected, since only the sinoatrial node is innervated
questions.why: Sympathetic fibers increase Ca2+ current in nodal tissue, so atrioventricular cells reach threshold and pass the impulse on faster, shortening the delay and the PR interval, which is useful at high heart rates when there is less time to spare. Slowed conduction with a longer delay is the parasympathetic effect. Block at high rates is what happens with excess vagal tone or disease, not with sympathetic drive. Both nodes are richly innervated by both branches of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.answerText: Conduction speeds up, so the delay is shorter

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Strong vagal stimulation reaches the atrioventricular node. What happens to the time between atrial and ventricular depolarization?
options: It shortens, because acetylcholine speeds nodal conduction
It lengthens, because acetylcholine slows nodal conduction
It is unchanged, because the vagus reaches only the sinoatrial node
It shortens, because a slower heart rate leaves more time for conduction
questions.why: Acetylcholine reduces Ca2+ current and increases K+ conductance in atrioventricular nodal cells, so they take longer to reach threshold and pass the impulse on, which lengthens the delay and the PR interval. Speeding conduction is a sympathetic effect. The vagus supplies the atrioventricular node as well as the sinoatrial node, which is why strong vagal activity can both slow the heart and block conduction. A slower rate does leave more time between beats, but that does not change how fast a single impulse crosses the node.
questions.answerText: It lengthens, because acetylcholine slows nodal conduction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which step in the conduction pathway accounts for most of the flat segment between the end of the P wave and the start of the QRS complex?
options: Spread of the impulse through atrial muscle
Conduction through the atrioventricular node
Conduction through the Purkinje fibers
Repolarization of the atria
questions.why: The line is flat because the tissue conducting at that moment, the atrioventricular node, is too small to generate a voltage the surface electrodes can see, and its slow conduction fills most of that 100 ms. Atrial spread produces the P wave itself, which comes just before this segment. Purkinje conduction is extremely fast and occurs immediately before and during the QRS. Atrial repolarization does occur around this time but is small and buried under the QRS complex, and it does not create the delay.
questions.answerText: Conduction through the atrioventricular node

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: In a normal heart, atrial spread takes about 30 ms, the atrioventricular node adds about 100 ms, and the His and Purkinje system takes about 30 ms. How long after the sinoatrial node fires do the ventricles begin to depolarize, and which ECG measurement matches that time?
options: About 0.13 second, matching the QRS duration
About 0.16 second, matching the PR interval
About 0.16 second, matching the QT interval
About 0.30 second, matching the PR interval
questions.why: Adding 30 plus 100 plus 30 gives 160 ms, or 0.16 second, and that is exactly what the PR interval measures: the time from the onset of atrial depolarization to the onset of ventricular depolarization, sitting comfortably inside the normal range of 0.12 to 0.20 second. The QRS duration measures only the ventricular depolarization that follows, normally under 0.12 second. The QT interval covers ventricular depolarization plus repolarization and runs closer to 0.40 second. The 0.30 second figure double counts the nodal delay.
questions.answerText: About 0.16 second, matching the PR interval

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An accessory pathway connects atrial muscle directly to ventricular muscle, bypassing the atrioventricular node. Predict the consequences for the PR interval and for ventricular filling.
options: A longer PR interval and reduced filling, because conduction takes an extra step
A shorter PR interval and reduced filling, because the ventricles fire too early
A shorter PR interval and improved filling, because the beat is more efficient
An unchanged PR interval, because the atrioventricular node still conducts normally
questions.why: The accessory route skips the only place in the heart that deliberately slows conduction, so ventricular depolarization begins early and the PR interval shortens. Losing the delay means the ventricles start contracting while the atria are still emptying, so the atrial contribution to filling is cut short and stroke volume suffers. An extra parallel route cannot lengthen the PR interval, since the impulse takes whichever path is faster. The node still conducts, but it is no longer the first to arrive, so the interval does change.
questions.answerText: A shorter PR interval and reduced filling, because the ventricles fire too early

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Purkinje fibers can depolarize spontaneously at about 20 to 40 per minute, yet they never pace a healthy heart. Why not?
options: They lose their pacemaker channels once the heart has matured
The sinoatrial impulse reaches them before their own drift does
The fibrous skeleton prevents any impulse they generate from spreading
Their threshold is too positive to be reached by any spontaneous drift
questions.why: This is overdrive suppression in its simplest form: at 70 beats per minute an impulse arrives every 850 ms or so, far sooner than a Purkinje cell needs to drift to threshold on its own, so the fast pacemaker resets the slow one on every beat. The channels are still there, which is why the fibers can pace once the sinoatrial impulse stops reaching them. The fibrous skeleton separates atria from ventricles and would not stop a ventricular impulse from spreading through ventricular muscle. Their threshold is reachable, just not quickly.
questions.answerText: The sinoatrial impulse reaches them before their own drift does

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An impulse from the sinoatrial node reaches the atria normally but never arrives at the ventricles. What does the ventricular myocardium do, and why?
options: It is driven by a slow escape pacemaker in the His and Purkinje system
It contracts at the atrial rate, because the atria and ventricles are mechanically coupled
It stops entirely, because ventricular tissue has no automaticity of any kind
It contracts at a faster rate, because the atrioventricular delay has been removed
questions.why: With the fast pacemaker cut off, the next tissue down the line drifts to its own threshold and takes over, giving a slow ventricular escape rhythm of roughly 20 to 40 per minute that keeps some output going. The chambers are coupled by pressure and valves, not by mechanical transmission of an impulse, so the ventricles cannot simply follow the atrial rate. Ventricular conducting tissue does have automaticity, which is precisely why the heart does not stop. Losing conduction cannot speed the ventricles up, since the impulse never gets there at all.
questions.answerText: It is driven by a slow escape pacemaker in the His and Purkinje system

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What defines the absolute refractory period of a cardiac muscle cell?
options: No stimulus of any strength can trigger a second action potential
A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger a second action potential
The cell responds normally but contracts more weakly
The cell is depolarized but cannot release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.why: During the absolute refractory period the fast Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen, so the cell simply will not fire again no matter how large the stimulus. A stimulus that is strong enough to work describes the relative refractory period, which follows the absolute one. A normal response with a weaker contraction is not a refractory state at all. Ca2+ release is happening vigorously during this period, which is why the cell is contracting.
questions.answerText: No stimulus of any strength can trigger a second action potential

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What makes the ventricular cell absolutely refractory for so long?
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is empty and cannot release more Ca2+
Fast Na+ channels stay inactivated until the membrane repolarizes
The Na+/K+ ATPase has not yet restored the resting ion gradients
Acetylcholine remains bound to the membrane throughout the contraction
questions.why: Inactivated Na+ channels only recover when the membrane returns toward its negative resting potential, and the long plateau holds the cell depolarized for about 200 ms, so recovery is postponed for most of the contraction. The sarcoplasmic reticulum still contains Ca2+; refractoriness is a membrane property, not a store depletion problem. The Na+/K+ ATPase restores gradients slowly and continuously and a single action potential barely dents them. Acetylcholine acts on nodal tissue and does not gate the ventricular refractory period.
questions.answerText: Fast Na+ channels stay inactivated until the membrane repolarizes

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Roughly how long is the refractory period of ventricular muscle?
options: About 2 ms
About 25 ms
About 250 ms
About 1000 ms
questions.why: The ventricular refractory period runs about 250 ms, which is close to the length of the action potential and therefore close to the length of the contraction itself. About 2 ms is the refractory period of a skeletal muscle fiber, which is why skeletal muscle can be stimulated again long before it relaxes. About 25 ms would still leave most of the contraction unprotected. A full second is longer than the entire cardiac cycle at a resting rate.
questions.answerText: About 250 ms

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What happens during the relative refractory period?
options: The cell cannot fire again under any circumstances at all
The cell fires normally but produces no contraction at all
A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential
The cell fires spontaneously without any stimulus being applied
questions.why: By the relative refractory period some fast Na+ channels have recovered but many have not, so a larger stimulus can recruit enough of them to fire, and the resulting upstroke is slower and smaller than normal. Complete unresponsiveness defines the absolute refractory period that precedes it. Firing without contracting would require a failure of excitation contraction coupling, which is a separate problem. Spontaneous firing is a property of pacemaker tissue, not a refractory state.
questions.answerText: A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger an action potential

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is tetanus in a muscle?
options: A sustained contraction from stimuli arriving faster than relaxation
A single maximal twitch produced by one unusually strong stimulus
A contraction that occurs without any action potential reaching the fiber
A prolonged relaxation caused by depleted Ca2+ stores in the cell
questions.why: Tetanus is summation taken to its limit: each new action potential adds Ca2+ before the previous release has been pumped away, so twitches fuse into one smooth maintained contraction. A single strong twitch is not tetanus no matter how large it is, because tetanus requires repeated stimulation. Contraction without an action potential does not occur in striated muscle. Depleted Ca2+ stores would weaken contraction, which is the opposite of a maintained one.
questions.answerText: A sustained contraction from stimuli arriving faster than relaxation

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How does the refractory period of skeletal muscle compare with the length of its own twitch?
options: The refractory period is about 2 ms and the twitch about 100 ms, so restimulation is possible
The refractory period and the twitch are both about 100 ms, so restimulation is impossible
The refractory period is about 250 ms while the twitch lasts about 100 ms, so the fiber must relax first
The refractory period is about 100 ms while the twitch lasts about 2 ms, so restimulation is impossible
questions.why: A skeletal fiber recovers its Na+ channels within a couple of milliseconds while the mechanical twitch is still developing over 100 ms, and that mismatch is the reason skeletal muscle can summate and be tetanized. A refractory period equal to or longer than the twitch is the cardiac arrangement, which is exactly what prevents tetanus there. A 250 ms refractory period is the cardiac value, not the skeletal one. A twitch of 2 ms confuses the mechanical event with the action potential.
questions.answerText: The refractory period is about 2 ms and the twitch about 100 ms, so restimulation is possible

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which part of the ventricular action potential does the absolute refractory period span?
options: Only the plateau phase
Only the resting period between action potentials
Only the upstroke itself
From the upstroke through most of repolarization
questions.why: Na+ channels inactivate at the top of the upstroke and stay inactivated as long as the membrane is depolarized, so the absolute refractory period covers phase 0, all of phase 2, and most of phase 3 until the membrane has repolarized to roughly -50 mV. Limiting it to the upstroke would leave the long plateau unprotected. Limiting it to the plateau would ignore that the cell is already unresponsive from the moment it fires. Phase 4 is when the cell is fully recovered and most excitable, which is the opposite of refractory.
questions.answerText: From the upstroke through most of repolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanized?
options: It has no sarcoplasmic reticulum, so Ca2+ cannot accumulate in the cytosol
Its cells are electrically isolated from one another, so stimuli cannot spread
Its contraction is too weak for individual twitches to add together usefully
Its refractory period lasts nearly as long as its own contraction
questions.why: By the time a cardiac cell can be excited again, the contraction it is already producing is nearly over, so there is no window in which twitches can overlap and fuse. Cardiac twitches are perfectly strong enough to summate if they were allowed to; the block is timing, not force. Cardiac muscle has a sarcoplasmic reticulum and uses it heavily during every beat. Cardiac cells are electrically connected by gap junctions, which is what lets the impulse spread cell to cell in the first place.
questions.answerText: Its refractory period lasts nearly as long as its own contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Suppose cardiac muscle could be tetanized. What would happen to pumping?
options: Output would be unchanged, because filling is driven by venous pressure
The ventricles would relax permanently and fill without any limit
Output would rise, because the ventricles would generate more force per beat
The ventricles could not refill, so output would fall to nearly zero
questions.why: A pump has to alternate between filling and emptying, so a maintained contraction leaves no diastole, the ventricles never refill, and after one or two beats there is nothing left to eject. Extra force is useless if the chamber is empty. Venous pressure does drive filling, but it cannot fill a chamber whose walls are locked in contraction and whose pressure exceeds venous pressure. Tetanus is sustained contraction, not sustained relaxation.
questions.answerText: The ventricles could not refill, so output would fall to nearly zero

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A second stimulus is delivered to a ventricular cell 100 ms after the upstroke, during the plateau. What happens?
options: A second action potential of normal size occurs
A second action potential of reduced size occurs
Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory
The cell hyperpolarizes and the contraction ends early
questions.why: At 100 ms the cell is still in the plateau with its fast Na+ channels inactivated, so no stimulus of any size can produce another action potential. A normal sized second action potential would require full recovery, which does not happen until the cell has repolarized. A reduced action potential is possible in the relative refractory period later in phase 3, not during the plateau. A stimulus delivers depolarizing current and cannot hyperpolarize the cell.
questions.answerText: Nothing, because the cell is absolutely refractory

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A stimulus is delivered to a ventricular cell 400 ms after the upstroke, once it has returned to -90 mV. What happens?
options: A normal action potential and a normal separate contraction
No response, because the refractory period lasts a full second
A reduced action potential, because Na+ channels are still recovering
A contraction that sums with the first one
questions.why: By 400 ms the action potential is over, the membrane is back at rest, and the Na+ channels have recovered, so the cell responds fully and produces an entirely separate beat. The refractory period is about 250 ms, not a full second, so the cell is no longer protected. Partial recovery describes the relative refractory period, which has already passed by 400 ms. Summation is impossible here because the first contraction has ended before the second action potential begins.
questions.answerText: A normal action potential and a normal separate contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A stimulus arrives during the relative refractory period of a ventricular cell. How does the resulting action potential compare with a normal one?
options: It has a faster upstroke, because the cell is already partly depolarized
It has a normal upstroke but no plateau at all
It is identical, because action potentials are all or none events
It has a slower upstroke and a lower peak, and conducts slowly
questions.why: Only some Na+ channels have recovered, so less inward current is available, the upstroke rises slowly to a lower peak, and because conduction speed depends on how fast each cell depolarizes its neighbor, the impulse also spreads more slowly. The all or none rule holds for a fully recovered cell; a partially recovered one gives a genuinely smaller response. Starting from a partly depolarized membrane reduces the channels available rather than adding speed. The plateau depends on L-type Ca2+ channels and is not the phase that fails here.
questions.answerText: It has a slower upstroke and a lower peak, and conducts slowly

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug lengthens the ventricular plateau from 200 ms to 400 ms. Predict the effect on the refractory period and on the highest heart rate the ventricles can follow.
options: A longer refractory period and a lower maximum rate
A longer refractory period and an unchanged maximum rate
A shorter refractory period and a higher maximum rate
An unchanged refractory period and a lower maximum rate
questions.why: The cell stays refractory until it repolarizes, so stretching the plateau stretches the refractory period with it, and beats that arrive before recovery simply cannot be conducted, which lowers the fastest rate the ventricles can sustain. The maximum rate cannot stay unchanged when the minimum interval between usable beats has grown. Lengthening the plateau cannot shorten refractoriness, since the two move together. The refractory period is not independent of action potential duration in cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: A longer refractory period and a lower maximum rate

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts summation in skeletal and cardiac muscle?
options: Both can summate, but cardiac muscle needs a much stronger stimulus to do it
Neither can summate, because both recover only after the twitch is over
Only skeletal muscle can summate, since it recovers before its twitch ends
Cardiac muscle can summate, but only at rates above 150 beats per minute
questions.why: The deciding factor is the ratio of refractory period to contraction time: about 2 ms against 100 ms in skeletal muscle, which leaves a wide window for a second stimulus, against roughly 250 ms against 250 ms in cardiac muscle, which leaves essentially none. Stimulus strength cannot overcome an absolutely refractory membrane, so no amount of extra current lets cardiac muscle summate. Skeletal muscle clearly does summate, which is how it grades force. Fast heart rates shorten both the action potential and the refractory period together, so summation still does not occur.
questions.answerText: Only skeletal muscle can summate, since it recovers before its twitch ends

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why must the heart relax fully between beats?
options: Ventricular filling happens during relaxation, so without it there is no volume to eject
The Na+/K+ ATPase can only work while the muscle is relaxed
The atrioventricular valves can only close while the ventricles are relaxed
Action potentials cannot be conducted while the muscle is contracting
questions.why: Stroke volume is limited by end diastolic volume, and the ventricles only fill when their walls are relaxed and chamber pressure is below atrial pressure, so relaxation time directly limits pump output. The Na+/K+ ATPase runs continuously and does not pause for contraction. The atrioventricular valves close at the start of contraction, not during relaxation; they open during relaxation. Cardiac impulses conduct through contracting muscle perfectly well, as the spread of each normal beat shows.
questions.answerText: Ventricular filling happens during relaxation, so without it there is no volume to eject

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A premature stimulus reaches ventricular muscle late in the relative refractory period. Trace what happens to that beat.
options: A small, slowly rising action potential and a weaker contraction
A normal action potential that produces a stronger contraction because it comes early
No action potential at all, because the cell is still absolutely refractory
A normal action potential that fuses with the previous contraction
questions.why: Late in phase 3 only a fraction of the fast Na+ channels have recovered, so the upstroke is small and slow, conduction from cell to cell is sluggish because each cell depolarizes its neighbor weakly, and less Ca2+ entry means a weaker beat. It cannot be normal, because normal requires full recovery. It is not silent either, since the absolute refractory period has already ended, which is what makes this window dangerous rather than safe. Fusion with the previous contraction would be summation, which the refractory period still prevents.
questions.answerText: A small, slowly rising action potential and a weaker contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: At a heart rate of 200 beats per minute, how much of each cardiac cycle is left for filling if ventricular contraction and its refractory period occupy 250 ms?
options: About 50 ms, which is far too little for adequate filling
About 150 ms, which is adequate at rest
About 300 ms, which is unchanged from resting values
About 550 ms, because the cycle lengthens at high rates
questions.why: At 200 beats per minute each cycle lasts 60000 divided by 200, which is 300 ms, and subtracting the 250 ms occupied by contraction leaves only about 50 ms of diastole. That collapse of filling time is why extremely fast rates reduce stroke volume and eventually cardiac output, and why the real heart shortens its action potential as rate rises. About 150 ms would require a 400 ms cycle, which is a rate of 150. About 300 ms is the whole cycle, not the part left over. Cycle length shortens as rate rises, never lengthens.
questions.answerText: About 50 ms, which is far too little for adequate filling

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An experimental drug shortens the ventricular refractory period to 50 ms without changing the length of the contraction. What becomes possible that normally is not?
options: The cell can be re-excited while it is still contracting, so twitches could summate
The cell can generate a larger single contraction with no change in Ca2+ entry
The atrioventricular delay would lengthen to compensate
Conduction through the ventricles would stop entirely
questions.why: The refractory period is the only thing keeping a second action potential from arriving mid contraction, so cutting it to 50 ms opens a long window during which a new stimulus can add Ca2+ to a cytosol that has not yet been cleared, and summation and tetanus become possible. A single contraction cannot grow larger without more Ca2+ reaching troponin. The atrioventricular delay is a property of nodal conduction and does not adjust in response to ventricular refractoriness. Shortening refractoriness makes the tissue more excitable, not less, so conduction would not stop.
questions.answerText: The cell can be re-excited while it is still contracting, so twitches could summate

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Skeletal muscle grades its force by summation and recruitment, but the heart cannot use either. How does cardiac muscle change the force of a beat instead?
options: By changing how much Ca2+ reaches the myofilaments and how far the fibers are stretched
By recruiting additional ventricular cells that were previously silent
By lengthening the refractory period so that each beat lasts longer
By increasing the amplitude of the action potential above its all or none level
questions.why: Because gap junctions make the ventricle contract as one unit and the long refractory period rules out summation, cardiac force is graded within each beat, by the amount of Ca2+ delivered to troponin and by the length tension advantage of a more filled ventricle. There are no reserve cells to recruit, since every ventricular cell is depolarized on every beat. A longer refractory period limits rate rather than adding force. Action potential amplitude is all or none in a fully recovered cell and is not the variable the heart uses.
questions.answerText: By changing how much Ca2+ reaches the myofilaments and how far the fibers are stretched

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which electrical event does the P wave represent?
options: Atrial repolarization
Depolarization of the sinoatrial node itself
Atrial contraction
Atrial depolarization
questions.why: The P wave is the voltage produced as depolarization sweeps across both atria, and atrial contraction follows it rather than being what the ECG records. An ECG shows electrical events only, so contraction is never what a wave represents. Atrial repolarization does happen, but it is small and hidden under the QRS complex. The sinoatrial node itself contains far too little tissue to produce a deflection at the body surface.
questions.answerText: Atrial depolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which electrical event does the QRS complex represent?
options: Ventricular repolarization
Ventricular contraction
Ventricular depolarization
Conduction through the atrioventricular node
questions.why: The QRS is the large deflection produced when depolarization spreads through the thick ventricular walls, and its size reflects the amount of muscle involved. Ventricular repolarization is the T wave, a slower and smaller event. Contraction is mechanical and begins shortly after the QRS, but it is not what the tracing records. Atrioventricular nodal conduction produces no visible deflection because the node is tiny; it appears as the flat segment before the QRS.
questions.answerText: Ventricular depolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which electrical event does the T wave represent?
options: Atrial repolarization
Ventricular relaxation
Ventricular repolarization
The plateau phase of the atrial action potential
questions.why: The T wave is the voltage change as the ventricles repolarize, and it is broader and lower than the QRS because repolarization spreads more slowly and less uniformly than depolarization. Atrial repolarization is buried within the QRS complex and is not seen separately. Ventricular relaxation is the mechanical event that follows the T wave. The atrial plateau is far too small an event to register at the body surface.
questions.answerText: Ventricular repolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What does the PR interval measure?
options: From the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex
From the end of the P wave to the end of the QRS complex
From the start of the P wave to the end of the T wave
From the peak of the P wave to the peak of the R wave
questions.why: The PR interval runs from the first sign of atrial depolarization to the first sign of ventricular depolarization, so it contains atrial spread plus the atrioventricular nodal delay, and most of it is the delay. Ending at the end of the QRS would add ventricular depolarization time and no longer isolate conduction from atria to ventricles. Running to the end of the T wave describes something closer to the QT interval plus the PR interval. Intervals are measured from onset to onset, not peak to peak, because the onsets mark when each event starts.
questions.answerText: From the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the normal duration of the PR interval?
options: 0.02 to 0.06 second
0.12 to 0.20 second
0.25 to 0.35 second
0.40 to 0.50 second
questions.why: A normal PR interval is 0.12 to 0.20 second, which is three to five small boxes on standard ECG paper, and most of that time is the atrioventricular nodal delay. A value of 0.02 to 0.06 second would be too short for the atria to depolarize, let alone for the node to hold the impulse. Values above 0.20 second define a first degree block. The 0.40 to 0.50 second range is closer to a normal QT interval.
questions.answerText: 0.12 to 0.20 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What does the QT interval measure?
options: From the end of the QRS complex to the start of the T wave
From the start of the P wave to the end of the T wave
From the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave
From the peak of the R wave to the peak of the T wave
questions.why: The QT interval spans ventricular depolarization and ventricular repolarization together, so it corresponds closely to the duration of the ventricular action potential and to ventricular systole. Measuring from the end of the QRS to the start of the T wave describes the ST segment, which is only the plateau portion. Starting at the P wave would include atrial events and the nodal delay. Peak to peak measurement misses the onset of depolarization and the end of repolarization, which are the boundaries that matter.
questions.answerText: From the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why is atrial repolarization not visible as its own wave on a normal ECG?
options: Atrial repolarization produces no ion movement and therefore no voltage at all
It appears only in the chest leads and never in the limb leads
The atria do not repolarize until the next beat has already begun
It happens during ventricular depolarization and is buried under the QRS
questions.why: Atrial repolarization generates a genuine but small signal that happens to coincide with ventricular depolarization, and the ventricular mass is so much larger that the QRS drowns it out. The atria certainly do repolarize within the same beat, otherwise they could not be excited again. Repolarization is K+ efflux and does generate voltage; it is simply overwhelmed. Lead choice does not rescue it, because the timing overlap is the same in every lead.
questions.answerText: It happens during ventricular depolarization and is buried under the QRS

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the normal duration of the QRS complex?
options: Less than 0.12 second
0.12 to 0.20 second
0.20 to 0.30 second
0.30 to 0.40 second
questions.why: Normal ventricular depolarization is complete in under 0.12 second, usually 0.06 to 0.10 second, because the Purkinje network distributes the impulse almost simultaneously. A QRS of 0.12 to 0.20 second is wide and indicates that activation is spreading through muscle rather than through the fast conducting system. The 0.12 to 0.20 second range is the normal window for the PR interval, not the QRS. Values above 0.20 second are far outside the normal range for ventricular depolarization.
questions.answerText: Less than 0.12 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Conduction through the atrioventricular node slows. Which ECG measurement lengthens?
options: The QRS duration
The QT interval
The PR interval
The T wave duration
questions.why: The PR interval contains the nodal delay, so anything that slows conduction between atria and ventricles stretches it while leaving the rest of the tracing untouched. QRS duration reflects how fast the ventricles depolarize once the impulse arrives, which is a His and Purkinje question, not a nodal one. The QT interval reflects ventricular depolarization and repolarization and is unaffected by how long the impulse waited at the node. The T wave reflects repolarization only.
questions.answerText: The PR interval

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A drug prolongs ventricular repolarization. Which ECG measurement lengthens?
options: The P wave duration
The ST segment only, with no change in QT
The PR interval
The QT interval
questions.why: The QT interval covers depolarization through the end of repolarization, so a slower phase 3 pushes the end of the T wave later and lengthens QT. The PR interval measures conduction from atria to ventricles and is unchanged by a repolarization effect. P wave duration reflects atrial depolarization only. The ST segment may shift too, but the point of the QT interval is precisely that it captures repolarization, so it cannot stay constant while repolarization slows.
questions.answerText: The QT interval

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A tracing shows a QRS complex lasting 0.16 second. What does that tell you about ventricular activation?
options: The atrioventricular node is conducting the impulse too quickly
The ventricles are repolarizing more slowly than they normally would
The ventricles are depolarizing faster than they normally would
Part of the ventricle is reached by slow muscle to muscle spread
questions.why: A wide QRS means ventricular depolarization is taking longer than the Purkinje system would allow, which happens when part of the ventricle has to be reached by slow cell to cell conduction through working muscle. A longer QRS is by definition slower activation, not faster. Atrioventricular conduction speed shows up in the PR interval and does not widen the QRS. Repolarization is the T wave and the QT interval, not the QRS.
questions.answerText: Part of the ventricle is reached by slow muscle to muscle spread

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Ventricular muscle mass increases substantially. What would you expect on the ECG?
options: A shorter PR interval, because conduction distance is greater
A smaller T wave, because repolarization requires less charge
A taller P wave, because atrial pressure rises
A taller QRS complex, because more muscle is depolarizing at once
questions.why: The size of a deflection reflects the amount of tissue depolarizing at that moment, so a thicker ventricular wall generates a larger voltage and a taller QRS. The P wave reflects atrial depolarization, which is not what has changed here. Greater distance would tend to lengthen conduction time, not shorten the PR interval, and the PR interval is dominated by the nodal delay in any case. More muscle repolarizing produces more voltage in the T wave, not less.
questions.answerText: A taller QRS complex, because more muscle is depolarizing at once

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which phase of the ventricular action potential does the T wave correspond to?
options: Phase 0, the upstroke
Phase 2, the plateau
Phase 3, repolarization
Phase 4, the resting potential
questions.why: The T wave is the surface record of ventricular repolarization, which is phase 3, when K+ efflux is no longer balanced by inward Ca2+ current. Phase 0 in millions of cells at once produces the QRS complex. Phase 2 is the plateau, during which the ventricles are uniformly depolarized and the tracing is flat. Phase 4 is the interval between action potentials, which appears as the flat line from the end of the T wave to the next P wave.
questions.answerText: Phase 3, repolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why is the segment between the end of the QRS and the start of the T wave normally flat?
options: The recording electrodes are electrically disconnected during this period
The atria are repolarizing and cancel the ventricular signal exactly
No ion movement is occurring anywhere in the heart at that moment
All ventricular cells sit at the same potential during the plateau
questions.why: Surface electrodes register differences in charge between regions, so when the whole ventricular mass is sitting in the plateau at the same potential there is no difference to detect and the trace stays on the baseline. Plenty of ion movement is happening, since Ca2+ is entering and K+ is leaving in every cell; it is the uniformity that hides it. The electrodes stay connected throughout. Atrial repolarization is much smaller than any ventricular signal and could not cancel one exactly.
questions.answerText: All ventricular cells sit at the same potential during the plateau

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why is the QRS complex much larger than the P wave on a normal ECG?
options: The recording electrodes are closer to the ventricles than to the atria
Ventricular depolarization lasts longer, which raises the recorded amplitude
Ventricular cells depolarize to a more positive peak voltage than atrial cells
The ventricles contain far more muscle mass, so more charge moves at once
questions.why: Deflection size on an ECG tracks the total amount of tissue changing charge at that moment, and the ventricular walls contain several times the muscle of the atria. Peak membrane voltage in a single cell is similar in the two chambers, so that is not the source of the difference. Electrode distance plays a small role in individual leads but does not explain the consistent size difference across leads. Duration and amplitude are separate measurements, and ventricular depolarization is actually quite brief.
questions.answerText: The ventricles contain far more muscle mass, so more charge moves at once

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An ECG shows a PR interval of 0.16 second, a QRS duration of 0.08 second, and a QT interval of 0.36 second at a rate of 75 beats per minute. What do these measurements indicate?
options: The PR interval is prolonged beyond normal
The QRS complex is abnormally wide
The QT interval is prolonged for this rate
All three intervals are within normal limits
questions.why: A PR interval of 0.12 to 0.20 second, a QRS under 0.12 second, and a QT near 0.36 to 0.44 second at a normal rate are all ordinary values, so this tracing shows normal conduction and normal repolarization. Prolonged PR means greater than 0.20 second, which 0.16 is not. A wide QRS means 0.12 second or more, and 0.08 is comfortably below that. A QT of 0.36 second at 75 beats per minute is normal, since QT shortens as rate rises.
questions.answerText: All three intervals are within normal limits

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A tracing at 60 beats per minute shows a normal P wave, a QRS of 0.09 second, and a QT interval of 0.60 second. Which cellular change best explains it?
options: Reduced K+ efflux during phase 3, which prolongs repolarization
Reduced Na+ influx during phase 0, which slows the upstroke
Slower conduction through the atrioventricular node
Increased K+ leak conductance at rest, which deepens the resting potential
questions.why: The QT interval is long while the QRS is normal, so depolarization is fine and the delay is in repolarization, which depends on outward K+ current during phase 3. Slower Na+ entry during phase 0 would widen the QRS, which this tracing does not show. Slowed nodal conduction would lengthen the PR interval instead. More resting K+ conductance would make the resting potential more negative but would if anything speed repolarization, not delay it.
questions.answerText: Reduced K+ efflux during phase 3, which prolongs repolarization

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A strip shows regular P waves and regular QRS complexes, but the distance from each P wave to the next QRS keeps changing. Which measurement cannot be meaningfully reported?
options: The QT interval, because the T waves belong to different beats
The P wave duration, because the atria are not depolarizing normally
The QRS duration, because the complexes are irregular in shape
The PR interval, because the P waves and QRS are unrelated
questions.why: A PR interval only means something when the same impulse produces the P wave and then the QRS, so when the two are marching at independent rates there is no interval to measure, only a changing coincidence. QRS duration is measured within a single complex and is perfectly reportable here, since each complex is itself regular. The QT interval is also measured within one ventricular beat, from that beat's QRS to that beat's T wave. The P waves are regular and normal in this description, so their duration can be measured too.
questions.answerText: The PR interval, because the P waves and QRS are unrelated

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: At a heart rate of 60 beats per minute the QT interval is 0.40 second. What fraction of each cardiac cycle are the ventricles electrically active, and what does the rest of the cycle represent?
options: About 60 percent, with the remainder representing atrial depolarization
About 40 percent, with the remainder representing the plateau phase
About 25 percent, with the remainder representing the atrioventricular delay
About 40 percent, with the remainder representing electrical diastole between beats
questions.why: At 60 beats per minute each cycle lasts 1.00 second, so a QT interval of 0.40 second occupies 40 percent of it, and the remaining 0.60 second is the time from the end of the T wave to the next QRS, when the ventricles are repolarized and refilling. The atrioventricular delay is roughly 0.10 second and accounts for only a small slice of the remainder. Atrial depolarization is the brief P wave, not the majority of the cycle. The plateau is contained inside the QT interval, so it cannot be the remainder.
questions.answerText: About 40 percent, with the remainder representing electrical diastole between beats

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On standard ECG paper, how much time does one small box represent?
options: 0.01 second
0.04 second
0.10 second
0.20 second
questions.why: Standard paper runs at 25 mm per second and each small box is 1 mm wide, so one small box is 1 divided by 25, which is 0.04 second. A value of 0.20 second is the large box, made of five small ones. A value of 0.10 second would not divide evenly into the grid at standard paper speed. A hundredth of a second is finer than the grid can resolve.
questions.answerText: 0.04 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How much time does one large box represent on standard ECG paper?
options: 0.04 second
0.10 second
0.20 second
0.50 second
questions.why: A large box contains five small boxes, and five times 0.04 second is 0.20 second, which is why five large boxes make one full second. The 0.04 second value belongs to a single small box. Neither 0.10 nor 0.50 second corresponds to any square on the standard grid, and using either would throw off every rate calculation.
questions.answerText: 0.20 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which rule gives heart rate from the number of small boxes between two R waves?
options: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes
Divide 300 by the number of small boxes
Multiply the number of small boxes by 10
Divide 60 by the number of small boxes
questions.why: There are 1500 small boxes in a minute, since each is 0.04 second and 60 divided by 0.04 is 1500, so dividing 1500 by the boxes between beats gives beats per minute. Dividing 300 is the rule for large boxes, and using it on small boxes underestimates the rate fivefold. Multiplying by 10 is the six second strip rule applied to QRS complexes, not to boxes. Dividing 60 by boxes would only work if each box were a full second.
questions.answerText: Divide 1500 by the number of small boxes

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How do you estimate heart rate from a six second rhythm strip?
options: Count the small boxes in the strip and divide by 6
Count the P waves in the strip and multiply by 4
Count the QRS complexes and multiply by 6, since the strip is 6 seconds
Count the QRS complexes in the strip and multiply by 10
questions.why: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute, so the number of beats in that window multiplied by 10 gives beats per minute, and this method works even when the rhythm is irregular. Multiplying by 6 would treat the strip as ten seconds long. Counting boxes and dividing by 6 measures time rather than rate. Counting P waves gives the atrial rate, which equals the ventricular rate only when every P wave is conducted.
questions.answerText: Count the QRS complexes in the strip and multiply by 10

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which findings define normal sinus rhythm?
options: An upright P before every QRS, a constant PR, and a rate of 60 to 100
A P wave after every QRS, a constant PR interval, and a rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute
An upright P wave before every QRS, a variable PR interval, and any rate
No visible P waves, a narrow QRS, and a rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute
questions.why: Sinus rhythm means the sinoatrial node started each beat and the impulse followed the normal path, which shows up as an upright P wave preceding every QRS, a PR interval that is the same on every beat, and a rate in the normal range. A P wave following the QRS would mean the atria were activated after the ventricles, so the beat did not begin in the sinoatrial node. A PR interval that varies from beat to beat means the P waves and QRS complexes are not linked. Absent P waves mean the atria are not depolarizing in an organized way.
questions.answerText: An upright P before every QRS, a constant PR, and a rate of 60 to 100

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: At what heart rate does bradycardia begin?
options: Below 100 beats per minute
Below 80 beats per minute
Below 60 beats per minute
Below 40 beats per minute
questions.why: Bradycardia is a resting rate under 60 beats per minute, the lower edge of the normal 60 to 100 range, and tachycardia is a rate above 100. A cutoff of 100 would label most normal resting hearts as slow. A cutoff of 80 sits in the middle of the normal range. A cutoff of 40 would miss the many rates between 40 and 60 that are genuinely below normal, although rates that low are usually a junctional or ventricular escape rhythm.
questions.answerText: Below 60 beats per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What defines a first degree heart block on an ECG?
options: A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with a QRS following every P wave
A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with occasional P waves not followed by a QRS
P waves and QRS complexes at completely independent rates
A QRS complex wider than 0.12 second with a normal PR interval
questions.why: In a first degree block every impulse still reaches the ventricles, it just takes too long crossing the atrioventricular node, so the PR interval is stretched beyond 0.20 second but each P wave is still followed by its own QRS. Dropped beats, where some P waves are not conducted, describe a second degree block. Complete independence of P waves and QRS complexes is third degree, or complete, block. A wide QRS is a problem in the ventricular conduction system, not at the node.
questions.answerText: A PR interval longer than 0.20 second, with a QRS following every P wave

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What defines a complete heart block on an ECG?
options: P waves are absent and the QRS complexes are irregular in timing
The PR interval lengthens progressively until a QRS is dropped
P waves and QRS complexes occur regularly but at independent rates
Every P wave is followed by a QRS, but the PR interval exceeds 0.20 second
questions.why: In complete block nothing crosses from atria to ventricles, so the sinoatrial node keeps pacing the atria at its own rate while an escape pacemaker below the block paces the ventricles at a slower rate, and the two are unrelated. P waves are present and regular in complete block; they are simply not conducted. A progressively lengthening PR interval before a dropped beat is one form of second degree block. A long but constant PR interval with every beat conducted is first degree block.
questions.answerText: P waves and QRS complexes occur regularly but at independent rates

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An ECG shows 20 small boxes between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
options: 15 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
100 beats per minute
questions.why: Dividing 1500 by 20 small boxes gives 75 beats per minute, and you can check it the long way: 20 boxes times 0.04 second is 0.80 second per beat, and 60 divided by 0.80 is 75. The value of 15 comes from applying the large box rule of 300 divided by boxes to small boxes instead. A rate of 60 would require 25 small boxes between beats. A rate of 100 would require 15 small boxes.
questions.answerText: 75 beats per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: An ECG shows exactly 5 large boxes between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
options: 50 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
75 beats per minute
300 beats per minute
questions.why: Dividing 300 by 5 large boxes gives 60 beats per minute, which makes sense because five large boxes is exactly one second. A rate of 75 would correspond to 4 large boxes. A rate of 50 would correspond to 6 large boxes. The figure of 300 is the rate for a single large box between beats, which would be an extraordinarily fast rhythm.
questions.answerText: 60 beats per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A six second rhythm strip contains 13 QRS complexes. What is the rate, and how is it classified?
options: 130 beats per minute, which is normal
13 beats per minute, which is bradycardia
78 beats per minute, which is normal
130 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
questions.why: Six seconds is a tenth of a minute, so 13 complexes times 10 gives 130 beats per minute, which is above the normal ceiling of 100 and therefore tachycardia. Multiplying by 6 instead of 10 gives 78 and treats the strip as ten seconds long. A rate of 130 cannot be called normal, since the normal range stops at 100. Reporting 13 forgets to scale the six second window up to a full minute.
questions.answerText: 130 beats per minute, which is tachycardia

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: The interval between R waves on a strip is 1.2 seconds. What is the rate, and how is it classified?
options: 50 beats per minute, which is bradycardia
72 beats per minute, which is normal
50 beats per minute, which is normal
120 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
questions.why: Rate is 60 seconds divided by the cycle length, and 60 divided by 1.2 is 50 beats per minute, which falls below 60 and is therefore bradycardia. A rate of 72 would mean a cycle length of about 0.83 second. Calling 50 normal ignores the lower limit of the normal range. The figure of 120 comes from treating 1.2 as if it were the rate rather than the interval.
questions.answerText: 50 beats per minute, which is bradycardia

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A strip shows an upright P wave before every QRS complex, a PR interval of 0.24 second that is identical on every beat, and a rate of 68 beats per minute. How is this classified?
options: Normal sinus rhythm with normal conduction
Sinus bradycardia with an otherwise normal tracing
Sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
Complete heart block with an escape rhythm
questions.why: Every P wave is conducted and the rate is normal, so the rhythm is sinus, but a PR interval of 0.24 second is longer than the 0.20 second limit, which means the impulse is being held too long at the atrioventricular node. Normal sinus rhythm would require a PR interval of 0.20 second or less. Sinus bradycardia would require a rate below 60, and 68 is within range. Complete block would show P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates rather than a fixed PR interval on every beat.
questions.answerText: Sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A strip shows P waves marching along at 82 per minute and QRS complexes at 34 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them. How is this classified?
options: Sinus bradycardia
First degree heart block
Complete heart block
Normal sinus rhythm with a slow ventricular response
questions.why: Two independent rates with no fixed PR interval means no impulse is crossing from atria to ventricles, so the sinoatrial node is pacing the atria while an escape pacemaker below the block drives the ventricles at 34 per minute. Sinus bradycardia would show a single slow rate with a P wave before each QRS. A first degree block still conducts every beat, so atrial and ventricular rates would be identical. Sinus rhythm by definition requires each QRS to be produced by the preceding P wave.
questions.answerText: Complete heart block

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A strip shows a rate of 96 beats per minute, an upright P wave before every QRS, and a constant PR interval of 0.16 second. How is this classified?
options: First degree heart block
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus tachycardia
Normal sinus rhythm
questions.why: All three criteria are met: the beat starts in the sinoatrial node as shown by the upright P wave, conduction is normal as shown by the constant PR interval within 0.12 to 0.20 second, and 96 falls inside the normal range of 60 to 100. Tachycardia would require a rate above 100, and 96 is close but still under the limit. A first degree block would require a PR interval longer than 0.20 second. Bradycardia would require a rate below 60.
questions.answerText: Normal sinus rhythm

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On a strip the P waves are 15 small boxes apart and the R waves are 50 small boxes apart, and no fixed relationship exists between them. State the atrial rate, the ventricular rate, and the rhythm.
options: Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 30, complete heart block
Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 50, first degree heart block
Atrial rate 30, ventricular rate 100, complete heart block
Atrial rate 60, ventricular rate 30, sinus bradycardia
questions.why: Using 1500 divided by small boxes, the atria are firing at 1500 divided by 15, which is 100 per minute, and the ventricles at 1500 divided by 50, which is 30 per minute, and because the two are unrelated the rhythm is complete block with a slow ventricular escape. A ventricular rate of 50 would require 30 small boxes between R waves. Swapping the two rates ignores that the closer spaced waves must be the faster rhythm. Sinus bradycardia requires every P wave to conduct, which cannot be true when the rates differ.
questions.answerText: Atrial rate 100, ventricular rate 30, complete heart block

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A strip shows 25 small boxes between R waves, an upright P wave before every QRS, and a PR interval of 0.32 second on every beat. State the rate and the rhythm.
options: 75 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
48 beats per minute, sinus bradycardia with a complete heart block
60 beats per minute, normal sinus rhythm
60 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block
questions.why: Dividing 1500 by 25 small boxes gives 60 beats per minute, which is the bottom of the normal range and not bradycardia, and the PR interval of 0.32 second is well beyond the 0.20 second limit, so this is sinus rhythm with a first degree block. Calling it normal ignores the prolonged PR interval. A rate of 75 would require 20 small boxes between R waves. A complete block cannot have a fixed PR interval on every beat, and 48 does not follow from 25 small boxes.
questions.answerText: 60 beats per minute, sinus rhythm with a first degree heart block

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: A patient's atria are depolarizing at 75 per minute but the ventricles are contracting at 35 per minute, independently. Which tissue is driving the ventricles, and why is the rate so low?
options: The atrioventricular node above the block, pacing at 40 to 60 per minute
Ventricular muscle itself, which depolarizes spontaneously when stretched
The sinoatrial node, conducting through a slow accessory pathway
A His and Purkinje escape pacemaker, firing at only 20 to 40 per minute
questions.why: When no impulse crosses from the atria, the fastest pacemaker below the block takes over, and ventricular conducting tissue drifts to threshold only 20 to 40 times a minute, which fits the observed 35. If the sinoatrial impulse were reaching the ventricles by any route, the two rates would be linked rather than independent. A junctional escape above the block cannot drive the ventricles, since the block lies between it and the ventricular muscle, and it would also give a faster rate of 40 to 60. Ordinary ventricular muscle has a stable resting potential and no pacemaker current, so it cannot generate a rhythm.
questions.answerText: A His and Purkinje escape pacemaker, firing at only 20 to 40 per minute

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On a strip the R to R interval varies between 20 and 25 small boxes, and each QRS is preceded by an upright P wave with a constant PR interval. What is the range of the heart rate, and does this meet the definition of tachycardia?
options: About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia
About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is tachycardia because the rhythm varies
About 75 to 100 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia
About 100 to 125 beats per minute, which is tachycardia
questions.why: Dividing 1500 by 25 gives 60 and dividing 1500 by 20 gives 75, so the rate swings between 60 and 75, entirely inside the normal range. Tachycardia is defined by rate alone, above 100 beats per minute, so variation in the interval does not make a rhythm fast. A range of 75 to 100 would require intervals of 15 to 20 small boxes. A range of 100 to 125 would require intervals of 12 to 15 small boxes.
questions.answerText: About 60 to 75 beats per minute, which is not tachycardia

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: In a lead II recording, which electrodes serve as the negative and positive poles?
options: Left leg negative, left arm positive
Right leg negative, right arm positive
Left arm negative, right arm positive
Right arm negative, left leg positive
questions.why: Lead II runs from the right arm as the negative pole to the left leg as the positive pole, which points down and to the left, roughly along the path the impulse travels through the heart. Left arm negative with right arm positive is a reversed version of lead I. Left leg negative with left arm positive reverses lead III. The right leg electrode is a ground reference and is not one of the recording poles in the standard limb leads.
questions.answerText: Right arm negative, left leg positive

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: How fast does ECG paper run during a standard recording?
options: 5 mm per second
25 mm per second
50 mm per second
100 mm per second
questions.why: Standard paper speed is 25 mm per second, which is what makes each 1 mm small box equal 0.04 second and each 5 mm large box equal 0.20 second. At 50 mm per second every interval would appear twice as wide and every measured duration would be doubled if you used the standard box values. Speeds of 5 or 100 mm per second are not clinical standards and would make the usual box rules meaningless.
questions.answerText: 25 mm per second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: What is the standard vertical calibration of an ECG recording?
options: 1 mm equals 1 mV
10 mm equals 1 mV
10 mm equals 10 mV
25 mm equals 1 mV
questions.why: Standard calibration makes 10 mm of vertical deflection equal 1 mV, which is why a calibration pulse two large boxes tall appears at the start of a proper recording. If 1 mm equalled 1 mV, every normal QRS would run off the paper. Ten millimeters for 10 mV would flatten normal complexes into near invisibility. The 25 mm figure belongs to the horizontal axis, as paper speed, not the vertical one.
questions.answerText: 10 mm equals 1 mV

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why is lead II usually chosen for a rhythm strip?
options: It records from the sinoatrial node directly, unlike the other limb leads
It is the only lead that is unaffected by skeletal muscle artifact
It is the only limb lead that records atrial activity at all
Its axis lies along the path the impulse takes, so waves are upright
questions.why: Depolarization normally travels from the upper right toward the lower left of the heart, and lead II looks along that same direction, so it produces the clearest upright P wave and the largest QRS, which makes counting and measuring easy. Every limb lead records atrial activity; lead II just shows it best. No surface lead records from the sinoatrial node itself, which is far too small to generate a surface signal. Muscle artifact contaminates any lead if the subject moves or tenses.
questions.answerText: Its axis lies along the path the impulse takes, so waves are upright

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which mechanical event follows the P wave?
options: Atrial contraction
Ventricular contraction
Closure of the semilunar valves
Ventricular filling by passive flow
questions.why: The P wave is atrial depolarization, and the atria contract a few tens of milliseconds later, once Ca2+ has reached the myofilaments. Ventricular contraction follows the QRS, not the P wave, and is separated from atrial contraction by the atrioventricular nodal delay. The semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular ejection, near the end of the T wave. Passive filling happens throughout diastole, before the P wave rather than because of it.
questions.answerText: Atrial contraction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which mechanical event follows the QRS complex?
options: Atrial contraction, with opening of the atrioventricular valves
Ventricular relaxation, with opening of the atrioventricular valves
Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves
Atrial relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves
questions.why: The QRS records ventricular depolarization, and contraction follows within a few tens of milliseconds, raising ventricular pressure above atrial pressure and slamming the atrioventricular valves shut, which produces the first heart sound. Atrial contraction follows the P wave, which comes earlier in the cycle. Ventricular relaxation follows the T wave. The semilunar valves close at the end of ejection rather than at its beginning.
questions.answerText: Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Which mechanical event follows the T wave?
options: Ventricular relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves
Ventricular contraction, with closure of the atrioventricular valves
Atrial contraction, with a rise in atrial pressure
Isovolumetric contraction of the ventricles
questions.why: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, and relaxation follows it, ventricular pressure falls below aortic and pulmonary pressure, the semilunar valves snap shut and produce the second heart sound. Ventricular contraction and atrioventricular valve closure follow the QRS, at the other end of ventricular systole. Atrial contraction follows the P wave. Isovolumetric contraction happens immediately after the QRS, at the start of systole, not after the T wave.
questions.answerText: Ventricular relaxation, with closure of the semilunar valves

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why is conductive gel applied under an ECG electrode?
options: It prevents current from the recorder from reaching the subject's skin
It blocks skeletal muscle signals while allowing cardiac signals through
It amplifies the cardiac signal before it reaches the recorder input
It lowers the electrical resistance between the skin and the electrode
questions.why: Dry skin is a poor conductor, and the voltages reaching the surface are only about a millivolt, so gel lowers the impedance at the contact and stops the signal from being lost in noise. Amplification is done by the recorder, not by the gel. An ECG only records, so no current is being sent into the subject that needs blocking. Gel cannot distinguish one tissue's signals from another's; muscle artifact is reduced by having the subject relax, not by the gel.
questions.answerText: It lowers the electrical resistance between the skin and the electrode

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On your subject's lead II strip, the PR interval measures 4 small boxes. What is its duration and is it normal?
options: 0.16 second, which is prolonged
0.04 second, which is normal
0.40 second, which is prolonged
0.16 second, which is normal
questions.why: Four small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.16 second, comfortably inside the normal PR range of 0.12 to 0.20 second. Calling 0.16 second prolonged applies the wrong cutoff, since prolongation begins above 0.20 second. Reporting 0.04 second uses the value of a single box instead of four. Reporting 0.40 second multiplies by 0.10 second per box, which is not the standard grid value.
questions.answerText: 0.16 second, which is normal

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: You measure a QRS complex spanning 2 small boxes. What is its duration and what does it tell you?
options: 0.08 second, indicating that ventricular activation is abnormally slow
0.20 second, indicating a bundle branch block is present
0.02 second, indicating an unusually fast ventricular rate
0.08 second, indicating normal ventricular conduction
questions.why: Two small boxes is 0.08 second, which is under the 0.12 second ceiling, so the impulse is reaching the ventricular muscle through the fast bundle branch and Purkinje network as it should. A duration under the normal limit cannot indicate slow activation. Reading 2 boxes as 0.20 second uses 0.10 second per box, which is not the standard grid value. QRS duration measures how long ventricular depolarization takes, not how often it happens, so it says nothing about rate.
questions.answerText: 0.08 second, indicating normal ventricular conduction

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: You measure the QT interval as 9 small boxes. What is its duration?
options: 0.09 second
0.18 second
0.36 second
0.45 second
questions.why: Nine small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.36 second, a normal QT interval at an ordinary resting rate. Reporting 0.09 second treats each box as 0.01 second. Reporting 0.18 second uses 0.02 second per box. Reporting 0.45 second uses 0.05 second per box, which is close to the correct value but not the standard grid.
questions.answerText: 0.36 second

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: During a simultaneous ECG and heart sound recording, when does the first heart sound occur?
options: At the peak of the T wave, as the ventricles begin to relax
Midway between the T wave and the next P wave
Just after the P wave, as the atria begin to contract
Just after the QRS complex, as the atrioventricular valves close
questions.why: The first heart sound is the atrioventricular valves closing, which happens as soon as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, a few tens of milliseconds after the QRS depolarizes the ventricles. Atrial contraction after the P wave is quiet in a healthy heart. Valve closure at the end of the T wave produces the second heart sound, not the first. The gap between the T wave and the next P wave is diastole, when both valve sets are quiet.
questions.answerText: Just after the QRS complex, as the atrioventricular valves close

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On the same recording, when does the second heart sound occur?
options: At the start of the QRS complex, as the ventricles depolarize
In the middle of the PR interval, as the impulse crosses the atrioventricular node
At the end of the T wave, as the semilunar valves close
Just before the P wave, as the ventricles finish filling
questions.why: The second heart sound is aortic and pulmonary valve closure, which happens when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the end of ejection, and that coincides closely with the end of the T wave. The QRS marks the start of ventricular systole, which is where the first heart sound belongs. Nodal conduction during the PR interval is silent, both electrically at the surface and mechanically. The interval before the P wave is late diastole, when the ventricles are filling quietly.
questions.answerText: At the end of the T wave, as the semilunar valves close

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Your subject's recording shows a fuzzy, high frequency baseline that disappears when the subject stops talking and relaxes the arms. What is the source?
options: Depolarization of the atrioventricular node reaching the surface
Repolarization of the atria becoming visible in this lead
A paper speed that has been set too high for the recording
Electrical activity from nearby skeletal muscle
questions.why: Skeletal muscle generates its own action potentials, and any contracting muscle near an electrode adds a rapid irregular signal on top of the cardiac trace, which is why subjects are asked to lie still and relax. The atrioventricular node is far too small to produce any surface signal at all. Atrial repolarization is a slow low amplitude event hidden inside the QRS, not a source of high frequency noise. Changing paper speed stretches or compresses the trace horizontally but does not add noise.
questions.answerText: Electrical activity from nearby skeletal muscle

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: Why does each wave of the ECG come slightly before the mechanical event it is associated with?
options: The mechanical event begins first and the electrode records it afterward
The recorder introduces a fixed electronic delay in the mechanical channel
Excitation contraction coupling takes time before force develops
Blood must move through the chambers before the signal reaches the skin
questions.why: Excitation contraction coupling has real steps: the action potential opens L-type Ca2+ channels, that Ca2+ triggers release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ binds troponin, and only then do cross bridges generate force, so contraction always lags depolarization by a few tens of milliseconds. The delay is physiological, not an artifact of the recording equipment. The electrical signal reaches the skin almost instantly, well before blood has moved anywhere. Reversing the order would mean muscle contracts before it is excited, which does not happen in cardiac muscle.
questions.answerText: Excitation contraction coupling takes time before force develops

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: On your strip, the interval from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave measures 10 small boxes. State the duration and what is happening mechanically at the end of that interval.
options: 0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to contract as the atrioventricular valves close
0.10 second, and the atria are contracting to complete ventricular filling
1.00 second, and the next beat is beginning at the sinoatrial node
0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to relax as the semilunar valves close
questions.why: Ten small boxes at 0.04 second each is 0.40 second, and that interval, the QT, covers ventricular depolarization through the end of repolarization, so its end marks the point where the ventricles stop generating force, pressure falls, and the semilunar valves close. Contraction and atrioventricular valve closure happen at the beginning of the interval, right after the QRS. Atrial contraction belongs to the P wave, well before the QRS. Reporting 1.00 second would require 25 small boxes.
questions.answerText: 0.40 second, and the ventricles are beginning to relax as the semilunar valves close

questions.topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology
questions.q: You record a subject at rest and again immediately after exercise. The heart rate rises from 60 to 150 beats per minute. Which part of the cardiac cycle shortens the most, and what is the consequence for the ventricles?
options: The PR interval shortens the most, so atrial contraction is lost
The QRS shortens the most, so ventricular activation becomes uneven
Diastole shortens the most, so there is much less time for ventricular filling
Systole shortens the most, so there is less time for ejection
