questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Blood flow in most normal vessels has what character?
options: Turbulent, with chaotic mixing across the vessel
Pulsatile only in veins and steady in arteries
Laminar, with concentric layers sliding past each other
Stationary during diastole and moving only in systole
questions.why: Normal flow is laminar, meaning the blood moves in concentric shells with the fastest layer in the center and the slowest against the wall, and this silent pattern is why a healthy artery makes no sound through a stethoscope. Turbulence appears only when velocity is high or a vessel is narrowed, and it is what makes bruits and Korotkoff sounds audible. Pulsatility is greatest in arteries and is damped out by the time blood reaches veins. Flow in arteries continues during diastole because elastic recoil keeps pushing.
questions.answerText: Laminar, with concentric layers sliding past each other

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Total peripheral resistance refers to what?
options: The resistance of a single arteriole
The combined resistance of the pulmonary circulation
The combined resistance of the entire systemic circulation
The resistance offered by the aortic valve during ejection
questions.why: Total peripheral resistance is the sum effect of every systemic vessel taken together, and because arterioles dominate that sum, changes in arteriolar tone are what move it. A single arteriole contributes only a tiny fraction of the total. The pulmonary circuit has its own resistance, which is far lower than the systemic value. Valve resistance affects ejection from the ventricle but is not part of the peripheral circuit.
questions.answerText: The combined resistance of the entire systemic circulation

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: An arteriole constricts so that its radius falls to half its original value. By what factor does its resistance change?
options: Resistance increases fourfold
Resistance increases sixteenfold
Resistance increases twofold
Resistance increases eightfold
questions.why: Resistance goes as 1 over radius to the fourth power, so cutting radius in half multiplies resistance by two to the fourth power, which is sixteen. A fourfold answer comes from squaring instead of raising to the fourth. A twofold answer treats radius as if it acted the way length does, in simple proportion. An eightfold answer comes from cubing. This steep dependence is exactly why arterioles are such powerful flow regulators.
questions.answerText: Resistance increases sixteenfold

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A vascular bed has a pressure gradient of 100 mmHg across it and a resistance of 20 mmHg per L/min. What is the flow?
options: 2 L/min
5 L/min
50 L/min
20 L/min
questions.why: Flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance, so 100 divided by 20 gives 5 L/min, a value close to a normal resting cardiac output. Twenty comes from dividing the gradient by five instead. Fifty comes from misplacing a decimal. Two comes from dividing resistance into the wrong quantity, that is, inverting the ratio.
questions.answerText: 5 L/min

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A surgeon replaces a segment of artery with a graft that is twice as long but has the same radius. What happens to the resistance of that segment?
options: It is halved
It quadruples
It doubles
It increases sixteenfold
questions.why: Length is in the numerator to the first power, so doubling the length doubles the resistance of that segment. Quadrupling and a sixteenfold rise would require squaring or raising to the fourth power, which applies to radius, not length. Halving would happen only if the tube got shorter. This is why the radius of the graft matters far more than its length when a surgeon chooses one.
questions.answerText: It doubles

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient with polycythemia has a hematocrit of 65 percent instead of the usual 45 percent. What is the direct effect on vascular resistance?
options: Resistance falls because viscosity falls
Resistance is unchanged because viscosity has no effect
Resistance rises because viscosity rises
Resistance rises because vessel length increases
questions.why: A higher red cell fraction makes blood thicker, and viscosity sits in the numerator of the resistance equation, so resistance climbs and the heart must generate more pressure to move the same flow. Viscosity falling would require fewer red cells, which is the anemia picture, not polycythemia. Viscosity clearly does affect resistance, which is why very high hematocrits raise cardiovascular risk. Vessel length does not change in this condition.
questions.answerText: Resistance rises because viscosity rises

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: An arteriole dilates so that its radius doubles while the pressure gradient across it stays the same. What happens to flow through it?
options: Flow increases twofold
Flow increases fourfold
Flow increases sixteenfold
Flow increases eightfold
questions.why: Doubling radius cuts resistance to one sixteenth, and with the pressure gradient held constant flow is inversely proportional to resistance, so flow rises by a factor of sixteen. Twofold treats radius as a first power term. Fourfold uses the square, which would be right if flow followed cross sectional area alone. Eightfold uses the cube. The fourth power is what makes small dilations so effective at redirecting blood.
questions.answerText: Flow increases sixteenfold

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which single change would raise flow through a vessel the most, assuming everything else is held constant?
options: Doubling the pressure gradient
Halving the vessel length
Halving the viscosity
Doubling the radius
questions.why: Doubling radius raises flow sixteenfold because radius enters to the fourth power, while each of the other three changes only doubles flow. Doubling the gradient doubles flow directly. Halving length halves resistance and so doubles flow. Halving viscosity does the same. All three are real effects, just far weaker than the radius term, which is the point of the fourth power relationship.
questions.answerText: Doubling the radius

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The pressure gradient across a vascular bed is tripled while its resistance is held constant. What happens to flow?
options: Flow is unchanged because resistance is unchanged
Flow increases ninefold
Flow increases by one third
Flow triples
questions.why: Flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient when resistance is fixed, so a threefold rise in gradient gives a threefold rise in flow. A ninefold answer squares the gradient, but no exponent applies to the pressure term. A one third rise inverts the relationship. Flow depends on both terms, so holding resistance constant does not freeze flow, it simply lets the gradient act alone.
questions.answerText: Flow triples

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In an inflamed tissue an arteriole dilates so that its radius doubles, and at the same time the mean arterial pressure feeding it falls slightly so the pressure gradient drops to half. What is the net change in flow through that arteriole?
options: Flow rises about eightfold
Flow rises about thirty twofold
Flow rises about twofold
Flow falls to about one eighth
questions.why: Doubling the radius drops resistance to one sixteenth, which alone would raise flow sixteenfold, and halving the gradient then multiplies that by one half, giving a net eightfold rise. Thirty two comes from multiplying by two instead of dividing. A twofold answer ignores the fourth power and treats radius linearly. A fall to one eighth would require the radius change to work against flow rather than for it. The lesson is that local dilation easily overwhelms a modest fall in driving pressure.
questions.answerText: Flow rises about eightfold

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A vessel constricts so its radius is halved, and at the same time the pressure gradient across it is doubled. Compared with the starting condition, flow through the vessel is now what?
options: One eighth of the original flow
One half of the original flow
One sixteenth of the original flow
Twice the original flow
questions.why: Halving radius raises resistance sixteenfold, so flow would fall to one sixteenth on its own, and doubling the gradient then multiplies that by two, leaving one eighth. One sixteenth ignores the doubled gradient. One half accounts for the gradient but treats radius as a first power term. Twice the original ignores the radius change entirely. Doubling the driving pressure cannot rescue flow through a vessel that has narrowed this much, which is the core problem in arterial stenosis.
questions.answerText: One eighth of the original flow

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient becomes severely dehydrated. Hematocrit rises from 45 to 60 percent while the heart continues to pump the same cardiac output. Predict the effect on mean arterial pressure and the reason.
options: Mean arterial pressure falls, because higher viscosity lowers resistance
Mean arterial pressure rises, because higher viscosity raises total peripheral resistance
Mean arterial pressure is unchanged, because viscosity does not enter the resistance equation
Mean arterial pressure rises, because the vessels have lengthened
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is the product of cardiac output and total peripheral resistance, so if output is held constant and viscosity drives resistance up, pressure must rise. Higher viscosity cannot lower resistance, since it appears in the numerator. Viscosity does enter the equation and is one of its three terms alongside length and radius. Vessel length is essentially fixed in an adult and is not what changed here. In real dehydration, volume loss usually pulls pressure down at the same time, so the viscosity effect partly offsets rather than dominates.
questions.answerText: Mean arterial pressure rises, because higher viscosity raises total peripheral resistance

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During exercise, many arterioles in skeletal muscle dilate at once, adding a large number of low resistance channels in parallel to the circuit. If cardiac output did not change at all, what would happen to total peripheral resistance and to mean arterial pressure?
options: Total peripheral resistance would fall and mean arterial pressure would fall
Total peripheral resistance would fall and mean arterial pressure would rise
Total peripheral resistance would rise and mean arterial pressure would rise
Total peripheral resistance would be unchanged because the vessels are in parallel
questions.why: Adding pathways in parallel always lowers the resistance of the whole circuit, because blood gains more routes to travel, and with output fixed a lower resistance means a lower pressure. Pressure cannot rise while resistance falls unless output rises with it, which is exactly what the body does during real exercise. Resistance does not rise, since dilation widens the vessels. Parallel arrangement is the reason resistance falls, not a reason it stays fixed.
questions.answerText: Total peripheral resistance would fall and mean arterial pressure would fall

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which vessels serve as the capacitance vessels of the circulation?
options: The veins
The arterioles
The capillaries
The elastic arteries
questions.why: Veins are thin walled and highly distensible, so they hold roughly two thirds of the total blood volume at low pressure and act as the reservoir the circulation draws on. Elastic arteries hold only a small volume at high pressure and act as buffers rather than reservoirs. Arterioles are the resistance vessels. Capillaries hold a very small fraction of blood volume at any instant and exist for exchange.
questions.answerText: The veins

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Exchange of gases, nutrients, and fluid between blood and tissue takes place mainly across which vessels?
options: The muscular arteries
The arterioles
The capillaries
The large veins
questions.why: Capillary walls are a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, which is thin enough for diffusion and filtration to occur across it, and they are so numerous that nearly every cell sits within a short diffusion distance of one. Arterioles have a smooth muscle coat that makes them too thick for meaningful exchange, though some exchange does begin there. Muscular arteries and large veins have multilayered walls built for conduction and capacitance, not transfer.
questions.answerText: The capillaries

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which vessels smooth the pulsatile output of the heart into a steadier forward flow?
options: The venules
The large elastic arteries
The capillaries
The arterioles
questions.why: The aorta and its large branches stretch during systole to store some of the ejected volume, then recoil during diastole and push that blood onward, which keeps flow going between beats. Arterioles control how much blood enters a tissue but do not store the stroke volume. Capillaries and venules operate at pressures too low and too steady for buffering to be their role, and by the time blood reaches them the pulse has already been damped out.
questions.answerText: The large elastic arteries

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which vessel type has the greatest total cross sectional area when all of its vessels are added together?
options: The capillaries
The arterioles
The aorta
The venae cavae
questions.why: There are billions of capillaries, and although each one is tiny, their summed cross sectional area is far larger than any other segment, which is why blood velocity is slowest there. The aorta has the largest single lumen but there is only one of it. Arterioles are numerous but far fewer than capillaries. The venae cavae have wide lumens but again there are only two, so their combined area stays well below the capillary total.
questions.answerText: The capillaries

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: At rest, roughly what fraction of the total blood volume is held in the systemic veins and venules?
options: About two thirds
About one third
About one tenth
Nearly all of it
questions.why: Roughly sixty to seventy percent of blood sits in the systemic venous side at any moment, which is what makes venoconstriction such an effective way to raise venous return. One tenth is closer to what the systemic arteries hold. One third understates the venous share considerably. Nearly all of it would leave nothing for the arteries, capillaries, heart, and pulmonary circulation, which together account for the remaining third.
questions.answerText: About two thirds

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Blood velocity is lowest in which part of the circulation?
options: The pulmonary artery
The aorta
The venae cavae
The capillaries
questions.why: Velocity equals flow divided by total cross sectional area, and since the capillary bed has by far the largest summed area, blood creeps through it, which gives red cells the seconds they need to unload oxygen. The aorta has the smallest cross sectional area of these choices and therefore the highest velocity. The venae cavae are wide but their combined area is far smaller than the capillary bed, so velocity picks back up there. The pulmonary artery behaves like the aorta in this respect.
questions.answerText: The capillaries

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The smooth muscle in the wall of an arteriole allows that vessel to do what?
options: Store blood at low pressure as a reservoir
Recoil elastically to sustain diastolic pressure
Allow proteins to cross into the interstitium
Change its radius and therefore the resistance it offers
questions.why: Arterioles carry a thick ring of smooth muscle relative to their small lumen, so contraction and relaxation of that muscle changes radius, and because resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, tiny changes there have large effects on flow. Storage at low pressure is the venous role. Protein movement across the wall belongs to capillaries, and even there it is limited. Elastic recoil is the property of the large conducting arteries.
questions.answerText: Change its radius and therefore the resistance it offers

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which vessels collect blood leaving the capillaries and are the first vessels of the venous side?
options: The venules
The metarterioles
The muscular arteries
The lymphatic capillaries
questions.why: Venules receive blood directly from capillaries, converge into veins, and because their walls are still thin, the smallest of them continue to allow some exchange and are a common site of white cell exit during inflammation. Metarterioles sit upstream of capillaries, on the arterial side. Muscular arteries are well upstream and carry blood toward tissues. Lymphatic capillaries pick up interstitial fluid rather than blood, and they drain to the lymphatic system, not into venules.
questions.answerText: The venules

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A drug produces a large fall in total peripheral resistance with almost no change in how much blood the venous system holds. Which vessels does it most likely act on?
options: Large veins
Capillaries
Arterioles
Elastic arteries
questions.why: Arterioles set most of total peripheral resistance, so a drug that lowers resistance sharply without shifting stored volume is acting there. A drug acting on large veins would move stored volume and change venous return, which is not what was described. Capillaries have no smooth muscle of their own and cannot be dilated directly. Elastic arteries are already wide and low resistance, so relaxing them changes buffering more than resistance.
questions.answerText: Arterioles

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Sympathetic stimulation causes venoconstriction. What is the immediate effect on the circulation?
options: Blood is shifted out of the venous reservoir toward the heart, raising venous return
Blood pools in the veins, lowering venous return
Capillary exchange surface area increases
Total peripheral resistance rises steeply because veins are the resistance vessels
questions.why: Squeezing the capacitance vessels reduces the volume they can hold, so blood is displaced forward into the right heart and venous return rises, which then raises stroke volume through the length tension relationship. Pooling is what happens when veins relax or when gravity works against return, not when they constrict. Venoconstriction does not add exchange surface. Veins contribute little to total peripheral resistance because their radii stay large, so constricting them changes capacitance far more than resistance.
questions.answerText: Blood is shifted out of the venous reservoir toward the heart, raising venous return

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: With aging, elastin in the aortic wall is replaced by stiffer collagen. What happens to pulse pressure?
options: Pulse pressure narrows, because the stiff aorta absorbs more of the stroke volume
Pulse pressure is unchanged, because buffering is a venous function
Pulse pressure widens, because the stiff aorta cannot buffer the stroke volume
Pulse pressure narrows, because arteriolar resistance falls with age
questions.why: A compliant aorta expands to accept part of the stroke volume, holding systolic pressure down and then recoiling to hold diastolic pressure up, so when it stiffens systolic rises and diastolic falls and the gap between them widens. A stiff vessel absorbs less, not more. Buffering is an arterial property and not a venous one. Arteriolar resistance tends to rise rather than fall with age, and in any case resistance mainly sets mean pressure rather than the size of the swing.
questions.answerText: Pulse pressure widens, because the stiff aorta cannot buffer the stroke volume

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Why does the very slow velocity of blood in the capillaries matter functionally?
options: It prevents red cells from being damaged by shear
It allows the capillary bed to store a large reserve of blood at low pressure between beats
It gives enough time for diffusion of gases and nutrients to reach equilibrium
It keeps flow turbulent so mixing is complete
questions.why: A red cell spends roughly a second in a systemic capillary, and diffusion needs that dwell time for oxygen to leave and carbon dioxide to enter before the cell moves on. Shear protection is not the reason velocity is low, though the low speed is gentle. Capillaries hold only about five percent of blood volume, so they are not a reservoir. Flow at these low velocities is laminar, not turbulent, and diffusion rather than mixing is what accomplishes exchange.
questions.answerText: It gives enough time for diffusion of gases and nutrients to reach equilibrium

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Across which vascular segment does mean pressure fall the most steeply?
options: The aorta and large arteries
The arterioles
The capillaries
The large veins
questions.why: Mean pressure drops from roughly 90 mmHg at the start of the arterioles to about 35 mmHg at the capillary entrance, the largest fall anywhere in the circuit, because that is where resistance is concentrated. The aorta and large arteries lose only a few mmHg over their length. Capillaries drop pressure further but over a smaller range. Large veins operate near right atrial pressure already and have little left to lose.
questions.answerText: The arterioles

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: By the time blood reaches the capillaries, the pulse produced by ventricular ejection has largely disappeared. What accounts for this?
options: The heart stops ejecting blood between beats so no pulse is generated
Elastic arteries store and release the pulse and arterioles damp what remains
Capillary walls are too thin to transmit a pressure wave
Venous valves block the pulse from moving forward
questions.why: The compliance of the large arteries absorbs the peak of each ejection and releases it during diastole, and the high resistance of the arterioles then smooths what is left, so capillary flow is nearly continuous, which protects the fragile exchange vessels. The heart does eject intermittently, but that is the source of the pulse rather than the reason it disappears. Capillary wall thinness does not filter pressure waves. Venous valves prevent backflow on the venous side and play no part in damping the arterial pulse.
questions.answerText: Elastic arteries store and release the pulse and arterioles damp what remains

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A clinician wants to lower the pressure the left ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Which vessels should the drug target?
options: Arterioles, to lower total peripheral resistance
Capillaries, to increase filtration
Large veins, to increase capacitance
Pulmonary veins, to lower left atrial pressure
questions.why: The load against which the left ventricle ejects is set mainly by arterial pressure, and arterial pressure is set by cardiac output and arteriolar resistance, so dilating arterioles is the direct route. Dilating large veins increases capacitance and lowers the volume returning to the heart, which reduces preload rather than the ejection load. Capillaries cannot be dilated directly and changing filtration there does not change ejection pressure. Lowering left atrial pressure affects filling, again a preload effect.
questions.answerText: Arterioles, to lower total peripheral resistance

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: An 80 year old has a blood pressure of 170 over 70 while a 25 year old has 120 over 80. Which explanation best accounts for the older reading, and what follows from it?
options: Venous capacitance has increased, so more blood is stored on the venous side and both systolic and pulse pressure climb as a result
A stiff aorta buffers poorly, so systolic rises and diastolic falls, widening pulse pressure and raising ventricular workload
Arteriolar dilation has lowered resistance, so systolic rises while diastolic falls
Capillary exchange has slowed, so pressure backs up into the arteries
questions.why: Pulse pressure is 100 mmHg in the older person and 40 in the younger, and a loss of aortic compliance explains both halves at once, since an unbuffered stroke volume drives systolic up and the missing recoil lets diastolic sag. Greater venous capacitance would reduce the volume reaching the heart and lower rather than raise systolic pressure. Arteriolar dilation lowers mean pressure and would not push systolic to 170. Capillary exchange operates far downstream and does not raise arterial pressure by backing up.
questions.answerText: A stiff aorta buffers poorly, so systolic rises and diastolic falls, widening pulse pressure and raising ventricular workload

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person loses one liter of blood. Sympathetic outflow constricts the veins strongly. Trace the consequence through to stroke volume.
options: Venous resistance rises sharply, so venous return falls and stroke volume falls further
Venous capacitance rises, so still more blood is stored in the peripheral veins, venous return falls further, end diastolic volume drops, and stroke volume falls with it
Venous capacitance falls, so stored blood is displaced forward, venous return and end diastolic volume are partly restored, and stroke volume is defended
Capillary pressure rises, so filtration adds volume to the blood and stroke volume rises above normal
questions.why: Because the veins normally hold most of the blood volume, tightening them recruits that reserve and pushes it toward the heart, which raises filling and, by the length tension relationship, protects stroke volume after a moderate bleed. Capacitance falls rather than rises during sympathetic activation. Veins are wide, so constricting them changes stored volume much more than resistance, and their small resistance change does not block return. In hemorrhage, capillary pressure falls and fluid moves from interstitium into blood, which helps, but it is a reabsorption effect, not filtration.
questions.answerText: Venous capacitance falls, so stored blood is displaced forward, venous return and end diastolic volume are partly restored, and stroke volume is defended

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The aorta has a cross sectional area of about 4 square centimeters and blood moves through it at about 40 centimeters per second. The capillary bed has a total cross sectional area roughly 700 times greater. Approximately how fast does blood move in a capillary, and why?
options: About 0.06 centimeters per second, because the same flow is spread over 700 times the area
About 40 centimeters per second, because flow must be conserved
About 700 centimeters per second, because narrow tubes speed blood up
About 4 centimeters per second, because velocity falls in proportion to vessel number
questions.why: Total flow is the same through every segment in series, and velocity equals flow divided by total cross sectional area, so dividing 40 by 700 gives roughly 0.06 centimeters per second, which is about a millimeter every two seconds. Keeping velocity at 40 confuses conservation of flow with conservation of velocity, which are not the same thing. Speeding up would happen if the total area shrank, as it does when capillaries converge back into veins. Dividing by vessel number rather than total area ignores how small each capillary lumen is.
questions.answerText: About 0.06 centimeters per second, because the same flow is spread over 700 times the area

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Two drugs are compared. Drug A dilates only arterioles. Drug B dilates only large veins. Which statement correctly separates their main effects?
options: Drug A mainly lowers total peripheral resistance and afterload, while Drug B mainly increases capacitance and lowers preload
Both drugs act mainly by lowering total peripheral resistance, since both dilate vessels
Drug A mainly increases capacitance and lowers preload, while Drug B mainly lowers total peripheral resistance
Both drugs act mainly by increasing capillary exchange surface area
questions.why: Arterioles set resistance because of their small radius and muscular walls, so dilating them drops arterial pressure and the load on the ventricle, while veins hold most of the blood volume, so dilating them lets blood pool and reduces the volume returning to fill the heart. Swapping the two reverses the roles of resistance and capacitance vessels. Dilation does not have the same consequence everywhere, because what matters is which property that segment dominates. Neither drug changes exchange surface area, which is set by how many capillaries are perfused rather than by venous or arteriolar diameter alone.
questions.answerText: Drug A mainly lowers total peripheral resistance and afterload, while Drug B mainly increases capacitance and lowers preload

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Systolic pressure is defined as what?
options: The average arterial pressure over one full cardiac cycle
The lowest arterial pressure reached during ventricular relaxation
The peak arterial pressure reached during ventricular ejection
The difference between the highest and lowest arterial pressures
questions.why: Systolic pressure is the high point of the arterial pressure curve, produced when the ventricle ejects blood into an aorta that is already full. The lowest point is diastolic pressure. The average over the cycle is mean arterial pressure, which sits nearer the diastolic value than the systolic one. The difference between high and low is pulse pressure, a derived number rather than a measured one.
questions.answerText: The peak arterial pressure reached during ventricular ejection

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Diastolic pressure represents what?
options: The pressure measured inside the ventricle while it is filling with blood from the atrium
The lowest arterial pressure, reached just before the next ejection
The average pressure driving flow to the tissues
The pressure in the right atrium between beats
questions.why: Diastolic pressure is the trough of the arterial curve, reached after blood has been draining into the tissues throughout diastole and just before the next stroke volume arrives, and it is sustained by elastic recoil of the large arteries. Ventricular filling pressure is a much lower number measured inside the chamber, not in the artery. The average driving pressure is mean arterial pressure. Right atrial pressure is close to zero and is the downstream end of the systemic circuit.
questions.answerText: The lowest arterial pressure, reached just before the next ejection

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Pulse pressure is calculated how?
options: Systolic pressure plus diastolic pressure, divided by two
Systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure
Diastolic pressure plus one third of systolic pressure
Mean arterial pressure minus right atrial pressure
questions.why: Pulse pressure is simply the size of the pressure swing within one cardiac cycle, so it is the systolic value minus the diastolic value, and it reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance. Averaging the two would give a rough midpoint, not the swing. The third option describes an incorrect version of the mean arterial pressure estimate. The last expression is the driving pressure for systemic flow, not the pulse.
questions.answerText: Systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Mean arterial pressure is best described as what?
options: The simple midpoint between systolic and diastolic pressure
The highest pressure the arteries experience during ejection
The pressure measured at the moment the first Korotkoff sound appears
The time weighted average arterial pressure across the whole cardiac cycle
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure averages pressure over time, and because diastole lasts longer than systole at rest, that average sits closer to the diastolic value than to the midpoint. The simple midpoint would overestimate it. The first Korotkoff sound marks systolic pressure. The highest pressure during ejection is also the systolic value. Mean arterial pressure is the number that matters most for tissue perfusion, which is why it is worth computing rather than eyeballing.
questions.answerText: The time weighted average arterial pressure across the whole cardiac cycle

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which expression estimates mean arterial pressure from a cuff reading?
options: Systolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure
Systolic pressure minus one third of the diastolic pressure
Diastolic pressure plus two thirds of the systolic pressure
Diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure
questions.why: The standard estimate starts at the diastolic floor and adds one third of the swing, because the heart spends about two thirds of each resting cycle in diastole. Starting from systolic and adding would put the estimate above the peak pressure, which is impossible. The remaining two expressions mix the terms in ways that have no physiological meaning and give values well outside the real range.
questions.answerText: Diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Why does mean arterial pressure lie closer to diastolic pressure than to systolic pressure at rest?
options: Diastole occupies a longer portion of each cardiac cycle than systole
Diastolic pressure is measured more accurately than systolic pressure
Arterial compliance is greater during systole than during diastole
Systolic pressure is only reached in the aorta and not in other arteries
questions.why: Because the mean is weighted by time, and roughly two thirds of a resting cycle is diastole, the average is pulled down toward the diastolic value. Measurement accuracy has nothing to do with where the true average sits. Compliance is a property of the vessel wall and does not switch between phases of the cycle in a way that would shift the average. Systolic pressure is reached throughout the arterial tree, and in fact peaks slightly higher in peripheral arteries than in the aorta.
questions.answerText: Diastole occupies a longer portion of each cardiac cycle than systole

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Mean arterial pressure is determined by the product of which two variables?
options: Stroke volume and pulse pressure
Heart rate and arterial compliance
Cardiac output and total peripheral resistance
Blood volume and venous capacitance
questions.why: Rearranging the flow equation for the whole systemic circuit gives pressure as flow times resistance, so mean arterial pressure is cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance. Stroke volume and compliance set the size of the pulse rather than the mean. Heart rate acts only through its contribution to cardiac output. Blood volume and capacitance influence how much blood returns to the heart, so they affect pressure indirectly through cardiac output rather than being the two direct terms.
questions.answerText: Cardiac output and total peripheral resistance

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which pressure best represents the driving force for perfusion of most organs?
options: Systolic pressure
Mean arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
Diastolic pressure
questions.why: Organs are perfused throughout the whole cardiac cycle, so what matters is the average pressure over that cycle, which is mean arterial pressure. Systolic pressure describes only the peak and overstates perfusion. Diastolic pressure describes only the trough, though it is the relevant one for the coronary arteries, which fill during diastole. Pulse pressure describes the size of the swing and says nothing about the average level.
questions.answerText: Mean arterial pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A blood pressure reads 120 over 80 mmHg. What is the mean arterial pressure?
options: About 93 mmHg
100 mmHg
About 87 mmHg
40 mmHg
questions.why: Pulse pressure is 120 minus 80, or 40 mmHg, and one third of 40 is about 13, so the mean is 80 plus 13, roughly 93 mmHg. One hundred is the simple midpoint, which overestimates because it ignores the longer duration of diastole. Eighty seven comes from subtracting rather than adding the third. Forty is the pulse pressure itself, not the mean.
questions.answerText: About 93 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient's blood pressure is 150 over 90 mmHg. What is the mean arterial pressure?
options: 120 mmHg
60 mmHg
100 mmHg
110 mmHg
questions.why: The pulse pressure is 60 mmHg, one third of that is 20, and adding 20 to the diastolic value of 90 gives 110 mmHg. One hundred twenty is the midpoint between the two readings and overestimates the true mean. One hundred comes from adding only ten. Sixty is the pulse pressure, which describes the swing rather than the average.
questions.answerText: 110 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A reading of 100 over 70 mmHg gives what pulse pressure?
options: 30 mmHg
80 mmHg
170 mmHg
10 mmHg
questions.why: Pulse pressure is the systolic value minus the diastolic value, so 100 minus 70 gives 30 mmHg, which is on the low side and would suggest a reduced stroke volume. Eighty is the mean arterial pressure for this reading, obtained by adding one third of 30 to 70. One hundred seventy is the sum of the two numbers, which has no physiological meaning. Ten is one third of the pulse pressure, an intermediate step in the mean calculation rather than the answer.
questions.answerText: 30 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Cardiac output is 5 L/min and total peripheral resistance is 20 mmHg per L/min. What is the mean arterial pressure?
options: 4 mmHg
100 mmHg
25 mmHg
50 mmHg
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance, so 5 times 20 gives 100 mmHg, a normal adult value. Four comes from dividing output into resistance, which inverts the relationship and would give a resistance rather than a pressure. Twenty five comes from adding rather than multiplying. Fifty halves the correct product for no reason the equation supports.
questions.answerText: 100 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Stroke volume increases while heart rate and total peripheral resistance stay the same. What happens to pulse pressure?
options: Pulse pressure is unchanged because resistance did not change
Pulse pressure narrows
Pulse pressure widens
Pulse pressure becomes equal to mean arterial pressure
questions.why: A larger stroke volume forced into the same arterial tree raises the systolic peak more than it raises the diastolic trough, so the swing between them grows. Narrowing would follow from a smaller stroke volume, as happens in hemorrhage. Resistance mainly sets the mean level rather than the size of the swing, so leaving it unchanged does not freeze pulse pressure. Pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure are different quantities and there is no reason for them to converge.
questions.answerText: Pulse pressure widens

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Total peripheral resistance doubles while cardiac output is held constant. What happens to mean arterial pressure?
options: It doubles
It falls by half
It is unchanged
It rises fourfold
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is the product of cardiac output and total peripheral resistance, so doubling one term while holding the other fixed doubles the product. A fall would require resistance to drop, not rise. It cannot stay unchanged, since resistance is one of only two terms in the relationship. A fourfold rise would require both terms to double, but output was held constant here.
questions.answerText: It doubles

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A reading of 90 over 60 mmHg gives what mean arterial pressure?
options: 75 mmHg
70 mmHg
80 mmHg
30 mmHg
questions.why: Pulse pressure is 30 mmHg, one third of that is 10, and 60 plus 10 gives 70 mmHg, which is at the low end of the range that keeps organs perfused. Seventy five is the midpoint of the two readings. Eighty adds twenty instead of ten. Thirty is the pulse pressure by itself.
questions.answerText: 70 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Two patients each have a systolic pressure of 160 mmHg. The first reads 160 over 100 and the second reads 160 over 70. Compare their mean arterial pressures.
options: The first has a mean of 120 mmHg and the second 100 mmHg, so the first has the higher mean perfusion pressure
The first has a mean of 100 mmHg and the second 120 mmHg, so the second has the higher mean perfusion pressure
Both have a mean of 130 mmHg because their systolic pressures are the same
The second has the higher mean because its pulse pressure is wider
questions.why: For the first, pulse pressure is 60 and one third of that is 20, giving 100 plus 20, or 120 mmHg. For the second, pulse pressure is 90 and one third is 30, giving 70 plus 30, or 100 mmHg. Identical systolic values therefore hide a 20 mmHg difference in mean pressure, which is why the mean is worth calculating. A wide pulse pressure does not raise the mean, since it comes here from a lower diastolic floor. Assuming equal means because the peaks match ignores the fact that diastole dominates the average.
questions.answerText: The first has a mean of 120 mmHg and the second 100 mmHg, so the first has the higher mean perfusion pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In septic shock, total peripheral resistance falls to half of normal while cardiac output rises to 1.5 times normal. If mean arterial pressure started at 100 mmHg, what is it now?
options: About 150 mmHg
About 100 mmHg, since the two changes cancel
About 75 mmHg
About 50 mmHg
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is the product of the two terms, so multiplying by 1.5 and then by 0.5 gives 0.75 of the starting value, or 75 mmHg. The changes do not cancel, because a halving is a larger fractional change than a fifty percent rise. One hundred fifty would follow if only the output change were counted. Fifty would follow if only the resistance change were counted. This is why a septic patient can be hypotensive despite a high cardiac output.
questions.answerText: About 75 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During heavy exercise, cardiac output rises from 5 to 20 L/min while total peripheral resistance falls to one third of its resting value. If resting mean arterial pressure was 90 mmHg, what is it during exercise?
options: About 30 mmHg
About 90 mmHg, since the changes offset exactly
About 360 mmHg
About 120 mmHg
questions.why: Cardiac output rises by a factor of four and resistance falls to one third, so the product changes by four thirds, and 90 times four thirds is 120 mmHg, a modest rise that matches what is measured during exercise. Three hundred sixty counts only the output change. Thirty counts only the resistance change. The changes nearly offset but not exactly, and the small net rise is what allows muscle to receive enormous flow without the arterial pressure either collapsing or spiking dangerously.
questions.answerText: About 120 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient has a mean arterial pressure of 70 mmHg with a measured cardiac output of 7 L/min. Working backward, what does this tell you about total peripheral resistance, and what kind of problem does it suggest?
options: Resistance cannot be determined without knowing the systolic and diastolic values
Resistance is about 490 mmHg per L/min, far above normal, pointing to intense vasoconstriction of the systemic arterioles throughout the body
Resistance is about 40 mmHg per L/min, twice normal, pointing to a failing heart
Resistance is about 10 mmHg per L/min, roughly half normal, pointing to widespread vasodilation rather than a pump or volume problem
questions.why: Rearranging the relationship gives resistance as mean pressure divided by cardiac output, so 70 divided by 7 is 10 mmHg per L/min against a normal near 20, meaning the vessels are abnormally dilated. Multiplying the two numbers instead of dividing gives 490, which is not a resistance at all. A failing heart would show a low output with a compensatory high resistance, the opposite pattern. Systolic and diastolic values are not needed once the mean is known.
questions.answerText: Resistance is about 10 mmHg per L/min, roughly half normal, pointing to widespread vasodilation rather than a pump or volume problem

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The myogenic response of an arteriole is what?
options: Vascular smooth muscle relaxes when the vessel is stretched by a rise in pressure
Vascular smooth muscle contracts when the vessel is stretched by a rise in pressure
Vascular smooth muscle contracts when local metabolites accumulate
Vascular smooth muscle relaxes when sympathetic nerve traffic increases
questions.why: Stretching the wall opens mechanically sensitive cation channels, depolarizing the smooth muscle and triggering contraction, so a rise in perfusion pressure is met with narrowing that holds flow steady. Relaxation on stretch would let flow climb with pressure and defeat autoregulation. Metabolite accumulation causes relaxation, not contraction, and that is the metabolic mechanism rather than the myogenic one. Sympathetic traffic acts through nerves and causes constriction, which is extrinsic control rather than an intrinsic wall response.
questions.answerText: Vascular smooth muscle contracts when the vessel is stretched by a rise in pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which local chemical change causes arteriolar dilation in an active tissue?
options: A rise in oxygen with a fall in carbon dioxide and H+
A rise in oxygen with a rise in adenosine
A rise in plasma sodium with a fall in plasma potassium
A rise in adenosine, carbon dioxide, H+, and K+ with a fall in oxygen
questions.why: Working cells consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide, acid, potassium, and adenosine, and each of those signals relaxes nearby arteriolar smooth muscle, matching delivery to demand. Rising oxygen with falling carbon dioxide is the signature of a tissue that is over supplied and would cause constriction instead. Plasma sodium and potassium concentrations are systemic variables and do not track local metabolism. Oxygen and adenosine move in opposite directions during activity, so they cannot both rise.
questions.answerText: A rise in adenosine, carbon dioxide, H+, and K+ with a fall in oxygen

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which substance released by endothelial cells causes vascular smooth muscle to relax?
options: Endothelin 1
Norepinephrine
Angiotensin II
Nitric oxide
questions.why: Endothelial cells make nitric oxide from arginine and it diffuses into the underlying smooth muscle, where it relaxes the cell and widens the vessel. Endothelin 1 comes from the same endothelium but is one of the strongest constrictors known, so it is the opposite arm of that control. Angiotensin II is a circulating hormone that constricts. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter released from sympathetic nerve endings and generally constricts through alpha receptors.
questions.answerText: Nitric oxide

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Endothelin 1 has what effect on arteriolar tone?
options: It has no effect on smooth muscle but increases capillary permeability
It causes strong vasodilation
It causes strong vasoconstriction
It relaxes veins only and leaves arterioles unaffected
questions.why: Endothelin 1 is a peptide released by endothelium that binds smooth muscle receptors and produces powerful, long lasting constriction, and it works alongside nitric oxide as the constricting half of endothelial control. Dilation is the nitric oxide effect. Permeability changes are driven mainly by histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Its actions are not restricted to veins, and it constricts rather than relaxes.
questions.answerText: It causes strong vasoconstriction

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle by raising the level of which second messenger?
options: Cyclic GMP
Cyclic AMP
Inositol trisphosphate
Diacylglycerol
questions.why: Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase inside the smooth muscle cell, cyclic GMP rises, and the resulting signaling lowers intracellular calcium so the cell relaxes. Cyclic AMP also promotes relaxation in vascular smooth muscle but is the messenger for beta adrenergic and prostacyclin signaling, not for nitric oxide. Inositol trisphosphate raises calcium and drives contraction, the opposite outcome. Diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C and likewise favors contraction.
questions.answerText: Cyclic GMP

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Active hyperemia refers to what?
options: The rise in local blood flow that follows an increase in tissue metabolic activity
The rise in local blood flow that follows a period of arterial occlusion
The maintenance of constant flow when perfusion pressure changes
The fall in local blood flow caused by sympathetic constriction
questions.why: Active hyperemia is metabolism driving its own blood supply, so when a muscle or gland starts working, its metabolites accumulate and dilate the arterioles feeding it. Flow rising after an occlusion is reactive hyperemia, which is triggered by the buildup during the period of no flow rather than by increased work. Holding flow constant across pressure changes is autoregulation. A sympathetic fall in flow is extrinsic control and is neither of these.
questions.answerText: The rise in local blood flow that follows an increase in tissue metabolic activity

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Reactive hyperemia refers to what?
options: The reduced flow seen when endothelin release increases
The surge in flow during the first minute of exercise
The steady flow maintained across a range of perfusion pressures
The surge in flow that follows release of a temporary arterial occlusion
questions.why: While flow is blocked, oxygen falls and metabolites build up in the tissue, so the arterioles dilate fully, and when the block is released the widened vessels allow a temporary flow far above baseline. Exercise onset produces active hyperemia, driven by work rather than by a period of no flow. Steady flow across pressures is autoregulation. Reduced flow with endothelin is a constricting response, not a hyperemia at all.
questions.answerText: The surge in flow that follows release of a temporary arterial occlusion

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Autoregulation of blood flow means what?
options: Blood flow rises in direct proportion to perfusion pressure
The medulla adjusts sympathetic outflow to the vessels in order to keep systemic arterial pressure constant
A tissue keeps its own blood flow relatively constant despite changes in perfusion pressure
The kidney adjusts blood volume to keep arterial pressure constant
questions.why: Autoregulation is a local property, so when perfusion pressure rises the arterioles constrict and when it falls they dilate, holding flow near a set level over a wide pressure range. Medullary adjustment of sympathetic outflow is the baroreceptor reflex, a systemic mechanism aimed at pressure rather than local flow. Flow rising in proportion to pressure is precisely what autoregulation prevents. Renal control of volume is a long term pressure mechanism, again systemic rather than local.
questions.answerText: A tissue keeps its own blood flow relatively constant despite changes in perfusion pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Perfusion pressure to a tissue rises suddenly. What does the myogenic response do, and what is the effect on flow?
options: The arterioles dilate, so flow rises sharply
The arterioles constrict, so flow falls far below its previous level
The arterioles constrict, so flow stays near its previous level
The arterioles do not respond, so flow rises in proportion to pressure
questions.why: The stretched wall contracts, raising resistance by about as much as the pressure rose, so the ratio of pressure to resistance and therefore flow is roughly preserved. Dilation would let flow climb and would expose the capillaries to damaging pressure. Constriction sufficient to drop flow well below baseline would overcorrect, and the response is graded rather than all or nothing. No response at all describes a vessel without myogenic tone, in which flow would simply track pressure.
questions.answerText: The arterioles constrict, so flow stays near its previous level

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A muscle begins contracting rhythmically. Predict the local flow response and its cause.
options: Flow falls, because the metabolites constrict the arterioles
Flow rises, because the myogenic response dilates the vessels in reply to lower pressure
Flow rises, because accumulating metabolites dilate the arterioles supplying the muscle
Flow is unchanged, because local control cannot override the resting level
questions.why: Adenosine, carbon dioxide, H+, and K+ rise and oxygen falls as the muscle works, and every one of those changes relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, so resistance falls and flow rises to meet demand. Metabolites dilate rather than constrict, which is what makes the match between supply and demand possible. The myogenic response is triggered by wall stretch, not by metabolic products, so it is not what drives this. Local control can raise muscle flow many fold, so it clearly overrides the resting level.
questions.answerText: Flow rises, because accumulating metabolites dilate the arterioles supplying the muscle

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A blood pressure cuff occludes flow to the forearm for one minute and is then released. What is observed and why?
options: Flow briefly exceeds baseline, because metabolites accumulated during the occlusion and dilated the arterioles
Flow briefly falls below baseline, because the vessels were compressed and remain narrowed
Flow returns exactly to baseline, because local control acts only during exercise
Flow briefly exceeds baseline, because the sympathetic nerves were cut off during the occlusion
questions.why: With inflow stopped, oxygen is consumed and vasodilator metabolites build up, so the arterioles are wide open the moment the cuff comes off and flow overshoots until the metabolites wash out. A fall below baseline would require lasting constriction, but the vessels are dilated, not narrowed. Local control operates continuously and is not limited to exercise. Sympathetic traffic is not interrupted by a cuff, and even if tone were withdrawn it would not explain the buildup that makes the overshoot proportional to the length of the occlusion.
questions.answerText: Flow briefly exceeds baseline, because metabolites accumulated during the occlusion and dilated the arterioles

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Blood flow through an artery increases, raising the shear stress on the endothelial lining. What follows?
options: Endothelial cells release more nitric oxide and the vessel dilates
Endothelial cells release more endothelin 1 and the vessel constricts
Smooth muscle contracts through the myogenic response and the vessel narrows
Nothing changes, because endothelium responds to pressure rather than flow
questions.why: Endothelial cells sense the drag of moving blood and respond by making nitric oxide, so an upstream artery widens to accommodate the flow its downstream bed has requested, a mechanism called flow mediated dilation. Endothelin release rises in injury and other settings, not as the normal answer to increased shear. The myogenic response answers stretch from pressure, and here the trigger is shear from flow. Endothelium senses both, so it is not blind to flow.
questions.answerText: Endothelial cells release more nitric oxide and the vessel dilates

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Increased endothelin 1 release in a vascular bed has what effect on resistance and local flow?
options: Resistance rises and local flow falls
Resistance falls and local flow rises
Resistance rises and local flow rises
Resistance is unchanged and only capillary permeability rises
questions.why: Endothelin constricts arteriolar smooth muscle, narrowing the vessel, and since resistance climbs steeply as radius falls, flow through that bed drops. Falling resistance would follow from nitric oxide instead. Resistance and flow cannot rise together at a fixed pressure gradient, since flow is pressure divided by resistance. Permeability is governed by other mediators and is not the main action of endothelin.
questions.answerText: Resistance rises and local flow falls

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A drug blocks the enzyme that makes nitric oxide in endothelial cells. What happens to arteriolar tone and arterial pressure?
options: Tone decreases and arterial pressure falls
Tone increases and arterial pressure rises
Tone is unchanged because nitric oxide acts only on veins
Tone increases but arterial pressure falls because flow is redistributed
questions.why: Endothelium releases nitric oxide continuously, so blocking its synthesis removes a background dilator signal, arteriolar smooth muscle contracts more, total peripheral resistance rises, and with cardiac output roughly unchanged mean arterial pressure climbs. Falling tone would require adding a dilator rather than removing one. Nitric oxide acts throughout the arterial tree, not only on veins. Pressure follows the product of output and resistance, so rising resistance cannot lower pressure while output holds.
questions.answerText: Tone increases and arterial pressure rises

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which metabolite is released by working cells and is considered a major local dilator in cardiac and skeletal muscle?
options: Adenosine
Albumin
Endothelin 1
Angiotensin II
questions.why: When ATP use outruns ATP production, adenosine appears in the interstitium and relaxes nearby arteriolar smooth muscle, which is why it is one of the strongest links between cardiac work and coronary flow. Albumin is a plasma protein that holds fluid in the capillary and has no role in setting tone. Endothelin and angiotensin II are both constrictors, so they would reduce flow to a working muscle rather than increase it.
questions.answerText: Adenosine

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: At the start of exercise, arterioles in a working muscle dilate until their radius has roughly doubled while the pressure gradient across the muscle bed is unchanged. Trace what happens and give the size of the flow change.
options: Metabolites relax the smooth muscle, resistance falls to about one sixteenth, and flow rises about sixteenfold
Metabolites relax the smooth muscle, resistance falls to about one half, and flow rises about twofold
Metabolites contract the smooth muscle, resistance rises sixteenfold, and flow falls to one sixteenth
The myogenic response dilates the vessel, resistance falls fourfold, and flow rises fourfold
questions.why: Accumulating adenosine, carbon dioxide, H+, and K+ relax the arteriolar wall, and because resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, doubling the radius cuts resistance to one sixteenth, so at an unchanged gradient flow rises by a factor of sixteen. A twofold answer treats radius as if it acted linearly. Contraction is the wrong direction for metabolites. The myogenic response answers stretch and would tend to oppose, not cause, this dilation.
questions.answerText: Metabolites relax the smooth muscle, resistance falls to about one sixteenth, and flow rises about sixteenfold

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Cerebral perfusion pressure falls from 100 to 70 mmHg. Autoregulation holds cerebral blood flow constant. By what fraction must cerebrovascular resistance change, and how is that achieved?
options: Resistance must rise to about 143 percent of its previous value, achieved by arteriolar constriction
Resistance must fall to about 30 percent of its previous value, achieved by arteriolar dilation
Resistance must fall to about 70 percent of its previous value, achieved by arteriolar dilation
Resistance does not need to change, because flow follows pressure only in the systemic circuit
questions.why: Flow is the pressure gradient divided by resistance, so holding flow constant while the gradient drops to seventy percent requires resistance to drop to seventy percent as well, and the vessels accomplish that by relaxing. Raising resistance would compound the fall in pressure and flow would drop further. Falling to thirty percent confuses the size of the pressure decrease with the resulting ratio. Cerebral vessels autoregulate strongly, so the relationship between flow, pressure, and resistance applies there as much as anywhere.
questions.answerText: Resistance must fall to about 70 percent of its previous value, achieved by arteriolar dilation

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In a person with damaged coronary endothelium, nitric oxide production is reduced and endothelin release is increased. Predict the effect on resting coronary tone and on the ability to raise flow during exercise.
options: Resting tone is lower than normal and the vessels dilate more during exercise, so flow rises more than normal
Resting tone is unchanged but exercise flow rises normally, since metabolic control replaces endothelial control entirely
Resting tone is higher than normal and the vessels dilate less during exercise, so the rise in flow is blunted
Resting tone is higher than normal but exercise flow rises normally, since endothelin is inactivated by adenosine
questions.why: Losing the background dilator while gaining a constrictor shifts the balance toward narrower vessels at rest, and it also removes the flow mediated dilation that normally helps upstream arteries widen when the bed downstream opens, so the maximum flow achievable during exercise is lower. Tone cannot fall when a dilator is lost and a constrictor is gained. Metabolic control still works, but it does not fully substitute for the endothelial arm, which is why exercise capacity suffers. Adenosine dilates but does not inactivate endothelin.
questions.answerText: Resting tone is higher than normal and the vessels dilate less during exercise, so the rise in flow is blunted

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Two forearms are occluded, one for 30 seconds and one for 3 minutes. On release, the longer occlusion produces a larger and longer flow overshoot. What best explains the difference?
options: The longer occlusion stretched the arteriolar walls more and for longer, so the myogenic response relaxed the smooth muscle further and kept it relaxed
More vasodilator metabolites accumulated and oxygen fell further during the longer occlusion, so the arterioles were dilated more and took longer to wash out
The longer occlusion recruited more sympathetic nerve traffic, which dilated the vessels on release
The longer occlusion raised arterial pressure upstream, so the driving gradient on release was larger
questions.why: Reactive hyperemia is graded to the metabolic debt, so a longer period without flow means a deeper fall in oxygen and a larger buildup of adenosine and other dilators, giving a wider vessel and a longer time for the signal to clear once flow resumes. Occlusion removes pressure from the vessels rather than stretching them, and the myogenic response to reduced stretch is dilation but it does not scale with duration this way. Sympathetic traffic constricts rather than dilates. Upstream pressure is set by the whole circulation and is not meaningfully raised by occluding one limb.
questions.answerText: More vasodilator metabolites accumulated and oxygen fell further during the longer occlusion, so the arterioles were dilated more and took longer to wash out

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which set names the four Starling forces acting at a capillary?
options: Capillary hydrostatic, lymphatic hydrostatic, plasma sodium, and interstitial sodium
Systolic, diastolic, pulse, and mean arterial pressure
Capillary hydrostatic pressure, venous hydrostatic pressure, total plasma osmolarity, and total interstitial osmolarity
Capillary hydrostatic, interstitial hydrostatic, capillary colloid osmotic, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
questions.why: The four forces are two hydrostatic pressures, one on each side of the wall, and two colloid osmotic pressures, again one on each side, and the balance among them sets the direction of fluid movement. Systolic and diastolic pressures describe the arterial waveform, not the capillary balance. Total osmolarity is nearly identical on both sides because small solutes cross freely, so it is the colloid, or protein, portion that matters. Sodium likewise crosses the capillary wall easily and exerts no lasting gradient across it.
questions.answerText: Capillary hydrostatic, interstitial hydrostatic, capillary colloid osmotic, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which Starling force is the main driver of fluid out of the capillary?
options: Interstitial hydrostatic pressure
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
Capillary colloid osmotic pressure
Capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: The blood pressure inside the capillary pushes fluid through the wall into the interstitium, and it is the largest of the outward forces. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure pushes in the opposite direction, back into the capillary, and is normally very small. Capillary colloid osmotic pressure pulls fluid inward and is the main opposing force. Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure does favor filtration but is much smaller than the hydrostatic push.
questions.answerText: Capillary hydrostatic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which Starling force is the main force pulling fluid back into the capillary?
options: Capillary colloid osmotic pressure
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
Capillary hydrostatic pressure
Lymphatic hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: Plasma proteins cannot cross the capillary wall easily, so they hold water in the vessel and generate an inward pull of roughly 25 mmHg that opposes filtration. Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes outward and is the force this one opposes. Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure pulls fluid the other way, out of the capillary, because it comes from the small amount of protein that has escaped. Lymphatic pressure is not one of the Starling forces, though lymph drainage does remove the fluid that filters out.
questions.answerText: Capillary colloid osmotic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Capillary colloid osmotic pressure is generated mainly by what?
options: Sodium and chloride dissolved in plasma
Red blood cells suspended in plasma
Glucose dissolved in plasma
Plasma proteins, especially albumin
questions.why: Albumin is small enough to be abundant but too large to cross the capillary wall in quantity, so it stays in the plasma and holds water there, accounting for most of the colloid osmotic pressure. Sodium, chloride, and glucose all cross the capillary wall freely, so their concentrations equalize and they exert no sustained osmotic pull across it. Red cells are confined to the vessel but are far too few in number to generate meaningful osmotic pressure.
questions.answerText: Plasma proteins, especially albumin

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What is the approximate value of capillary colloid osmotic pressure in a healthy person?
options: About 5 mmHg
About 25 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
questions.why: Plasma proteins generate roughly 25 mmHg of inward pull, a value that stays nearly constant from one end of the capillary to the other. Five mmHg is closer to the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure in many tissues. Sixty mmHg is far above what plasma protein concentrations can produce. One hundred mmHg is near mean arterial pressure and has nothing to do with the protein osmotic force.
questions.answerText: About 25 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Capillary hydrostatic pressure changes in which way from the arterial end of a capillary to the venous end?
options: It rises, from roughly 15 mmHg to roughly 35 mmHg
It falls, from roughly 90 mmHg to roughly 40 mmHg
It stays constant at roughly 25 mmHg along the whole length
It falls, from roughly 35 mmHg to roughly 15 mmHg
questions.why: Pressure drops as blood moves along the capillary because of the resistance of the vessel itself, so the outward push weakens from about 35 mmHg at the start to about 15 mmHg at the end, and that fall is what reverses the net direction of fluid movement. Rising pressure would require an upstream source partway along, which does not exist. Staying constant would leave the direction unchanged along the whole length. Values near 90 mmHg belong to arteries, upstream of the arterioles that drop pressure so steeply.
questions.answerText: It falls, from roughly 35 mmHg to roughly 15 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In capillary exchange, filtration and reabsorption are defined how?
options: Filtration is movement of protein out of the capillary and reabsorption is movement of protein back in
Filtration is diffusion of oxygen out and reabsorption is diffusion of carbon dioxide in
Filtration is bulk fluid movement out of the capillary and reabsorption is bulk movement back in
Filtration happens in the lymphatics and reabsorption happens in the capillaries
questions.why: Both terms describe bulk flow of fluid across the capillary wall, with filtration meaning outward into the interstitium and reabsorption meaning inward into the plasma. Protein movement is small and does not define these terms, though the protein that does escape is what the lymphatics must return. Gas movement is diffusion down partial pressure gradients and is a separate process from bulk flow. Lymphatics collect filtered fluid but do not filter it themselves.
questions.answerText: Filtration is bulk fluid movement out of the capillary and reabsorption is bulk movement back in

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure has what effect on fluid movement at the capillary?
options: It favors filtration by pulling fluid out of the capillary
It favors reabsorption by pulling fluid into the capillary
It has no effect because interstitial protein concentration is zero
It favors filtration by pushing fluid out of the capillary
questions.why: A small amount of protein leaks into the interstitium and is not immediately cleared, so it exerts an osmotic pull toward the tissue side, adding to the outward forces. Pulling fluid inward is what the plasma proteins do from the other side of the wall. Interstitial protein is low but not zero, and it rises sharply when permeability increases or lymph drainage fails. It acts by osmosis rather than by pushing, which is what hydrostatic pressures do.
questions.answerText: It favors filtration by pulling fluid out of the capillary

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: At the arterial end of a capillary, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 35 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure is 0 mmHg, capillary colloid osmotic pressure is 25 mmHg, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure is 3 mmHg. What is the net filtration pressure?
options: 10 mmHg favoring filtration
7 mmHg favoring reabsorption
13 mmHg favoring filtration
63 mmHg favoring filtration
questions.why: Add the outward forces, 35 plus 3 equals 38, add the inward forces, 0 plus 25 equals 25, and subtract to get 13 mmHg pushing fluid out. Ten comes from ignoring the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure. A reabsorption answer would require the inward forces to exceed the outward ones, which happens at the venous end rather than here. Sixty three comes from adding all four values instead of taking the difference between the two groups.
questions.answerText: 13 mmHg favoring filtration

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: At the venous end of a capillary, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 15 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure is 0 mmHg, capillary colloid osmotic pressure is 25 mmHg, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure is 3 mmHg. What is the net pressure and direction?
options: 7 mmHg favoring filtration
10 mmHg favoring reabsorption
13 mmHg favoring reabsorption
7 mmHg favoring reabsorption
questions.why: Outward forces total 15 plus 3, or 18 mmHg, inward forces total 25 mmHg, and the difference of 7 mmHg pulls fluid back into the capillary. Ten comes from leaving out the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure. Thirteen is the arterial end value. A filtration answer reverses the sign, but at this end the protein pull has become the larger of the two groups.
questions.answerText: 7 mmHg favoring reabsorption

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Why does the net direction of fluid movement reverse between the arterial and venous ends of a capillary?
options: Capillary colloid osmotic pressure falls along the capillary while capillary hydrostatic pressure stays nearly constant along it
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure rises steeply along the capillary and reverses the balance
Both pressures fall, but the colloid osmotic pressure falls faster
Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary while capillary colloid osmotic pressure stays nearly constant
questions.why: Resistance along the capillary drops the hydrostatic push from about 35 to about 15 mmHg, while the proteins that generate the inward pull cannot leave the vessel, so their roughly 25 mmHg holds steady, and the balance therefore tips from outward to inward partway along. Colloid osmotic pressure does not fall, and in fact it rises very slightly as water leaves and concentrates the protein. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure changes very little and is too small to reverse anything on its own.
questions.answerText: Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary while capillary colloid osmotic pressure stays nearly constant

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient with liver disease makes less albumin, so capillary colloid osmotic pressure falls from 25 to 15 mmHg. What happens to net filtration?
options: Reabsorption increases, because the interstitium now holds relatively more protein
Filtration decreases, because less protein means less osmotic push outward
Filtration is unchanged, because hydrostatic pressure did not change
Filtration increases, because the inward pull holding fluid in the capillary has weakened
questions.why: Plasma protein pulls fluid inward, so losing ten mmHg of that pull leaves the hydrostatic push less opposed and more fluid crosses into the interstitium at both ends of the capillary. Plasma protein pulls rather than pushes, and it works to retain fluid, so less of it cannot mean less filtration. Filtration depends on all four forces, so an unchanged hydrostatic pressure does not freeze the outcome. Reabsorption falls rather than rises, which is why hypoalbuminemia causes edema.
questions.answerText: Filtration increases, because the inward pull holding fluid in the capillary has weakened

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A blood clot obstructs a vein draining a limb, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure. What happens at the capillaries downstream of the clot?
options: Net reabsorption increases and the interstitium dries out
Nothing changes, because the clot is on the venous side and Starling forces are arterial
Net filtration increases and fluid accumulates in the interstitium
Capillary colloid osmotic pressure rises to match, so the balance is preserved
questions.why: Blocking outflow backs pressure up into the capillary, raising the outward hydrostatic force at both ends, so more fluid is pushed out and less returns. Reabsorption would require a lower capillary pressure, which is the opposite of what a venous obstruction produces. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is set by both the arteriolar inflow and the venous outflow, so a venous problem changes it directly. Plasma protein concentration does not rise to compensate, and if anything the fluid loss is what raises it slightly, far too little to restore the balance.
questions.answerText: Net filtration increases and fluid accumulates in the interstitium

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which end of a systemic capillary normally shows net filtration, and which shows net reabsorption?
options: Reabsorption at the arterial end and filtration at the venous end
Filtration at both ends, with all returned fluid handled by lymphatics
Filtration at the arterial end and reabsorption at the venous end
Reabsorption at both ends, with fluid supplied only by lymphatics
questions.why: The hydrostatic push is high where blood enters and has fallen well below the protein pull by the time blood leaves, so fluid exits early in the capillary and re enters late. The reverse pattern would require pressure to climb along the capillary. Filtration exceeds reabsorption slightly overall, so lymphatics do return a net surplus, but that does not mean both ends filter. Reabsorption at both ends would leave the interstitium without the fluid turnover it depends on.
questions.answerText: Filtration at the arterial end and reabsorption at the venous end

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Inflammation makes a capillary leaky, so protein escapes and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure rises from 3 to 12 mmHg. What is the effect on fluid movement?
options: More reabsorption, because protein in the interstitium draws fluid back into the capillary
More filtration, because the outward osmotic pull from the interstitium has grown
No change, because only capillary side forces matter
More reabsorption, because capillary colloid osmotic pressure rises by the same amount
questions.why: Protein sitting in the interstitium pulls water toward itself, and since it is outside the vessel that pull adds to filtration, which is why inflamed tissue swells. Interstitial protein cannot draw fluid back into the capillary, because osmotic pull acts toward the side with more protein. Both sides of the wall contribute forces, which is the whole point of having four of them. Capillary colloid osmotic pressure falls slightly when protein leaks out rather than rising.
questions.answerText: More filtration, because the outward osmotic pull from the interstitium has grown

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In a tissue, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 30 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure is 2 mmHg, capillary colloid osmotic pressure is 28 mmHg, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure is 6 mmHg. Determine the net pressure and its direction.
options: 6 mmHg favoring filtration
2 mmHg favoring reabsorption
6 mmHg favoring reabsorption
