34 mmHg favoring filtration
questions.why: Outward forces are capillary hydrostatic plus interstitial colloid osmotic, 30 plus 6, or 36 mmHg. Inward forces are interstitial hydrostatic plus capillary colloid osmotic, 2 plus 28, or 30 mmHg. The difference is 6 mmHg pushing fluid out. Getting the same magnitude with the opposite direction means the two groups were subtracted the wrong way around. Thirty four comes from grouping the two capillary values against the two interstitial values, which mixes hydrostatic and osmotic forces incorrectly.
questions.answerText: 6 mmHg favoring filtration

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In nephrotic syndrome, albumin is lost in the urine and capillary colloid osmotic pressure falls to 15 mmHg. At the venous end of a capillary, hydrostatic pressure is 15 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure is 0 mmHg, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure is 3 mmHg. What now happens at the venous end?
options: Net filtration of 3 mmHg, so fluid leaves the capillary even at the venous end
Net reabsorption of 3 mmHg, unchanged in direction from normal
Net reabsorption of 7 mmHg, the same as a healthy capillary
No net movement, because the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures are both 15 mmHg
questions.why: Outward forces are 15 plus 3, or 18 mmHg, inward forces are 0 plus 15, or 15 mmHg, so 3 mmHg now pushes fluid out where a healthy capillary would pull 7 mmHg in. Losing the reabsorbing end entirely is why these patients develop widespread edema. Seven mmHg of reabsorption is the normal value with colloid osmotic pressure at 25 mmHg. The two 15 mmHg values do not cancel to zero, because the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure of 3 mmHg tips the balance outward.
questions.answerText: Net filtration of 3 mmHg, so fluid leaves the capillary even at the venous end

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: As plasma moves along a capillary and fluid filters out, what happens to capillary colloid osmotic pressure, and why does this matter?
options: It falls steadily, because protein filters out along with the water
It is unchanged, because the capillary wall is freely permeable to protein
It rises slightly, because protein stays behind while water leaves, which strengthens reabsorption near the venous end
It falls sharply along the capillary, matching the fall in hydrostatic pressure, so the two forces stay in step from one end to the other
questions.why: The capillary wall holds back most protein, so removing water concentrates what remains and the inward pull edges upward as blood travels, adding a little to the reversal already produced by the falling hydrostatic pressure. Protein does not filter out in quantity, which is exactly why the pull persists. The wall is not freely permeable to protein, and if it were there would be no colloid osmotic pressure at all. The colloid osmotic pressure does not fall in parallel with hydrostatic pressure, and if it did the direction would never reverse.
questions.answerText: It rises slightly, because protein stays behind while water leaves, which strengthens reabsorption near the venous end

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In left heart failure, pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure rises to 45 mmHg at the arterial end and 30 mmHg at the venous end, with capillary colloid osmotic pressure 25 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure 0 mmHg, and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure 3 mmHg. What is the pattern along the capillary?
options: Net filtration of 23 mmHg at the arterial end and net reabsorption of 8 mmHg at the venous end, the usual pattern in a healthy capillary
Net filtration of 23 mmHg at the arterial end and 8 mmHg at the venous end, so fluid leaves along the whole length
Net filtration of 20 mmHg at the arterial end and 5 mmHg at the venous end
Net reabsorption at both ends, because colloid osmotic pressure is unchanged
questions.why: At the arterial end outward forces are 45 plus 3, or 48, against 25 inward, giving 23 mmHg of filtration, and at the venous end 30 plus 3, or 33, against 25 gives 8 mmHg still pushing outward. The capillary has lost its reabsorbing segment, which is how pulmonary edema develops. Twenty and five come from omitting the interstitial colloid osmotic pressure. Reabsorption at either end would require the protein pull to exceed a hydrostatic pressure that is now far above normal.
questions.answerText: Net filtration of 23 mmHg at the arterial end and 8 mmHg at the venous end, so fluid leaves along the whole length

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Edema is defined as what?
options: An excess accumulation of fluid inside cells
An excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space
An increase in circulating plasma volume
An increase in the protein concentration of plasma
questions.why: Edema is fluid that has left the capillaries and collected between the cells, so it is an interstitial problem rather than an intracellular or intravascular one. Swelling inside cells is cellular edema and follows osmotic shifts across the cell membrane rather than the Starling balance. A larger plasma volume can contribute to edema by raising capillary pressure, but it is not the same thing. Plasma protein concentration usually falls rather than rises in the forms of edema caused by protein loss.
questions.answerText: An excess accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which change in Starling forces produces edema in congestive heart failure?
options: Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
Increased capillary colloid osmotic pressure
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: A failing heart cannot move blood forward efficiently, so pressure backs up through the veins into the capillaries and the outward push rises at both ends of the capillary. A lower capillary pressure would favor reabsorption and reduce swelling. A higher capillary colloid osmotic pressure would pull more fluid in, again opposing edema. A lower interstitial colloid osmotic pressure removes an outward force and would also reduce filtration.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Edema caused by a fall in plasma albumin works through which force?
options: Reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure
Reduced capillary colloid osmotic pressure
Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
Increased capillary colloid osmotic pressure
questions.why: Albumin is what holds water inside the capillary, so losing it lowers the inward pull and leaves the hydrostatic push less opposed at every point along the capillary. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is unchanged by the protein loss itself. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure rises as fluid accumulates, but that is a consequence rather than the cause. A rise in capillary colloid osmotic pressure would protect against edema, not produce it.
questions.answerText: Reduced capillary colloid osmotic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In a burn or an acute inflammatory reaction, edema develops mainly by which mechanism?
options: Increased capillary permeability, letting protein escape into the interstitium
Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure throughout the capillary bed of the injured area
Increased plasma albumin synthesis by the liver
Increased lymphatic pumping into the venous system
questions.why: Mediators such as histamine pull endothelial cells apart, so protein crosses the wall, the plasma pull falls while the interstitial pull rises, and fluid follows the protein out. A lower venous end pressure would favor reabsorption. More albumin would strengthen the inward pull and resist edema. Faster lymphatic drainage removes interstitial fluid and protects against swelling rather than causing it.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary permeability, letting protein escape into the interstitium

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Lymphedema results from what?
options: A rise in plasma albumin that overloads the capillaries
A fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure that halts filtration
Obstruction or loss of lymphatic vessels, so filtered fluid and protein cannot be returned
Excessive reabsorption of fluid at the venous end of every capillary in the affected limb and trunk
questions.why: Lymphatics normally carry away the small surplus of fluid and the protein that escapes each day, so blocking them lets both build up in the tissue. Higher plasma albumin would hold more fluid in the vessel and reduce swelling. Reduced filtration would leave the interstitium drier, not wetter. Excessive reabsorption pulls fluid back into the blood, again the opposite of what produces edema.
questions.answerText: Obstruction or loss of lymphatic vessels, so filtered fluid and protein cannot be returned

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which organ synthesizes the plasma albumin that generates capillary colloid osmotic pressure?
options: The kidney
The spleen
The liver
The bone marrow
questions.why: Hepatocytes make albumin and release it into the plasma, which is why severe liver disease lowers colloid osmotic pressure and causes edema and ascites. The kidney does not make albumin, though it can lose it into the urine when the glomerular filter is damaged. The spleen filters blood and recycles red cells. Bone marrow produces blood cells, not plasma proteins.
questions.answerText: The liver

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Pitting edema, in which a thumbprint remains in swollen skin, indicates what?
options: Increased blood volume within the capillaries
Excess fluid trapped inside skin cells
An increase in subcutaneous fat
Excess mobile fluid in the interstitial space
questions.why: When the interstitial gel is overloaded with free fluid, pressing displaces that fluid sideways and it takes time to flow back, leaving a pit. Fluid inside cells cannot be displaced by pressure this way, so cellular swelling does not pit. Fat is compressible but rebounds immediately. Blood inside capillaries is quickly refilled from upstream, so it also does not leave a lasting indentation.
questions.answerText: Excess mobile fluid in the interstitial space

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which mechanism of edema is characterized by a rise in interstitial colloid osmotic pressure?
options: Increased capillary permeability
Reduced plasma protein concentration
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased arteriolar constriction
questions.why: A leaky capillary lets protein cross into the interstitium, so the tissue side gains osmotic pull and holds fluid there. Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out but leaves protein behind, so the interstitial protein concentration is actually diluted. Reduced plasma protein lowers the pull inside the vessel rather than raising it outside. Arteriolar constriction lowers capillary pressure and reduces filtration.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary permeability

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient with right heart failure has swollen ankles and distended neck veins. Which mechanism of edema fits best?
options: Reduced plasma protein from impaired synthesis
Lymphatic obstruction from scarred lymph channels
Increased capillary permeability from inflammatory mediators
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous congestion
questions.why: A right ventricle that cannot keep up lets pressure rise behind it, which is visible in the neck veins and transmitted back to the systemic capillaries, raising the outward push. Impaired albumin synthesis is a liver problem and would not distend the neck veins. Inflammatory permeability produces local, warm, red swelling rather than symmetric dependent edema with venous congestion. Lymphatic obstruction is usually confined to the drainage territory of the blocked vessels.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous congestion

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A child with severe protein malnutrition has a swollen abdomen and low serum albumin. Which mechanism of edema is at work?
options: Increased capillary permeability from a systemic allergic reaction
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from heart failure
Reduced plasma protein lowering capillary colloid osmotic pressure
Lymphatic obstruction from parasitic infection
questions.why: Without dietary protein the liver cannot make enough albumin, the inward pull at the capillary falls, and fluid stays in the interstitium and body cavities. Heart failure would show venous congestion and would not lower albumin. An allergic reaction produces rapid, often generalized swelling with normal albumin. Parasitic lymphatic obstruction produces swelling limited to the drainage region rather than the pattern seen with a low serum albumin.
questions.answerText: Reduced plasma protein lowering capillary colloid osmotic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Minutes after a bee sting, the skin around the site becomes red, warm, and swollen. Which mechanism produced the swelling?
options: Reduced plasma protein from renal loss
Increased capillary permeability caused by histamine release
Lymphatic obstruction caused by the venom
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous obstruction
questions.why: Histamine from mast cells dilates arterioles, which brings the redness and warmth, and separates endothelial cells, which lets protein and fluid escape, so swelling appears within minutes. Renal protein loss takes days to lower albumin and would cause generalized rather than local swelling. Venom does not physically block lymphatics. Venous obstruction would produce a cool, dusky limb rather than a hot red area.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary permeability caused by histamine release

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A woman develops persistent swelling of one arm months after surgery that removed the axillary lymph nodes on that side. Which mechanism explains it?
options: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure in the arm
Lymphatic obstruction preventing return of filtered fluid and protein
Reduced plasma protein from surgical blood loss
Increased capillary permeability from chronic inflammation
questions.why: Removing the nodes removes the drainage route, so the fluid and protein that normally filter out of the arm capillaries each day accumulate, and the swelling is confined to that limb. Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the arm is unchanged by node removal. Blood loss during surgery does not produce a lasting fall in albumin months later, and it would affect the whole body rather than one arm. Chronic inflammation would produce redness and tenderness alongside the swelling.
questions.answerText: Lymphatic obstruction preventing return of filtered fluid and protein

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A clot in a deep leg vein is followed by swelling of that leg. Which mechanism of edema does this represent?
options: Increased capillary permeability from clot proteins
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from blocked venous outflow
Lymphatic obstruction from the clot
Reduced plasma protein from consumption of clotting factors
questions.why: A clot obstructing the vein raises the pressure everywhere upstream of it, including the capillaries, so the outward push climbs and fluid accumulates in that leg. Clot proteins do not open the capillary wall. The clot sits in a vein and does not block lymphatic vessels, which run alongside but separately. Clotting factor consumption does not lower total plasma protein enough to change colloid osmotic pressure meaningfully.
questions.answerText: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from blocked venous outflow

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A cashier who stands all day notices ankle swelling by evening that resolves overnight. What is the mechanism?
options: Standing damages the capillary wall, increasing permeability
Standing lowers plasma albumin, reducing colloid osmotic pressure
Gravity raises capillary hydrostatic pressure in the feet, increasing filtration
Standing shuts down lymphatic vessels in the leg permanently
questions.why: In a standing column of blood, the weight of that column adds substantially to capillary pressure in the feet, so filtration outpaces reabsorption during the day and lying down at night removes the gravitational load and lets it reverse. Albumin concentration does not change with posture in a way that would explain this. Standing does not injure the capillary wall. The lymphatics keep working, and the muscle pump moving them along is exactly what is missing during quiet standing.
questions.answerText: Gravity raises capillary hydrostatic pressure in the feet, increasing filtration

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Two patients have leg edema. The first has a serum albumin of 1.8 g/dL and large amounts of protein in the urine. The second has a normal albumin, distended neck veins, and an enlarged liver. Which pairing of mechanisms is correct?
options: Both have edema from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, one from renal and one from cardiac causes
The first has edema from increased capillary permeability and the second from lymphatic obstruction
The first has edema from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure and the second from reduced capillary colloid osmotic pressure
The first has edema from reduced capillary colloid osmotic pressure and the second from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: Urinary protein loss with a very low albumin points squarely at a weakened inward pull, while normal albumin with venous congestion in the neck and liver points at pressure backing up into the capillaries from a failing right heart. Swapping the two mechanisms ignores the albumin values, which are the deciding clue. Neither picture involves the local heat and redness of a permeability problem or the regional distribution of a lymphatic blockage.
questions.answerText: The first has edema from reduced capillary colloid osmotic pressure and the second from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In lymphatic filariasis, worms block the lymphatic vessels of a limb. Trace the effect on interstitial protein, interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, and net filtration.
options: Interstitial protein is diluted, interstitial colloid osmotic pressure falls, and net filtration decreases, so the swelling stabilizes and then slowly resolves on its own
Interstitial protein accumulates, interstitial colloid osmotic pressure rises, and net filtration increases further, so the swelling worsens over time
Interstitial protein accumulates, capillary colloid osmotic pressure rises to match, and net filtration returns to normal
Interstitial protein accumulates but has no osmotic effect, so swelling depends only on hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: One of the main jobs of the lymphatics is to remove escaped protein, so blocking them lets protein build up in the tissue, and that protein pulls still more fluid out of the capillary, a self reinforcing cycle that explains the massive limb swelling this disease produces. Dilution would require the protein to be cleared, which is exactly what is blocked. Capillary colloid osmotic pressure does not rise to compensate. Interstitial protein is osmotically active, which is why it is one of the four Starling forces.
questions.answerText: Interstitial protein accumulates, interstitial colloid osmotic pressure rises, and net filtration increases further, so the swelling worsens over time

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Edema fluid is sampled from two patients. One sample is protein poor and the other is protein rich. Which mechanisms do these findings point to?
options: Protein rich fluid fits raised capillary hydrostatic pressure or low plasma protein, while protein poor fluid fits increased permeability or lymphatic blockage
Both samples should be protein poor, since protein cannot cross a capillary wall under any conditions
Protein poor fluid fits raised capillary hydrostatic pressure or low plasma protein, while protein rich fluid fits increased permeability or lymphatic blockage
Both samples should be protein rich, since filtered fluid always carries plasma protein with it
questions.why: When the wall is intact and lymphatics work, extra filtration pushes out a nearly protein free ultrafiltrate, so the fluid is thin. When the wall leaks, protein comes with the fluid, and when lymphatics are blocked, the protein that normally escapes each day is never retrieved, so both leave a protein rich fluid behind. Reversing the pairing contradicts what each mechanism does to the wall and to drainage. Protein does cross in small amounts normally and in large amounts when permeability rises, so neither all or nothing answer holds.
questions.answerText: Protein poor fluid fits raised capillary hydrostatic pressure or low plasma protein, while protein rich fluid fits increased permeability or lymphatic blockage

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient receives several liters of intravenous normal saline rapidly. Explain how this can produce edema, naming the forces involved.
options: Plasma volume expansion raises capillary hydrostatic pressure while the added protein free fluid dilutes plasma protein and lowers capillary colloid osmotic pressure, so both forces push toward filtration

Saline increases capillary colloid osmotic pressure because sodium is osmotically active across the capillary wall, so fluid is pulled out of the vessel and into the tissue spaces of the limbs and lungs
Saline blocks lymphatic drainage, so filtered fluid cannot be returned
Saline damages the endothelium, so permeability rises and protein escapes
questions.why: Two of the four Starling forces move at once here, since the extra volume raises the pressure inside the capillary and the fluid added contains no protein, so the concentration of albumin falls and the inward pull weakens. Sodium crosses the capillary wall freely, so it exerts no colloid osmotic pull there, which is why saline distributes through the extracellular fluid rather than staying in the vessel. Saline neither obstructs lymphatics nor injures endothelium. This is why large volume resuscitation so often leaves patients puffy.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume expansion raises capillary hydrostatic pressure while the added protein free fluid dilutes plasma protein and lowers capillary colloid osmotic pressure, so both forces push toward filtration

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: About how much fluid does the lymphatic system return to the bloodstream each day?
options: About 3 liters
About 0.3 liters
About 30 liters
About 100 liters
questions.why: Roughly three liters of filtered fluid are collected from the interstitium and returned to the venous circulation each day, which is close to the entire plasma volume, so the system is not a minor accessory. Three tenths of a liter would be far too little to keep the interstitium from flooding. Thirty liters overshoots by an order of magnitude and exceeds the surplus that filtration actually leaves behind. One hundred liters is not a plausible figure for any daily fluid movement in the body.
questions.answerText: About 3 liters

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Of the fluid filtered out of systemic capillaries each day, roughly how much is reabsorbed directly back into the capillaries?
options: About 3 of the roughly 20 liters filtered
All 20 liters, leaving nothing for the lymphatics
About 17 of the roughly 20 liters filtered
About 10 of the roughly 20 liters filtered
questions.why: Around twenty liters filter out and about seventeen return at the venous end of the capillaries, leaving the three liter surplus that the lymphatics must carry. Reversing the numbers would make the lymphatic load nearly six times what it actually is. If all twenty returned there would be no lymph at all, and no route for escaped protein to get back. Ten liters would leave a surplus far larger than the lymphatic system carries.
questions.answerText: About 17 of the roughly 20 liters filtered

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: How does interstitial fluid enter a lymphatic capillary?
options: Through tight junctions that require active transport
Through overlapping endothelial flaps that open inward when interstitial pressure rises
Through small pores in a continuous basement membrane, driven by an osmotic gradient across the wall
Through the same fenestrations used by blood capillaries
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are blind ended tubes whose endothelial cells overlap like roof shingles, and rising interstitial pressure pushes those flaps inward so fluid and protein enter, then the flaps fall shut and prevent backflow. Tight junctions would seal the vessel and no bulk uptake could occur. There is no active pumping of fluid at this step, and lymphatic capillaries have an incomplete basement membrane rather than a continuous one. Blood capillary fenestrations are far smaller and do not admit protein in bulk.
questions.answerText: Through overlapping endothelial flaps that open inward when interstitial pressure rises

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The thoracic duct drains lymph from which regions of the body?
options: The left arm and the left side of the head and neck, but not the abdomen, the pelvis, or the legs
Everything except the right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax
The lower limbs and abdomen only
The entire body, with no separate duct
questions.why: The thoracic duct handles roughly three quarters of the body, including both legs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and thorax, while a much smaller right lymphatic duct covers the remaining upper right quadrant. Limiting it to the left arm and head leaves out the entire lower body, which is its largest source. Limiting it to the lower body leaves out the left upper quadrant. There are two ducts, not one, which is why lymph from the right arm follows a different route.
questions.answerText: Everything except the right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The right lymphatic duct drains which region?
options: The right leg, the right side of the abdomen, and the right side of the pelvis
The right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax
The entire right half of the body
The right lung only
questions.why: The right lymphatic duct serves only the upper right quadrant, a relatively small territory, and empties near the right subclavian vein. The right leg and right abdomen drain into the thoracic duct instead. The whole right half of the body would include those lower regions, which is why the split is by quadrant rather than by side. The right lung is part of the territory but not the whole of it.
questions.answerText: The right upper limb and the right side of the head, neck, and thorax

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Where does the thoracic duct empty its lymph into the bloodstream?
options: Directly into the left atrium of the heart, alongside the pulmonary veins
At the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
Into the abdominal aorta
Into the hepatic portal vein
questions.why: Lymph rejoins the blood on the venous side, at the angle where the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins meet, where pressure is low enough for the lymph to flow in. Emptying into the left atrium would bypass the venous return path and is not how the duct is arranged. The aorta is an artery at high pressure, so lymph could not enter it. The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver and is not a lymphatic destination.
questions.answerText: At the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What propels lymph along the lymphatic vessels?
options: A dedicated lymphatic heart that beats about 60 times a minute
Osmotic pull generated by plasma proteins in the subclavian vein
The pressure generated by the left ventricle during systole, transmitted through the arteries and capillaries into the lymphatics directly
Smooth muscle contraction of the vessel segments plus the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps, with valves preventing backflow
questions.why: Lymph moves because the walls of the collecting vessels contract rhythmically and because surrounding muscles and breathing squeeze the vessels, while one way valves make each squeeze produce forward movement. Humans have no lymphatic heart. Ventricular pressure is almost entirely dissipated by the time blood reaches the capillaries, so none of it is available to drive lymph. Osmotic pull in a vein cannot draw lymph the length of the body.
questions.answerText: Smooth muscle contraction of the vessel segments plus the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps, with valves preventing backflow

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What happens to lymph as it passes through a lymph node on its way back to the blood?
options: It is filtered and screened by immune cells before continuing on
It is concentrated by removal of water so its volume is halved
It is oxygenated by contact with capillary blood
It is returned to the interstitial space it came from
questions.why: Lymph nodes sit along the lymphatic route so that macrophages and lymphocytes can inspect fluid coming from the tissues and mount a response to anything foreign in it. Nodes do not concentrate lymph by removing water, and lymph volume changes little across them. Oxygenation happens in the lungs and has nothing to do with nodal function. Lymph continues forward toward the ducts rather than returning to the tissue.
questions.answerText: It is filtered and screened by immune cells before continuing on

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which sequence correctly traces fluid from the interstitial space back to the bloodstream?
options: Interstitial fluid, lymph node, lymphatic capillary, collecting lymphatic vessel, lymphatic trunk, lymphatic duct, and then the subclavian vein
Interstitial fluid, venule, lymphatic capillary, lymph node, lymphatic duct, subclavian vein
Interstitial fluid, lymphatic capillary, collecting lymphatic vessel, lymph node, lymphatic trunk, lymphatic duct, subclavian vein
Interstitial fluid, lymphatic duct, lymph node, lymphatic capillary, lymphatic trunk, subclavian vein
questions.why: Fluid enters the smallest blind ended lymphatic capillaries, moves into larger collecting vessels, passes through at least one node, joins a trunk, and reaches a duct that empties into a subclavian vein. Putting the node before the capillary reverses the order, since fluid must be collected before it can be filtered. Venules are blood vessels and are not part of the lymphatic path. Ducts are the last step, not the first, so any sequence that starts there is backwards.
questions.answerText: Interstitial fluid, lymphatic capillary, collecting lymphatic vessel, lymph node, lymphatic trunk, lymphatic duct, subclavian vein

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Lymph formed in the right hand returns to the blood by which route?
options: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct into the superior vena cava directly
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
questions.why: The right upper limb is within the territory of the right lymphatic duct, which empties near the right subclavian vein. The thoracic duct serves the rest of the body and drains on the left, so it is the wrong duct and the wrong side for the right hand. Lymph does not enter the superior vena cava directly, since each duct joins at a subclavian junction. Pairing the thoracic duct with the right subclavian mixes the two systems.
questions.answerText: Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Lymph formed in the left foot returns to the blood by which route?
options: Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Left lymphatic duct into the inferior vena cava
Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
questions.why: Both lower limbs drain upward through the abdominal trunks into the thoracic duct, which ascends through the chest and empties on the left side. The right lymphatic duct serves only the upper right quadrant, not the legs. The thoracic duct empties on the left, not the right. There is no vessel called the left lymphatic duct, and lymph does not enter the inferior vena cava.
questions.answerText: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Why can lymphatic capillaries take up protein from the interstitium when blood capillaries cannot reabsorb it?
options: They actively transport protein using ATP driven pumps
They have a higher internal colloid osmotic pressure that pulls protein in
Their overlapping flaps leave large openings that admit protein along with fluid
They break protein down into amino acids that then diffuse across
questions.why: The gaps between the overlapping endothelial cells of a lymphatic capillary are far larger than the clefts of a blood capillary, so albumin passes through easily when interstitial pressure pushes the flaps open. There is no protein pump doing this work. A higher internal colloid osmotic pressure would pull water, not protein, and the pull would develop only after protein had already entered. Lymphatics transport protein intact rather than digesting it.
questions.answerText: Their overlapping flaps leave large openings that admit protein along with fluid

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: If the thoracic duct were completely obstructed, what would happen to plasma volume and plasma protein over the following days?
options: Both would rise, because fluid would back up into the circulation
Plasma volume would fall but plasma protein would rise as the remaining protein concentrated
Both would fall, because filtered fluid and escaped protein could no longer be returned
Neither would change, because blood capillaries reabsorb all filtered fluid anyway
questions.why: The lymphatics are the only route back for the roughly three liters and the protein that escape each day, so blocking the main duct strands both in the tissues and the plasma is progressively depleted. Fluid cannot back up into the circulation past an obstruction that lies between the tissue and the vein. Protein concentration falls rather than rises, since protein is being lost to the interstitium faster than water in relative terms. Blood capillaries reabsorb most but not all of what they filter, which is precisely why the lymphatic route is essential.
questions.answerText: Both would fall, because filtered fluid and escaped protein could no longer be returned

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient is completely immobile in bed. What happens to lymph flow from the legs, and why?
options: It falls, because the skeletal muscle pump that normally compresses lymphatic vessels is inactive
It rises, because resting metabolism produces more interstitial fluid
It is unchanged, because lymphatic smooth muscle alone provides all the driving force
It falls, because lymphatic valves close permanently during inactivity
questions.why: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the lymphatic vessels between them, and with the valves directing each squeeze upward, movement is a major driver of lymph return, so immobility removes it and flow drops. Resting metabolism does not generate more interstitial fluid than activity does. Lymphatic smooth muscle contributes real propulsion but not enough to keep flow at normal levels without the external pumps. Valves open and close passively with pressure and do not lock shut.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the skeletal muscle pump that normally compresses lymphatic vessels is inactive

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A small amount of albumin escapes from a capillary in the left calf. Trace its full route back to the bloodstream and name where it rejoins the blood.
options: Interstitium, venule, femoral vein, inferior vena cava, right atrium
Interstitium, lymphatic capillary, hepatic portal vein, liver sinusoids, hepatic vein, inferior vena cava, and then the right atrium of the heart
Interstitium, lymphatic capillary, right lymphatic duct, right subclavian vein
Interstitium, lymphatic capillary, collecting vessels of the leg, inguinal nodes, lumbar trunks, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, left subclavian vein
questions.why: Protein too large to re enter the blood capillary is taken up by lymphatic capillaries, carried through the nodes of the groin and the lumbar trunks into the dilated cisterna chyli, and then up the thoracic duct to rejoin the blood at the left subclavian junction. Re entry through a venule would require the protein to cross a blood capillary wall, which is what it could not do in the first place. The right lymphatic duct does not serve the leg. The portal vein carries blood from the gut, not lymph from the limbs.
questions.answerText: Interstitium, lymphatic capillary, collecting vessels of the leg, inguinal nodes, lumbar trunks, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, left subclavian vein

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: If lymphatic return stopped entirely, what would happen to plasma volume, and over what time scale would this become life threatening?
options: Plasma volume would fall by roughly 0.3 liters per day, so weeks would pass before any problem appeared
Plasma volume would fall by roughly 3 liters per day, so circulatory collapse would follow within a day or two
Plasma volume would rise, since fluid would be retained in the vessels
Plasma volume would stay constant, since the kidneys would simply retain more water
questions.why: About three liters leave the circulation each day and depend on the lymphatics to come back, and since total plasma volume is only around three liters, losing that much daily is rapidly fatal. Three tenths of a liter a day understates the loss tenfold. Volume falls rather than rises, because the fluid is stranded outside the vessels. Renal retention adds water to the extracellular space, but without lymphatic return that water keeps filtering into the interstitium and does not preserve plasma volume.
questions.answerText: Plasma volume would fall by roughly 3 liters per day, so circulatory collapse would follow within a day or two

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During vigorous exercise, lymph flow can rise more than tenfold. Give the two main reasons.
options: Sympathetic nerve outflow pumps the lymph forward directly, and a rise in plasma albumin draws interstitial fluid into the lymphatic capillaries of the working limb
Rhythmic muscle contraction compresses lymphatic vessels, and higher capillary pressure and permeability increase the volume filtered into the interstitium
Lymph nodes contract to push fluid forward, and lymphatic valves open wider under pressure
The heart rate rises, and the resulting arterial pulse propels lymph along the ducts
questions.why: Exercise both increases the load, because working muscle capillaries filter more fluid, and increases the pumping, because contracting muscles squeeze the vessels that carry that fluid away. Sympathetic nerves influence lymphatic smooth muscle but do not do the bulk of the pumping, and plasma albumin does not rise during exercise. Lymph nodes are not contractile pumps. The arterial pulse is largely damped out before the capillaries and does not drive lymph.
questions.answerText: Rhythmic muscle contraction compresses lymphatic vessels, and higher capillary pressure and permeability increase the volume filtered into the interstitium

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The thoracic duct is torn during chest surgery, and milky fluid collects in the pleural space. Why is the fluid milky, and what is lost besides water?
options: The duct carries arterial blood that has separated into plasma and cells during transit, so red cells and clotting factors are lost as well
The duct carries lymph from the intestinal lacteals rich in chylomicrons, so fat, protein, and lymphocytes are lost along with the fluid
The duct carries cerebrospinal fluid, so glucose and electrolytes are lost
The duct carries bile from the liver, so bile salts and pigments are lost
questions.why: Lymphatics of the small intestine absorb dietary fat as chylomicrons, and that lymph joins the thoracic duct, giving it a milky appearance after a meal, so a torn duct spills fat along with the protein and the lymphocytes lymph normally carries. The thoracic duct carries lymph, not arterial blood, so red cells are not its content. Cerebrospinal fluid circulates within the central nervous system. Bile drains through the biliary tree into the duodenum and never enters the thoracic duct.
questions.answerText: The duct carries lymph from the intestinal lacteals rich in chylomicrons, so fat, protein, and lymphocytes are lost along with the fluid

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The skeletal muscle pump aids venous return by what action?
options: Contracting muscles release nitric oxide that relaxes venous smooth muscle
Contracting muscles dilate the deep veins so more blood can be stored
Contracting muscles increase arterial pressure and push blood through the capillaries faster
Contracting muscles compress the deep veins and squeeze blood toward the heart
questions.why: Veins running between and within muscles are thin walled, so every contraction flattens them and the blood inside is forced along, with valves ensuring the movement is toward the heart. Dilating the veins would increase pooling and reduce return. Arterial pressure does rise during exercise but that is a separate effect and is not what the pump does to veins. Nitric oxide relaxation would widen the vessels and encourage storage rather than emptying.
questions.answerText: Contracting muscles compress the deep veins and squeeze blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What is the function of the valves in peripheral veins?
options: They regulate the resistance of the vein by opening and closing partially
They generate the pressure that drives venous return
They separate oxygenated from deoxygenated blood within the vein
They prevent backflow so that each compression moves blood toward the heart
questions.why: Venous valves are passive one way flaps, so when a muscle squeezes a vein the blood can only go forward, which converts random compression into directed flow. They are not resistance regulators, since they are either open or shut rather than graded. All blood in a systemic vein is deoxygenated, so there is nothing to separate. Valves direct flow but generate no pressure of their own.
questions.answerText: They prevent backflow so that each compression moves blood toward the heart

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During inspiration, what change in pressures aids venous return?
options: Intrathoracic pressure rises while abdominal pressure falls, widening the gradient toward the heart
Intrathoracic pressure falls and venous valves close to hold blood in the abdomen
Both intrathoracic and abdominal pressures fall equally, so no gradient develops
Intrathoracic pressure falls while abdominal pressure rises, widening the gradient toward the heart
questions.why: The diaphragm descends, which drops the pressure around the thoracic veins and simultaneously compresses the abdominal contents, so blood is pulled and pushed toward the right atrium at the same time. Reversing the two pressures describes expiration and would oppose return. Equal falls in both compartments would create no gradient, but the diaphragm moving between them guarantees they change in opposite directions. Valves open to allow this forward movement rather than closing to block it.
questions.answerText: Intrathoracic pressure falls while abdominal pressure rises, widening the gradient toward the heart

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Venoconstriction is produced by which signal acting on which receptors?
options: Sympathetic norepinephrine acting on alpha adrenergic receptors on venous smooth muscle
Parasympathetic acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors on venous smooth muscle
Circulating nitric oxide acting on endothelial receptors in the venous wall
Sympathetic norepinephrine acting on beta receptors on venous endothelium
questions.why: Veins carry a sympathetic innervation whose norepinephrine binds alpha receptors on the smooth muscle and contracts it, reducing the volume the veins can hold. Parasympathetic fibers have essentially no innervation of systemic veins. Nitric oxide relaxes rather than constricts, and it is made locally by endothelium rather than circulating as a hormone. Beta receptor activation in vessels favors relaxation, and the receptors that matter here sit on smooth muscle rather than endothelium.
questions.answerText: Sympathetic norepinephrine acting on alpha adrenergic receptors on venous smooth muscle

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Venous return is defined as what?
options: The volume of blood ejected by the right ventricle each beat
The total volume of blood held in the systemic veins and venules at any given moment in time
The volume of blood flowing from the systemic veins into the right atrium each minute
The pressure in the large veins as they enter the thorax
questions.why: Venous return is a flow, measured per minute, and over any sustained period it must equal cardiac output, since blood cannot accumulate indefinitely on either side. The volume stored in the veins is venous capacitance, a volume rather than a flow. What the right ventricle ejects per beat is stroke volume. Pressure at the thoracic inlet is central venous pressure, which influences return but is not the same quantity.
questions.answerText: The volume of blood flowing from the systemic veins into the right atrium each minute

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What is the approximate normal right atrial pressure in a healthy person lying down?
options: About 0 mmHg
About 25 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 90 mmHg
questions.why: Right atrial pressure sits near zero, essentially atmospheric, which is what makes it the low pressure end of the systemic circuit and gives blood somewhere to flow toward. Twenty five mmHg is closer to pulmonary artery systolic pressure. Sixty and ninety mmHg belong to the arterial side, and pressures that high in the right atrium would abolish the gradient driving venous return.
questions.answerText: About 0 mmHg

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Venous return matters for stroke volume because of which relationship?
options: It sets afterload, and lower afterload produces a stronger contraction
It sets total peripheral resistance, and lower resistance produces a larger stroke volume
It sets heart rate, and a faster rate produces a larger stroke volume
It sets end diastolic volume, and greater stretch of the ventricle produces a stronger contraction
questions.why: The blood arriving at the heart fills the ventricle, and the resulting stretch improves the overlap of the contractile filaments so the next beat ejects more, which is the length tension relationship applied to the whole chamber. Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome, set mainly by arterial pressure rather than by venous filling. Heart rate is set by the pacemaker and autonomic input, and a faster rate can actually shorten filling time. Total peripheral resistance is an arteriolar property.
questions.answerText: It sets end diastolic volume, and greater stretch of the ventricle produces a stronger contraction

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: When a person stands up, what happens to venous pressure in the veins of the feet?
options: It falls to near zero, because gravity pulls blood away from the feet and toward the chest and abdomen
It is unchanged, because venous valves hold pressure constant
It rises sharply, by roughly 80 to 90 mmHg, because of the weight of the column of blood above
It rises by about 5 mmHg, the same amount as in the neck veins
questions.why: A vertical column of blood exerts a hydrostatic pressure proportional to its height, so foot veins in a standing adult carry roughly ninety mmHg more than they do lying down, which is why leg veins distend and filtration into the foot rises. Gravity pulls blood toward the feet, not away from them. Valves interrupt the column when muscles are active but cannot abolish the hydrostatic pressure during quiet standing. Neck veins actually see pressure fall on standing, since they are above the heart.
questions.answerText: It rises sharply, by roughly 80 to 90 mmHg, because of the weight of the column of blood above

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person stands still at attention for several minutes. Predict what happens to venous return and stroke volume.
options: Venous return is unchanged because venous valves prevent any pooling
Blood is forced upward by gravity, so venous return rises and stroke volume rises
Venous return falls but stroke volume rises to compensate
Blood pools in the leg veins, so venous return falls and stroke volume falls
questions.why: Without muscle contraction, the hydrostatic column distends the leg veins and several hundred milliliters collect there, so less blood reaches the right atrium, end diastolic volume drops, and the length tension relationship gives a smaller stroke volume. Gravity pulls blood downward, not upward. Stroke volume follows filling, so it cannot rise while venous return falls unless contractility increases, which is a reflex response rather than an automatic compensation. Valves reduce pooling during movement but cannot prevent it when the muscles are still.
questions.answerText: Blood pools in the leg veins, so venous return falls and stroke volume falls

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person who has been standing still begins to walk. What happens to venous return?
options: It falls, because walking increases the metabolic demand of the legs
It rises, because the skeletal muscle pump empties the leg veins toward the heart
It is unchanged, because the hydrostatic column is the same when walking as when standing
It falls, because muscle contraction compresses the arteries supplying the legs
questions.why: Rhythmic contraction squeezes the deep veins, and the valves make each squeeze move blood upward, so pooled volume is returned and venous pressure in the feet actually drops well below the standing value. Higher metabolic demand raises flow through the legs but does not trap blood there. The hydrostatic column is only part of the picture, since the pump interrupts it segment by segment. Arterial compression during contraction is real but brief and does not reduce venous return over a walking cycle.
questions.answerText: It rises, because the skeletal muscle pump empties the leg veins toward the heart

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person takes a slow deep breath in. What is the immediate effect on venous return to the right atrium?
options: It decreases, because the lungs expand and compress the great veins
It is unchanged, because breathing affects only the pulmonary circulation
It increases, because intrathoracic pressure falls while abdominal pressure rises
It decreases, because the diaphragm blocks the inferior vena cava
questions.why: A deep inspiration drops the pressure surrounding the thoracic veins and right atrium while the descending diaphragm raises abdominal pressure, and that widened gradient pulls blood forward. Expanding lungs do not compress the great veins, which lie in the mediastinum. The respiratory pump acts on the systemic venous return, so the effect is not confined to the pulmonary circuit. The vena cava passes through the diaphragm without being occluded by it during normal breathing.
questions.answerText: It increases, because intrathoracic pressure falls while abdominal pressure rises

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In a person with incompetent venous valves in the legs, what is the consequence during standing?
options: Blood moves upward more easily, so venous return increases
Blood refluxes downward and pools, so venous pressure in the legs stays high and venous return is reduced
Arterial inflow to the legs is blocked by the failed valves, so the legs become pale, cold, and painful on walking
Lymphatic drainage increases enough to keep leg volume completely normal
questions.why: Working valves let the muscle pump lower venous pressure in the legs with each step, so when they fail, blood falls back between contractions, the veins stay distended, capillary pressure stays high, and less blood returns centrally. Failing valves cannot make upward movement easier, since their whole purpose is to prevent the downward leak. Arterial inflow is unaffected by venous valve disease. Lymphatics do carry more fluid but are eventually overwhelmed, which is why chronic venous insufficiency produces swelling and skin changes.
questions.answerText: Blood refluxes downward and pools, so venous pressure in the legs stays high and venous return is reduced

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Sympathetic activation during a fright causes venoconstriction. What is the effect on venous return and stroke volume?
options: Both decrease, because narrower veins offer more resistance to flow
Neither changes, because veins contribute nothing to circulatory control
Venous return increases but stroke volume falls because filling time is shortened
Both increase, because the veins hold less blood and more reaches the heart
questions.why: Squeezing the capacitance vessels shifts stored blood forward, filling rises, and the stretched ventricle ejects more. Veins are wide enough that constricting them changes stored volume far more than resistance, so flow is not impeded. Sympathetic activation does shorten filling time by raising heart rate, but the increased filling pressure and contractility more than offset that in this setting. Veins hold most of the blood volume, so they are central to circulatory control rather than passive.
questions.answerText: Both increase, because the veins hold less blood and more reaches the heart

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A patient is placed on positive pressure mechanical ventilation, which raises intrathoracic pressure during inspiration. What happens to venous return?
options: It falls, because the gradient from the peripheral veins to the right atrium is reduced
It rises, because the lungs push blood out of the thorax and into the heart
It is unchanged, because venous return depends only on blood volume
It rises, because higher airway pressure improves the respiratory pump
questions.why: Normal inspiration lowers the pressure around the right atrium and pulls blood in, so reversing the sign of that pressure raises right atrial pressure and narrows the gradient driving return. Higher pressure in the chest impedes inflow rather than pushing blood into the heart. Blood volume matters but so does the pressure gradient, which is what changed here. The natural respiratory pump depends on negative intrathoracic pressure, so positive pressure works against it, which is why hypotension is a known hazard of this therapy.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the gradient from the peripheral veins to the right atrium is reduced

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person prone to leg swelling wears graduated compression stockings while standing at work. What is the mechanism of benefit?
options: External compression lowers plasma protein concentration, reducing filtration
External compression raises arterial pressure in the leg, so more blood is delivered to the tissues of the foot and ankle
External compression closes the lymphatic vessels, so fluid stays in the blood
External compression limits venous distension, so less blood pools and venous return is better maintained
questions.why: Squeezing from outside opposes the distending hydrostatic pressure, so the veins hold less, capillary pressure stays lower, and more blood remains available to fill the heart. Arterial delivery is not the problem in dependent pooling and stockings are not designed to raise it. Closing lymphatics would trap fluid in the tissue and worsen swelling. Plasma protein concentration is set by liver synthesis and losses, not by external pressure on a limb.
questions.answerText: External compression limits venous distension, so less blood pools and venous return is better maintained

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A soldier standing rigidly at attention on a hot day becomes lightheaded and faints. Trace the sequence from posture to loss of consciousness.
options: Pooling in the legs raises venous return, stroke volume rises, arterial pressure rises above its normal range, and the resulting reflex bradycardia slows the heart enough that cerebral perfusion fails and fainting follows
Standing raises intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return and overfills the ventricle
Heat causes arteriolar constriction in the skin, arterial pressure rises, and cerebral vessels constrict in response

Pooling in the legs lowers venous return, end diastolic volume and stroke volume fall, cardiac output and mean arterial pressure fall, and cerebral perfusion drops below the level needed for consciousness
questions.why: Quiet standing removes the muscle pump while gravity distends the leg veins, and the chain from reduced filling to reduced stroke volume to reduced pressure ends at the brain, which is above the heart and least tolerant of a pressure drop. Pooling reduces rather than increases venous return. Heat causes cutaneous vasodilation, not constriction, and that dilation makes the pooling worse rather than raising pressure. Standing does not raise intrathoracic pressure, and marching in place would prevent the whole sequence by restoring the pump.
questions.answerText: Pooling in the legs lowers venous return, end diastolic volume and stroke volume fall, cardiac output and mean arterial pressure fall, and cerebral perfusion drops below the level needed for consciousness

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A person performs a Valsalva maneuver, straining hard against a closed glottis and raising intrathoracic pressure to 40 mmHg for ten seconds. Predict venous return and stroke volume during the strain and immediately after release.
options: During the strain venous return and stroke volume fall, and on release both rise sharply as the trapped venous blood surges into the thorax
During the strain venous return and stroke volume rise, and on release both fall as blood is redistributed to the legs and the veins of the abdomen
Venous return falls during the strain but stroke volume is maintained by the length tension relationship
Both are unchanged throughout, since intrathoracic pressure affects only the lungs
questions.why: Raising the pressure around the right atrium narrows the gradient driving blood into the chest, so filling and therefore ejection fall during the strain, and when the pressure is released the accumulated peripheral volume rushes in and stroke volume overshoots. Rising return during a strain would require intrathoracic pressure to fall. The length tension relationship is precisely why stroke volume cannot be maintained when filling drops, since less stretch means less force. Intrathoracic pressure acts on every structure in the chest, including the great veins and the heart.
questions.answerText: During the strain venous return and stroke volume fall, and on release both rise sharply as the trapped venous blood surges into the thorax

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: An astronaut returns from six months in microgravity with a reduced blood volume and poorly conditioned venous responses. Predict what happens when standing upright on Earth, and why.
options: Venous return rises because the veins are unusually compliant and drain quickly
Pooling is exaggerated and poorly opposed, so venous return, stroke volume, and arterial pressure fall steeply and orthostatic intolerance results
Arterial pressure rises on standing because total peripheral resistance is elevated after prolonged weightlessness, so no orthostatic symptoms occur at all
Stroke volume is preserved because reduced blood volume lowers the amount available to pool
questions.why: In microgravity there is no hydrostatic column to resist, so plasma volume falls and the venoconstrictor and muscle pump responses that normally defend upright posture go unused, leaving the astronaut with less blood and weaker defenses when gravity returns. Compliant veins fill more and drain less, so they worsen the problem. Peripheral resistance responses are blunted rather than elevated. A smaller total volume does not protect stroke volume, since the fraction that pools comes out of an already reduced supply.
questions.answerText: Pooling is exaggerated and poorly opposed, so venous return, stroke volume, and arterial pressure fall steeply and orthostatic intolerance results

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Lying down, a person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. On standing, stroke volume falls to 55 mL and the baroreceptor reflex raises heart rate to 90 beats per minute. Compare cardiac output before and after.
options: Cardiac output falls sharply, from about 5.04 L/min to about 3.96 L/min
Cardiac output falls only slightly, from about 5.04 L/min to about 4.95 L/min, because the faster rate nearly offsets the smaller stroke volume
Cardiac output rises, from about 5.04 L/min to about 6.30 L/min, because heart rate rose by 25 percent
Cardiac output is unchanged at 5.04 L/min, because the baroreceptor reflex restores stroke volume to its original value within a minute
questions.why: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so lying down gives 72 times 70, or 5040 mL/min, and standing gives 90 times 55, or 4950 mL/min, a difference of only about 2 percent. The sharp fall would result if heart rate had not risen at all. Output cannot rise here, since the stroke volume fell proportionally more than the rate climbed. The reflex works by raising rate and resistance rather than by restoring stroke volume, which stays low until the legs move.
questions.answerText: Cardiac output falls only slightly, from about 5.04 L/min to about 4.95 L/min, because the faster rate nearly offsets the smaller stroke volume

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What produces the Korotkoff sounds heard during blood pressure measurement?
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves transmitted down the arm
Contraction of the arterial smooth muscle beneath the cuff
Turbulent flow through an artery that the cuff has partially compressed
Friction between the cuff and the skin as pressure is released
questions.why: Squeezing the artery to a narrow opening speeds the blood passing through it and breaks the smooth laminar pattern, and that turbulence is audible. Valve closure produces the heart sounds heard over the chest, not the sounds heard at the elbow. Arterial smooth muscle contraction is silent. Cuff friction would be heard regardless of cuff pressure, whereas Korotkoff sounds appear and disappear at specific pressures.
questions.answerText: Turbulent flow through an artery that the cuff has partially compressed

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The first Korotkoff sound heard as cuff pressure falls marks what?
options: Diastolic pressure
Systolic pressure
Mean arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
questions.why: The first sound appears the moment cuff pressure drops just below the peak arterial pressure, so a small jet of blood forces its way through at the top of each beat. Diastolic pressure is marked by the disappearance of the sounds, not their onset. Mean arterial pressure is calculated from the two readings rather than heard directly. Pulse pressure is the difference between them and likewise is not a moment in the auscultation.
questions.answerText: Systolic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: The disappearance of the Korotkoff sounds as the cuff continues to deflate marks what?
options: Mean arterial pressure
The point of maximum turbulence
Systolic pressure
Diastolic pressure
questions.why: Once cuff pressure falls below the lowest arterial pressure, the artery stays open through the entire cycle, flow becomes laminar again, and the sounds stop. Systolic pressure is marked by the first sound rather than the last. Mean arterial pressure is derived from both endpoints and has no audible marker. Maximum turbulence occurs somewhere in the middle of the range, where the sounds are loudest, not where they vanish.
questions.answerText: Diastolic pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Which artery is auscultated during a standard blood pressure measurement?
options: The brachial artery at the antecubital fossa
The radial artery at the wrist
The carotid artery in the neck
The femoral artery in the groin
questions.why: The cuff wraps the upper arm and the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery just below the cuff, where the compressed vessel produces its sounds. The radial artery is used to palpate a pulse but lies too far distal for the cuff to compress it directly. The carotid cannot be compressed by an arm cuff and should never be occluded. The femoral artery requires a thigh cuff and is not the standard site.
questions.answerText: The brachial artery at the antecubital fossa

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: Why should the cuff be positioned at the level of the heart during measurement?
options: Because the stethoscope only transmits sound properly at that height
Because a cuff above or below heart level adds or subtracts hydrostatic pressure from the reading
Because arterial smooth muscle tone varies with the height of the limb relative to the rest of the body
Because the heart rate changes when the arm is raised or lowered
questions.why: Blood pressure varies with vertical distance from the heart because of the weight of the column of blood, so placing the cuff at heart level removes that offset and lets you read the pressure the heart is actually generating. Stethoscope acoustics do not depend on limb height. Arterial tone does change somewhat with position, but the hydrostatic offset is much larger and is the reason for the rule. Heart rate is not meaningfully altered by arm position.
questions.answerText: Because a cuff above or below heart level adds or subtracts hydrostatic pressure from the reading

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: What is the effect of using a cuff that is too narrow for the person's arm?
options: The reading is falsely low
The systolic value is falsely high and the diastolic falsely low
The reading is falsely high
The reading is unaffected as long as the cuff can be fastened
questions.why: A narrow cuff spreads its pressure over too little tissue, so more cuff pressure is needed to compress the underlying artery and the recorded numbers exceed the true ones. A falsely low reading comes from a cuff that is too wide for the limb. The error affects both endpoints in the same direction rather than splitting them. Fastening is not the criterion, since cuff width relative to arm circumference is what determines accuracy.
questions.answerText: The reading is falsely high

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: While cuff pressure is above systolic pressure, no sound is heard. Why?
options: The artery is completely occluded, so there is no flow to make turbulence
Flow is continuous and laminar, so it is silent
The stethoscope is compressed by the cuff and cannot transmit sound
The artery has dilated fully and offers no resistance
questions.why: When the cuff exceeds the highest pressure the heart generates, the vessel is squeezed shut for the entire cycle and no blood passes, so there is nothing to hear. Continuous laminar flow explains the silence below the diastolic reading, which is the other silent zone. The stethoscope sits distal to the cuff and works normally. The artery is compressed rather than dilated at these pressures.
questions.answerText: The artery is completely occluded, so there is no flow to make turbulence

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: After the cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the sounds stop. What is the flow condition then?
options: Flow has stopped entirely because the artery has collapsed
Flow is continuous through the whole cardiac cycle and laminar, therefore silent
Flow is intermittent but too weak to produce sound
Flow is still turbulent but shifts to a frequency above the range of human hearing
questions.why: Once the cuff no longer narrows the artery at any point in the cycle, blood moves in smooth concentric layers, which produces no audible sound. Collapse and absent flow describe the silence above systolic pressure, at the other end of the range. Flow is continuous rather than intermittent at this point, which is precisely why turbulence ends. The sounds do not shift out of the audible range, they cease because the turbulence itself ends.
questions.answerText: Flow is continuous through the whole cardiac cycle and laminar, therefore silent

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A student measures blood pressure on a large arm using a standard adult cuff that barely fits. How will the recorded values compare with the true pressure?
options: Both systolic and diastolic will read lower than the true values
Both systolic and diastolic will read higher than the true values
Systolic will read higher and diastolic lower, widening the pulse pressure
The values will be accurate because the cuff was able to close
questions.why: A cuff that is too small for the limb transmits less of its pressure to the artery, so higher cuff pressures are required to occlude and to release it, inflating both numbers. Low readings would come from an oversized cuff. The error shifts both endpoints together, so pulse pressure is not systematically widened. Whether the cuff fastens says nothing about whether its bladder covers enough of the arm circumference.
questions.answerText: Both systolic and diastolic will read higher than the true values

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A student measures blood pressure with the subject's arm resting in their lap, well below heart level. What is the effect on the reading?
options: The reading is falsely low because blood pools away from the arm
The reading is falsely high because hydrostatic pressure adds to the arterial pressure
Only the diastolic value is affected, since it is measured last
The reading is unaffected because the cuff measures pressure relative to the arm
questions.why: Every centimeter the artery lies below the heart adds hydrostatic pressure from the column of blood above it, so a dependent arm reads several mmHg too high. Blood does not pool away from a dependent limb, it pools into it. The offset applies through the whole measurement, so both endpoints shift. The cuff reads the pressure in the artery beneath it, which includes the gravitational component, so limb position matters.
questions.answerText: The reading is falsely high because hydrostatic pressure adds to the arterial pressure

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A student deflates the cuff very slowly, taking well over a minute. What error is most likely?
options: No error occurs, since slower deflation always improves accuracy
The artery relaxes and the systolic value reads falsely high
The Korotkoff sounds become louder, so both values read falsely low
Venous congestion builds in the forearm and the diastolic value reads falsely high
questions.why: Prolonged cuff pressure traps blood in the forearm veins, which distends the limb and muffles the transition, so the sounds persist longer than they should and diastolic is overestimated. Slow deflation does not raise the systolic reading, since the first sound is still detected at the correct pressure. Congestion tends to muffle rather than amplify the sounds. Deflation at roughly two to three mmHg per second is the accuracy target, and going far slower introduces this error.
questions.answerText: Venous congestion builds in the forearm and the diastolic value reads falsely high

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A subject moves from lying down to standing. What is the expected normal blood pressure and heart rate response after a minute?
options: Systolic rises sharply, diastolic falls sharply, and heart rate slows
Both systolic and diastolic rise substantially and heart rate slows
Both systolic and diastolic fall by more than 20 mmHg and heart rate is unchanged
Systolic falls slightly, diastolic rises slightly, and heart rate increases modestly
questions.why: Standing lets blood pool in the legs, so stroke volume and therefore systolic pressure dip, while the baroreceptor reflex raises heart rate and constricts arterioles, which lifts diastolic pressure and largely defends the mean. A drop over 20 mmHg with no rate change is the abnormal pattern that defines orthostatic hypotension. Systolic rising sharply on standing is not a normal response. Bradycardia on standing would deepen the fall in output rather than compensate for it.
questions.answerText: Systolic falls slightly, diastolic rises slightly, and heart rate increases modestly

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During moderate dynamic exercise such as cycling, what happens to systolic and diastolic pressure?
options: Systolic rises substantially while diastolic stays about the same or falls slightly
Both rise by about the same amount
Systolic stays about the same while diastolic rises substantially above its resting value
Both fall, because muscle arterioles dilate
questions.why: A larger stroke volume and faster ejection drive the systolic peak up, while widespread dilation in working muscle lowers total peripheral resistance and keeps the diastolic floor from climbing, so pulse pressure widens. Equal rises would mean resistance had increased along with output, which is the isometric rather than the dynamic pattern. Systolic cannot stay flat when cardiac output rises several fold. Both values falling would leave no driving pressure for the enormous muscle flow required.
questions.answerText: Systolic rises substantially while diastolic stays about the same or falls slightly

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A student releases the cuff pressure very quickly, dropping it about 10 mmHg per second. What error results?
options: Systolic is overestimated and diastolic is underestimated, because the sounds are heard earlier and persist longer than they should
Both values are overestimated by roughly the same amount
Systolic is underestimated and diastolic is overestimated, because the endpoints are passed before they can be heard
Only the systolic value is affected, since it comes first
questions.why: With the needle falling fast, several mmHg pass between heartbeats, so the first audible beat occurs below the true systolic pressure and the last audible beat occurs above the true diastolic pressure, narrowing the recorded range. The opposite pairing would require the sounds to be heard before they exist. Both endpoints are affected, and they shift toward each other rather than in the same direction. This is why a controlled two to three mmHg per second deflation is taught.
questions.answerText: Systolic is underestimated and diastolic is overestimated, because the endpoints are passed before they can be heard

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: While cuff pressure lies between systolic and diastolic pressure, what is happening in the artery?
options: Blood flows continuously but slowly through a fully open artery
The artery is completely closed for the whole cycle and the sounds come from the cuff pressing on the skin of the arm
Blood spurts through a narrowed opening during part of each cycle, producing intermittent turbulent flow
Blood flows backward during diastole through incompetent arterial valves
questions.why: In this pressure window the artery opens only while arterial pressure exceeds cuff pressure, so a jet passes through a partly squeezed vessel once per beat and the resulting turbulence is what you hear. Continuous open flow describes conditions below the diastolic reading, where sounds cease. A completely closed artery is the state above systolic, and the cuff itself makes no sound. Arteries have no valves along their length, so backflow of that kind does not occur.
questions.answerText: Blood spurts through a narrowed opening during part of each cycle, producing intermittent turbulent flow

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A subject reads 120 over 80 lying down and 90 over 60 after one minute of standing. Calculate both mean arterial pressures and interpret the change.
options: Mean arterial pressure falls from about 93 to 70 mmHg, a drop consistent with orthostatic hypotension
Mean arterial pressure falls from about 100 to 75 mmHg, a normal postural response
Mean arterial pressure rises from about 93 to 100 mmHg because the reflex overcompensates
Mean arterial pressure is unchanged at about 93 mmHg because pulse pressure narrowed
questions.why: Lying down, pulse pressure is 40 and one third of it is about 13, so the mean is 80 plus 13, roughly 93 mmHg. Standing, pulse pressure is 30 and one third is 10, so the mean is 60 plus 10, or 70 mmHg. A fall of that size, with systolic dropping 30 mmHg, is well beyond the small dip expected normally. Using the midpoint of the two readings gives 100 and 75 and overestimates both means. The mean clearly changed, so the narrowed pulse pressure did not hold it constant.
questions.answerText: Mean arterial pressure falls from about 93 to 70 mmHg, a drop consistent with orthostatic hypotension

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: A subject reads 120 over 80 at rest and 170 over 80 during steady cycling. Calculate pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure for each and explain the pattern.
options: Pulse pressure widens from 40 to 90 mmHg but mean arterial pressure falls to about 80 mmHg because resistance dropped
Pulse pressure widens from 40 to 90 mmHg and mean arterial pressure rises from about 93 to 145 mmHg, tracking the midpoint of the systolic and diastolic values recorded during exercise
Pulse pressure is unchanged at 40 mmHg and mean arterial pressure rises from 93 to 110 mmHg
Pulse pressure widens from 40 to 90 mmHg and mean arterial pressure rises from about 93 to 110 mmHg, because stroke volume rose sharply while muscle vasodilation held resistance down
questions.why: At rest, 120 minus 80 gives a pulse pressure of 40, and 80 plus one third of 40 gives about 93 mmHg. During exercise, 170 minus 80 gives 90, and 80 plus 30 gives 110 mmHg.
