The mean rises only modestly because arteriolar dilation in working muscle offsets much of the rise in cardiac output. A mean of 145 is the midpoint of the exercise reading and overestimates it. Pulse pressure clearly widened, and the mean rose rather than fell, since output climbed more than resistance dropped.
questions.answerText: Pulse pressure widens from 40 to 90 mmHg and mean arterial pressure rises from about 93 to 110 mmHg, because stroke volume rose sharply while muscle vasodilation held resistance down

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: In dynamic exercise diastolic pressure typically stays flat, but during sustained isometric exercise such as a hard handgrip it rises noticeably. What explains the difference?
options: Isometric exercise raises plasma viscosity, which raises diastolic pressure
Dynamic exercise raises stroke volume while sustained isometric exercise lowers it, so diastolic pressure falls during the dynamic form of work and rises during the isometric form
Dynamic exercise activates the parasympathetic system while isometric exercise activates the sympathetic system
Dynamic exercise dilates a large muscle mass and lowers total peripheral resistance, while sustained contraction compresses vessels within the muscle and raises resistance
questions.why: Diastolic pressure tracks total peripheral resistance closely, so opening large numbers of muscle arterioles during rhythmic work keeps it from climbing, while a maintained contraction squeezes those same vessels shut and pushes resistance up. Stroke volume rises in both forms of exercise, though more in the dynamic form, so it does not explain the diastolic split. Both forms of exercise activate the sympathetic system. Viscosity changes little over minutes and is far too small an effect to account for the difference.
questions.answerText: Dynamic exercise dilates a large muscle mass and lowers total peripheral resistance, while sustained contraction compresses vessels within the muscle and raises resistance

questions.topic: Vascular Physiology
questions.q: During a lab exercise trial, a student hears Korotkoff sounds continue all the way down to zero on the manometer. What is the best interpretation and what should be recorded?
options: The subject has no diastolic pressure, so a value of zero should be recorded
The cuff has a leak, so the systolic value should also be discarded
The stethoscope is pressing too hard on the artery and creating the sounds itself, so the whole measurement should be discarded as meaningless and repeated on the other arm
High flow through the artery keeps turbulence audible below the true diastolic pressure, so the point where the sounds become muffled should be recorded as diastolic
questions.why: After exercise, and in other high output states, blood moves fast enough to stay turbulent even when the cuff is barely compressing the artery, so the muffling point is used as the diastolic endpoint and noted as such. A diastolic pressure of zero is physiologically impossible in a living person, since elastic recoil sustains arterial pressure between beats. Excessive stethoscope pressure can create artifact, but the fix is to lighten the pressure and repeat rather than to assume the whole reading is meaningless. A cuff leak would cause pressure to fall uncontrollably and would not selectively prolong the sounds.
questions.answerText: High flow through the artery keeps turbulence audible below the true diastolic pressure, so the point where the sounds become muffled should be recorded as diastolic

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What physical change do the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus actually detect?
options: Stretch of the arterial wall
Oxygen content of the arterial blood
Carbon dioxide content of the blood
Velocity of blood flowing past them
questions.why: Baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors. A higher pressure distends the vessel wall, the nerve endings woven into that wall are stretched, and they fire faster, so pressure is sensed indirectly through wall deformation. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the stimuli for the peripheral chemoreceptors of the carotid and aortic bodies, which sit close by but report a different variable. Flow velocity is not sensed directly anywhere in the arterial tree, and a vessel can carry fast flow at low pressure.
questions.answerText: Stretch of the arterial wall

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which cranial nerve carries baroreceptor signals from the carotid sinus to the medulla?
options: The vagus nerve (cranial X)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
The facial nerve (cranial VII)
The trigeminal nerve (cranial V)
questions.why: Carotid sinus afferents run in the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and enter the medulla with cranial nerve IX. The vagus is the correct answer for the aortic arch receptors, and swapping those two is the most common error on this pathway. The facial and trigeminal nerves supply the face and jaw and carry no arterial pressure information.
questions.answerText: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which nerve carries baroreceptor signals from the aortic arch to the medulla?
options: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
The phrenic nerve
The vagus nerve (X)
The spinal accessory nerve (XI)
questions.why: Aortic arch afferents travel in the aortic depressor nerve, a branch of the vagus, so cranial nerve X is both the sensory route from the arch and the motor route back to the SA node. Glossopharyngeal is correct for the carotid sinus, one level higher in the neck. The phrenic nerve is motor to the diaphragm and the spinal accessory supplies neck muscles, so neither carries pressure information.
questions.answerText: The vagus nerve (X)

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Where is the integrating center for the baroreceptor reflex located?
options: In the hypothalamus
In the cerebellar cortex
In the pontine tegmentum
In the medulla oblongata
questions.why: The cardiovascular control center lies in the medulla oblongata, where afferent traffic is compared against the operating point and converted into sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow. The hypothalamus does drive cardiovascular changes with temperature and emotion, but it acts on the medullary centers rather than replacing them. The pons modulates breathing rhythm and the cerebellum coordinates movement; neither integrates this reflex.
questions.answerText: In the medulla oblongata

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which medullary nucleus receives the incoming baroreceptor signals first?
options: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
The nucleus tractus solitarius
The nucleus ambiguus
The rostral ventrolateral medulla
questions.why: The nucleus tractus solitarius is the sensory entry point for glossopharyngeal and vagal baroreceptor afferents, and it distributes that input to the outflow nuclei. The nucleus ambiguus and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus are sources of parasympathetic output to the heart, so they sit on the efferent side, not the afferent side. The rostral ventrolateral medulla drives sympathetic outflow and is inhibited by signals coming out of the nucleus tractus solitarius, which places it one step downstream.
questions.answerText: The nucleus tractus solitarius

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Mean arterial pressure falls from 95 to 70 mmHg. What happens to the firing rate of the carotid sinus baroreceptors?
options: It decreases, because the wall is stretched less
It is unchanged, since only high pressure is sensed
It increases, then settles back to the old baseline
It increases, because the reflex is switching on
questions.why: Firing rate tracks wall stretch, so a lower pressure means less stretch and fewer action potentials per second. This is the step students invert most often: the reflex is triggered by a drop in afferent traffic reaching the medulla, not by a rise in it. A receptor that reported only high pressure would leave the body with no defense against hypotension. The transient rise followed by a return to baseline describes receptor adaptation to a sustained high pressure, which is the opposite situation.
questions.answerText: It decreases, because the wall is stretched less

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which nerve and which receptor carry out the parasympathetic slowing of the SA node?
options: Cardiac nerves, acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors
Glossopharyngeal nerve, acetylcholine onto muscarinic sites
Vagus nerve, acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors
Vagus nerve, norepinephrine onto beta-1 receptors
questions.why: Vagal postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto muscarinic (M2) receptors in the SA node, which slows the pacemaker depolarization and lowers heart rate. Norepinephrine and beta-1 receptors belong to the sympathetic limb, which does the opposite, so pairing them with the vagus mixes the two systems. Nicotinic receptors do appear in the autonomic pathway, but at the ganglion between the two neurons, not at the cardiac target. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensory traffic in from the carotid sinus and sends no motor fibers to the heart.
questions.answerText: Vagus nerve, acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Norepinephrine released onto a systemic arteriole constricts it by acting on which receptor?
options: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors
Beta-2 adrenergic receptors
Muscarinic cholinergic receptors
Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
questions.why: Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle raise intracellular Ca2+ and contract the vessel, which is how sympathetic outflow raises total peripheral resistance. Beta-1 receptors are the cardiac target of the same transmitter and change rate and contractility rather than vessel diameter. Beta-2 receptors dilate vessels in skeletal muscle but respond mainly to circulating epinephrine, not to norepinephrine released from nerve terminals. Muscarinic receptors are cholinergic and are not part of the sympathetic vasoconstrictor pathway at all.
questions.answerText: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient stands up quickly and blood pools in the leg veins. In the first few seconds, what does the medullary cardiovascular center do with sympathetic outflow?
options: Increases it, because baroreceptor firing has fallen
Decreases it, because baroreceptor firing has fallen
Increases it, because baroreceptor firing has risen
Leaves it unchanged until pressure drops below 60 mmHg
questions.why: Pooling lowers venous return and arterial pressure, the receptors stretch less and fire less, and that loss of firing removes inhibition from the sympathetic center, so outflow rises. Decreasing sympathetic outflow keeps the correct afferent direction but inverts the central step, since less baroreceptor traffic releases the brake rather than applying it. Saying that firing has risen gets the sensor backwards, because firing falls when pressure falls. Waiting until 60 mmHg would mean tolerating a large drop before responding, and the reflex in fact operates continuously around its normal set point.
questions.answerText: Increases it, because baroreceptor firing has fallen

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A clinician presses firmly over the carotid sinus, stretching the sinus wall. What happens to heart rate?
options: It rises, because the pressure blocks blood flow to the brain
It is unchanged, since the stretch is mechanical, not vascular
It rises, because the medulla reads the signal as low pressure
It falls, because the medulla reads the signal as high pressure
questions.why: The receptor cannot tell pressure from any other source of stretch, so external compression increases firing, the medulla concludes that pressure is high, vagal outflow rises and sympathetic outflow falls, and heart rate drops. A rising heart rate would require the sign to be inverted twice over, since extra stretch means more firing, and more firing means less sympathetic drive. Reduced cerebral flow would trigger a chemoreceptor and ischemic response that raises pressure, but that requires far more severe compression than a sinus massage. The mechanical stimulus is exactly what these endings are built to detect, so calling it irrelevant misreads the receptor.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the medulla reads the signal as high pressure

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Mean arterial pressure rises to 120 mmHg. What happens to vagal traffic to the heart, and what does that do?
options: It is unchanged, since only sympathetic outflow is adjusted
It falls, letting the intrinsic SA node rate emerge
It rises, slowing the SA node
It falls, slowing the SA node
questions.why: Higher pressure means more stretch, more afferent firing, and a medullary response that raises vagal output while lowering sympathetic output, so the SA node slows. Falling vagal traffic would unmask the faster intrinsic pacemaker rate near 100 beats per minute, which is what happens when pressure drops, not when it rises. Pairing falling vagal traffic with a slower SA node joins the right effect to the wrong cause, since less vagal traffic can only speed the heart. Both limbs are adjusted reciprocally in this reflex, so leaving the vagus out misses half the response.
questions.answerText: It rises, slowing the SA node

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient takes a beta-1 blocker. Which part of the baroreflex response to a fall in blood pressure is blunted?
options: The constriction of capacitance veins
The rise in heart rate and contractility
The constriction of systemic arterioles
The fall in baroreceptor firing rate
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors are the cardiac targets of sympathetic outflow, so blocking them removes the chronotropic and inotropic part of the response while everything else still works. Arteriolar and venous constriction run through alpha-1 receptors and are untouched by a beta-1 blocker. Baroreceptor firing is a sensory event in the vessel wall and is not adrenergic at all, so no adrenergic blocker changes it.
questions.answerText: The rise in heart rate and contractility

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: In an animal experiment all baroreceptor afferents are cut. What does the medulla do, and why?
options: Raises vagal outflow, reading silence as low pressure
Makes no change, since the reflex needs an active signal
Raises sympathetic outflow, reading silence as low pressure
Lowers sympathetic outflow, reading silence as high pressure
questions.why: Ongoing baroreceptor firing is a tonic brake on the sympathetic center, so cutting the afferents removes that brake entirely and mean arterial pressure rises and becomes unstable. Lowering sympathetic outflow reverses the sign, treating no signal as if it meant a strong one. Raising vagal outflow would be the response to more firing, not less, so that answer keeps the right premise and draws the wrong conclusion. Expecting no change at all misses that the resting reflex is always firing, which makes the absence of a signal informative in itself.
questions.answerText: Raises sympathetic outflow, reading silence as low pressure

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Sympathetic outflow to the systemic veins increases after a fall in pressure. What is the immediate hemodynamic result?
options: Venous return falls because the veins hold more blood
Afterload rises while preload stays unchanged
Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls sharply
Venous return and ventricular preload increase
questions.why: The systemic veins hold about two thirds of the blood volume, so squeezing them shifts stored blood toward the heart, raising end diastolic volume and stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism. Constricted veins hold less blood, not more, so the answer with venous return falling has the geometry backwards. Afterload is set by arterial pressure and arteriolar tone, not by the veins. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is governed mainly by arteriolar resistance upstream, and it falls in hemorrhage because arterioles constrict, not because veins do.
questions.answerText: Venous return and ventricular preload increase

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient takes an alpha-1 blocker and then has a fall in blood pressure. Which compensatory change still occurs normally?
options: The rise in heart rate through beta-1 receptors
Constriction of the systemic capacitance veins
The overall rise in total peripheral resistance
Constriction of the splanchnic and renal arterioles
questions.why: An alpha-1 blocker leaves the cardiac limb of the reflex intact, so the fall in baroreceptor firing still produces a tachycardia through beta-1 receptors on the SA node. Splanchnic arteriolar constriction, venoconstriction, and the resulting rise in total peripheral resistance all depend on alpha-1 receptors and are the very responses the drug removes. This is why alpha blockade so often produces orthostatic hypotension with a fast pulse.
questions.answerText: The rise in heart rate through beta-1 receptors

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A trauma patient has lost about a liter of blood and mean arterial pressure is 72 mmHg. Trace the reflex and pick the correct pair of changes.
options: Baroreceptor firing rises, sympathetic outflow rises
Baroreceptor firing falls, sympathetic outflow rises
Baroreceptor firing falls, sympathetic outflow falls
Baroreceptor firing rises, sympathetic outflow falls
questions.why: Blood loss lowers pressure, the arterial walls stretch less, and firing in cranial nerves IX and X falls. That reduced traffic removes inhibition from the medullary sympathetic center, so outflow to the heart and vessels rises, giving tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Any option with firing rising has the sensor backwards, since receptors report the pressure that exists, not the pressure the body wants. The pairing of falling firing with falling sympathetic outflow is the classic sign error: it treats the afferent signal as excitatory when it is inhibitory.
questions.answerText: Baroreceptor firing falls, sympathetic outflow rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: An older patient faints while buttoning a shirt collar that presses on the carotid sinus. Which sequence explains the faint?
options: Wall stretched, firing up, sympathetic up, pressure up
Wall stretched, firing up, vagal outflow up, heart rate down
Wall stretched, firing down, sympathetic up, heart rate up
Wall compressed, firing down, sympathetic up, pressure up
questions.why: The collar deforms the sinus, the receptors read that deformation as a high pressure, and the medulla answers with more vagal outflow and less sympathetic outflow, so heart rate and pressure fall far enough to drop cerebral perfusion. The two sequences in which firing falls have the afferent step inverted, treating a stretched receptor as a quiet one. The sequence that ends in a rise in pressure gets the sensing right but then has the medulla answer a high pressure by raising it further, which would be positive feedback rather than a reflex correction.
questions.answerText: Wall stretched, firing up, vagal outflow up, heart rate down

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient has had a mean arterial pressure near 160 mmHg for two years, yet the baroreflex is not driving it down. What best explains this?
options: The medulla has stopped responding to afferent input
The vagal fibers to the heart have degenerated
The receptors were destroyed by the sustained pressure
The reflex has reset and now defends the higher pressure
questions.why: Baroreceptors adapt over hours to days, so a chronically high pressure comes to produce close to normal firing and the medulla treats 160 mmHg as the value to protect. The reflex still works, and it will still correct a sudden rise or fall around that new operating point, which is why resetting explains chronic hypertension without abolishing acute regulation. The receptors are not destroyed, the medulla is not deaf, and the vagus is not degenerated in any of these patients; all three would predict a reflex that fails on acute challenges, which is not what is observed.
questions.answerText: The reflex has reset and now defends the higher pressure

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient on a beta-1 blocker stands up and blood pressure drops further than it would without the drug. Which limbs of the reflex are intact and which are missing?
options: Vasoconstriction intact, rise in heart rate blunted
Vasoconstriction blunted, rise in heart rate intact
Both limbs blunted, since the drug blocks all outflow
Neither limb affected, since the drug acts on the kidney
questions.why: Standing lowers baroreceptor firing and raises sympathetic outflow as usual, and the alpha-1 arteriolar and venous responses go ahead normally because the drug does not touch alpha receptors. Only the beta-1 cardiac response is lost, so heart rate cannot climb enough to hold cardiac output while stroke volume is low, and pressure falls further. Calling vasoconstriction blunted and the heart rate response intact swaps the receptor families. Saying both limbs are blunted overstates a drug that is selective for beta-1 and leaves central outflow untouched, and putting the drug in the kidney confuses a beta blocker with a diuretic.
questions.answerText: Vasoconstriction intact, rise in heart rate blunted

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which cells release renin, and what triggers them?
options: Collecting duct principal cells, when plasma K+ rises
Adrenal cortical cells, when plasma volume falls
Juxtaglomerular cells, when renal perfusion falls
Macula densa cells, when tubular Na+ delivery rises
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole act as pressure sensors and secrete renin when perfusion pressure drops, when sympathetic outflow rises, or when the macula densa reports low NaCl delivery. The macula densa is a sensor that signals those cells; it does not itself secrete renin, and it drives renin release when sodium delivery falls, not rises. Principal cells respond to aldosterone rather than making a hormone, and the adrenal cortex makes aldosterone, which is several steps downstream of renin.
questions.answerText: Juxtaglomerular cells, when renal perfusion falls

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What reaction does angiotensin converting enzyme catalyze?
options: It converts inactive renin into active renin
It converts angiotensin II into aldosterone
It converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I
It converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II
questions.why: Angiotensin converting enzyme, found in high concentration on pulmonary capillary endothelium, clips two residues off angiotensin I to make the active hormone angiotensin II. Cleaving angiotensinogen to angiotensin I is the job of renin, and confusing those two steps makes the whole cascade collapse into one. Renin is secreted in an already active form after intracellular processing. Aldosterone is a steroid made in the adrenal cortex in response to angiotensin II, not a chemical conversion product of it.
questions.answerText: It converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What is the direct action of angiotensin II on systemic arterioles?
options: It dilates muscle vessels and constricts skin
It constricts them and raises resistance
It dilates them by releasing nitric oxide
It has no direct effect on systemic vascular tone
questions.why: Angiotensin II is one of the most powerful vasoconstrictors in the body, acting on AT1 receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle to raise resistance and therefore mean arterial pressure within minutes. Nitric oxide release is an endothelial dilator pathway that angiotensin II opposes rather than triggers. The hormone has renal actions as well, but they are additional to the vascular ones rather than a substitute for them. Selective dilation of muscle beds with constriction of skin describes the pattern of exercise and circulating epinephrine, not angiotensin II.
questions.answerText: It constricts them and raises resistance

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion from which tissue?
options: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex
The posterior pituitary
The zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex
The adrenal medulla
questions.why: The outer zone of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa, makes aldosterone, and angiotensin II and a rising plasma K+ are its two main stimuli. The adrenal medulla is chromaffin tissue that releases epinephrine under sympathetic drive, a much faster and shorter acting system. The zona fasciculata makes cortisol under the control of ACTH, not angiotensin II. The posterior pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone, which also defends blood pressure but through water rather than sodium.
questions.answerText: The zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What are the two main tubular actions of aldosterone?
options: More Na+ reabsorption and more K+ secretion
More Na+ reabsorption and more K+ reabsorption
More water reabsorption through aquaporin channels
More Na+ excretion and more K+ retention
questions.why: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing the number of sodium channels and Na+/K+ ATPase pumps, so sodium is reabsorbed and potassium is secreted into the tubular fluid. Water follows the reabsorbed sodium osmotically, which is how a sodium hormone ends up expanding blood volume. Sodium and potassium move in opposite directions here, so reabsorbing both loses the exchange that makes aldosterone excess produce a low plasma K+. Aquaporin insertion is the action of antidiuretic hormone, and excreting sodium while retaining potassium describes the effect of blocking aldosterone rather than of having it.
questions.answerText: More Na+ reabsorption and more K+ secretion

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: From which structure is antidiuretic hormone released into the blood?
options: The atrial myocardium
The posterior pituitary
The anterior pituitary
The adrenal cortex
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone is made in hypothalamic neurons whose axons run down the pituitary stalk and release the hormone from their terminals in the posterior pituitary directly into the circulation. The anterior pituitary is glandular tissue that makes its own hormones under hypothalamic releasing factors, so it stores nothing from the hypothalamus. The adrenal cortex is the source of aldosterone and the atrial myocardium is the source of atrial natriuretic peptide, the two other volume hormones on this list.
questions.answerText: The posterior pituitary

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What does antidiuretic hormone do at the collecting duct?
options: It inserts aquaporin-2 channels so water is reabsorbed
It inserts sodium channels so sodium is reabsorbed
It blocks water reabsorption so urine volume rises
It increases potassium secretion into the tubular fluid
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone signals principal cells to move stored aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane, making a normally water tight epithelium permeable so water is drawn out into the concentrated medullary interstitium. Sodium channel insertion and potassium secretion are aldosterone effects, and telling the two hormones apart is the point: aldosterone moves salt with water following, while antidiuretic hormone moves water alone. Blocking water reabsorption is what happens when the hormone is absent, as in diabetes insipidus, where urine output can exceed ten liters a day.
questions.answerText: It inserts aquaporin-2 channels so water is reabsorbed

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What stimulus causes release of atrial natriuretic peptide?
options: A rise in plasma potassium concentration
Sympathetic stimulation of the ventricular wall
Stretch of the atrial wall as volume rises
A fall in atrial filling pressure during rest
questions.why: Atrial myocytes act as volume sensors: when venous return and atrial filling rise, the stretched cells release atrial natriuretic peptide, which then promotes sodium and water loss and brings volume back down. A fall in filling pressure does the opposite and turns the hormone off, which is why it is low in hemorrhage. A rising plasma K+ is a stimulus for aldosterone, and sympathetic drive raises contractility rather than triggering this peptide.
questions.answerText: Stretch of the atrial wall as volume rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A narrowing of one renal artery lowers perfusion pressure to that kidney. Predict renin release and systemic blood pressure.
options: Renin rises and systemic pressure falls
Renin falls and systemic pressure rises
Renin falls and systemic pressure falls
Renin rises and systemic pressure rises
questions.why: The stenosed kidney senses a low perfusion pressure and cannot tell that the rest of the body is normal, so it secretes renin, the cascade generates angiotensin II and aldosterone, and systemic pressure climbs. The kidney is defending its own perfusion at the cost of the whole circulation, which is why this is a recognized cause of secondary hypertension. Any answer with renin falling misreads the trigger, and any answer with pressure falling ignores what angiotensin II and aldosterone do once they are made.
questions.answerText: Renin rises and systemic pressure rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient takes a drug that inhibits angiotensin converting enzyme. Predict plasma angiotensin II and aldosterone.
options: Angiotensin II is unchanged, and aldosterone falls
Angiotensin II falls, and aldosterone falls with it
Angiotensin II falls, but aldosterone rises instead
Angiotensin II rises, because renin is inhibited
questions.why: Blocking the converting enzyme stops the production of angiotensin II, and because angiotensin II is the main stimulus for aldosterone secretion, aldosterone falls as a consequence. That is one hormone pulling the other, not two independent effects. Aldosterone cannot rise when its main stimulus is removed, unless plasma K+ climbs enough to drive it directly. Saying angiotensin II rises because renin is inhibited confuses the two enzymes, since renin is upstream and untouched by this drug, so angiotensin I accumulates while angiotensin II falls.
questions.answerText: Angiotensin II falls, and aldosterone falls with it

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which hormone retains water without a matching gain of sodium, and therefore lowers plasma osmolarity?
options: Aldosterone
Atrial natriuretic peptide
Angiotensin II
Antidiuretic hormone
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone opens a water pathway in the collecting duct while leaving solute handling alone, so pure water is added to the body and plasma osmolarity falls. Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium with water following, which expands volume while keeping osmolarity close to normal, and that is the distinction between the two. Atrial natriuretic peptide removes sodium and water rather than retaining either. Angiotensin II raises pressure mainly through vasoconstriction and by driving the other two hormones, so its water effect is indirect.
questions.answerText: Antidiuretic hormone

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Plasma osmolarity rises from 290 to 302 mOsm/L. Predict antidiuretic hormone secretion and urine concentration.
options: Hormone falls, urine becomes more concentrated
Hormone falls, urine becomes more dilute
Hormone rises, urine becomes more concentrated
Hormone rises, urine becomes more dilute
questions.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors are sensitive to shifts of only one or two percent, so a 12 mOsm/L rise strongly stimulates antidiuretic hormone release, water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. The two options with the hormone rising but urine diluting or the hormone falling but urine concentrating break the link between the hormone and its own renal action. Falling hormone with dilute urine is the correct response to drinking a large volume of water, which is the opposite stimulus.
questions.answerText: Hormone rises, urine becomes more concentrated

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: An adrenal tumor secretes aldosterone continuously. Predict plasma potassium and blood pressure.
options: Potassium falls and blood pressure rises
Potassium rises and blood pressure rises
Potassium falls and blood pressure falls
Potassium rises and blood pressure falls
questions.why: Sustained aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption, which expands extracellular volume and raises pressure, and it drives potassium secretion, which drains plasma K+ over time. Potassium and sodium move in opposite directions through the principal cell, so any answer with both potassium and blood pressure rising has that exchange backwards. A falling blood pressure would be the picture in adrenal insufficiency, where aldosterone is missing and sodium is lost in the urine, and there plasma K+ climbs instead.
questions.answerText: Potassium falls and blood pressure rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent. What does this do to glomerular filtration when renal perfusion is low?
options: It raises renal blood flow and filtration together
It holds filtration up despite the low renal blood flow
It lowers filtration by reducing glomerular capillary pressure
It has no net effect, since both arterioles constrict
questions.why: Squeezing the vessel downstream of the glomerulus dams blood inside the capillary tuft, so glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration are preserved even while total renal blood flow is falling. Constricting the afferent arteriole instead would do the reverse and cut filtration, which is the confusion this card is built around. Filtration and flow move in opposite directions here, so the option pairing them together misses the point of selective efferent tone.
questions.answerText: It holds filtration up despite the low renal blood flow

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient receives a large intravenous saline infusion. Predict atrial natriuretic peptide secretion and urinary sodium excretion.
options: Peptide falls and sodium excretion rises
Peptide falls and sodium excretion falls
Peptide rises and sodium excretion rises
Peptide rises and sodium excretion falls
questions.why: Volume expansion stretches the atria, atrial natriuretic peptide is released, and it raises filtration while blocking sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, so sodium and the water that follows it leave in the urine. The name of the hormone states its action, so a rise in the peptide with less sodium in the urine contradicts itself. A falling peptide belongs to volume depletion, where the atria are underfilled and the body is trying to keep sodium rather than lose it.
questions.answerText: Peptide rises and sodium excretion rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A hiker drinks nothing for eight hours in the heat. Plasma osmolarity is 302 mOsm/L and blood volume is down about 6 percent. Which set of changes fits?
options: Hormone up, aldosterone down, urine volume up
Hormone down, aldosterone up, urine volume down
Hormone down, aldosterone down, urine volume up
Hormone up, aldosterone up, urine volume down
questions.why: Sweating loses more water than salt, so osmolarity rises and drives antidiuretic hormone, while the volume loss lowers renal perfusion and drives renin, angiotensin II, and aldosterone. Both hormones conserve fluid, so the urine becomes small in volume and concentrated. The answers that raise one hormone while lowering the other split a pair that moves together, since in dehydration the osmotic and volume signals point the same way. Suppressing both with a large urine volume describes the state after drinking a lot of water, which is the opposite challenge.
questions.answerText: Hormone up, aldosterone up, urine volume down

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient starts an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Trace the effect on efferent arteriolar tone and then on glomerular filtration rate.
options: Efferent tone falls, so filtration pressure and rate fall
Efferent tone rises, so filtration pressure and rate rise
Efferent tone falls, so filtration pressure and rate rise
Efferent tone is unchanged, and filtration rate is unchanged
questions.why: Angiotensin II is what holds the efferent arteriole constricted, so removing it opens that vessel, blood leaves the glomerulus more easily, capillary hydrostatic pressure drops, and filtration rate falls even though renal blood flow rises. The step that trips students is that flow and filtration move in opposite directions here. Efferent tone cannot rise when the hormone that produces it is gone, and it cannot fall while filtration climbs, since the pressure in the tuft is what drives filtration.
questions.answerText: Efferent tone falls, so filtration pressure and rate fall

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: In heart failure the atria are chronically stretched and atrial natriuretic peptide is high, yet the patient still retains salt and water. What explains this?
options: The peptide has no renal actions in adult humans
High peptide levels reverse and cause sodium retention
The kidneys stop filtering, so no hormone can act
Low output drives renin, which overrides the peptide
questions.why: The failing heart delivers a low cardiac output, the kidney reads that as volume depletion, and renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone, and antidiuretic hormone all rise. Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes them but is outmatched, so the net result is retention and edema even with a high peptide level. This is a good illustration that hormones are a balance, not a switch. The peptide keeps its normal actions and does not reverse direction at high concentration, and filtration continues, though it falls as perfusion drops.
questions.answerText: Low output drives renin, which overrides the peptide

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A drug blocks the aldosterone receptor in the collecting duct. Predict urine sodium, plasma potassium, and blood volume after several days.
options: Urine sodium up, plasma potassium up, blood volume down
Urine sodium up, plasma potassium down, blood volume down
Urine sodium down, plasma potassium up, blood volume up
Urine sodium down, plasma potassium down, blood volume down
questions.why: Without aldosterone signaling, principal cells make fewer sodium channels and pumps, so sodium is left in the tubule and lost in the urine, water follows it, and blood volume falls. The same pump drives potassium secretion, so blocking it also keeps potassium in the plasma, which is why this class of drug is called potassium sparing. Losing sodium while also losing potassium describes a loop or thiazide diuretic, which works upstream and leaves aldosterone free to dump potassium. Retaining sodium is what aldosterone itself does, not what its blockade does.
questions.answerText: Urine sodium up, plasma potassium up, blood volume down

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Cardiac output is the product of which two variables?
options: Stroke volume and peripheral resistance
End diastolic volume and ejection fraction
Heart rate and stroke volume
Heart rate and mean arterial pressure
questions.why: Cardiac output is the volume ejected per beat multiplied by the number of beats per minute, so a resting value near 70 mL times 70 beats per minute gives about 5 L/min. Mean arterial pressure is the result of cardiac output working against resistance, not one of its factors. End diastolic volume times ejection fraction gives stroke volume, one step short of cardiac output, which makes it the most tempting wrong answer here.
questions.answerText: Heart rate and stroke volume

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What produces the very first rise in heart rate at the onset of exercise?
options: Venous return stretching the SA node directly
Withdrawal of vagal tone to the SA node
A surge of sympathetic outflow to the ventricles
A rise in circulating aldosterone
questions.why: At rest the vagus holds the SA node well below its intrinsic rate, so simply releasing that brake raises heart rate within one or two beats, faster than any transmitter or hormone could act. Sympathetic outflow does rise, and it carries the increase above about 100 beats per minute, but it takes seconds to build and so cannot explain the first beats. Aldosterone acts on the kidney over hours and has no direct effect on rate. Stretch of the SA node by filling does modestly raise rate, but it is a small contributor and it follows the rise in venous return rather than leading it.
questions.answerText: Withdrawal of vagal tone to the SA node

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which change explains most of the rise in stroke volume during moderate exercise?
options: Greater venous return raising end diastolic volume
A rise in aortic pressure raising afterload
A longer filling time at higher heart rates
A fall in contractility offset by the faster rate
questions.why: The muscle pump, the respiratory pump, and venoconstriction all push more blood back to the heart, filling stretches the ventricle, and the Frank-Starling mechanism converts that stretch into a larger ejection. Increased contractility from sympathetic drive adds to this by lowering end systolic volume. A higher afterload opposes ejection and lowers stroke volume, so it works against the observed change. Filling time gets shorter, not longer, as heart rate climbs, and contractility rises rather than falls in exercise.
questions.answerText: Greater venous return raising end diastolic volume

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What happens to total peripheral resistance during moderate whole body exercise?
options: It is unchanged, because the two effects cancel
It falls, because blood becomes less viscous
It falls, because the muscle arterioles dilate
It rises, because sympathetic outflow increases
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is such a large fraction of body mass that opening its arterioles drops whole body resistance despite strong constriction in the gut and kidneys. This is why mean arterial pressure rises only modestly while cardiac output can triple. Sympathetic outflow does rise, but its effect on the total is outweighed by local metabolic dilation in the working muscle. Blood viscosity changes very little during exercise and slightly increases with fluid loss, so it is not the reason resistance falls.
questions.answerText: It falls, because the muscle arterioles dilate

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which vascular beds receive a smaller share of cardiac output during exercise?
options: The pulmonary and bronchial circulations
The splanchnic and renal circulations
The coronary and cerebral circulations
The skeletal muscle and skin circulations
questions.why: Sympathetic alpha-1 constriction is strongest in the gut, liver, and kidneys, and cutting their share frees a large volume of flow for working muscle. Coronary and cerebral flow are protected, since the heart is working harder and the brain must be perfused at all times. Muscle and skin both take a larger share, muscle for metabolism and skin for heat loss. The pulmonary circulation must carry the entire cardiac output by definition, so its flow rises exactly as much as the systemic side does.
questions.answerText: The splanchnic and renal circulations

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What happens to cerebral blood flow during moderate exercise?
options: It roughly doubles along with cardiac output
It falls sharply as muscle takes priority
It swings widely with each breath
It stays close to its resting value
questions.why: Cerebral vessels autoregulate tightly and have little sympathetic vasoconstrictor influence, so flow is held near 750 mL/min across a wide range of pressures and workloads. Doubling would follow cardiac output blindly, which is exactly what autoregulation prevents. A sharp fall would risk syncope in the middle of activity, and the brain is one of the beds the body protects rather than sacrifices. Flow does vary a little with the PCO2 changes of breathing, but not enough to describe as wide swings.
questions.answerText: It stays close to its resting value

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What causes the arterioles inside working muscle to dilate?
options: Circulating aldosterone acting on smooth muscle
Withdrawal of parasympathetic vasodilator nerves
A fall in local tissue temperature
Local metabolites such as adenosine, K+, and CO2
questions.why: Active hyperemia is a local mechanism: contracting fibers release adenosine and K+, produce CO2 and H+, and consume oxygen, and all of those relax nearby arteriolar smooth muscle so flow matches demand. Aldosterone is a renal hormone with no direct arteriolar dilating action. Systemic arterioles receive essentially no parasympathetic innervation, so there is no parasympathetic tone to withdraw. Working muscle gets warmer, not cooler, and that warming adds a little more dilation.
questions.answerText: Local metabolites such as adenosine, K+, and CO2

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Roughly what is cardiac output in a healthy adult at rest?
options: About 5 L/min
About 1 L/min
About 15 L/min
About 25 L/min
questions.why: A resting stroke volume near 70 mL and a rate near 70 beats per minute give close to 5 L/min, which also equals the whole blood volume circulating once per minute. About 1 L/min would not meet resting oxygen demand and is closer to the flow through a single organ such as the kidneys. Values of 15 to 25 L/min belong to moderate and maximal exercise, and only a trained athlete reaches the top of that range.
questions.answerText: About 5 L/min

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A runner has a heart rate of 150 beats/min and a stroke volume of 120 mL. What is cardiac output?
options: 1.8 L/min
30 L/min
18 L/min
12.5 L/min
questions.why: Multiply 150 beats per minute by 120 mL per beat to get 18000 mL/min, which is 18 L/min, a realistic value for hard exercise. The 12.5 L/min answer comes from dividing rather than multiplying. The 1.8 L/min answer is a decimal slip of one place and is well below even resting output, which is a useful check on any result. The 30 L/min answer exceeds what all but an elite endurance athlete can reach.
questions.answerText: 18 L/min

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Cardiac output during exercise is 20 L/min and heart rate is 160 beats/min. What is stroke volume?
options: 125 mL
80 mL
320 mL
questions.why: Rearranging cardiac output equals rate times stroke volume gives 20000 mL divided by 160 beats, which is 125 mL per beat. The 80 mL answer is a resting stroke volume and would give only 12.8 L/min at this rate. The 320 mL answer comes from multiplying instead of dividing and exceeds the volume a ventricle can hold. The 12.5 mL answer is off by a factor of ten and is far too small to support any exercise.
questions.answerText: 125 mL

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Skeletal muscle receives about 20 percent of cardiac output at rest. What happens to muscle blood flow during heavy exercise?
options: Share rises but total muscle flow stays about the same
Share is unchanged while total cardiac output rises
Share rises only because cardiac output falls elsewhere
Share rises above 80 percent as total output rises
questions.why: Two things multiply together: cardiac output can rise from 5 to 20 L/min or more, and muscle takes a much larger slice of it, so absolute muscle flow can rise more than twentyfold. If the share rose while flow stayed flat, the extra output would have to go somewhere else, and no other bed expands like this. An unchanged share would mean muscle gained only as much as everything else, which cannot support the observed oxygen consumption. Cardiac output does not fall anywhere during exercise, so explaining the larger share that way contradicts the central fact of the response.
questions.answerText: Share rises above 80 percent as total output rises

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: During exercise systolic pressure rises while diastolic pressure stays roughly flat. What happens to pulse pressure?
options: It widens
It narrows
It is unchanged
It falls to zero
questions.why: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic, so raising the top number while the bottom number holds steady must widen the gap. The larger stroke volume ejected into the aorta is what raises the systolic peak. A narrowing pulse pressure is the signature of a falling stroke volume with vasoconstriction, as in early hemorrhage, which is the opposite pattern. A pulse pressure of zero would mean no pulsatile ejection at all.
questions.answerText: It widens

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Why does diastolic pressure fail to rise much during exercise even though cardiac output triples?
options: Venous return falls once the muscle pump starts
Total peripheral resistance falls at the same time
The heart spends longer in diastole at high rates
Blood viscosity drops sharply during exercise
questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times resistance, so a large rise in output paired with a large fall in resistance leaves pressure only modestly higher, and the diastolic number, which reflects runoff into dilated muscle beds, barely moves. Diastole gets shorter as heart rate rises, not longer, so the answer about filling time has that backwards. Viscosity is essentially unchanged, and venous return rises rather than falls when the muscle pump is working.
questions.answerText: Total peripheral resistance falls at the same time

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: The skeletal muscle pump squeezes the deep veins during rhythmic exercise. What is the effect on the heart?
options: Preload falls, so heart rate must rise to hold output
Contractility rises directly, independent of filling
Preload rises, so stroke volume rises by Frank-Starling
Afterload rises, so stroke volume falls
questions.why: Contracting muscle compresses the veins running through it, and one way valves make the displaced blood move only toward the heart, so filling and end diastolic volume increase and the ventricle ejects more per beat. Afterload is set by arterial pressure, which the venous side does not control. Preload rises rather than falls, which is why stroke volume can climb while filling time is getting shorter. Contractility does increase in exercise, but through sympathetic beta-1 stimulation, not through the mechanical pump.
questions.answerText: Preload rises, so stroke volume rises by Frank-Starling

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: The heart already extracts about 70 percent of the oxygen from coronary blood at rest. How does it meet the extra demand of exercise?
options: By extracting a larger fraction of the oxygen
By switching entirely to anaerobic metabolism
By lowering its own oxygen consumption per beat
By increasing coronary blood flow
questions.why: With extraction already near its ceiling, the only remaining variable is flow, so coronary arterioles dilate in response to local metabolites and flow rises several fold during exercise. Skeletal muscle, which extracts only about 25 percent at rest, does have extraction in reserve, and mixing up the two beds is the common error here. The heart cannot run on anaerobic metabolism for more than moments. Oxygen consumption per beat rises with contractility, so it cannot be part of the solution.
questions.answerText: By increasing coronary blood flow

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A person on a beta-1 blocker exercises at a workload that would normally give a heart rate of 150 beats/min, but reaches only 110. What happens to stroke volume and cardiac output?
options: Stroke volume falls, and cardiac output falls with it
Stroke volume is unchanged, and cardiac output is normal
Stroke volume rises further, but cardiac output falls short
Stroke volume and cardiac output both reach normal values
questions.why: A slower rate leaves more time for filling, so end diastolic volume and stroke volume rise more than they otherwise would, and the Frank-Starling mechanism partly compensates. The compensation is incomplete because the drug also blunts contractility, so cardiac output and exercise capacity end up below normal. Full compensation would make beta blockade invisible during exercise, which it is not. Stroke volume falling would require reduced filling, but filling actually improves at the lower rate.
questions.answerText: Stroke volume rises further, but cardiac output falls short

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: During exercise sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow rises throughout the body, yet arterioles inside the working muscle dilate. What resolves this contradiction?
options: Working muscle has no alpha-1 receptors on its vessels
Local metabolites override the constrictor signal
Sympathetic nerves do not reach skeletal muscle arterioles
Central sympathetic outflow is switched off during exercise
questions.why: Local control wins where metabolism is high, a phenomenon called functional sympatholysis, so the same neural signal that constricts gut and kidney vessels is overridden inside the contracting muscle. This is exactly what the body needs, since the constriction elsewhere redirects flow to the beds that can take it. Skeletal muscle arterioles are richly innervated and do carry alpha-1 receptors, which is why resting muscle constricts normally. Central outflow rises during exercise rather than switching off, which is what makes the local override necessary.
questions.answerText: Local metabolites override the constrictor signal

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: An athlete runs for an hour in the heat without drinking. Late in the run, stroke volume is falling and heart rate is climbing at the same workload. What explains this?
options: Sweat loss and skin pooling cut venous return
The heart has run out of glycogen, so contractility fails
Peripheral resistance rises steeply and blocks ejection
Sympathetic outflow is withdrawn to protect the heart
questions.why: Plasma volume falls with sweating and a large share of the remaining volume sits in dilated skin veins for heat loss, so filling drops and stroke volume with it. Heart rate rises to defend cardiac output, and the drifting rate at a constant workload is the visible sign. The heart uses fatty acids and lactate as well as glucose and does not simply run out of fuel in an hour. Resistance falls during exercise rather than climbing, and sympathetic outflow increases as the pressure signal weakens, which is the opposite of withdrawal.
questions.answerText: Sweat loss and skin pooling cut venous return

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Cardiac output triples during exercise and arterial pressure rises modestly. Why does the baroreflex not simply push the pressure back down?
options: The reflex responds only to falls in pressure, never to rises
Central command resets the reflex to a higher operating point
The receptors are damaged by the higher exercise pressure
Exercise disconnects the afferents from the medulla
questions.why: Signals from the motor cortex and from receptors in the working muscle shift the baroreflex set point upward, so the medulla now treats the raised pressure as correct and continues to regulate around it. The reflex is not abolished, which is why a sudden drop during exercise still produces a fast correction. Receptors are not damaged by exercise pressures and the afferents keep conducting the whole time. The reflex is bidirectional at any set point, so calling it a one way system misdescribes the whole mechanism.
questions.answerText: Central command resets the reflex to a higher operating point

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which compensation for blood loss begins within seconds?
options: The baroreceptor reflex
Aldosterone driven sodium retention
Erythropoietin driven red cell production
Plasma protein replacement by the liver
questions.why: The baroreflex is neural, so it acts within a heartbeat or two: firing falls, sympathetic outflow rises, and heart rate, contractility, and vessel tone all increase before any hormone has been made. Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone act over minutes to hours through the kidney. Erythropoietin restores red cells over days to weeks, and hepatic plasma protein synthesis takes days, so both are late repairs rather than immediate defenses.
questions.answerText: The baroreceptor reflex

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: About how much blood volume can a healthy adult lose before mean arterial pressure usually begins to fall?
options: About 40 percent
About 70 percent
About 10 percent
About 1 percent
questions.why: Compensation is good enough that a loss of roughly a tenth of blood volume, close to the volume of a blood donation, leaves mean arterial pressure nearly normal, though heart rate rises and pulse pressure narrows. A one percent loss is far too small to challenge the system at all. By 40 percent most patients are in severe shock with a clearly low pressure, and a 70 percent loss is not survivable without immediate replacement.
questions.answerText: About 10 percent

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: After hemorrhage, fluid moves from the interstitium into the capillaries. What drives that shift?
options: A fall in plasma colloid osmotic pressure
A rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure
A rise in interstitial osmotic pressure
A fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.why: Arteriolar constriction and low arterial pressure both lower the hydrostatic pressure inside the capillary, so plasma colloid osmotic pressure now dominates the Starling balance and fluid is pulled inward, adding as much as a liter to plasma volume over hours. This transcapillary refill dilutes the blood, which is why hematocrit drops after the bleed. A falling plasma colloid pressure would push fluid out instead of drawing it in. A rise in capillary hydrostatic pressure is what happens in heart failure and produces edema, the opposite movement.
questions.answerText: A fall in capillary hydrostatic pressure

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which hormones restore plasma volume over the hours after blood loss by conserving salt and water?
options: Atrial natriuretic peptide and cortisol
Epinephrine and thyroid hormone
Erythropoietin and parathyroid hormone
Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone
questions.why: Angiotensin II drives aldosterone, which holds sodium, and the fall in volume drives antidiuretic hormone, which holds water, and together they cut urine output sharply while thirst adds new fluid. Atrial natriuretic peptide falls in hemorrhage because the atria are underfilled, so it is the wrong direction entirely. Epinephrine acts on the heart and vessels within seconds rather than restoring volume, and thyroid, parathyroid, and erythropoietin do not manage salt and water balance in this setting.
questions.answerText: Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Which compensation for blood loss takes weeks rather than hours?
options: Replacement of the lost red blood cells
Constriction of the splanchnic arterioles
Increased sympathetic outflow to the heart
Movement of interstitial fluid into capillaries
questions.why: Erythropoietin from the kidney stimulates the marrow, but making and maturing red cells takes weeks and needs adequate iron, so oxygen carrying capacity is the slowest thing to recover. Splanchnic constriction and increased cardiac sympathetic outflow are both parts of the baroreflex and appear within seconds. Fluid movement into the capillaries begins within minutes and is largely complete within a day, so it restores volume long before the cells are back.
questions.answerText: Replacement of the lost red blood cells

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What happens to pulse pressure early in significant hemorrhage?
options: It disappears entirely
It narrows
It widens
It is unchanged
questions.why: A smaller stroke volume lowers the systolic peak while intense arteriolar constriction holds the diastolic pressure up, so the gap between the two numbers shrinks. Narrowing pulse pressure is one of the earliest signs of blood loss and often appears while mean arterial pressure still looks normal. A widening pulse pressure is the exercise pattern, driven by a large stroke volume and dilated muscle beds. The pulse does not disappear until circulatory collapse is far advanced.
questions.answerText: It narrows

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: What is the physiological definition of shock?
options: Loss of more than one liter of circulating blood
A heart rate sustained above 100 beats per minute
Tissue perfusion too low to meet metabolic demand
Any systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg
questions.why: Shock is defined by delivery, not by any single number: when blood flow cannot supply the oxygen tissues need, cells shift to anaerobic metabolism and lactate rises. That is why a patient can be in shock with a normal blood pressure, if compensation is holding the pressure up while flow is already inadequate. A low systolic reading, a given volume lost, and a fast heart rate are all findings that may accompany shock, but each can be present without shock and absent with it.
questions.answerText: Tissue perfusion too low to meet metabolic demand

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: In irreversible shock, what happens to arterioles that had been strongly constricted?
options: They are replaced by newly grown collateral vessels
They lose tone and dilate despite maximal drive
They constrict further until flow stops completely
They regain normal tone as the reflex recovers
questions.why: Prolonged hypoxia and acidosis paralyze vascular smooth muscle and the receptors become unresponsive to catecholamines, so the vessels dilate even though sympathetic outflow is at its maximum, and peripheral resistance collapses. That loss of the last compensating mechanism is what makes the state irreversible. Further constriction would maintain pressure rather than losing it, and a recovery of normal tone describes a patient who has been resuscitated in time. New vessel growth takes weeks and has no role in an event measured in hours.
questions.answerText: They lose tone and dilate despite maximal drive

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient has lost 15 percent of blood volume. Predict heart rate, total peripheral resistance, and urine output.
options: Heart rate up, resistance down, urine output up
Heart rate down, resistance up, urine output down
Heart rate up, resistance up, urine output up
Heart rate up, resistance up, urine output down
questions.why: Baroreceptor firing falls, sympathetic outflow rises, and the result is tachycardia, widespread vasoconstriction including the renal arterioles, and a sharp drop in urine output that is reinforced by aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone. Falling resistance would give away the pressure the reflex is trying to defend. A slower heart rate would be the response to a pressure that was too high, not too low. Rising urine output would waste the very volume the body is trying to keep.
questions.answerText: Heart rate up, resistance up, urine output down

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Why does urine output fall sharply after hemorrhage?
options: Renal constriction plus antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone
The kidneys are permanently damaged by the fall in pressure
Antidiuretic hormone secretion is suppressed by the volume loss
Filtered sodium is excreted faster than the tubules reabsorb it
questions.why: Three mechanisms point the same way: sympathetic constriction of the afferent arteriole lowers filtration, antidiuretic hormone reabsorbs water, and aldosterone reabsorbs sodium with water following. Low urine output is therefore an early and sensitive marker of hypovolemia. Acute kidney injury can follow prolonged hypotension, but the initial fall in output is a normal defense, not damage. Volume loss stimulates antidiuretic hormone rather than suppressing it, and sodium is conserved rather than dumped.
questions.answerText: Renal constriction plus antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Immediately after acute blood loss the hematocrit is nearly normal, but it falls over the next several hours. Why?
options: The bone marrow halts red cell production immediately
Plasma proteins leave the circulation faster than cells do
Whole blood is lost first, then interstitial fluid enters
Red cells are destroyed by the sympathetic response
questions.why: Hemorrhage removes plasma and red cells in the same proportion, so the ratio between them is unchanged at first, and only when transcapillary refill adds cell free fluid does the hematocrit drop. This is why an early normal hematocrit never rules out significant bleeding. Catecholamines do not lyse red cells, and the marrow responds to blood loss by making more cells, not fewer. Protein loss would raise the hematocrit by concentrating the cells rather than diluting them.
questions.answerText: Whole blood is lost first, then interstitial fluid enters

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Why are cerebral and coronary blood flow relatively spared while the gut and kidneys are constricted?
options: Their arterioles are too large in diameter to constrict
Blood is redirected to them through the venous system
They autoregulate and resist sympathetic constriction
They receive extra sympathetic vasodilator fibers
questions.why: Brain and heart hold their own flow through local metabolic and myogenic control and carry sparse alpha-1 innervation, so the systemic vasoconstriction that shifts blood away from other organs passes them by. This is why a patient can be cold and oliguric while still awake. There is no sympathetic vasodilator supply to these beds in humans. Their arterioles are ordinary resistance vessels with normal smooth muscle, and blood cannot be routed to an organ through veins, which carry flow away.
questions.answerText: They autoregulate and resist sympathetic constriction

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Sympathetic outflow constricts the systemic veins after blood loss. What does this achieve?
options: It raises afterload so the heart works harder
It lowers venous return to protect the lungs
It raises capillary pressure and refills the tissues
It shifts stored venous blood back toward the heart
questions.why: The veins normally hold about two thirds of the blood volume, so constricting them acts as an internal transfusion, restoring filling and stroke volume without any new fluid. Afterload is determined by the arterial side, so venoconstriction does not set it. Lowering venous return would worsen the very problem the body is fighting. Capillary hydrostatic pressure actually falls in hemorrhage, and that fall is what pulls interstitial fluid into the blood rather than pushing fluid out.
questions.answerText: It shifts stored venous blood back toward the heart

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient taking a beta blocker has significant blood loss. Which usual sign of compensation is blunted?
options: The narrowed pulse pressure
The rise in heart rate
The fall in urine output
The cool and pale skin
questions.why: Beta-1 receptors carry the tachycardia, so blocking them removes the most familiar early sign while the alpha-1 responses go on working. Skin pallor and coolness come from alpha-1 constriction, the narrowed pulse pressure follows from a low stroke volume against constricted arterioles, and the fall in urine output comes from renal constriction and from hormones. All three are therefore preserved, which is worth knowing, because the patient can be much further into hemorrhage than the pulse suggests.
questions.answerText: The rise in heart rate

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: Put the compensations for a 20 percent blood loss in the order in which they take effect.
options: Baroreflex, fluid refill, salt and water hormones, red cells
Salt and water hormones, baroreflex, red cells, fluid refill
Fluid refill, red cells, baroreflex, salt and water hormones
Red cells, salt and water hormones, baroreflex, fluid refill
questions.why: Neural signaling is fastest and acts in seconds, movement of interstitial fluid into the capillaries begins within minutes and continues for hours, renal salt and water conservation builds over minutes to hours and holds the gains, and red cell replacement takes days to weeks. The hormonal and fluid steps do overlap in time, but the fluid shift starts first and needs no new hormone to begin. Every other ordering puts a slow mechanism before a fast one, which would leave a gap of seconds to minutes during which pressure was undefended.
questions.answerText: Baroreflex, fluid refill, salt and water hormones, red cells

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: In progressive shock, a low cardiac output lowers coronary perfusion, which weakens the heart, which lowers cardiac output further. What kind of loop is this?
options: Negative feedback, which will restore pressure on its own
Feedforward control, which anticipates the next fall
An oscillation that settles into a new steady state
Positive feedback, which worsens the decline further
questions.why: Each turn of the loop makes the next turn worse, which is the definition of positive feedback, and it explains why shock can pass a point where compensation alone can no longer recover it. Negative feedback is what the baroreflex provides, opposing the change rather than amplifying it, and if this loop behaved that way shock would be self limiting. Feedforward control acts before a disturbance rather than in response to one. A self limiting oscillation would settle at a lower but survivable output, which is exactly what progressive shock does not do.
questions.answerText: Positive feedback, which worsens the decline further

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: After hours of severe hypotension the precapillary sphincters relax while the venules stay constricted. Predict capillary hydrostatic pressure and plasma volume.
options: Capillary pressure rises, fluid leaves the blood, volume falls
Capillary pressure falls, fluid enters the blood, volume rises
Capillary pressure holds steady, so plasma volume is unchanged
Capillary pressure rises, so fluid is drawn into the blood
questions.why: Local hypoxia and acidosis paralyze the smooth muscle of the sphincters first, so the inflow gate opens while the outflow gate stays shut, and pressure builds inside the capillary until it exceeds plasma colloid osmotic pressure and fluid is forced into the tissue. That loss of plasma volume deepens the hypovolemia and is one route into irreversible shock. A falling capillary pressure with fluid entering the blood describes the early compensated phase, when both ends are constricted. The answer that raises capillary pressure and still draws fluid inward gets the pressure right but the flow backwards, since a high capillary pressure pushes fluid out.
questions.answerText: Capillary pressure rises, fluid leaves the blood, volume falls

questions.topic: Cardiovascular Regulation
questions.q: A patient has lost about 25 percent of blood volume. Blood pressure is 112/94 mmHg, heart rate is 128, the hands are cold, and blood lactate is high. What does this pattern show?
options: The high lactate proves the blood loss was less than 10 percent
Compensation holds the pressure while perfusion is already poor
Perfusion must be adequate, since the blood pressure is normal
Compensation has failed, since the pressure would otherwise be high
questions.why: The narrow pulse pressure, the tachycardia, and the cold hands are all signs of intense sympathetic vasoconstriction, and the raised lactate proves that tissues are running anaerobically even though the mean pressure looks acceptable. This is compensated shock, and reading the pressure alone would miss it. Normal pressure never guarantees normal perfusion once vasoconstriction is doing the work. Failed compensation would show a low pressure and often a falling heart rate, and a high lactate points to more blood loss rather than less.
questions.answerText: Compensation holds the pressure while perfusion is already poor
